Part I 


Herodotus’ Hermeneutical Dilemma and His Table of 


Historians with Prophetic-like Voices 


1 Herodotus’ Hermeneutical Dilemma, Prophet-like Voice, 


and an Estranged Heir Named Luke 


1.1 Framing the Question around Herodotus’ Imaginary Meeting 


with his Historiographical Heirs 


Writing history in the shadow of the Homeric tradition and drama, Greek histori- 
ans contended with each other about issues such as the choice of subject, genre, 
and style. Some persistent questions concerned the place of the realm of the di- 
vine in historical discourse. What place, if any, should historians accord to per- 
ceptions of the divine and religious experiences of the divine in their accounts of 
human history? And should historians provide examples of piety and impiety for 
the moral education of their readers? These questions gave rise to a hermeneuti- 
cal dilemma that was dealt with in various ways from the beginning of Greek his- 
toriography with Herodotus, Thucydides, and Xenophon, and it continued well 
into the first century CE, with the likes of Flavius Josephus, Plutarch, and Luke. 


The logic of the dilemma can be summarised as follows: although human 


agency formed the core of Greek historiography, it was never considered suffi- 
cient in itself. Perceptions of divine agency, informed by tradition and belief, 
were a legitimate part of interpreting and expressing human history. Moreover, 
examples of practised religion, as well as claims of human and divine interaction, 
supported this interpretative approach. This is evidenced in patterns of piety and 
impiety and divine reward and retribution. Thus, a theological premise under- 
pinned this approach to historiography. Historians disagreed on a number of 
points, but they all conceded that the divine realm – however conceived – was 
greater than the human realm and shaped the development of human history. In 
this respect, a significant yet often overlooked feature of Greek historiography is 
its theological nature. This presented a hermeneutical dilemma for Greek histori- 
ans, and it continues to present a hermeneutical challenge to their interpreters in 
various disciplines. 


Although historiography was considered distinct from the works of Homer, 


Hesiod, and the tragedians, the mythopoetic tradition – expressed through vari- 
ous literary genres – also influenced Greek historiography. This characteristic 
was seen to require nuance. When Herodotus describes the Greco-Persian Wars, 
he often refers to the divine realm, albeit differently from Homer. Similarly, 
when Thucydides describes the Peloponnesian War, he modestly includes refer- 
ences to the divine and practised religion, but not in the same way as Homer or 


Herodotus. Then came Xenophon who refers to the divine realm more often than 
Thucydides, but still differently from him and Herodotus. The question, then, was 
not whether to include references to the influence of the divine realm but how to 
represent it appropriately. This hermeneutical dilemma persisted beyond their 
time and was addressed in various creative ways by Greek-speaking historians 
from different periods, cultures, and theistic worldviews. The result is a multiplic- 
ity of historiographical voices – prophetic-like voices of various forms and inten- 
sities – responding to the questions, interests, and expectations of their audi- 
ences. Yet it is above all Herodotus who is responsible for this enduring strand of 
Greek historiography. The writings of his successors, who grappled with his lega- 
cy, bear witness to this in diverse ways. Their unique perceptions of the divine 
are responses to the hermeneutical dilemma. 


This book surveys this enduring feature of history-writing, from Herodotus 


to Luke, and then focuses on the works of these two Greek historians who demon- 
strate how historiography exhibited tradition and innovation through theological 
reflection on their subjects and for their audiences. Rather than seeking to dis- 
cern the veracity of their claims about the divine, this research explores the 
methods employed to depict the divine and the reasons behind their use. 


Herodotus’ ‘heroic’ project. Around 450–420 BCE Herodotus conducted and shared 
his enquiries, both through speeches and texts.1 This endeavour culminated in an 
extraordinarily multifaceted narrative. He seems to have wanted to set the record 
straight on many issues. For one, his audience needed to know not only what had 
happened during the Greco-Persian Wars (490; 480/479 BCE), but also how and why 
it had happened and who had been affected by it. Given the cultural circumstances, 
this prodigious victory over the Persians had to be told in a different way (i.e., in 
prose) than, for example, Aeschylus’ tragedy, The Persians. Although Herodotus 
knew that part of his audience would not appreciate his opinion, he acknowledged 
Athens as “the saviours of Greece” (7.139.5).2 The Athenians, however, were not 
alone; significant help was needed from the human and divine realms. Herodotus 
displays many prominent contributions by non-Athenians in opposition to the 
spread of the Persian Empire. But this story, from Herodotus’ perspective, would 
have been incomplete if he had not also integrated perceptions of the divine realm 
into his rendition of the story.3 In the above passage, Herodotus certainly gives cred- 
it to Athens, but he carefully qualifies this by stating that the Athenians’ role as sav- 
iours was still subordinate to divine assistance, namely, “after the gods” (7.139.5).

For these things we ourselves did not accomplish, but both the gods and the heroes, 
who were envious of one man who might rule over Asia and Europe, who was both 
profane and arrogant. This one treated sacred things and personal things in the 
same way, having burned and toppled the statues of the gods and also flogged the 
sea violently and sank shackles into it. (8.109.3) 


In Herodotus’ argument, Themistocles places this victory in light of a larger issue, 
the Eurasian conflict, which is characterised by two major themes: abuses of hu- 
man rule and sacrilegious behaviour. 


As an author, Herodotus seems to avoid both these dangers, presenting ac- 


tions and speeches that give honour where honour is due, either to humans or to 
the gods. In this sense, his work contributed to other acts of piety in the fifth cen- 
tury that honoured the gods.4 Likened to a monument, a work of such a compre- 
hensive narrative was still lacking.5 The salvation of the Greek alliance against 
Persia was interpreted in the light of contemporary hopes and practices for di- 
vine deliverance.6 Herodotus’ work attempts to make sense of this through the 
medium of prose, a new development in Greek literary history.7 This was no easy 
task, for Herodotus was on hallowed ground, literarily and theologically, writing 
in the shadow of the Homeric tradition, which had made the agōn (contest, con- 
flict, struggle) a central component.8 Moreover, given the literary productivity of 
the fifth century in theatre, philosophy, and history, the standards and expecta- 
tions for Herodotus’ contribution to social and political life must have been high.9 


Moreover, Herodotus’ narrative responded to another challenge on the 


rhetorical level: his audience’s own troubled times. While Herodotus was proba- 
bly still writing down his enquiries around 425 BCE (perhaps, even later), some of

his audience was facing the tragedy of another great war, now known as the Pelo- 
ponnesian War (431–404 BCE). According to Thucydides, this war was even great- 
er than the Trojan War and the Greco-Persian Wars (1.1.2–3; 1.23.1–3). This time 
it was an internal conflict, between two centres of power, Athens and Sparta, and 
their allies. Athens, “the saviours of Greece,” had now become the instigator of 
this terrible internecine struggle, and Herodotus saw the stark irony. Like the Per- 
sians, the Athenians were animated by the “imperial impulse”: that universal, ar- 
rogant drive for power that, sooner or later, always fails and gives way to greater 
powers.10 It fails, in part, because, according to the historiographical record, the 
divine realm does not let it succeed indefinitely. It concerns the obsession for 
more territory and power and how the divine realm regularly levels it.11 For this, 
Herodotus gave the Athenians an upbraiding and a warning12 about the disgrace 
of being the new Persians against their own kinsfolk.13 A message was needed to 
set the record straight: an explanation that would put the past and the present 
into perspective for all Greek-speaking people, but particularly for Athens. 
Herodotus’ project was therefore a bold one in troubled times. 


As he dealt directly and indirectly with the two wars, Herodotus collected a 


vast number of stories from a variety of sources and cultures. Many of these re- 
counted divine action and speech, as well as human efforts to solicit divine assis- 
tance. Herodotus did not ignore this element in his long and detailed history. Like 
other contemporary acts of piety, his act of historiographical piety involved the 
recognition of divine activity, both general (e.g., ‘the god’) and particular (e.g., 
‘Apollo’). But how could he do this in a pious way? He produced a narrative that 
shared certain characteristics with Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey.14 This included 
claims of interaction between the divine and human spheres, which appear 
throughout the nine books of the Histories. In this regard, Herodotus’ endeavour 
was doubly courageous, as he also recognised the risks of speaking about the gods 
(e.g., 2.3.2; 2.65.2).15 He composed his collection of enquiries assuming his audi- 
ence’s position between two interrelated realms: the divine and the human. This

Herodotus’ successors seated around his table. Writing in this way, Herodotus set 
in motion a literary development that enjoyed – and still does enjoy – a wide- 
spread legacy.17 Through his elegant prose, he showed the Greek-speaking world 
how one could account for the past on a vast scale. His influence is manifest in his 
first successors, Thucydides and Xenophon, who described various stages of the 
Peloponnesian War. With Herodotus, they formed the first core group in the 
Greek historiographical canon. But Herodotus had many other imitators, some of 
whom lived many years later and in distant places such as Berossus (flor. 290 
BCE, Babylonia), Manetho (flor. 280 BCE, Egypt), and Flavius Josephus (37 – 
ca. 100 CE, Judea). They all wrote in Greek, resulting from the Hellenisation of 
their peoples by Alexander the Great and his successors.18 For some of Herodotus’ 
heirs, it is easy to imagine a conversation with him, ‘the Father of history’ (Ci- 
cero’s epithet for him, Leg. 1.5). Some conversations – in Greek, of course – 
would probably be relaxed, for example, with Timaeus of Tauromenium (ca. 350– 
260 BCE) and Theopompus (ca. 378/7 – ca. 320 BCE). Others would be perhaps 
more strained as with his critics, e.g., Ctesias of Cnidus (late fifth century BCE) 
and Plutarch (ca. 50–120 CE). 


Conversations between Herodotus and Luke may even seem like a blind 


date, glancing at each other and wondering why they are sitting face to face at the 
same table. Literarily, one sees the logic in pairs such as Homer and Herodotus; 
Herodotus and Thucydides; and with more contextualisation, Herodotus and Plu- 
tarch. But rarely does one utter Herodotus and Luke, the first Christian historian 
(first century CE) in the same sentence, let alone in the same paragraph.19 But 
there is nothing ostensibly strange about this imaginary conversation. Luke was 
either a Greek or a Hellenised Jew from the diaspora, with an excellent command 
of the Greek language, and he lived and composed his work about events and

Acts of the Apostles (hereafter ‘Luke-Acts’ when referred to together), were at the 
crossroads of Jewish and Greek historiography, telling a story for the oikoumenē 
(Luke 2:1), moving from the Roman province of Judea through many other prov-

of these two historians cries out for clarification. A defence of this apparently 
strange pair begins with a few premises, some of which are easier to ask the read- 
er to acquiesce while others will require more justification in later sections. 


Although this research has a particular focus on Herodotus and Luke, it is 


important to note that they are placed within literary and cultural continuity and 
viewed in light of a particular historiographical strand. Thus, it can be beneficial 
to envisage a conversation involving them alongside Herodotus’ other successors 
seated at Herodotus’ table. Each of his literary heirs would share about the im- 
mense political and cultural vicissitudes during the span of five hundred years. 
Luke’s experience of life under Roman rule would make him a valuable source of 
insight, along with other historians of this era. For some, Luke’s presence at 
Herodotus’ table may seem logical, while for others he may seem out of place. 
Perhaps he should be redirected to the room where Demetrius, Jason of Cyrene, 
and Justus of Tiberias have organised a colloquium on Jewish history. Still, others 
might say that he is perfectly entitled to attend both sessions and not be dismissed 
as an unworthy impostor. In fact, why not invite those three Greek-speaking his- 
torians to join Herodotus’ group?21 As with Herodotus and his successors, Luke 
also had a message to convey: namely, an experience of the imperial impulse of 
Rome and how it was ultimately subordinate to divine rule. 


In addition to the literary and geopolitical elements, another key aspect for 


appreciating Herodotus’ legacy is theological. From a narratological perspective, 
it is a voice akin to that of a prophet, playing a hermeneutical role. This pertains to 
the level of attention historians give to the divine realm when describing human 
history for their readers. It will be argued that Greek historians, from Herodotus 
to Luke, wrote history through a theistic lens, and it was an element expected by 
their audiences who continued to have an interest in the divine – according to 
their perceptions – in human experience and in historiography. It forms one of 
the underlying and continuous strands that shaped their historiographical styles. 
This prophet-like voice influenced, for example, how they chose and described 
events and how they portrayed people, e.g., as pious or impious. Also, a consistent 
theme in their writings is that the divine realm is perceived by these authors and

We address this question briefly here and examine it further in Chapter 4.22 


Luke, an estranged but deserving heir of Herodotus? Luke was also on hallowed 
ground when he set his mind to writing history. This kind of writing had been 
going on for some time in Greek and Jewish traditions. So, for curious and en- 
lightened audiences scattered around the Mediterranean, Luke applied himself to 
produce a well-researched history (Luke 1:1–4). It is helpful to recall a few things 
about Luke’s writings, traditionally named the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the 
Apostles. Luke did not write them for a publication project called ‘The New Testa- 
ment’. Their inclusion in this later Christian compilation can obscure his unique 
contribution to Greek history-writing for at least two reasons. 


First, Luke’s works are often separated from the Greek historiographical tra- 


dition because they are aligned with Jewish and Christian history and theology. 
Their estrangement grew as a result of the nineteenth-century division between 
the disciplines of Theology and Philology.23 This is unfortunate, since these re- 
search fields are mutually enriching and contribute together to our understand- 
ing of Greco-Roman history and the ways it was recounted, especially as it was 
experienced at the margins of the Roman Empire.24 Second, the two volumes are 
separated by the Gospel of John in New Testament canonical lists, which can give 
the impression that they were meant to be read separately from the beginning. 


For these reasons, Luke’s works are primarily studied within biblical re- 


search and often separated from one another in commentary series. One will not 
find them in the ‘Loeb’ or ‘Cambridge Greek and Latin Classics’ series. To include 
Luke in one of these reputable series requires first putting them back together 
before they were separated in canonical lists and circulated separately in textual

the “Acts of the Apostles” (trans. McKinney et al.) (2002); now in its – slightly modified – sec-

traditions.25 This approach enables us to consider how Luke might have unders- 
tood his own project when he wrote for a broad audience, under Roman imperial 
rule in the Mediterranean basin, and dedicated them to a certain Theophilus, 
probably around the last quarter of the first century CE. This is their ‘pre-canoni- 
cal’ context, about which we can imagine their reception, as F. Gerald Downing 
suggests, at a dinner party to which this Theophilus invites his guests to hear a 
reading from one or both scrolls.26 This prompts us to remember that Luke told a 
story in Greek for Greeks (and Greek-speakers) about a socio-religious movement 
with origins in the Roman province of Judea. From the beginning, Luke’s writings 
were a part of Greek literature, history, and theology. 


A step further in this literary reconnection concerns the type of literature 


that Luke claims to write. He calls it a διήγησις (Luke 1:1), an account of events, 
which were of particular importance from his perspective.27 This is in general the 
nature of history-writing. Luke is unique among the canonical evangelists in sev- 
eral ways. For example, he displays a greater self-awareness of historiography, 
and he is the only one to write two volumes and connect them through common 
themes. At the beginning of his second volume (Acts 1:1), Luke refers to the first 
volume as his first λόγος, another term used to describe a narrative or a section 
of a written work.28 Luke proposes his second volume to be the follow-up λόγος or 
διήγησις. He thus invites his audience to receive his two scrolls as one narrative 
in two parts and as works of history. His prefaces display how Luke places his 
writings in connection with the Greek historiographical tradition. These prefaces 
and their claims will be examined in Chapter 4. 


During the latter part of the first century CE, Luke composed his two-volume 


work with the conviction that the object of his enquiry and his insights were valu- 
able to his contemporaries (Luke 1:1–4). Other notable historians of the Roman 
Imperial period who wrote in Greek include Josephus, Plutarch, and Arrian. Still, 
other historians drew inspiration from the Greek tradition and wrote in other 
languages, such as the Latin historians Livy and Tacitus. They all claimed to have 
something to tell, accounts of events that were significant enough to pass on to 
their readers (Livy 1.0.3; Tacitus, Ann. 1.1).

It is important here to note the relevance of Herodotus in Luke’s times,29 


even five hundred years after the publication of his Histories.30 All the historians 
above, regardless of their cultural background, knew Herodotus because he was a 
part of the Greek literary canon, already from the early stages of the Hellenistic 
period.31 One may not have agreed with Herodotus’ interpretation of the Greco- 
Persian Wars or his way of writing history, but he was a popular author, along- 
side Thucydides and Xenophon in the historiographical tradition, and Homer and 
Hesiod in the mythological tradition. This point will be further discussed in Chap- 
ter 2. 


Finally, the geopolitical reach of Luke’s two volumes must be mentioned. 


One may assume, without having read them, that they only tell a Jewish story, 
restricted to an isolated Roman province. Yet Luke’s account begins in Jerusalem 
in ca. 5/4 BCE, and it ends in Rome, with the apostle Paul’s two-year captivity in 
60–62 CE during Nero’s reign (54–68 CE). Like Herodotus’ Histories, Luke’s ac- 
count attempted to deliver a literary work that had not yet appeared according to 
his project’s aims and methods (cf. Luke 1:1–4). It also explains an unlikely victo- 
ry-story, includes political commentary with theological support, in a way that 
made sense to his audience. It will be seen that Luke’s account, from beginning to 
end, has a global reach as well as claims of universal import. It is solidly ground- 
ed in the Jewish theological, Greek cultural, and Roman Imperial contexts. Luke is 
in fact interested in the intersection between divine and human rule. Thus, al- 
though it is still common to confine Luke to the world of biblical literature, it is 
unlikely that Luke understood himself and his project exclusively in this way. It is 
more probable that Luke had both in mind, writing within the Jewish and Greek 
traditions. 


Indeed, it is certainly ordinary to consider Herodotus’ influence on histori- 


ans like Ctesias of Cnidus, Ephorus of Cyme, Polybius, and Plutarch. But it is as- 
tonishing that Herodotus could inspire many others to write histories, centuries 
later and in Greek, about the Egyptians, Babylonians, Romans, and Jews. Helleni- 
sation made Herodotus known to the likes of Manetho, Berossus, Polybius, and 
Josephus. The Greek language enabled these authors to disseminate their own en- 
quiries to a much broader context. Hence, Herodotus and the Greek language be-

came the primary sources of inspiration for the composition of prose history. And 
Luke was one of the beneficiaries of this legacy.32 


Reconnecting Herodotus and Luke. Herodotus and Luke, as historians of 


Greece, share substantial links. Their accounts, although they are for Greek- 
speaking audiences, are global in nature, covering multiple peoples and develop- 
ments taking place under (threats of) foreign rule. Their histories have both 
moral and didactic weight, addressing the concerns and interests, explicitly and 
implicitly, of their own audiences under foreign rule. To do this more comprehen- 
sively, their narratives are told from a theistic standpoint, incorporating their 
own experiences as well as those of their characters in the core narrative, but 
also those from the distant past. Luke delineates the experiences of a multicultur- 
al movement that shares a common set of religious beliefs, spanning from Jer- 
usalem to Rome, under the dominion of the Roman Empire and under consider- 
able Greek cultural influence. Luke’s account, thus, builds on and connects both 
Greek and Jewish histories and historiographies.33 


The exploration of the works of these two authors provides a comprehensive 


understanding of ancient historiography and the literary and theistic unity that 
exists between them. Despite the manifest differences between them, their histo- 
ry-writing functions as didactic acts for their readers, thereby establishing a link 
between these two fathers of history and others seated around Herodotus’ table. 
It provides, therefore, a significant – and often underestimated – strand for con- 
ducting research on classical and biblical historiography in unison. 


Contextualised in this way, within this Greek historiographical line, to imag- 


ine Herodotus and Luke at the same table – with many historians in between 
from a wide variety of peoples and cultures yet all Greek-speakers – is more plau- 
sible. Additional elements, given below and in other chapters, justify the continui- 
ty between the two historians and Luke’s place at the historiographers’ table. But 
what about the five hundred years in between them? Historians in antiquity ac- 
knowledged this theological strand running through the historiographical record, 
but they differed as to the extent to which they integrated it into their writings. 
This is the ‘hermeneutical dilemma’ that will be discussed in the following section 
and expanded in Chapter 2. There, the question is explored about how one could 
break from the Homeric mythological tradition of writing and still compose histo- 
ry.

1.2 The Hermeneutical Dilemma: Divine Agency and Historiography 


(An Ancient Problem) 


The mythological legacy of Homer and Hesiod exerted a significant influence on 
the development of Greek historiography, and Herodotus made it one of its dis- 
tinctive features. This influence subsequently spread to other geographical and 
cultural areas.34 In order to examine this historiographical strand, the develop- 
ment of which will be outlined in Chapter 2, the discussion is initiated with an 
overview of the interpretative challenges that historians in antiquity were faced 
with. Undeniably, historiography and theology have a complex history, and 
Herodotus is partly to be blamed or thanked for their intertwining. But one of his 
predecessors, Hecataeus of Miletus, had already evoked this unease with the 
mythological past: “Hecataeus of Miletus speaks thus: I write what seems to me to 
be true; for the Greeks have many tales that seem absurd to me” (fr. 1).35 He- 
cataeus’ Genealogies, though extant now only in forty fragments, show already a 
rationalising interpretation of the family claims of divine origin. Conversely, 
Herodotus also critiques Hecataeus’ claims to divine lineage (2.143.4). 


However, it is Herodotus who is the most important link between the 


mythopoetic and historiographical traditions. Homer and Herodotus influenced 
the way historians dealt with the distant past as well as with contemporary per- 
ceptions of divine agency. Herodotus’ connection with Homer is particularly 
strong. Just as Homer seems to have imparted some historical knowledge within 
mythologically laced poetry, so Herodotus imparted mythological elements in his- 
toriographical prose. Herodotus himself was literarily and theologically a son of 
Homer,36 but he was not uncritical of him.37 Various epithets for Herodotus attest 
to this literary agnation, combining epic and historiography, such as the ‘Prose 
Homer of History’ in the Salmakis Inscription and the ‘most Homeric’ (Ὁμηρι- 
κώτατος) of Longinus (de subl. 13.3). Although somewhat hyperbolic, historio- 
graphically speaking, Herodotus can even be called ‘the modern Odysseus’ due to 
his inquisitive nature and extensive travels.38 


The task of writing a comprehensive history in the shadow of Homer, He- 


siod, and other cultural influences is difficult to imagine. The mythological past 
presented two main challenges: the unverifiability of the stories of the distant

past and the presence of the divine realm, the gods, or other supernatural forces 
in these traditions.39 And, regarding the second element, a fundamental question 
was that “While the gods may be absolute, human perceptions of them are not.”40 


These questions created a certain epistemological uncertainty that was problem- 
atic for historians and contributed to a literary shift, from the mythopoetic to the 
historiographical. Herodotus and Thucydides played a key role in this, as they 
“[…] confronted epic poetry and tried to substitute new models for those offered 
by Homer; both men responded to the needs of an age that sought more extended 
and reliable knowledge (Herodotus especially), to be utilized in particular for the 
formation of a governing class (Thucydides especially).”41 Historians negotiated 
this problem by deciding what value the distant past could add to their own proj- 
ects (even if only metaphorically or symbolically), and to what extent they could 
integrate stories involving the divine realm into their interpretation of historical 
development. Here, then, is the dilemma: how could historians incorporate – 
even honour if so desired – perceptions of the gods and heroes, or other super- 
natural forces, into their narratives? Based on the historiographical record, the 
question seems to be one of ‘how to do it’ rather than on ‘whether to do it’. The 
latter was not the dilemma in Herodotus’ legacy. 


Indeed, Herodotus offered to the world something that was different, both 


generically and religiously, from that of his eminent literary forebear.42 This 
choice marks a “twofold relation of break and filiation between myth and histo- 
ry.”43 This was one of the hermeneutical challenges encountered by Herodotus, 
and it subsequently became a dilemma for his heirs and for historiography in 
general. The historiography of Herodotus and Thucydides required thinking 
through a series of hermeneutical questions, one of which pertains to the influ- 
ence of theological beliefs on the interpretation and expression of historical 
events.44 


How did Herodotus negotiate this hermeneutical dilemma? A few examples 


will serve to open the discussion and will be developed throughout the study. In 
an important remark towards the end of his long work, Herodotus makes the 
claim: “It is indeed clear, from many proofs, that divine forces are at play in cir- 
cumstances […]” (9.100.2).45 This is unmistakably the language about perceptions 
of divine agency. It is perhaps the greatest presupposition about the divine in his 
entire work, and thus also one of his hermeneutical principles, which seeks to in-

terpret divine activity when it is permissible or justifiable. In short, for Herodotus 
the divine realm was not without witness. The above aside arguably sums up his 
position, which is expressed in various ways throughout his work. Yet this narra- 
tive remark comes at the very end of his work when he comments on the alleged 
chronological coincidence between the battles of Plataea and Mycale. Other 
asides, some of which will be examined below, remind us that this question is not 
so easily resolved. 


Arguments supporting Herodotus’ stance on belief and piety must be bal- 


anced against other hermeneutical principles perceived in other narrative re- 
marks. With regard to divine agency, Herodotus can hardly be described as trig- 
ger-happy. Typically, he does not see a demon instigating every action, nor does 
he anthropomorphise the gods in the melee of battles. Nor is he a naive fable- 
monger. He makes this clear to his audience in various remarks. For example, in 
qualifying an account of the Argives’ peculiar behaviour, he writes: “I am obliged 
to say what is said. But I am certainly not obliged to believe it all, and as for me, 
let this statement stand for the whole story (λόγον)” (7.152.3).46 This critical prin- 
ciple clearly means that he does not blindly trust the stories passed on to him. 
Even so, what he ultimately accepts as reliable accounts may not convince read- 
ers of his time or of later times. This is part of the dilemma that he has left 
through his legacy. Since the most extraordinary things can happen in this world 
and accounts of such events abound, discernment is required. His interest in 
things incredible (παράδοξα), marvellous (θαυμάσια), or unbelievable (ἄπιστα) of- 
ten earns him a mention as a predecessor of the ‘paradoxographers’. However, 
his work cannot be reduced to this later literary genre (third c. BCE).47 His inter- 
pretative approach, as well as his role before his audience, is further illustrated 
by another aside regarding his Egyptian sources: “Now as for the things said by 
the Egyptians, let them be useful to those to whom such tales are plausible; as a 
principle for this whole story (λόγον) I write down the things said by all through 
hearsay (ἀκοῇ)” (2.123.1).48 


In short, Herodotus acknowledges divine action and extraordinary events in 


the world, but he does not believe everything that is told to him, and he expects 
his readers to apply the same hermeneutical discernment.49 In this way, he shows 
an openness to his world, given its amazing complexity and forces, both visible 
and invisible. In addition, he shows openness to his readers by acknowledging the

hermeneutical dilemma that he faced, as well as the considerable variety of sto- 
ries he received and their (sometimes) questionable reliability. He invites his 
readers to interpret the stories critically within their polytheistic worldview. He 
assumes their belief and interest and does not provide all the details that modern 
readers might wish to have. 


In discussing Herodotus’ approach to the interpretation of the divine sphere, 


some scholars place too much emphasis on other statements from Book 2.50 These 
statements show a side of Herodotus that seems to set limits to his discussion of 
the divine. For example, he will talk about the gods only when his narrative oblig- 
es him to do so (2.3.2; 2.65.2). Then, when discussing the names or denominations 
of the gods, he seems to relativise the discussion by saying: “Now as for the mat- 
ters concerning the gods – except only their names – I am not keen to explain 
what I heard, considering all humans equally knowledgeable about them. If, how- 
ever, I do make mention of them, I do so because the story compels me” (2.3.2). 


Each of these statements must first be studied in the context of Book 2 before 


its value for all the Histories can be judged.51 For when one begins a study of 
Herodotus’ view and use of the divine in this way, then the discussion takes a 
more sceptical approach. Yet his audience has already heard much about divine 
agency in Book 1, enough to begin to shape their reception of the macronarrative, 
and they will encounter many more in which Herodotus’ beliefs are explicitly 
stated. So, if there are so many recorded perceptions of the divine, then it is in 
accordance with his principle “because my account leaves me no choice.” Never- 
theless, there is a certain reservation about and restriction of attention pertaining 
to the divine sphere. This is partly a reflection of Herodotus’ hermeneutical 
dilemma. He trusts his audience to know certain things. Given his audience’s 
knowledge and expectations, on the one hand he integrates the divine into his 
narrative differently from Homer and Hesiod. On the other hand, he does not 
hermetically exclude the divine from his explanation of the prodigious victory 
over the Persians. His approach is a via media; historiographically, he avoids 
these excesses. 


If the above statements reflect something of the historical Herodotus behind 


the narrative voice(s), then we have an idea of his hermeneutical principles and 
the limits of his own investment in theological traditions.52 So, what exactly does 
he believe? And what difference does it make in the reading of his nine-volume 
work? These are two questions that continue to be debated, and which we will

In addition to the above hermeneutical principles, Herodotus offers a 


glimpse of certain other principles of divine ordinance and agency that are regu- 
larly and artfully woven into his history. These principles suggest the belief that 
divine rule is omnipresent. Wherever one lives and whatever names one gives to 
the divine,53 the gods and the heroes – or other non-human forces – have the last 
word.54 Conversely, the mutability of human destiny is ever-present and often po- 
sitioned in relation to the divine realm. Human fate is portrayed as precarious at 
both the individual and collective levels (cf. the dialogue between Croesus and 
Solon, 1.29–33). Consequently, the interaction between the divine and human 
spheres is constantly placed before his audience. Indeed, Herodotus refers so fre- 
quently to religious attitudes, rituals, and divine agency that this emphasis plausi- 
bly reflects the interests and expectations of his audience.55 However, partly be- 
cause of this emphasis on bidirectional movement, i.e., the interaction between 
the divine and human realms (e.g., rituals, pious and impious exempla, oracles, 
and divine intervention), his historiographical legacy has always been ambiva- 
lent. His holistic approach was – and still is – both praised and criticised.56 In- 
deed, the world described by Herodotus, human and divine, resembles that of a 
kaleidoscope with patterns of multiple features. 


Related to the previous point, Herodotus’ inclusion of the divine realm was 


seen as falling short of the mark in two ways. I present them briefly here, as they 
will be clarified in the next chapter. First, some historians thought that Herodotus 
resorted too often to divine intervention in the description of historical develop- 
ments and in the moral evaluation of individuals and groups. Although his Histo- 
ries broke with the poetic tradition of Homer and Hesiod and began the process 
of demythologising historiography,57 some historians thought that Herodotus did 
not demythologise enough. Secondly, it seems that Plutarch thought that Herodo- 
tus’ representation of the gods was inadequate. Even though this aspect is fre- 
quently expressed through allusions or speeches, Herodotus was criticised for not

History writing had already been going on for some time by the middle of 


the fifth century BCE, but a historical production such as Herodotus’ was differ-

composed many of his logoi for public reading meant that they could reach a wid-

Herodotus, particularly in relation to his hermeneutical dilemma. 


Considering Herodotus as one of the pioneers of classical Greek historiogra- 


phy, the present project builds on the assessment that Herodotus’ kind of history 
not only “did not succeed in putting myth out of business,”60 but prolonged, nu- 
anced, and underpinned it. By anchoring his history in this tradition, the result 
was a work of piety and education for his audience. Was this a dilemma or an 
opportunity for his audience and his successors? Or did Thucydides put an end to 
this dilemma and make subsequent historiography essentially secular?61 I think 
this is erroneous, and it calls into question Hermann Strasburger’s statement 
about the effect that, for example, Thucydides and the Sophists had on the rela- 
tionship between mythology and historiography:

alters. Seine mündlichen Gewährsmänner aus der Väter- und Großvätergeneration 
waren zumeist noch völlig durchdrungen von der Identität zwischen religiöser und 
historischer Weltbetrachtung, die sich seit dem Zeitalter der Sophistik und des Thu- 
kydides für das Altertum nie wieder ungebrochen hergestellt hat.62 


Did Herodotus’ kind of historiē (or “display/performance of his enquiry” ἱστορίης

have had no serious reservations about it, and divine action (of various kinds) 
became a permanent feature of historiography. Herodotus became both heir and 
bequeather of this hermeneutical question. Chapter 2 develops this from Thucy- 
dides to Lucian of Samosata. The next section examines how this hermeneutical

1.3 Modern Reception of Herodotus’ Hermeneutical Dilemma 


(A Modern Problem) 


Before examining how some modern interpreters have dealt with Herodotus’ 
hermeneutical dilemma, we first look briefly at some related questions and ex- 
pressions often used about the Histories and their influence on historiography. 
These are various facets of a complex issue, where abstract terms are often used 
and even contested.64 Accordingly, this section does not provide a detailed survey 
of the scholarly literature on the vast topics of ‘Herodotus and religion’ or 
‘Herodotus and the divine’. Almost every introductory book or essay on the Histo- 
ries contains a chapter or a section on these topics.65 In addition, other subjects 
are often treated under ‘Herodotus and religion’ such as ‘myth and history’, ‘truth 
and fiction’, ‘religion and history’, and ‘faith and history’. Each of these will be 
briefly described below. The dichotomous nature of these categories is obvious. 
They are, however, not watertight, because they are interrelated and shed light 
on some aspects of Herodotus’ understanding of the relationship between the di- 
vine and human realms. All of these pairs contribute to an understanding of reli- 
gion and theology in the Histories as well as a prophetic-like feature in ancient 
historiography. 


Of the four groups above, the modern reception of the hermeneutical dilem- 


ma most closely resembles the question of ‘myth and history’.66 But myth is gener- 
ally understood to be much broader than mere discourse about the divine realm. 
Broadly speaking, it concerns stories from or about the distant and unverifiable 
past. A key line of enquiry is how Herodotus used material from Homer, Hesiod, 
and other earlier sources, and how he both imitated them and distanced himself 
from them. As a master storyteller, Herodotus has a definite penchant for all sorts 
of interesting stories from the distant past, whether or not they contribute signifi- 


64 
Many modern terms are used by scholars to describe ancient beliefs and practices with the 
intention of not being blatantly anachronistic. ‘Religion’ is one of them, and has been prob- 
lematised by Nongbri (2013) and Barton and Boyarin (2016). Certain abstract expressions 
present their own difficulties, but they can, when explained, be useful for the analysis of 
Greek religious beliefs and practices as portrayed in historiography. For example, for a good 
argument defending the use of ‘religion’ and ‘polytheism’, see Pirenne-Delforge (2020) 9–23. 
Andreas Schwab also acknowledges the risks of reducing ‘religion’ to a single definition, in-

Schwab 2020, 31–32). Likewise, for ‘belief’ and ‘beliefs’ in relation to religious practice in 
Greek religion, see Versnel (2011) Appendix 4 and Harrison (2025).

cantly to his main questions. He includes these accounts in his history because he 
has received them, and, plausibly, because he thinks his audience might find 
them interesting. This also has some historiographical value. 


The question of myth is often treated with another pair, ‘truth and fiction’, 


which is clearly a central question in the history of historiography, and the pri- 
mary dilemma in Herodotean reception.67 In principle, Herodotus says that he re- 
lates what he hears, openly acknowledging his use of oral tradition. He also recog- 
nises that his sources are of varying reliability. But just as Herodotus was accused 
of falsehood in antiquity (e.g., by Ctesias and Plutarch), modern scholarship has 
not failed to add to it.68 The reasons for this have to do with the material that he 
presents to his readers and the value he attaches to it. But this does not necessari- 
ly lead to the judgement that Herodotus was naive about the difference between 
fact and fiction, or generally unreliable in his historical representation.69 


When it comes to ‘religion and history’, it is an understatement to say that 


Herodotus has a keen interest in the religious beliefs and rituals of different cul- 
tures. He is truly cosmopolitan in this respect. He considers them to be an integral 
part of the customs (nomoi) of peoples and attributes an almost sacred status to 
them.70 The respect or non-respect of nomoi leads to a wealth of highlighted ex- 
amples of piety and impiety. This information must have been of some impor- 
tance to him and his audience (Greeks and Greek speakers). However, this is only 
one facet of his larger story, which cannot be reduced to an ethnographic study of 
practised religion. 


Finally, ‘faith and history’ involves the study of personal involvement or in- 


vestment in the religious beliefs and practices. It moves the question from the 
theology of the Histories to the theology of Herodotus. What did he really believe? 
How did his religious experiences influence his understanding of the divine 
realm? Was he, for example, an initiate of the Samothracian mysteries?71 Did he 
receive priestly training, given his frequent contact with priests in various parts 
of the world and his interest in their rituals? Or was he more like the so-called 
Sophists, supposedly uninterested in the divine realm? In short, how did his piety 
(if any) influence his writing of history? All of the above are relevant to the study 
of Herodotus, as they are to any historian of antiquity. These elements also reveal 
a certain tension that persists in historical research, namely whether history and 
theology or religion can be profitably studied together.72

In the light of this overview of related issues, we turn to the modern recep- 


tion of Herodotus’ hermeneutical dilemma. If the primary dilemma in Her- 
odotean reception has been the question of Herodotus’ truthfulness and reliabili- 
ty, modern scholarship has shown some unease about Herodotus’ inclusion of 
reports involving the divine realm.73 Historians recognise that this element is 
prevalent in the Histories and cannot easily be ignored. Their questions are essen- 
tially on two levels, the descriptive and the normative. John Gould has described 
this dilemma for modern historians as “a constant and recurring unhappiness 
over the part played by religion in Herodotus’ text.”74 The main reasons for histo- 
rians’ disappointment with Herodotus are two: his “apparent superficiality” 
about divine causation and his lack of separating the good material from the bad, 
which, it is assumed, all good historians must do.75 The inclusion of gods is also 
perceived by moderns as a lack of objectivity. Less inclusion of the divine realm 
seems to imply more objectivity, veracity, and reliability. 


This leads historians to try to make him appear more sceptical, and his lack 


of “analytical clarity” on matters of religion, especially “the phenomena of other 
religious traditions than his own.”76 Indeed, early modern scholarship has some- 
times criticised Herodotus for his reliance on divine agency.77 He was pejoratively 
labelled naive or pagan.78 The mixture of the descriptive and the normative has 
been at the heart of this modern reception dilemma. Its appeal to greater objectiv- 
ity in historiography is understandable, but ancient historians worked with limit- 
ed resources and diverse worldviews. Guy Lachenaud rightly points out that 
those who judge historians such as Herodotus too harshly for their religious or 
philosophical leanings are not exempt from this in their own methods and writ- 
ings.79 As Luke Pitcher pithily concludes: “Ancient historiography is not always as 
ancient, or modern historiography as modern, as is often supposed.”80 Neverthe- 
less, one can discern a “turning-point” in scholarship, as Hugh Lloyd-Jones notes – 
which is more generous towards Herodotus.81 With regard to Herodotus and the

Major proposals for solutions and challenges to Herodotus’ hermeneutical dilem- 
ma. Three major works signal a significant shift away from sceptical, perhaps 
positivist, approaches towards a more equitable view of Herodotus’ attitude to 
the divine as a part of ancient historiography. As the summary will show, despite 
these major works, there is still no consensus, and three general views remain in 
tension. I will offer a proposal for reconciling these views through a viable and 
conciliatory approach. 


Guy Lachenaud’s Mythologies, religion et philosophie de l’histoire dans Hé- 


rodote is one of the major works that marked a trend towards a non-judgemental 
assessment of Herodotus’ integration of the divine with the human realm. Lache- 
naud is critical of scholars who are too harsh or superficial in their assessment of 
Herodotus’ religious and philosophical views, often because of “préjugés défavo- 
rables.”82 Lachenaud brings balance to the discussion and almost delivers an apol- 
ogy for the great historian. Unfortunately, due to its length (761 pages), depth 
(note the title), and untranslated French text, scholarship has not taken advan- 
tage of this useful work.83 Lachenaud presents a Herodotus who is neither overly 
rationalistic nor relativistic about divine intervention. Rather, he is open-minded 
and generally positive about religion as it is expressed in other cultures, yet with- 
out seeking to develop a syncretistic religion or a kind of primitive monotheism. 
An important contribution is Lachenaud’s comparison of Herodotus’ views with 
those in philosophical and literary works of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE. 


Lachenaud does not classify Herodotus as a philosopher, but he explores 


how Herodotus negotiates religious issues within real contexts of historical devel- 
opment. Religious expression and geographical movement allow him to explore 
the interrelationship between the divine and human spheres without making this 
his primary intention.84 The divine is always present in the narrative (a kind of 
universal logos), and its expressions should not be considered a separate domain 
from the rest of his work. Rather, it is intertwined with the rest, which leads to a 
significant interpretative key: one should read Herodotus without separating “le 
géographe, l’historien, le moraliste, le penseur, l’homme religieux.”85 For Lache- 
naud, Herodotus explores the universal logos in human history without develop- 
ing a sacred history. The divine and human spheres are not autonomous, but are 
interdependent, existing through contractual relationships.86 The close connec- 
tion between the history of religions and geography grounds this reality. The

strength of Lachenaud’s study in relation to the hermeneutical question is that it 
upholds the very possibility of doing a theological reading of Herodotus as a part 
of a holistic approach that integrates different facets of a complex narrative. 


Thomas Harrison’s watershed publication in 2000 (and slightly revised pa- 


perback edition in 2002) also astutely critiqued modern dismissals of Herodotus’ 
interest in the divine.87 The strength of his book is that he allows Herodotus to 
speak for himself and to allow for the possibility that his texts and narrative voic- 
es may also reflect fifth-century religious thought and, by extension, Herodotus’ 
own beliefs. Harrison’s thematic analysis is supported by a wealth of examples 
from the Histories and thorough interaction with earlier scholarship of various 
tendencies. In defence of his position, Harrison points out some of the hermeneu- 
tical errors committed by modern scholarship. 


First, for some scholars, Herodotus was clearly wrong, because that is not 


the purpose of history-writing (i.e., normative concerns).88 In short, it seems too 
easy to let Herodotus be Herodotus. Allowing him to express his interpretation of 
the world through his belief in the divine would be to jeopardise his credibility as 
a historian. As a result, some scholars have attempted to vindicate him as the ‘Fa- 
ther of history’ by finding a way to excuse him from this troublesome element. In 
their view, the extensive presence of the divine realm must have a historical ex- 
planation, based on some contextual element in the fifth-century milieu (here, 
the descriptive aspect). For example, certain solutions can be placed under an 
“entertainment theory,” that is, the blame to some extent shifts from Herodotus to 
the expectations of his audience.89 If Herodotus included so much discourse on 
religion and the divine, it was mainly to please his audience or readership. This 
attempt, however, to exculpate Herodotus is unconvincing. 


Another proposal is that certain sections of the Histories are more serious 


than others. For example, the earlier parts of his work contain much more about 
the divine realm than the later parts.90 His thought evolves as the story progress- 
es. Another view finds that Herodotus’ rhetoric represents a transition from un- 
critical to more rational. This linguistic mimesis – it is claimed – is simply the 
way people talked, which was a rhetoric of traditional ideals and beliefs that was 
both accessible and pleasing to people at different levels of society. However, this 
rhetoric – it is argued – was already in the process of being eclipsed, for example 
in the work of Thucydides, a putatively purer form of historiography.91 There are 
some underlying assumptions in these proposals. An individual who produced a 
work as sophisticated as the Histories must be more intelligent than a simple 
polytheist and, quite plainly, Herodotus’ integration of the divine is not the way

a plausible framework that shows how to move from ‘religion found in the Histo-

Jon Mikalson’s Herodotus and Religion in the Persian Wars appeared in 2003, 


a few years after Harrison’s publication. A glimpse of the timeliness of this and 
other studies is underscored: “Oddly, though, until very recently little attention 
has been paid to the whole – to the picture of Greek religion that emerges from 
the writings of this observer and practitioner of Greek religion in the classical pe- 
riod.”95 Mikalson begins with Lachenaud’s study and compares it with Harrison’s 
(2000). His emphasis “on the whole” illustrates well his contribution to the devel- 
opment that allows Herodotus to interpret history from his own worldview. Since 
Lachenaud and Harrison’s studies are organised thematically, Mikalson’s com- 
plements them in that he adopts mainly a narrative approach, showing how the 
vertical and horizontal axes of religion develop continuously and interconnected- 
ly. The bulk of the book is devoted to this narrative development in the Histories 
in Mikalson’s Chapter 2 “A Religious Account of the Persian Invasions.”96 Mikal- 
son supplements this synchronic approach diachronically by providing examples 
of Greek literature as well as material culture that highlight traditional piety in 
relation to the Greco-Persian Wars. In this regard, Mikalson convincingly shows 
how Herodotus’ narrative provided Greek culture with something valuable that 
was not available in other gestures of piety in the fifth century.

weak voice in scholarly discussion. These works, however, have not removed all 
the “unhappiness” evoked by Gould.97 But if one can speak of any kind of move-

asked. To illustrate this, one might entertain a conversation among colleagues 
about whether Herodotus would have been better off omitting any discussion of 
religious beliefs and practices. If we can imagine a Herodotean narrative world 
without religion, how would this silence have affected his legacy in antiquity? 
And how would it change modern historians’ appreciation of his work? Respons- 
es to this question would probably be mixed.99 Would it necessarily mean that 
Herodotus was an atheist? Would it even be possible to tell many of his stories 
with the divine simply removed, or would it remain implicit? 


Three general views: one holistic approach? Reactions to an imagined omission of 
all things religious and divine from the Histories function as a foil for what we 
find there. The risk, of course, is that much of Herodotus would be silenced. It 
would demythologise his work and denature his own narrative voice. This is 
clearly anachronistic and unhistorical. In recent research, the subtly derogatory 
tone has been attenuated, especially as questions and approaches have moved 
from the referential to the rhetorical. 


Thus, broadly speaking, three general positions remain perceptible in Her- 


odotean scholarship.100 It is important to recognise that these positions are nei- 
ther impermeable nor necessarily exclusive. This rift in scholarship reveals cer- 
tain a priori hermeneutical choices about Herodotus’ relationship to his cultural 
milieu. The underlying questions are: Who had the greatest influence on him in 
terms of thought and piety? Homer, Hesiod, Hecataeus, or the Sophists, e.g., Hip- 
pias, Antiphon, Gorgias, Protagoras, and Prodicus? These questions are valuable, 
of course, but another question that is worth considering is whether scholars al- 
low for any theological innovation in the Histories. It may be helpful to think in 
terms of degrees of appropriation and differentiation of existing concepts. 


The first view emphasises Herodotus’ preference for human agency, as a 


quasi-rationalist who allows little or no place for divine causation in historical 
discourse.101 This would align Herodotus with the Ionian and Athenian intellectu-

Which of the three positions above is the most plausible? Does Herodotus 


have a discernible and consistent voice throughout the nine volumes on the di- 
vine? Could Herodotus want to keep his readers guessing, raising dust here and 
there, so that, like everything else in human experience, things are shifting and 
therefore ambiguous? This seems extreme, since repetitive patterns (e.g., motifs 
and themes) orient his audience to receive his historical explanations through the 
lens of a theistic worldview, nuanced by perceptions of human and divine inter- 
action. This interpretation is closely aligned with the second position. However, 
as noted above, these three categories are not watertight. For example, even 
Lateiner’s rationalising tendency leaves some room for divine agency, as is evi- 
dent in his helpful table “Explanation in Herodotus: Some Important Narra- 
tives.”107 Many of these are interpreted (e.g., by Harrison and Mikalson) as clear 
examples of Herodotus’ perception of divine causation. 


Given Herodotus’ holistic approach to the world and his didactic position 


vis-à-vis his audience, my approach, which is mainly narratological and theologi- 
cal, integrates aspects of these three views. I do, however, give more attention to 
the second view, which has a more synchronic orientation than the others. These 
three views can be combined in this formulation: (1) Herodotus constructs his 
historical explanation largely through accounts of human action, but this is not 
complete for his investigation, and, thus (2) he provides explanations from sour- 
ces that illustrate perceptions of the divine through tradition and belief, and (3) 
on a socio-historical level, a human-divine interaction manifests itself in a variety 
of bidirectional activities throughout the world, resulting in clear patterns of pie- 
ty and impiety, and, correspondingly of divine reward and retribution. These are 
all part of human culture and are worth exploring for Herodotus and his audi- 
ence, because they shed light on the nomoi of the peoples and on the reasons for 
global and internecine conflicts. 


In the next section, I outline a holistic approach to the hermeneutical dilem- 


ma as the methodological basis, articulated in three main points: (1) the reception 
history of Herodotus, which can be extended to include Christian historiography, 
especially the writings of Luke; (2) the notion of the ‘prophetic voice’ as a link 
between historians of the Greek tradition; and (3) a narratological and theologi- 
cal reading of these prophetic-like voices displayed in the writings of Herodotus 
and Luke, as bookends on two sides of the continuum of Greek historiography.

1.4 Addressing the Hermeneutical Dilemma via Ancient Reception 


History, the Prophetic Voice of Historiography, and 


Its Demonstration in Herodotus and Luke 


1.4.1 Following Ancient Reception History around Herodotus’ Table of Historians 


As the main link between the mythopoetic tradition and historiography, Herodo- 
tus is often viewed as the inspiration for the inclusion of divine agency in prose 
historiography. From the beginning of the history of his reception, this element 
did not go unnoticed, and it became a problem for ancient and contemporary 
readers. But what parts of this question were problematic for earlier readers and 
for later readers? Are they the same? Or are there differences or nuances? 


In the above introductions to the ancient and modern reception history of 


Herodotus’ hermeneutical dilemma, there is some overlap at the normative level. 
The ancient question remains: What place, if any, should be given to divine agen- 
cy in historiography? Concerning various aspects of this question, ancient and 
modern historians have one thing in common. They all want to set the record 
straight: either to defend Herodotus against misinterpretations that would dena- 
ture him and denigrate his work, or, conversely, to correct him. 


On the descriptive level, however, there is some disagreement between an- 


cient and modern interpreters. What explains the massive presence of the reli- 
gious and the divine? What is Herodotus’ own attitude to the divine? And who 
cares? This line of enquiry opens the door to the perspectives of other authors on 
this thorny question. For instance, why would Plutarch take such a strong posi- 
tion against Herodotus’ representation of the gods some five hundred years lat- 
er? What did it matter to Plutarch in his time? Similarly, why does Luke want to 
set the record straight about Jewish and polytheistic beliefs and practices? Why 
did this matter in the second half of the first century CE? And how does Herodo- 
tus figure in these questions? 


To explore the above questions, one way of shedding light on this hermeneu- 


tical dilemma is to survey the ancient reception of Herodotus and to consider his 
work from the perspective of ancient authors in the Greek historiographical tra- 
dition, thus placing the three contemporary positions in the light of the ancient 
ones. This approach may help to reduce the interpretative pitfall raised by Latein- 
er’s question: “[…] do our muddy categories of the Historical map onto the an- 
cient Greeks’ or even one ancient Greek’s?”108 It is like opening a discussion 
among Herodotus’ successors, who are seated around his table explaining how 
they understood their host historian. This way of doing research on the history of 
interpretation of Herodotus has value, but it also has its limitations. Practically 
speaking, a complete history of the reception of this question, like any other com-

parative question in antiquity, is incomplete because of all the missing texts in 
the historical record. To ascertain the views of his successors on this question to 
some extent, it is necessary to examine what is available in their writings, for ex- 
ample: specific comments on Herodotus’ use of divine agency, implicit remarks 
on the question whether positive or negative, and their own use of divine agency 
in their voices or in those of their characters (e.g., in speeches, conversations, and 
prayers). Chapter 2 provides an overview of these questions. 


1.4.2 The Prophetic Voice and Role of Historiography 


Since the comparison of the work of historians with prophetic-like activity has 
already been evoked above, and since the main points of this concept will be de- 
veloped more fully in Chapter 3, I will briefly introduce its value for the study of 
Herodotus, Luke, and other ancient historians in relation to the stated hermeneu- 
tical dilemma. 


We return briefly to the analysis of Herodotus’ approach as it exemplifies 


the logic of this historiographical strand to varying degrees in the writings of his 
successors. The prophetic-like voice is meant in a narratological sense, that is, as a 
hermeneutical role played by historians for their readers. This aspect helps to ex- 
plain the evidence in the Histories as outlined above: 


(1) 
Human agency is essential to Herodotus’ investigation, but it is not sufficient; 


(2) Divine agency, informed by tradition and belief, provides a fuller description; 
(3) Examples of claims of human and divine interaction support this interpreta- 


tive approach, as evidenced by patterns of piety and impiety, and divine re- 
ward and retribution. 


The prophetic historiographical strand can be summarised in five points. As hu- 
man causality cannot provide a complete explanation of life and its activities, 
points two and three in the above list add a significant nuance to the narrative 
argumentation. The authorial voice takes on a prophetic-like voice in the narrative 
development. In order to strengthen this voice, the author may resort to a reli- 
gious metanarrative to ground the core story in a larger story, and to claim episte- 
mological source(s) that evoke divine origin or divine activity. Finally, this 
prophetic voice has the potential to play a prophetic role outside the narrative, in 
the world of the audience, seeking to address contemporary issues and generate 
certain existential pragmatic aims. Historiography can be said to have a prophet- 
ic-like voice to the extent that the narrative exhibits one or more of the above 
elements. The strength of a narrator’s prophetic voice depends on the frequency 
and relevance of these elements to the overall story, as a singular part of the nar- 
rative representation of the past. 


1 Prophet-like Voice, and an Estranged Heir Named Luke 
47 


It is also assumed that this prophetic voice reflects in some way the expecta- 


tions and interests of the audience. The divine is a part of their world. It matters 
to them. The prophetic voice then seeks to make a difference to the audience on 
two levels, as mentioned earlier: to explain the events of the core narrative and to 
offer an interpretation of the audience’s own history, a message intended to com- 
municate or influence a social vision in which the divine sphere has some rele- 
vance to humanity. This is related to the first level, the narrative world, as the 
author’s prophetic voice, depending on its strength, depicts a sacred landscape in 
which the divine is brought to the attention of the reader and how this affects the 
plot (i.e., the progressive exploration of the story’s questions). Divine presence 
can be represented as operative, in a general sense, guiding the larger story on 
the macro-level, and in specific situations at the micro-level. In addition, all things 
related to the divine realm, such as sacred precincts, rituals, festivals and games, 
also maintain the audience’s interest in human-divine interaction. 


These criteria establish the general parameters of the methodology in Chap- 


ter 3, as well as the basis for comparing our authors in Chapters 4 to 12. They will 
also be referred to as required when surveying the hermeneutical dilemma in 
Chapter 2. 


1.4.3 Herodotus and Luke at Herodotus’ Table: 


A Comparative Demonstration of the Prophetic Voice 


Research helps us to address the concerns of modern interpreters and enter the 
cultural contexts and narrative worlds of Herodotus and Luke. The hermeneuti- 
cal dilemma is one of the obstacles to achieving a plausible interpretation. How- 
ever, suppressing their prophetic-like voices would mean suppressing cultural 
artefacts that bear witness to the beliefs of the historians and their characters. 
This research proposes parameters for safeguarding and promoting this aspect of 
historiography, which can be considered part of historical poetics. 


Placing Herodotus and Luke at the same table with Herodotus’ successors is, 


like other models, an artificial construct. But it attempts to be plausible by provid- 
ing a justification for the choices of Herodotus and Luke and the latter’s rightful 
place in Herodotus’ legacy. This is particularly important for an interdisciplinary 
study that invites readers to read texts that may be unfamiliar to them. Through- 
out the study, explanations will be provided to facilitate engagement with our au- 
thors’ texts. 


Here I outline the framework of the study, which consists of four sections. 


The first section, Chapters 1–3, serves to frame the question and provide a work- 
ing methodology for theological study of ancient historiography. The aim is to ex- 
plore the writings of Herodotus and Luke on their own terms, not to force one 
into the mould of the other. I recognise the danger of parallels. But the fact that 


Part I Herodotus’ Hermeneutical Dilemma and His Table of Historians 
48 


they are not isolated cases, and that they represent two points on a line, shows 
that we are dealing with continuity and discontinuity in Greek history, literature, 
and theology. Their similarities and differences must be respected. To this end, a 
synchronic approach such as narratology, supported by historical research, helps 
to focus on the uniqueness of the intrigues of the Histories and Luke-Acts and the 
literary devices of their narrators. 


The second section (Chapters 4–6) introduces the comparison proper. Chap- 


ter 4 establishes this comparison on the basis of multiple contexts, seeking to link 
the two authors by exploring their worlds, narrative prefaces, and audiences. 
Both are cosmopolitan men, keenly interested in peoples and the geopolitical re- 
lations between them. The pains that they took to compose their engaging narra- 
tives show that they wished to influence cultural spaces that were Greek-speaking 
and, arguably, multi-ethnic. Chapters 5 and 6 help to develop a theological under- 
standing of their writings. Both authors anchor their stories, explicitly and implic- 
itly, in larger religious metanarratives. In light of this, they propose a ‘divine plu- 
past’ upon which the core narrative is constructed. Theological differences aside, 
these plupast sections are, narratively, very similar in that they both strengthen 
their prophetic voices. In other words, their audiences are invited to explore sto- 
ries in relation to a larger narrative in which the divine had already manifested 
itself through words and deeds. Chapter 6 provides a cursory overview of the ‘di- 
vine constellations’ of the Histories and Luke-Acts, that is, what is meant by ‘di- 
vine’ and who the actors are in their narratives. This offers a glimpse of the 
worldviews that Herodotus and Luke may have held and assumed from their au- 
diences. While perceptions of the divine realm are occasionally explicitly evoked, 
they are more frequently implied within the development of the narrative argu- 
mentation. 


The third section (Chapters 7–9) is devoted to exploring Herodotus’ prophet- 


ic-like voice in the Histories. Herodotus explores humanity under the threat of 
imperialist powers and how the rule of the divine realm intervened during the 
Greco-Persian Wars. He accomplishes this against the backdrop of two great 
wars: the Trojan War and the Peloponnesian War, which was in force at the time 
of redaction.109 Although the outcome of the Greco-Persian conflict was known to 
readers, their own context was still hostile. The Persians were still present in 
Asia, and relationships between the Greeks had become more aggressive. There- 
fore, they needed to understand how the broader story fit together and how it 
related to their own political situation. Herodotus thus addresses universal ques- 
tions such as freedom, servitude, imperialism, and salvation. For him, the whole 
geopolitical conflict was also a spiritual and religious one. Divine agency in shap- 


109 
For Herodotus’ representation of Athens’ decisive role in the victory over the Persians but 
also his warning for their imperialistic behaviour qua the new Persians in the Mediterranean, 
see Moles (2002). 


1 Prophet-like Voice, and an Estranged Heir Named Luke 
49 


ing history and human participation in it had a role to play that could not be ig- 
nored. 


This is Herodotus’ role for his audience, as a historian with a prophet-like 


role, both for the honour of the gods and the education of his audience.110 As their 
interpreter, he stands in between them, putting the pieces together, writing with 
“oracular authority”111 and in certain passages “almost as a χρησμολόγος him- 
self.”112 His interpretation of history from a theistic perspective gave him an inim- 
itable prophetic voice. He thus sets in motion a moral and theological purpose 
that is so deeply perceptible throughout his work, encouraging his audience to 
learn from this remarkable theological-laden history.113 As Charles Fornara con- 
cisely states: “History became moral and Herodotus didactic.”114 Divine rule is a 
force to be reckoned with, and, if possible, to live in harmony with, in the hope of 
better fortune. So, whether through Homer or Herodotus, divine rule would re- 
main a constant in Greek literature. 


The fourth section explores Luke’s prophetic voice in his Gospel of Luke and 


the Acts of the Apostles. Chapters 10–12 show how Luke produced a literary mon- 
ument that immortalised those who participated in a story that, from Luke’s per- 
spective, could not have happened without divine intervention. Perceptions of the 
divine are shown to be working towards a plan, moving outwards from the Ro- 
man province of Judea. Like Herodotus’ story, this one is also considered from the 
audience’s experience of foreign rule, so Luke places divine rule at the centre of 
the intrigue in relation to the universal themes of freedom, servitude, imperial- 
ism, and salvation. Luke begins and ends his story as an invitation to the widest 
possible audience. His preface (Luke 1:1–4) enters a cultural space still influ- 
enced by Herodotus, his successors, and, of course, Homer. The end of the second 
volume (Acts 28:23–31) depicts the communication of a claimed realisation of 
what is announced at the beginning of the first volume: news of the salvation of 
God (τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ, Acts 28:23 // Luke 2:30; 3:6) and the kingdom of God 
(ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ, Acts 28:28 // Luke 1:33) are offered to all peoples. Paradoxi- 
cally, these claims of divine intervention come at a time when human domination 
in the form of the Roman Empire seems to have reached its apogee. As in the con- 
text of Herodotus, how might this message have appealed to Luke’s audience? Or 
be understood as a subversive warning to the imperial powers? This is also a sto- 
ry of hope for liberation from oppression. Like the prophetic voice of Herodotus, 
Luke’s voice also focuses on divine rule over human forms of rule. This compo- 
nent is present throughout the historiographical tradition.

Luke’s use of rhetorical devices shows that he does not wish to suppress the 


prophetic voice of historiography, but to offer an alternative theistic perspective 
through which divine rule can be understood. Like Plutarch’s critique of Herodo- 
tus’ theology, Luke proposes something theologically different, at times confirm- 
ing some of his characters’ views of the divine and rejecting others. Moreover, he 
does this skilfully through the rhetorical art of historiography. 


1.5 Conclusion 


Both Herodotus and Luke turn the past into history through their records of it, 
illustrating part of the range of Greek historiography. This raises some questions 
that every generation faces. What can be learned from the received traditions? 
How does the divine realm – whatever its name or force – fit into life and histo- 
ry? Herodotus and Luke (and their characters) disclose some ideas about these 
questions, some similar and others different. The divine realm was important to 
them, as was piety. To interpret their stories without these elements is to quell 
their prophet-like voices for their audiences. Their legacies are too important to 
human history for that. The comparison between their works is less about conti- 
nuity of theme (e.g., military conflict) or as grand narratives of eras. Luke-Acts is 
not itself a grand narrative, but it builds on the knowledge of one (i.e., Israel’s 
metanarrative). Instead, the parallels are found in their cultural themes and 
spaces, historiographically and theologically. The need, then, is to read Herodotus 
and Luke (and their heirs) both theologically and historiographically. 


Rather than carving out parts of the Mediterranean (e.g., Judea) as if they 


were not part of Greek history, studying Herodotus and his heirs at the same ta- 
ble means that their estrangement can be mended through a holistic approach 
with historical, literary, and theological accents. Despite their differences, there is 
theistic and thematic continuity. At Herodotus’ table sit a variety of historians 
from different regions and cultures, such as Berossus, Manetho, Polybius, and 
Josephus. Chapter 2 fleshes this out by demonstrating that this unity in diversity 
offers Luke a place at Herodotus’ table and in classical studies.115

2.1 Introduction 


Herodotus left his successors in antiquity and modern historians of historiogra- 
phy with a hermeneutical dilemma. Some of the questions raised in antiquity 
have remained problematic to this day. Both groups have tried to defend or criti- 
cise Herodotus on various issues.1 One of these is the place of the divine realm – 
however it is defined – in the writing of history. In this chapter, we focus on the 
first group, the historians of antiquity, hailing from different peoples and reli- 
gious backgrounds. They seem to have raised two main questions with respect to 
Herodotus’ theological legacy: What place does divine agency have in historiogra- 
phy? And when one has recourse to it, what knowledge of the divine should be 
transmitted? While it is true that the perception and presence of the divine realm 
vary among Herodotus’ successors, their texts do not show a continuum between 
two opposites: the gods who are active and no divine realm at all. This may be 
true in modern interpretations of our authors, but historiographical texts in the 
Greek tradition testify to a continuity of various theistic and rhetorical expres- 
sions. There appear to be no atheists (in the modern sense) seated around 
Herodotus’ table.2 


As the principal link between Homer, Hesiod, and the historians, Herodotus 


links the mythopoetic past to contemporary history in prose.3 Greek, Roman, Jew- 
ish, and Christian historians read him well into the first centuries CE and reacted 
differently to his hermeneutical and literary challenge. To keep the discussion to 
a manageable size, the survey is delimited by the reception history of Greek-writ- 
ing historians who have something to say about their forebear’s recourse to di-

also be considered an heir of Herodotus and have a place at his table. 


A few preliminary remarks are necessary before beginning this survey. Oc- 


casionally, authors from other literary traditions (e.g., Aristotle and Lucian) and 
languages (e.g., Cicero and Livy) are included to supplement the discussion. Since 
some authors do not (as far as we know) offer specific commentary about divine 
agency, attention is also given to their integration of the divine in their own 
works as an indication of consent or censure of Herodotus’ example. The ques- 
tion, however, is not simply one of counting the number of mentions of the gods 
or the godhead. Rather, the questions concern how historians integrated the di- 
vine into the narrative argumentation of their objects of enquiry. 


The assessment may also appear somewhat uneven in the treatment of our 


authors for a few reasons. Fragmentary authors do not leave much evidence, but 
they should not be ignored because of their limited contribution to the discussion. 
It is a fact, however, that the study of the reception of Herodotus, as of any an- 
cient historian, is severely limited by the fact that only one fortieth (or 2.5 per 
cent) of the classical historical works has survived.6 The number of historians 
whose works are incompletely attested – 856 of whom are reported in Felix Jaco- 
by’s Die Fragmente der griechischen Historiker – continues to grow and is being 
addressed in Brill’s New Jacoby, Second Edition.7 


Conversely, I devote more attention to Thucydides and Polybius, because it is 


often assumed that they had little or no interest in divine agency in historical 
composition. This point is crucial to our understanding of the hermeneutical 
dilemma. Finally, other authors who, like Polybius, wrote their histories in Greek
