Another point worth recalling is that historians generally used material 


from their predecessors freely, but often without any explicit recognition. This is 
certainly true of Herodotean reception which is characterised by frequent bor- 
rowing well into the first centuries CE. Felix Jacoby’s remark reminds us that 
“polemic usually names its object, borrowings are anonymous.”8 This is aptly ech- 
oed by Simon Hornblower as “explicit abuse and silent exploitation.”9 As this was 
generally perpetuated by Greek historians, Arnaldo Momigliano applies it to the 
mixed reception of Herodotus: “Admittedly, the Greeks and Romans were not apt 
to kneel in silent adoration before their own classical writers. Historians were 
especially open to accusations of dishonesty. But no other writer was so severely 
criticized as Herodotus.”10 Of course, Herodotus was not the sole target of criti- 
cism and polemic.11 Polybius’ list of faults committed by Timaeus is even longer 
than Plutarch’s tirade against Herodotus.12 


Fortunately, the history of the reception of Herodotus has had a happy end- 


ing, at least until the present day. As Momigliano pointed out in 1958, Herodotus’ 
methods and results have been vindicated by modern research.13 He was “suc- 
cessful in his enterprise” and “can be trusted.”14 His reputation in modern schol- 
arship has come a long way from the bleak evaluation that his work was already 
old at the time of publication, or that no one read him after Thucydides, Ctesias, 
and Theopompus, or that Alexandrian philology paid him little attention.15 And, 
although for centuries, if not millennia, Thucydides’ model of contemporary po- 
litical history was often regarded as the only serious way of doing history, mod- 
ern historical methods have shown that research into the distant past, foreign 
lands and peoples can be done, and, not least, with the tools used by Herodotus 
(e.g., ὄψις, ἀκοή, γνώμη, ἱστορίη; i.e., autopsy, hearsay, judgement, and en- 
quiry).16 The following survey demonstrates that Herodotus, despite sometimes 
fierce and ungracious criticism, remained one of the pillars of historiography.

2.2 The Hermeneutical Dilemma from Thucydides to Plutarch 


2.2.1 Classical Period (Fifth century BCE–323 BCE) 


The literary milieu of the fifth century BCE was rich and varied, offering much 
cross-fertilisation of rhetorical devices and ideas, not the least of these the rela- 
tionship between divinity and humanity.17 While writings of the fifth century of- 
fer no direct mentions of Herodotus or his Histories, allusions and various paral- 
lels have been proposed between Herodotus and the tragedies of Sophocles and 
Euripides (more difficult to demonstrate), and the comedies of Aristophanes with 
plausible references in the Birds of 414 BCE but more securely up until the Achar- 
nians (425 BCE).18 These parallels and their authors’ interests in common Her- 
odotean themes – such as piety, impiety, as well as divine reward and retribution 
– offer suggestive paths for the present question. 


Nevertheless, wishing to remain mainly within the historiographical legacy 


of Herodotus, our attention turns immediately to Thucydides (ca. 460–ca. 400 
BCE) who is often praised as the second – or even the true – father of Greek histo- 
riography.19 Next to Homer, Herodotus was arguably Thucydides’ greatest source 
of inspiration, but also probably one of his main objects of theoretical critique.20 


Herodotean intertextuality in Thucydides’ The Peloponnesian War is impressive. 
Simon Hornblower finds as many as 139 parallel passages.21 In Thucydides’ eyes, 
the father of epic and the father of history were exemplary as regards their 
choice of subjects and literary beauty, but both left him with hermeneutical faults 
that needed correction.22 As Thucydides’ Pericles comments, Homer’s praises and 
charming words failed to interpret the facts correctly (τῶν δ᾽ ἔργων τὴν ὑπό-

The conspicuous quietness or reticence of Thucydides has attracted some 


scholarly attention. It may then seem unprofitable to accord so much space to the 
person who apparently integrated so little of the divine in his narrative. It is note- 
worthy that – despite Thucydides’ apparent lack of interest in divine agency – 
commentators often address the question of Thucydides’ beliefs, probably, as 
stated, because he writes in the wake of the great Herodotus.25 In short, what does 
this difference reveal about him? Should he not have written more about divine 
agency and order? Could the differences between the fathers of history be used to 
support his decision to use a different hermeneutical model, i.e., a rationalistic 
approach?26 Indeed, on the surface, Thucydides does seem to reflect more the

surprisingly missing in Thucydides’ account.28 Hellmut Flashar agrees, but re-

Jordan has produced a helpful and dense catalogue of Thucydides’ knowledge 
and use of the religious dimension in his work.30 Thus, it seems too strong to af-

Similarly, Lisa Hau concludes that Thucydides’ moral didacticism is constructed 
on a world without gods.34 Thucydides’ beliefs may seem enigmatic, as William 
Furley summarises, to the extent that one can argue for an agnostic, rationalist 
position or a traditionally pious one.35 But it is unwarranted to suggest an atheis- 
tic stance in the modern sense on the basis of this silence,36 and it is also implausi- 
ble with respect to Thucydides’ cultural milieu.37 


Given the tragic nature of his account, it may also be argued that he thought 


that one could only blame humans for the catastrophe of the conflicts between 
Athens and Sparta and their allies. Thucydides portrays a painful and recent de- 
feat in which he took part as a general in the Athenian army. His failure to rescue 
Amphipolis in 424 BCE against the Spartan general Brasidas forced him into polit- 
ical exile. Not only was Thucydides on the losing side of the war, but he was also 
held responsible for some of it. Running through the work then is a general and 
thorough disappointment with human behaviour. It resembles a historiographi- 
cal lament on society of which religion was a key element of its fabric. 


It can be argued that the divine had let human agency run its course, the 


latter ignoring, as it were, the warnings that were manifest before and during the 
Peloponnesian conflict. The gods may seem absent because of the extent of hu- 
man impiety. From Thucydides’ worldview, his account may then be a mirror to 
what he perceived to be accurate. This is still a theistic approach. Rather than a 
contradiction, it could make sense of what appears to be divine indifference. One 
cannot help to see the irony in an apparent unbelieving stance and a prophetic- 
like affirmation to tell things the way they are for posterity: “When Thucydides 
decided to write a true narrative of the Peloponnesian War, this narrative for him 
entailed showing the truth about the absence of divine justice and the dying out 
of simple morality in the world. In this way he intended to make his work useful 
for readers wanting to see the world ‘with perfect clarity’, and thus make it ‘a

All agree that Thucydides’ world is comparatively quiet about the divine, 


and, as Furley concludes, this aspect must be intentional, “as no other literary 
genre of the period dispenses with the gods in the same way.”40 But Furley is also 
right in distinguishing Thucydides’ reticence on divine agency on the one hand 
and religion as a social phenomenon on the other.41 The knot that many would 
like to unravel is what explains this apparent deliberate choice to be so discreet 
about divine agency. 


First, Thucydides appears to be taking distance from his predecessors re- 


garding this point.42 Herodotus, for example, appears to be the target or one of the 
targets for Thucydides’ reproach to his poetic and prose forebears: 


ἐκ δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων τεκμηρίων ὅμως τοιαῦτα ἄν τις νομίζων μάλιστα ἃ διῆλθον 
οὐχ ἁμαρτάνοι, καὶ οὔτε ὡς ποιηταὶ ὑμνήκασι περὶ αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τὸ μεῖζον κοσμοῦντες 
μᾶλλον πιστεύων, οὔτε ὡς λογογράφοι ξυνέθεσαν ἐπὶ τὸ προσαγωγότερον τῇ ἀκρο- 
άσει ἢ ἀληθέστερον, ὄντα ἀνεξέλεγκτα καὶ τὰ πολλὰ ὑπὸ χρόνου αὐτῶν ἀπίστως ἐπὶ 
τὸ μυθῶδες ἐκνενικηκότα […]. 


Nevertheless anyone accepting the broad facts of my account on the arguments I 
have adduced will not go wrong. He [the reader] will put less faith in the glorified 
tales of the poets and the compilations of the prose chroniclers (λογογράφοι), 
whose stories are written more to please the ear than to serve the truth, are inca- 
pable of proof, and for the most part, given the lapse of time, have passed into the 
unreliable realms of romance […] (1.21.1, trans. Hammond; cf. also 6.2.1).

Yet this so-called attack on Herodotus cannot be unequivocally demonstrated. It may be di-

composed as a permanent legacy, not a showpiece for a single hearing,” Waterfield rightly 
describes as an “unanswerable question” (Herodotus 2008, 486 n. 241). Pierre Ponchon ob- 
serves Thucydides’ insistence on the rupture between his predecessors. The fact that Herodo- 
tus is a significant source of information does not necessarily mean that Thucydides wished 
to extend this literary genre that was only developing at this point. Thucydides seems to have 
wanted to write something different. Although later historians saw continuity between the 
two authors and their works, Thucydides may not have intended his project to be aligned 
with Herodotus’ or others: Ponchon (2017) 40–43. Zacharias Rogkotis provides evidence for 
greater continuity and less rupture between the two authors in Rogkotis (2006) 57–86.

With these cutting remarks and others, Thucydides seeks to sway his readers to 
opt for his more solid methodology and composition.43 He openly displays his au- 
thority, arguing that facts are more enduring and meaningful than questionable 
reports for momentary pleasure (1.22.4). Yet this critique is general. It neither 
aims explicitly at Herodotus nor at accounts involving the divine sphere. His re- 
ception then of Herodotus is ambivalent when one considers the high degree of 
Herodotean intertextuality in The Peloponnesian War. Hornblower aptly de- 
scribes Thucydides’ complicated reception of his predecessor: “Thucydides may 
have disapproved of Herodotus’ methods and outlook, but he was not above 
showing off how well he could ‘do a Herodotus’ when he felt like it.”44 


A patently clear example of this is found at the beginning of his work, and it 


is highly informative about the hermeneutical dilemma in historiography. De- 
spite his apparent reticence to include the divine in his description of the past,45 


Thucydides wishes to go beyond Herodotus by claiming the superiority of his sub- 
ject (i.e., the Peloponnesian War was greater than previous wars) and, surpris- 
ingly, by giving proofs of this from unusual activity in the realm of nature. Unlike 
unsupported stories of old, Thucydides’ contemporary history appeals to newly 
attested facts, which include a great frequency of earthquakes, solar eclipses, 
droughts, famine, and the plague that occurred prior and during this greatest of 
wars (1.23). 


Although not explicitly attributed to the divine, Thucydides uses this rhetori- 


cal device to buttress his argument that something of unprecedented magnitude 
had taken place. Thucydides thus invites his readers, at the end of his introduc- 
tion, to interpret this dreadful military conflict from an implicit theistic perspec- 
tive. If reticence about the gods follows in his account, this bold claim ac- 
knowledges that divine communication through nature was indeed occurring as 
in ancient times: “The matters received earlier by hearsay, scarcely confirmed by 
fact, were no longer incredible” (1.23.3). P. J. Rhodes is prepared to recognise this 
statement as “exceptional” but tempers it with “Thucydides is tempted to see sig- 
nificance” in these natural events.46 Yet here the Athenian historian simulta- 
neously gives credit to stories of the past that could not be verified then but can 
now be somewhat substantiated because of present-day occurrences. The rhetori- 
cal force is unmistakable; greater forces, which go unnamed, were shaping the

it not be due to divine retribution and human frailty? Regarding the first ques-

brought to the fore in several places.47 


Thucydides’ implicitly theistic approach may serve as an example of the ten- 


sion or awkwardness evidenced in the historiographical tradition. Does the ex- 
plicit inclusion of the divine make one a logographos, who offers more in terms of 
aesthetic pleasure but falters in reliability?48 Later Polybius will also appeal to the 
unusual convergence of multiple natural and human phenomena as a work of 
Tyche (Hist. 1.1, 4). Like Polybius, a few intellectuals use this motif, albeit with 
variations (e.g., Aristotle and Plutarch). Thucydides’ interest in religion clearly 
concerns less the existence and influence of the gods than how both sides of the 
war used expressions of piety in practice and rhetoric to gain advantage over the 
other.49 But what if Thucydides feels profound disappointment because he was on 
the losing side and because he perceives that the gods are silent due to men’s 
impiety? 


This is another difference between the two fathers of historiography con- 


cerning the divine-human relationship, which Herodotus resolutely did not ne- 
glect. They appear to represent two opposing views on the inclusion of the divine 
in historical discourse. Yet since Thucydides never criticises Herodotus on this 
point, it may be impossible to know what he really thinks about that issue, just as 
it is problematic to decipher his own faith through his writings. Was Thucydides

It is more plausible to consider his rhetoric about the divine as subtle but not 


indifferent. For example, in addition to his grand statement of cosmic participa- 
tion in the strife of men (1.23.3), Thucydides mentions other eclipses (2.28; 4.52.1) 
which can be understood as similar signs of global importance. Many earth- 
quakes (πολλοὶ σεισμοί) in various regions are also mentioned in connection with 
the second outbreak of the plague in Athens (3.87). This seems uncoincidental, for 
these natural phenomena are also supported by attention to religious phenome- 
na. This appears to be the case in light of other evidence, cursorily discussed here. 
First, the fulfilment of oracles is also occasionally mentioned (2.17.2; 3.96.1). Sec- 
ond, exempla of piety and impiety also suggest a pious worldview in that Thucy- 
dides views that winners and losers reaped what they had sown. Generally, the 
Athenians are depicted as losing their confidence in the gods (2.52–53; 2.47.4). 
They even seek oracles to discern whether divine disfavour is upon them, which 
is confirmed by two oracles (2.54.2–5). The psychological effects on the populace 
are thus here underlined with great flair. 


On the other hand, Thucydides portrays the Spartans as “the most punctil- 


ious in the observance of religious formalities.”52 Athens rarely consults Delphi, 
and they failed to do so before embarking on the disastrous Sicilian expedition.53 


Also, while only two Athenian leaders express proper religious attitudes – Peri- 
cles (2.38.1; 2.64.2) and Nikias (6.9.1; 7.69.2; 7.77.2–3)54 – in contrast, Spartan 
leaders are frequently portrayed as seeking help from the gods (Stheneleides, 
1.86.5; Pausanias, 2.71.2; Archidamos, 2.74.2).55 The general Brasidas receives one 
of the highest evaluations, owing much to his exemplary piety (4.87.2–6; 5.10.2). 
He is singled out as the only commander in the entire war who acknowledges 
divine help for victory in battle (4.116.2). Another example of Thucydides empha- 
sising piety in his own voice is found in his appreciation of certain aspects of the 
Peisistratid tyranny in Athens (6.54.5–6). Among his assertions of the many 
things that the tyrants did well is that “they provided sacrifices for the temples” 
(ἐς τὰ ἱερὰ ἔθυον). It seems that Thucydides is doing more than listing facts. Rath- 
er, he is expressing his own opinion on tyrants, who were generally unpopular in

As a part of Thucydides’ characterisation, another point to consider is the 


place of the divine and religion in the speeches that Thucydides represents. Ed- 
ward Armstrong analyses four texts (in connection with other texts from antiqui- 
ty), showing that each of them frequently displays religious language that con- 
tributes to the interpretation of these key scenes revealing a military failure.56 


The literary devices employed underline the functions of religion in discourse, 
which serve to guide readers in their interpretation of military failures to mo- 
bilise and examine their own understanding of justice and morality in relation to 
the divine sphere. 


Furthermore, since thought about the divine realm was closely connected to 


discourse on morality in antiquity, research has explored the question whether 
Thucydides’ writing is also amoral, as some have suggested.57 This can hardly be 
the case since Thucydides’ forthright moral evaluations contribute to the substan- 
tiation of a core sense of moral decency in Thucydides himself. The very vocabu- 
lary of moral categories evinces moral (and possibly also pious) character. It 
seems plausible that a reader from his generation could understand that the pla- 
gue and Athens’ defeat in Sicily were forewarned by various forms of divine com- 
munication. Regarding the former, Thucydides allows Pericles to offer the follow- 
ing interpretation: 


[…] καὶ δι᾽ αὐτὴν οἶδ᾽ ὅτι μέρος τι μᾶλλον ἔτι μισοῦμαι, οὐ δικαίως, εἰ μὴ καὶ ὅταν 
παρὰ λόγον τι εὖ πράξητε ἐμοὶ ἀναθήσετε. φέρειν δὲ χρὴ τά τε δαιμόνια ἀναγκαίως 
τά τε ἀπὸ τῶν πολεμίων ἀνδρείως· ταῦτα γὰρ ἐν ἔθει τῇδε τῇ πόλει πρότερόν τε ἦν 
νῦν τε μὴ ἐν ὑμῖν κωλυθῇ. 


[…] And because of this [the plague], I know that I am hated even more, yet unjust- 
ly, unless you also give me credit for anything good you happen to accomplish. We 
must inevitably endure the things sent by the gods and with courage the things of 
war. For such was customary for our city in the past, so let it not be a hindrance to 
you now. (2.64.1–2). 


This seems to disaffirm the statement by Rosalind Thomas: “In placing ‘human 
nature’ at the centre of history so emphatically, he also implicitly rejected any 
idea that the divine might play a part in either individual actions, or the larger 
patterns of history.”58

Thucydides, I think, counts on his audience’s discernment in this regard. In 


sum, while Thucydides does not employ a thorough theistic hermeneutical treat- 
ment, he neither rejects a priori the reality of divine agency nor a restrained the- 
istic approach. Ironically, then, Thucydides displayed the fulfilment of Herodotus’ 
(prophetic-like) warning to Athens.59 The entire story is about a human tragedy 
and the evil that caused it, and it ironically echoes Pericles’ words: “our city as a 
whole is an education for Greece” (2.41.1). For Thucydides, divine rule was not 
absent but operated mainly behind the scenes. Whatever one makes of Thucy- 
dides’ handling of the hermeneutical dilemma, he certainly did not prohibit 
Herodotus’ theistic approach nor quench his legacy, which is patently clear in 
Xenophon, Thucydides’ immediate successor. 


Before moving on to Xenophon, a brief note is justifiable for a contemporary 


of Herodotus and Thucydides, Antiochus of Syracuse (flor. late fifth c. BCE; FGH 
555), who may have wished to complete what Herodotus did not provide con- 
cerning the history of Sicily and of Italian cities up until 424 BCE.60 His fragments 
(via Strabo) show interest in the role of the oracles in the founding (and ensuing 
disputes) of Rhegion, Kroton, Satyrion, and Taras.61 Delphi and other oracular 
centres were almost always consulted before establishing colonies, and historians 
were keen to point this out in their histories, which became an important motif in 
the historiographical tradition.62 


In the writings of Xenophon (ca. 430–354 BCE), intertextual connections to 


Herodotus’ Histories become more explicit.63 He is voluntarily indebted to 
Herodotus, in the opinion of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who comments on Xen- 
ophon’s imitation of Herodotus concerning subject matter, arrangement, and lan- 
guage (Pomp. 4). For this and other reasons, Dionysius describes Xenophon as 
Ἡροδότου ζηλωτής (“a zealous one [i.e., a follower] of Herodotus” Pomp. 4.1). 
Theologically, like Herodotus, Xenophon exemplifies the hermeneutical dilemma 
by integrating divine agency in his works, but who also may have been wishing to 
bring a corrective nuance to Herodotus’ theology via Socrates’ influence.64 Given

that there is no direct commentary on this issue, we must look at his integration 
of the divine in his own works. 


Although Xenophon’s Hellenica resumes Thucydides’ narrative on the Pelo- 


ponnesian War from 411 BCE, he prefers Herodotus’ historiographical style. In- 
stead of describing details of battles, Xenophon chooses to concentrate on the 
moral lessons one can learn from leaders within those conflicts. In the Hellenica, 
he is insistent on seeing the hand of the divine in Sparta’s fall (Hell. 5.4.1), and he 
offers a maxim about divine retribution: “Now then one could point out many 
other instances, both Greek and barbarian, in which the gods do not overlook 
those who act profanely or practise unholy things” (Hell., 5.4.1). This is also a 
common motif in Greek literature in general and historiography in particular. 
Xenophon describes ‘the god’ (ὁ θεός) as the cause for the Battle of Mantinea to be 
perceived as being won by both sides: “[…] but the god acted in such a way that 
both sides set up trophies as if they had achieved victory, and neither side prohib- 
ited those setting them up” (7.5.26). Here this dual interest in the divine is clear: 
historiography also serves to illustrate divine agency (when deemed necessary) 
to inculcate piety in audiences. This moralising didactic aspect is undeniably a 
key link with Herodotus.65 As Lisa Hau points out, divine justice is often not far 
from the picture as a “historical force,” which advocates “piety as a cardinal vir- 
tue” as seen, especially, in Herodotus, Xenophon, and Diodorus.66 


Another parallel with the Histories concerns the divine as a part of an over- 


arching story. For example, throughout the Anabasis, Xenophon frequently dis- 
plays religious rituals and divine activity, which are linked to the storyline (i.e., 
Xenophon’s perilous adventure with mercenaries from Greece to Mesopotamia 
and back).67 First, Xenophon’s part in the story (told in third person) is offered to 
the audience as an exemplary pious leader who regularly seeks divine guidance 
(via oracles and signs).68 Divine activity is highlighted through responses to Xen- 
ophon and his comrades. All this is framed by an entertaining conversation, 
which opens the work, in which Socrates reproaches Xenophon for having 
wrongly inquired at Delphi whether he should join the mercenaries going to 
Babylon (3.1.4–10). Jan Haywood aptly summarises the role of the divine in the 
Anabasis: “It is clear that the events that unfolded between 401 and 399 BCE are 
inextricably bound up with the divine. For Xenophon, the numinous is the very 
fabric of the Anabasis; it was, after all, a supra- and super-human consultation 
with Apollo and Socrates respectively that Xenophon records as the basis of his 


divine in historical causation, Xenophon has implicitly rewritten the episode as a correction 
to Herodotus’ theology: Ellis (2016) 73–91.

subsequent rôle in this now iconic voyage.”69 Xenophon is thus one of the most 
welcoming heirs and imitators of Herodotus (and of Homer) through his historio- 
graphical rhetoric and in his unequivocal mentions of the divine-human interac- 
tion as a part of unified macronarratives.70 


Ctesias of Cnidus (late fifth to early fourth cent. BCE) is far less appreciative of 
Herodotus than Xenophon. In his history of Persia (Περσικά), Ctesias takes issue 
with his forebear on numerous details regarding the Persians. Although Ctesias 
lived for some time at the Persian court, it is not certain that Herodotus ever trav- 
elled to Persia. Consequently, Ctesias calls Herodotus a λογοποιός (a fable-mon- 
ger).71 However, the fragments of Ctesias’ work lend little credibility to this un- 
warranted attack. It is also unclear from his material whether he criticises 
Herodotus for his recourse to divine agency. 


Two other fragmentary authors, Ephorus of Cyme (405–330 BCE) and 


Theopompus of Chios (378–after 320 BCE), who are known for their ‘rhetorical 
historiography’, appear more welcoming heirs to Herodotus’ legacy than Ctesias. 
No critique of the use of divine agency is perceptible. Ephorus produced a univer- 
sal history, emulating the scope of the Histories. He shows his respect to Herodo- 
tus by claiming that he did not wish to criticise Herodotus by correcting certain 
details of a particular event along with a superior moralising of it (apud Diod. 
10.24.1).72 Theopompus’ contribution to Herodotus’ legacy is the enigmatic Epito- 
me of Herodotus, which may have been “the first demonstrable epitome of an ear- 
lier work in antiquity.”73 It is understood to be a collection of excerpts from the 
Histories in two books (see T 1, fr. 1–4), either as a separate work or a part of the 
Philippica, and thus a significant testimony of Herodotus’ influence in the fourth 
century.74 Theopompus had ample opportunities for borrowing from Herodotus, 
and he shares with him multiple interests including marvels (θαυμασία, cf. Book 8 
and part of Book 9; fr. 64–84) and myth, about which he claims to have surpassed 
Herodotus and other authors (fr. 381).75 


A fitting illustration of the mixed reception of Herodotus in the fourth centu- 


ry BCE is the way Aristotle describes Herodotus. While Aristotle (384–322 BCE; 
FGH 646) – himself not a historian – describes Herodotus as a μυθολόγος (fable-

2.2.2 Hellenistic Period (323–31 BCE) 


Moving now to the early Hellenistic period, Jacoby ascribes to Herodotus the sta- 
tus of a ‘Klassiker’ of history, even if it is more difficult to ascertain direct influ- 
ence on authors of this period.79 Oswyn Murray detects a shift in intensity in the 
reception of Herodotus during this period: 


But it is the early Hellenistic writers who seem most heavily indebted to Herodotus. 
They never tire of denouncing him, and declaring his information to be unreliable. 
That was of course necessary in order to assert (often falsely) their own indepen- 
dence of his narrative, and their allegedly better sources of information: it was a 
game which had been played with equal dishonesty by Ctesias earlier.80 


Timaeus of Tauromenium (c. 340–270 BCE; ‘Timaios’ FGH 566) was one of the 
most important historians between Ephorus and Polybius.81 Thanks to several 
parallels to his great forebear, Timaeus deserves the title “the Herodotus of the 
west.”82 His interests, like Herodotus, were broad and interwoven in his now frag- 
mentary work, Sicilian History. His use of myths, religion, marvels, and paradoxa 
attracts one of Polybius’ sharpest critiques (Polyb. 12.24).83 Timaeus was also criti- 
cal of his predecessors, which earned him the epithet Epitimaeus (‘slanderer’, cf. 
Ister T 1, 11, 16). Herodotus may have been one of his targets, but this is uncer- 
tain. In any case, his integration of divine agency, as well as human-divine inter-

The fragments available from a variety of writings of Duris of Samos 


(ca. 340–270 BCE; FGH 76) appear to provide little concerning direct Herodotean 
reception. As a historian himself (e.g., the Μακεδονικά), however, his criticism of 
Ephorus and Theopompus (in the proemium of F 1) is suggestive. He claims that 
they lack μίμησις καὶ ἡδονή, that is, “a realistic and lifelike depiction with its en- 
suing pleasures.”84 This suggests he was an appreciable advocate for Herodotus’ 
style: “The fact that Duris chose a Herodotean model illustrates not only his 
predilections, but also the lasting power of the work the ‘father of history’ com- 
posed.”85 In addition, one of Duris’ works, Homeric Problems, may have included 
helpful insight on the Homeric-Herodotean interpretative link.86 


As a further corrective to modern research on Herodotean reception, Mur- 


ray shows persuasively how Herodotus had significant influence on the writings 
of Nearchus (a childhood friend of Alexander the Great), Hecataeus of Abdera 
(ca. 360–290 BCE), Megasthenes (ca. 350–290 BCE), Berossus (flor. 290 BCE), and 
Manetho (flor. 280 BCE).87 These and other historians “saw the new world of 
Alexander through Herodotean eyes, and sought to give the Herodotean tradition 
a more systematic basis.”88 


These historians will be discussed below, but, first, we consider the contribu- 


tion of Hieronymus of Cardia (born ca. 360 BCE; FGH 154; extensively referred to 
in Diod. Books 18–20). Concerning political and military history, he is certainly a 
successor of Herodotus alongside Thucydides. Noteworthy is his “political sub- 
text” in his discussion of the Nabatean Arabs (Diod. 19.94ff.), which Hornblower 
suggests was a message to his patron Antigonus Gonatas as a plea for freedom. I 
differ with Hornblower when he says that this presentational model, which could 
also advise and warn autocrats, is “not at all how Herodotus saw the purpose of 
history.”89 Perhaps he means not explicitly or directly advising, but Herodotus 
was surely doing this implicitly.90 Herodotus’ rhetorical aims do not rest on the

Hecataeus’ work on Egypt was the first under Alexander’s successors, the 


Diadochoi. He uses Herodotus extensively, even though he criticises him as unre- 
liable. His manner of organising his work became a model for ethnographical re- 
search, combining Herodotean methods with philosophical categories. It followed 
an arrangement of logical principles, one of which – it should be noted – was the 
mythical period.91 Hecataeus influenced authors such as Berossus and Manetho, 
who are particularly important for our discussion as they are ‘crossover histori- 
ans’, i.e., non-Greeks making known their peoples’ histories to a broader audi- 
ence, especially to their Greek rulers. Flavius Josephus, and to a degree also Luke 
(if he was not Greek), can be seen as doing comparable things from a similar his- 
toriographical perspective under Roman rule. Integration of the divine realm 
plays a part in the construction of the identity of a group or people. 


Herodotus remained an authority on Babylonia and Egypt, despite the criti- 


cisms of Berossus in his Βαβυλωνικά (or Χαλδαϊκά) and of Manetho in his Αἰγυ- 
πτιακά.92 These two heirs of Herodotus, namely, “Clio’s Other Sons,”93 did not hesi- 
tate to correct him when they thought he was in error. It is noteworthy that both 
these historians were priests, which again shows the link between religious ser- 
vice and history-writing.94 Josephus makes reference to both historians in Against 
Apion (1.73 and 1.129). 


Berossus, a priest of Baal in Babylon, wrote under Antiochus I of the Seleucid 


dynasty.95 No direct acquaintance with Herodotus is perceptible, but he clearly 
writes within the Greek tradition following the principles by Hecataeus of Ab- 
dera.96 Wishing to explain his people’s history to their new rulers (the Greeks), 
Berossus illustrates the significance of the distant past to ancient audiences by 
writing about their mythology (Book 1), the ten mythical kings of Babylon (Book 
2), which are followed by general history (Book 3).97 


Manetho, high priest of Heliopolis, wrote under the Ptolemaic dynasty. He 


follows Hecataean structure and philosophy, and he challenges Herodotus con- 
cerning Egyptian history (according to Josephus, Ag. Ap. 1.73 = T 7a). Manetho 
may have even produced a pamphlet Against Herodotus (cf. F 13). Manetho is a 
bit more gracious towards Herodotus, who was not acting out of malice but out of

Later in the Hellenistic period, one finds another ambiguous reception of 


Herodotus by Agatharchides (ca. 215 to after 145 BCE). He depicts Herodotus with 
still another epithet: ὁ πολυπράγμων (Diod. 1.37). This could be taken positively, 
as does Murray, “a tireless investigator,” which evinces his holistic approach to 
history, or negatively, someone who is simply “curious after knowledge” (LSJ, see 
e.g., Polyb. 9.1.4). In any case, enthusiasm for Herodotus in this period is illustrat- 
ed by the publication of a commentary (now lost) on Herodotus’ Histories by 
Aristarchus of Samothrace (ca. 217–144 BCE), head of the Library in Alexandria. 


This brief treatment of Hellenistic historians from various peoples supports 


Murray’s claim that historiographical surveys of this period often neglect 
Herodotus’ influence and are thus “seriously distorted and inadequate.”100 Again, 
what is reported above is only a minute portion of the lost texts which probably 
gave explicit attention to Herodotus or displayed his influence. Again, as for other 
periods, it is best to recognise the parallel legacies of Herodotus and Thucydides 
also in the Hellenistic period.101 One reason for an interest in political history- 
writing is due to Polybius (ca. 200–120 BCE), a political historian, who could be 
quite pedantic towards Herodotus’ line of historians. 


While Polybius writes his own history, he teaches his audience how to do it 


correctly. This makes him an excellent figure for exploring historiographical 
questions. Ironically, however, Polybius neither highlights Herodotus, nor even 
mentions him. This silence about Herodotus could be interpreted variously, as re- 
spect or indifference towards him, as he does show some grace and appreciation 
for his predecessors of long ago who wrote for moral instruction (1.1) and with 
limited resources (3.59). Yet too much of Polybius’ work is missing to come to a 
sound conclusion regarding this reticence towards his forebear. Since Polybius’ 
focus was on Rome’s ascension and with a stronger accent on political historiog- 
raphy,102 he appears more an heir of Thucydides than of Herodotus. Nevertheless, 
it would be injudicious to rule out Herodotus’ influence regarding method and 
divine agency. Hornblower is surely right: “Nobody who had thought hard about 
how to do history or geography, as Polybius certainly did, could fail to have as- 
similated Herodotus almost with his mother’s milk.”103 In fact, as with the treat-

Regarding Herodotus’ hermeneutical dilemma, the pater historiae is proba- 


bly one of Polybius’ targets when he objects to the exaggerated recourse to divine 
agency in historical discourse.105 Historians, he affirms, should avoid the popular 
usage of bringing the divine into discussion when human or natural agency is 
apparent (3.47–48; 36.17; and e.g., specifically, not Fortune (τυχή) for humanly- 
faulted shipwreck at 1.37). Yet a careful reading of Polybius militates against an 
overly rationalist reading of his approach and work. Sacred geography and exem- 
pla of piety and impiety punctuate the work (e.g., 4.20, 35, 62, 73; 5.9–12). This 
implies that he had an evaluative belief system, which is evident in his heavily 
moralising tone. For example, although his use and views of traditional myths is 
ambivalent, it is not at all always negative, which suggests a degree of acceptance 
of the activity of supra-natural forces in human history. He occasionally employs 
mythical references in his narration, and he does not reject Homer’s description 
of the Trojan War and Odysseus’ wanderings as wholly fabulous as they also con- 
tain historical facts (34.2.9–11).106 


The strongest argument for this is his understanding of world history, which 


is sustained by a repeated use of τυχή (‘Fortune’ or ‘fortune’) in reaction to hu- 
man actions (for reward 3.63 and retribution 2.20; 4.81), but even more so in a 
larger realm, the span of human history.107 So, while Polybius discourages unnec- 
essary recourse to the divine, he does recognise that greater forces cause human 
history to move forward. Despite his criticism of Timaeus’ interest and use of 
myths (12.24), he often justifies his approach and supports his narrative through 
the notion of τυχή in the sense of fortune, fate or divine providence, particularly 
for explaining the ultimate design for the emergence of Rome as a world power 
(and logically also for the decline of others, e.g., Sparta at 4.81).108 However, he

neither defines τυχή nor does he use it consistently.109 This ambiguity has con-

control (1.1.2). Indeed, it is not easy to decide which nuance (or a combination

that his ideas about it changed during the many years of redaction. Yet to reduce 
it to the last nuance seems unjustifiable, given the contexts of its usage as well as 
Polybius’ emphasis on proper behaviour to the gods. Likewise, Polybius also occa-

23.17.10 θεῶν προνοίας).112 These uses are similar to Herodotus’ divine provi-

From the discussion above, Polybius’ integration of the divine realm appears to 
follow this logic: as in human experience events happen that cannot be reduced 
to human causation, so historians mirror this reality in their writings. Polybius 
was like his contemporaries in that they recognised the existence of the gods, but 
they could only be sure of their intervention in exceptional situations.114 Polybius 
perceived divine activity in the convergence of so many factors (e.g., the death of 
several kings in the same period) allowing for the emergence of Rome. Thus, the 
‘imperial impulse’ is supported by cosmic developments. This is the intriguing 
and elusive part in history and historiography to which even Thucydides seems to 
admit, by evoking unprecedented natural phenomena preceding the Peloponne- 
sian War. Similarly, for Polybius, Rome’s emergence as a world power is extraor- 
dinary, evoking wonder, and demanding contemplation (1.1–2). It is both the 
fruit of their own military prowess (1.63.9) and of Τυχή or τυχή (1.4.2). Incidental- 
ly, but not insignificantly, he does recognise Roman piety in an important aside 
(3.112). Again, it concerns human and divine participation in a larger frame of 
world history, which of course Herodotus often fleshes out. One also notes, for 
example, the ambiguity at 3.118 where τυχή even works against Rome in singular 
events, but they still achieve world domination thanks to Τυχή. This illustrates 
well Polybius’ apparently inconsistent use of τυχή, for his understanding of histo- 
ry integrates mainly what is explainable but also what is greater than normal hu- 
man processes.115 This process – in the world and in history writing – is for Poly- 
bius rational, but it also presupposes belief in his Τυχή and τυχή, which can be 
illustrated by parts of his discussion in 1.4: 


[…] τὸ γὰρ τῆς ἡμετέρας πραγματείας ἴδιον καὶ τὸ θαυμάσιον τῶν καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς και-

(1.4.1, 4–5, Thucydides, 2009) 


First, he asserts the explicability of Roman success: “Based on these books and the 
preface in them, let it be clear to readers that they [the Romans], equipped both 
with sound reasoning and resources, pursued their purpose and its completion” 
(1.3). Then, he imitates Thucydides’ claims to unparalleled movements, divine 
and human, that demand (but surpass) rational explanation. Just as the force of 
Fortune sets in motion converging world events, so it also sets in motion and sub- 
stantiates the goal for Polybius’ project and model of universal history (which for 
him is clearly superior to local history!) for his fellow historians. For all his read- 
ers, but especially for his Greek readers, Polybius’ aim is to demonstrate that this 
historical development must be accepted, given that Τυχή is one of the primary 
causes behind it. 


Herodotus’ shadow is certainly visible here; his hermeneutical dilemma is 


not dissolved but only attenuated. The fact that Rome became the master of most 
of the oikoumenē in the space of almost fifty-three years (1.1) cannot be reduced 
to human agency alone. It is both a spectacle to be admired (θέαμα) and a lesson 
to be learnt (μάθημα) compared to other great developments (1.1.6). Furthermore, 
Polybius’ mirroring approach to human and divine/supra-natural history via his- 
toriography will receive a glorified status by Diodorus Siculus (see below). In the 
legacy of Herodotus,116 we note that Polybius’ contribution is both a political and 
moral act,117 and it is undergirded by an awareness of the divine. Appropriately, 
perhaps, Polybius concludes his Histories with a prayer for his own prosperity 
(39.19). The two levels of the prophetic voice of historiography are thus modestly 
exemplified in Polybius.118 


When considering authors from the Roman Republic period, Cicero (106–43 


BCE) should be mentioned briefly for his comments on the Herodotean legacy. 
Despite Herodotus’ ambivalent reception history up to Cicero’s times, the great 
Latin orator coined the honorific title that has crossed the centuries: pater histori- 
ae (De legibus 1.1). In the following lines, Cicero notes that Herodotus recounts a 
good number of fables, although these are not said to be concerning the divine. In 
any case, these few lines illustrate well Herodotus’ ambivalent reception history

seems to have culminated in Cicero’s famous quote. This synthesis of Herodotus’ 
conflicting reception, says Momigliano, shows how Cicero was “conforming to a 
traditional opinion about Herodotus.”119 


Moving now to Greek authors in the late Hellenistic period under Roman rule, 
Diodorus Siculus (ca. 90–ca. 30 BCE) and Dionysius of Halicarnassus (ca. 60–ca. 7 
BCE) offer some significant insight on Herodotus and his hermeneutical dilemma. 
Murray describes this period of reception thus: “Only in the late Hellenistic peri- 
od does Herodotus seem to have suffered a slight eclipse as a serious writer to be 
studied. Dionysius of Halicarnassus might praise his literary merits; but Diodorus 
did not use him; and the great majority of the references to Herodotus in Strabo 
come not from his own reading but through earlier writers, like Eratosthenes.”120 


Hornblower, however, nuances this apparent ‘eclipse’: “By the time of Dionysius 
of Halicarnassus and Livy, that is to say the time of the emperor Augustus, 
Herodotus was a classic who could be argued with on his own terms, pillaged, 
and adapted freely; it was no longer so necessary to prove one’s own indepen- 
dence by declaring Herodotus to be a fool or a liar.”121 


Similar to other authors of this epoch, Diodorus Siculus does not credit 


Herodotus explicitly (but does mention him in 10.24.1); yet he uses him either di- 
rectly or indirectly through Ephorus.122 Despite this, Diodorus is an important link 
at the turn of the first century BCE for this historiographical strand in Herodotus’ 
reception history because of his use of prophet-like language to describe histori- 
ography and his own integration of activities of the divine realm throughout his 
Bibliothēkē.123 Like other historians, he seeks to compose a universal history, 
which begins with mythological origins and ends in 60 BCE. 


Scholarly research has explored various aspects of Diodorus’ attention to the 


place of the divine in history,124 which point towards connections to elements al- 
ready treated in this survey.125 For example, Diodorus’ attention to portents, 
prophecies, and oracles provides evidence for identifying his sources.126 Echoing 
Polybius in particular, Diodorus employs τυχή to describe divine guidance in hu-

man history (e.g., 18.59), as well as other well-known nuances of this term, rang-

interest in divination as an example of the divine-human link, which figures fre- 
quently in Xenophon’s Anabasis.128 The prominence of Diodorus’ moralising ap- 
proach is well-known, and the relationship between divine justice and piety and 
impiety is arguably the most important moral theme throughout his work, as it is 
relevant to both individuals and states (cf. e.g., 8.15).129 


For these reasons, we can have a better appreciation for Diodorus’ introduc- 


tory tribute to historiography (1.1–3). It is unsurpassed in historiographical litera- 
ture, because he argues that the writing of history mirrors various operations of 
Divine Providence in human history (ἡ θεία πρόνοια, 1.1.3; cf. Herodotus’ use of 
divine providence in the realm of animals, Hist. 3.108.2). Consequently, he can 
describe history as “the prophetess of truth” and “the mother-city of philosophy” 
(1.2). In fact, it is the historian’s responsibility to explain changes in τυχή (18.59). 
History, thus, performs an important function for society by preparing “manners 
for nobility” (1.2.2) and by illustrating this life as “the guardian of the high 
achievements of illustrious men” (1.2.2). In short, Diodorus theorises like no other 
historian had done about the dual prophetic function of history-writing, which 
monumentalises divine activity – in its various general and specific manifesta- 
tions – and edifies audiences with its strong moral emphasis. 


Dionysius of Halicarnassus (born ca. 60 BCE) is highly relevant to our discus- 


sion despite the comparative lack of attention he has received in research.130 Like 
Polybius and Diodorus, Dionysius was a Greek who wrote under Roman rule, 
overlapping the Republican and Imperial periods. During the reign of Caesar Au- 
gustus, he published various treatises on rhetoric, individual orators, and letters. 
His De Thucydide is valuable for his postulations about history-writing.131 His writ- 
ings display his interest in the relationships between history, rhetoric, and aes- 
thetics. Here we focus on his twenty-volume Roman Antiquities (Ῥωμαϊκὴ ἀρχαιο- 
λογία, Books 1–10 are complete while 11–20 in excerpts), parts of which betray 
Herodotean influence. More than any other, Dionysius discussed the importance 
of Herodotus for his epoch. Being from Halicarnassus, he may have had a certain 
empathy for Herodotus and consequently been somewhat biased in his evalua- 
tion of Thucydides who, he believed, was in several ways inferior to Herodotus

Like other historians, Dionysius experienced life under foreign rule and wit- 


nessed the transformation of Roman governance, from republic to empire, hav- 
ing lived in Rome from ca. 30/29 to at least 8/7 BCE when he published Book 1 
(Ant. Rom. 1.7). But Dionysius’ approach to the ‘imperialist impulse’ is unique. 
Rather than opposing Rome’s desire for conquest, explicitly or subtly, he justifies 
it, even theologically. He is proud to be an acculturated Greek in Rome (1.7.2), and 
his message to his audience is clear as his content and style all serve to glorify the 
great Roman state, now an empire under Augustus Caesar. He appears to be a 
contented Greek in these circumstances: “Dionysius used the legends of Rome’s 
origins to demonstrate that it was really a Greek city, and his whole history is an 
erudite panegyric of Roman virtues.”134 


In this, we perceive already part of his contribution to the hermeneutical 


dilemma. He is aware of the difficulties that Greek mythology poses, which eluci- 
dates his disposition towards myths with caution (εὐλαβῶς, 2.20.2). But he also 
scolds “those who practice godless philosophies” (ὅσοι […] τὰς ἀθέους ἀσκοῦσι 
φιλοσοφίας) and “denigrating all the manifestations of the gods” (ἁπάσας διασύ- 
ροντες τὰς ἐπιφανείας τῶν θεῶν, 2.68.2). For him, Roman representation of the 
myths and their theology (θεολογία as “science of things divine”) are superior to 
the Greek mythological tradition (2.20.2). Theology and piety go hand in hand in 
his criticism of the masses, who, being ignorant of philosophy, can fall into two 
errors when interpreting the stories about the gods: to despise the gods due to 
their own misfortune or to act impiously by committing shameful deeds that are 
attributed to the gods (2.20.2). 


He is confident in his own understanding of theology (“I am acquainted as 


anyone with these matters”) – certainly not agnostic135 – and employs it unfailing- 
ly in his universal history.136 Indeed, to achieve this ambitious project, unsurpris- 
ingly, he also begins his investigation with mythical beginnings and stops at the 
first Punic War, that is, up to the point where Polybius begins his history (1.8.1– 
2).137 Interestingly, then, rather than being Polybius’ chronological continuator, 
Dionysius provides background to his predecessor’s histories, some of which is

2.2.3 Roman Imperial Period: Some Key Contemporaries of Luke 


We continue this survey of the Herodotean hermeneutical dilemma by observing 
how Cicero’s understanding of Herodotus is reflected by authors of the Roman 
Imperial period: Flavius Josephus (ca. 37–100 CE), Plutarch (ca. 50–120 CE), Arri- 
an of Nicodemia (86–160 CE), and Lucian of Samosata (born ca. 120).143 The first 
two historians are particularly valuable since Josephus came from a priestly fam- 
ily and Plutarch was a priest of Delphi. Quite naturally, both are interested in the 
role of the divine in human history.144 


Among various aims in his writings, Josephus seeks to make known Jewish 


history, religion, and culture to a broad audience in first century CE. Like Ber- 
ossus and Manetho, Josephus is a crossover historian using the Greek language

service to the Romans through his divinely-inspired dreams. He also asserts that 
he had prophesied the emergence of Emperors Vespasian and Titus (Bell. 3.400–

Writing from Rome, having been adopted by the Flavian family, another ele- 


ment worth consideration is whether he also writes history with a message for 
the rulers. Josephus uses subtle language to speak to his context and to the Ro- 
mans, because they destroyed the temple and Jerusalem, the holy city of an an- 
cient people. This may also be a warning to them, like Herodotus’ work warned 
the Athenians of their imperialist undertaking.147 


As a part of his general approach, he levels a polemic against Greek histori- 


ography as being inferior to Eastern historiography (see e.g., C. Ap. 1.1–5). To 
drive the point home, he makes a list of errant historians and caps it off with 
Herodotus. In the succession of historians who told falsehoods and were correct- 
ed one after the other – all had Herodotus as target (C. Ap. 1.3).148 Again, this type 
of negative evaluation can be misleading in exploring Herodotus’ real reception 
by historians, because Josephus also shows favourable uses of the Histories. As 
regards Herodotus’ use of divine agency, Josephus offers no specific critique. Giv- 
en his openly favourable interpretation of history through a (mono)theistic 
hermeneutic, we can conclude that he would not in principle object to recourse to 
the divine, but that he would reject Herodotus’ theology.149 On this point, his con- 
temporaries, Plutarch and Luke, would agree, as will be shown.

prosperity never stays too long in one place and what was once great is now small 
and vice versa (Hist. 1.5.4). Josephus reads then from this perspective, employing 
the Histories in his own polemics as well as correcting its alleged errors. 


While Josephus uses the Histories to support his polemic against Greek histo-

ethnographic customs. For example, concerning the custom of male circumcision 
among the eastern peoples, Herodotus was correct in that the Jews (whom 
Herodotus does not explicitly mention) were the only ones in Palestine (not the 
Phoenicians, nor the Syrians whom he does mention) who practised circumci- 
sion. Herodotus knew this, because he might have seen and reported it, thus exer- 
cising the principle of autopsy. 


In another passage (Antiquities 8.260–2), Josephus corrects Herodotus on 


two points related to the campaign of Sesostris in Palestine-Syria (Hist. 2.202–3). 
The name of the Pharaoh is wrong (it should be ‘Isok’), and this Pharaoh only 
marched against one people, not many, without resistance. Yet the biblical texts 
do not mention surrendering “without a fight” (see 1 Kgs 14:25–26 and 2 Chr 
12:9). Thus, he seems to follow Herodotus on one point, but not on another. 


Then Josephus moves on to speak of circumcision, but he misquotes Herodo-

the practice of circumcision independently of the Egyptians. The result is that 
Josephus, by attempting to practise better historiographical principles, tries to 
“‘out – Herodotus’ Herodotus.”151 In a few other occurrences, Josephus shows his 
respect for Herodotus by evoking him as an authority concerning ethnographic

read by Josephus but was respected by him as the great predecessor of historical

own table. Josephus was perhaps a reluctant heir of Herodotus, but an heir all the 
same. While discussing the intermingling of historiography and theology (i.e., the 
hermeneutical dilemma) would not have been a problem, agreeing on the theo- 
logical substance of their aggregation would have been an issue to debate. 


Similar to Ctesias, Plutarch of Chaeronea (ca. 50–after 120 CE) is on the oppo- 


site side of the reception spectrum, not in terms of divine causality but in terms of 
empathy towards Herodotus. We can imagine in him an uncomfortable presence 
at Herodotus’ table. Plutarch might even disavow any literary agnation with 
Herodotus. True, he wrote – in his words – biographies, but his writings are now 
generally recognised as a part of the Greek historiographical tradition. This 
makes Herodotus his literary forbear. Like Berossus and Manetho, Plutarch was 
also a priest (of the great oracular centre Delphi) and lived under foreign rule. 
Regarding the hermeneutical dilemma, Plutarch is intriguing. On the one hand, 
among others in our survey, he has great interest in divine influence on human 
affairs. On the other hand, Plutarch clearly has one of the greatest axes to grind 
with Herodotus. He offers him the gravest of epithets: “the father of lies.”153 This 
slanderous accusation is chiefly due to political and religious objections, as well 
as the threat that Herodotus posed to wholesome education. Herodotus mattered, 
because he was widely read and still had considerable influence. Plutarch thus 
aims to correct Herodotus’ portrayal of Greek history and theology. 


Besides the fact that Herodotus does not put the Boeotians in favourable 


light (who unlike other Greeks were allies with the Persians), the underlying his- 
toriographical critique is Plutarch’s own understanding of the purpose of history- 
writing (i.e., mainly moral instruction)154 and the role of the historian.155 Although 
Plutarch generally accepts Herodotus’ account of the Persian Wars, he tells the 
story differently, highlighting what is constructive for moral formation, that is, 
what future generations can learn from examples.156 Of course, Herodotus has his 
reasons for doing so; he shows the victories and the defeats of all, and one can 
learn from all of them. Yet Herodotus was not only “unfair” to other Greek cities, 
but he also seemed partial to Athens. In addition, for Plutarch, Herodotus also 
showed too much interest, often positive, in the barbarians; hence, his epithet 
φιλοβάρβαρος (Her. mal. 2.857a). Why show the glory of the barbarians and the 
failures of the Greeks? Plutarch’s reactions illustrate the desire by Greek and 
non-Greek historians who wanted to correct what they felt was in error in the 
Histories, especially concerning their own peoples. Their vantage point – some

More serious still was Herodotus’ religious influence on Plutarch’s genera- 


tion. Just as Homer was problematic for Greek education even several centuries 
later, so also was Herodotus.158 Plutarch’s theology, being greatly influenced by 
Platonic thought, could not accept Herodotus’ description of the gods. Plutarchan 
research – thanks especially to Brent159 – has set aside the hypothesis that, as Plu- 
tarch aged, he moved from a rational, philosophical position to a traditional view 
of the gods. Religious accounts, even so-called ‘superstitious’ ones, are found 
throughout his corpus. Also, scholars have given greater attention to the compati- 
bility of his religious and philosophical thought. Plutarch, like other contempo- 
rary authors, draws from and affirms philosophical thought based on religious 
sources.160 Platonic thought did not make him less of a believer in the gods; rath- 
er, he understood them differently, in a better light. 


This was also the core of his problem with Herodotus’ theology. John Marin- 


cola’s essay “Defending the Divine: Plutarch on the gods of Herodotus,” is highly 
informative for a particular view of the hermeneutical dilemma at the end of the 
first century CE.161 Plutarch’s de Herodoti malignitate (On the Malice of Herodotus) 
provides an example of how an ancient work such as Herodotus’ could still be 
used and critiqued some five hundred years later. In this substantial critique of 
Herodotus, Plutarch offers multiple points, and he begins with his disagreement 
concerning the divine realm. It was customary in Greek culture to give “priority 
to the divine,” that is, by dealing with divine affairs first and then human af- 
fairs.162 Despite Plutarch’s stark critique of Herodotus, both authors display per- 
ceptions of the divine realm in various ways in their works. That is what they 
have in common. In fact, Plutarch does not criticise Herodotus because he in- 
cludes the divine in his work but because he portrays it incorrectly.163 In Plu- 
tarch’s view, Herodotus is wrong for three reasons: (1) he deliberately misrepre- 
sents the nature of individual deities or heroes;164 (2) he misrepresents the true

nature of the divine in general;165 and (3) he omits significant incidents in which 
divine agency clearly assists human characters.166 Marincola points out two ele- 
ments that clarify Plutarch’s harsh critique. First, Plutarch is working with a Pla- 
tonic understanding of the divine as source of all good things and cannot be ac- 
cused – as those who practise superstition – of being the author of evil and 
misfortune. Herodotus, however, seems at ease with the idea that the divine 
realm can distribute both good and bad things as a part of a greater scheme. Sec- 
ond, Plutarch received substantial traditional material related to the Greco-Per- 
sian Wars and thus could expand on several passages where Herodotus had al- 
ready included details concerning the divine (e.g., in the descriptions of the Battle 
of Plataea, Hist. 9.61–65). Plutarch, again, is interested in passing down true 
knowledge of the divine for the sake of his audience’s moral education. Despite 
his literary qualities, Herodotus, like Homer, was an obstacle to that goal. 


In sum, Plutarch knew the power of historiography, which, since the beginn- 


ing, not only described events, people, and places, it also carried a message. It 
worked on two temporal levels simultaneously: the past of the historical repre- 
sentation and the present of the audience. This is the threat that Plutarch saw in 
the Histories. Again, Herodotus mattered some five hundred years later, not only 
for content but also for theological and moral instruction. Similar to Josephus and 
Luke, Plutarch offers alternative ways of understanding the divine realm at work 
in history. 


Finally, this survey closes with two further authors who merit our attention 


about the hermeneutical dilemma, as they generously round out the period fol- 
lowing the publication of Luke’s writings. Arrian of Nicomedia (86–160 CE) is a 
later contemporary of Luke, but he offers some noteworthy links for our survey. 
He studied under the Stoic philosopher Epictetus, and he served under the Roman 
Emperor Hadrian as legate of Cappadocia (131–137 CE). He was also at a cultural 
crossroads. Literarily, he saw himself as a second Xenophon and wished to offer 
to the world a tribute to Alexander the Great similar to what Homer had done for 
Achilles.167 Arrian thus locates himself in the line of Herodotus and those who 
were influenced by the mythopoetic tradition. While commenting on the Theban 
Dionysus and his attacks against warlike tribes, he gives an idea of how he deals 
with the hermeneutical dilemma: “But it is not right to make a minute examina- 
tion of the tales told about divine figures from long ago. For these matters are not 
trustworthy to one who composes in accordance with probability; but when one 
adds the divine element to a story, these matters do not seem wholly untrustwor-

Although not considered a historian, Lucian of Samosata is included here,

knowledge. The same is true for his treatise How to Write History. Of course, Lu- 
cian’s critique of Greek mythology is evident in his satiric dialogue between Zeus 
and Cyniscus in Zeus Catechized. Again, it is necessary to be careful with qualifi-

criticise the mythopoetic tradition or aspects of Greek religion. This was Marcel

the opposite conclusion of Caster in the analysis of the same body of evidence.171 


This reflects similar debates, mentioned above, concerning, for example, the (re- 
al) beliefs of Thucydides and Polybius. 


2.3 Conclusion: Various Theistic Views Shaping the 
Hermeneutical Dilemma of Greek Historiography 


This survey has attempted to show how the hermeneutical dilemma, which had 
passed down from the mythopoetic tradition through Herodotus to the historio- 
graphical tradition, was shaped by his successors from the fifth century BCE to 
the end of the first century CE and a little beyond. The discussion included com- 
ments and allusions concerning Herodotus’ right or wrong use of the divine 
realm in his Histories. Attention was also given to how he himself was used and 
commented upon in order to assess his significance for Greek historiography. The 
limitations to this survey were also recognised, such as the fact that most works 
of history are lost (i.e., fragmentary and missing texts), as well as the lack of spe- 
cific credit given to Herodotus and unfair criticism of his pioneering work. I now 
highlight some of the key elements that emerged within the Greek historiographi- 
cal tradition, including Greek and non-Greek authors who extended their histori- 
cal contributions to Greek-speaking audiences. It has been noted that the influ-

ence of Hellenistic culture over a vast area after Alexander’s death allowed for 
greater participation by non-Greeks in the development of historiography. 


First, concerning the historiographical line, from Herodotus to Arrian, the 


divine realm was consistently incorporated into explanations of both distant and 
recent past events. This appears to have been a given for Greek historians and 
their various cultural contexts. There are two main criticisms levelled at Herodo- 
tus. In the transition from mythology to historiography, Herodotus did not go far 
enough to demythologise the distant past, and he also misrepresented the charac- 
ter of the gods/divine. But these points do not lead to a censorship about the di- 
vine realm, a kind of imposed secularism. The notion that the historiographical 
record moves from traditional pious thinking to a more rationalising neutral 
hermeneutic can be discarded. No steady progression of demythologisation is 
perceptible within the Herodotean legacy from Thucydides to Arrian.172 


While recognising the flourishing intellectual milieu of the fifth century BCE, 


it is plausible to set aside the notion that there was a fifth-century Enlightenment 
that succeeded in replacing Herodotus’ polytheistic worldview of which the His- 
tories is evidence.173 In other words, although he shared many interests with the 
Sophists and other intellectuals of his time, this influence did not destabilise his 
theological worldview. If the ancients did not criticise him for his belief in the 
gods, it seems defensible to discard the position that considers Herodotus as a 
kind of rationalist sophist. On the contrary, I extend Harrison’s argument that 
theological thinking was a part of historiography from the beginning by showing 
that this feature continued throughout the first five hundred years.174 We can 
therefore assume then that the inclusion of the divine resonated with audiences 
in antiquity. This historiographical strand was important to the authors and their 
audiences, who expected to find it in historical works. History writing always 
contained theological and religious elements reflecting the interplay between the 
vertical and horizontal axes of the divine and the human. Historians described 
what they perceived as reality for the edification of their audiences (cf. Diodorus’ 
praise of historiography). 


Second, the historiographical record reveals significant differences in the 


perception of what ‘divine’ means, both within Greek theological expression, 
such as between Herodotus and Plutarch, and even more so between Herodotus 
and Josephus, and later with Luke. But, again, Greek historiography has always 
had recourse to the divine, however one might have understood the divine realm. 
This means that various theistic views of the world and its history circulated and 
shaped the way audiences understood the role of the divine in distant and recent 
history for their own peoples but also for the cosmos as a whole. A problematic

issue that resurfaces at various points is the validity of the distant past as a part of 
historiographical rhetoric. Many historians include mythological origins (e.g., in 
divine plupast sections) to anchor their core narratives. Although in some cases it 
is impossible to ascertain the historical value that they ascribe to these stories of 
the distant past, it is nonetheless an element that runs through the historiographi- 
cal record. Herodotus was certainly not alone in this approach. 


Third, there are differences in the intensity or use of the divine. A spectrum 


ranges from intense integration of the divine, such as in Herodotus, Xenophon, 
Theopompus, Josephus, and Plutarch to weaker expressions such as in Thucy- 
dides and Polybius. Again, the question is not how often one finds words refer- 
ring to the divine or divine figures, but how they are integrated, narratologically, 
in the overall story (macro-level) and in individual scenes (micro-level). Writers 
who include both elements with greater frequency show a stronger theistic ex- 
pression, and, thus, a stronger prophetic-like voice. 


Fourth, like other literary genres, theological thought could also permeate 


historiography and contribute to the way people understood the divine and its 
influence on human history. It is an integral part of the moral component of his- 
toriography – especially with regard to the pairs ‘piety and impiety’ and ‘recom- 
pense and retribution’ – and thus plays a part in the service historians rendered 
to societies. Namely, the divine was integrated – as audiences would have expect- 
ed – into the moral fabric of historical discourse. 


Fifth, historiography can be viewed as an expression of ancient piety. 


Whether this is intentional or accidental is not always easy to ascertain. Narrative 
asides, the integration of divine activity, as well as negative and positive exempla 
help to construct an assessment of a historian’s degree of intentionality. Since the 
ancients expressed their belief, trust, and hope in the divine realm in various 
ways (e.g., sacrifices, monuments, prayers and hymns for recognition of divine 
assistance), writing history that acknowledges divine activity – whether favour- 
able assistance or retribution – can also be considered as a material form of an- 
cient piety.175 We have seen what ancient sources reveal about Herodotus’ theo- 
logical legacy. His successors do not raise the question whether Herodotus 
believed in divine agency. Nor do they describe him as a rationalist sophist or a 
sceptical scholar. Plutarch, however, criticises Herodotus for not accurately de- 
scribing the true nature of the gods. For him, the Histories is not a work of piety 
but of irreverence, and readers should not be deceived, because Herodotus teach- 
es false ideas about the gods. This critique from a priest-historian at the end of the 
first century CE confirms how the writing of history could be perceived as bear- 
ing positive or negative influence on readers, just as Homer’s works were per- 


175 
On general beliefs about divine activity as evidenced in Greek literature, see Harrison (2007) 
371–384.

ceived. This reinforces the link between theology and history in ancient historiog- 
raphy and its moral role for society. 


Sixth, by integrating the divine to explain past events, whether distant or re- 


cent, historians also addressed contemporary issues facing peoples and individu- 
als in their own times. In exercising this theological interpretation, proclamation, 
and application of the past, it can be said that historians could play a prophet-like 
role for their respective societies. In this way, they both honour the divine – in its 
various general and specific manifestations – and edify their audiences with a 
moral emphasis. For example, historians living under oppressive regimes might 
use various, often subtle, rhetorical devices to warn oppressors or to encourage 
the oppressed. Conversely, claims of divine intervention are often used to subs- 
tantiate the founding of cities or even to justify a global regime such as the Roman 
Empire (e.g., by Dionysius). The extent to which a historian exercises a prophet- 
like function can be measured by examining his context, his aims, and the rhetor- 
ical devices he uses to achieve them. The nine elements that distinguish this 
strand of historiography were introduced in Chapter 1 and will be the subject of 
Chapter 3 (section 3.4). 


Finally, we now move on to a consideration of the theological, not just histo- 


riographical, connection between Herodotus and Luke. Based on this survey, it is 
unwarranted to set a rift between Herodotus and his successors and Luke based 
on theological grounds. Some have suggested as much. For example, Daniel Mar- 
guerat understands Greek history to be more rational than biblical historiogra- 
phy: 


Luc se situe à l’exact confluent des courants historiographiques juif et grec. Ses 
procédés narratifs sont largement empruntés à ce qui constituait le standard 
culturel dans l’Empire romain, à savoir l’histoire telle que l’écrivent les Grecs. Mais 
à l’opposé de l’idéal d’objectivité de l’historiographie hérodotéenne et thucydi- 
dienne, Luc raconte une histoire confessante.176 


This is where the hermeneutical dilemma comes to the fore. The comparison is 
problematic for several reasons. How objective was the Greek historiographical 
tradition? Are objectivity and belief in divine agency in conflict? Were Herodotus 
and Thucydides more objective because they were – if they were – less confes- 
sional? In Marguerat’s definition, they appear to be ‘unconfessional’ and conse- 
quently more objective. Luke, on the other hand, is described as confessional, in- 
terested only in divine agency, and therefore distanced from his Greek 
historiographical predecessors: 


176

precisely at the meeting point of Jewish and Greek historiographical currents. His narrative

the Greeks wrote it. However, contrary to the ideal of objectivity found in Herodean [sic] and

La recherche de causalité qui anime la quête historienne gréco-romaine est chez

But several Greek historians often show the divine realm working behind or in 
collaboration with human agency, especially those with a strong prophetic voice 
such as Herodotus, Xenophon, Diodorus, Josephus, and Plutarch. 


Steve Walton follows Marguerat’s interpretation: “Luke is located at the 


crossroads of Jewish and Greek historiography, sharing features with both. How- 
ever, he writes a confessional history, so Acts is not pure Greek history (which 
valued objectivity). Luke shares the quest for causes in Greek historiography but 
admits divine causes as primary.”178 In the light of the above historiographical 
overview, these assessments are also erroneous for a few reasons. No “pure 
Greek history” ever existed, and, to use Marguerat’s expression, ‘confessional his- 
tories’ are present from the beginning, if one means that some aspect of ‘confes- 
sion’ or theistic framework contributes to historical discourse. 


This drives an unnecessary wedge between Greek, Jewish, and Christian his- 


toriographies. Luke can therefore find a place at Herodotus’ table, because theo- 
logical thinking was a part of Greek historiography from the beginning, expressed 
through various theistic frameworks. In sum, Herodotus’ theological legacy 
waxed and waned, but it was never extinguished. Herodotus remains one of the 
greatest representatives of this historiographical strand for two reasons: (1) his 
pioneering work as a link between the mythopoetic tradition and prose history 
and (2) his narratological integration of the divine in the description of the global 
geopolitical conflict of the Persian Wars and for an audience that also faced the 
‘imperialist impulse’ of Athens. From this point of view, Herodotus exemplifies 
the prophetic voice of historiography that was imitated by his successors. Not 
only that, but above all, he also sets the precedent for what historiography had 
become and still is. 


We now turn to the final part of the preliminary discussion of this study in 


which I elaborate on the meaning and utility of the ‘prophetic voice’ of Greek his- 
toriography, which was cursorily introduced in Chapter 1. Together, these three 
chapters provide a methodological basis for the investigation of the lives and 
works of Herodotus and Luke or any historian of antiquity.

3 The Prophet-like Voice of Historiography: 
Writing the Divine as One’s Audience Expects 


“He is neither bard nor soothsayer but between the two; he is Herodotus.” 
(Hartog 2000, 395) 


3.1 Introduction 


The Greek historiographical tradition provides ample evidence for the juncture of 
historical and theological reflection performed through prose narrative. Indeed, 
temporally, Greek historiography never ceased to be theological, and, geographi- 
cally, it extended on a global level through the spread of the Greek language. This 
facilitated an encounter with traditions displaying other theistic expressions in 
historiography. Like Herodotus, Greek and non-Greek historians responded to the 
hermeneutical dilemma by employing various narrative devices to integrate per- 
ceptions of the divine realm, to varying degrees of intensity, both in the global 
narrative structure (macronarrative) and in its constituent smaller narrative 
units (micronarratives). The historiographical record, then, displays theistic con- 
tinuity, interest, and mutual influence rather than rupture, indifference, and 
rhetorical failure. The survey in Chapter 2 has contended that the issue was not 
necessarily whether the divine realm should be reflected in historiography but 
how perceptions of the divine realm should be integrated rhetorically and theo- 
logically. The combination of the two provides a framework for understanding 
them as having a prophet-like function for their respective audiences. This ele- 
ment is the subject of the present chapter. 


As the final chapter of the methodological section, prior to the parallel study of 


Herodotus and Luke, the discussion here seeks to respond to the issue above by elu- 
cidating the meaning of ‘prophetic voice’ as an integral part of responding to audi- 
ences’ expectations.1 The question is first framed by exploring the value of the nar- 
rative rhetoric of historiography, focusing on audience expectations within the 
rhetorical triad of author, text, and audience.2 Second, I discuss the expressions 
‘prophetic history’ and ‘prophetic historiography’ in Jewish and Christian studies 


1 
Hans Robert Jauss (1970, 7) explains the social function as a missing element in literary theo-

and show how they may be applied profitably to Greek historiography as a part of 
the audiences’ expectations. Finally, the historiographical time frame explored here 
(fifth century BCE to first century CE) calls for a methodology that takes into con- 
sideration the intermingling of cultural activities, in public and private venues, such 
as historical discourse, theological reflection, and storytelling. To this end, I propose 
that ‘prophetic voice’ brings these elements together as a constructive tool for theo- 
logical and narratological analysis of perceptions of the divine in works of history. 
The discussion provides a list of rhetorical features to look for in this prophetic-like 
voice whose rhetorical force can contribute to an audience’s experience and forma- 
tion. As such, the analysis of historians’ prophetic voices can be a valuable tool 
especially for this network of disciplines: historiography, hermeneutics, theology/ 
religion/ethics in antiquity, and narratology.3 


3.2 The Rhetorical Aspect of Historiography: 


An Author-Audience Complicity 


Narrative theory and why historiography matters. In classical and biblical scholar- 
ship, the questions of literary genre in general and historiography in particular 
continue to enjoy considerable attention.4 As regards ancient historiography, 
among other literary genres,5 it may be categorised as an interconnected but dis- 
tinct “recurrent literary form.”6 In addition, scholars recognise the variety of his- 
toriographical expression, such as local histories, ethnographies, biographies, and 
extensive socio-political histories.7 Despite their differences in content and form, 
they all share an implied interest from audiences. In antiquity, history-writing en- 
joyed – and it still enjoys – a unique appeal as a literary genre. To know the past 
matters; hence, historiography also matters. Herodotus, Thucydides, Polybius, 
and Diodorus (inter alii) proclaim this in their own terms.8 That the rhetorical as- 
pect was intrinsically significant in history-writing may be viewed in the very de- 
scription of genre from an audience’s perspective. Nino Luraghi’s definition of 
‘genre’ illustrates this well: “a set of historically and culturally specific expecta- 
tions with which an audience approaches a text.”9 


3 
Ethics has its rightful place here as a significant element of historiography, which is ethical 
formation or ‘moral history’: “a narrative of historical events that presents them in a moral 
light and aims to draw moral lessons from them.” Hau (2016) 72.
