For a better understanding of this literary reality, narratology has made a sig- 


nificant contribution to historical and biblical research.10 Essentially, storytelling 
matters, because it responds to a human need for narrative: “As accounts of what 
happened to particular people in particular circumstances and with specific conse- 
quences, stories have come to be viewed as a basic human strategy for coming to 
terms with time, process, and change […]”.11 Individuals, families, colonies, and peo- 
ples wanted to make sense of their existence, and they needed someone to do the 
hard work of gathering, organising, and telling the story. For example, Herodotus’ 
understanding of historiē is illustrated by his first presentation of divergent stories 
(Hist. 1.5), about which Carolyn Dewald observes: “[…] everything told about the 
past is in fact tendentious, and is merely the version that the person telling it wants 
you to hear. That is why one needs historiē, or investigation, to help decode a story 
and sift the wheat from the chaff.”12 In effect, a representation of the past has the 
force of ‘normalisation’, which consists of “bringing a collection of events into nar- 
rative coherence […] It renders them plausible, allowing one to see how they all 
‘belong’.”13 Narrative then has the capability of responding to this human need for 
understanding. It is thus an interpretative process – a complex and creative activity 
– in view of providing some service for an intended audience. It is a way of “pro- 
cessing the past” for an audience’s present needs, because people long to see how 
they belong to their own society and to the broader world.14 


Aristotle, mythos, and audience reception. Aristotle considered this type of reflec- 
tion important, as attested by his Poetics, one of the first theoretical treatments 
about what makes theatre (and thus also literature) successful. Essentially, his 
discussion explores how theatrical productions can elicit emotions in spectators. 
Various examples of good and bad techniques are provided. But even Aristotle’s 
well-known (and debatable) argument that poetry (i.e., the composition of fic- 
tional stories) is superior to history implies this potential value for the consumers 
of theatrical production. He describes it this way, helpfully using Herodotus as an 
example: 


ὁ γὰρ ἱστορικὸς καὶ ὁ ποιητὴς οὐ τῷ ἢ ἔμμετρα λέγειν ἢ ἄμετρα διαφέρουσιν· εἴη 
γὰρ ἂν τὰ Ἡροδότου εἰς μέτρα τεθῆναι καὶ οὐδὲν ἧττον ἂν εἴη ἱστορία τις μετὰ 
μέτρου ἢ ἄνευ μέτρων· ἀλλὰ τούτῳ διαφέρει, τῷ τὸν μὲν τὰ γενόμενα λέγειν, τὸν δὲ 
οἷα ἂν γένοιτο. διὸ καὶ φιλοσοφώτερον καὶ σπουδαιότερον ποίησις ἱστορίας ἐστίν· 
ἡ μὲν γὰρ ποίησις μᾶλλον τὰ καθόλου, ἡ δ᾿ ἱστορία τὰ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον λέγει […].

The difference between the historian and the poet is not that between using verse 
or prose; Herodotus’ work could be versified and would be just as much a kind of 
history in verse as in prose. No, the difference is this: that the one relates actual 
events, the other the kinds of things that might occur. Consequently, poetry is more 
philosophical and more elevated than history, since poetry relates more of the uni- 
versal, while history relates particulars […]. (1451b, trans. Halliwell, LCL 199) 


For Aristotle, poetry has greater value than history because of what it can pro- 
duce for and in audiences due to its philosophical value. Of course, the attraction 
of factual history is that it proposes to explore events and their consequences.15 


Narratively, then, it distinguishes itself regarding the question of pragmatics as 
“the rhetoric of the real,”16 having the potential, like fictional narrative, to elicit 
emotions as well as lasting effects.17 In sum, both fictional and factual-based myth- 
oi (i.e., ‘intrigues’ or ‘plots’) can coexist in society, as Aristotle points out, seeking 
to produce emotions during the reception phase and to facilitate the assimilation 
of moral teaching.18 


One may question Aristotle’s view about poetry being superior to history, 


but he appears to have intuited this vital notion in narrative theory, which is the 
central role of mythos in fictional and non-fictional works.19 The link between the 
story and the audience is the intrigue (or plot). For this reason, mythos should not 
be reduced to a mere story structure, sequence of events, or causal network. Rath- 
er, it is better located within the reception itself, as that which drives the recep- 
tion forward, the audience’s expectations and questions that may develop and 
change as the story progresses, adding to their desire for narrative closure. For 
this reason, the theory of historical and fictional storytelling has learned to give 
greater room to the audience’s participation – to keep them in the equation – to 
consider how narratives respond to audiences’ expectations.20 This includes the

sometimes do not get all their facts straight. But a basic understanding between writers and

time-honoured devices such as curiosity and suspense, as well as surprise via in- 
novative features.21 Historiography is no exception to this general rule. 


Emplotment, plot, and explotment. To flesh out how history can elicit emotions but 
also take part in the audience’s moral formation, three complementary terms 
help to visualise a narrative’s journey: emplotment, plot, and explotment. I sum- 
marise here my discussion of them elsewhere.22 In similar ways, Hayden White’s 
‘emplotment’ and Paul Ricoeur’s mise en intrigue call attention to the fact that his- 
toriography’s ‘making sense of the past’ is only one way of depicting events, time, 
and people.23 This process involves making choices as to content, order, and rep- 
resentation, which are evident in the opening lines of the Histories.24 The attrac- 
tive thing about history-writing as narrative is that it seeks to make sense of the 
past for a particular group of readers. In the end, the produced ‘history’ will be- 
come a unique performance for them. This leads to the process of literary engage- 
ment, the intrigue, the interplay between text and audience. 


Second, the intrigue is latent in this textual performance and must be acti- 


vated by audiences. They must turn the pages and explore the questions, result- 
ing in a cognitive, ethical, temporal, and experiential narrative journey. Audi- 
ences encounter events, people, and questions about them. But it is not restricted 
to an informational encounter, since historical representation includes “moral 
and ideological valences” instilled by historians.25 These features then become ex- 
istential links between historians, the explored time periods, their histories, and 
their readers. This rhetorical ‘moralising’ aspect was an integral part of ancient 
historiography from the beginning, as cogently argued by Lisa Irene Hau in her 
book Moral History from Herodotus to Diodorus Siculus and summarised here: 
“Moralising in historiography was not an isolated genre feature, then, but was 
part of what connected historiography with its society, a way of creating a fellow- 
feeling between author and reader by placing them in a common world of well- 
known and generally accepted values.”26 


The third part of a narrative’s journey, ‘explotment’, is what all historians 


hope for: acceptance and assimilation of their histories in their audience’s histor- 
ical consciousness. Their emplotment expects an explotment. Audiences are invit-

In sum, since Aristotle’s times, genres have evolved and others have been born, 
but an element that has not changed is that readers, listeners, and spectators 
have been, formally and informally, trained to distinguish between literary gen- 
res and to adjust their expectations accordingly. They may pose dreaded ques-

of history is that the history’s content reflects the real world. See Anderson (2014): “We’re 
changed not only by lived experience but also by read experience – by the books that we’ve

tions to any storyteller such as ‘So what?’ and ‘What difference does it make?’28 


Whether a comic book, a daily paper, or Xenophon’s Hellenica, all literature has 
the power to shape our thinking and way of living. Consequently, this raises ques- 
tions about historiography’s narratological and rhetorical value, what it does, 
how it performs, and to what ends. 


Why Herodotus matters for this question. This question may not appear necessary 
for Classicists, but it is useful to address it here for other readers. Herodotus nev- 
er pauses his narration to spell out his views on the usefulness of history-writing. 
It appears to be understood by his audience. Polybius, however, does this often 
(e.g., 8.2.1–11). Herodotus’ preface evokes the importance of preserving the mem- 
ory of great and marvellous deeds and of explaining historical causes, especially 
concerning the conflict between the Greeks and the barbarians (Hist. Proem).29 


These commemorative and encomiastic functions served to honour people wor- 
thy of esteem and inspire audiences to emulate them, as well as to be amazed at 
the great diversity of humanity.30 


These and other elements in the Histories have captured scholarly attention 


concerning Herodotus’ attempt to meet certain audience expectations. Charles 
Fornara, for example, argued convincingly that Herodotus produced a moral and 
didactic composition.31 Beyond the informational wealth of the Histories, one per- 
ceives therein Herodotus’ effort to drive home certain attitudes, mindsets, even 
messages, to his contemporaries. Often this narrative strategy is not overt, but 
various macronarrative elements and rhetorical devices underline these overall 
aims.32 What makes Herodotus’ Histories a great read, millennia later, is his abili- 
ty to involve audiences in his own research and questions and link them together 
through the main thread of an intercontinental struggle for power. Audiences’ ex- 
ploration of questions that seek resolution is what drives the narrative and its 
reception (i.e., its unique intrigue).33 In this regard, John Marincola, while recog- 
nising continuity between the poetic tradition and prose historiography, de- 
scribes the rhetorical import of Herodotus’ approach:

Herodotus says at the outset that his work is the result of his research (historiē), his 
human attempt to understand the world in all its particularity, and he displays 
throughout a willingness to reveal to his audience the fractured and incomplete na- 
ture of his own knowledge. In accepting this imperfect truth with all its gaps, suppo- 
sitions, and best guesses, Herodotus may be said to inaugurate a new method of 
learning and understanding.34 


This implied complicity between Herodotus and his audience is noteworthy. Rath- 
er than an abrupt rupture with his literary heritage, Herodotus integrated vari- 
ous types of literary forms in his Histories35 with the aim of investigating the past 
with and for his readers.36 His legacy illustrates well how there has always been a 
complicity between producers and consumers of historiography. It responds to a 
fundamental human need to understand life through narrative. As Lachenaud 
acutely states, historiography places “humanity between the past and the fu- 
ture.”37 Audiences allow themselves to be placed in this (potentially vulnerable) 
position and expect this performative act from their historians, however painful 
their re-enactments may be. Cognitive, experiential, and emotional facets are thus 
interwoven.38 Historiography is intrinsically rhetorical in its production and re- 
ception, precisely because some degree of explotment is expected. 


Given this strong moral and didactic element in Greek historiography, ques- 


tions worth asking are how theistic discourse facilitated and supported these au- 
dience-centred objectives, how historians sought to respond to their audiences’ 
expectations and, more strongly, to respond to some of their existential concerns. 
The prophetic voice, as will be further contended, interprets the past and speaks 
to their present, including perceptions of the divine as a valid part of the intrigue. 
We now consider how scholars have used ‘prophecy’ and ‘prophetic’ in relation 
to Jewish and Christian historiography and whether this could be constructive in 
the study of Greek historiography.

3.3 ‘Prophetic history’, ‘Prophetic historiography’ 


or ‘Prophetic voice’? 


Various expressions have been used to describe texts that include divine-human 
interaction in ancient narratives: heroic historiography,39 theological historiogra- 
phy,40 sacred or divine history,41 apologetic historiography,42 revealed history,43 


kerygmatic history,44 and, later, also hagiography.45 Each expression has its own 
focus, nuances, and limits. They are not necessarily in conflict with one another 
nor with the meaning of a prophetic role in historiography. These are all exam- 
ples of ideological literature in that a specific worldview is assumed and at times 
explicitly evoked or contended. The expressions ‘prophetic history’ and ‘prophet- 
ic historiography’ have not been used in the field of classical research (if biblical 
studies are excluded), but they are employed in biblical research. The latter 
seems quite normal, given the nature of Jewish historiography with its conver- 
gence of prophets and historical writings. We will first look at their uses in re- 
search on Jewish and Christian literature and then explore the links with the 
Greek historiographical tradition via the expression ‘prophetic voice’. 


Jewish historiography and prophetic expressions. In research on the Hebrew Bible, 
the connection between prophets and history-writing is obviously not a recent de- 
velopment. One could even say that this is part of the DNA of Jewish historiogra- 
phy. For example, Jewish tradition attributes the title of ‘former prophets’ (נביאים 
ראשונים 
nevi’im rishonim) to a block of narratives often called the ‘historical books’ 


(Joshua, Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel, and 1 and 2 Kings). In addition, Josephus made 
the claim that only prophets could write history, and this was, in part, thanks to 
divine inspiration.46 


In line with these historical references linking prophets to history-writing, 


David Petersen proposes the expression ‘prophetic historiography’ as one of sev- 
eral literary forms within prophetic prose accounts (distinct from prophetic 
forms of ‘poetic speech’). He defines the term then, not necessarily as a complete 
macronarrative, but as a literary form: “Prophetic historiography is a prose liter- 
ature that recounts events in the world of public affairs and the ways in which

Israel’s historical and moral consciousness and the claim to divine inspiration in 
relation to written historical narratives. 


Another substantial example of prophetic historiography is the book of 


Chronicles (in two volumes). Although Scott Hahn does not define the term specif- 
ically, he uses ‘prophetic historiography’ throughout his article to describe how 
the Chronicler retold the covenantal history between God and Israel.50 In Jewish 
tradition, the Chronicles evince zakhor, that is, a remembrance of this divinely 
established relationship. The Chronicler’s fusion of history and prophecy is “char- 
acterized by the author’s profound assimilation and interpretation of the 
covenantal and liturgical worldview of the Hebrew Bible.”51 Chronicles can be 
rightly considered haggadic, or homiletic, in that its purpose goes beyond the 
mere communication of historical information. Rather, these texts are intended 
to lead audiences to attentive reflection on their own part in this sacred history.52

Christian historiography and prophetic expressions. In the study of Christian histo- 
riography, in light of Jewish literature and history, scholars have also employed 
‘prophetic historiography’ and ‘prophetic history’. This also appears quite 
straightforward given that, for example, all four canonical gospels assume and 
show continuity between Israel’s history and Jesus’ life and movement in which 
prophets and prophetic writings are integrated. Jesus was of course Jewish and 
understood by the evangelists as being the heir to the throne of King David (e.g., 
Mark 11:10; Matt 21:9; Luke 1:32; John 7:42). To support this, very early in their 
narratives, the evangelists (here in the example of Luke’s Gospel) bring in the 
figure of John the Baptist as “prophet of the Most High” (Luke 1:76) and precursor 
of Jesus (Luke 1:17, 76). Jesus is also closely associated with the Jewish prophetic 
line, not only through John the Baptist (“in the spirit and power of Elijah” Luke 
1:17), but also through other contemporary expressions of prophetic activity 
(Luke, chap. 1 and 2), and through Israel’s earlier prophets, those who wrote and 
those who did not (e.g., Elijah and Elisha).53 


To explore the expressions ‘prophetic historiography’ and ‘prophetic histo- 


ry’, we focus here on the reflections of two scholars, Robert Hall and Gregory 
Sterling, who both consider Josephus a key parallel for studying Luke’s writings 
within the Hellenised Jewish milieu. Robert Hall’s book, Revealed Histories: Tech- 
niques for Ancient Jewish and Christian Historiography, provides useful defini- 
tions and nuances of ‘revealed history’, and applies them to several Jewish and 
Christian writings.54 He uses various terms interchangeably,55 but the term that 
most directly concerns our discussion is ‘prophetic history’, which he qualifies as 
‘interpretative’ and ‘inspired’:

retained. Prophetic histories which relate events experienced by the historian but 
interpreted by revelation will be called interpretative prophetic histories. Prophet-

nistic, and do not reflect sufficiently Luke’s understanding of the identity of Jesus’ 
movement as a part of the Jewish social and theological world. Compared to 
Hall’s definitions, Sterling’s use of ‘prophetic history’ raises the question whether 
a historiographical writing can be considered prophetic even when the author 
does not identify himself specifically as a prophet or within a prophetic line. But, 
in most cases, individuals who exercise a prophetic function are called ‘prophets’ 
by the narrators.64 This also raises the question of whether the Greek historio- 
graphical line can be understood as displaying prophetic-like characteristics. 
Strictly speaking, ‘prophetic history’ and ‘prophetic historiography’ can be used 
to describe a particular subgenre of historiography or a literary form in relation 
to people who are the subjects of historical discourse or who composed historical 
texts, such as prophets, seers, diviners, as well as priests and scribes. In a broader 
sense, then, given this discussion and Chapters 1 and 2, other types of individuals 
also played prophet-like roles in society that contributed to the development of 
ancient Greek historiography. We will now examine more closely this broader 
function, the ‘prophetic voice’, in the Greek historiographical tradition. 


Historiographical ‘prophetic voices’ in the Greek tradition. Except for the role of 
priests (e.g., Berossus, Manetho, and Plutarch), historians of antiquity generally 
do not present themselves as exercising one of the above societal roles. Their 
works, however, invite their audiences to explore the world through various the- 
istic perspectives. Herodotus never claims to have performed his investigation 
through mystical inspiration. He also does not refer to himself as a prophet, a 
seer, or by any other religious expression. He does, however, interpret history via 
various perceptions of divinely connected acts and speech for his audience.65 His 
sources provided this information, and he performed the act of interpretation 
upon them. According to the historiographical record, his successors do some- 
thing similar, again without claiming a prophetic status in society. I contend then 
that Greek historiography is implicitly prophetic, whereby historians exercise a 
prophet-like interpretative role for their readers, without calling themselves or 
being called prophets (or by another mediatory expression) in the traditional 
sense. Rather, it concerns a historiographical function, similar to that of a ἑρμη- 
νεύς, as interpreters and expositors of human history through theistic lenses. 


If ‘prophetic’ may seem unsuitable to describe an element of history-writing 


in the Greek tradition, a point that may be overlooked – especially by biblical 
scholars – is that the Greeks had their own widespread traditions of human inter- 
mediaries claiming the ability to impart divine communication (e.g., προφήτης,

tion so as to make it conform to their own authorial voice and the needs of their 
story. And so they are not a mirror that exactly reflects the practices of divination 
and the personae of seers; yet they do refract attitudes and methods that must 
have had resonance for their audiences. This interplay between representation 
and reality is subtle and not always easy for us to analyze.67 


Flower rightly signals the narrative and theological role of narrators for their au- 
diences. The presence of this prophet-like activity in a variety of literature pre- 
supposes knowledge and expectations of it by audiences throughout the Mediter- 
ranean basin and the Near East. It was simply a part of life in various domains. 
The study of Greek historiography must also take into consideration this holistic 
perspective in societies which resisted strict compartmentalisation of religious 
expression, as J.-P. Vernant concisely states, “La religion grecque, c’est un do- 
maine où le chercheur est obligé de ‘penser ensemble’ le religieux et le politique, 
l’anthropologie et l’histoire, la morale et la vie quotidienne.”68 


Of course, prophetic activity was practised in different ways in the ancient 


world, and here the extensive comparative research of Martti Nissinen is particu- 
larly instructive. Through comparative studies on prophets and prophecy in an- 
tiquity, Nissinen proposes this broad definition of ‘prophet’: “as someone who in- 
termediates allegedly divine knowledge by non-technical means.”69 In this regard, 
several general components allow for common ground and comparative research 
of prophecy in various fields.70 The point of this definition is to illustrate the com- 
mon social activity, throughout the Mediterranean basin, of human mediation of 
knowledge about the divine realm (being and activity) to human recipients. We

are not arguing here that all Greek historians performed the work of prophets, 
seers, or diviners in various cultures.71 Some of them may have done so. But the 
notion of ‘prophetic voice’, used in the present study, serves to compare histori- 
ans to prophets as intermediaries of perceptions of divine being or activity based 
on their deduction of natural and historical developments as well as received 
knowledge of oracles, signs, omens, etc., which, together, influence their interpre- 
tation and description of singular events or the overall story to their audiences.72 


The intention is not to relativise the rhetorical potential of historical transmission 
of knowledge of divine being or activity, but only to distinguish it from the recog- 
nised societal roles of prophets, seers, and diviners. 


As regards historiographical research, then, we return to the question of the 


rhetorical force of historiography in order to explore this prophetic-like function. 
First, it is helpful to recall what historiography has in common with other literary 
forms within social life. Hans Robert Jauss has concisely described this as the 
‘horizon of expectations’. Literature, in particular history, preserves real experi- 
ences, but it “also anticipates unrealized possibilities, widens the limited range of 
social behavior by new wishes, demands, and goals, and thereby opens avenues 
for future experience.”73 History opens new understandings for the audiences’ 
past, present, and future. Various trajectories can be imagined, hoped for, and 
perhaps even averted. Historiography with a prophetic voice brings an additional 
dimension to this situation. The idea of greater forces guiding history, and the po- 
tential for human beings working with or against these forces in shaping future 
outcomes, offers readers an intriguing perspective. 


For sure, Greek historiography does not work with the covenant relationship 


(i.e., between God and a people) understood by Jewish and Christian historiogra- 
phy, but it does reveal the Greeks’ (and other peoples’) perception of the enduring 
presence of the divine in history. Some general principles can be extracted from 
that realm. For example, by hearing or reading history, audiences learn that cer- 
tain actions enhance the probability of a better life under the rule of the divine, 
while others most likely diminish it. Audience expectations mirror social life 
which displays an amalgam of practical concerns, ethics, historical consciousness, 
as well as a (conscious or unconscious) worldview or theology. The prophetic 
voices of historians speak to those expectations, seeking to inform, educate, and 
shape their values. We see then the social relevance of this prophet-like role, re-

turning again to Jauss: “From the point of view of the aesthetics of reception its 
social function in the ethical realm is equally to be understood in the modality of 
question and answer, problem and solution, through which it enters the horizon 
of its historical effect.”74 The use of rhetoric based on theism has the effect of in- 
cluding the divine in this equation of thought and experience at both the corpo- 
rate and individual levels. 


In this respect, modern historians have explored how the emergence of his- 


tory-writing corresponded to societal concerns and desires. As in Jewish and 
Greek historiographies, some scholars have also identified a prophetic or divina- 
tory element in this literary development. François Hartog, for example, explores 
the interrelationship between divination and history in various cultures.75 Unsur- 
prisingly, Herodotus plays a fundamental role in Hartog’s reconstruction and 
comparative study (as in other studies discussed below), so it will not be dwelled 
upon here. Hartog explores the development of history in the Greek-speaking 
world through three ‘sense-making’ figures in society: the soothsayer, the bard, 
and the historian. He locates Herodotus in this configuration: “If the inquiry (thus 
defined) both evokes the wisdom of the bard and breaks with it, Herodotus also 
appeals to a second register of knowledge (that we have already met), the divina- 
tory one. Herodotus historei but he also sêmainei. He investigates and he shows, 
reveals, signifies.”76 Herodotus performs his investigation with an “oracular au- 
thority.”77 For example, Herodotus displays his interpretative ability via the 
Pythia’s reply to the Siphnians, who wanted to know about the longevity of their 
prosperity (3.57–58). The Siphnians were not able to interpret the oracle, neither 
at the time of its reception nor at the time of its fulfilment when the Samians 
came to request a loan. Herodotus reveals the interpretation to his readers, citing 
the Pythia’s response. 


In the same vein, Thomas Harrison’s “‘Prophecy in reverse’? Herodotus and 


the Origins of History” argues that history-writing was theological from the begin- 
ning.78 Yet Herodotus’ Histories is more than a divinely threaded narrative, it has 
a “prophetic quality” permeating the story, from the chronological perspective of 
fulfilled prophecies and omens in relation to the Persian Wars.79 This element 
takes on additional strength when placed in relation to the Peloponnesian War 
during which Herodotus recorded his findings. Some of these passages must have 
resonated with Herodotus’ audience, and thus “the proleptic references take on 
something of the quality of prophecies.”80 It is a type of prophetic prefiguration in

that it brings an additional component to the emplotment.81 This suggests that

Jewish and Christian historiography.82 Greek historiography can also be con- 
sidered prophetic-like because of its theistic interpretation of the past, its message 
for the audience’s context and concerns, and, occasionally, its forewarning of fu- 
ture events. 


The proleptic value of expressions involving the divine is thus significant, 


both narratively and rhetorically. For example, Irene de Jong demonstrates that 
although most of the prophecies in the Histories are ultimately realised, Herodo- 
tus’ characters and readers both encounter a hermeneutical challenge when in- 
terpreting ambiguous prophecies, dreams, and portents.83 As the narrative pro- 
gresses, Herodotus provides them with more clarity, but in the meantime, the 
characters and readers experience “riddling prolepses” involving puzzlement 
and requiring “patient decoding.” Indeed, through these devices, a ‘prophetic fu- 
ture’ may be discerned throughout the Histories.84 


Rhetorically, Harrison identifies the moral lessons to be learned from the 


presence and actions of the divine in numerous scenes described by Herodotus. 
For example, he suggests that reversals of fortune and miracles serve as remin- 
ders to people to pay attention to the gods, and that injustice and wrongdoing will 
be punished.85 Also, on the macronarrative level, Herodotus’ attention to the di- 
vine contributes to certain assumed patterns, a type of ‘moralism’ which reminds 
readers that just as the divine wrought revenge at the end of the Histories, it is 
also “referring forward ominously to the Athenian empire of Pericles.”86 


Despite the differences in views on the divine in the fifth century, in which 


traditional and sceptical expressions cohabited, both were a part of a culture that 
generally believed that the gods were active in the human realm. Religious beliefs 
and practices imbued Greek political life, and especially in domestic contexts (i.e., 
family or household piety).87 The Histories, as well as other literature, mirror 
what audiences knew in social life, and it is reasonable to assume that they ex-

pected to find it in Herodotus’ enquiries. Herodotus’ message – or his overall

things to do and not do. Rather, it speaks of “a recommended mindset, a humility, 
infused by mindfulness of the gods.”89 Herodotus had a moral message, which 
was supported by a theistic framework. In short, as Hau rightly comments: 
“Moral didacticism forms the backbone of the work.”90 Likewise, his successors 
buttress their moral rhetoric by way of explicit and implicit inclusion of the di- 
vine. 


Like Hartog and Harrison, Mark Munn also tackles the question ‘Why histo- 


ry’? Munn boldly extends the discussion by drawing attention to the political utili- 
ty of both Herodotus and Thucydides as competing voices to those of other inter- 
preters of the past and the present via oracles, omens, etc.91 Both historians 
provide ample evidence for the serious use of oracles and omens in political and 
military matters.92 Given the timeliness of their writings during the Peloponne- 
sian War, their histories brought another kind of voice to reflect on public mat- 
ters, by simultaneously not neglecting the divine realm and providing a more sol- 
id basis for guidance in political matters.93 Despite their differences in the 
handling of τὰ θεῖα, Herodotus’ and Thucydides’ writings were both intended to 
be “hortatory and protreptic” especially for the governing class.94 It was “the gap 
between authority and reliability” that needed to be bridged by “a new standard” 
for understanding the world.95 We see here the historiographical prophetic voice 
in action, providing commentary on the past in light of present societal concerns. 
This is the conviction that underlies Thucydides’ claim that his writings will also 
help to understand the future and thus be valuable for all times (1.22.4). Religious

With Hartog, Harrison, and Munn, we have returned to the roles and appar- 


ent rivalry between the fathers of Greek historiography, Herodotus and Thucy- 
dides. This serves to illustrate that prophetic-like voices were heard in the earliest 
period of development of Greek historiography and that – in this regard – there 
was no theistic rupture between Herodotus and Thucydides. True, the representa- 
tion of perceptions of the divine and its degree of intensity are conspicuous be- 
tween them, and between their successors, but there is not a theistic rift. For this 
reason, a strand of prophetic voices in Greek, by Greeks and non-Greeks, provides 
common ground for various theological traditions. The concept of ‘prophetic 
voice’ does not intend to relativise these differences or to impose terms on the 
Greek tradition. Rather, the proposed approach in this monograph seeks to re- 
spect native categories relating to intermediary functions of divine communica- 
tion and to consider their influence in historiographical expressions to particular 
audiences from the fifth century BCE to the end of the first century CE.97 In this 
sense, the survey of Greek historiography in Chapter 2 supports the hypothesis 
that Herodotus and Luke are two central expressions of Greek historiography 
with a prophetic voice.98 Viewing the world from a theistic perspective (i.e., theo- 
logical reflection) mattered to them and to their audiences.99 In this way, τὰ θεῖα 
and τὰ ἀνθρωπικά are joined existentially.

3.4 Reading the Historians Theologically through 


Their Prophetic Voices: A Methodology 


In the light of the working definition of ‘prophetic voice’ provided in Chapter 1 
and elucidations of it in Chapter 2 and in this chapter, this section sets out some 
of its key elements, as discernible in the historiographical record as a methodo- 
logical basis for exegetical analysis. Presenting them here in a concise form will 
be helpful for the following analysis of the histories of Herodotus and Luke, as 
well as for theological readings of other historians. The advantage of the list be- 
low is that it is applicable to historical texts of various theistic expressions. 


But it cannot be considered exhaustive; rather, it seeks to highlight certain 


elements in historical prose that contribute to the overall construction of the his- 
torians’ prophetic voices.100 It is important to note from the outset that ‘prophetic 
voice’ is not reduced to the narratorial remarks by historians. Rather, in addition 
to it, the prophetic voice can incorporate multiple voices and rhetorical devices, 
at the macro- and micronarrative levels that bring the presence of the divine to 
the fore and contribute to the historians’ teaching to their contemporaries. In 
short, the prophetic voice helps to connect the creative work of emplotment with 
its hoped-for explotment. We begin here with a broad perspective and narrow 
down the view by looking at rhetorical strategies that contribute to the prophetic 
voice. There is some overlap between the categories. 


(1) Participation in the narrative argumentation. The prophetic voice in historiog- 


raphy brings perceptions of the divine into the narrative world in various 
ways, as a part of the overall narrative argumentation and its rhetorical 
strategies. It highlights the interaction between the divine and human 
spheres, which can be depicted in both directions, divine intervention in hu- 
man history as well as human action towards the divine sphere. These two 
axes contribute to the overall cognitive and emotional reception of the ques- 
tions of the historical narrative (i.e., ‘intrigue’). The strength of the prophetic 
voice depends on how many of (and how frequently) the following elements 
are employed to guide the audience through the narrative. For example, in 
reflecting on the audience’s perspective, it is constructive to observe where 
and how they encounter these prophetic characteristics in the narrative (e.g., 
beginning, end, key moments). Are these elements new or retold elements to 
the audience? Are there patterns in the larger narrative that contribute to 
motifs or themes? Elements such as these contribute to the audience’s explo- 


100 
This narrative theological methodology is distinct from, yet complementary to, a more the- 
matic approach to studying religion in the Histories, as demonstrated by Schwab (2020), 
which adapts and applies Klaus Hock’s model (Hock 2002). The result is a multidimensional 
approach that presents findings across five chapters concerning specific aspects of foreign 
religion (cf. the description of Schwab’s approach, 28–33).

ration of the narrative’s questions and their desire for their closure. Addi- 
tionally, literary forms are employed to explore the divine-human relation- 
ship, such as narratorial remarks, description (telling) or portrayal (show- 
ing) of actions and speeches, including both positive and negative exempla. 


(2) Historians’ posture towards the divine. Here a variety of questions can be ex- 


plored. For example, what indications do historians provide, explicitly or im- 
plicitly, about their views of the divine realm and its activity in the human 
sphere? How do they depict divine beings? How do their positive or negative 
representations compare with other representations of their contemporaries 
or successors? Do divine beings participate in the development of the narra- 
tive’s agōnes, e.g., in cooperation or competition with other forms of divine 
or human rule? Do historians identify themselves with a particular religious 
role or a mediating function (e.g., priest), thus underlining a link between 
practised religion and historiography?101 In addition, some of the following 
features may be discernible and contribute to our understanding of histori- 
ans’ views of the divine, allowing us to attempt to discern the contours of 
their theological framework. 


(3) Historians’ posture towards their audiences. Historical prose carries the nar- 


rative voices of historians for their generations, which may be explicit or im- 
plicit, ranging from a limited audience to a general multicultural audience. 
By adopting a theistic perspective (and perhaps a claim to understanding of 
the divine realm), the narrative voice of the historian may be charged with 
greater authority, consequently increasing its potential for rhetorical influ- 
ence. This illustrates in a unique way the didactic function that ancient histo- 
rians performed in their societies. How then do historians position them- 
selves in relation to their readers and in society? How do historians 
demonstrate their self-awareness, authority, and role through their relation- 
ship to and understanding of the divine? All of these elements are reinforced 
when historians address a broad Greek-speaking multicultural audience. 


(4) Historians’ posture towards religious traditions and metanarratives. The 


prophetic voice is often an expression of an existing religious metanarrative. 
Historians may assume that their audiences have knowledge about a particu- 
lar tradition (e.g., their divine beings and rituals). The Greek mythopoetic 
tradition, for example, assumes a polytheistic worldview, which influenced 
the development of a cultural metanarrative and the historiography of the

Greeks. This narrative strategy can achieve at least two things. It substanti- 
ates the recounted history, and, consequently, it extends – from one genera- 
tion to the next – a religious heritage and/or a prophetic/oracular tradition.102 


The term ‘divine plupast’ helps to underline how stories that evince the di- 
vine realm and chronologically predate the core part of a narrative can bol- 
ster the narrator’s argumentation. This often involves continuity and discon- 
tinuity, analogy and dissimilarity in relation to divine activity. The rhetorical 
contribution of the above elements is the formation of audiences’ piety (see 
‘existential rhetorical aims’). In this regard, given the audience’s knowledge 
of earlier and contemporary literature, intertextuality is often a significant 
rhetorical feature (e.g., citations, allusions, and textual parallels [or echoes] 
of sacred and profane texts). Various literary devices may be used to evoke 
familiar religious symbolism from literary and non-literary sources. Alterna- 
tively, historians may opt for a critical and polemical stance towards reli- 
gious traditions (and characters representing them) that they do not consider 
to be reliable expressions of the divine realm (e.g., sometimes serving as lit- 
erary foils). 


(5) Epistemological sources about the divine. In relation to the previous element, 


the prophetic voice as an interpretative activity implies an understanding of 
the divine sphere, which can be claimed implicitly or explicitly, as a result of 
direct or indirect reception of sources. This fact relates to the way in which 
historians availed themselves of these sources (autopsy, interviews, hearsay, 
texts, material culture, etc.). In turn, sources provide ‘proofs’ (τεκμήρια) 
about divine activity (e.g., signs, omens, oracles, miracles) to substantiate an 
explanation. Alternatively, do historians or their characters make claims for 
divine revelation or interpretation from the divine realm?103 From their per- 
spective, historians may include intermediaries between the divine and hu- 
man spheres to support their own voices. Narratively, it is crucial to distin- 
guish, as much as possible, between these auctorial and actorial perspectives 
of the divine, and how they are used to offer theological nuance to a scene. 
Historians, then, may refer to individuals or groups as sources of informa- 
tion. Speeches containing perceptions about the divine in history are particu-

ing project: “it seemed good to me and the Holy Spirit.” This variant is found in Old Latin 
manuscripts (itb,q), which appear to borrow from a letter-writing context in Acts 15:28: “For it

larly common.104 This raises the question of the correspondence of interpreta- 
tion between the speaker and the narrator. In addition, historians often inte- 
grate stories from the ancient or recent past (i.e., ‘divine plupast’, cf. Hdt., 
Hist. 1.2; Thuc. 1.16). Are these stories considered to be true in fact, or true 
only in their moral value? Historians may also distance themselves from 
such stories and perhaps use them as negative exempla, e.g., to characterise 
corrupt seers or false prophets. Do their prophetic voices challenge or com- 
plement other mediating personages in society, and thus play an alternative 
role in making the divine known to humanity? 


(6) Existential rhetorical aims. Historians of antiquity, it is assumed, sought to re- 


spond to the ‘horizon of expectations’ of their audiences.105 Their narratives 
can then be seen as messages to their audiences, namely, how their emplot- 
ment sought also an explotment in the contexts of their audiences. Temporal- 
ly, this connects the two horizons of the prophetic voice, which involves the 
interpretation of the period being narrated and addresses the contemporary 
concerns of the audience’s time. Audiences are invited to explore their reli- 
gious heritage via historical representation. In terms of piety and impiety, 
what moral and religious values might audiences be encouraged to embrace? 
How might this aspect contribute to the creation, development, and (re)defi- 
nition of the audiences’ identity, both individually and collectively? 


(7) Historians’ posture towards human rule. Intrigues of human rule are ubiqui- 


tous in ancient history. This issue can be explored by observing how divine 
rule is positioned in relation to human structures of rule to support or coun- 
ter the imperial impulse as examples of hegemonic hybris.106 A critical voice, 
especially towards leaders, may be developed throughout a narrative that de- 
cries bad choices and negative examples. This element depends on the rela- 
tionship between historians and the audiences for whom they write, which 
may be the royal court or the ruling classes.

Greek historiography was to illustrate ethical standards by providing good

E.g., Herodotus challenges forms of imperialistic powers (Persia and Athens). Dionysius of 
Halicarnassus supports Rome’s rise to power; and Luke reminds his readers that the disciples 
wanted to know if Jesus was going to restore the kingdom to Israel, and, apparently, against 
Rome’s wishes. 


3 Writing the Divine as One’s Audience Expects 
111 


and bad examples. Because it is such an extensive feature, I list it separately, 
although it is closely related to the previous two points. On both the vertical 
and horizontal axes of religious behaviour, historians provide exempla to en- 
courage piety and discourage impiety. This, of course, contributes significant- 
ly to the message and the desired explotment. Historians may develop pat- 
terns of exempla that acclaim one group while denigrating another. In 
relation to rule and authority, various types of leaders are common subjects 
of exempla. 


(9) Divine presence through material culture. A subtle feature that can be under- 


estimated is the presence of the divine through material objects evoked in the 
narrative. Occurrences of this feature may go unnoticed because of their 
inanimate appearance. In antiquity, however, material culture could be un- 
derstood as a channel for divine presence and serve as a reminder to pay 
homage to the gods. This element then contributes to an audience’s en- 
counter in the narrative with ‘divine things’, such as their territory, sacred 
places, and rituals. Some references may have been very familiar to audi- 
ences while others may be new to them. The subtlety of this feature depends 
on an audience’s knowledge of references to the divine, the amount of atten- 
tion paid to their representation, and their connection to the narrative’s 
questions. 


The strength of the prophetic voice in historiography depends on the degree and 
intensity to which historians incorporate the above elements in such a way that 
the interplay between the divine and the human emerges as a part of the histori- 
an’s narrative account of the past. The link between emplotment and explotment 
depends not just on the historian’s presumed relationship with the divine and di- 
vinely imparted knowledge, but also on how they help audiences to explore the 
divine in the intrigue of the narrative: expectations seeking fulfilment and ques- 
tions seeking closure. 


3.5 Conclusion 


The issue for historians in antiquity was not necessarily whether perceptions of 
the divine realm should be represented in historiography but how they could be 
incorporated rhetorically and theologically for their respective interests and au- 
diences. This chapter has argued that the combination of the rhetorical and the 
theological provides a framework for understanding historical writings with 
prophetic-like characteristics as an integral part of their responses to the ques- 
tions, concerns, and interests of their audiences. The ‘prophetic voice’ in histori- 
ography, which emerged among other voices in the fifth century, was another 


Part I Herodotus’ Hermeneutical Dilemma and His Table of Historians 
112 


way of dealing with the hermeneutical dilemma bequeathed by the mythopoetic 
tradition. 


The proposed methodology explores this feature within the rhetoric of histo- 


riography, in the rhetorical triad of author, text, and audience, as an interpreta- 
tive and didactic process. Every ‘history’ can be seen as a unique performance 
that expects to be experienced by an audience. Through this author-audience 
complicity, the historian’s emplotment desires a positive explotment, that is, an 
integration into the thinking and life of an audience. How then did theistic dis- 
course contribute to the fulfilment of these audience-centred aims, that is, re- 
spond to the horizon of expectations of the audience and to their existential 
needs? 


As for the nomenclature of this phenomenon, certain notions drawn from 


Jewish and Christian historiographical research, such as ‘prophetic history’ and 
‘prophetic historiography’, can be appropriated for Greek historiography. The ex- 
pression ‘prophetic voice’ helps to highlight the ‘prophet-like’ function of histori- 
ans, who – explicitly or implicitly – performed a mediating function of interpre- 
tation and proclamation between the divine and human realms. This feature 
reflects how audiences in antiquity expected to encounter theological discourse 
in a variety of Greek literature, hence the unsurprising and reasonable integra- 
tion of knowledge of the divine in history as a stock part of ancient historiogra- 
phy. 


Historiography with a prophetic voice brings an additional element to his- 


torical narratology by exploring the idea that greater forces intervene in human 
history, as well as the possibility of working with or against these forces in the 
realisation of possible trajectories that open before audiences. In this sense, 
Greek historiography may also be considered to have a prophetic trait in its theis- 
tic interpretation of the past, its message for audiences’ context and concerns, 
and, occasionally, its forewarning of future events. Herodotus’ example is funda- 
mental to understanding how the hermeneutical dilemma influenced his succes- 
sors. His theistic framework supported his didactic role towards his audience and 
offered them a moral message. 


To varying degrees, Herodotus’ successors played the same role in society, 


dealing with the hermeneutical dilemma in their own way, using a variety of 
rhetorical strategies and devices to explain perceptions of the divine to their audi- 
ences. For this reason, we may speak of the historiographical prophetic voice in 
the singular, but also in the plural, as a unique expression of an alternative voice 
to other societal voices such as bards, seers, and diviners. The frequency and in- 
tensity of their prophetic voices reflect their understanding of the influence of the 
divine realm in human history and how they choose to express this rhetorically 
and theologically. 


We now turn to the second part of the research, with chapters that introduce 


some thematic comparisons of the prophetic voices of Herodotus and Luke, 


3 Writing the Divine as One’s Audience Expects 
113 


which in turn prepare for the exegetical chapters in the third part. As bookends 
in relation to the hermeneutical dilemma, we begin to consider how Herodotus 
and Luke spoke into their own contexts by interpreting history from theistic per- 
spectives as a part and extension of – perhaps even as a substitute for – other 
prophetic voices.

4 Connecting Herodotus and Luke: Their Worlds, Incipits, 


and Multicultural Audiences 


The previous chapters have demonstrated historiographical and theistic continui- 
ty between Herodotus and Luke. It is now time – in this second section of three 
chapters – to consider their lives, contexts, and parts of their works in parallel, 
and – with some imagination – in conversation with one another at Herodotus’ 
table. This chapter has two overlapping functions. It compares their lives and 
contexts as well as specific texts of their works, beginning here with the incipits, 
the opening lines of the narratives.1 These incipits raise questions concerning 
their audiences and narrative aims for them. In both works, a multicultural audi- 
ence can be discerned given the global interests in the narratives themselves. 
Herodotus’ interest in, perhaps even affection for, Greeks and non-Greeks, had 
wider political implications for one who appears to have resisted unconditional 
alliance to any state. Towards the end of the first century CE, Plutarch labelled 
Herodotus with the disparaging epithet of φιλοβάρβαρος (‘a lover of barbar- 
ians’).2 I think the same could be said of Luke, Plutarch’s contemporary. Despite 
their worlds being in turmoil – i.e., the Greeks and other peoples under political 
and military threat – Herodotus and Luke were able to produce narratives that 
are perhaps remarkably open to outsiders or to the other. Both historians lived in 
multicultural contexts and appeared to have valued them. This also reflects the 
composition and interests of their audiences, for whom they establish geopolitical 
connections on a grand scale and draw conclusions in response to manifestations 
of the imperial impulse. As the chapter presents both authors and their contexts 
in parallel, readers may wish to skim through documentation they are already 
familiar with. 


4.1 Their Lives and Worlds: Powers in Conflict and Flux 


Ideally, these biographical summaries should be established on information pro- 
vided by Herodotus and Luke themselves or by contemporary, reliable sources. 
Unfortunately, information is sparse for both authors. Their choices of topics, in-

Herodotus. 


4.1.1 Herodotus and His World 


If sources are excluded outside the Histories, not much material is left about 
Herodotus’ life.3 Fortunately, Herodotus often uses first person commentary. His 
frequent asides allow his presence to be felt and render the narration more per- 
sonable, as if one were in the audience during a public reading.4 One hears, for 
example, what Herodotus himself had seen and heard, and how he had obtained 
his sources. He openly shares insights, opinions, as well as doubts about historical 
reports.5 But he chooses to tell his audience very little about his life and the cir- 
cumstances in which he composed his writings. 


The opening line of the Histories functions as the title: Ἡροδότου Ἁλικαρνησ- 


σέος ἱστορίης ἀπόδεξις ἥδε. It describes the nature of the work and identifies the 
author-narrator as Herodotus of Halicarnassus (modern Bodrum, Turkey). Esti- 
mations of his lifespan range from the earliest ca. 490 to the 410s BCE.6 He was 
most likely born in Halicarnassus approximately between ca. 490 and 479 BCE at 
the time of the Persian Wars.7 The multicultural context of this coastal city is dis- 
tinctive. It was founded ca. 900 BCE by Troezen (a city-state in the Argolic penin- 
sula), which was, according to Herodotus, of Dorian origin (1.144; 7.99.3).8 In 
Herodotus’ times, Halicarnassus was in the region of Caria; consequently, a sig- 
nificant percentage of the inhabitants had Carian names. It was also well connect-

is that Herodotus grew up here when the city was under Persian rule, though lo- 
cally governed by a Carian dynasty. During the Persian Wars, Halicarnassus 
fought alongside the Persians under Artemisia, the Carian queen and admiral 
(Hist. 7.99). 


According to one source (see the Suda excerpt below), Herodotus migrated 


to Samos because of conflicts with Lygdamis, the Carian tyrant and grandson of 
Artemisia. After the Aegean coast was liberated by the Greeks, Halicarnassus be- 
came a part of the Delian League (478/7 BCE) and continued its allegiance as an 
Athenian naval station even after Athens’ allies revolted in 412.10 After Herodo- 
tus’ death in the 420s or 410s, probably in Thurii, Caria became a Persian prov- 
ince and thus Halicarnassus was again under Persian rule. Consequently, Herodo- 
tus and his contemporaries, in the space of around 150 years, experienced both 
political instability and full subjugation of the Aegean coast, under the alternating 
reigns of the Lydians, Persians, and Greeks. 


Although ancient reception of the Histories affirms Herodotean authorship 


and Halicarnassus as his place of origin, a textual variant brings an additional 
element to Herodotus’ multicultural identity.11 Some manuscripts have Ἡροδότου 
Θουρίου. Thurii was a Greek colony in the southern peninsula of Italy. This vari- 
ant goes as far back as Aristotle (Rhet. 3.9). Plutarch also has knowledge of nu- 
merous examples of this textual amendment (Mor. On Exile 604).12 The variant 
with ‘Halicarnassus’ should not be doubted, since the ancient sources supporting 
Halicarnassus are almost unanimous. For example, an inscription (Syll.3 46) at- 
tests to the Carian names of ‘Lyxes’ (his father) and of ‘Panyassis’ (his uncle or 
cousin) and to the Greek name ‘Theodorus’ (his brother), appearing in other Cari- 
an-Greek families from Halicarnassus.13 


Based on his Histories, we gather that Herodotus travelled extensively, for 


example, in Asia Minor, Phoenicia, Egypt and other parts of North Africa, possibly 
also the Black Sea region.14 Apart from the specific mentions of visits, other clues 
suggest actual presence in certain areas.15 His metanarrative remarks such as

scriptions), which had been a recognised literary dialect since Homer.20

with the Dorian Greeks south of Halicarnassus.22 Also, the Suda omits the travels

Herodotus’ contact with Athens is also found in some ancient sources. Plu-

Herodotus) accuses Herodotus of flattering the Athenians in exchange for finan-

Athens on the proposal of Anytos” (Her. mal 26, 862b).27 It is deduced that Herodo-

erudite, for example, Pericles, Protagoras, Sophocles, and Euripides (cf. Plutarch, 
An seni 785b).28 A tradition also tells that Thucydides was moved to tears when he 
heard a lecture of Herodotus in Athens (Marcellinus, Life of Thucydides, 54).29 The 
point is that if Herodotus spent time in Athens, he certainly benefited from and 
contributed to this productive literary milieu with its cross-fertilisation of ideas 
from politics, philosophy, medicine, and theatre.30 He thus had direct contact with 
those who shaped Athenian democratic rule and its intense phase of expansion.

Other places merit attention. Delphi was an important source for Herodo- 


tus.31 It is one of the most crucial locations for understanding the entire narrative, 
and as such it will often feature in later sections. He also speaks of a meeting with 
Archias in Sparta (Hist. 3.55.2), and with Tersander of Orchomenus in Boeotia 
(Hist. 9.16.1, 5). Later attacks on Herodotus speak of his alleged hostility towards 
the Corinthians and the Thebans, because he was not paid for his readings, and 
because the Thebans did not allow him to address their youth.32 Regarding Magna 
Graecia (the coastal region of Italy colonised by the Greeks), Herodotus mentions 
Sybaris, but never Thurii, so his connection with the latter colony must be drawn 
from other sources. The textual variant mentioned about Thurii was understood 
by ancient scholars to be an indication of biographical fact, and not an invention. 
That Herodotus wrote part of his project in Magna Graecia can be deduced from 
the passage where Herodotus explains terms of distance used in Attica (Hist. 
4.99.5). Asheri reconstructs this period thus: 


Herodotus’ emigration to Thurii may thus be a true biographical episode. Chrono- 
logically, it is entirely possible that Herodotus, after staying in Athens, joined for a 
while the new Panhellenic colony of Thurii, founded in 444/3 BC, as did other con- 
temporary intellectuals, such as Protagoras and Hippodamus of Miletus. For a 
while, Thurii became Herodotus’ adopted fatherland and competed for this honour 
with Halicarnassus […] It is impossible to establish whether he died at Thurii, as 
the biography in the Suidas claims, or whether he went back to Athens. We cannot 
even establish the year of his death: we can only fix a terminus ante quem non: 430 
BC.33 


In sum, regarding Herodotus’ lifespan, only approximate calculations can be ex- 
trapolated from the above data. Given that ancient historians do not provide se- 
cure methods for dating his life,34 modern researchers generally place him be- 
tween the 480s and 420s (based on his stay in Thurii up to at least 430 BCE).35 


Earlier dates for his death are also proposed, as early as the 410s.36 The birth year 
of circa 484 is based on Herodotus’ fortieth year (his acmē) and the foundation of 
Thurii (444/3 BCE). Another tradition purports that Herodotus was 53 at the be- 
ginning of the Peloponnesian War, thus 431 + 53 = 484 BCE. We are left with these 
general figures.

searcher-narrator, he is intensely curious and culturally attuned, having an “un-

biased and pluralistic outlook as a historian.”38 He takes genuine interest in other 
peoples and their cultures, near and far. The two distant cities, Halicarnassus and 
Thurii, attest to this and suggest that he is a Greek of the periphery and conver- 
sant with the Greeks of Asia, Magna Graecia, and Europe. Indeed, his life is 
marked off by two great conflicts involving the Greeks and other peoples: the 
Greco-Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War. This fact, and a possible exile, 
may explain why he travelled and explored those places and peoples for himself. 
Greek colonisation and Persian imperialism facilitated and forced contact with 
other ethnic groups. 


In the light of this general profile and the cultural sensitivity manifest in his 


Histories, scholars have explored Herodotus’ appreciation of Greek culture, as 
well as a fascination with the ‘other’, what was different, among the non-Greeks 
and how this influenced his research.39 As will be discussed in relation to his in- 
cipit, one of the driving questions is why relations between the Greeks and the 
barbarians (i.e., the non-Greeks) were so hostile. His perspective is constantly 
outward-looking. As such, politically, Herodotus is difficult to pin down, as John 
Gould notes: “Herodotus’ own apparent perception of himself as a Greek without 
clear and exclusive ties to either of the rival segments of Greek colonists is itself 
interesting and says something of his relative cultural and intellectual freedom 
and lack of constraining loyalties.”40 He is both profoundly of Greek culture and 
cosmopolitan in outlook.41 As Lachenaud observes, Herodotus resists being placed 
in one location: “Hérodote est véritablement apolis: aucune cité grecque, même 
Athènes, ne peut être considérée comme sa patrie, à la fois le centre autour 
duquel il organiserait son histoire et le foyer d’où rayonnerait toute vérité re- 
ligieuse, morale et politique.”42 Though in a sense apolis, Herodotus was thor- 
oughly geopolitical in thought, exploring geography, ethnography, and religion as 
real factors in global relations. The world was in flux, constantly evolving be- 
tween shifts in world powers. Again, Herodotus knew first-hand the dangers of 
the imperial impulse. This was the world he described and in which he lived and 
to which his prophetic voice spoke. 


4.1.2 Luke and His World 


We now move forward some five hundred years to a period when the Greeks 
lived again under another major political power, the Roman Empire. The works

the developments of this force from the West and its impact on the oikoumenē. 
Despite this political subjugation, Greek culture and language continued to exert 
significant influence on the peoples dominated by the Roman Empire, one of 
which was the Jewish people. By the first century CE, most of the Jewish people 
lived in the diaspora due to forced and willing emigration beginning in the eighth 
century BCE. This brought the Jews into contact with Greeks and Greek-speakers 
in various regions. One key proof of this cultural influence is the production of 
Jewish-authored texts in Greek, e.g., 2 and 3 Maccabees (first century BCE) and 
the compositions of Josephus and Philo (first century CE).43 In addition, from the 
second century BCE on, translations of Hebrew Scriptures in Greek were pro- 
duced in Alexandria.44 


Subsequently, the earliest Christian writings emerged. These were written in 


Greek mainly by Jewish authors and were intended for a broad audience. This 
includes the four canonical Gospels, of which ‘Luke’ is the most prolific of the 
evangelists, given that he is the only one to have written a sequel. Around the 
time when Plutarch accused Herodotus of being a φιλοβάρβαρος, Luke was com- 
posing his own global and multicultural narrative, the Gospel of Luke and the Acts 
of the Apostles. One of the difficulties for research about Luke concerns his pre- 
cise identity and context. The question is not without interest because of the au- 
thor’s claims of eyewitness reports in the second volume. For this reason, this sec- 
tion is longer than the one on Herodotus. We will make a proposal regarding this 
question, but whoever the author may have been, we know approximately where 
and when he lived, that is, in the Mediterranean Basin during the second half of 
the first century CE, perhaps even extending into the second century. The conven- 
tional attribution to ‘Luke’ is used, which is justified below in light of ongoing 
deliberations within biblical scholarship. 


The narrative’s historical period ca. 5–4 BCE–62 CE. Regarding Luke’s knowledge 
of the context of the recounted narrative, it is perhaps not surprising that one of 
the first attested questions after Jesus’ resurrection is on the political level and 
certainly in response to the imperial impulse of the Roman Empire. It concerns 
one of the lingering questions in the disciples’ minds: “Is this the time when you 
will you reestablish the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6). Apparently setting aside 
the question as being beyond their knowability, Jesus responds by shifting their 
focus to their own mandate (1:7–8): “It is not for you to know the times or periods 
that the Father has set by his own authority. But you will receive power when the 
Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all

Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” Luke’s writings reflect this shift 
in emphasis. While the geopolitical scene is not ignored by Luke, it becomes 
subordinate to the theme of God’s purposes for global reconciliation. Likewise, 
given this shift of interest and lack of compositional context, we are confronted 
with the difficulty of placing Luke securely in a precise region and time period. 


It can, however, be affirmed that Luke was well informed of major political 


developments and administrative functions of the recounted period in Luke-Acts, 
beginning with the births of John the Baptist and Jesus in 5–4 BCE until Paul’s 
two-year stay in Rome ca. 60–62 CE. The disciples’ question above reflects the as- 
pirations of some parts of Jewish society in the first century CE. The increasing 
tension between the Jewish people and the Romans is well documented.45 Similar 
to Herodotus who lived in between wars, Luke also could speak of comparatively 
recent developments not long before his birth and their consequences during his 
lifetime. In rapid succession, the Romans had gained control of Syria (64 BCE), 
Palestine (63 BCE), and Egypt (31 BCE). The reign of Augustus (27 BCE–14 CE) – 
during which Jesus was born – marked the beginning of the Empire and estab- 
lished stability in his time. Yet it also created a legacy of imperial succession that 
would burden Roman leadership on the imperial and provincial levels. From Au- 
gustus until Trajan – Luke’s probable end of life around the end of the first centu- 
ry – the imperial title had changed thirteen times. On a provincial level, among 
many examples, Jewish history was marked particularly by the collaboration of 
the Herodian dynasty with Rome. Periodic heavy-handedness by both sides led to 
multiple Jewish revolts. The First Jewish-Roman War (66–70 CE) resulted in the 
heaviest of blows through the destruction of Jerusalem and her temple in 70 CE. 
But the fight for independence for some was still a dream worth fighting for (e.g., 
the Kitos War in 115–117 CE; Bar Kochba revolt in 132–135 CE). Jesus’ movement 
continued to develop during these troubled times. Whatever Luke’s ethnicity 
might have been, he most certainly grew up and lived in regions subjugated by 
the Romans. Knowledge of the fatal blow to the Jewish centre of worship would 
not have left Luke unmoved. Like Paul, he may have been a non-ethnic Roman 
but a Roman citizen, and favourable to Jewish history and culture. This undoubt- 
edly influenced Luke’s historiography. 


Traces of Luke’s authorial presence and lifetime, ca. 20–100 CE. If these are the 
general contours of the recounted historical period with some echoes of Luke’s 
own life context, what do we know about ‘Luke’ within his Roman dominated 
world? Similar to the quest for Herodotus’ identity, the search for the author of 
the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles remains elusive (cf. Appendix II for 
additional information on Luke’s profile). In the incipits of both works, the au- 
thor provides no elements of a typical formal introduction: name, patronymic,

For a survey, see Marshak (2010) 40–55.

and name of city. While the author identifies himself nowhere, he mentions the 
addressee, Theophilus, at the beginning of both works (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1). That 
Theophilus knew the author seems indisputable.46 Theophilus’ identity, however, 
is also obscure, since Luke does not provide any information about him. It is pos- 
sible that Theophilus acted as a sponsor, providing funds for the literary project. 
But first we will explore the internal and external evidence supporting the tradi- 
tion of the name ‘Luke’ being attached to these ancient documents. Further be- 
low, we will come to the question whether the book titles can be useful for this 
enquiry. We consider first the internal evidence. 


Internal evidence of authorial presence. The apparent desire by the author to re- 
main in the background could lead to the resolution to respect the author’s 
wish.47 Yet there is good evidence that the author’s identity was known to his 
readers despite the omission of his name.48 The relevance of knowing more about 
Luke as author parallels the quest for Herodotus’ biography and role as histori- 
an: “If we do not accept as true that the historical author Herodotus visited the 
places he said he visited, we are bound to judge the investigatory principles en- 
dorsed in the Histories in a different way than if we take the narrator at face val- 
ue.”49 The same principle should be applied to Luke as well, since it does influence 
our interpretation of the author’s claims for reliability and autopsy. Luke is 
claiming to write a history of recent events, part of which he claims to have wit- 
nessed.50 I think a good argument can be made for the traditional attribution, 
since, internally, one can trace the textual presence of the author-narrator 
throughout the two volumes.51 


Authorial presence appears in various ways such as first-person speech and 


especially specific commentary (i.e., evaluative remarks, narrative asides). First, 
despite textual anonymity, the author makes use of first-person singular and plu- 
ral in the first incipit: ἐν ἡμῖν (Luke 1:1), ἡμῖν (Luke 1:2); κἀμοί (Luke 1:3), and in 
the second incipit, ἐποιησάμην (Acts 1:1). The second and third occurrences draw 
attention to the author’s implication in the composition, whereas the first occur- 
rence appears to claim something that Herodotus could mostly not do, that is, to

This leads to the more specific occurrences of eyewitness claims through the ‘we 
passages’ scattered in the latter part of the second volume (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5– 
21:18; and 27:1–28:16).52 These passages are textual clues of more explicit order 
and raise various questions related to the previously mentioned uses of first-per- 
son speech. Taken at face value, the ‘we passages’ are eyewitness claims as Paul’s

and some exegetes accept these occurrences as authentic claims to participation 
in some of the narrated scenes. Yet three other views have been proposed. The 
‘we passages’ were (1) retained from sources claiming to be eyewitnesses; (2) fic- 
tional claims to eyewitness as a mere rhetorical device; or (3) a “conventional 
eyewitness” used when literarily demanded.53 No consensus has been reached 
about these passages.54 Some of this is certainly due to the tendency of biblical 
scholarship to be more critical than historiographical research supports. We can 
at least recognise the textual elements reminding the audience of the author’s 
presence and authority, which sustain his claim to rigorous methodology in re- 
search and composition (Luke 1:1–4). His project is located in the category of con- 
temporary history. The events of the first book were not part of his eyewitness 
range (ca. 5/4 BCE until 30 CE). But his objects of study were as accessible as 
Herodotus’. Luke’s participation in the story probably began when he joined 
Paul’s team sometime before his first eyewitness claim in Troas around the year 
50 CE (Acts 16:8–11).

presence.55 In the first volume, the narrator’s parenthetical remarks are not evi-

External sources for authorship. We now turn to these external sources, which are 
unanimous in attributing the two volumes to a Λουκᾶς mentioned in New Testa-

mentioned only in Pauline literature. The three occurrences in three letters are 
expressed in Paul’s voice in closing sections with greetings and contextual infor-

Acts can be traced back to the latter part of the second century CE, thus approxi-

author can be found in Clement of Alexandria (Strom. 5.12), Tertullian (Marc. 
4.2), Origen (in Euseb. H.E. 6.25), and other documents.59

that the author of Acts insufficiently represents details of Paul’s life and typical 
Pauline themes (i.e., those found in his undisputed letters). Some find these ap- 
parent discrepancies irreconcilable, arguing that if Luke (or any other fellow 
worker) really journeyed with Paul and knew his teaching, he would have been 
better informed and followed more closely the autobiographical descriptions in 
Paul’s letters.64 Although these arguments have some weight in the question, they 
are not convincing enough to discard the traditional view that the ‘we passages’ 
are authentic and could plausibly be Lukan. 


Like Herodotus, Luke displays rhetorical authority, mastery of multiple contexts, 
and literary brilliance. Similar to many of his historiographical predecessors, 
Luke lived in times of political subjugation with periods of tension and occasional 
rebellion. The imperial impulse of Rome kept people in their place, but it also in- 
cited some groups to dream of, fight and die for liberty (e.g., Jewish rebels in the 
Jewish Wars and the Acts of the Apostles). Luke tells of a people who lived under 
Roman rule, but who also had the kingdom of God on their lips and in their 
hearts. Roman authorities generally allowed for religious expression as long as it 
did not transgress Roman law (cf. Luke’s depiction of Paul’s audiences before Fe- 
lix and Festus). A political reading of Luke-Acts can therefore be seen as a people

4.2 Herodotus and Luke’s Projects through Their Incipits 


4.2.1 The Narratological Value of the Incipits 


The incipits in the Histories and in Luke-Acts represent the initial point of contact 
between the authors and their audiences. They serve the rhetorical function of 
establishing a ‘reading pact’ with the audience, enabling to understand what to 
expect from the narrative. Since a historical narrative can also be considered a 
(textual mimetic) performance, prepared for the audience in mind, the incipit is 
an invitation to explore the past, experience it, and learn from it. It prepares 
them for the exploration of central questions, displayed through selected events, 
characters, and places. By ‘incipit’, as regards the Histories, I am referring to the 
opening lines of the work as a part of the larger ‘proem’ or ‘preface’ (Hist. 1.1– 
5).65 


Much has been written about the prefaces of the Histories and Luke-Acts.66 


For some readers, the following discussion will cover some familiar ground, but it 
will focus on these incipits through the lens of their prophetic voices via narrative 
theory. One element that marks a break from earlier Greek and Jewish literature 
is that neither Herodotus nor Luke appeal (in their incipits) to the divine sphere 
or claim direct reception of divine revelation. For example, Hesiod, at the beginn- 
ing of Theogony, claims to have received direct revelation from the Muses (Theog. 
23–24), and they charged him to sing about what he had heard about the past, the 
future, and the gods (Theog. 29–31). Similarly, at the beginning of Works and 
Days, after invoking the Muses (Op. 1), Hesiod expresses his wish to be a herald of 
divine communication: “And, Perses, I would tell of true things.” (Op. 10). In addi- 
tion, Homer’s opening words of the Iliad and Odyssey are interpreted as poetic- 
religious calls to the Muses to inspire through their divine power and speak 
through the bard. Homer also appeals in later sections to the Muses for knowl- 
edge of the past (e.g., 2.484–493; 11.218–219; 14.508–509; 16.112–113). Similarly, 
in Jewish literature, one finds expressions that signal divine communication 


65 
For the proem, see Immerwahr (1956) 247–251. 


66 
Until 1956, see the selective bibliography in Immerwahr (1956) 247–248 n. 11. 


4 Connecting Herodotus and Luke 
131 


through prophetic utterances, often at the beginning of the book, such as “The 
LORD summoned Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting” (Lev 1:1; cf. 
Num 1:1; Josh 1:1); or “An oracle. The word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi” 
(Mal 1:1; cf. Zeph 1:1; Hag. 1:1; Zech 1:1). Or the claim for divine communication 
may come later in the text: “the word of the Lord came to [prophet’s name]” (Gen 
15:1; Luke 3:2) or “thus says the Lord” (Ezek 12:10). 


By comparison, the incipits of the Histories and Luke-Acts are much subtler 


theologically, most likely because it was not necessary to mention this to their au- 
dience. They claim above all knowledge and insight, but they do not claim direct 
access to divine revelation. Herodotus had received information, for example, 
from informants in Delphi and priests in Egypt, etc. Luke also claims to be the 
recipient of information from a chain of “eyewitnesses and servants of the word” 
(Luke 1:2). Thus, they have discovered through investigation, apprehended 
through personal reflection, and handed down what they considered worthy of 
transmission. 


We now examine the two incipits. Both are short and in the modern critical 


editions display one sentence (punctuated by five and four commas respectively). 
The incipit of the Histories in Greek (cf. Wilson’s edition) contains forty-one 
words (thirty-nine words if <δὴ καὶ> are excluded). Luke’s incipit (Luke 1:1–4) 
contains forty-two words (Nestle-Aland 28th ed.). In both incipits, their unique 
voices are heard clearly through their aims, which evince both tradition and in- 
novation. 


4.2.2 The Histories 


Text, structure, and translation. As noted above, the incipit in the Histories is both 
concise and straightforward concerning the themes that will be presented. It is, 
however, a long, complex, and creative sentence in three parts (cf. structure be- 
low).67 


Ἡροδότου Ἁλικαρνησσέος ἱστορίης ἀπόδεξις ἥδε,
