Commentary. In relation to the Homeric tradition and fledgling historiographical 
tradition, we can observe how Herodotus exhibits elements of tradition and inno- 
vation. The commentary below follows the three-part structure indicated above. 


(1) The first line functions as the “title-page and general table of contents.”75 In 
light of the following syntactical structure, one could replace the non-verbal title 
with a verbal one such as: “Herodotus of Halicarnassus displays here his en- 
quiry.”76 Herodotus identifies himself as author, breaking with Homeric poets, but 
joining others such as Theognis (sixth-century elegiac poet) who speaks of putting 
his ‘seal’ (σφραγίς) on his poems (Theognidea, 19–23; cf. also Hecataeus, FGH 1 F 
1; Thucydides, Hist. 1.1). The textual variant ‘Halicarnassus’ or ‘Thurii’ has al- 
ready been treated above. Rhetorically, however, the use of one or the other may 
have intrigued his audiences. Literarily, Halicarnassus situates him within the 
rich Ionian tradition. Politically, as a Greek, he is on the periphery and may be 
reluctant to show support for either Athens or Sparta. His homeland was – and 
presumably in spirit still was – Halicarnassus, on the frontline, at the crossroads 
of great empires. ‘Thurii’ might have also drawn the audience’s attention, be- 
cause of the political intricacies and cultural richness of this Panhellenic Atheni- 
an colony. Does he take sides with greater Ionia in his representation of the Per- 
sian Wars as well as in his contemporary commentary on Athenian subjugation? 
Will Ionia be free again? Thurii, on the other hand, is not mentioned once, so it 
seems less intriguing in relation to the latter part of Herodotus’ life. But, above 
all, the incipit introduces the break with Homer in form and content, i.e., it pres- 
ents itself as a prose enquiry (“research” [Purvis]; “Forschung” [Feix]; and 
“recherches” [Legrand]). But like Homer, the oral element can be discerned via 
ἀπόδεξις77 which can be translated as ‘display’, ‘presentation’, as in ‘publication’78 


or even ‘performance’.79 This may be an indication of the close relationship be- 
tween Herodotus’ public readings and writings. His narrative style illustrates 
this, as he often invites his audience to explore with him competing versions of 
the same story and their consequences.

repetition of subjects from preceding line: “[…] en particulier, ce qui fut cause que Grecs et

(2) The second part displays Herodotus’ creativity through the multiple parallels 
contained in the first two final clauses (cf. α, β, γ). The first final clause expresses 
Herodotus’ desire to preserve the memory of human achievements, which risk 
fading away by the force of time. He does not specify whether these are good or 
bad erga (‘deeds’ and ‘works’).80 Interpreted with the parallel in the third clause, 
it appears that Herodotus wishes to preserve, for society’s collective memory, any 
type of human deed that can serve this purpose. This functional role places 
Herodotus in the bardic tradition which announces deeds of the past. But unlike a 
narrator of fiction or a faithful transmitter of traditional stories, Herodotus has 
had to perform historical investigation “calling attention to himself as inquirer, 
collector, informer, editor, and judge of native accounts and received tradi- 
tions.”81 This authoritative position finds a parallel in the incipit of the Gospel of 
Luke in which the author displays a reliable didactic voice; one who gathers and 
transmits from collective memory for the audience’s edification. 


The second final clause builds logically on the first, by paralleling τὰ γενόμενα ἐξ 
ἀνθρώπων and ἔργα μεγάλα τε καὶ θωμαστά. They, however, are not necessarily 
synonymous, understood as separate entities in which the second is greater in 
quality (distinguished in grade). Like Homeric epic tradition (Il. 9.189; Od. 1.338), 
Herodotus’ enquiry serves to immortalise the κλέος (‘fame’ or ‘glory’) of those 
who deserve it. In this way, Herodotus shows how “the historian is heir of the 
bard.”82 The participle (ἀποδεχθέντα) provides an additional qualification in the 
phrase τὰ μὲν Ἕλλησι, τὰ δὲ βαρβάροισι ἀποδεχθέντα in that these accomplish- 
ments are still understood as being in the human sphere, that is “by the Greeks 
and the barbarians.” In any case, the μεγάλα τε καὶ θωμαστά signals to the reader 
that extraordinary deeds or works will be encountered in the performance; in- 
deed, nothing is banal here. This also highlights ‘the greatness of the subject’, 
which became a motif in Greek historiography.83 In addition, the μέν […] δέ 
clause in τὰ μὲν Ἕλλησι, τὰ δὲ βαρβάροισι ἀποδεχθέντα leaves no doubt that 
Herodotus will not restrict his exposition to things Greek; his net is spread broad- 
ly to catch whatever is magnificent, even among the barbarians (i.e., non- 
Greeks). His universal interest is thus explicitly stated from the beginning. His re- 
flection on and moral evaluation of people from all groups show that he was “a 
fine disciple of Homer and Aeschylus.”84

(3) Finally, in the last clause of the incipit, Herodotus makes it clear – what could 
seem to be a “last but not least” item – that his narrative will set forth the com- 
plex and protracted cause (αἰτίην, singular in the Greek) that led the Greeks and 
the non-Greeks to war with each other.85 Indeed, the conjunctions τε […] καί (in 
τά τε ἄλλα καί […]) have the function of linking the clause to previous clauses86 


and marking additional information, so that various expressions could render its 
force in nuancing τὰ ἄλλα (“the other matters,” “all else” = “for the rest”):87 “in 
addition,” “and especially,” “and in particular,” “as well as,” or “and even.” With 
regard to the expression δι’ ἣν αἰτίην, Herodotus is particularly concerned to ex- 
plore the “blame, offence, responsibility” of their conflicts.88 The theme of causali- 
ty runs deep in the Histories. In addition, among many other leaders, Croesus ap- 
pears first chronologically as the cause for hostility between these two ethnic 
categories (1.5.3). His audience, however, will discover that this general frame- 
work, Greeks and barbarians, will not be sufficient for explaining all the geopolit- 
ical intrigues. Hostility and rivalry among the Hellenes themselves are wide- 
spread throughout the entire narrative. Furthermore, the ongoing conflict of the 
Peloponnesian War forms the political backdrop for exploring the Histories. 


The mention of warfare in the final line is not isolated from the previous topics 
promised, since “great and marvellous works” will be displayed in a great num- 
ber of scenes of military conflict. This, of course, is also a Homeric theme, which 
continued to enjoy the interest of historiographers and their audiences after 
Herodotus. Although the presence of the divine is not explicitly mentioned here, 
we know from the narrative proper that readers will discover that some of the 
main reasons for initiating and waging military conflict are due to perceived di- 
vine activity. Various key episodes underline this point, which in fact – if Herodo- 
tus had wanted to restrict his enquiry to the human sphere – could have been 
omitted. Yet, from Herodotus’ perspective, the gods are involved in humans’ 
geopolitical struggle for power and independence, so that he could not narrate 
such events without this critical aspect. 


In conclusion, expressing the three clauses in their positive forms, Herodo- 


tus sets out to achieve three objectives for his public: to keep the deeds of human- 
ity afresh in society’s collective memory; to acclaim those deeds worthy of hon- 
our, fame, and interest; and finally, to explain the causes of geopolitical hostility 
between Greeks and barbarians. Framed in this way, given the circumstances 
and social discourse of the fifth century BCE, Herodotus stimulated his audience’s

theological rhetoric to achieve this. 


4.2.3 Luke-Acts 


Text, structure, and translation. The incipit in Luke-Acts (Luke 1:1–4) is a complex 
sentence, equally succinct to Herodotus’. It is structured through terse expres- 
sions in five parts. One main clause supported by four subordinate clauses, two 
before and two after. Textual traditions do not present significant variants.89 This 
incipit can be considered as an introduction to the two volumes of Luke-Acts. In 
turn, the incipit in Acts (1:1–2) can be seen as part of the recapitulation that eluci- 
dates the main incipit and links the two volumes.90 Here is the text followed by a 
literal translation, with a few alternate renderings:

μένων ἐν ἡμῖν πραγμάτων, 2 καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται καὶ ὑπη-

Commentary. As in the commentary on Herodotus’ opening lines, the discussion 
on Luke’s incipit will follow the syntactical order above. 


(1) The first subordinate introduced by ἐπειδήπερ (‘since’)91 indicates the reason 
for Luke undertaking this literary project: “many” others had already composed 
accounts. We are not told how many accounts nor the authors’ names. This affir- 
mation places his work within a tradition. Luke adds his voice to the conversa- 
tion, recognising the works of previous authors, without explicitly naming, prais- 
ing, or criticising them. Yet the fact that he resolves to write an additional account 
implies that he wishes to offer to his readers something different. In terms of con- 
tent, this is clear, since he adds new material in his first volume not available in 
other gospels, and the second volume is entirely unique. It is also clear by the 
object of his διήγησις that he employs the term in the sense of recounting the 
past, thus historiographical. For the author, these πράγματα are in the sphere of 
the recent past, πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν (“that have taken place among us”). 
The value of ἐν ἡμῖν has been discussed above, but it is worth repeating that this 
plural presence (again in 1:2) contributes to the incipit’s rhetorical force, because 
he represents a group. Moreover, it is plausible to consider these actions with an 
additional nuance, given the prophetic-voice of Luke-Acts, that is, not only “events 
that took place” but also “events that have been fulfilled,” that is, by God, in the 
sense of the divine passive. Luke places a high priority on the aspect of divine 
fulfilment throughout the two volumes. In summary of the opening clause, Moles 
is certainly correct: “After this immediate generic ‘signal’, readers must read the 
rest of the Preface historiographically, as the narrative broadly confirms.”92 


Hence, audiences’ expectations are already being shaped by the first line, which 
are fully supported by the following clauses. 


91 
A NT hapax, ἐπειδήπερ. 


92

(2) The second subordinate begins in verse 2 and is introduced by καθώς,93 which 
serves to connect the written traditions (evoked in the first clause) to authorita- 
tive sources for (most of) the account. Here the author claims an unbroken chain 
of tradition (παρέδοσαν), from those “from the beginning” to the author’s genera- 
tion (ἡμῖν). Again, Luke claims a position among the collective presence that is 
within reach of the earliest witnesses. Luke uses two expressions to qualify this 
group: αὐτόπται (eyewitnesses) and ὑπηρέται τοῦ λόγου (servants of the word). 
The first is patently important for the Greek historiographical tradition, as it 
claims obtaining knowledge through those who could give a first-hand account. 
The second expression describes how the eyewitnesses performed another role as 
“servants of the word”. Apart from the possible nuance of divine fulfilment in 
πεπληροφορημένων, the epithet “servants of the word” is the only clue of Chris- 
tian language in the incipit. One can assume that Theophilus and other Christian 
readers understood the expression with an intended nuance of λόγος. In other 
words, about which ‘word’ had those eyewitnesses become servants, given the 
polyvalence of λόγος? Was it equally meaningful to novices? Two possibilities 
seem plausible: “the word” could signal the person of Jesus (John 1:1, 14), or 
more probably, the message (teaching) of and about Jesus.94 In short, it can be 
understood as an ellipsis95 for the word/account/message of/about God/the Lord as 
fully revealed through Jesus’ teaching and deeds. Support for this interpretation 
is the use of λόγος in Acts 1:1 as a reference to the preceding volume (i.e., Gospel 
of Luke), which continues, as it were, the account of Jesus’ acts and teaching (τὸν 
μὲν πρῶτον λόγον ἐποιησάμην περὶ πάντων, ὦ Θεόφιλε, ὧ ν ἤρξατο ὁ Ἰησοῦς 
ποιεῖν τε καὶ διδάσκειν). 


(3) The main clause follows logically this claim of authoritative tradition in that it 
contains the most personal textual signal (κἀμοί) by the author in the incipit. It is 
expressed through the verb δοκέω with the infinitive (γράψαι) and qualified by 
the compound form κἀμοί – (“to me as well”) in the dative.96 Here and in the reca- 
pitulative incipit of Acts (ἐποιησάμην, 1:1), the author declares his role, presence, 
and authority as a part of the interpretative community for the compilation of the 
two works. In the syntactical layout above, the narrator and the addressee are 
separated by the subordinate clause of means, which will be discussed, for syn-

tactic purposes, further below. Rhetorically, this technique (in the author-reader 
contract) serves to assure Theophilus of the diligent work that has gone into the 
production of the two-volume work. In short, the author asserts that he has done 
his part, and that no doubts should be cast on the quality and trustworthiness of 
his work. 


Further above, it was mentioned that the author remains anonymous in the 


incipits of Luke and Acts and throughout the narrative proper. But it can be ar- 
gued that the author’s name was on the titulus (title page), so that Theophilus 
knew the author’s name. Despite this detail, the author does not provide any in- 
formation about Theophilus, nor about his relationship with him, nor about The- 
ophilus’ social rank. Since the name ‘Theophilus’ means ‘friend of God’ or 
‘beloved of God’, some exegetes do not exclude the possibility that it is a pseudo- 
nym for all readers who consider themselves ‘friends of God’. The equivalent 
name in Hebrew is Yedidya (or Jedidja, Heb. יְדִידְיָהּ 
cf. 2 S 12.25). This name, real or 


fictional, could have resonated with readers of both Greek and Jewish origin. 
However, Theophilus may be a historical figure, e.g., the patron of Luke’s re- 
search or a figure in the Roman administration, similar to the way Flavius Jose- 
phus addresses his patron Epaphroditus in the preface to his work The Jewish An- 
tiquities (Ant. 1.pr). The use of the epithet ‘most honourable’ or ‘excellent’ 
(κράτιστος) might support this hypothesis, supported also by other uses of this 
honorific title for high-ranking personages in Acts (Felix in 23.26 and Festus in 
24.3 and 26.25). 


What then explains the use of anonymity by an author wishing to establish 


his authority towards his audience? Historical precedents of anonymity are com- 
mon in Greco-Roman and Jewish historiographical traditions.97 Luke may have 
wanted to imitate his predecessors in the Jewish tradition in which most histori- 
cal books do not provide the author’s name in the incipit or elsewhere. In the 
Hebrew canon, the only exception is Nehemiah.98 This is clearly the opposite case 
for ‘prophetic’ books for whom the prophet-authors are named specifically.99 In 


97 
For anonymity in Latin literature, see Geue (2019). 


98 
Anonymous historical writings in the Hebrew Bible in which the author does not specifically 
identify himself: the Torah (or Pentateuch, Genesis-Deuteronomy), Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 
and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings, 1 and 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Esther. Nehemiah is the only exam- 
ple of specifically claimed authorship. 


99 
The distinction between historical and prophetic books can be problematic because both can 
contain historical and prophetic material (and other literary forms). Evidence for this is the 
Hebrew expression “former prophets” to describe the historiographical writings from Joshua 
to Samuel. “Prophetic” books, on the other hand, all claim specific authorship, often with pat- 
ronym and origin. The prefaces almost always contain a prophetic formula such as “the word 
of the Lord that came to Joel” or “vision of Obadiah”. For completeness, I list these writings 
here, which logically carry their authors’ names: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, 
Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. The book 
of Daniel does not contain a prophetic formula in the preface and begins with third person 
narration. Later, however, six occurrences show prophetic awareness “I Daniel”, and subs- 
tantiate evidence for authorship claims (8:15, 27; 9:2; 10:2, 7; 12:5).

addition, the author of the third gospel mentions that he was aware of other ac- 
counts similar to his project, but he does not name them. One of these was cer- 
tainly the Gospel of Mark, which he uses extensively in the first volume. He most 
likely knew the Gospel of Matthew, as well as other sources like the Logienquelle 
(or ‘Q’ for Quelle), and, possibly, also John’s Gospel.100 Irrespective of the question 
of literary dependence, all four canonical gospels, as the texts stand, are textually 
anonymous. So, Luke seems to have observed this early Christian tradition. 


But another influence that may have inspired Luke’s anonymity is the Gre- 


co-Roman tradition.101 The omission of formal identification finds its primary 
precedent in none other than Homer. Henceforth, authors of various literary gen- 
res either imitated Homer or preferred to claim authorship for various reasons.102 


Hesiod, a contemporary of Homer, names himself specifically (Hes. Theog. 22). 
Hecataeus, Herodotus, and Thucydides also lay claim to their works in their pref- 
aces. However, the next great historian, Xenophon, prefers to remain anonymous 
in two of his major works, Anabasis and Hellenica. It must be recognised, howev- 
er, that Xenophon, despite his use of the pseudonym Themistogenes of Syracuse 
(Hell. 3.1.2), is the main character and third-person narrator in the Anabasis, in 
order to give the impression of objectivity (Plut. Mor. 345).103 In the latter work, 
Hellenica, Xenophon may have omitted his name because he was continuing the 
narrative of the Peloponnesian War, which had ended abruptly in Thucydides’ 
work. 


Polybius and Diodorus also omit their names in their proems, given that 


those opening lines served, above all, to underline the importance of their chosen 
themes.104 Successively, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Josephus, and Appian men- 
tion their names. Arrian, however, prefers anonymity (Anab. 1.12.5), probably for 
polemical reasons against historians’ self-exalting prefaces (perhaps specifically 
against Appian).105 It should also be noted that Roman historians never adduce “a 
formal introduction of themselves into the text.”106 In light of these precedents of 
anonymity in Jewish and Greco-Roman prefaces, it is not unusual that Luke pre- 
fers to keep his name in the background, emphasising instead his theme,

methodology, and objective for his audience. Presumably, for him, his name in

(4) The third subordinate clause boldly describes how the author produced his 
work (research and composition). The clause is built around one participle (παρη- 
κολουθηκότι) and three adverbs (ἄνωθεν, ἀκριβῶς, and καθεξῆς). The participle 
is grammatically linked to κἀμοί. Again, the link between author and the sources 
of tradition is bolstered; he has closely followed (traced), from the beginning 
(adv. ἄνωθεν), all of them (πᾶσιν). That which he has received and written is ‘ac- 
curately’ (ἀκριβῶς) handed on. The third adverb καθεξῆς describes the sequential 
quality of the composition. 


(5) The last subordinate clause signalled by ἵνα explains the purpose (or at least 
the main one) for the account. Luke shows awareness that Theophilus had al- 
ready received Christian written accounts or verbal reports.108 It seems also that 
Luke recognises a certain quality of this information since his account serves to 
underline the (already) ‘solid’ nature of the teaching. Again, direct address to 
Theophilus appears as in the main clause. It may also be that this direct address 
to Theophilus reflects the treatises in Greek literature which are addressed to in- 
dividuals but are intended for a wider readership (e.g., Letter of Aristeas; Plut., 
Life of Theseus 1.1). By bringing a fuller account, based on reliable sources and 
accurate research, Theophilus and the wider public can know more fully the so- 
lidity of the λόγος of and about Jesus and confidence in his movement. This 
rhetorical aim may be understood as undergirding the entire two-part narrative. 
The aspects of careful work, listed above, emphasise both the author’s claim for 
his abilities as historian and the reliability of the content, that is, its ἀσφάλεια 
(‘certainty’, lit. ‘non-slipperiness’). Also, the use of ἐπιγινώσκω (with ἐπί nuancing 
γινώσκω) accentuates the meaning ‘to know exactly (fully, completely)’.109

In sum, Luke invites his audience to receive his writings as part of the historio-

cal influences, particularly the Jewish literary heritage and earlier accounts about 
Jesus’ deeds and teachings. Rhetorically, he invites his readers to explore his two- 
volume work as a work of history, both for their instruction and edification (cf. 
the prefaces in Luke 1:1–4 and Acts 1:1–3). 


4.3 The Global Nature of Their Writings and of Their Audiences 


Herodotus and Luke present themselves as cosmopolitan in experience and 
knowledge. But what of their audiences? Evidence (some already mentioned 
above) supports the claim that both historians wrote for multicultural audiences. 
The significance of this is that they are extending their stories as a part of greater 
metanarratives that include theistic perspectives. Although their perceptions of 
the world are different, they do, however, offer in their unique way multicultural 
worldviews that are inclusive and enthralling. Their writings, presumably, res- 
onated with people like them, contemporary cosmopolitans. Herodotus consis- 
tently displays a cultural inclusivism through his interest in all of humanity and a 
theological polytheism that encompasses a variety of multicultural religious ex- 
pressions. Likewise, one of Luke’s theological accents is to demonstrate a soterio- 
logical inclusiveness of all peoples, that is, God himself seeks reconciliation with 
them irrespective of their ethnic or social status (e.g., Luke 24:46–48). Both au- 
thors speak in ways that their audiences might feel included in these program- 
matic metanarratives, which are the focus of Chapter 5. 


That said, Herodotus and Luke do not describe their intended audiences. 


One may assume, based on the notion of interest, without which no narrative has 
significant potential for favourable reception, that the stated themes in the incip- 
its reveal something of the interests and expectations of their audiences. The con-

tent mirrors in part what they wanted to hear for their own edification and enter- 
tainment. This reflects an underlying notion of narrativity: most narratives are 
anthropomorphic since humans enjoy reading about humans, especially about 
themselves, or about those who are like them.112 Essentially, narratives can be ex- 
plored as reflections of the “human adventure,” “the evolution of human exis- 
tence,” as “a succession of transformations.”113 In this sense, the works of Herodo- 
tus and Luke display various developments and facets of the human experience 
on a global level. Moreover, although Herodotus’ incipit is more explicitly global 
than Luke’s, both histories depict significant geographical movement from begin- 
ning to end. Both intertwine local reports of human activity from various regions, 
as threads of greater multinational themes throughout their works. 


4.3.1 The Histories 


As stated in the section on the incipit in the Histories above, two clear elements 
demonstrate Herodotus’ interest in the global arena: (1) his mention of works ac- 
complished among Greeks and barbarians, and (2) his attempt to explain the hos- 
tilities between these two extensive blocks of ethnic identity from a Greek per- 
spective. Based on these opening lines, his project is global in scope. Herodotus’ 
curiosity, presumably, reflects the audience’s desire to know more about the 
world and how various cultures fit together. Herodotus is interested in other peo- 
ples for their part in the Eurasian conflicts and simply for their ‘otherness’. 


This can be supported by two complementary aspects regarding Herodotus’ 


audiences for his oral performances and for his final composition. The relation 
between the two, that is, whether the existing forms of the Histories reflect what 
Herodotus delivered in oral performances, has been studied in great detail and 
has not resulted in consensus.114 The best approach is to hold the two in tension, 
concurring with Waterfield, “No one would claim, then, that Herodotus recited 
the entire work, over any number of days and nights; but at the same time it 
would be foolish to deny that he could have, and even might have, given recita- 
tions of chunks of it.”115 Herodotus could have read one scroll at a time, similar to

The process of research, writing, and oral delivery. Rosaria Munson’s discussion 
on Herodotus’ original audiences attempts to reconstruct the compositional sett- 
ing(s) and the audiences that may have enjoyed readings of (parts of) the Histo- 
ries.118 The Histories may have represented a record of performances or potential 
ones. The redactional work on this collection may have been revised over a long 
period. Some references to events in the text point to moments when he was writ- 
ing, but there are no dates about publication of a complete text. Scholars have 
noticed significant echoes in the fifth-century tragedies and comedies that suggest 
early knowledge of the Histories in Athens.119 Thucydides (from Athens) certainly 
knew Herodotus’ work, but it is not clear how and when he became acquainted 
with it, whether first as an auditor and then as a reader.120 Yet, in one important 
aside (Hist. 7.138–9), it is evident that Herodotus is not addressing an exclusively 
Athenian audience, since he expresses the opinion – knowing that it “will offend 
a great many people” – that the war with Persia would have never been won 
without Athens. Nevertheless, it is difficult to ascertain whether this parenthetical 
remark reflects the implied readership for the whole of the Histories or for that 
particular part of the narrative. Like many other contemporary Greek intellectu- 
als from Asia, Herodotus spent much of his life travelling, yet this did not hinder 
his intellectual pursuits or make him dependent on Athens’ cultural milieu.121 


Some idea of the final redactional activity can be deduced from the text it- 


self. Munson notes that explicit references to events between 479 (the last histori-

Besides the evidence pointing to reception of readings in Athens, Thurii has 


also been suggested as one of the primary audiences that received parts or all of 
the composition. Yet, as stated above, Herodotus neither mentions Thurii specifi- 
cally, nor his travels in the West. We also do not know when he joined the Panhel- 
lenic colony in Thurii or how long he lived there. Nevertheless, gleaned from the 
work itself, various passages “reveal familiarity with that part of the world or ap- 
pear to address listeners for whom Southern Italy was home.”125 Thurii was sup- 
ported by Athens to further its influence in Italy. The new colony had a utopian 
feel to it, because people from various cities, even with divergent perspectives, 
were invited to set its foundations. In this sense, Panhellenic (i.e., what the 
Greeks have in common) could also include some diversity of origins and culture 
in the Greek-speaking world. Thus, the political and cultural circumstances in 
Thurii may have provided a receptive audience for Herodotus’ knowledge of the 
world and lessons drawn from it. This then may have been the “ultimate implied 
audience.”126

various sources that suggest the gradual process of writing as well as knowledge 
of the Histories by the literary elite in Athens, support for the multicultural inter- 
est in the Histories can be assumed from the content itself. Herodotus is admired 
for his diplomatic and fair treatment of foreign peoples and their customs, which 
Asheri describes: “In this respect too, Herodotus shows himself a fine disciple of 
Homer and Aeschylus. Also, in this attitude it is clear how he could easily be 
branded as philobarbaros, as committing an act of political and cultural betray- 
al.”127 Plutarch, to whom this epithet ‘barbarian-friend’ is ascribed, hyperbolically 
deplores Herodotus’ excessive (and biased) multicultural interest: “He is also 
such a pro-barbarian that he acquits Busiris of the charge of human sacrifice and 
murder of strangers. He bears witness to the strict piety and justice of all Egyp-

One must remember that Plutarch’s context was not the same as Herodotus’, but

Regardless of Plutarch’s opinions on Herodotus, it is important to take notice 


of these facts within the narrative itself. Herodotus’ coverage of numerous peo- 
ples (Lydians, Persians, Babylonians, Massagetae, Egyptians, Ethiopians, Indians, 
Scythians, Libyans, Thracians, etc.) is not only a reflection of his curiosity in their 
customs, but also, in some cases, evidence of his movements in which he had 
more than conversations with his informants, but perhaps also audiences from 
those places. In sum, Herodotus’ interest in a significant number of peoples may 
mirror the audience(s) for whom he spoke and wrote. In its broadest sense, some 
treatments of these peoples could be the result of presentations on, or at least 
conversations with, those particular groups. 


Audience for the long, written composition. To drive a rigid wedge between 
Herodotus’ public lectures and his (final) scrolls is not plausible.130 How the 
smaller sections accreted to a longer, final document is not entirely clear. But, as 
Bakker argues, the written form itself can also be understood as an enactment of 
Herodotus’ enquiries, as he invites readers to explore with him various reports 
and consequential narrative trajectories.131 Yet the question remains concerning 
the audience for the written documents, the “final composition” as it were. Here, 
again, we encounter some degree of uncertainty, thus reconstructions remain hy- 
pothetical. 


Stewart Flory’s provocative article, “Who read Herodotus’ Histories?,” also 


supports the idea of a limited literary elite as primary audience, owing to the lim- 
ited number of potential readers and reading situations of the long work in 
Herodotus’ times.132 For Flory, “there is no convincing evidence that the work was 
even widely known in the late fifth century.”133 He finds the evidence unconvinc- 
ing that the allusions to Herodotus in fifth-century tragedies and comedies sup- 
port knowledge and appreciation of the Histories by the general population. 
While Flory does not deny the possibility of public readings of excerpts, he rejects 
the idea that public readings were organised for listening to the entire work as 
we know it (Flory estimates fifty or more hours).134 Thus, for example, he dismiss- 
es Lucian of Samosata’s anecdote about Herodotus’ reading at Olympia’s four-

scrolls135 and the final collection could not have been commensurate for memori- 
sation (in comparison to shorter readings of poetry), nor for public readings with 
limited attention spans.136 In addition, the minimal literacy for participation in 
Athenian democracy was not sufficient for the private reading of Herodotus’ 
writings.137 Yet the Histories were not impossible to read, nor written in a vacu- 
um. What the evidence suggests for Herodotus’ target group is a circle of intellec- 
tuals who had the literacy, leisure, and interest to read or listen to the entire work 
(over a given period via multiple sittings).138 Again, the Panhellenic (and multicul- 
tural?) community in Thurii may have provided an ideal situation for Herodotus 
to collect and connect the various excerpts through multiple narrative threads. 
Whatever the circumstances were surrounding the final collection of the entire 
project, it is certainly plausible that Herodotus performed readings, at least of ex- 
cerpts, upon request in various parts of the world where he travelled. It seems 
judicious to hold these in tension, diachronically (i.e., a history of public readings 
with accompanying scripts) and synchronically (i.e., a final collection of these 
readings, reformulated in a written project). 


In conclusion, more narrowly, a multicultural audience with shared curiosi- 


ty for the greater world might also be reflected in this vast palette of ethnograph- 
ic treatments. The final redaction in Thurii for a Panhellenic group of intellectu- 
als, as suggested by Munson, and supported by Flory’s contribution that some 
group of elites, such as the literary elite in Athens and elsewhere, may be the 
most plausible alternative for such an extensive work in its final written form.

based on evidence in the two volumes pertaining to language, literary genre, con-

Language. Regardless of Luke’s ethnicity, many Jews in the diaspora continued to 
use Greek as their main language well into the Roman Imperial period, as did 
many other peoples. The significant impact of Hellenisation on Jewish communi- 
ties dismisses a strict dichotomy between Greek and Jewish livelihood.140 All of 
the texts in the New Testament were written in Greek to address the needs of 
multicultural churches at the end of the first century and – especially for the gos- 
pels as messages about Jesus – to reach as many people as possible. It follows 
then that Luke’s writings were accessible to Jewish and non-Jewish readers and 
auditors.141 Luke also provides glosses for Hebrew terms for non-Jewish readers 
(e.g., Acts 1:19). As stated above, Luke’s addressee, “Theophilus,”142 may have res- 
onated with readers who considered themselves or aspired to be friends of God.143 


Literary genre. Based on discussions above on the influence of the Greek historio- 
graphical tradition, it may be asserted that Luke not only chose to write in Greek 
to reach a greater public, but he also expressed his thoughts through a well- 
known literary genre in the Mediterranean basin.144 Luke anchored his descrip- 
tion of the past in a way that made sense to people of his times. By evoking a 
historiographical methodology in the first incipit (Luke 1:1–4), Luke used a mode 
of discourse that could be interpreted by the literary elite, and that was accessible 
to auditors of the general public. It was the cultural space that he wished to en- 
gage with. 


To this end, Luke proposes a theological and geopolitical experience – which 


begins in Jerusalem and must end in Rome145 – through a variety of literary de- 
vices and content that first-century audiences appreciated: inspiring and intrigu-

It is necessary to introduce briefly the question of the literary distinctiveness 


of Acts. As will be noted in the introductory section to Chapter 10, Luke’s first vol- 
ume is largely dependent on Mark’s Gospel and, to a lesser degree, on other sour- 
ces. His second volume, however, appears to be largely his own creation. Except 
for his own claimed participation in certain scenes (i.e., the ‘we passages’), his 
sources are not indicated.149 They still remain elusive to modern research.150 Fur- 
thermore, this account of the first thirty years of Jesus’ movement does not find 
any contemporary equal, worthy of comparison.151 Thus, compared to the first 
volume, the second volume reflects, to a greater degree, the author’s experience 
and knowledge.152 This partly explains why biblical scholarship continues to dis- 
cuss the generic differences between Luke and Acts, and consequently whether 
the two volumes should be interpreted together.153 Yet some differences between 
the two volumes are readily understandable. The events presented in the second 
volume are closer to the narrator’s lifetime and he is closer to them, culturally 
and geographically, admitting that he may have come from Asia Minor or 
Greece.154 In short, the second volume is more distinctive in its narrative than the 
first, which relies on Mark’s Gospel.

become more appealing and relevant to traditional interests in Classical studies, 
as the narrative moves from Judea westward through the Mediterranean Basin to

Rome.155 The focus on events originating in the Levant and moving through the 
Near East also aligns with the expansion of Classical studies to include a broader 
understanding of the ancient world beyond Greece and Rome. For example, 
Luke’s knowledge of imperial judicial procedures is reliable.156 His level of Greek 
also places him among the educated elite, a man of culture.157 One of Luke’s inter- 
ests, then – like crossover historians such as Berossus, Manetho, and Josephus158 – 
was to make known a marginal story from a distant Roman province and a lesser- 
known religion, showing their relevance and consequences for the oikoumenē. 
Theologically, like the writings of his contemporaries, e.g., Josephus and Plutarch, 
Luke’s project serves to provide an alternative view of the divine realm and, con- 
sequently, also of the Empire.159 His narrative “defends the divine,” as Jesus’ 
movement comes in contact and (at times) clashes with competing religious nar- 
ratives.160 In Acts, this becomes especially relevant as Luke depicts – through acts 
and speeches – the superiority of Jesus as a ‘saviour god’ compared to the gods of 
the peoples. 


Globally relevant content. Although the content initially focuses on events and 
people in Judea and anchored in the history of Israel, hints in the first chapters 
signal the author’s interest in drawing his readers into an exploration of a divine 
plan that will be accomplished among the Jews and other peoples.161 Reducing 
this to a Jewish story in a falsely homogenous Jewish context disregards Judea as 
a Roman province and a part of the Roman story and greater Mediterranean nar- 
rative. Early on, Luke anchors the story in the greater Roman administration 
(Luke 2:1–2; 3:1–2). The divine plan, announced at the beginning of Luke’s Gos- 
pel, passes through a great number of cultural spaces, from Jerusalem to Rome, 
via the message of ‘the kingdom of God’.162 Ethnically speaking, then, it was in- 
tended to be a meaningful narrative to a broad audience.

If the offer of divine reconciliation to all peoples is the main theme of Luke’s 


narrative, spiritual opposition to God’s plan appears early through the counter- 
proposal of the διάβολος in the temptation scene (Luke 4:1–13). This ‘devil’ at- 
tempts to sabotage God’s plans through Jesus by offering an appealing proposi- 
tion: authority and glory of all the kingdoms of the world (πάσας τὰς βασιλείας 
τῆς οἰκουμένης, 4:5–6). In short, the devil is said to know God’s intentions to con- 
duct a plan of salvation extended to all peoples; thus, he counters it with a more 
alluring adventure with respect to making an impact on the peoples. This may be 
understood as a foil for understanding Luke-Acts. 


Consequently, Luke’s literary project depicts a multicultural human experi- 


ence that is consistently shaped by divine intervention. To this end, Luke relates 
episodes that illustrate both Jewish and non-Jewish reception and rejection of 
God’s project of reconciliation for all peoples.163 This recalls the narratological 
principle that readers desire to hear stories about people, especially about them- 
selves or people like them. Luke gives regular attention to non-Jewish individuals 
and structures, especially Roman rule and administration. Roman narrative pres- 
ence resonated with all readers – citizens and all others. Luke highlights positive 
depictions of Romans, especially centurions.164 Negative examples are mainly tak- 
en from the elite, such as Pontius Pilate (condemnation of Jesus, Luke 23:1–23); 
Felix (corrupt; unjustly detained Paul, Acts 24:26–27) and Festus (unable or un- 
willing to resolve Paul’s case, Acts 25:1–26:32). The regular presence of various 
Caesars is also good to note for background, but they do not intervene directly in 
episodes and are not explicitly placed in negative light.165 Foremost among Ro- 
mans is the apostle Paul, chief protagonist of the second book. Paul incarnates the 
various narrative and cultural strands, as an ethnic Jew and Roman citizen from 
Greek Tarsus, a “not insignificant city” (Acts 21:39). 


This dual interest in Jews and non-Jews may be considered Luke’s unique 


contribution in relation to the other canonical evangelists whose literary projects 
do not specifically recount Jesus’ reception among the peoples. Consequently, 
Luke’s choice of content encourages various types of persons in his audience to 
consider the story and their part in this global project of reconciliation (of which

Geography. The geography of Luke-Acts also implies not only a global authorial 
perspective, but also a wide-ranging interest on the part of the readers. These 
writings correspond well with other contemporary descriptions of the juncture 
between Jewish and non-Jewish peoples (e.g., Josephus and Philo). The macro- 
level movement is from Jerusalem to Rome, from the first scene with Zechariah in 
the temple (Luke 1:5–25) to the last scene with the apostle Paul in semi-captivity 
(Acts 28:16–31). In between these religious and political capitals, there is move- 
ment of the word about Jesus – as a message or report about him – alluded to in 
the first incipit (Luke 1:2). Acts 1:8 also orients the audience’s expectations by 
framing the rest of the work through Jesus’ order to his disciples to be witnesses 
well beyond traditional Jewish regions.166 The Pentecost scene in Jerusalem ex- 
plicitly highlights this (Acts 2:1–13). Therein Luke provides an extensive list of 
peoples, from East to West, which are represented by individuals.167 He also ex- 
plains that they heard God’s praises in their own language (and not in one lan- 
guage such as Greek or Hebrew). The movement of the word about Jesus is de- 
picted as beginning centripetally in Jerusalem, then continuing from that point on 
centrifugally, taking place in many cases far away from Jewish traditional lands, 
as Jesus’ witnesses accomplish their mandate (Acts 1:8).168 


First reading. With these observations, we may try to reconstruct the first readers 
of Luke’s writings, that is, the immediate context of reception of his two-part nar- 
rative. Similar to Flory’s exploration of Herodotus’ immediate real readers, F. 
Gerald Downing proposes a plausible context for the first reading of Luke-Acts.169 


Some qualifications are necessary for this comparison. First, one must keep in 
mind that Luke’s project was significantly shorter than Herodotus’ multi-scroll 
work. Also, we do not know the length of time that passed between the composi- 
tion and reception of Luke’s first volume and the second. But it is easy to imagine 
that such reading events were not difficult to organise in the first-century context.

social condition was required to enter this network of Jesus’ followers. This nar- 
rative world was very familiar to them; this was their world. 


4.4 Conclusion 


The Histories and Luke-Acts are works of historians who were cosmopolitan in 
experience and knowledge. The Greek context of Herodotus and the Greco-Ro- 
man context of Luke each influence their writing by shaping the size of their 
worlds and therefore the narratives, as well as the agōnes therein. Herodotus 
wrote between two great wars and saw patterns emerging while writing in the 
face of the internecine Peloponnesian War. Luke knew the Jewish hostility to- 
wards the Romans, and he wrote – as an insider of a growing movement in Asia 
and Europe – in the wake of the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE. Chapters 7–12 
explore how their histories respond to the contemporary challenges of their audi- 
ences.

Through their incipits, they present themselves as narrators who apply a 


methodology to explore the stated themes, seeking to stimulate and educate audi- 
ences having similar interests. They tell stories that were presumably considered 
relevant to their potentially ethnically diverse, Greek-speaking audiences. To this 
end, both literary projects link and make known local events as globally relevant 
and connected. And some of Herodotus’ ethnographic research may have been 
new to his audience. Their histories become a part of the world’s history, as re- 
ports from various regions were linked together through various threads in the 
narrative in order to explore societal themes, e.g., political, ethnographical, and 
religious. They could contend for geopolitical and religious causes and effects. In 
so doing, they were able to contribute to the development of a global theistic 
worldview, including the presence of the gods or the God of Israel. This under- 
lines well the rhetorical strength of global prophetic voices. Their prophetic voic- 
es were unique and have had lasting legacies. But for the sake of clarity, it is good 
to restate that I am not claiming that this link between Herodotus and Luke is 
unique to the two of them. The first section gave a broad view of Greek historiog- 
raphy with a focus on the prophetic voice as a common strand evidenced in the 
historiographical record. 


Having considered the value of the incipit, the next chapter addresses an- 


other significant narrative device: the ‘plupast’. Through this technique, histori- 
ans anchored their core narratives in the flow of previously occurred past events. 
Herodotus and Luke employ this technique theologically, namely, how a ‘divine 
plupast’ can authenticate a core narrative by demonstrating the perceived influ- 
ence of the divine realm on past events that had already occurred.

5 Extending Theistic Metanarratives: The Divine Plupast 


in Herodotus’ Histories and in Luke-Acts 


We have seen how Herodotus and Luke use their opening lines to orient their 
audiences’ expectations. Another rhetorical choice that they had to consider was 
at what point in history should their stories begin in order to prepare their read- 
ers to enter the world of the core narrative. Perceptive historians think about 
their audiences’ cognitive needs so that they can engage with the narrative’s 
main themes. Instead of beginning in medias res, Herodotus and Luke, like other 
historians, describe prior events and epochs leading to the historical period un- 
der examination. This initial temporal backdrop is congenially called ‘the past be- 
fore the past’ or the ‘plupast’. Hermeneutically efficient and narratively captivat- 
ing, plupast sections can be valuable for audiences, since “stories build on other 
stories; writers and readers apply familiar codes in order to make sense of what 
they say and what they read.”1 In historical discourse, an explicit or implicit part 
of this hermeneutical code may be a theistic metanarrative, a broader story of the 
divine realm undergirding the core narrative. 


One of the hermeneutical challenges for Herodotus and his successors was 


precisely how to integrate the divine into historical prose. One way was to anchor 
their histories through previous theological expressions, for example, stories 
about the divine from the distant or recent past, religious beliefs, practices, sym- 
bolism, objects, and even names of divinities. The argument of this chapter is that 
Herodotus and Luke build on various components of theistic metanarratives that 
had influenced their own prophetic voices. As a result, through the act of writing, 
they extend these narratives in space and time, well beyond their local and occa- 
sional oral presentations. 


The present chapter and the following one delve into their ‘divine plupast’ to 


consider how such stories contribute to the development of their core narratives 
and audiences’ reception. The next chapter builds on this by considering their ‘di- 
vine constellations’, expressions of the divine in general and what kinds of beings 
were considered divine. Consequently, in a preliminary sense, both chapters pre- 
pare for the analysis of the core narratives in Chapters 7–9 on the Histories and 
Chapters 10–12 on Luke-Acts. Below, we first flesh out the notion of plupast and 
its value for historiography, then we survey the ‘divine plupast’ on the macronar- 
rative level of the Histories and Luke-Acts. Finally, we explore two key plupast 
episodes that have programmatic value for the overall narratives. 


1 
Pelling (2013) 1–20. 


5.1 The Plupast in Historiography 


5.1.1 The Historian’s Plupast 


The notion of a ‘historian’s plupast’ is a constructive way of describing various 
narrative techniques evoking the past that precedes the historian’s focused past 
(or core narrative). However, one will search in vain for a definition of plupast in 
modern dictionaries. In the introductory chapter of Time and Narrative in Ancient 
Historiography: The ‘Plupast’ from Herodotus to Appian, Jonas Grethlein and 
Christopher Krebs2 provide a general description of the ‘author’s plupast’,3 which 
I summarise and expand here. ‘Plupast’ is inspired by the nomenclature and logic 
of the ‘pluperfect’ verbal tense (in English and various European languages), 
which allows speakers to provide background information for understanding the 
main topic expressed through other tenses.4 As in other languages, the pluperfect 
is normally not used extensively to carry a narrative discourse. Rather, it is used 
to punctuate the narrator’s description or a character’s discourse. In a similar 
way, the historian’s plupast, scattered throughout a narrative, adds fullness of 
historical detail by giving an additional retrospective view. Compared to other 
frequently used terms, such as intertextuality and exemplarity, Grethlein and 
Krebs consider ‘plupast’ more inclusive and capable of illuminating “the tempo- 
ral complexity of ancient historical narratives.”5 Three categories help classify oc- 
currences of the plupast: time, voice, and form of reference. The first two are 
drawn mainly from narrative theory, while the third “lies outside the narratologi- 
cal framework.”6 


The first element, ‘time’, is similar to other expressions describing textual 


anachronisms, looking backwards in time such as analepsis, retrospection, flash- 
back, and epic regression.7 The historian’s plupast can be internal or external in 
relation to the core narrative. The former refers to actions completed within the 
historian’s narrative, and the latter to actions extending beyond the narrative

Grethlein and Krebs (2012) 1–16.

discussion of the definition is primarily limited to the section by Grethlein and Krebs.

regression’) is natural to human story-tellers, as any reader who has been a narrator knows 
well.”

framework.8 In essence, the use of plupast “allows the historian to extend the 
scope of his narrative.”9 Moreover, borrowing from Gérard Genette’s theory on 
time, the temporal aspect can be further described by ‘reach’, which means how 
far back in time the reference carries the narration, while ‘extent’ signifies the 
duration of an event.10 


The second element, ‘voice’ (or ‘focus’), explores how the plupast can be re- 


called by the narrator (historian) or by a character within the narrative. These 
uses of authorial and actorial voices add various layers and complexity to the 
temporal aspect. Their references to the past need not be limited to exempla 
(moral lessons), since plupast material can be evinced for various purposes. In 
addition, these retrospective interpretations can provide intriguing comparisons 
between the points of view of historians and their characters. 


The third category, ‘form of reference’, is the broadest, since it includes mul- 


tiple elements that transmit memory of the plupast. These analeptic elements can 
be quite overt (e.g., events and quotations) or subtle such as embedded elements 
within the narrator’s or historical character’s description. Grethlein and Krebs 
describe four elements, but the list is certainly not exhaustive. Of course, the most 
basic form of the plupast belongs to the narrator’s (or speaker’s) description of 
prior events with regard to the primary narrative. To this, one can add plupast 
forms of intertextuality (but not exclusively limited to texts), which are very com- 
mon, such as quotations, allusions, literary topoi, and metaphors. Plupast forms 
can also integrate non-intertextual elements such as material entities (e.g., tab- 
lets, temples, monuments) or general concepts that do not necessarily allude to a 
particular source (e.g., political and military theory). It may also include lists or 
catalogues such as military logistics, political figures, or even human and divine 
genealogies. All of these have the rhetorical capacity to recall the plupast in a 
meaningful way and provide additional layers of temporal complexity. 


These analeptic elements evoking the plupast can be explored via three 


main questions: “To which time does the plupast refer (in absolute terms and in 
relation to the narrative)? Who focalises and narrates the plupast? By what 
means is the plupast evoked?”11 The section below elucidates how this type of 
analysis can offer interesting angles for historiographical research. In section 5.3 
we will consider two passages, one each from Herodotus and Luke, that particu- 
larly exhibit the force of the rhetorical plupast in preparation for the reception of 
the core narrative.

5.1.2 The Plupast’s Value for Historiographical Research 


Undeniably, the concept of plupast owes much to other interpretative methods 
describing temporality in narratives. The advantage of this historiographical con- 
cept over others is that “the framework of the plupast offers a fuller view of the 
dynamic play of historical narratives with different levels of the past.”12 In the 
following part of the introductory chapter, Grethlein and Krebs explain how this 
approach of describing the past adds to historical enquiry. They mention two us- 
ages of the historian’s plupast: (1) the historian’s plupast within historical seman- 
tics,13 and (2) the historian’s plupast as metahistory.14 I summarise these briefly. 


As regards historical semantics, the historian’s plupast helps understand the 


construction of historical meaning through the juxtaposition of plupast and past, 
each one illuminating the other through “similarities, contrasts and refractions.”15 


This temporal interplay via the voice of the narrator or a character creates addi- 
tional layers of meaning and invites readers to reflect on their own historical un- 
derstanding. This becomes particularly stimulating when comparing diverse ver- 
sions of an event by the historian for his external audience and by a historical 
character for his internal audience. The result can potentially destabilise the nar- 
rative, causing readers to think critically about the past. 


Consequently, the historian’s plupast sheds light on metahistory, the self- 


definition of historiography, and the self-understanding (even self-fashioning) of 
the historian. Thus, for example, the use of a plupast element recalled by a histor- 
ical character is similar to the epic song-within-song. Thus, in the hands of the 
historian, the plupast becomes a type of mise en abyme, in that “an act […] is em- 
bedded in a commemorative text.”16 Certainly, writing history and recalling the 
past are not identical, but they are both acts of memory and were (and still are) 
influenced by rhetorical techniques.17 In this sense, the use of the plupast by his- 
torians and their characters reflects the pragmatic dimension of oral and written 
historical narratives. The historian’s use of the plupast can highlight lessons 
learned from the past that support rhetorical aims, but it can also underline dif- 
ferences in perspectives, thus creating dissonance between the author and cer- 
tain characters. From this angle, one can explicate historical nuances, such as ex- 
amples of synkrisis evincing resemblance between historian and characters and 
embedded speeches. Again, they may shed additional light, not only on the char- 
acters, but on the personae of the historians themselves (i.e., their self-fashion- 
ing) as well as their own understanding of their craft.

5.1.3 Theistic Metanarratives via the Historian’s Plupast 


That historians link earlier traces of the divine to their own narratives is support- 
ing evidence that historians can perform a prophet-like role in their own soci- 
eties. These plupast narratives may include explicit or implicit theological ele- 
ments. We can speak of the extension of smaller theistic narratives, and, on a 
larger scale, even theistic metanarratives. ‘Theistic metanarrative’ is not restrict- 
ed to the transmission of an official, theological dogma, but rather it refers to 
those generally accepted beliefs and stories about the divine sphere. That is, the 
nature and interventions of God, gods, and other spiritual beings as well as the 
names by which they are invoked (cf. Chapter 6). 


As a part of their prophetic voices, Herodotus and Luke connect their own 


narratives to previous theistic metanarratives, thus prolonging the former stories 
in time and extending them in space. Herodotus and Luke anchor their own histo- 
ries against this backdrop. By making them available orally and textually, these 
historians monumentalise these theistic frameworks for their generations and 
those to follow. From the historian’s perspective, the shadow of the plupast has an 
effect not only on the interpretation of the past, but even of the present and fu- 
ture: “The eyes of the Greek historian envisage history as a space in which plu- 
past, past, present and future mirror one another as in a kaleidoscope.”18 How 
much more so, then, when the divine is perceived as being in some ways 
supratemporal and able to influence the course of history. 


The rhetorical strength of the divine plupast consists of various techniques 


evoking earlier divine interventions. These may resonate with audiences who al- 
ready know the stories and help them to grasp recounted historical events. Debo- 
rah Boedeker’s essay “Epic Heritage and Mythical Patterns in Herodotus” helpful- 
ly clarifies how Herodotus draws upon mythical patterns from Homer and other 
authors and blends them in his historical discourse of more recent events.19 The 
result is often a narrative with an overlapping of the mythical and historical. Uni- 
versal concerns are echoed, paralleled, and blended, especially in those narrative 
contexts where oral rhetorical techniques are employed to engage internal and 
external audiences. Consequently, in certain passages, it becomes difficult to 
tease out the historical from the mythical. For example, within the broad narra- 
tive framework of the Trojan War for Herodotus’ Persian Wars,20 Agamemnon’s 
dream that leads him to defeat Troy (Il. 2.1–40) finds an intriguing parallel in 
Xerxes’ dream which leads the Persians to invade Greece (7.12–18). Another ex- 
ample is Herodotus’ description of divine retribution falling on Artaÿctes, who 
had robbed from the shrine of the hero Protesilaus in Troy (9.116–20). This story

is richly illuminated by Homer’s story of Protesilaus, who was the first Greek vic- 
tim at Troy (Il. 2.695–709).21 Through this, Herodotus underlines divine activity 
within the ancient Europe-Asia conflict. 


In various ways, then, narrative patterns may contribute to the theological 


construction of the broader story and consequently help audiences to gain a 
deeper understanding of the divine sphere. A few syllogisms can be examined: 
“As this divinity had acted in that situation, so also he or she acted here.” Alterna- 
tively, “It is known that this divinity acts in this way; thus, it was not surprising 
that he or she also acted in this way.” This may be due to an established pattern in 
previous epochs by means of (collective and cumulative) observation or imagina- 
tion of divine interventions. In a word, this can be understood as the develop- 
ment of a divine plupast. These and other types of theological formulas can be 
powerful techniques for supporting a micronarrative, and when used regularly 
and perhaps strategically enough, even an entire macronarrative.22 Thomas Har- 
rison aptly evinces this – commenting on the nature of Herodotus’ work – that 
“the origins of history-writing were (to a significant degree) theological.”23 The 
point is that the histories of Herodotus and Luke are both anchored in existing 
theistic traditions, which they presuppose or evoke as divine plupasts in support 
of their own core narratives. 


We may consider both historians as pioneers of a particular historiographi- 


cal tradition, but they were not historians with prophetic voices in a void; they 
extend the prophetic voices of their own theistic heritages. By doing so, they em- 
bed divine interventions in the chain of cause and effect in the human sphere. 
This raises various questions: In what ways do their histories reflect the recep- 
tion of a theistic heritage? In what ways does a divine plupast help to anchor the 
recounted history? How does Herodotus incorporate the mythopoetic traditions 
in his narrative? Does he use something identifiable as a spatium mythicum in his 
narrative strategy, distinguishing it from or embedding it in his spatium his- 
toricum?24 As regards Luke, how does the history of the relationship between God 
and Israel support the author’s claims about Jesus of Nazareth and his movement 
that extends from Jerusalem to Rome? Besides this clearly evoked theistic meta- 
narrative, what other religious traditions does Luke use or assume in his narra- 
tive? And are there competing theistic metanarratives at work in the authorial 
and actorial perceptions of the divine? 


Plupast theory helps to address these questions. This shows that background 


studies and narrative theory are complementary exegetical approaches that help

unpack the material transmitted in plupast form. To explore these questions, 
when discussing the divine plupast of our historians’ works, it is helpful to re- 
member two elements. First, historians often presuppose a religious metanarra- 
tive and thus do not argue for its validity, such as the existence of a divine dimen- 
sion and its intervention in human affairs, hence the necessity of human 
responses (e.g., worship, reverence, obeisance) and appropriate uses of material 
objects devoted to cultic practices (e.g., temples, sacrifices). Herodotus and Luke 
generally assume that their audiences agree with their understanding of the di- 
vine. They expect their audiences to fill in those pieces of information that are not 
explained regarding the theistic metanarrative that they have received and now 
call to mind.25 There are, to my knowledge, no explicit religious polemics ad- 
dressed to their audiences. 


Second, a plupast on a macronarrative level may also be assumed by authors 


in their narratives. Gaps may be present that need to be filled in by readers (or 
need to be accepted as not pertinent).26 Proofs are provided when deemed neces- 
sary. When historians consider a plupast element important enough to mention, 
they do so explicitly in various ways. Some of the first questions, then, that an 
author of historical narrative must consider are: At what point in time should the 
narrative begin? How much of previous contexts must be provided so that read- 
ers can fully enter the world of the focused narrative? On a macronarrative level, 
plupast material used by historians can be very brief. Mark the Evangelist intro- 
duces John the Baptist in a few verses (1:1–8) then moves on to Jesus’ baptism by 
John (1:9–11). Conversely, Polybius tells his audience that he will begin with the 
140th Olympiad (Hist. 1.3), but he uses the first two books to explain Roman and 
Carthaginian history to his Greek readers. The narrative proper begins with Book 
3. Below I propose a view of how Herodotus and Luke orient their readers tempo- 
rally and hermeneutically, as they insert divine plupast sections at the beginning 
of their works and in other parts scattered throughout.

5.2 Extending Theistic Metanarratives through a Divine Plupast 


in the Histories and in Luke-Acts 


5.2.1 Divine Plupast on the Macronarrative Level in the Histories 


We begin by viewing Herodotus’ project on a macronarrative level in order to 
consider any theistic elements in the plupast material.27 As the narrative devel- 
ops, Herodotus will consistently provide much more plupast material. Here we 
focus on the first main section of Herodotus’ plupast. The incipit announces that a 
focus will be on aspects of the plupast, namely, the cause(s) of the conflicts be- 
tween the Greeks and the barbarians – of whom the Persians will be the main 
actors.28 


At what point in the narrative does Herodotus begin his narrative proper, 


viz. the actual conflicts between Greeks and barbarians? And what is prior to that 
narrative focus? In the discussion below, Croesus is understood as the link be- 
tween the Greeks and the barbarians.29 The shift from the plupast and the past 
turns on him, with his presence overlapping in both parts. The boundaries could 
be extended in either direction.30 I think, however, that Herodotus wishes to give 
a good sense of what Croesus had done and who he was, so that the reader could 
better understand what factors contributed to Croesus’ foolish decision to attack 
Cyrus (1.46–56). There is a link between Herodotus’ authority as historian and 
the divine authority he draws from the oracle in the Croesus logos.31 In this sense, 
Croesus and the Lydian kingdom are the geopolitical hinge between the Greeks 
and the Persians. This chapter, therefore, fleshes out the first part of what Harri- 
son refers to as the “causative skeleton” of the Histories.32 


Despite Herodotus’ numerous digressions, and digressions within digres- 


sions, the overall structure of the nine books discloses his focus on the reigns of 
one Lydian king, Croesus (560–547) and four Persian kings: Cyrus (559–530) in 
Book 1, Cambyses (530–522) in Book 2 and the first third of Book 3, Darius (521– 
486) in the rest of Book 3 and Books 4–6, and Xerxes (486–465/4) in Books 7–9.33 


In light of this overall structure, Herodotus’ initial focus (on the Lydian kings up

at the centre of the narrative […] the military campaigns of the four kings against

After the incipit, Herodotus moves quickly to the question about existing ex- 


planations of the causes of hostility between the Greeks and the barbarians. He 
sets aside traditions pointing to guilty parties in the abduction of four women: Io, 
Europa, Medea, and Helen. The Persians blame the Phoenicians for the first ab- 
duction, and they accuse the Greeks for the first military aggression. The Phoeni- 
cians deny the blame and point to Io’s own part in arriving in Egypt (i.e., via an 
affair with a ship captain in Argos). According to the Persians, the root problem 
for hostility between them and the Greeks – a clear reference to Homer’s Iliad – 
is the military aggression against King Priam and Ilium (i.e., Troy, situated in 
Asia). The Persians’ anachronistic argument is that Asia had already belonged to 
them, while the Greeks possessed Europe.35 This forms the basis for viewing the 
world as divided into these two major geographical blocs, a division which runs 
through the entire narrative.36 


For Herodotus, these versions of the distant past are insufficient. This is the 


first example of many where Herodotus clearly signals to his readers the limits of 
traditional material. These stories of Eurasian rivalry do not provide a solid basis 
for his enquiry. He claims to have more reliable information (1.5.3), which allows 
him to point out the verifiable cause of the hostilities. He knows the name of the 
culprit, but he withholds it from readers briefly until 1.6.1. It is Croesus, king of 
the Lydian Empire. He is the initial cause – but not the only cause – of this geopo- 
litical conflict. In the following lines, we can detect the contours of Herodotus’ 
plupast and past: “Now the Persians and the Phoenicians report these things. As 
for me, I shall not say whether one thing or another happened, [plupast →] but I 
do know the one [i.e., Croesus] who first committed unjust acts towards the Hel- 
lenes. Having described him [past →] I shall proceed with my account going 
through both small and great cities in detail” (1.5.3).37 He wishes to proceed to the 
rest of the story (προβήσομαι ἐς τὸ πρόσω τοῦ λόγου), but first he provides some

Author’s plupast = History preceding the Greco-Barbarian conflicts, i.e., not ac- 
cording to these versions of the story (1.1–5), but Herodotus’ version (1.6–45), 
which includes the identification of Croesus as initial culprit. A few important 
statements help to visualise how Herodotus distinguishes the plupast from the 
past on a macronarrative level. 


– “Before the reign of Croesus, all the Hellenes were free, because, before his time, 


the Cimmerian army came to Ionia not to subjugate cities but to plunder” 
(1.6.3). 


– “After Alyattes died, his son Croesus was thirty-five years of age when he re- 


ceived the kingdom. The first Hellenes he attacked were the Ephesians” (1.26.1). 


Since Croesus is a barbarian from the Hellenic perspective, and he is the initial 
cause of the Greco-Barbarian conflicts, all that includes the identification of Croe- 
sus with the Greeks is plupast on a macronarrative level. Outright subjugation 
seems to be in Herodotus’ mind as he singles out Croesus as the initial culprit. In 
other passages, he indicates that previous Lydian kings “took” Greek cities before 
Croesus: Gyges (716–678) took Colophon; Ardys (678–629) took Priene; Sadyattes 
(629–617) took Smyrna. But Croesus took away the Ionian Greeks’ independence 
in a collective sense. 


Author’s past = Greco-Barbarian conflicts continuing with Croesus and the Per- 
sian kings – 1.46 onward 


Once that has been established, Herodotus can proceed with the rest of his story – 
his focused past about the Greco-Barbarian conflicts – which continues with 
Croesus’ decision to attack Cyrus (1.46–56).38 This structural analysis shows how 
the large plupast section contributes to understanding Croesus’ rise to power and 
to the entire work.39 Indeed, this section introduces major themes such as the 
fragility of humans and states, divine sovereignty, and the contested geopolitical 
blocks of Europe and Asia. Here the focus will be on Book 1, chapters 6 to 25 to

The divine plupast before Croesus, the first cause of Greco-Barbarian hostilities. 
Having set aside rival alternative stories and resolved that Croesus was the initial 
cause of the Greco-Barbarian conflicts, Herodotus now provides his first digres- 
sion, an analepsis concerning royal intrigues before Croesus. Our interest will fol- 
low the hints of divine presence and intervention instead of providing a detailed 
presentation of these episodes. In this plupast material, readers discover that 
some peculiar things had happened in ca. 716 BCE that caused a major shift in 
political power, from the line of the Heraclidae to the Mermnadae. The transition 
goes from Candaules, the last of the Heraclid kings of Sardis, to Gyges (Candaules’ 
favourite bodyguard), the first of the Mermnad line of kings until it reaches Croe- 
sus five generations later.40

aristocratic families.43 According to David Asheri, the genealogy is generally unre-

Second, Herodotus signals an act of divine approval via prophecy regarding 


this royal line. The Heraclidae were entrusted with the kingdom of the Lydians by 
their princes.45 This transfer of power (ἡγεμονίη, 1.7.1) was confirmed by an ora-

and the dynasty is said to have remained in their hands for a period of five hun- 
dred and five years until Candaules (for this period, 1221–716 BCE).46 References 
to oracles for divine direction or support are a common motif in the Histories. 


Third, an allusion to the power of fate is present in the change of destiny for 


the Heraclid royal line (1.8.2). The principal cause of Candaules’ ruin appears 
somewhat ambiguous. Was it due to fate or to Candaules’ bringing destruction on 
himself because of his obsession with his wife’s beauty? Or both? The divine and 
the human seem to cooperate in his downfall. In a parenthetical remark, Herodo- 
tus foreshadows Candaules’ destiny: χρόνου δὲ οὐ πολλοῦ διελθόντος (χρῆν γὰρ

gone by (for it was necessary that evil should come to Candaules), when he spoke 
thus to Gyges.”48 Robin Waterfield’s translation (among others) underlines the 
work of fate by rendering the parenthetical clause in the indicative at the beginn- 
ing of the sentence: “Candaules was destined to come to a bad end, and so after a 
while he said to Gyges […].” In any case, what follows these temporal and causal 
phrases is the king’s foolish behaviour and ruinous proposal to Gyges.49

insists that Gyges must gaze upon the queen’s exceptional beauty, for, he says, 
“men trust their ears less than their eyes” (1.8.2). Initially, Gyges’ outright refusal 
appears exemplary (1.8.2–4) exclaiming, “I ask you to not ask me what is con- 
trary to custom (ἀνόμων)” (1.8.4). Candaules’ behaviour crossed the line of decen- 
cy and self-control, and this was an open invitation to divine wrath. The principle 
evoked by Gyges before the act, “May everyone look after his own things” (1.8.4), 
was violated. Therefore, Candaules must be punished.51 Indeed, this section is full 
of principles and aphorisms, each character using them in his or her defence. 


Yet the king’s plan prevailed, and Gyges was caught by the queen. She 


knows well that his act was a major infringement of νόμος. Someone must pay, by 
death, either the king who planned it or Gyges who saw her nakedness.52 Neither 
rebuking nor consulting her husband, the queen gives Gyges an ultimatum: ei- 
ther his own death or the assassination of the king with her help. Unsurprisingly, 
Gyges chooses the latter, and, through the death of Candaules, the Heraclid dy- 
nasty is shattered in 716 BCE. This harsh verdict, the judgement of death, is sup- 
ported by a common theme in the Histories: the violation of customs is often fol- 
lowed by divine retribution (τίσις).53 For example, in Book 3, Herodotus, 
commenting on King Cambyses’ insanity for his murders and acts of sacrilege in 
Egypt, cites Pindar’s axiom: “Custom is king of all” (3.38.4).54 There, Herodotus is 
making the point that only a madman would violate the cherished customs of a 
people in such a flagrant manner. In the case of Candaules and Gyges, although 
Herodotus does not explicitly evoke divine intervention here, his perception of 
the act can be understood as such because of his remarks about Candaules’ im- 
pending ruin and the sacred respect for customs.55

confirm or reject Gyges’ claim (1.13.1). The oracle (τὸ χρηστήριον) ordained that 
Gyges should occupy the throne (ἀνεῖλέ τε δὴ τὸ χρηστήριον καὶ ἐβασίλευσε οὕτω
