Moving then to the human dimension of religion, Herodotus mentions later 


(1.14) that Gyges became a generous supporter of the Delphic oracle by sending 
an enormous number of votive offerings (ἀναθήματα). This Gyges was also the 
first non-Greek, after the Phrygian king Midas, who gave offerings to Delphi. This 
religious connection between the Lydian Empire and Delphi was noteworthy for 
Herodotus (confirmed by many other examples), because he passes quickly over 
Gyges’ military exploits and other deeds in a few sentences (1.15.1). Gyges re- 
spected Delphi, which was positive from Herodotus’ perspective. 


However, the sixth and final element shows that Gyges received additional 


information from the Pythia (priestess of Apollo) that confirmed who really was 
in control, namely the gods and fate. The oracle also stated that vengeance for the 
Heraclidae would be taken, not on Gyges, but on his posterity in the fifth genera- 
tion of the Mermnadae (1.13; cf. table in 5.2.1). The Lydians and their kings disre- 
garded this part of the oracle until it was fulfilled. Gyges had a good deal, not so 
for Croesus. Did Herodotus really believe these prophetic utterances? It seems so, 
since he takes the time to describe its fulfilment. Indeed, apparently, Croesus was 
ignorant of all this until the Pythia revealed it to him when Croesus despairingly 
lamented his defeat at the hands of Cyrus and wrongly accused Apollo of his lack 
of support (see 1.91). Thus, the short-lived dynasty of Gyges underlines the theme 
of rising and falling of men, kings, and city-states. This concludes the discussion 
about the divine past concerning the shift in power from Candaules to Gyges, the 
first king of the Mermnad line. 


Other instances of the divine plupast between Gyges and Croesus. On a macronar- 
rative level between Gyges and Croesus (1.15–25), Herodotus recounts briefly the 
reigns of Ardys and Sadyattes (1.15–16). What draws Herodotus’ attention is the 
conflict between the Lydians and the Milesians, and particularly the Lydians’ mil- 
itary strategy of crop burning for eleven consecutive years (1.17–18). At this point 
in the narrative (1.19), Herodotus presents the first example of many that con- 
cerns human offence to sacred structures. He assures his readers that he has re- 
ceived this information from the Delphians and other details from the Milesians 
(1.20). In the twelfth year, this annual burning of Milesian crops grew out of con- 
trol and burned down the temple of Athena in Assesus. Their apparent lack of 
reaction to this sacrilege is astonishing: no one took much notice of it. Back in 
Sardis, however, Alyattes became very ill and was not able to recover. Herodotus 
does not know what pushed Alyattes to think that it might be a good idea to con- 
sult the oracle in Delphi. But he did so, and his messengers to Delphi were told 


Part II Herodotus and Luke: Preparing to Hear Their Prophetic Voices 
170 


right away that the Pythia would not respond to their questions until the temple 
of Athena had been rebuilt. The principle is clear: no reparation for the damage, 
no oracle. 


Some lines later (1.22), Herodotus reveals that Alyattes obeyed the Pythia’s 


command, and he made double reparation, building two temples for Athena in 
Assesus. This resulted in Alyattes’ recovery. Further on, Herodotus reports that 
Alyattes thanked Delphi with a very generous gift (still present in Delphi in 
Herodotus’ times). The Lydian royal family thus knew the powers of Apollo in 
Delphi and this relationship would intensify through the experiences of Croesus. 
Another implicit lesson is drawn for Herodotus’ readers: always show respect to 
sanctuaries, shrines, and temples – indeed, to anything belonging to the gods. If 
they are treated sacrilegiously, Herodotus demonstrates that divine retribution 
will follow sooner or later (e.g., the story of Cambyses, 3.37). This foreshadows 
the motif of Persian impiety, particularly the destruction of sacred objects, and 
the subsequent Greek desire for vengeance (e.g., 8.144.2). 


Finally, before reaching the stories about Croesus in 1.26, Herodotus accords 


much space (1.23–24) to the tale about Arion, the famous cithara-player, who was 
saved by a dolphin after being thrown overboard by deceitful sailors. Arion ar- 
rives back safely to Taenarum, then returns to Corinth. Herodotus does not ex- 
plicitly mention a divine intervention, but he does qualify this tale as something 
extraordinary (θῶμα μέγιστον), which evokes one of Herodotus’ main objectives 
in the preface: to recount “the great and marvellous works” (ἔργα μεγάλα τε καὶ 
θωμαστά). A subtle cue to the divine, however, has been found in Arion’s perfor- 
mance to the sailors as a prayer to Poseidon for salvation from drowning.57 This 
would explain the miraculous rescue via a dolphin. 


In the end, Herodotus relates that the doubting Periander, after inquiry (ἱστο- 


ρέεσθαι, 1.24.7), finally believed the story.58 Further, a statuette of a dolphin car- 
rying a man (dedicated by Arion according to the Corinthians and the Lesbians) 
was still in Taenarum in Herodotus’ day (1.24). Scholars have seen Periander’s 
move from unbelief to belief through inquiry to be self-referential to Herodotus. 
Here, divine intervention is subtle, as is his lesson drawn from it.59 In addition, 
David Branscome – through a great number of parallels – shows that the Arion 
logos plays a key role in preparing audiences to interpret the Solon–Croesus lo- 
gos.60 This is another example of a story in the Histories that perhaps seems silly

171 


or unimportant but has much more narrative and ideological significance than at 
first sight. 


In sum, at the very beginning of the Histories, the divine within the plupast 


on the macronarrative level creates an atmosphere in which the divine and the 
human meet, where the divine commends and condemns, and the human rises 
and falls. This marks the beginning of a pattern that underlines divine sovereign- 
ty over human affairs and the moral lessons that can be drawn from this reality.61 


Theologically, Herodotus’ ‘divine plupast’ (Book 1.1–45) orients readers temporal- 
ly and hermeneutically for the rest of the Histories. The beginning of a theological 
pattern that underlines divine sovereignty over human affairs (often frail and 
precarious). The imperial impulse is thus countered from the start of the Histo- 
ries: the Heraclid and Mermnad dynasties both cease, and the Lydian kingdom is 
absorbed into the Persian kingdom. 


Didactically, we also find the beginning of patterns of lessons drawn from 


this reality: excess in behaviour and divine retribution, respect of νόμοι, and re- 
spect of structures devoted to the divine. No one is exempt from these principles. 
True even for a king or an empire, the frailty of human existence is the gist of 
Herodotus’ words, which foreshadow many examples: “For many cities that were 
great long ago are now small and those that are great in my time were once small, 
so then knowing that human fortune does not stay long in the same place, I shall 
mention both equally” (1.5.4). Herodotus almost whispers to his audience: “Learn 
from Croesus’ life. The first lesson has been drawn. Readers, tread carefully.” This 
precarious state is brutally summed up by Solon, the Athenian sage, in his con- 
cluding words to Croesus: “In my opinion, whoever has the most, carries on, and 
then finishes life happily, this is the right one, O King, and wins for himself the 
name. But it is necessary to consider the end of every issue how it turns out, be- 
cause, indeed, the god who has shown happiness to many people has ruined them 
completely” (1.32.9). 


Rhetorically, then, one finds in this section the reflection of Herodotus’ self- 


fashioning as historian, speaking to his audience with a prophetic voice. He ac- 
complishes this by extending a shared theological metanarrative with his audi- 
ence and by elaborating his objective to consolidate Greek identity (i.e., the gods 
as fundamental elements of cultural identity; cf. 8.144.2). In this way, through 
these initial examples of the divine plupast, Herodotus recommends a teleological 
interpretation of human existence, and, implicitly, also of his own work.62 A look- 
ing forward to an end goal (teleology) and backward (‘futures past’) is thus per- 
ceivable (and necessary) not only from nature, but also from the opening chap- 
ters of Herodotus’ enquiry. The use of “still there to my day” also helps to bridge 


61 
For the rhetorical force of this early part in relation to the macronarrative, see Kindt (2006) 
35, 46–48. 


62 
For a thorough study of teleological interpretation in historiographical explanations, see 
Grethlein (2013) 1–26; 185–223 on Herodotus.

the past with Herodotus’ present, which drives home the value of verisimilitude 
and principles concerning divine agency. 


5.2.2 Divine Plupast on the Macronarrative Level in Luke-Acts 


We now turn to the presence of a divine plupast on a macronarrative level in 
Luke-Acts, noting how Luke brings in the divine sphere in various ways. The nar- 
rative function of Luke 1:5–4:13 is preparatory for the reception of the greater 
narrative. The main narrative interest of Luke’s two volumes is the exploration of 
Jesus as teacher and saviour and the ensuing effects thereof on the lives of his 
followers and on individuals and groups, among the Jews and non-Jews. Plupast 
and past from the author’s perspective turns on the hinge of Jesus’ implementa- 
tion of his mandate: 


Author’s plupast: Causes and preparation of Jesus’ mandate (Luke 1:5–4:13) 
Author’s past: Jesus’ implementation of his mandate (Luke 4:14–24:53) 


Unlike the incipit in the Histories, the incipit in the Gospel of Luke is somewhat 
oblique about the plupast-past distinction. The mention of “servants of the word 
or (Word)” (Luke 1:2) suggests that the focus will be on the word of (or about) 
God/Jesus or on those who teach the word.63 The incipit in Acts, however, spells it 
out by pointing to the core narrative that Luke will focus on. There we read that 
the first book (the Gospel of Luke) relates primarily to what “Jesus did and taught 
from the beginning until the day when he was taken up to heaven” (Acts 1:1, my 
italics). It may be assumed then that the narrative proper concerns Jesus’ imple- 
mentation of his mandate as an adult, which, narratively, begins in Luke, chapter 
4. It is important to note that Jesus does not actually teach or perform miracles in 
the section 1:5–4:13. This long section functions in narratological terms as an ‘ini- 
tial orientation’ for readers.64 Thus, if we interpret retrospectively the incipit of 
the first volume in light of the second incipit, it is plausible that the logos of the 
“the servants of the word” refers to the logos of and/or about Jesus. The questions 
that drive the core narrative concern his identity and mandate (as introduced in 
Luke 1:5–4:13), and those individuals among the Jews and non-Jews who would 
receive him and his message. 


Other reasons for viewing Luke 1:5–4:13 as plupast material are that Luke 


provides background information concerning John the Baptist as Jesus’ prophetic

8:4, 14, 25; 10:36, 44; 12:24; 13:48.

a child, and the public confirmation of Jesus as messiah via John’s baptism of 
him, a voice from heaven, and – to secure this firmly – via an extended genealogy 
through the narrator’s voice. At this point, the genealogy serves the narrative 
function of bringing the first major section of the work to a close, clearly spelling 
out the divine origin and identity of Jesus of Nazareth before shifting the main 
narrative focus to the subject mentioned above. This explanation is justified 
through the comparison of the narrative strategies in Mark which begins with a 
very short introduction to John’s ministry in medias res (1:2–8) and in Matthew, 
which begins with a genealogy followed by plupast material, prior to the beginn- 
ing of Jesus’ ministry recounted in Matthew 4. 


Some of the divine plupast in Luke 1:5–4:13 have been mentioned above. 


Here I will briefly indicate divine action and speech in this section: angelic ap- 
pearances, prophetic activity, and signs of divine presence. First, the angel Gabri- 
el is sent by God to announce two miraculous births to some improbable protago- 
nists. The first child is promised to Zechariah and Elizabeth who was “barren,” 
and they were both “advanced in years” (1:7). The second child is promised to 
Mary, who, in her own words, had not known a man (1:34). The mandates and 
the names of the two divinely appointed children are also clearly announced. 
John would prepare the people for the Lord (1:17), and Jesus would become great 
as Son of the Most High and reign over the house of David (i.e., Israel; 1:32–33). 
The Holy Spirit then provides further information about their mandates by giving 
prophetic utterances to Elizabeth (1:41–45), Zechariah (1:67–79), Simeon (2:25– 
35), and, implicitly, also to Anna (2:36–38). In addition, between the prophecies 
of Zechariah and Simeon, another angel (“an angel of the Lord”) is sent to an- 
nounce to a group of shepherds that Jesus’ birth had happened, and that this son 
would be “a saviour, who is Christ the Lord” (2:11). Thus, Chapters 1 and 2, which 
are only found in the Gospel of Luke, provide this and other pertinent information 
to orient readers in their understanding and experience of the narrative to fol- 
low. 


Chapter 3 then focuses on the implementation of John’s mandate, which 


Luke emphasises by indicating John’s prophetic status. John receives divine com- 
munication (“the word of God came to John […]”; 3:2), which is in turn supported 
by a quotation from Isaiah 40:1–3 that shows that John is the fulfilment of this 
ancient oracle (Luke 3:4–6). Luke then summarises John’s ministry (3:3, 18–20) 
and shows John in action (3:7–17), culminating in his confession about the com- 
ing Messiah, which illustrates the qualitative difference between the two individ- 
uals (3:16–17):

John answered all of them by saying, “I baptize you with water; but one who is 
more powerful than I is coming; I am not worthy to untie the thong of his sandals. 
He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, 
to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his granary; but the chaff 
he will burn with unquenchable fire.” 


This prophetic preparation leads to the divine confirmation of Jesus at the mo- 
ment of his baptism by the presence of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and 
by a voice from heaven saying, “You are my Son, the Beloved, with you I am well 
pleased” (3:22). Finally, as mentioned above, Luke provides a genealogy of Jesus 
(3:23–38) that works back from his (legal, but non-biological) father Joseph (“as it 
was supposed” in 3:23 which underlines the aforementioned miraculous birth) 
all the way to “Adam, the son of God” (3:37). Here the ‘reach’ and the ‘extent’ of 
the divine plupast is quite long. 


Therefore, through the narrator’s showing and telling in these first three 


chapters, readers are prepared to enter the first section in which Jesus, like John, 
performs his mission, which marks the beginning of the narrative core of Luke- 
Acts, that is, from 4:14 on. In between, however, Luke inserts an additional plu- 
past scene in which Jesus is tempted to abdicate his divine identity and mission. 
This will be considered below as an example of the plupast in a singular episode. 
In sum, the divine plupast on the macronarrative level is transmitted through 
various plupast forms of divine action and speech in order to supply this back- 
drop against which the narrative core will be developed. 


5.3 Key Divine Plupast Passages and ‘Forms of reference’ 


on the Micronarrative Level 


Moving from these broad sweeps of periods on the macronarrative level to a 
sharper focus on the micronarrative level, two key passages in our authors’ writ- 
ings exhibit examples of the divine plupast preceding the core narrative (as out- 
lined above). These passages are particularly significant for an understanding of 
their histories and can be understood as being programmatic. They both partici- 
pate in the plupast sections on a macronarrative level, bolstering the religious di- 
dactic tone already set forth in previous passages. Classicists and biblical scholars 
know these passages well on account of their programmatic import in their 
works. Herodotus continues his narration by recounting the visit of Solon to Croe- 
sus (Hist. 1.29–33) some time before Croesus declares war on Cyrus (1.46–75). Af- 
ter describing the preparations for Jesus’ ministry in Chapters 1–3, Luke contin- 
ues his narrative by recounting the temptation of Jesus in the desert by the 


5 The Divine Plupast in Herodotus’ Histories and in Luke-Acts 
175 


διάβολος (4:1–13). Luke places this episode just before Jesus publicly announces 
his mandate in the synagogue of his hometown, Nazareth (Luke 4:14–30). 


This discussion follows up on the discussion of ‘forms of reference’ for plu- 


past material (4.1.1). Theologically, plupast forms of reference provide additional 
depth to the author’s (assumed) theistic metanarrative.65 In the treatment of the 
two passages from the Histories and Luke-Acts below, we shall observe some of 
these. I list here some of the most common that are explored below and in the 
following chapters. First, the most explicit way is when Herodotus and Luke 
evoke divine acts and speech of spiritual beings in previous times and places. 
Through them, audiences are invited to consider the weight of these examples for 
the interpretation of subsequent events in the narrative proper. Second, struc- 
tures and materials related to the devotion of spiritual beings (e.g., Delphi, sanctu- 
aries, the temple in Jerusalem) are significant in the development of a spiritual 
landscape or a sacred geography, so that readers understand what is devoted to 
the holy and what ought to take place there.66 Objects dedicated to the divine, 
such as temples, texts, tombs, and bones, are frequently embedded in accounts of 
past events and do not require detailed descriptions.67 Third, oral and written 
sources evoking the divine (e.g., oracles, inscriptions) that predate the core narra- 
tive. Examples of intertextuality are very common, such as summaries of conver- 
sations, quotations, allusions, and echoes.68 These sources may be referred to as 
written or oral. Our historians may handle these sources in different ways (e.g., 
with belief or disbelief), and they can be expressed through a variety of voices. 
The use of recognised sources evoking the divine reinforces our authors’ authori- 
ty as historians with prophetic voices.69 Finally, Herodotus and Luke use expres-

5.3.1 The Divine Plupast in Solon’s Visit to Croesus (Hist. 1.29–33) 


Solon’s visit to Croesus in Sardis is one of the most studied passages in the Histo- 
ries due to its early appearance and programmatic weight.71 Here, I build on scho- 
larly insights by fleshing out the presence of the divine in this plupast passage. 
Herodotus’ presentation of the narrative suggests that he is essentially in sympa- 
thy with Solon’s theological views and moral values, which are substantiated in 
the rest of the Histories.72 


Placed between Croesus’ royal lineage and Solon’s visit to him in Sardis, 


Herodotus provides a synopsis of the expanding Lydian kingdom (1.27–28). Re- 
garding Croesus’ imperial impulse, on the one hand, Croesus changed his plans 
for subduing the Aegean Islands, thanks to a certain shrewd Bias of Priene (or 
according to another version, Pittacus of Mytilene at 1.27). On the other hand, 
Herodotus provides an impressive list of the peoples that Croesus had subjugated 
in Asia Minor (except for the Cilicians and Lycians, 1.28). This background infor- 
mation shows that Croesus is both power hungry and yet somewhat naive. These 
two weak points will push him, unknowingly, to his defeat at the hands of Cyrus. 
This passage then links the summary of his subjugating and his own subjugation 
by the Persians, and their subsequent desire to have all of Asia and the Hellenic 


in discourses, and occasionally through his own voice. Herodotus refers often to his conversa- 
tions with priests (e.g., in Egypt).

thorial past on a macronarrative level because of its geopolitical position between 
the Lydians, Persians, and Greeks, as well as its part in unravelling the doom an-

plupast position is that audiences needed to know this part to fully grasp how the 
Greeks entered into conflict with the Lydians and with the Persians. Here, 
through the person of Solon, Croesus encounters one of the best thinkers of 
Greece and rejects his counsel. 


Herodotus’ use of the Solon figure has raised questions about its historicity 


and quasi legendary impression.74 Solon was from Athens and had already 
earned a solid reputation for his political and philosophical contributions. He was 
later included as one of the seven sages of Hellas.75 Herodotus portrays him as 
one of the wise advisors who are often rebuffed in the Histories. After Solon’s 
tour of Croesus’ treasuries, the conversation proper takes place almost in private, 
as if no other participants or bystanders were present and it ends abruptly 
(1.30.2–1.33). Regardless of its historical value, historiographically, it serves a 
programmatic purpose within the overall narrative. The two men’s qualities are 
compared, as are their approaches to judging human prosperity (εὐδαιμονίη). 
Loyalty towards others and humility before the gods are highlighted values. 
Wealth and power, however, are no guarantee of ultimate fortune, for one can 
only hope not to be visited by misfortune and finish well one’s final days on 
earth. 


With his kingdom at the height of its prosperity, Croesus receives the visit of 


Solon the sage. Like other sages who had come there (1.29), Solon was apparently 
curious to explore the phenomenon of the Lydian kingdom with its great wealth. 
In Herodotus’ depiction, Solon’s visit will mark the turning point in Croesus’ life 
and kingdom, acting as a catalyst to expose Croesus’ folly. Herodotus sets up the 
contrast between the characters of the two men by providing plupast material 
regarding Solon (1.29–30). This is an example of a plupast within a plupast sec- 
tion. Solon’s impressive reputation had preceded his arrival, as evinced by Croe- 
sus’ flattery of Solon’s wisdom, travels, and pursuit of knowledge. This is one of 
the many positive examples that may have inspired audiences (and most likely 
Herodotus himself) to emulate Solon’s qualities. 


This leads to the highlighted dialogue focused on an existential question that 


ironically will trigger Croesus’ doom. Given this opportunity to meet such a rep- 
utable man as Solon, Croesus cannot resist asking him one question: Who is the

happiest man you have ever seen? If we compare this question to the verdict pro- 
leptically (and prophetically) announced later by Herodotus at 1.34: “After Solon 
had gone away, a great retribution from a [the] god seized Croesus, because, as 
one might infer, he considered himself to be the happiest of all men.” We have 
here the confirmation of a theological depiction of this meeting. This is further 
supported by other divine plupast elements in the dialogue, the bulk of which is 
Solon’s response at the insistent bidding of Croesus who longs to appear at the 
top of the list of the happiest people.76 


Solon gives two examples of people in the past who qualify as the happiest 


persons. These in turn are plupast exempla for Herodotus. Neither of these exam- 
ples please Croesus. Solon justifies his choices based on the fact that these people, 
Tellus of Athens and the brothers Cleobis and Biton of the Argives, not only lived 
exemplary lives, but they also died in honourable ways. Solon consistently ap- 
plies the existential principle that one can only judge a person’s happiness by 
evaluating his or her life from beginning to end. Tellus died a glorious death in 
battle in service of his people (1.30). The brothers also died honourably because 
of their sacrificial love for their mother (1.31). The lives of all three were held as 
exemplary and monumentalised by their people, respectively by a “public funer- 
al” and “statues.” These are some of the first mise en abyme of Herodotus’ promise 
to display “great and marvellous works” (1.1.0). 


In the example of Tellus, Solon does not explicitly bring out the divine, only 


Tellus’ quality of life. Implicitly, his honourable life and death would be wel- 
comed by the gods and glorified in the afterlife. In the second example, however, 
Solon provides several theological justifications. First, the brothers Cleobis and 
Biton take action during a festival of Hera at Argos at which time their mother 
needed to go urgently to Hera’s temple. Other reasons for this are not given. Her 
health was rapidly declining, and she sought divine healing. Her sons acted 
valiantly and pulled their mother by cart for forty-five stades. The overexertion 
killed them both. From a human perspective, it was perhaps a tragedy, but Solon 
speaks prophetically, interpreting from a theistic perspective: “they died in the 
best possible way; in fact, the god used them to show that it is better for a person 
to be dead than to be alive” (1.31.3). Owing to this supreme act of filial devotion, 
their mother prayed before the statue of Hera so that Hera might honour Cleobis 
and Biton by giving them “whatever it is best for a human being to have” (1.31.4). 
This was indeed a risky prayer, for after participating in the rites and feasting, 
the young men went into the temple to rest, and both died. For them, an hon- 
ourable death was presumably better than any other further earthly achieve- 
ments. Subsequently, their glory was celebrated by statues dedicated at Delphi, 


76 
See Immerwahr (1966) 156. 


5 The Divine Plupast in Herodotus’ Histories and in Luke-Acts 
179 


for “they had been the best of men.”77 In this case, the gods, represented by Hera 
and Apollo, favoured this family. Theologically, through Solon’s voice, Herodotus 
extended the belief that dying with honour was better than living a long life on 
earth without honour. 


At this second example, Croesus became furious, because he was now ou- 


tranked by two commoners. How could he not figure among the happiest of men? 
This prompts Solon to expound on his choices of those happiest persons (the ob- 
ject of 1.32). In short, Solon argued that human life is fragile enough, and what 
makes things worse is that the divine sphere is ever-present and not always 
benevolent. He summarises this with an aphorism: “Croesus, you put the ques- 
tion to me about human matters, knowing that the god is entirely envious and 
troubling” (1.32.1). Solon exploits the topos of divine jealousy as regards human 
happiness.78 This introduces the important theme of divine retribution, which is 
depicted for various reasons in the Histories (e.g., human hybris or divine envy).79 


This is confirmed as soon as Solon departs: “Straightaway, while he [Croesus] 
was asleep, a dream came to him, which revealed the truth about the evil things 
that were going to happen concerning his son” (1.34.1). 


The repeated principle is that a rich man may be more fortunate than the 


common man for a time, but only his death will tell whether he really had a hap- 
pier life than the other (cf. sections 5, 7, 9). Existence can be so fragile that Solon 
reduces it to this extent: “But it is necessary to consider the end of every issue 
how it turns out, because, indeed, the god who has shown happiness to many peo- 
ple has ruined them completely” (1.32.9). Solon’s prophetic word, in a short time, 
would become reality in Croesus’ life and his empire.80 The two plupast exempla 
and the theological statements were not enough to bring Croesus to reason. He 
was too enamoured with his success to grasp how it all hung in the balance. 


Here the macro- and the micronarrative levels mirror each other. Herodotus 


had prefaced his work by saying that prosperity does not stay long in the same 
place (1.5.4), and the proof of this manifests itself overtly in Croesus and the Lydi- 
an kingdom, the initiator of military strife between the Greeks and the barbar- 
ians. Yet Croesus had had his chance to heed Solon’s wisdom, change direction,

and avoid (or at least delay) personal and national calamity. Herodotus, however, 
expresses Croesus’ obstinacy by describing how he disparaged Solon and even 
considered him a great fool (1.33). His demeanour towards the divine and the hu- 
man would usher his fated destruction, announced in the days of Gyges (1.13.2). 
Later, however, Solon is vindicated in the audience’s eyes by Croesus’ own decla- 
ration (on his funeral pyre) that Solon had spoken with divine help (σὺν θεῷ) and 
by Croesus’ desperate cry for his wise advisor (1.86.3). 


The dialogue between Solon and Herodotus highlights various items of plu- 


past material regarding the divine: exempla of piety (sons and their mother), a 
literary topos on honourable death, general statements about divine activity, and 
the presence of temples as tokens of the sacred and divine approval (via answ- 
ered prayer). Finally, on a metahistorical level, Solon’s persona and the plupast 
material offer a glimpse of how Herodotus may have understood himself as one 
who understood something about the divine and human spheres.81 The plupast 
material embedded in this dialogue offers much material for theological reflec- 
tion. Through Solon’s voice, Herodotus extended the Greek divine metanarrative 
about the gods’ ambivalent influence on human existence as well as the value of 
an honourable death. Indeed, the theological import of this episode is confirmed 
through Plutarch’s critique of Herodotus for having defamed the gods in such a 
way, and using, dishonestly, Solon’s voice to do it.82 Narratively, this first major 
episode mirrors Herodotus’ consistent interest in the divine/human relationship 
concerning the fate of individuals and kingdoms. The end of one’s life can only 
tell whether one has been truly happy or not. Likewise, the end of Croesus’ story 
points to the aim of the Histories, which gives counsel to individuals, city-states, 
and kingdoms about true happiness before the gods and humanity. 


5.3.2 Luke’s Use of the Divine Plupast in the Devil’s Counterproposal 


(Luke 4:1–13) 


Examples of the divine plupast teem the pages of Luke-Acts. Here we consider 
several instances in an exceptional Lukan passage: the description of the devil’s 
temptation of Jesus in the desert. It is the last episode of plupast material, situated 
some time before the episode in the synagogue of Nazareth (4:16–30). Justifica- 


81

82

181 


tion for situating this passage in the plupast on the macronarrative level (Luke 
1:5–4:13) is that the temptation scene builds on the audience’s exploration of Je- 
sus’ identity and mission, between the genealogy and Jesus’ implementation of 
his mandate. It is the link between all that has been said about Jesus through vari- 
ous voices and his public announcement of his mandate in the synagogue of Naz- 
areth. Like the Solon-Croesus conversation, the dialogue between Jesus and the 
devil provides key information for understanding some of the theological accents 
in the rest of Luke’s two-volume work. Moreover, both scenes represent the open- 
ing of alternative narrative trajectories. If Croesus had been attentive to Solon’s 
wisdom, he might have made better choices and diverted (for some time at least) 
divine judgement on himself, his family, and dynasty. Likewise, in the present 
passage, if the devil had been successful in enticing Jesus to accept his proposal, 
then the entire story would have taken another direction. These crucial moments 
take place in the context of conversations between two individuals with divergent 
perspectives and with no intervention of other participants. 


Due to its mystical nature, the encounter between Jesus and the devil obvi- 


ously presents challenges concerning its historicity. Jesus is assumed to be the ul- 
timate source of this story since he is said to be alone with the devil. It is indeed 
one of the rare instances where no witnesses are present or implied. Like Herodo- 
tus, Luke assumes that his audience has some understanding and belief of the di- 
vine realm. The devil is assumed to be known as a spiritual creature and receives 
no description. Temporally, the scene takes place sometime after Jesus’ return 
from the Jordan (4:1), which evokes the baptism episode (Luke 3:21–22). Led by 
the Holy Spirit, Jesus enters an undefined, isolated region (ἐ ν τῇ ἐ ρήμῳ , 4:1) and 
is tempted “for forty days,” a biblical (and true plupast) temporal marker to 
mean ‘for some time’. This temporal expression places Luke’s account of Jesus’ 
story in continuity with other biblical narratives.83 Luke also describes physical 
movement (seemingly in a mystical sense): the devil leads Jesus up (ἀ ναγαγὼν 
αὐ τὸν) and presents to him in an instant all the kingdoms of the world (πάσας τὰς 
βασιλείας τῆ ς οἰ κουμένης, 4:5). Then, the devil brings Jesus to Jerusalem and pla- 
ces him on the highest point of the temple (ἐ πι ̀ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱ εροῦ , 4:9). Luke 
does not say how this was done. We are faced then with a characteristic of an- 
cient historiography: reports of apparitions of spiritual beings in the human 
sphere. This belief is assumed by Luke. Herodotus also assumes this, never justi- 
fies it, and presents a few cited messages of spiritual beings as well as numerous 


83

again to describe the period of Jesus’ post-resurrection appearances (Acts 1:3).

reports of divine interventions in human history.84 Luke generally presents an- 
gels and demons and does not offer speculation on their existence or activity. 
They are reported as protagonists and antagonists as a part of the human experi- 
ence. 


The divine plupast appears especially within their dialogue. Up to this point 


in the narrative, the devil had not been presented by Luke, who appears to as- 
sume his audience’s knowledge of this spiritual being. It is likely that Luke could 
assume this, based on a high degree of intertextuality, either from Israel’s Scrip- 
tures or from other Christian literature or oral teaching available to Luke’s read- 
ers.85 Christian audiences, like the one to whom Luke was writing, will have re- 
ceived some teaching about spiritual beings (e.g., angels and demons), 
particularly if they had already had parts or all of one of the gospels. It is plausi- 
ble that some of the first audiences had already heard the story from one of the 
parallel passages of the temptation scene (Mark 1:12–13; Matt 4:1–11).86 


Since Chapter 6 will present more about the nature of this διάβολος, I men- 


tion here only that Luke later presents this character, elsewhere in the narrative, 
as Satan (Σατανᾶς) and Beelzebul (Βεελζεβούλ). The objective of this encounter is 
to tempt Jesus (ἡ μέρας τεσσεράκοντα πειραζόμενος ὑ πὸ τοῦ διαβόλου, 4:2). The 
underlying test concerns whether Jesus might avail himself of his right to divine 
power and glory, if he is truly the Son of God. Yet, similar to the unclean spirit a 
bit later (4:34), the devil knows Jesus’ identity. The question for the devil is not 
whether Jesus is the Son of God, but rather if he can derail Jesus from accomplish- 
ing God’s plan. The devil’s strategy consists of evoking various connections with 
the divine sphere: sacred scriptures, places, and beings. Jesus’ response in de- 
fence is to recall authoritative principles based on Israel’s Scriptures. 


Other plupast elements can be observed in the temptation episode. The lack 


of introduction of ‘the devil’ is a plupast item as it implies knowledge of this char- 
acter as an adversary from Israel’s history. Also, the expression “son of God” 
harks back to the angel Gabriel’s words (1:35), and the intertextual expression “it 
is written” (4:4) assumes knowledge of Israel’s Scriptures. This is valid for the 
other citations in the conversation to those sacred texts (4:8, 10, 12). Also, the 
mention of Jerusalem as a Jewish holy city and the temple as the cultic centre of 
Israel anchor the story in the Jewish metanarrative (4:9). Finally, spiritual beings 
(angels), who have already been encountered in the first three chapters, are 
evoked (4:10–11) to underline the additional supernatural help available to Jesus, 
who responds to the devil’s quotation with another quotation. The plupast mate-

rial referring to Israel’s religious heritage serves to undergird the clash between 
Jesus and his spiritual adversary. For this reason, Luke’s depiction of this allows 
readers to appreciate the differences between the two characters and their re- 
spective allegiances, the kingdom of God, and the kingdoms of men. The devil’s 
counterproposal can be boiled down to the lure of the imperial impulse. Jesus’ 
life had been presented as a response to human need (Luke 1:79; 2:32) for the 
Jews and the peoples. So, rather than God’s plan of reconciliation for the peoples, 
the devil offers subjugation and rule over them. Two theologically supported nar- 
rative trajectories are now understood to be in conflict. 


From this encounter between Jesus and the devil in the desert, the narrative 


continues by focusing on Jesus’ contact with the human sphere and diverse reac- 
tions to him. Luke summarises an undefined time of success and acceptance of 
his mandate in Galilee (4:14–15), which is followed, ironically, by a rejection 
scene in the synagogue of Nazareth (known by the audience as his hometown, 
cf. 1:26; 2:4, 39, 51). This interplay between plupast and past elucidates and fore- 
shadows reactions to Jesus’ mandate in the spiritual and human realms. For ex- 
ample, the devil knew who Jesus was and wanted to sabotage his role in God’s 
plan. In the following scene, the synagogue people of Nazareth knew Jesus, but 
they failed to accept his claim of fulfilment of the prophetic role in Isaiah’s 
prophecy (cf. Luke 4:18–19; Isa 61:1–2 LXX; Isa 58:6). By recounting these two 
scenes, Luke links Jesus to Israel’s religious metanarrative, prophetic line, as well 
as the topos of the rejection of prophets. Luke seeks to confirm, for his audience, 
Jesus’ divine nature and role in addition to the antagonistic forces in the spiritual 
and human spheres. In this way, Luke extends knowledge of this scene and the 
underlying theistic metanarrative in space and time. 


5.4 Conclusion 


Historians could begin their narratives almost at any time or point in history. 
Herodotus and Luke chose their chronological limits and their foci from previous 
epochs in relation to their audiences’ knowledge and interest. This provided a 
frame for their focused pasts, their core narratives. I have proposed that the plu- 
past on a macronarrative level shows how our historians began their enquiry, 
where they started in time, and how this decision affects a theological reading of 
the rest of their narratives, and how it is linked to their objectives in the incipits. 
This comparison on a macronarrative level shows how each author provided not 
only a historical, chronological introduction, but also a theistic and moral frame- 
work within which the rest of the stories develop. Pragmatically, then, audiences 
enter the assumed worldview and theistic metanarrative, which will continue 
throughout without justification. Important moral lessons raised early in the nar- 
rative will be developed throughout.

184 


Herodotus is keen on showing how prosperity is no guarantee of lifelong 


success. The divine plupast prepares the reader for a theological and religious 
evaluation of events and characters. Candaules and Croesus are proof of that. 
Overstepping one’s boundaries, violating customs, and displaying a haughty spir- 
it attract the gods’ attention and invites divine retribution. Conversely, Solon and 
his exempla are proposed as models for knowing and hoping to not incur the 
wrath of the gods. 


Through the plupast section of Luke’s narrative, audiences learn about Je- 


sus’ identity and mandate. Those who oppose him are opposing God’s plan. In 
both works, consistent moral frames of reference are developed through a theo- 
logically supported worldview. But this raises the question of what the divine 
spheres look like, how they are composed, and more importantly, how they are 
perceived by the authors and their characters. The next chapter provides an over- 
view of these perceived divine spheres to help interpret the passages discussed in 
Chapters 7–12. 


5 The Divine Plupast in Herodotus’ Histories and in Luke-Acts 
185 


6 Divine Constellations of Herodotus’ Histories and Luke-Acts 


It is understandable that readers unacquainted with either Herodotus or Luke 
might assume that neither one is interested in both the geopolitical and divine 
spheres. It may be one or the other, but not both. However, in ancient times most 
people would not have considered these spheres to be completely separate enti- 
ties. This assumption reflects the lingering doubt that some may have about 
bringing Herodotus and Luke together in theistic continuity. I think this is mistak- 
en. In both works, the imperial impulse is at the forefront, and this is certainly 
not overlooked by the divine in the reported perceptions.1 This chapter works on 
an epistemological level, seeking to explore how Herodotus and Luke may have 
perceived the nature of the divine, those beings occupying a place both within 
and outside the limited human realm. The chapter’s preparatory function is to 
familiarise readers with the theological frameworks underlying this narrative in- 
terest, which will be examined in Chapters 7–12. There, it will be shown how the 
geopolitical and theological are intertwined, that is, how divine actors are inter- 
preted within the developments of human history. Rather than presenting a the- 
ology of the Histories or Luke-Acts, this chapter surveys the divine characters that 
feature in these theological compositions. 


Chapter 2 showed how this theistic continuity runs through the Greek histo- 


riographical tradition in which, like other historians, Herodotus and Luke write 
as theists keeping an eye on the interface between the geopolitical and divine 
realms. One example of this – that will be explored in Chapters 7–12 – is how 
oppression and enslavement are often depicted as impious acts. This element un- 
derlines one of the tensions between divine and human forces. Our authors’ the- 
istic understanding of the world is clearly holistic. This does not deny the obvious 
differences in their histories and historiographies, but it does argue that both 
have a high view of divine rule, over and above human forms of rule and agency. 
In their worldviews, and theistic frameworks, these spheres cannot be unders- 
tood as separate elements in a closed system.2 


However, this raises the question of how they – as historians speaking with 


a prophetic-like voice in their contexts – seem to conceive of the divine realm. 


1 
This understanding of the world is also not unusual since politics and practised religion in 
antiquity were not at all watertight categories. 


2 
Various expressions for the description of an understanding of the world or reality, including 
the visible and the invisible, such as ‘beliefs’, ‘worldview’, etc. We have already considered 
the validity of speaking of such things with respect to antiquity and historians. I am here fol- 
lowing Harrison in viewing religious conceptions or beliefs as “one area of Herodotus’ ‘world 
view’”. Harrison (2002) 11. 


Two facts about their prophetic voices emerge here. On the one hand, despite the 
five hundred years that separate our two historians, there is a shared belief that 
the divine realm not only exists but also influences and governs the course of hu- 
man history. On the other hand, although both authors are theists, their under- 
standing of the divine is quite different. Their ‘theologies’, articulated through 
historical discourse, represent the theistic worldviews through which they con- 
struct their narratives.3 It would be unhelpful to force one into the worldview of 
the other. What, then, can be said to refer to the divine for them within their the- 
istic frameworks? Which divine beings are involved in influencing the human 
sphere? Are there any discernible similarities or differences between their repre- 
sentations of the divine and the metanarratives that they have received and ex- 
tended? That is, are there points of continuity or discontinuity? Are there theolog- 
ical innovations? We are thus considering their perceptions of the divine – or 
more often – their descriptions of others’ perceptions of divine activity. Previous 
chapters have explored the worlds of Herodotus and Luke, and the worlds of the 
plupast as the foundation upon which their core narratives are constructed. In 
this way, this chapter provides a helpful theological transition between Chapters 
4–5 and Chapters 7–12. 


6.1 The Divine and Proofs of Activity (τεκμήρια): 
A Common Assumption of Herodotus and Luke 


Both Herodotus and Luke work with the epistemological assumption that their 
audiences share their views that the divine sphere exists and is active in the hu- 
man sphere. Therefore, they do not provide an extensive defence to justify their 
decision to speak of the divine. They do, however, operate with a sensible apolo- 
getic that emerges naturally in the narration, as if they had anticipated objections 
from sceptical readers about certain types of stories. We begin with Herodotus, 
giving him more space since Luke’s view of the divine comes to the fore more 
often and more explicitly. 


In the incipit of Book 1, Herodotus states his focus on those ἔργα accom- 


plished by humans, both Greeks and non-Greeks. Nevertheless, it is clear from his 
long narrative that it would be unprofitable to disregard divine agency and rule 
as an essential part of his work. For Jon Mikalson, following Harvey Yunis’s study, 
Herodotus shares with his contemporaries three common beliefs: the gods’ exis- 
tence, their attention to human affairs, and the reciprocity between the divine 
and human spheres.4 Mikalson thinks that these three core beliefs required little

substantiation for Herodotus’ readers, as they were already familiar with this 
concept.5 


Although Herodotus does generally not imitate Homer in describing divine 


agency through anthropomorphic representation, he does intersperse his narra- 
tive with episodes evincing divine presence and intervention.6 Perhaps, due to 
this distinctive feature, Herodotus occasionally reveals a degree of self-conscious 
reflection about his own beliefs in the divine. For a cautious, almost apologetic, 
aside, he says at 9.65.2: “I think, if one must think about the deeds of the divine, 
the goddess herself did not allow them entry, because they had burned her tem- 
ple at Eleusis.”7 Since this comment appears close to the end of his long work and 
readers have already encountered the theme of divine wrath due to sacrileges, it 
is not surprising that Herodotus attributes this intervention to Demeter, whose 
burnt sanctuary he had not previously brought to his readers’ attention.8 Also, he 
offers various formulations lest he neglect the divine sphere,9 speak about it in- 
correctly (2.45.3)10 or question the reliability of prophecies (8.77). The same is 
true about certain stories when he expresses a more rational reading, uncertainty 
or hesitancy, e.g., Arion and the dolphin (1.23–28); belief in Poseidon’s creation 
of the Peneius gorge (7.129.4); and the divine epiphany to Adeimantus and the 
Corinthians at Salamis (8.94). In some instances, plain disbelief can be noted, e.g., 
regarding sexual relations between gods and mortal women (1.182); the parents 
of Targitaus being Zeus and a daughter of the river Borysthenes (4.5.1); and Skyl- 
lias’ amazingly long dive (8.8.2–3). 


Further examples shed light on his general epistemological approach to the 


divine realm that we attempt to piece together. These must be properly contextu- 
alised and not taken too hastily as evidence of a deeply sceptical mindset. For ex- 
ample, regarding Egyptian beliefs and practices, he nuances his treatment for his 
contemporaries: “Now as for the things said by the Egyptians, let them be useful 
to those to whom such tales are plausible; as a principle for this whole story (λόγ- 
ον) I write down the things said by all through hearsay (ἀκοῇ)” (2.123.1). This ap- 
proach to hearsay is echoed in other passages but not necessarily regarding the 
divine.11 Yet it appears that he treats Egyptian religion both with respect – owing 
to their ancient customs – and with some distance, for example, when he de-

scribes them as being “extraordinarily religious, more than any other people” 
(2.37.1; θεοσεβέες δὲ περισσῶς ἐόντες). Their exuberant attention to rituals may 
also be evidence of a certain excess in beliefs in stories that would have been dif- 
ficult to accept by non-Egyptians like Herodotus and some of his audience. 


These statements should be held in balance with others, for example, where 


Herodotus takes a bolder stance on his beliefs in the divine. For him, the traces of 
the divine were clear enough to warrant belief. In addition to the remark about 
Demeter’s retributive intervention mentioned above (9.65), I briefly list others 
below, which will be discussed in more detail in the following chapters (see also 
Appendix 1 for the question of ‘miracles’ in Herodotus). 


Herodotus describes an earthquake in Delos as an omen (τέρας), which he 


further supports by an oracle (χρησμός) indicating the divine origin of the earth- 
quake. His interpretation: “This was an omen sent by the god, surely, to warn 
people of the trouble that was to come” (6.98.1). The link between the geopolitical 
and divine spheres is tightly woven as “the coming evils” (τῶν μελλόντων ἔσεσθαι 
κακῶν) that would be wrought chiefly through Darius, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes 
whom he names specifically (6.98.2). In another instance, Herodotus perceives di- 
vine vengeance for expiation of a crime, namely, the Spartans’ unjust killing of 
Persian ambassadors (7.137.1–2). His aside reads thus: “[…] it is clear to me that 
this was a divine act of wrath” (7.137.2). 


Also, while Herodotus knows that prophecies can be shown to be false and 


misinterpreted – because he does point this out on a number of occasions – in 
one passage, he allows his readers to grasp something of his approach and appre- 
ciation for prophetic communication: “I do not speak against the oracles as if they 
are not truthful, nor do I wish to try and refute the ones that speak clearly […] in 
light of this, and so clearly said by Bacis, I do not dare contradict the oracles nor 
do I give ear to others in this regard” (8.77). 


Finally, in his description of the battle at Mycale, Herodotus frames the pas- 


sage theologically: “It is indeed clear, from many proofs (τεκμήρια), that divine 
forces are at play in circumstances […]” (9.100.2).12 He supports this further by 
adducing evidence of traces of divine activity in parallel between the battles of 
Plateia and Mycale. For him, there was no doubt that the Persians were defeated 
with the help of the divine. This aside being found so late in the work, it serves 
historiographically to summarise his approach to divine agency rather than to in- 
troduce it. 


Given these brief statements in his own voice and his numerous and consis- 


tent references to the divine throughout his narrative, it is impossible not to 
recognise Herodotus’ belief in the context of the fifth century BCE. The issue is 
not whether the gods exist, but whether one can attribute certain occurrences to 
the divine realm and show their relevance to understanding the development 


12 
Morgan (2022) 53–58. 


Part II Herodotus and Luke: Preparing to Hear Their Prophetic Voices 
190 


and outcome of the Persian Wars. Chapters 7–9 will explore these and other ins- 
tances in more detail. As Chapter 2 demonstrates, other historians followed 
Herodotus in this approach to various degrees. Their worldviews would simply 
not allow them to impose a chasm between the divine and human realms. Geopo- 
litical questions were thus regularly perceived as displaying traces of the divine 
and religious spheres. 


How then does Luke fit into this long tradition of the divine in historiogra- 


phy? Luke’s believing posture hardly needs justification given that his two-part 
narrative concerns principally a divine figure, Jesus of Nazareth, who brings a 
message “from on high” and is himself at the centre of the message. Additionally, 
divine activity by God and the Holy Spirit, as well as by angelic beings, permeates 
the narrative. Nevertheless, Luke occasionally brings in language of authentica- 
tion and verification, as if, like Herodotus, some of his readers may have had a 
sceptical view of his report or his theology. In both prefaces, one finds efforts to 
demonstrate the reliability of his factual reporting. He leads his readers to explore 
for themselves how characters react when they encounter the divine or receive 
new information about it.13 For example, on the road to Emmaus, Cleopas asks 
Jesus (whom he does not recognise post-resurrection): “Are you the only stranger 
in Jerusalem who does not know the things that have taken place there in these 
days?” (Luke 24:18). Amusingly, Cleopas describes this Jesus to the resurrected 
Jesus as “a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people” 
(24:19). Likewise, Paul emphasises his faith in public knowledge of divine inter- 
ventions in his defence before Festus, the governor of Judea: “Indeed the king 
knows about these things, and to him I speak freely; for I am certain that none of 
these things has escaped his notice, for this was not done in a corner” (Acts 
26:24). This pattern aims at confirming belief in Luke’s readers, that is, to be cer- 
tain of these things, rather than doubting them.14 Again, as it was true for the His- 
tories, the question is not about the existence of the divine but whether this Jesus 
and his movement are truly accompanied by divine favour and assistance. Below 
are a few examples that substantiate Luke’s theistic epistemology. 


We have already seen that Luke’s first preface offers no explicit mentions of 


the divine sphere. But from the first passage on, divine interventions are evoked 
to describe the circumstances regarding John the Baptist, Jesus, then his disciples 
of the earliest generations. This chain of witnesses culminates in the person of

Paul of Tarsus who brings the message of ‘the salvation of God’ and proclaims 
‘the kingdom of God’ in Rome (Acts 28:23–31). At the core of this message are the 
resurrection and ascension of Jesus that are recounted at the end of the Gospel of 
Luke (24:1–49) and recapitulated at the beginning of the second volume (Acts 
1:1–11). This literary device underscores the theological unity of the work.15 


In the second preface, Luke – similar to Herodotus in 9.100.2 – evokes τεκμή- 


ρια, which from Aristotle on, rhetorically speaking, was the strongest word avail- 
able for describing solid evidence.16 Luke addresses his readers thus: “After his 
[Jesus’] suffering he presented himself alive to them by many convincing proofs, 
appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God” 
(Acts 1:3, my emphasis). In addition to τεκμήρια, Luke describes Jesus and his 
disciples through other expressions claiming divine intervention, e.g., δυνάμεις 
(‘deeds of power’), τέρατα (‘wonders’), and σημεῖα (‘signs’).17 


In the Greek historiographical tradition, Herodotus and Luke are like two 


bookends in a line of historians writing with theistic perspectives. They explain 
how divine activity was relevant for their audiences, as a part of geopolitical de- 
velopments of multicultural import. In addition, these stories would not have 
been possible to write (from their perspective) without some belief in divine ac- 
tivity, given that the stories were improbable if reduced to cause and effect via 
human agency. 


6.2 Perceptions of Divine Beings 


We have considered how Herodotus and Luke assume and show the existence 
and participation of the divine in human history. This section surveys the compo- 
sition of the divine realm in Herodotus and Luke. Previous chapters have given a 
glimpse of their beliefs in the divine realm and activity. Here we consider their 
theological vocabulary for divine or spiritual beings within their worldviews. 
Again, we begin with Herodotus. 


6.2.1 The Histories 


As stated above, Herodotus’ writings reflect some common Greek beliefs of the 
Classical period.18 In the discussion below, a summary is given of what Herodotus 
seems to consider ‘divine’, that is, those beings that possessed or achieved a status 
above limited mortal life and that received worship. For him, the gods can inter-

vene in ways that humans cannot. Because of their power and extravagant ef- 
fects, unexplainable on a human level, their kinds of deeds then constitute the 
‘miraculous’.19 The way that Herodotus speaks of these beings can be summarised 
in three groups: the gods, the heroes, and the divine.20 In general, continuity with 
the traditional Greek religious metanarrative is abundantly clear. The first two 
groups represent distinct personalities, while the third speaks of divine being or 
action in a more general, or simply less specific, sense. Occasionally, Herodotus 
takes time to elaborate on their origins and activity.21 Harrison warns us that a 
systematic treatment is not without difficulties, due to the fact that distinctions 
between divine figures are not always clear and some internal contradictions do 
exist.22 Consequently, it is preferable to explore what Herodotus has chosen to re- 
veal according to his own terms and contexts without attempting to iron out the 
wrinkles to create a unified system of thought. Herodotus was surely no “closet 
monotheist” and is best described as an adherent to a polytheistic worldview, 
which was far from being in decline in the fifth century BCE.23 This perspective of 
reality, as put forth above, is a “rooted assumption” in Herodotus’ entire work.24 


Since Herodotus mentions a significant number of divine beings – Greek and for- 
eign – what follows is a summary of the three designations above.25 


6.2.1.1 The gods 


The Olympian gods are credited with the greatest contribution to the victories of 
the Greeks over the barbarians. While the gods of Olympus are mentioned, not all 
receive specific honours for help in victories (e.g., Ares, Hephaestus, and Diony- 
sus do not). Three gods are recognised for their significant interventions and also 
in various regions: Zeus of Olympia, Apollo of Delphi, and Poseidon of the Isth- 
mus. Despite their cults and festivals being attached to those three regions, their

the Greeks for their final triumph over Persian forces (9.81.1). 


The main qualities attributed to Zeus Olympios are freedom and deliver-

mysterious Pythia at Delphi, which was involved in almost every major military 
event in the Histories.30 The significant exception is the battle of Marathon.31 It 
was to “the god of Delphi” that the Greeks vowed to dedicate the possessions of 
other Greeks who surrendered to the Persians (7.132). Also, after the victory at 
Plataea, so important was Apollo’s part in Greek devotion that his name appears 
first in the list of recipients of tithes (9.81). An additional point is that Apollo’s 
sanctuary (of the three main gods) lay on the path of the Persians; thus, there 
were occasions for direct encounters with them. Poseidon also receives praise as 
saviour for his key maritime interventions on behalf of the Greeks at Artemisium 
and the coast of Euboea (7.192) as well as at Potidaea (8.129).32

divine figures intervened in the Greco-Persian conflicts when battles took place 
close to their sanctuaries. They interceded in the human sphere mainly to protect 
their own precincts, for revenge concerning sacrilegious acts against those same 
structures, and for castigation in cases of hybris exhibited by individuals and 
groups. 


A final designation worth brief commentary is μοῖρα. Since Herodotus does 


not describe this term, we notice that he uses it in the singular to indicate ‘fate’ 
and in the plural Μοῖραι to indicate, possibly, beings.34 Intriguingly, these two nu- 
ances are found, e.g., at 1.91 where the Pythia responds to Croesus’ complaint 
against Apollo for not defending him appropriately (i.e., according to Croesus’ 
generous propitiation). But the Pythia subordinates even the gods to the power of 
fate (1.91.1) and consequently Loxias (i.e., Apollo) could not divert the Fates 
(1.91.2). This personification of the Moirai evinces Hesiod’s description in his The- 
ogony (904–906).35 This second usage appears an isolated case in the Histories 
based on the Delphic setting. It is intriguing for its value in understanding how 
Herodotus may have viewed what could happen behind the scenes in the divine 
realm, namely, that even the gods may be subordinate to a greater power, fate 
itself.36 Similarly, to conclude this section on the gods, noteworthy is the divine 
subordination of Pallas (i.e., Athena) to Zeus in a Delphic oracle to the Athenians, 
which begins thus: “Pallas cannot placate Olympian Zeus, pleading with many 
words and shrewd counsel […]” (7.141.3).37 So, again, Herodotus passes on two 
examples of divine subordination through Delphic oracles, rather than imitating 
the dramatic style of Homer.

the Histories. These spiritual beings share in the divine, because they were either 
denizens of the heroic age or humans who received cult status after their 
deaths.38 Herodotus appears to believe in them both and does not make a distinc- 
tion between them (e.g., Heracles and Onesilus).39 They were also well-known by

and Telamon (8.64). Still, compared to the Olympian gods (notwithstanding some 
inconsistency in this distinction), the heroes were more geographically restricted

Autonous, the local heroes of Delphi, who routed the Persians from the sanctuary 
(8.38–39).43 Typically, heroes are described as being physically large and beauti- 
ful, qualities which are considered divine in Greek culture. Like the gods, they are 
propitiated for good fortune (5.114.2; cf. 6.105.2), but they can also resent human 
fortune and punish humans for their acts of injustice (9.120.1–2).44

6.2.1.3 General Designations of the Divine 


Herodotus uses various expressions to speak of divine beings, such as ὁ θεός (‘the 
god’ and fem. ἡ θεός)45 or οἱ θεοί (‘the gods’), τὸ θεῖον (‘the divine’), ὁ δαίμων (‘the 
daimon’), and τὸ δαιμόνιον (‘the daimonion’).46 They appear often and consistently 
throughout the Histories. An outline of their uses is complicated by the fact that 
all of these terms require nuanced treatments, since rigid definitions do not fit all 
contexts evoked by Herodotus.47 Sometimes they are used synonymously; thus, 
distinctions are not always clear.48 Other times, within the same logos or even 
within the same paragraph, Herodotus might use one or another in an inconsis- 
tent sense.49 Thus, interpretations of these expressions must be explored for each 
occurrence. Scholars generally concur that Herodotus uses them in accordance 
with contemporary Greek literature; hence, no innovations are perceptible.50 An 
attempt then will be made here to point out general observations. 


In several cases, Herodotus uses these expressions (as other writers of his 


times) to indicate that a divinity was responsible for a particular action, but 
Herodotus (or a historical character) does not know the name of the god.51 Thus, 
the uses of these expressions can be twofold in that it allows him to recognise 
divine assistance and to avoid a haphazard guess as to its attribution. In these 
situations, Herodotus makes use of τὸ θεῖον or θείη τύχη (‘divine chance’).52 Yet he 
does not hesitate to offer a reasonable deduction, for example, when a miracu- 
lous action occurs near a god’s sanctuary as in the presumed interventions of Po- 
seidon in Potidaea (8.129.3) and Demeter in Plataea (9.65.2).53 In addition, this 
group of expressions is not necessarily a ‘catch-all’ category, since each one can 
be used to refer back to a divinity that has already been mentioned, which is an 
anaphoric usage for stylistic purposes to avoid repetition.54

Another nuance of these expressions is to evoke ‘the divine’ in a collective 


sense, which recognises both individuality within a corporate nature or sphere, 
even race. Linforth, for example, proposes ‘godkind’ in a similar way that one 
uses ‘humankind’ (τὸ ἀνθρώπινον). Thus, when Herodotus evokes ‘the divine’, he 
may have in mind the entire sphere or any part of those who share in the divine 
(apparently without distinction between categories). For this reason, Herodotus 
can recall examples in which aspects of divine “unity and multiplicity” exhibit 
their influence on humankind.55 Linforth expresses this cogently: “This divine 
race, godkind, set over against mankind, is very real, and its part in the affairs of 
men and the universe is plain for all to see. One can detect its influence in the 
world with more or less certainty, and one can form opinions concerning its gen- 
eral character; but little can be known about it from within.”56 


It is noteworthy (perhaps more beneficial for readers of biblical literature) 


that Herodotus does not speak in terms of two antagonistic forces, i.e., good and 
evil divine beings. This is in stark contrast to the evil or unclean spirits or demons 
found in Luke’s writings (and other New Testament narratives). For Herodotus, 
the term daimon is most often interchangeable with ‘god’, also in the description 
of individual divine beings.57 Some pejorative overtones may stem from the hu- 
man perspective in rhetorical situations.58 


Herodotus, however, does record perceptions of humanlike qualities dis- 


played in divine beings (e.g., envy, betrayal, revenge, and exaggerated punish- 
ment).59 For example, with regard to human affairs, Solon describes (for Croesus) 
the divine not only as envious but also troublesome (φθονερόν τε καὶ ταραχῶδες, 
1.32.1).60 Indeed, the divine is one of the highlighted sources of human misfortune 
in the Histories as is graphically depicted in Croesus’ subsequent downfall (cf. the 
parallel in relation to Polycrates’ success and cruel death related in 3.40–43; 
3.122–125). However, divine figures are depicted as addressing humans directly, 
often to reprimand them for behaviour that is considered displeasing or improp- 
er.61 These interventions always influence the characters and Herodotus’ inter- 
pretation.

Other perceptions of humanlike behaviour by the divine are found in Croe-

Finally, it is appropriate to consider briefly a few significant differences be- 


tween the Histories and the mythological tradition received by Herodotus. He 
generally does not dwell on theogony,63 nor on the physical appearance64 of divine 
beings, nor on their interrelations as in the narratives of Homer and Hesiod.65 


Rather than recounting actions that are taking place in the heavenly realms and 
in an anthropomorphic manner, Herodotus generally portrays divine activity in a 
sober way. Their interventions generally lead to some kind of rational end. This 
again is a step away from the mythopoetic portrayals. Another key distinction is 
that Herodotus describes divine activity from a retrospective viewpoint in light of 
what happened afterwards and what he had heard from his sources. Again, he 
was a mediator of this religious metanarrative but not a mere mouthpiece of it.66 


In sum, Herodotus often points to the divine realm as one of the most significant 
forces in the overall agōn between peoples and individuals.

6 Divine Constellations of Herodotus’ Histories and Luke-Acts

6.2.2 Luke-Acts 


Like the Histories, Luke’s literary work is also theologically driven from start to 
finish. Luke, however, offers no sustained reflection on the geography of the land, 
the politics of the day, or any other element unless it serves to illustrate the out- 
working of God’s plan of reconciliation between him and humanity.67 On the oth- 
er hand, Luke-Acts, like the Histories, is not a treatise of theological speculation. 
Rather, it is a narrative that highlights key divine works and speech for the benefit 
of humanity against the backdrop of Roman imperial structures. Like Herodotus, 
Luke also assumes that his readers have a good understanding of the underlying 
religious metanarrative: Jewish religion and beliefs, as well as other religious be- 
liefs and practices. He expects his readers to know (or have someone who can 
explain) the history of the relationship between God and Israel. Again, continuity 
is capital for Luke. When he introduces Zechariah, a priest of the temple in Jer- 
usalem, he does not deem it necessary to elaborate extensively on this priest, nor 
the temple, nor the divinity that is worshiped there. In short, it is a narrative that 
expects readers to fill in the assumed fonds de connaissance. If then, Luke-Acts is 
not a manual of theology, how does Luke represent divine nature and activity? 
Who are the main actors of the divine sphere? Here we encounter a theological 
and terminological issue that highlights a significant difference between our two 
authors. Luke’s worldview assumes one God and other beings are not in the same 
existential category. Thus, ‘divine’ must be qualified according to Luke’s terms. 
Yet limiting the discussion to what only fits the category of ‘divine’ alone would 
neglect a significant part of the world of non-human creatures, that is, angels and 
evil spirits (i.e., demons and the devil). ‘Spiritual’ (as opposed to mortal) seems to 
be a better solution, but it is not without problems.68 This discussion is limited to 
the evidence available in Luke’s writings and is occasionally illustrated by data 
from the New Testament. The references given below, however, do not always 
indicate the full number of occurrences of a given expression. 


67 
The notion of salvation or deliverance attributed to God appears very early in Luke’s Gospel 
(via σωτήριον in Luke 2:30; 3:6 and σωτηρία in 1:69, 71, 77. These occurrences help express 
the sense of expectation of divine intervention conveyed through various characters. The 
idea of divine salvation is picked up in later passages in Luke and in Acts (e.g., σωτήριον in 
Acts 28:28 and σωτηρία in Luke 19.9 and Acts 4:12; 13:26, 47; 16:17; 27:34). 


68 
Neither are the categories ‘visible’ and ‘invisible’ helpful as will be seen in Chapters 10–12 
and as elucidated in Wilson (2019) 353–370.

6.2.2.1 Divine beings: ὁ θεός, ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, κύριος, and πνεῦμα (τοῦ θεοῦ) 


and τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον. 


ὁ θεός. Luke establishes very early in his narrative that ὁ θεός means the God of 
Israel (Luke 1:16, 68; 7:16; 13:17).69 The same God who acted in Israel’s history is 
the same God who sends Jesus to his people (Acts 3:13; 5:29–32; 13:17, 23). Thus, 
an overwhelmingly monotheistic position is assumed throughout the work. This 
fact is so forceful that a pagan reader of the first century with little contact with 
the Jewish people or Jesus’ movement might have been astonished that of the 289 
occurrences of θεός in Luke-Acts only a few designate the gods of other peoples 
(e.g., Acts 7:40 and the names of pagan gods, 7:42–43; 12:22; 14:11; 17:23; 19:26, 
37; 28:6). The adjective ὕψιστος, with or without the article, also designates Is- 
rael’s God as the ‘the most high’. This can be understood as a superlative from 
either a polytheistic perspective (i.e., the highest god among many gods, cf. per- 
haps Luke 8:28 and Acts 16:17) or from a monotheistic perspective (i.e., the high- 
est God of the gods that are believed to exist, Luke 1:32, 35, 76; 6:35; Acts 7:48). 


ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. Given the monotheistic principle underlying the work, it is neces- 
sary to address the expression ‘son of God’ found in several passages. Luke pres- 
ents Jesus as “the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1:32), “Son of the Most High God” 
(Luke 8:28), and “the Son of God” (1:35; 4:3, 9; 4:41; 22:69; Acts 9:20). These ex- 
pressions assert an indissoluble relationship with the God of Israel.70 Luke does 
not delve into the question whether Jesus existed before his birth in Bethlehem, 
as is affirmed in other NT texts and later creeds. Like other NT authors, Luke por- 
trays Jesus having self-awareness of a particularly special relationship to the ‘Fa- 
ther’, e.g., as an adolescent (2:46–51) and as an adult (9:26; 10:21–24; 22:29, 42). 
During his life and especially after his death and resurrection, however, Jesus is 
described as having powers that go beyond the constraints of a normal human 
body. After his resurrection, he appears to two disciples on the road to Emmaus 
(Luke 24:13–35) and shortly afterwards to the disciples in Jerusalem (Luke 
24:36–49). Then Luke describes Jesus’ departure (or return) to heaven (ἔξοδος, 
Luke 9:31) which is told twice (Luke 24:50–53 and Acts 1:9–11). In the Acts of the 
Apostles, Luke takes up the narrative again by speaking of Jesus’ presence with 
his disciples “for forty days” (1:4). Thereafter, Luke portrays Jesus as continuing 
to manifest his presence to his disciples: for example, through his baptism by

κύριος. Similar to θεός, the expression κύριος is used in different ways in Luke-

πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον (e.g., Luke 3:22; Acts 1:16; 5:3). Another occurrence, τὸ πνεῦμα 
Ἰησοῦ (Acts 16:7), may be understood as either the Holy Spirit (to avoid repetition 
of the “Holy Spirit” in Acts 16:6) or as another example of Jesus’ post-Ascension 
presence. 


6.2.2.2 Other Spiritual Beings of Different Status 


Luke describes a world that is affected by other spiritual beings who support and 
oppose God’s established order and his plan of reconciliation for humanity (Acts 
26:18). Luke assumes his readers’ acceptance of this cosmic conflict and there- 
fore the existence of these beings. He does not argue for nor speculate upon these 
realities. Luke does not engage in the debate concerning the existence of angels or 
spirits (Acts 23:8), of which he is aware. Angels and demons form these two basic 
groups, the first being protagonists and the second antagonists. No neutral 
ground between these two antithetical camps exists in Luke’s narrative. This cat-

ἄγγελος. Angels appear early and extensively in Luke-Acts.76 Luke assumes that 
their existence requires no explanation for his readers, some of whom must have 
been acquainted with angelic activity reported in Israel’s Scriptures.77 As in most 
European languages, this word is often transliterated in English by ‘angels’, based 
on the verb ἀγγέλλω (to send) from which this expression derives. Alternatively, 
one can also translate the word with ‘messengers’, ‘emissaries’, and ‘sent ones’. 
The idea behind this expression, from Luke’s point of view, is that God sends 
these spiritual beings to perform certain tasks.78 They are at his service within the 
scope of his ordered creation and plan of reconciliation. For example, they deliv- 
er messages from God (e.g., to Zechariah [Luke 1:11–19], Mary [Luke 1:26–38], 
and Paul [Acts 27:23–24]) and they worship God (Luke 2:13). They also send, as- 
sist, and punish humans (e.g., Acts 8:26; 12:7; 12:23; 27:24). From a narratologi- 
cal perspective, they are portrayed as protagonists in the overall agōn in Luke- 
Acts. 


In contrast to angels, another group of spiritual beings exists who are antag- 


onistic towards God and to those in right standing with God. The word πνεῦμα, 
for example, does not guarantee that it is the Holy Spirit at work, because the 
same word is used to speak of antagonistic spirits. These spirits of lesser power 
and moral quality are described in various ways (via adjectives and epithets, 
etc.). Luke does not speculate on their existence or their origins, whether they 
were, for example, originally also angels and then lost this status due to their re- 
bellion against God. He always depicts them in a negative light. A hierarchy with- 
in this group is also perceivable, starting with the creature treated here below.

role with regard to God’s kingdom and authority.
