6.3 Conclusion 


The works of Herodotus and Luke show theistic continuity with their respective 
received metanarratives as regards the composition of the divine realm. Both au- 
thors share the belief that the divine realm exists and intervenes in human affairs 
on both the individual and geopolitical levels. The divine and human spheres are 
perceived as interconnected rather than watertight categories. Rather than seek- 
ing to justify this worldview as valid, both assume it. This belief structure pro- 
vides readers with a theological framework through which to interpret their his- 
tories. 


Two significant differences are notable: the theological composition of the 


divine and their depiction of it. While Herodotus exhibits a polytheistic under- 
standing of the world, Luke works with a monotheistic framework, received 
mainly through the Jewish religious heritage. Herodotus generally does not por- 
tray the divine in a mythopoetic fashion, which separates him from his predeces- 
sors and connects Herodotus with Luke by their medium of prose history. 
Herodotus typically narrates in a deductive manner, depicting his perception or 
his characters’ perceptions of how the divine was active in given situations. Luke 
also does this, but he often shows divine figures at work, for example, in the act of 
performing miracles. 


Both authors understand the divine realm to contain multiple actors. 


Herodotus speaks of the gods, the heroes, and in more general ways, such as ‘the 
divine’ or ‘the god’ to point out divine activity without attributing it to a specific 
divinity. No cosmic conflict can be noted in the Histories, only traces of some di- 
vine activity that may have been understood as having occurred behind the 
scenes.83 Luke, on the other hand, views the world as monotheistic. ‘God’ means 
the God of Israel. But the divine is understood also through the coactivity of the 
God of Israel, his son Jesus, and the Holy Spirit. Fully expressed trinitarian formu- 
las are not present in Luke-Acts.84 However, his audience is expected to under- 
stand the unity between the three divine figures as well as their cooperation in 
the accomplishment of the divine plan of salvation for humanity. With respect to 
this last element, Luke-Acts does depict conflict between God and spiritual antag- 
onists, namely, Satan and demons, who are working against God’s order and 
plan. Angels, on the other hand, are seen as spiritual protagonists working in 
God’s service and helping humans. 


In Chapters 7–12, it will be seen that both authors consistently display divine 


rule over human structures. In this, the divine and geopolitical realms are per- 
ceived as interrelated, which was a distinctive characteristic of ancient Greek his- 


83 
E.g., Apollo (Λοξίας) not being able to divert the ‘Fates’ (Hist. 1.91) or Athena’s plea to Zeus to 
change his course of action (Hist. 7.141.3) 


84 
Such as the trinitarian expressions produced at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and the 
First Council of Constantinople (381 CE). 


6 Divine Constellations of Herodotus’ Histories and Luke-Acts 
205 


toriography. A significant difference, however, between the two works is whether 
divine agency is perceived as working towards an ultimate goal.

7.1 Introduction: A Narratological and Theological Reading 


of the Geopolitical Intrigue 


Having considered Herodotus’ artful use of the ‘divine plupast’ in Chapter 5, we 
continue to explore his unique voice among the diverse literary voices of the late 
fifth century. This is his prophetic-like voice. A few preliminary remarks are in 
order for Chapters 7–9, which cover the rest of the nine volumes and their focus 
on Greek resistance to five oppressive foreign kings: Croesus, Cyrus, Cambyses, 
Darius, and Xerxes. Building on previous discussions in Chapters 2 and 3, I frame 
the ensuing discussion with a brief explanation of my approach. 


Chapters 7–9 presuppose a familiarity with the scope of Herodotus’ account 


of the Greco-Persian Wars, as well as an understanding of how this macronarra- 
tive spoke to the concerns of his audiences during the Peloponnesian War. Narra- 
tively, Herodotus is mainly working on two temporal levels: the recent past and 
the present. Much of this story would have had existential resonance with 
Herodotus’ audience (as summarised in 4.3.1). Some of the underlying questions 
for audiences in the latter part of the fifth century BCE were remarkably similar. 
Tyranny and subjugation had raised their ugly heads again, particularly through 
Athens, and Persia was still a threat. Narrative tension is at its highest when these 
moments arise, creating a sense of hopelessness when the Greeks and their allies 
are on the verge of defeat. Indeed, freedom is at stake throughout the nine vol- 
umes. This is the narrative backdrop that acts as a foil for the audience’s experi- 
ence of the Histories. It is part of the plot and the explotment. 


Theologically, Herodotus operates on and between two levels, the divine and 


the human. Due to the significant quantity of reported divine activity, it is not 
possible to provide a detailed analysis of all of the examples in the following 
chapters. The main criterion for selecting the episodes is their value in under- 
standing the overall aims of the Histories, particularly in terms of how the themes 
of imperial impulse and divine rule are connected. Herodotus’ literary genius 


brings out their interaction through his prophetic voice. Within the narrative, 
geopolitical oppression is perceived as offensive to both the divine and human 
realms. However, in Herodotus’ world, the divine has the final say. 


As a theological reading, my contribution is complementary to works al- 


ready referred to many times, especially those of Harrison and Mikalson. Harri- 
son’s Divinity and History: The Religion of Herodotus is a perceptive and detailed 
treatment of thematic elements that make the theological landscape of the Histo- 
ries so rich and intriguing. Mikalson’s Herodotus and Religion in the Persian Wars 
also has thematic chapters, but the main contribution is the narrative description 
of divine activity, appearing continuously and connectedly throughout the Histo- 
ries. Mikalson’s rich diachronic treatment (orienting audiences forward and 
backward in classical literature and material culture) is highly valuable, but it 
interrupts the narrative flow and the sense of continuous presence of the divine 
within the audience’s encounter of the narrative (i.e., the intrigue). My approach 
aims to avoid this by confining diachronic information primarily to the footnotes. 
I attempt to keep to the narrative flow by highlighting how the divine realm is 
continually brought to the audience’s attention through various narrative de- 
vices, and by focusing more closely on how Herodotus’ prophetic voice depicts 
the interrelationship between the human and divine realms during the reigns of 
the five aforementioned kings. As with Greek historiography in general, Herodo- 
tus’ story encompasses politics, military affairs, but also theology and ethics. 
These aspects cannot be viewed in watertight compartments. Herodotus’ prophet- 
ic voice invites his audience to explore these interconnected questions, both ex- 
plicitly and often implicitly. The result is a geopolitical survey with a theological 
underpinning. 


While I try to provide sufficient context for readers to appreciate the value 


of the focused episodes within the narrative flow, some readers may find addi- 
tional support helpful such as Strassler’s The Landmark Herodotus, a summary of 
the Histories such as Sean Sheehan’s A Guide to Reading Herodotus’ Histories, or 
at least a comprehensive chapter summary of the Histories.1 


We will now turn to some of the key instances of the relationship between 


the divine and the human. Given that the ‘plupast’ material was surveyed in the 
previous chapter, that is, the prelude to direct conflict between the Greeks and 
Persians, the discussion below will follow the order of the reigns of the barbarian 
kings. It will begin with Croesus of Lydia, followed by the Persian kings Cyrus and 
Cambyses. Chapters 8 and 9 will then focus on events during the reigns of Darius 
and Xerxes. 


1 
Strassler (2018); Sheehan (2018). E.g., Scanlon (2015) 26–68. 


Part III Hearing Herodotus’ Prophetic Voice 
210 


7.2 Croesus and Divine Retribution (Hist. 1.26–92) 


Croesus reigned in ca. 560–546 BCE. His tragic contribution to the story can be 
summarised thus: he subjugates the Greek cities in Asia, then he is defeated by 
Cyrus, the great Persian king. Herodotus introduces Croesus as early as Book 1.5, 
and he provides sustained attention on this Lydian king in 1.26–92. In between 
those sections, as it was noted in Chapter 5, plupast material on the royal Lydian 
line was provided. The beginning of conflicts via divine judgement for Gyges’ 
murder of Candaules finally fell on Croesus, King of Lydia. Interpreting his fate 
solely on this point, one may think that Croesus was an innocent victim upon 
whom the timebomb exploded. Nevertheless, Herodotus provides several clues 
leading to the perception that Croesus also contributed to this judgement. This 
was not a random divine intervention without cause; Croesus was an accomplice 
in his own downfall. His pompous interaction with Solon and subsequent attitude 
towards life under the gods’ rule merited their wrath. Furthermore, from the 
Greek perspective, Croesus was guilty of jeopardising Greek liberty for two rea- 
sons: he subjugated the Greek cities of Ionia (1.26.1 and 1.6.3), and he provoked 
Cyrus to enter war. This then led to the subjugation of all of Asia by Persian 
forces. Herodotus states this plainly: “Before the reign of Croesus, all Greeks were 
free” (1.6.3). 


We have already explored Solon’s visit as pivotal in Croesus’ private life in 


relation to the divine and how subsequently “the weight of divine anger descend- 
ed on Croesus” (1.34). We now consider additional divine interventions that led to 
the next step in bringing the Persian Empire into conflict with the Greek cities. 
Herodotus develops the line of divine judgement on Croesus by relating in detail 
the tragic death of Croesus’ son Atys (1.34–43). Herodotus prefaces this long story 
by indicating that divine vengeance was upon Croesus (1.34). This is confirmed 
through a dream that Atys would be killed by an iron spear. Croesus takes this 
warning seriously by doing everything he can to protect his favourite of two sons 
(the other son was born speech-impaired and is nameless in the narrative). That 
this dream is going to be fulfilled becomes steadily evident. A Phrygian, named 
Adrastos (i.e., ‘Unable-to-Escape’), arrives at Croesus’ door in order to receive rit- 
ual purification for having shed blood through bad luck. This ‘Unable-to-Escape’ 
will also bring bad luck to Croesus’ family. While Adrastos ironically was protect- 
ing prince Atys during a hunting trip, Adrastos misses the wild boar and strikes 
Atys with a deadly blow. Adrastos subsequently kills himself over the tomb of 
Atys (1.45.3). Divine causation in this tragedy is brought out in two ways. Croesus 
expresses his deep agony by evoking various epithets of Zeus as witness of his 
great misfortune: God of Purification, Protector of the Hearth, and as God of 
Guest Friendship (1.44.2).2 This is confirmed by Croesus, who, in response to 


2 
See Linforth (1926) 4. 


7 Croesus, Cyrus and Cambyses under Divine Rule 
211 


Adrastos’ plea for death, states that this tragedy was to be blamed on some god 
(1.45.2). The destruction of Croesus and his empire were at the mercy of the gods. 
And the tragedy wasn’t over; the situation was going to get worse. 


After two years of mourning Atys’ death, Croesus finds new vigour through 


learning that Cyrus had defeated Astyages, King of the Medes (550 BCE) in Cap- 
padocia and thus the power of Persia was steadily becoming a greater threat to 
the Lydian kingdom. An additional element is that Croesus was Astyages’ brother- 
in-law (cf. 1.73.1–2). Croesus now faces the question whether he should strike 
Persia pre-emptively, before it was too late. In this logos, Croesus’ attitude to- 
wards the divine reflects his mixture of piety and irreverence, especially his ex- 
cessive scepticism for testing the oracles, and not heeding Solon’s wisdom. He 
seeks counsel from an impressive number of oracles at the same time in order to 
test their veracity. This significant prophetic activity will lead to a clash between 
the Lydian and Persian kingdoms. Divine causation is at work. 


The oracle of Delphi wins the first test, and Croesus continues by testing it 


again, hoping to obtain a favourable response by offering sacrifices and lavish 
gifts to the Delphic Apollo (1.50–52). He also sends gifts to the shrine of the hero 
Amphiaraus.3 As for the question whether Croesus should attack Persia or not, 
both oracles respond similarly. If he attacks, a great empire will be destroyed, and 
he should seek the friendship of the most powerful of the Hellenes (1.53.3). Croe- 
sus interprets this as divine approval, but he still seeks confirmation from Delphi 
asking whether his kingdom would last for a long time. The answer again pleased 
Croesus, giving him greater confidence that his family would remain in power 
forever. Yet Croesus interpreted both oracles incorrectly: his empire was the 
great empire to fall, and it would certainly not recover. Is this result to be unders- 
tood as divine trickery or Croesus’ tomfoolery? Herodotus intimates his interpre- 
tation: “Having given gifts to Delphi, Croesus consulted the oracle a third time, for 
since he had received the truth by way of the oracle, he was filling himself with 
it” (1.55.1). He did, however, recognise his need for the help of the Greeks, accord- 
ing to oracular sources (1.53). This led Croesus to do some research on the most 
powerful city-states, which turned out to be the Lacedaemonians and the Atheni- 
ans (1.56). 


For this reason, before recounting the military encounter with the Persians, 


Herodotus offers to his audiences a significant digression (1.56–70) about the ori- 
gins of the Hellenes, and particularly the Athenians and the Spartans who were in 
Croesus’ scope as potential allies. In this long section, Herodotus provides several 
examples of divine acts, but none are central to the thread of geopolitical conflict 
instigated by divine sources. They do, however, keep the audience’s attention on 


3 
Herodotus also informs his audiences that the shield and the spear sent by Croesus were still 
present in the temple of Ismenian Apollo in Thebes (1.52).

divine presence.4 Additionally, Herodotus’ prophetic voice is at work on two lev- 
els as he brings into focus Athens and Sparta, the two major geopolitical powers 
of the Peloponnesian War. In this way, Herodotus is preparing his audience for a 
theological interpretation of subsequent events of the core narrative but also of 
events of their times. 


Having provided this geopolitical parallel, Herodotus resumes the narration 


about the looming military conflict between Croesus and Cyrus (1.71–73). 
Herodotus makes it clear that the gods were ultimately behind Croesus’ provoca- 
tion of Cyrus. This, at least, is Croesus’ claim, perhaps in an attempt to remove his 
guilt, which by way of his own folly and misinterpretation of a Delphic oracle, led 
Croesus to provoke Cyrus (1.72.2). This overall perception of divine instigation in 
the story is confirmed ironically. Another wise advisor, similar to Solon, is pre- 
sented in the person of Sandanis (1.71.2–4). He comments that he was glad that 
the gods never put into the heads of the Persians the idea of attacking the Lydi- 
ans. It appears, however, that they did this to Croesus, and perhaps because of 
this that Sandanis was not able to dissuade Croesus from attacking Cyrus. 
Herodotus also reports that Croesus “was yearning to conquer land in addition to 
his own portion (1.73.1); which is clearly code for hybris. With (supposed) divine 
backing and Sparta’s agreement to assist him (1.69–70), Croesus thought he had 
every reason to expect success (1.71.1). This will not be the case. Despite various 
warnings, Croesus crosses the Halys River, leading his army into direct conflict 
with the Persian army in Cappadocia (1.71–73). The Persians rout the Lydians 
and follow them all the way back to Sardis, which they capture (1.76–84). 


As for Croesus, he is miraculously delivered in two ways, the first is implicit- 


ly divine and the second is explicit. When Croesus is about to be killed in battle, 
his mute son speaks for the first time in his life – actually he screams – informing 
Persians soldiers of Croesus’ identity (1.85.3). That the boy’s action was divinely 
motivated, Herodotus deduces from a Delphic oracle announcing to Croesus, 
sometime earlier in peaceful times, that the day he heard his mute son speak 
would, ironically, be a wretched day (1.85.2). Indeed, this is the day he loses his 
freedom and great wealth. But the Lydian king is spared and brought to Cyrus for 
judgement. In the latter’s presence, Croesus should have died a second time. 
Stretched out on a pyre in blazing flames, he is saved by rain falling from a cloud- 
less sky (1.86–87). Croesus called upon Apollo to deliver him if, perchance, any of

This second divine intervention is noteworthy for its effects on both kings, 


for both are trying to ascertain, from opposite perspectives, how this all hap- 
pened. This section provides a narrative hinge between the Lydian and Persian 
kings. Both kings now sitting side by side are – figurately speaking – at the feet of 
Solon, whose teaching is audibly restated by Croesus in the flames and recounted 
to Cyrus. Now these two enemies of Greece are, paradoxically, divinely illuminat- 
ed on the precarious nature of human existence and life under divine rule. Cyrus 
thus learns with Croesus, and he resolves to preserve Croesus’ life and those of 
the fourteen Lydian boys on the pyre (1.86.6). 


Cyrus recognised the wisdom of Solon’s words, and he also feared divine ret- 


ribution. This passionate experience drives Cyrus to raise the question that every- 
one was trying to fathom: “Croesus, what sort of a man convinced you to wage 
war against my country coming before me as my enemy rather than my friend?” 
(1.87.3). Curiously, Croesus, even after his deliverance, maintains his version of 
the story, blaming divine provocation as the source of their military conflict: “O 
king, I did these things for your fortune but it was to my misfortune. The cause of 
these matters was the god of the Hellenes who incited me to wage war. For no one 
is so senseless as to choose war instead of peace, because in times of peace sons 
bury their fathers, while in times of war fathers bury their sons. But that this hap- 
pened in this way was perhaps something pleasant to the gods” (1.87.3–4).5 It will 
be seen below that Croesus, despite divine intervention, continues with the same 
mindset, contending with the gods for such an unfair treatment. 


As for Cyrus, having witnessed this divine deliverance, the new master of 


Asia recognises that somehow Croesus must have a special place in the gods’ 
hearts (1.87.2). He is a “good man” and deserves to remain alive and serve in the 
king’s court (1.88–89). Cyrus applies Solon’s message to his own life and fears di- 
vine retribution. Although he is perplexed by Croesus’ grudge against the god 
(i.e., Apollo, 1.90.2), he allows his Lydian rival to send messengers to Delphi for 
an explanation about this disappointing defeat. 


Herodotus leads his audience to explore theologically Croesus’ polemical ex- 


change with Delphi (1.90–91). The Pythian priestess informs Croesus that Apollo 
receives credit for this intervention and was even responsible for delaying the 
destruction of Sardis, which had been decreed by the Fates (1.91.3). This passage 
suggests two bits of intriguing material. First, it is even impossible for a god to 
escape destiny (1.91.1). Second, Apollo was only able to delay but not thwart Croe- 
sus’ destiny (1.91.2).6 These clarifications open a window to perceptions of the di-

Croesus, upon reception of the oracle’s response, acknowledges that he 


alone was to blame. Later in the narrative, Croesus recognises again his fault in 
the fall of Sardis (1.155.3). In this way, Herodotus closes the logos about Croesus 
by offering his (correct) interpretation of the events, placing the divine and hu- 
man dimensions in their proper places, and even how one ought to handle puz- 
zling oracles (1.91.4–6). There is then a genuine divine-human participation in 
the downfall of the Lydian kingdom: the Fates decreed it, Delphi forewarned it, 
and Cyrus carried it out (1.95.1). But Croesus destroyed his own empire (1.86.1). 
This is the motif of divine and human interaction that continues until the end of 
Book 9. 


Despite the preceding commentary on Croesus’ behaviour, one may draw a 


positive evaluation of Croesus at the end of his life. This confirms the lessons im- 
parted by Solon, whose name Croesus invoked on the pyre, recognising that Solon 
was right and even divinely inspired (1.86.3). Croesus is now depicted as a pious 
man, and one may presume that he died happier than if he had remained in Sar- 
dis amidst his great riches.8 Curiously, we are not told about his death.9 But it is 
reported that he accompanied Cyrus and Cambyses on their journeys. Nonethe- 
less, geopolitical power is now in the hands of the Persians who are masters of 
Asia as well. 


Herodotus has imparted some vital lessons to his audiences. Moles was right 


that “Solon in some sense represents Herodotus, which the sequel confirms, and 
coheres with the careers of the great sophists and Herodotus, all of whom visited 
Athens extensively.”10 More space is allotted to Croesus than to other kings be- 
cause of the narrative importance of this long section in the first book of the His- 
tories. Many scholars have noted the religious and moral tone that it gives to the 
rest of the nine volumes.11 Playfully and accurately, Pelling describes this section 
as “Educating Croesus.”12 But, narratively, this is equally an education for all read-

ers and listeners.13 Indeed, this warning is particularly appropriate to the kings of 
the East, who, as will be seen, demonstrate an exaggerated sense of self-confi- 
dence (Selbstsicherheit) before humankind and godkind.14 This continued reflec- 
tion on the Persian rulers will reinforce the lessons learned from Solon. 


Far from being a warning to those in high places alone, Herodotus’ contem- 


poraries are invited to consider its value for the rest of the story and for them- 
selves. Whether one is a colossal despot, a wealthy satrap, or a commoner, life 
under the gods’ rule is not to be taken lightly. Herodotus had introduced this sec- 
tion with a theistic underpinning. Solon states that the gods are jealous of human 
prosperity (1.32.1), and this is confirmed in Herodotus’ own comment that “a 
nemesis from god” had fallen upon Croesus after Solon’s departure (1.34.1). This 
“apparently” (ὡς εἰκάσαι) occurred because Croesus had considered himself the 
happiest man of all. This thematic development is strengthened with multiple ref- 
erences to the notion of ‘fortune’, which is defined by Solon, not in terms of 
wealth, but in terms of e.g., good health and children, and, finally, a good death 
(see 1.32.5–7; and via Croesus in 1.86–87). Solon had shown in his second exam- 
ple of happiness that it was the brothers of common stock who – because of their 
honourable death for their mother’s sake – were the happiest. Thus, as Solon an- 
nounced, one must keep the end in mind, because, ultimately, the divine realm 
has the final word. This is one of the key elements of the theology and moral fab- 
ric of the Histories. The remaining sections follow closely the thread of divine 
geopolitics through which these principles are driven home by our master narra- 
tor. Even Cyrus, despite his extraordinary background, will not elude these inex- 
orable principles under divine rule. 


7.3 Cyrus and the Continuing Subjugation of the Greeks in Ionia 


(Hist. 1.95–216) 


The narrative hinge connecting the Lydian and Persian rulers allows the audi- 
ence to appreciate how Cyrus encounters the logic of the theistic worldview de- 
scribed by Herodotus. Narratively, without Croesus, the Persians might not have 
entered such a deep conflict with the Greeks. Without Croesus, the story would be 
incomplete. The direct line of divine involvement in the passage of human power 
is clearly stated in Croesus’ own words, which appear later in the narrative, when 
Croesus prefaces his counsel and allegiance to Cyrus: “O King, as I told you when 
Zeus gave me to you, that if I saw one, I would avert any disaster from your house 
with all my strength” (1.207.1). 


13 
See Immerwahr (1966) 154 and Pelling (2006) 172–173. 


14

Cyrus is portrayed as a witness to the miraculous events surrounding Croe- 


sus’ deliverance at his execution and the transformation of his character. For 
Herodotus, the lesson is clear: life under the gods can be brutal. From this van- 
tage point, Cyrus has a distinct advantage over Croesus. The former knows that it 
pays to live respectfully under divine rule and perhaps avoid the same mistakes 
committed by his Lydian counterpart. From the audience’s perspective, this ap- 
plies equally to Cyrus’ successors, which allows for greater audience participa- 
tion in the evaluation of individuals, both great and small. What then is the theo- 
logical evaluation of Cyrus, who destroyed the empire of Croesus and became the 
undisputed leader of Asia (1.95.1)? Herodotus primarily dedicates the rest of Book 
1 to this remarkable figure (1.94–216), with not a few plupast digressions.15 Cyrus’ 
tragic end provides still another anecdote confirming Solon’s (and, presumably, 
Herodotus’) teaching (1.214).16 


The long retrospective section about the period before Cyrus’ rule demons- 


trates Herodotus’ concern to show divine providence and fulfilment supporting 
this renowned figure (1.96–129). Herodotus reports two dreams of Astyages, king 
of Media from 584 to 550. The first dream concerns his daughter, Mandane, who 
urinated so much that his city and all of Asia were filled (1.107). His second 
dream also involves his daughter from whose genitals a vine extended to cover 
Asia (1.108). The interpreters, the Magi, take these dreams very seriously, because 
both dreams specifically concern Asia. Herodotus adduces this prophetic activity 
so as to enhance the story’s importance. It also adds to the overall accent on 
prophetic activity in relation to kings and kingdoms and divine bearing on world 
history. 


For fear of the dreams, Astyages marries his daughter to a Persian, whose 


name is Cambyses.17 Mandane becomes pregnant and gives birth to Cyrus. Astyag- 
es’ plan to kill Cyrus is thwarted by a combination of human actors. Herodotus 
recounts how Cyrus grew up and was recognised to be the fulfilment of Astyages’ 
dreams. Humanly speaking, that which should not have happened did happen on 
account of divine and human interventions. Herodotus summarises this interpre- 
tation through the voice of Harpagus: “O son of Cambyses, the gods are watching 
over you, because, if not, you would not have reached such fortune; now you 
must avenge yourself against your murderer Astyages! For you would have died 
according to his desire, but thanks to the favour of the gods and mine, you have 
survived” (1.124.1b–2a). The fact of being set aside by divine providence (θείῃ

τύχῃ) supported his confidence in overthrowing the Medes for the sake of liberty

whether Greek or Persian, are active behind the scenes to shape the geopolitical 
landscape. It was now Cyrus’ turn to bring order in the human sphere, namely, 
the task of political liberation.18 


Like other kings, Cyrus moves beyond his initial victory of liberation to sub- 


jugate other targets. He has in sight the Assyrians (Babylon), the Bactrians, the 
Sacae, and the Egyptians, and he delegated the Ionian question to his subordi- 
nates (1.153.4). His hunger for domination eventually leads to his own downfall. 
Subsequently, Persia crushes the Lydian revolt (1.157) and takes Ionia (except for 
Miletus, thanks to a pact) through the leadership of Harpagus (with various di- 
gressions recounted in 1.162–169). Harpagus continues Persian conquest by con- 
quering the Carians, the Caunians, and the Lycians (1.171.1). Herodotus is atten- 
tive to point out that this was the second time Ionia was enslaved (οὕτω δὴ τὸ 
δεύτερον Ἰωνίη ἐδεδούλωτο), thus drawing a clear parallel between Croesus and 
Cyrus (Lydia and Persia, 1.169.2). In Herodotus’ view, geopolitical encroachment 
and enslavement eventually lead to divine jealousy and judgement.19 This now 
will play itself out in the conquests of Cyrus, who, in the meantime, had other 
prey in his sights rather than the Asians (1.177). But Herodotus’ narrative on this 
part is limited to those especially interesting matters, e.g., Cyrus’ capture of Baby- 
lon but also his defeat at the hands of the Massagetae. Herodotus’ narrative focus 
rings clear on these two peoples in 1.178 and 1.201, as both peoples are described 
as particularly strong, the Assyrians for their cities and the Massagetae for their 
warlike disposition. 


The conquest of Assyria has its showcase in the capture of Babylon.20 At the

punishing the river Gyndes by weakening it (1.189–190). Herodotus does not pro- 
vide commentary on this event, allowing his audiences to fathom this sacrilegious 
act.21 The religious nature of this scene is striking. It is the drowning of one of 
Cyrus’ ‘white horses’ that are sacred to the sun (1.89; 3.90; 7.40) that causes him

Narratively selective, Herodotus turns to Cyrus’ next prey, the Massagetae, 


who lived to the east of the Caspian Sea (1.201). Cyrus’ intense desire of subjuga- 
tion is underlined by Herodotus: ἐπεθύμησε Μασσαγέτας ὑπ᾽ ἑωυτῷ ποιήσασθαι 
(1.201). Yet this was “a numerous and warlike people,” which begs the question – 
especially in light of their geographical location – why Cyrus wished to subjugate 
them. Further on, Herodotus reveals his motives (1.204.2). Of the “many things,” 
two are singled out: Cyrus’ belief in his origin as being “more-than-human” and 
his good fortune in military campaigns. Here again the link between the divine 
and the human realms emerges as a main factor in the narrative line of cause and 
effect. Convinced of the gods’ favour (1.209.4), Cyrus thought himself unstop- 
pable, being of divine provenance and having a spotless military record. How 
could the Massagetae possibly oppose the Persian war machine? Highly impor- 
tant for the narrative is that the Massagetae were led by a woman, Tomyris 
(1.205; see Croesus’ remark in 1.207.5). Cyrus was voracious for more land and 
power, succinctly echoed in the queen’s words: “Since you will not accept this 
counsel, and by no means keep the peace, if you indeed wish so greatly to put the 
Massagetae to the test […]” (1.206.2). The irony of hybris is building up; Cyrus will 
deserve his downfall, and it is predicated by Croesus’ advice to cross the Araxes 
River (1.207.5). By crossing the river, he is in the line of other kings who, because 
of their hybris, tempt the gods.23 


Indeed, according to Herodotus’ representation, Cyrus still had another 


chance to avoid his disaster. A dream comes to him while he is in Massagetae ter- 
ritory (1.209). In the dream, he sees Darius, the son of Hystaspes, with a pair of 
wings, one covering Asia and the other covering Europe. Through the voice of 
Cyrus, Herodotus is preparing his audience for the thread that will eventually 
manifest itself. Darius will be a legitimate successor with a keen interest in Asia 
and Europe. Yet Cyrus mistakenly believes that this young man of twenty is plott- 
ing against him while he is away.24 Cyrus believes that the gods watch over him 
and warn him of imminent danger. However, like Croesus, he misinterprets the 
signs.25

Herodotus’ prophetic voice emerges with oracular authority by providing 


the right interpretation and inviting his audience to consider the warnings that 
follow from it. The dream had been given to Cyrus by a god (ὁ δαίμων) to warn 
him of his impending death (1.210.1). Consequently, Darius’ father Hystaspes re- 
turns to Persia to keep an eye on him, and in the meantime, Cyrus is killed by the 
Massagetae. Lessons are to be drawn from this fatal ending, which ironically echo 
Croesus’ story. The question of domination for Europe and Asia; thus, liberty is at 
stake. This thread is again brought to the fore through the depiction of divine in- 
tervention. While the Lydian royal line was decreed to fall, Cyrus was entirely at 
fault for his own divine judgement. He was in the wrong for two main reasons, 
which would become pitfalls for his successors. He did not respect the ever-pres- 
ent gods, whom he presumptuously thought to be always on his side, while he 
impiously pushed the ‘normal’ geographical limits of his power by attacking the 
Massagetae. Additionally, while he protected his own royal lineage by sending his 
son Cambyses back to Persia before the battle, he prompted the bitter end for 
Spargapises, Tomyris’ son (1.213). Second, through his incorrect interpretation of 
the divine warning (1.209), he became an accomplice to his own destruction 
(1.210.1). 


Croesus, although still a prisoner, apparently died in good health.26 Cyrus, 


however, was ridiculed by a female ruler who made him drink (post-mortem) the 
blood of his wrath, which she had pledged in the name of her god, the sun (ἥλιον 
ἐπόμνυμί τοι τὸν Μασσαγετέων δεσπότην, 1.212.3).27 Herodotus invites his audi- 
ence to weigh this subtle indication of divine intervention for the sake of Queen 
Tomyris and her people.28 Despite her invoking the Massagetae god and referring 
to Helios as despotēs, Cyrus had completely disregarded Tomyris’ terms. This ex- 
pression is also used to describe Cambyses in 3.89.3 because he was “harsh and 
arrogant.” This severe description of Helios illustrates well the earlier discussion 
of life under the gods as being brutal. Cyrus’ violent death drives this point home, 
and it ends Book 1, followed only by a brief discussion of the military and social 
customs of the Massagetae.29 Despite their military defeat, the Persians retain con- 
trol of the centre of power, at least in relation to the Eurasian conflict. Herodotus 
thus continues his enquiry with Cyrus’ heir, Cambyses, whose reign and death 
also prompt theological reflection. 


26 
The last word we hear about Croesus in relation to Cyrus is that the latter delegated his son 
Cambyses to accompany Croesus back to Persia (1.208).

7.4 Cambyses’ Campaigns against Egypt and Ethiopia (Hist. 2.1–3.66) 


The narrative of Cambyses’ reign (2.1–3.66) focuses almost exclusively on his rule 
in Egypt. It is well-known that all of Book 2 appears to be a long digression about 
Egypt. Direct geopolitical intrigues between the Greeks and the Persians are al- 
most completely set aside. But this is only apparent, because – from both Persian 
and Greek points of view – this section continues to develop the intrigue about 
political domination of the Mediterranean basin. If the Mediterranean and its 
coastlands are at risk, then logically the Greek city-states are also deeply affected. 
Consequently, for Greek audiences, this part of the enquiry must have held par- 
ticular interest. In addition, Book 2 presents numerous examples of the historical 
and cultural links between the Greeks and the Egyptians. For example, Herodotus 
discusses the origins of the worship of the gods (e.g., 2.4.2; 2.50–52; 2.58.1; 2.82– 
83). In this regard, Egypt appears in the very first story of Book 1 where Io is re- 
ported (by the Persians!) to have been brought to Egypt (1.1.4).30 The significance 
of this is that Io’s son (with Zeus), Apis (gr. Epaphos), is one of the major gods of 
Egypt who becomes a protagonist in the fatal end of Cambyses. Another notewor- 
thy connection is that the eminent Solon had visited Egypt before going to Sardis 
to meet Croesus (1.30.1).31 All of this serves to highlight the magnitude of Egyptian 
culture, both its antiquity and its peculiarities, as well as its relevance for the 
geopolitical and theological story. The result is a rich spiritual landscape in Egypt 
and Ethiopia, which contributes to a theological reading of the rule of Cambyses. 


How then does Herodotus represent the relationship between the Greeks 


and the Persians? At the very beginning of Book 2, Herodotus reports that Camby- 
ses considered the Ionians and the Aeolians to be his father’s slaves.32 For this 
reason, Cambyses forced them to serve in his conquest of Egypt. Thus, the Eura- 
sian conflict is assumed as it is extended to Egypt. The reason for Cambyses’ inter- 
est in Egypt lies in the fact that Egypt had made an alliance with Croesus between 
555 and 546 which also included Babylon. Once Babylon had been subjugated, it 
seemed reasonable to Cambyses to enslave Egypt as well.33 Herodotus provides 
other reasons for Cambyses’ conquest, but, if they are true, they are only supple- 
mentary to his desire for further conquest (i.e., Amasis’ trickery involving Nitetis 
instead of his own daughter for Cambyses; and Cambyses’ youthful boast of his 
future overthrow of Egypt, 3.1–3). 


30 
Herodotus also brings a lengthy critical discussion of the story of Helen and Alexander (Paris) 
(2.113–20), as well as a corrective to the story about Rhodopis (2.134–135). 


31 
Ionians and Carians were also key for Greek and Egyptian relations as they assisted Psam- 
metichus’ ascent to Egyptian rule and for their transmission of knowledge about Egyptian 
history (2.154). A story about Elis and Egypt is told about how the grand Egyptian wisdom 
tradition gave counsel to the Elians regarding the question of fairness in the Olympic games 
(2.160).

Herodotus picks up this thread with the Ionians and the Aeolians as Hellenes in 3.1.1.

Herodotus also includes the Ionians (2.15–17) and the Hellenes (e.g., 2.20) – 


apparently not making a distinction between these designations (summed up by 
“Hellenes” at 2.1.2) – in his discussions about the differences of interpretation re- 
garding a variety of topics: the origins of humanity, religion, geography, etc.34 He 
attempts to provide correct information, for example, regarding the physical lim- 
its of Egypt. He argues that it encloses all residents of the Nile valley. As proof of 
this, after having done his own thinking on the subject, he confirms it with an 
oracle from Ammon (2.18.1).35 Thus, in his correction of the Ionians’ interpreta- 
tion according to which the limits of Egypt are determined by the Nile Delta alone 
(2.15–17), he argues that Egypt, being much greater in size, can be rightly con- 
sidered a fourth part of the earth, along with Europe, Asia, and Libya. This high- 
lights the grandeur of Egypt, and, consequently, the scope and stakes of Persia’s 
subjugation of this ancient people and culture. 


Of course, Herodotus could have omitted much of the material presented in 


Book 2 so as to focus more on events during Cambyses’ reign, between Cyrus and 
Darius. However, Herodotus undoubtedly gives Egypt the attention it deserves in 
order to be complete in his overall investigation of the regions explored.36 Since 
Cambyses’ focus is on Egypt (2.1–3.16) and Ethiopia (3.17–26), Herodotus offers 
significant narrative space to describe the geography, history, and customs of 
these peoples. This is where Herodotus, the geographer, cultural-anthropologist, 
and theologian shines.37 The lengthy treatment of the grand culture and history of 
Egypt provides a backdrop by which to compare the squalid victory of Cambyses 
who shows no appreciation for their cultural sophistication or their gods, the 
height of which is his slaying of the sacred Apis bull in Memphis. In Herodotus’ 
representation, Cambyses is sacrilegious, which fits well with the description of 
the following Persian kings. Herodotus is raising red flags for his audience. 


In contradictory fashion, Herodotus states that he will not repeat much of 


what he gathered in Egypt about the gods, and yet he provides some of the most 
detailed religious commentary in all his work about religious practices (2.3.2). In 
one of his most important asides about the divine, Herodotus states that he will 
broach the subject of the divine only when the story demands it for explanatory

Herodotus writes that he knows more about Egyptian religious practices, but he 
prefers not to divulge this information owing to his reverence for the divine 
(2.171.1–2). This, however, does not stop him from continually comparing knowl- 
edge and practice of the relationship between the divine and human spheres. His 
treatment, in this part of the narrative, lacks illustrations of divine intervention 
that have been encountered thus far in the narrative. Attention to the divine 
sphere, however, is very much kept before the eyes of the audience. 


Herodotus’ description of Egypt and Ethiopia is a multifaceted spiritual land- 


scape, which provides the backdrop for a theological reading of the reign of Cam- 
byses. The divine realm is very much present in the narrative through discus- 
sions on Egyptian gods, temples, and worship practices. This is indeed the irony: 
while Egypt is reported to be full of the divine, their gods are not able – or are 
unwilling – to avert Cambyses’ victory. Furthermore, Cambyses openly refuses to 
respect the divine in Egypt. This irreverent attitude will literally come back to 
stab him at the end of his days, far from Egypt.39 A theological reading then re- 
quires attention to details that Herodotus may not explicitly point out. For exam- 
ple, just after the death of the Egyptian king Amasis (570–526 BCE) and before 
military conflict with the Persians, an extraordinary thing happened at the begin- 
ning of the brief rule of Amasis’ son Psammenitus: it rained in Thebes, which in 
those times never happened (3.10.3). Given that Herodotus remarks that nothing 
really important happened during the reign of forty-four years of Amasis, now an 
unheard-of natural event is reported without interpretation. Most likely it is to be 
derived as a portent heralding immanent trouble for Egypt at the hands of Persia. 


Hence, Herodotus continues his intricate storyline about kings and the di- 


vine. Some of the motifs introduced in relation to Croesus and Cyrus are devel- 
oped with respect to Cambyses, and thus provide an unbroken chain with Darius, 
Xerxes, and other political leaders that follow. Interestingly, the thread about Per- 
sian conquest is picked up again at the end of Book 2 where Herodotus introduces 
Amasis, whose kingdom and son would be overthrown by Cambyses. This be- 
comes the narrative hinge between Books 2 and 3. 


Herodotus paints a favourable picture of Amasis, who, significantly, is a Hel- 


lenophile. Book 2 ends therefore with the Hellenes and the Egyptians on friendly 
terms.40 Amasis shows his respect for the Hellenes by giving lavish gifts to various 
Greek centres of worship (2.182.1–2). Book 3, however, begins with Egypt and 
Persia at odds (for the reasons given above). But what part do the Greeks play in 
this? The Greeks of Asia Minor are enlisted on the side of the Persians via en-

With little difficulty, Cambyses conquers Psammenitus in 525 BCE. Yet, simi- 


lar to other kings described by Herodotus, Cambyses commits the tragic error of 
stepping too far in Egypt by violating Egyptian customs, exhibiting cruelty (3.11– 
14), and offending their gods. In fact, of all the Persian kings, Cambyses seems to 
have had the most difficult relationship with the divine realm. He is openly and 
consistently sceptical and antagonistic towards the gods. With this demeanour to- 
wards the divine, the audience is prepared to foresee a knotty future for Camby- 
ses, who turns his attention to the conquest of Ethiopia. 


In prophetic fashion, the Ethiopian king, who remains unnamed in the nar- 


rative, reveals a recurring element about the divine geopolitical thread in the His- 
tories. He recognises the treachery of Cambyses’ diplomats, and he sends word 
back to the Persian king who should be thankful that the gods had not turned the 
thoughts of the Ethiopians on his country (3.21.3). Cambyses’ attitude towards 
them and the king’s reply echoes the story of Cyrus and Queen Tomyris. Camby- 
ses had now reached too far and was going to pay for his imperial impulse and 
hybris. His anger at the reply of the Ethiopian king caused him to make two fatal 
decisions: his departure for Ethiopia without sufficient provisions and the dis- 
patch of a large army against the Ammonians in the desert in order to burn their 
temple of Zeus, which is also an oracular site. Neither part of the army reached 
their destination. In Herodotean manner, one may understand this as a divine 
intervention, deduced by the story of a large sandstorm burying the Persian con- 
tingent in the desert (3.26.3). No traces were left of them. 


Cambyses’ lack of mental stability (3.25.2) gets worse upon his return to 


Memphis. At this point in the narrative, the link between the divine and the royal 
family increases significantly. In an ironic measure, it was said that the god Apis 
(gr. Epaphos) had appeared in those days in Memphis. This god’s manifestation 
was extremely rare, and the Egyptians, as custom demanded, were celebrating it 
grandly. Cambyses understood this falsely as their way of celebrating his terrible 
military misfortunes.41 Subsequently, in addition to having the rulers of Memphis 
killed and the priests beaten, he also committed a great sacrilege by stabbing the 
Apis in the thigh. The animal, believed to be a divine manifestation in the form of 
a calf, died on the altar. 


From the Egyptians’ perspective, Cambyses’ mental state, which was already 


poor, only grew worse after this wicked act (διὰ τοῦτο τὸ ἀδίκημα ἐμάνη, 3.30.1). 
Herodotus signals again the link between the divine and the royal line by admitt- 
ing the possibility of impiety as a result of Cambyses’ insanity (3.33). To support

this, he offers a curious bit of information about Cambyses. It was said that he 
suffered a “sacred disease” from birth, namely, epilepsy, whose symptoms resem- 
bled the ecstatic seizures of diviners (3.33). Later, Herodotus confirms this by stat- 
ing that his blatant acts of mockery of the gods and other impieties were proofs of 
his madness (3.37–38). 


More divine activity is reported to have followed Cambyses. Having rejected 


the apparition of Apis at Memphis, he now receives his own apparition in a 
dream. A messenger from Persia reveals that someone named Smerdis is sitting 
on the throne and that his head is touching the sky (3.30.2). This time Cambyses 
takes the revelation seriously and sends someone to kill his brother Smerdis, also 
a son of Cyrus (3.30.3). Leaving his readers in suspense about important details of 
this dream, Herodotus resumes the tragic story of Smerdis’ murder below. Other 
acts of Cambyses’ madness are reported, including the murder of his wife (3.31– 
32), the murder of a young boy (Prexaspes’ son, 3.35); and the attempted murder 
of the still-living Croesus (3.36). But more follows. Cambyses commits sacrilegious 
acts in the temples of Hephaestus and of the Cabiri (3.37). Then, before moving to 
a digression on Sparta, Herodotus concludes this section on Cambyses with ex- 
plicit commentary: the king was clearly out of his mind, for no one would per- 
form such acts against other people’s religious concerns and customs that are so 
dear to them (3.38).42 


Then, by way of a digression in 3.39–60, Herodotus sets aside the Persian 


storyline in order to explore the political intrigues behind the Spartan War in 525 
BCE. This parenthesis offers a few noteworthy points about perceptions of the di- 
vine realm in which a parallel is developed.43 While the Spartans were waging 
war against Samos, Cambyses was attacking Egypt. King Amasis had made an al- 
liance with Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos. Amasis was worried that Polycrates’ 
great fortune would soon run out, given that the god (τὸ θεῖον) is jealous of hu- 
man fortune (echoing Solon’s counsel to Croesus). Amasis suggests a way to avert 
divine jealousy, which is that Polycrates must give up something he esteems of 
highest value. Polycrates throws away a decorous signet ring into the sea. But a 
fisherman brings it back to Polycrates, having found it in the belly of a fish. When 
Amasis received this story from his counterpart, he broke off his alliance with the 
Samian tyrant, reasoning that, sooner or later, Polycrates would suffer great mis- 
fortune (3.43). Despite noting some success against the Spartans, Herodotus, final- 
ly at 3.125, tells of the cruel death that befalls Polycrates through the hands of 
Oroites, a Persian governor. Polycrates’ death – according to Herodotus – ful-

Following these anecdotes about Polycrates and various battles, the rest of 


Book 3 brings back into focus the Persian Empire, which goes through political 
instability between the death of Cambyses in 522 BCE and the accession of Darius 
as legitimate heir in 521 BCE.44 In 3.64–66 Herodotus concludes his treatment of 
Cambyses’ rule by mentioning multiple contacts between the divine sphere and 
Persian rule. Two events reveal how the divine and human realms operate in par- 
allel in Cambyses’ death. First, Herodotus links Cambyses’ fate by resuming the 
story about the dream of a conspiracy led by a certain Smerdis. However, the au- 
thor of this usurpation, revealed in the dream as Smerdis, was not his brother, 
but a homonymous magus who, with his brother Patizeithes, wishes to deliver the 
empire into their hands (3.61.1–3). In this way, Cambyses, having misinterpreted 
the dream, participates, like Croesus and Cyrus, in bringing about his own down- 
fall. It cost his brother’s life, his kingdom, and ultimately his own life (3.65.4). 
Mikalson rightly comments, “Most of the dreams Herodotus reports give signs of 
failure or disaster and what they predict is inescapable.”45 In addition, Cambyses 
reports that an apparition (ὄψις) and a god (ὁ δαίμων) had warned him in the 
dream (3.65.2, 4). This is how divine presence and intervention are perceived. His 
dream about Smerdis functions as a portent; nothing can prevent its fulfilment. A 
theological reading suggests that the gods knew this beforehand, that the dream 
was a test that would reveal the king’s true character.46 In Cambyses’ own words: 
“for it is not in human nature to avert what is going to happen” (3.65.3), and di- 
vine activity is reported to have helped bring about the fulfilment of Cambyses’ 
fated downfall. 


The second act of divine-human interaction is articulated through the great 


irony of Cambyses’ death. Having learned about his error in interpretation, he 
clumsily mounts his horse and mortally wounds himself in the thigh, at the same 
place where he had stabbed the Apis calf (3.64.3; cf. 3.29.1). Cambyses who had 
impiously rejected the gods of Egypt in Egypt, died at the hands of an Egyptian 
god far from his land of worship. In fact, Cambyses’ death in Ecbatana had been 
foreordained by an oracle. Cambyses had accepted this favourably as Ecbatana of 
Media, but he actually died in Ecbatana of Syria (3.64.3–5). Divine retribution is 
again underlined with reference to political leadership, through an apparition 
and a wound. Also, the divine implementations of the names Smerdis and Ec- 
batana to lead Cambyses to believe one thing for another is patently devious.

Cambyses died after seven years and five months of rule, leaving no children at 
all (3.66.1–2). Surely, Herodotus’ audience could not consider this man blessed by 
the gods, even after his confession of remorse for his brother’s murder and for 
his sins (3.65.1–7). 


Cambyses’ bit of piety rises to the occasion concerning the question of royal 


succession. The rule must never pass again to the Medes, he exclaims. In doing so, 
he invokes “the gods of the royal house” (3.65.6). These deities are the protectors 
of this line of kings and will ensure, as he wishes, that sovereignty remains in the 
Achaemenid royal family. Following this devout injunction, he announces bless- 
ings or curses, depending on his family’s obedience to his final wishes (3.65.7). 
The curse is particularly revealing, as he acknowledges his own tragic life and 
threatens the Achaemenids with these words in case of disobedience: “[…] but if 
you do not recover the rule nor attempt to recover it, then I pray that the opposite 
will happen to you, and, moreover, that the same end of life might befall every 
Persian in the same way that it befell me” (3.65.7). In this way, the divine geopolit- 
ical intrigue remains present in the minds of the participants and Herodotus’ au- 
dience. 


7.5 Conclusion 


Herodotus’ prophetic voice weaves multiple theological and geopolitical threads 
in his treatment of the reigns of Croesus, Cyrus, and Cambyses. The theological 
underpinnings of the overarching narrative are consistently brought to the fore- 
front through illustrations of divine intervention, such as acts, oracles, and por- 
tents, as well as through Herodotus’ description of the reciprocal relationship be- 
tween worshippers and their gods (especially in Book 2). This narrative interest 
creates a rich spiritual landscape for the audience to explore. Herodotus’ narra- 
tive is not speculative theology. Rather, it is one interpretation of the reality of 
human experience, for individuals and peoples alike. Reading this against the 
backdrop of the Peloponnesian War would certainly have enhanced the audi- 
ence’s reception of the ‘miraculous story’ of the Greeks’ victory against the Per- 
sians. Furthermore, these stories and the theological framework stimulate 
Herodotus’ audience to reflect on how the lessons learned (e.g., the risks of 
amassing fortune, hybris, and disrespecting the divine) could inform their experi- 
ence of internecine conflict. 


The geopolitical agōn is perceived by most, if not all, of Herodotus’ focalised 


characters to be partly due to divine involvement, even instigation (e.g., Croesus 
attacking Cyrus). But the desire for expansion, the imperial impulse, is mainly at- 
tributed to human nature. The Eurasian conflict widens when Cyrus enters the 
scene, and it extends further under Cambyses to involve a greater part of the 
Mediterranean when Egypt is added to the number of territories under Persian 


7 Croesus, Cyrus and Cambyses under Divine Rule 
227 


rule. Herodotus depicts divine-human interaction in the fall of these kings. Their 
participation in their fall comes mainly through acts of hybris. The gods keep this 
in check, and they punish them for acts of sacrilege, for example, the mishandling 
of oracles and offences to nature (e.g., rivers). Even the narrative digressions in 
Books 2 and 3 have their function in creating a spiritual and moral landscape 
through which readers virtually travel. For example, theological continuity cross- 
es geographical and ethnographic boundaries through the numerous links be- 
tween the gods’ origins and names, particularly between Egypt and Greece. More- 
over, cultural customs, including many religious practices, are shown to be 
necessarily authoritative, even for foreign rulers. For Croesus, Cyrus, and Camby- 
ses, divine retribution for sacrilegious actions is shown to reach human rulers 
indiscriminately in their home territories or abroad, inspired by the imperial im- 
pulse. Following Cambyses’ tragedy, a new period opens in Persia’s history under 
the reign of Darius (521–486 BCE). The next chapter examines how Herodotus 
leads his audience to explore how Darius and others fare under divine rule.

8 Darius under Divine Rule: Persia’s First Invasion of Greece 


(Hist. End of Book 3, Books 4–6) 


You whose fortunate fate surpassed all mortals in bliss, how enviable you 
were when you saw the light of the sun and led a life of such happiness that 
Persians looked on you as a god! And now too I envy you, because you died 
before seeing the depths of our present suffering. It will take you very little 
time, Darius, to hear the whole story: to all intents and purposes, the for- 
tunes of Persia are utterly ruined. 


Queen Atossa to the ghost of Darius in Aeschylus’ The Persians (trans. Som- 
merstein, LCL 145) 


8.1 Introduction 


Herodotus’ first three books describe, among many things, the founding of the 
Persian Empire, alongside early developments in Greece, and show how the di- 
vine realm (in its various perceived manifestations) shaped the lives and reigns 
of Croesus, Cyrus, and Cambyses. Herodotus’ audience is now well prepared to 
observe divine involvement in the geopolitical agōn of the Persian invasions, led 
by Darius and Xerxes, in Books 4–9. This chapter zeroes in on Herodotus’ 
prophetic voice in the description of Darius’ imperial impulse. The end of Book 3 
describes Darius’ ascension to the throne with the help of the divine. Books 4–6 
concentrate on his failed subjugation of the Scythians, the repression of the Ioni- 
an Revolt, and then the Persians’ humiliating defeat at Marathon. Along the way, 
Herodotus imparts lessons through numerous anecdotes about divine rule. Sever- 
al motifs are picked up again in the narrative and interwoven with respect to 
Darius’ rule. For example, his lack of piety, even sacrilege, leads to social discord. 
The humiliation of individuals, cities, states, and peoples involves the destruction 
of their homes and cities, as well as their temples and customs. In Herodotean 
thinking, aiming to subjugate people has religious and moral connotations and 
implications. All of this contributes to the main theme for Herodotus’ audience: 
the agōn for the rule of Asia and Europe. Audiences of the late fifth century knew 
that Darius had failed to conquer the latter. But how did he fail? Who was respon- 
sible for this first massive failure? And were the gods perceived by Herodotus or 


by his characters to be helping or hindering Darius’ imperial impulse to rule both 
continents? 


8.2 The Accession of Darius and the Beginnings of his Reign 


(Hist. 3.61–160) 


In the remainder of Book 3, Herodotus explores three main points: Darius’ acces- 
sion to the throne, the breadth of his realm and administration, and the beginn- 
ings of his reign vis-à-vis other peoples and individuals. Herodotus gives us here a 
glimpse of the type of king Darius would become during his reign from 521 to 486 
BCE. Herodotus’ prophetic voice is distinctive as he points out perceptions of di- 
vine activity, from Darius’ extraordinary climb to power to his humiliating 
demise after the great defeat at Marathon in 490. Significant attention is given in 
this chapter to the beginnings of this part of Darius’ reign because of the depic- 
tion that Herodotus provides about the divine and human realms. This prepares 
his audience to interpret and experience Darius’ imperial impulse to subjugate 
other peoples beyond the borders of his vast kingdom. 


Like the succession between Cyrus and Cambyses, Darius obtained kingship 


thanks in part to divine judgement on Cambyses. The passage from one king to 
the next is accompanied by divine intervention. Yet the divine geopolitical thread 
is stronger in Darius’ case in that his accession to the Persian throne is not hand- 
ed over to him simply by divine right. Cambyses had no heir, and Darius, son of a 
satrap, must fight for his claim to the throne by dealing with the Magi who had 
successfully tricked everyone back in Persia. This was aided, among Cambyses’ 
contingent, by the Persians’ scepticism of Cambyses’ confession (3.66) and by 
Prexaspes’ denial of having killed Smerdis, Cyrus’ son! It will take a combination 
of human and divine agency to allow Darius to make his way to the throne. A 
theological reading will elucidate Herodotus’ emphasis on divine involvement in 
these early stages of Darius’ rise to power. 


Support for Darius’ plan to overthrow the Medan Magus comes through Go- 


bryas, one of the seven conspirators, who recalls with insistence Cambyses’ curs- 
es (uttered in 3.65.7 and recalled in 3.73.2). They must act now or else risk divine 
judgement. This injunction convinces ‘the Seven’ (οἱ ἑπτά), and “having prayed to 
the gods,” they departed straight away for Susa. Unbeknownst to Darius and his 
conspirators, the Magis’ rule was being publicly and unexpectedly challenged by 
Prexaspes in Susa (3.75). The Magi had considered him a loyal collaborator in 
their scheme. However, upon the palace tower, Prexaspes betrays the Magi by re- 
vealing their deception to a great crowd. Smerdis, son of Cyrus, really was dead; 
thus, Smerdis the Magus was an imposter. He then invokes similar curses to those 
of Cambyses on the Persian people if they do not overthrow the Medan rule of the 


Part III Hearing Herodotus’ Prophetic Voice 
230 


Magi. In Herodotus’ eyes, Prexaspes showed himself to be an admirable man by 
challenging the Magi and throwing himself off the tower for the Persian cause. 
This evinces the wisdom of Solon: Prexaspes died with a clear conscience and 
was perhaps a happy man. 


Meanwhile, the seven conspirators learn of these events midway, which 


causes them to reconsider whether the timing was right for their intervention. 
The debate is fierce, but, here again, divine assistance gives them courage to carry 
out Darius’ plan. While they are debating, seven (not five or six) pairs of hawks 
flew by, chasing two pairs of vultures. The Seven conclude that this omen con- 
firms their decision, “being emboldened by the birds” (3.76.3).1 Darius’ idea to 
present themselves directly at the palace doors proved to be providentially 
backed as well, as Herodotus notes in an aside: “they passed by making use of the 
divine escort (παρίεσαν θείῃ πομπῇ χρεωμένους)” (3.77.1). Herodotus is building 
up a case for divine approval of Darius’ march to the throne; it is greater than 
coincidence or human achievement. The ruling Magi are beheaded, evoking the 
hawks’ plucking apart of the vultures, and many Magi are murdered throughout 
Persia. 


The Seven now turn their attention to the form of government that should 


be organised (3.80–88). A debate ensues about the benefits of democracy, oli- 
garchy, and monarchy, the last of which Darius extols. Again, his opinion suc- 
ceeds and logically the next question is who will be the monarch. The Seven, of 
whom Otanes has excluded himself, resort to the natural realm to decide the mat- 
ter. The proposal was the following: the first horse of one of the six contenders 
that makes a sound the following day would indicate the new monarch. Darius 
and his groom Oebares hatch a plot to ensure that the lot falls on Darius. Oebares 
makes it happen. But just when the audience may think that this has occurred 
purely out of human trickery, Herodotus provides evidence of divine agency. Im- 
mediately after Darius’ stallion whinnied, a divine sign confirmed the choice: on 
this clear day, lightening appeared and thunder sounded, as if it were a sign of 
divine agreement (3.86).2 Herodotus does not call this extraordinary event a sign 
or an omen, because, as in other places, he assumes his audience’s ability to un- 
derstand it as such. That Darius has divine endorsement is immediately recog- 
nised by his companions as they bow down before him. Darius and the Persians 
are again under divine rule. By including the role of divine portents in the acces- 
sion of Darius to the throne, Herodotus leads his audience to explore how this will 
unfold throughout Darius’ life.

8 Darius under Divine Rule 
231 


Once Darius had gained control of Persia, he reigned from 521 to 486. During 


this period, geopolitical conflicts were numerous and great. In his treatment, 
Herodotus quickly mentions that the question of the subjugation of Asia passed 
through Cyrus to Cambyses, and then to Darius (3.88.1). The subjugation of Asia 
was assured, which included the Ionian Greeks. The conflict continued and would 
not go unchallenged. Would Europe and Asia be governed by the same man as 
Cyrus had once dreamt (1.209)? This question will engage the audience’s atten- 
tion throughout the remaining six books. Herodotus displays perceptions of how 
human and divine protagonists shaped the development of this matter. This point 
is clearly illustrated by the idea of divine jealousy at the prospect of one man rul- 
ing both Asia and Europe (8.109). 


Herodotus’ remarks guide the interpretation of Darius’ reign. The latter 


“ruled over the whole of Asia, except for Arabia” (3.88.1; via an agreement with 
Cambyses in 3.5–9), and “everything was full of his force” (3.88.3). Darius, it was 
said, reigned like a “retailer” due to his love for profit (3.89.3). He ensured this 
through satrapies. Yet Herodotus gives a clue of Darius’ sense of self-realisation 
when he highlights his “first act,” which was the erection of a monument with 
this inscription: “Darius, son of Hystapses, with the excellence of his horse ([…] 
the horse’s name […]) and of his groom Oebares, won the throne of Persia” 
(3.88.3). Darius celebrates his power and honours his groom and his horse, whose 
name was also in the inscription (Herodotus says), but not the name of any of the 
gods. This may be a subtle way of alluding to Darius’ lack of devotion to his gods 
and lack of respect for the Greek gods whose territory he was going to enter.3 


Before considering examples of divine involvement during Darius’ reign, we 


review how he handled relations at the beginning, with Greeks and non-Greeks, 
both individuals and peoples. This is a significant part of the portrait painted by 
Herodotus. First, Herodotus gives an overview of the various Persian satrapies 
and their annual tribute (3.89–97). Unsurprisingly, Herodotus first lists the 
westernmost provinces, of which the first four are all in Asia (3.90). Thus, the Io- 
nian Greeks remained under Persian enslavement. Chapters 3.88 to 5.29 treat the 
events leading to the Ionian revolt in 499 BCE (5.30–6.33). This is the geopolitical 
thread that will trigger the Persian invasions, which begin with Mardonius’ expe- 
dition in 493–492 and are followed by the campaign of Datis and Artaphrenes 
(son of Artaphrenes) in 490 (6.94–120). The narrative leads the audience to ad- 
mire the greatness of his territory and wealth. Questions may arise as to which 
peoples might be added to this already prosperous kingdom and whether Darius’ 
gods and rival peoples’ gods would be perceived as helping or hindering his im- 
perial impulse. As per Herodotus’ practice, he weaves ethnographic material in 
between his stories of attempts of conquest. Here he provides material on the In- 
dians in the eastern part of the empire (3.98–105), then he covers the other ends 


3

232 


of the empire on a variety of subjects (3.106–117). This is the human landscape 
that fills the pages of the Histories, describing the hunger of an individual for 
more power over real people, not just subjects, but peoples with their own cher- 
ished histories and customs. 


Next, Herodotus displays various examples of Darius’ ability to handle 


threats to the stability of his kingdom such as Intaphrenes (one of the Seven, exe- 
cuted for treason, 3.118–119); Oroetes, an impious governor of Sardis (also put to 
death, 3.120–128); and Democedes of Croton, Darius’ doctor who led Persian 
spies to Hellas then escaped (3.129–138). This last individual played a key role in 
motivating Darius to conquer territories in Europe. Democedes succeeded in us- 
ing Queen Atossa to convince Darius to show the Persians his authority and to 
keep his people occupied by war. He should attack the Greeks first, said Atossa. 
Also, in that passage, Herodotus reveals that Darius had already devised a plan to 
make a bridge over to Europe and attack the Scythians. Atossa convinces him, 
however, to focus first on the Greeks, and so he sends spies to gather information 
before embarking on a military expedition (3.134). Despite the spies’ reports 
(3.135–138), Darius decides instead to capture Samos. Herodotus, however, does 
not indicate divine influence in these deliberations. 


Nevertheless, through these passages, Herodotus is bringing his audience 


closer to the main line of interest of his narrative. He underlines this point by 
saying that those spies were the first Persians to come from Asia to Hellas 
(3.138.4), and, in the following line, that Samos was the first of the cities, Greek or 
non-Greek, to be seized by Darius (3.139.1). The question of whether one man, 
Darius, might one day rule over Europe and Asia is being impressed upon the au- 
dience. 


The reason for capturing Samos first was not due to an oracle, but due to a 


favour owed to a Greek named Syloson (exiled brother of Polycrates of Samos!), 
who had given a generous gift (a red cloak) to Darius while he served Cambyses 
in Egypt (told in 3.139–141). This meeting some years before was in Herodotus’ 
judgement “good luck” (εὐτυχίη, 3.139.2), because Syloson requested that the is- 
land be returned to him and not Maeandrius, the guarantor of Polycrates. 


Despite Maeandrius’ best intentions before the people to honour Zeus the 


Liberator and to become his chief priest, his act of apparent piety was never 
recognised by the Samians nor honoured by the god himself. The Samians lost 
their liberty, so more Greek territory was added to the Persian Empire (3.142– 
148). Herodotus never leads his audience to entertain the idea that the Greeks 
were guaranteed protection by their gods, as per entitlement. The Greeks could 
only hope for some benefits through their acts of devotion, e.g., sacrifices, and for 
a fair chance to defend themselves.4 Subsequent acts of Maeandrius, however, 


4 
Mikalson (2003) 29–30. For the function of acts of devotion such as sacrifice, see e.g., Naiden 
(2015) 463–476.

233 


cast doubts on his level of devotion to Zeus and the people; he was motivated by 
self-preservation and wealth (3.143–149). This is another motif that receives at- 
tention in the lives of various leaders, Greeks and barbarians, during Darius’ 
reign (e.g., Miltiades, Histiaeus, and Mardonius). 


Audiences, however, hear about the first specific case of Persian hybris going 


beyond what was necessary to carry out their plans (3.147). Their ‘drag-net meth- 
od’ swept clean the island of Samos (3.149.1; cf. method explained in 6.31). The 
troops killed Samians, against the orders of Darius, wherever they were found, 
including in sanctuaries (3.147.2). Acts of sacrilege such as this would become a 
key factor in the gods defending the Greeks, namely for the sake of their own 
honour. Zeus the Liberator and other gods (called upon frequently) would liber- 
ate the Greeks not because of favouritism but because of their own honour, as 
well as to maintain a balance of power in Asia and Europe.5 One may deduce that 
the gods had already begun their work of vengeance for this sacrilege, since 
Herodotus reports in a curious note how, sometime later, Otanes the Persian gen- 
eral tried to repopulate the island in response to a dream (ὄνειρος) and because 
of a genital disease (3.149). Some humour through divine activity is not to be 
missed. Although the content of the dream is absent, it was sufficient to move 
Otanes to action. Also, the physical punishment attacking the means of reproduc- 
tion (his genitals) – thus, also the means of repopulation (συγκατοικίζω, ‘popu- 
late’) – symbolises a reversal in human fortune, spurned by the divine, as Herodo- 
tus lets his audience assume. 


Book 3 ends with the revolt of Babylon and its long siege by the Persians, 


who were unable to overthrow the city. Here Herodotus brings in another exam- 
ple of divine assistance without which the Persians would not have taken Baby- 
lon. Darius had tried every stratagem in the space of twenty months. It took a 
“marvellous thing” (τέρας) to incite to action a certain Zopyrus (son of Megabyzus 
– one of the Seven) who hatched an equally remarkable plot involving self-muti- 
lation. Zopyrus appears to have been chosen for this portent in that a mule in his 
possession gave birth. Zopyrus sought no one for assistance in its interpretation, 
as he remembered well the taunting words of a Babylonian: “for when you take 
our city when mules will have foals” (3.151.2). Zopyrus reasoned that the portent 
was a divine promise of a successful siege, which was not at all in sight. No, this 
indeed was of divine origin: “For it was by a god’s help that the man was able to 
speak and that his own mule was able to give birth” (σὺν γὰρ θεῷ ἐκεῖνόν τε 
εἰπεῖν καὶ ἑωυτῷ τεκεῖν τὴν ἡμίονον, 3.153.2). Consequently, Zopyrus makes this 
his mission with the ambition to become a great man in Persian history.6 Encour-

aged by the divine, Zopyrus envisages human and divine complicity as the only 
hope for a Persian victory, and so he feigns being a Persian defector with a muti- 
lated nose and ears. At the cost of his own health and thousands of Persian sol- 
diers sacrificed at the gates of Babylon (3.157–159), Zopyrus is ironically the 
hero.7 Unlike Cyrus who took Babylon quickly and astutely, Darius is not at all 
portrayed for his military prowess. This foreshadows his subsequent failures, 
such as in Scythia and Greece. This narrative of Zopyrus is a clear example of 
Herodotus’ prophetic voice, providing extraordinary detail and serving once 
again to demonstrate that Darius is governed by the divine. 


8.3 Darius against the Scythians and the Libyans (Hist. 4.1–205) 


Having recaptured Babylon, Darius turns his attention to subjugating the Scythi- 
ans. From a Greek perspective, this might be dismissed as merely an inter-barbar- 
ian conflict. It is, however, more profound than this, as it falls within the greater 
implications of the Eurasian agōn. Herodotus dedicates almost all of Book 4 to this 
additional failure of Darius (4.1–144). The last part of the book treats the conflicts 
between the Libyans and the Persians (4.145–205). Setting aside plupast material, 
the events of the core narrative here took place around 513 BCE, which was still 
sometime away from the beginning of the Ionian Revolt in 499. 


In the opening lines, Herodotus states that Scythia was the cause of political 


conflict with Persia. The former had infiltrated Asia to the point that they had 
dominion of the Medes for twenty-eight years (4.1.2). Darius was provoked and 
resolved to punish the Scythians (4.1.1; 4.4). Herodotus does not repeat Darius’ 
plans for invasion described in Book 3 (i.e., his conversation with his wife Atossa, 
3.133–134) nor does he suggest here any divine instigation in this geopolitical 
conflict. From the Persian point of view, the provocation began with the Scythi- 
ans. Before rushing to judgement on Darius, audiences must wait to hear the in- 
terpretation of another point of view later in Book 4 (119.2–3). Perhaps the divine 
was involved in encouraging the Scythian-Persian conflict after all. If so, the 
crossing into Europe was virtually assured. 


As elsewhere, Book 4 contains a wealth of material on ethnography and ge- 


ography. This includes religious practices8 and mythological traditions.9 The latter 


soldiers to believe in victory and fight with greater confidence. Zopyrus would have received 
a certain place of honour all the same. Hérodote (1967) 180 n. 2.

being examples of the divine plupast, which enriches the sacred landscape of the 
Histories. Book 4, however, does not offer many instances of divine activity direct- 
ly related to the geopolitical thread under study.10 Nevertheless, some points merit 
attention. 


Herodotus points out that many of the Greek gods were worshiped by the 


Scythians. The main gods are Hestia, Zeus, and his wife Earth (in their pantheon), 
as well as secondary deities Apollo, Celestial Aphrodite, Heracles, and Ares. Royal 
Scythians also worship Poseidon (4.59.1). Contrary to Greek custom, they do not 
make statues, altars, or temples to honour their gods, except to Ares (4.59.2). 
Herodotus does not hold back his knowledge about their soothsayers who are nu- 
merous in Scythia and who use willow rods to prophesy (4.67.1). There are also 
the Enarees, ‘women-men’ (or hermaphrodites), who received their method of 
divination from Aphrodite (4.67.2). 


An event that cannot remain untreated here is the story of Scylas, a Scythian 


king (4.78–80), because it concerns another ruler who is judged by the interaction 
of divine and human agency. Herodotus tells this anecdote to illustrate how 
Scythians fiercely held to their traditions and did not allow foreign customs to 
enter their culture. As in the case of Candaules (1.8.2), Herodotus prefaces the sto- 
ry with a proleptic clause regarding the king’s fate: “It was necessary, however, 
for bad things should happen, and the occasion for this is as follows” (4.79.1). Scy- 
las was unusual in that he nurtured a fondness for Greek culture and religion. His 
secret, magnificent house in the city of the Borysthenites was protected by 
sphinxes and griffins.11 He went so far as to be initiated into the Mysteries of 
Dionysus. Prior to initiation, divine disapproval manifested itself through a “great 
portent” (φάσμα μέγιστον, 4.79.1). The god hurled a thunderbolt on Scylas’ house 
(ἐς ταύτην ὁ θεὸς ἐνέσκηψε βέλος) which burned down completely (4.79.2). Scylas 
ignored this sign and pursued his project of initiation. His people became aware 
of this sacrilege and had Scylas executed by his brother (4.80.5). This anecdote 
supports the solemn theme of the sacredness of national customs, which under- 
lines the severity with which the Scythians handled important matters. Once 
more, Herodotus invites his audience to reflect on another encounter between 
royal families and the divine realm. This pattern continues with increasing 
prominence in the remaining books.
