Interestingly, before resuming the core narrative (started in 4.1), Herodotus 


is compelled to add a note about the natural wonders of those lands (e.g., great 
rivers and plains), but only one deserves a short note: a huge footprint of Hera- 
cles can be seen in a rock along the Tyras River (4.82). Heracles enjoyed popular 
attention and worship even in those parts of the world. How does this make a 
difference in history and interpretation? The sacred grounds of Heracles in the 
Marathon conflict will prove to be of encouragement for the Greek troops. 
Herodotus then resumes his account: “So much now for that matter, I shall return 
to the account which I set out to tell from the beginning” (4.82). 


Worthy of note at the resumption of the story is the fact that Artabanus, Dar- 


ius’ brother, attempts to persuade him to abandon his conquest of Scythia. His 
efforts fall on deaf ears. This is the first instance of a parallel action that will be 
repeated when Artabanus later warns his nephew Xerxes against attacking the 
Greeks, particularly Athens (7.10). In the latter case, however, divine appearances 
cause Xerxes and Artabanus to proceed with their plans to attack Greece (7.12– 
18). 


Through the Scythian logos, Herodotus highlights the perception of divine 


involvement in Darius’ pursuit of global rule. Darius arrives at the Thracian 
Bosphorus, where a new bridge connects Asia to Europe. A pivotal moment in the 
narrative occurs when Darius is said to have enjoyed the spectacular view, from 
either the promontory or the temple (4.85.1).12 This symbolic act intimates that 
Darius is assuming a quasi-divine posture, thus the culmination of a sacrilegious 
act connecting land that God had kept separate (cf. mirrored by Xerxes’ plans at 
7.8 A). Darius then crosses over into Europe (4.89.1) and erects various monu- 
ments of his presence moving through Thrace towards Scythian territory. 
Herodotus lists the various Thracian tribes who are easily subdued (4.93) and of- 
ten signals their beliefs and practices regarding the divine.13 The Scythians con- 
clude that they do not have the means to defeat Darius’ forces (4.102), and they 
request help from neighbouring peoples. Some of them agree to help, but others 
refuse with this justification:

Had you not yourselves been the aggressors in your trouble with Persia, we should 
have considered your request justified; we should have granted what you ask and 
been willing enough to fight at your side. But the fact is, you invaded Persia with- 
out consulting us, and remained in possession of it as long as God allowed you, and 
now the same God is urging the Persians to pay you back in your own coin. 
(4.119.2–3, trans. de Sélincourt) 


Their response is informative in that they recognise divine involvement in two 
stages. First, the god (ὁ θεός) allowed Scythian aggression in Asia; now, he stirs up 
the Persians to retaliate (καὶ ἐκεῖνοι, ἐπεί σφεας ὡυτὸς θεὸς ἐγείρει, 4.119.3).14 The 
theme of divine geopolitical agōn is thus extended to inter-Barbarian relations. 
This is an example of how Herodotus uses later material to tie up loose ends. In- 
deed, Darius wanted to punish the Scythians (4.4). Although the blame lies with 
the Scythians, the divine realm permitted it to happen. Their neighbours’ refusal 
obviously weakens the Scythian coalition, which places them in the situation of 
underdogs before the Persians. Will their gods defend them? Or would Darius act 
as the means of divine retribution? From Herodotus’ point of view, the former 
seems more probable. In response to Darius’ frustrating appeal to the Scythians 
to give up or fight, Idanthyrsus, the Scythian king, boldly challenges the Persians 
to destroy their forefathers’ tombs, for this would be a legitimate reason to fight. 
Idanthyrsus refuses to be threatened with slavery, because they have no masters 
except, as he says, “Zeus from whom I sprang, and Hestia the Scythian queen” 
(4.127). The mention of slavery infuriated the Scythians. Only their gods could 
merit the title of master, for the Scythians’ existence depended on them (cf. 4.59). 
Significantly, we have here a parallel story of liberation: Scythia and Greece in 
the face of Persia. Kings come and go, only life under divine rule remains. 


Herodotus resumes the narration by underlining Darius’ incompetence as a 


military chief, since the Scythians competently frustrated his attempt to subjugate 
them (4.128–142). Moreover, the Scythians were almost able to convince the Ioni- 
ans to attempt their own revolt (4.137–139) exclaiming with pride: “Good luck go 
with you, and thank the gods and the Scythians for your freedom” (4.136.4). In 
Herodotus’ story-world, this is articulated by a pious and cautious ruler; it is al- 
ways good to acknowledge the gods for their part in military success. The two ele- 
ments are again mentioned together: divine intervention with reference to politi- 
cal freedom.

After Darius’ departure for Asia, Megabazus continued to subdue other peo- 


ples that had not submitted to Persia (4.143–144; 5.1–27). Herodotus now turns 
his attention to another sequence of Darius’ imperial impulse: the subjugation of 
Libya. Less pronounced than other sections, Herodotus here provides other ex- 
amples of conflicts between Greeks and Persians in other places in the Mediter- 
ranean. Here it concerns mainly the Greek colonies in North Africa. Perhaps un- 
surprisingly, Greek presence there is justified by a persistent succession of 
oracles from Delphi. As in the previous section regarding the Scythians, this final 
section about Libya has numerous examples of Herodotus’ interest in the divine 
realm and religious practices. One of the most extensive logoi about dealings be- 
tween communities and the Delphic oracle is found here (4.149–159). It concerns 
the Pythia’s command to Battus I to found a colony in Libya. He refused to do so 
several times, but various experiences and consultations in Delphi convinced him 
and others that Apollo was not going to change his mind. This explains the 
Greeks’ presence in Libya via the colonisation of Cyrene.15 Herodotus then re- 
counts other experiences with the Delphic oracle involving Battus’ relatives, in- 
cluding his son Arcesilaus I (4.159–160), his grandson Battus II (4.161), and his 
great-grandson Arcesilaus III, who was murdered by his brothers and the inhabi- 
tants of Barca (4.162–164), and the latter’s mother, Pheretima, who took revenge 
on the Barcaeans (4.205). As always, Herodotus devotes much narrative space to 
geographic and ethnographic description, which also contributes multiple refer- 
ences to the sacred landscape (4.168–199). Once satisfied with this ‘digression’, 
his “So much for this subject” introduces his return to the question of the Persian 
invasion (4.200–205). The highlights here are the conquest of Barca and the fail- 
ure to capture Cyrene. Also, queen mother Pheretima’s desire for revenge on Bar- 
ca (interrupted in 4.167) is fulfilled with the help of Egyptian forces. She, howev- 
er, goes too far in her treatment of those responsible for her son’s death. 


Herodotus uses this anecdote to conclude Book 4 with a principle highlight- 


ing divine rule: “accordingly, exceedingly strong acts of vengeance are odious in 
the eyes of the gods” (4.205). Divine intervention through natural causes is for 
Herodotus unmistakable here; Pheretima “died badly” (ἀπέθανε κακῶς) due to 
worms.16 Here Herodotus explicitly underlines divine envy.17 Due to her excessive 
cruelty, she got her just desserts.18 This example contributes to the motif of royals

who are guilty of cruelty against rulers and their families: e.g., Cyrus and Queen

to acts of brutality or hybris, punished by the gods who maintain their rule over 
humanity. 


8.4 Darius’ Subjugation of Thrace and Re-subjugation of Ionia 


(Hist. 5.1–126) 


Despite fewer references to divine intervention compared to other books, this 
book should not be underestimated with respect to Herodotus’ prophetic voice. 
He carefully weaves multiple strands leading to the Ionian Revolt, which sparks 
greater conflicts between the Greeks and Darius. The first lines of Herodotus’ 
‘books’ help his audience to remember the main storyline. Indeed, Herodotus 
picks up quickly the theme of the Greco-Persian agōn (left off in 4.144): the first 
victims in the Hellespont of Darius’ General Megabazus are the Perinthians (5.1– 
2). This story introduces the subjugation of Thrace (5.1–27), including ethno- 
graphic commentary on its inhabitants and the lands beyond (5.3–10). Theologi- 
cal commentary resumes swiftly in Book 5. After the report of divine judgement 
on Queen Pheretime at the end of Book 4, Herodotus indicates that an oracle by 
an unspecified god (χρήσαντος τοῦ θεοῦ) was the cause of the Paeonians’ attack 
on the Perinthians (5.2). This was a bit of divine plupast about the Perinthians 
whom he mentions as the first to be subdued by the Persians. In customary fash- 
ion, Herodotus identifies foreign gods with Greek deities: Ares, Dionysus, Arte- 
mis, as well as Hermes, who is worshipped by the kings (5.7).19 


From this point until the end of Book 9, Herodotus pays less attention to eth- 


nic and geographical description and more to the historical developments of the 
peoples involved, including retrospective political commentary. In keeping with 
Herodotean style, these plupast sections, which support the core narrative, con- 
tain multiple examples of divine intervention.20 This additional layer of Herodo- 
tus’ prophetic voice responds to his audience’s expectations and shapes their ex- 
perience of the narrative. 


Thrace, in Herodotus’ view, was not to be underestimated because of its 


great size, being second only to India. But the Thracians could not achieve signifi- 


19 
For Ares and Dionysus Thracian origins, see How and Wells (1936) 2: 3. 


20 
E.g., the Pythia’s role in establishing Cleomenes’ ancestor as the superior king of Sparta to 
Demaratus (Book 6.51–52) and the versions of Athens and Argos about Cleomenes’ death 
based on a shared religious belief (i.e., retribution for acts of sacrilege) (6.75). On these “com- 
peting narratives” having the common goal of discrediting Sparta and Cleomenes, see Kindt 
(2012) 78–80. 


Part III Hearing Herodotus’ Prophetic Voice 
240 


cant power because they were not united, neither by rule nor by purpose. There- 
fore, Persia, under the leadership of Megabazus and Otanes, incorporated Thrace 
into its empire (4.143–4; 5.1–27). Herodotus, however, inserts an intriguing story 
of how Persian envoys were murdered in Macedonia (5.17–22). Alexander I is de- 
scribed as originating from the Argive Greeks. He cunningly thwarts both Persian 
subjugation and subsequent retaliation for the murder of seven envoys and their 
entire contingent. Consequently, a brief Greco-Persian interlude is recounted be- 
fore returning to Megabazus’ trip back to Sardis, the Persian central base in Asia. 


Thrace was a part of Europe; thus, the Europe-Asia agōn remains firmly in 


Herodotus’ outline. They, however, are not a part of the Hellenes. Hence, this part 
builds on the intra-Barbarian storyline. Herodotus’ main interest moves to the de- 
velopments leading to the revolt of the Greek colonies in Ionia, coined ‘the Ionian 
Revolt’. This subject receives significant narrative space (5.99–103 and 5.116– 
6.32). Indeed, Feix perceives this shift by dividing the Histories in two parts: the 
first part being “Die Griechen in den Kolonien und die Barbaren” (1.6–4.205) and 
the second, from Book 5 on, “Die Perser und das griechische Mutterland” (5.1– 
9.122). This explains the reason for fewer sections of ethno-geographical com- 
mentary than in the first four books.21 In fact, the abundant retrospective sections 
concerning shifts in power and forms of government help audiences to under- 
stand the struggle of the Ionians and other Greeks for freedom. This includes 
those who had fallen under Persian control and those who anticipated Persian 
occupation of their lands. Narrative tension may be assumed to be steadily grow- 
ing, not only for the exploration of the main questions but also because – like 
Herodotus – some of Herodotus’ audience had lived or were living in those very 
areas and could perhaps feel, as if they were there, the heaviness of this immi- 
nent threat. 


Our author’s aside in 5.28 signals the shift to the Ionian Revolt: “Otanes ach- 


ieved such works when he led as general. After not too much time, there was re- 
lief from the bad happenings, but a second time came when evil arose out of Nax- 
os and Miletus”. Naxos was very prosperous, and Miletus was ‘the glory of Ionia’. 
However, previous lines deal with a potential threat of a Greek revolt by Histi- 
aeus who had received Miletus and Myrcinus in Thrace as a gift from Darius. Dar- 
ius listened to Megabazus’ warning that Histiaeus could potentially instigate con- 
flict and that it was better never to let him have control over an administrative 
district or go back to Greece (5.23–24). As it will be seen, Darius, even until Histi- 
aeus’ death, struggled to implement this policy. 


In his account about Aristagoras and the Ionian Revolt, Herodotus subtly in- 


corporates notions of divine foreknowledge and involvement in the events that 
directly impacted the decline of Greco-Persian relations. In our retelling of the 
events leading to the Ionian Revolt, we focus on the key moments when divine 


21 
See Feix’s section “Plan und Aufbau des Werkes,” Herodot (2006b) 1431–1434.

intervention is mentioned in the quest to liberate the Ionians. This means leaving 
out much of the intriguing political history of Athens, Sparta, and Aegina (and 
many others, 5.39–96). Therein, Herodotus provides commentary on sacred areas 
and several examples of divine plupast interventions, both in action and speech 
(e.g., 5.42–47). 


We now return to Histiaeus, who, ironically, from Susa, instigates Aristago- 


ras, his son-in-law and first cousin, to lead the revolt. Histiaeus succeeds, as this 
was an opportune solution for Aristagoras’ own problems relating to the failure 
to subdue Naxos (5.31–36). Aristagoras convinces the Milesian leaders and over- 
throws many Persian tyrants in other Ionian cities (5.36–38). This is not enough, 
however. He needs the support of Sparta, so he approaches King Cleomenes. His 
terse speech elucidates several major themes in the Histories, namely, the urgen- 
cy surrounding the themes of freedom and subjugation, which are mixed with 
personal expediency. These are best understood and highlighted against the back- 
drop of the greater agōn throughout the Histories: 


[…] Ἰώνων παῖδας δούλους εἶναι ἀντ᾽ ἐλευθέρων ὄνειδος καὶ ἄλγος μέγιστον μὲν 
αὐτοῖσι ἡμῖν, ἔτι δὲ τῶν λοιπῶν ὑμῖν, ὅσῳ προέστατε τῆς Ἑλλάδος. [3] νῦν ὦν πρὸς 
θεῶν τῶν Ἑλληνίων ῥύσασθε Ἴωνας ἐκ δουλοσύνης ἄνδρας ὁμαίμονας […] 


[…] That Ionians should have become slaves in place of free men is a bitter shame 
and grief not only to us, but to the rest of Greece, and especially to you, who are the 
leaders of the Greek world. We beg you, therefore, in the name of the gods of 
Greece, to save from slavery your Ionian kinsmen […] (5.49.2–3, trans. de Sélin- 
court) 


Aristagoras evokes several points in his attempt to persuade Cleomenes: the trag- 
edy of Ionian subjugation; Greek unity; Spartan military prowess as leaders; and, 
significantly, the invocation of the gods as his witnesses. Aristagoras failed to con- 
vince Cleomenes, so the story continues without Spartan help (another Her- 
odotean motif). The question arises whether the gods will help in this noble, yet 
self-centred project. This will be seen as these points are further developed in the 
direct conflicts with the Persians. 


After Sparta’s refusal, Aristagoras goes to the second great ally, Athens (in- 


troduced in 5.55 and resumed in 5.97), who was needed to rout the Persians from 
Ionia.22 If ever one could speak of perfect timing, this was it. The Athenians had 
already placed themselves in a delicate situation by refusing to obey the order of 
the Persian Artaphrenes to reinstate Hippias as tyrant, the most important exile 
of the tyrannical Pisistratidae and traitor to Persia (5.96).23 This was the simmer-

5.97.1).

ing of direct conflict with Persia. Aristagoras was then the man of the moment, for 
he offered everything he could think of, and, although he had failed to convince 
one man, Cleomenes, he “succeeded with thirty thousand Athenians” (5.97.2)! 
Athens decides to send twenty ships for the Ionian cause. Here Herodotus’ 
prophetic voice comments on Athens’ support: “These ships were the beginning 
of evils for Greeks and barbarians” (5.97.3). This celebrated phrase brings to the 
fore the dramatic heights of this crucial turning point in European history.24 


The Athenians, with Ionian forces, focus their attack on Sardis, which had 


also been the centre of Lydian-Persian hostility, leading to direct contact with Io- 
nian Greeks and Cyrus’ Persia. The forces succeeded in taking all but the acropo- 
lis. Herodotus then considers an important detail. Inadvertently, the lighting of 
one house led to a great fire which became the cause of a great error: the burning 
of the temple of Cybele, a Lydian goddess (identified, however, with Demeter, the 
Great Mother and Aphrodite).25 Whether accidental or not, a sacred building was 
destroyed, and in Herodotean theology, this would not go unnoticed in the divine 
realm (e.g., the burning of Athena’s temple in Assesus and divine reparation, 
1.19.1 and 1.22.3). After significant silence of the divine element (barring plupast 
material), the political and the religious spheres are reconnected. Athens was 
now going to be the enemy of Persia (5.96), which awakens the wrath of Darius 
and subsequent implication of the gods. Upon learning about the destruction 
caused in Sardis, Darius, in fact, entreats Zeus for revenge: “[…] and inquiring as 
to the identity of the Athenians, when he received the response, he asked for his 
bow. He took it and loaded an arrow and shot it upwards to the heaven. As he 
sent it through the sky, he said: ‘O Zeus, may it be granted to me to take venge- 
ance against the Athenians!’” (5.105.1–2). 


Divine intervention is entreated; but would it be granted? Audiences knew 


the answer, but they needed to see how developments led to Darius’ failure of 
this wish, which is clearly stated at the end of Book 6 and the beginning of Book 7. 
Mikalson comments on the consequences of the destruction of Sardis and Cy- 
bele’s temple, and Darius’ reaction: “The burning of sanctuaries, as reprisals, 
would become a distinctive feature of the forthcoming Persian attacks on the 
Greeks for the next eighteen years, and it was in this gross impiety that Herodotus 
would find one of the major causes of the ultimate defeat of Persians.”26 Indeed, 
Darius’ desire to bring the Athenians to justice was so strong that he ordered one 
of his servants to say thrice at dinner, “Master, remember the Athenians” 
(5.105.2).

Great irony surfaces in Herodotus’ description of this and subsequent devel- 


opments. The story has now come full circle between the reigns of Croesus and 
Darius. Ionia is the source of conflict, and Sardis is again the epicentre and link 
between the Greeks and Persians. Moreover, Darius prays to the most-high god in 
the Greek and Persian pantheons (‘Zeus’ without epithet). An important detail in 
this invocation is that Zeus, as the father of Perseus who was the father of all Per- 
sians, could grant supremacy to Darius over all other peoples.27 Yet the height of 
irony is that Darius allows Histiaeus, a Milesian Greek, who had instigated 
Aristagoras to revolt in the first place (5.105–7), to attempt to resolve the situation 
in Ionia!28 The perception of Darius is that he has Zeus and Histiaeus on his side to 
make things right. Herodotus proleptically alerts his readers to this bad decision: 
“The purpose of this [Histiaeus’ proposal] was to deceive Darius – and it was suc- 
cessful” (5.107). He succeeded partly thanks to his pledge in the name of the royal 
gods (θεούς […] βασιληίους, 5.106; cf. 3.65.6). This sounds very much like a reli- 
gious and political war. Proof of this is the strange tradition that followed. The 
people of Amathus (in Cyprus), who had refused to join the Ionians and sen- 
tenced Onesilus to death because of his siege against them, are given the chance 
by an unnamed oracle to have good fortune thereafter. The condition is that they 
must bury the head of Onesilus and honour him as a hero with a yearly animal 
sacrifice (5.114–5).29 In this case, the god behind this command was on the Ioni- 
ans’ side.30 Herodotus notes that this tradition was still going on in his time. 


A following line tersely states the movement in the direction of Persian vic- 


tory in Cyprus and throughout the remaining regions: “Thus the Cyprians were 
free for a year, but were once more subjugated” (5.116). The Carians, however, 
demonstrate their valorous opposition, and Herodotus depicts the religious lands- 
cape by stating that some Carians found refuge in Labraunda in the sacred grove 
of Zeus Stratios (ἐς Λάβραυνδα ἐς Διὸς στρατίου ἱρόν, 5.119.2). “Zeus of the Army” 
may be mentioned here to underline the god-fearing character of the Carians.31 


On the divine side, no miracles or oracles are mentioned, neither sacrifices nor 
prayers on the human side. Our author, nonetheless, keeps the divine ever-pres- 
ent before his audience. 


Consequently, Book 5 ends with Persian victories in the Hellespont, Propon- 


tis, Caria, Ionia, and Aeolis. It also ends with the defeat and death of Aristagoras, 
whom Herodotus describes with a litotes as a “not one of excellent mind” (ψυχὴν

8.5 End of the Ionian Revolt, Sparta’s Intrigues, and Athenian Victory 


at Marathon (Hist. 6.1–140) 


The highlights of Book 6 can be organised into three parts: the reconquering of 
the regions involved in the Ionian revolt (6.1–33), Sparta’s internal and external 
political intrigues (6.50–93), and the victory of the Athenians at Marathon in 490 
BCE (6.94–120).32 Most of the mentions about divine realm occur in relation to 
Marathon and bolster the account of this extraordinary defeat of the Persians. 
Herodotus mobilises divine explanation to legitimise Athenian resistance theolog- 
ically after their allegedly impious burning of the Persian temple of Cybele. The 
events in Book 6, excluding the plupast material, take place around the years 496 
to 489, during the latter part of the reign of Darius who dies in 486. 


The first chapters, as said above, lead the audience to explore the fate of His- 


tiaeus and of Miletus. Their downfall serves as an example of the re-subjection of 
the regions that had hoped to break the Persian yoke. An important motif begins 
to gain greater attention: the sacrilegious destruction of sanctuaries. This is due, 
but only in part, to the Persians’ revenge for the burning of Cybele’s temple in 
Sardis. It is used as a threat by the Persians, a sort of bargaining chip, to invite 
their foes to avoid destruction of their personal property and sacred patrimony 
(6.9.3). Noteworthy are Herodotus’ repetitions of the word pairs ‘houses and tem- 
ples’ (6.13.2) and ‘cities and temples’ (6.25, 32). 


Several valorous attempts at thwarting re-subjection are highlighted and of- 


fer a glimpse of the intertwining elements of divine and human participation. At 
Lade, Dionysius, the Phocaean commander, seeks to motivate the Ionians to equip 
themselves properly for military engagement: “our circumstances, men of Ionia, 
lie on a razor’s edge, either to be free or slave, or for that matter like runaway 
slaves” (6.11.2). Victory for Ionia is only possible, he recognises, if the gods do 
their part: “[…] if the gods deal equally, I promise that either our enemies will not 
join us in battle, or, if they do enjoin us, they will be soundly defeated” (6.11.3).33 


Dionysius is counting heavily on the fair treatment of the gods (θεῶν τὰ ἴσα νεμόν- 
των); they might have a chance if the gods reduce the obvious disparity. Although 
the Ionians were motivated to action, this did not last, for, in Herodotus’ estima- 


32 
For a description of the religious aspects of the Ionian revolt, see Mikalson (2003) 24–37. 


33 
A stimulating parallel of evoking divine favour before battle is found in Thucydides’ repre-

tion, they were not of stout character. They even complained against Dionysius as 
one imposing a greater type of enslavement: “What god have we offended to be 
filled up with such things?” (6.12.3). The motifs of slavery and freedom and their 
cost continue to resound in Herodotus’ narrative.34 The Ionian confederation falls 
apart: the Ionians, the Samians, and the Lesbians. Only the Chians continue to 
resist (6.15–16). The Athenians had thrown in the towel long before, and the 
Spartans were not interested, so there was little hope for lasting freedom. 


The fall of Miletus in 494 BCE, where the revolt had begun under Aristago- 


ras, becomes the focal point from 6.18 on. Describing the Persians’ attack by land 
and sea, Miletus falls in the sixth year after Aristagoras’ revolt. This, Herodotus 
says, corresponded to an oracle about Miletus: “[…] they enslaved the city, as a 
result the disaster coincided with the oracle concerning Miletus” (6.18).35 The re- 
sult clause shows how the disaster coincides or agrees with, even accomplishes, 
the oracular utterance: ὥστε συμπεσεῖν τὸ πάθος τῷ χρηστηρίῳ τῷ ἐς Μίλητον 
γενομένῳ. Herodotus then provides his audience with some plupast material. The 
Argives had consulted Delphi about the safety of their city (6.19.1). Interestingly, 
Apollo’s response was a ‘shared oracle’ (ἐπίκοινον χρηστήριον), which addressed 
the Argives and the Milesians. For the moment, our author holds back his inter- 
pretation on the Argives for later (at 6.77.2) and focuses on the Milesians, setting 
forth the interpretation succinctly. To dramatise it fully, Herodotus cites the ora- 
cle in view of the transpired events: 


[…] “καὶ τότε δή, Μίλητε κακῶν ἐπιμήχανε ἔργων, 
πολλοῖσιν δεῖπνόν τε καὶ ἀγλαὰ δῶρα γενήσῃ, 
σαὶ δ᾽ ἄλοχοι πολλοῖσι πόδας νίψουσι κομήταις, 
νηοῦ δ᾽ ἡμετέρου Διδύμοις ἄλλοισι μελήσει.” 


[…] “You then, Miletus, contriver of wicked deeds, 
Shall be a feast for many, and a splendid prize; 
Your wives shall wash the feet of many a long-haired man, 
And others shall care for our shrine at Didyma.” (6.19.2, trans. de Sélincourt) 


As a good prophet or oracle-monger would do, Herodotus recalls the oracle and 
explains it. The unspecified agents of divine intervention allow the oracle to be 
fulfilled through human agents.36 Miletus is punished for its trickery, and it has 
effects in the social sphere: women are enslaved by the Persians (the “long-

haired man”) and their sacred patrimony is lost. Their temple in Didyma (= 
Branchidae, 5.36), near Miletus, including shrine and oracle, is both robbed and 
burnt.37 This then is the showcase of several occurrences of sacking of cities and 
sacred precincts. Samos, however, of all the Ionian rebels, was spared, and 
Herodotus notes again the word pair: neither town nor the temples were burnt 
(6.25.2). 


Herodotus then brings out another act of treachery by Histiaeus and sup- 


ports it with theological commentary. Histiaeus was still at large and looking for 
allies. Chios was his next choice, but they rejected him. Herodotus underlines the 
wind of misfortune brought by Histiaeus by applying a general principle of ‘life 
under divine rule’: “It seems that there is nearly always a warning sign of some 
kind, when disaster is about to overtake a city or a nation” (6.27.1). These were 
the signs (σημήια) sent by the god to serve as warnings: the death of ninety-eight 
choir boys by the plague; the death of one hundred and nineteen school children 
from a collapsed roof; and the defeat at the battle of Lade (6.27.2). Histiaeus was 
at the heart of their misfortunes (6.27.3). 


He, however, would not go unpunished for all the harm he had committed 


before and after this event: he was judged by Artaphrenes and Harpagus. First, 
he was impaled, then his head was cut off, then mummified and sent to Darius in 
Susa. The paradox of Darius’ reaction is that he was angry at his servants for such 
a harsh treatment. Herodotus ventures that Darius would have even forgiven him 
(6.30.1)! The recounting of Histiaeus’ death coincides with the recounting of the 
end of the Ionian Revolt, which Herodotus summarises by evoking the Persian 
threat to the rebels cited above: “[…] and they burnt the cities with their temples. 
In this way the Ionians were enslaved a third time, once by the Lydians and two 
consecutive times by the Persians” (6.32). Another full circle of cause and effect – 
with divine and human parallel activity – is drawn for the audience, namely, 
what deities do to humans, and what humans do for and against deities. Darius 
has not forgotten the Athenians. Will the gods forget what the Persians have done 
to their sanctuaries in Ionia? This question is a key element driving the story 
from one epoch to the next. 


Herodotus then leads his audience to the Chersonese, the peninsula on the 


European side of the Hellespont, to consider the towns that had already been tak- 
en or remained to be subjected (6.33). This leads to a parenthesis exploring the 
leading Greek families of this area, the family of Miltiades son of Cimon (who was 
of the family of the Philaïdai). Herodotus supports this theologically, with divine 
plupast material concerning oracles and genealogical links to Ajax (6.34–35). This 
focus on Miltiades’ family is significant because Miltiades would become one of 
the heroes at the battle of Marathon. In the face of adversity in the Chersonese, 
Miltiades was forced to return to Athens (6.40–42). A foil for this aristocratic and

military profile comes from the Persian side in the person of Mardonius (first in-

Herodotus relates an episode that is often overshadowed by the events of 


Marathon, in which a divine intervention thwarts an invasion by Mardonius. The 
aim of his expedition in 493–492 BCE was to conquer Eretria and Athens, but he 
also subjugated all who were in his path (6.44.1).38 Herodotus does not explicitly 
mention divine intervention in this conquest, but his reference, here and else- 
where, to the divine operating through nature, suggests that he may have per- 
ceived the gods at work.39 Mardonius’ fleet was nearly destroyed by a gale along 
the coast of Athos, around three hundred ships and over twenty thousand men. 
These men were killed by wild beasts (θηρίων), dashed against the rocks, 
drowned, or died of hyperthermia (6.44.3). Mardonius also lost a great number of 
his troops on land at the hands of the Brygi, Thracians of Macedonia (6.45.1). 


Despite some success, these significant losses on land and sea forced Mardo- 


nius to abandon the Persian plan to subjugate Eretria and Athens. Mardonius re- 
turned to Asia “having waged war disgracefully” (αἰσχρῶς ἀγωνισάμενος, 6.45.2). 
Mardonius will have another chance to subjugate Europe. For now, though, Dar- 
ius orders Datis and Artaphrenes (nephew of Mardonius) with a new strategy to

the loyalty of the Greek city-states and Asiatic coastal towns; Greek refusal is sig- 
nalled at 6.94.1. Surprisingly, Aegina submits to him, resulting in an immediate 
conflict with Athens and Sparta. This, then, opens a significant parenthesis about 
Sparta’s internal and external intrigues (6.50–93),40 which we will leave without

Darius’ servant continued to repeat to him ‘Remember Athens’, and Darius 


did remember. This time he entrusted the expedition to Datis and Artaphrenes. 
Again, their mission is to enslave Athens and Eretria. Their new strategy seems 
better organised, departing from Samos and moving through the Cyclades (6.95). 
The island of Naxos was their first victim, due to their previous failure to capture 
it during the Ionian Revolt (5.28). Despite the Naxians fleeing to the hills, the Per- 
sians showed no mercy, enslaving them and burning their city and temples (6.96). 
The motif of sacrilege resurfaces, but the Persians have too much respect for De- 
los to treat the Delians in the same way as the Naxians.41 They acknowledge this 
island as the home of Apollo and Artemis. After offering immense amounts of 
frankincense upon the altar, the Persians honour their promise and sail for Ere- 
tria (6.97). Here, Herodotus inserts a significant remark about an earthquake and 
its meaning, which is supported by an oracle. After the Persians’ departure, the 
island was shaken strongly, as Herodotus reports: “it was shaken the first and the 
last up to my day.” He perceives this marvel (τέρας) as an unequivocal portent 
sent by the god (ὁ θεός) to warn of the terrible things to come (6.98.1).42 Herodotus 
interprets this unusual natural event this way: 


[…] καὶ τοῦτο μέν κου τέρας ἀνθρώποισι τῶν μελλόντων ἔσεσθαι κακῶν ἔφαινε ὁ 
θεός. ἐπὶ γὰρ Δαρείου τοῦ Ὑστάσπεος καὶ Ξέρξεω τοῦ Δαρείου καὶ Ἀρτοξέρξεω τοῦ 
Ξέρξεω, τριῶν τουτέων ἐπεξῆς γενεέων, ἐγένετο πλέω κακὰ τῇ Ἑλλάδι ἢ ἐπὶ εἴκοσι 
ἄλλας γενεὰς τὰς πρὸ Δαρείου γενομένας, τὰ μὲν ἀπὸ τῶν Περσέων αὐτῇ γενόμενα, 
τὰ δὲ ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν τῶν κορυφαίων περὶ τῆς ἀρχῆς πολεμεόντων. 


[…] It may well be that the shock was an act of god to warn men of the troubles 
that were on the way; for indeed, during the three generations comprising the 
reigns of Darius the son of Hystaspes, and of his son Xerxes and his grandson Ar- 
taxerxes, Greece suffered more evils than in the twenty generations before Darius 
was born – partly from the Persian wars, partly from her own internal struggles 
for supremacy. (6.98.1–2, trans. de Sélincourt) 


This is supported by a short oracular utterance of unspecified source: “I will 
shake Delos too, though it was unshaken before” (6.98.3). Mikalson underlines the 
role that Herodotus assumes here: “[…] almost as a soothsayer, he launches into 
an interpretation of the omen in terms of the next sixty years of Greek history.”43

(circa from the 480s and possibly into the 410s). This is one of Herodotus’ stron-

ural event and an oracle announce together this period of global military conflict 
and destruction.44 It also illustrates well Herodotus’ dual interest in Persian and 
Greek responsibility in the devastation. 


The Persians’ respect for the gods shown in Delos was short-lived, since, af- 


ter arriving in Euboea, Herodotus tells of their burning and robbing of sanctuar- 
ies in Eretria. The reason is plainly stated: it is revenge for the sanctuaries de- 
stroyed by the Greeks in Sardis (6.101.3). But Darius had not forgotten the 
Athenians. They take revenge against the Eretrians by taking their treasury and 
destroying what is dear to them. These are clear acts of humiliation. The narra- 
tive tension building on this question is overwhelming: sooner or later, the gods 
will make their power known. This contrasts with the Persians’ growing enthusi- 
asm for their victories as they head towards Athens (6.102). Due to its strategic 
value, Marathon is carefully chosen by a Greek traitor, Hippias, son of the tyrant 
Pisistratus (6.102). On the other side, a family rival, Miltiades, son of Cimon, is 
among the ten Athenian generals. Hegemony of Athens depends on the outcome 
of this rivalry. 


Yet Herodotus reminds his audience that this outcome is not only due to mil- 


itary prowess; rather, the divine realm has its role to play and can push the bal- 
ance in one direction or the other. For this reason, Herodotus does not hesitate to 
insert an apparition story in which the god Pan appeared to Pheidippides, the 
messenger sent by the Athenian generals to solicit the help of the Spartans. This 
encounter between Pheidippides and Pan was visual and oral, as the god prom- 
ised to be helpful, as in the past, despite their lack of attention to him (6.105). This 
message was transmitted to the generals before their departure for Marathon. 
Herodotus does not mention the psychological aspect, but it may be assumed that 
this divine gesture may have been perceived as a word of encouragement to Athe- 
nian leaders and soldiers, who “believed Pheidippides’ story” (6.105.3). This ex- 
emplum finds a parallel in the victory in Mycale (9.100) where Greek troops were 
emboldened by divine presence and word of victory in Plataea.45 


Somewhat ironically, the Spartans refused to leave straight away to help 


Athens because of a custom (οὐ βουλομένοισι λύειν τὸν νόμον), on the ninth day 
of the month, the Carneia, in honour of Apollo Carneius, celebrated from the sev- 
enth day to the fifteenth, that is, up until the full moon. During this time, they 
were unable to engage in warfare (6.106). This meant that the first battle between 
the Greeks and Persians in Marathon was fought without Athens’ strongest allies. 
Would the gods make it fair for all? Herodotus seems to think so, as he provides a

Miltiades counts on both the divine and the human for success. The gods must

Athens will become the first city.49 The desire for domestic, even global glory was 
certainly an alluring card to play by Miltiades.50 Athens received the backing of 
Callimachus and of the gods, for the sacrifices were favourable (καὶ τὰ σφάγια 
ἐγίνετο καλά, 6.112.1).51 The Athenian army entered battle in a peculiar, menac- 
ing running formation, emboldened as they were to press the Persians. 


Herodotus devotes little narrative time to describing the importance of this 


battle. Nevertheless, he states, “They fought at Marathon for a long time” 
(6.113.1). After routing the Persians on land, the Athenian army had to run quick- 
ly to Athens before the Persian ships could moor there and then release their 
wrath on the city, its temples, and inhabitants. Having done this, the Athenians 
pitched camp on the sacred precinct of Heracles in Cynosarges (an unknown loca- 
tion). Heracles, again, was their protector. Quite amazingly, perhaps miraculously 
in Herodotus’ view, the Persians lingering in the harbour of Athens then must 
have thought another incursion would be pointless. So, they sailed back to Asia. 


After the standard reporting of casualties on both sides (6 400 Persians and 


192 Athenians), Herodotus discloses to his readers stories of divine activity. A 
‘surprising thing’ (θῶμα) occurred when Epizelus, an Athenian soldier, became 
instantly blind while fighting a Persian. The former, however, was not killed, pro- 
tected as he was by an apparition (φάσμα). A giant hoplite with a long beard that 
covered his shield killed the adversary (6.117).52 While Herodotus’ description of 
the battle is short, he gives significant attention to Pan’s apparition as well as to 
that of the giant hoplite.

Juxtaposed here, these two anecdotes bolster the entire narrative strategy 


that Herodotus has used throughout the Marathon logos: divine presence and ac- 
tivity made the difference in the Athenian victory.53 The victory was perceived as 
no less a miracle than the divine activity reported here.54 The Athenians ac-

Mede.55 Ironically, the Spartans finally arrived for the battle as promised, but they 
were too late. At the battlefield of Marathon, witnessing the bodies, the Spartans 
rightfully acknowledged and congratulated Athens for their heroic victory

can finish poorly, especially when driven by selfish reasons to the point of 
breaching sacred customs. Analeptically, this reinforces Solon’s solemn warning: 
“But it is necessary to consider the end of every issue how it turns out, because, 
indeed, the god who has shown happiness to many people has ruined them com- 
pletely” (1.32.9). Like Cyrus and Cambyses, Miltiades finished poorly. He died of a 
gangrenous infection in his thigh and left to his descendants a fine of fifty talents 
for deceiving the Athenians (6.136.3).59 


8.6 Conclusion 


Book 6 concludes with a final anecdote about Miltiades, which fills in a gap about 
the conquest of Lemnos by the Athenians, since it had been mentioned as a bar- 
gaining chip in Miltiades’ defence (6.137–140). This is a clear example of the di- 
vine plupast, whereby Herodotus presents two sides about a conflict between the 
Athenians and the Pelasgians, the latter of whom were sent away by the former. 
Lemnos became one of their homes. Not forgetting their ill treatment, the Pelas- 
gians avenged themselves by seizing Athenian women and making them their 
concubines back in Lemnos. These women and their children became a source of 
great opposition and division to the point that the ‘pure Pelasgians’ murdered 
these impure mothers and children.

These crimes resulted in divine judgement: the birth rate dropped among

they refused to hand over their land, stating that they would do so only on one 
condition: “whenever a ship sails with the north wind from your land to ours on

The inhabitants of Hephaestia departed, but not those of Myrina, who were be-

This anecdote underlines Miltiades’ reputation, reminding readers that the 


divine realm takes note of wrongdoings and acts to establish order in the human 
sphere. It also sheds light on the causes of inter-Hellenic warfare, a topic of great 
interest to a late fifth-century audience. It is, however, a peripheral event that 
precedes the return of the narrative’s main focus, which resumes in the opening 
lines of Book 7. Darius is furious about his army’s defeat at Marathon by the Athe- 
nians. He will continue to “remember Athens,” but the Eurasian agōn will ulti- 
mately be left to his son, Xerxes.

9 Xerxes under Divine Rule: Persia’s Second Invasion 


of Greece (Hist. 7.1–9.122) 


The last three books of the Histories are structured around five major battles: 
Thermopylae in Book 7, Artemisium and Salamis in Book 8, and Plataea and My- 
cale in Book 9.1 The expedition led directly by Xerxes himself ends at 8.129 when 
he returns to Susa. Mardonius then leads the campaign until his death at Plataea 
(8.130–9.64); the subsequent battles are headed by Artabazus and Artaÿctes. 
These individuals serve as contrasting figures that highlight various interconnect- 
ed themes throughout Herodotus’ work: the pursuit of absolute power (i.e., the 
imperial impulse) and its impact on divine rule and human freedom in the con- 
text of the Eurasian agōn. Book 7 provides the most intense psychological insight 
into Xerxes’ character of all the books in the Histories concerning men with seem- 
ingly unlimited power. Xerxes and his successors are humiliated by the gods for 
their acts of impiety and injustice. The underlying theological premise is that, as 
divine rule brings world powers under control, global social disorder moves to- 
wards a greater sense of balance. 


9.1 Xerxes and Hellas: The Land that Only Xerxes Ought to Own 


(Hist. 7.1–239) 


Book 7 is one of the most straightforward books of the Histories. The narrative 
goal is to explore Persia’s third invasion (i.e., after those of Mardonius and Dar- 
ius) under the reign of Xerxes (reign 486–465/4 BCE). Movement is from Susa to 
Thermopylae, the latter being a strategic passage between Thessaly and Locris, 
linking the north with central and southern Greece. The narrative covers ten 
years. It begins with the report to Darius about the Persian defeat in Marathon in 
490, which is followed by initial preparations to attack Greece, various stations 
during the expedition, and finally ending with the Greeks’ loss in Thermopylae in 
480. 


Compared to previous books, Book 7 contains much less ethno-geographic 


commentary (except the origin of the Macedonians and Alexander’s genealogy, 
7.137–139). Herodotus’ audience has truly entered the heart of the problem. The 


1 
Immerwahr proposes that Books 7–9 (“despite their great length”) can be grouped together 
under one campaign logos, that of Xerxes and Mardonius. If so, the logos continues until the 
end of the book when Xerxes returns to the narrative: Immerwahr (1966) 126–147. 


stakes are greater now, since almost all the Greek city-states become involved, on 
one side or the other, including Sparta. One can imagine that the audience might 
have felt the narration of the events to a greater degree.2 Narratively speaking, 
the previous books, in comparison to the magnitude of this invasion, appear 
preparatory for the climax in Books 7–9. 


Along with the focus on Persia’s massive forces and Xerxes’ personality, 


Herodotus invites his audience to continue to explore key themes such as abso- 
lute rule versus freedom, loyalty to one’s allies, and the effects of piety and impie- 
ty in the social sphere. The risk of complete domination of Asia and Europe be- 
comes acute, which is continuously counterbalanced by values evinced in key 
protagonists, such as faithfulness to Greek identity and their nomoi. Values or 
lack of values are explored as Greek allies react to the Athenians’ plea for help. 
Life under divine rule is also consistently brought to the audience’s attention. The 
question of whether the gods would permit Xerxes to act with impunity and ulti- 
mately rule over Asia and Europe is a complex one. If the Histories concluded 
with Book 7, it could be posited that the Greeks were destined to fail and that the 
gods did not undertake sufficient measures to impede this king’s quest for greater 
power. However, it must be noted that the conclusion of Book 7 does not signify 
the termination of the conflict, but rather the cessation of hostilities. 


The subsequent description of divine intervention in Books 7 is composed of 


five parts.3 Part 1 (7.1–25) describes the debates and dreams that lead to the 
preparations for the invasion. Part 2 (7.26–56) describes Xerxes’ travels to and 
crossing of the Hellespont. Part 3 (7.57–131) covers the Persians’ march from the 
Hellespont to Therma, including a catalogue of the infantry (61–83), cavalry (84– 
88), and navy (88–99). Part 4 (7.132–177) depicts how Greek leaders and city- 
states respond to Athens’ plea for help. Part 5 (7.178–239) describes military con- 
flict on land and sea around Thermopylae. Concerning attention given to the di- 
vine realm, Herodotus’ prophetic voice is particularly strong in this the longest 
book of the Histories. Finally, it is significant that Herodotus was probably born 
during the first years of Xerxes’ reign, around 484. 


9.1.1 Preparations for the Invasion (Hist. 7.1–25) 


Book 7 opens with Darius’ fury against Athens, which in several instances is un- 
derstood as the representative of all the Greek city-states.4 Darius’ goal is still

I have adapted the outline by Sheehan (2018) 194.

258 


vengeance (“remember Athens!”). Herodotus reminds his audience of Darius’ 
anger for the first Hellenic affront in Sardis.5 Whatever reservations he might 
have had when Atossa tried to convince him to attack Greece, it was now his own 
conviction, even an obsession. Egypt comes back into the picture, since Darius is 
also angry with the Egyptians for their revolt. He begins preparations to fight 
both. Consequently, Darius must name a successor, which causes another royal 
intrigue. In the end, Xerxes is selected because he was born when Darius was 
king. Perhaps equally important, Xerxes was the son of Atossa, daughter of Cyrus, 
who had great influence. 


Darius, however, dies in 486 after thirty-six years of rule, “and so he was not 


permitted to seek vengeance against either the revolted Egyptians or the Atheni- 
ans” (7.4).6 With these words, Herodotus underlines the vengeful atmosphere in 
the Persian court.7 Darius’ death left two open questions for Xerxes: will he “re- 
member Athens”? And what kind of king will he be compared to his predeces- 
sors? 


Some indications of response to these questions are found in 7.5. Xerxes, in 


fact, was not interested in attacking Greece, but he did muster his army against 
Egypt and apparently swiftly quells the rebellion in 485. It is evident that Herodo- 
tus wishes to revisit the topic of the Eurasian agōn, given the paucity of informa- 
tion he provides regarding the campaign in Egypt (7.7). It is equally noteworthy 
how the project of revenge against Athens alone transforms into a plan of domin- 
ion of the whole of Greece (7.5.1; 7.7.1; 7.8b–c). Consequently, the causes of the 
expedition against Greece must be explored: what will finally cause Xerxes to 
change his mind? Will the divine have any part in this? Various individuals seek 
to impose their views on Xerxes. Onomacritus and Mardonius argue for the inva- 
sion, while Artabanus pleads against it. Once again, Herodotus presents the influ- 
ences as a complex blend of human and divine agency. Vannelli rightly points out 
the literary quality and programmatic weight of Herodotus’ depiction of the de- 
bate in Susa. Key points cover a vast palette of material, “historical, politico-mili- 
tary, ethical, religious, and even psychological,” which picks up and develops pre- 
vious discussions in the Histories.8 


Herodotus immediately integrates an appeal to divine support that comes 


through Onomacritus, an oracle-monger (chresmologos). Once more, the audi- 
ence delves into the relationship between the divine source of oracles and their

strategic application for persuasion and manipulation.9 Onomacritus had been 
brought all the way to Susa by the Athenian aristocracy, the Pisistratids, who 
were seeking to restore tyranny in Athens.10 This collector and editor of oracles of 
Musaeaus presents to Xerxes only good oracles, such as the bridging of the Helle- 
spont by a Persian and how the army would march from Asia to Greece. But he 
veils from Xerxes any prophecies that might suggest unfavourable situations. Due 
to Onomacritus’ interpretations and, ironically, the Greek aristocrats’ pressure, 
Xerxes is induced to attack Greece (7.7.1). However, the debate about the invasion 
is not quite over; neither is the subject of divine influence. 


As a prelude to the major events still to come, Xerxes’ speech sheds light on 


his decision to invade Greece. First, he himself claims divine support: “but it is 
god leading us in this way and by pursuing it, it will be for the better for us” 
(7.8α.1). Xerxes is confident that the divine (the god is unspecified) supports his 
enterprise. He wants to continue in the traditions of his three forefathers. The 
two goals are stated: “satisfaction and revenge,” that is, to enlarge the empire for 
glory and to take revenge against their enemies, the Greeks and the Egyptians. 
Xerxes also reminds his court of the burning of the sacred groves and sanctuaries 
as key motives for revenge against Athens (7.8β). For this, he will build a bridge 
over the Hellespont to cross from Asia to Europe. 


Xerxes laces his speech with several mentions of the divine, which evince 


the hybris of the imperial impulse. He assumes that he has divine assistance for 
the realisation of his projects: “we will produce a Persian land that borders with 
the sky, the domain of Zeus” (7.8.γ.1, γῆν τὴν Περσίδα ἀποδέξομεν τῷ Διὸς αἰθέρι 
ὁμουρέουσαν). The union of the divine and human spheres will be realised 
through him, but not quite the way he had hoped. He also speaks of creating “one 
territory” and “thus the guilty shall bear the yoke of servitude as well as the inno- 
cent” (7.8.γ.3). All these proclamations function to awaken in Herodotus’ audi- 
ence the sensation of one who is going to fall greatly. How and Wells capture the 
irony regarding θεός […] ἄγει: “Since the phrase is fatalistic, and as a rule implies 
impending ruin, it is in the mouth of Xerxes ominous.”11 


Mardonius praises Xerxes magnanimously and emphasises the weakness of 


the Greeks. So, why should Persia fear them? Will the Greeks really oppose Xerx- 
es? Will they not follow the example of other peoples who do not resist? Mardo- 
nius bolsters Xerxes’ own convictions. All is going well until Xerxes’ uncle, Arta- 
banus, dares to express his reluctance to drag Persia into another war with this

You can see how the god blasts living things that are prominent and prevents their 
display of superiority […] It is the god’s way to curtail anything excessive. And so 
even a massive army may be destroyed by a small force if it attracts the god’s re- 
sentment and he sends panic or thunder, until they are shamefully destroyed. This 
happens because the god does not allow anyone but himself to feel pride. (7.10ε, 
trans. Waterfield) 


Artabanus then counters by uttering a series of curses on Mardonius (7.10ζ–θ). 
Xerxes is furious with Artabanus and publicly belittles him, condemning his un- 
cle to stay with the women in Persia during the campaign against Greece. Xerxes 
then repeats the key elements of his speech. He must rule according to the nomos 
set by his forefathers; the Athenians would invade again, just as they did in Sar- 
dis; hence, revenge is the only course of action (7.11). All of this seems clear, but 
then Herodotus builds up narrative tension by reporting further information 
about what “the Persians say” (7.12.1). Xerxes, upon further reflection on Arta- 
banus’ warnings, changes his mind and decides, before falling asleep, to an- 
nounce, the following day, that there would be no invasion of Greece. Herodotus, 
however, now brings in the influence of divine activity, which opposes Xerxes’ 
change of mind. Three times a divine figure appears and speaks directly to his 
interlocuters: twice to Xerxes and once to Artabanus (7.12–18). The goal of these 
apparitions is to lead Persia into war, which, ironically, is what Xerxes had assert- 
ed in his first speech (7.8α).12 


In the first nocturnal vision, a “tall and handsome man” (7.12.1) fails to dis- 


suade Xerxes despite menacing words: “Are you deliberating, Persian, to not lead

This is the turning point: now Xerxes and Artabanus know what the god 


wants. The phantom’s chilling words evoke divine rule: “Yet neither later nor at 
present will you escape unpunished for trying to avert what must happen” 
(7.17.2).15 Artabanus tells Xerxes straightaway what he saw and heard. Even

Massagetae, Cambyses against the Ethiopians, Darius against the Scythians. Arta-

en destruction overtaking the Greeks, I turn aside and change my judgment” 
(7.18.3). This statement emphasises again the theological thread supporting the 
structural unity of the Histories: human and divine involvement are perceived as 
working in parallel to foster Persian imperialism.16 In fact, the next day, Xerxes 
announces that preparations must begin for the invasion. Persia is again at war.

However, through the divine presence in the dream and its interpretation, 


Herodotus continues to seal the looming sense of dread. Xerxes has a third dream 
in which he is crowned with an olive bough whose branches cover the entire 
earth. Yet the crown suddenly disappears from his head. Unsurprisingly, the Magi 
offer a favourable interpretation of the first part: Xerxes will subjugate the world. 
Yet, like Onomacritus, they also neglect the part that could lead to a negative in- 
terpretation: the disappearance of the crown. Herodotus is again raising expecta- 
tions of Xerxes’ downfall.17 The interpretation of the dream in favourable terms 
has an immediate effect on the Persian nobles who do their utmost to fund the 
costly invasion. According to Herodotus, this ransacked the continent (7.19). The 
preparations take four years (484–481), and the expedition begins in 480. 


9.1.2 The March to and over the Hellespont Bridge (Hist. 7.26–56) 


Once the question of the expedition has been resolved – owing to the menacing 
divine apparitions to Xerxes and Artabanus – Herodotus leads his audience to ex- 
plore Xerxes’ movements to the Hellespont and its crossing. Human greatness 
and bravado are placed in contrast with the forces of nature and divine 
sovereignty. The illusory depiction of Xerxes as the Zeus on earth is pursued. 
Herodotus depicts the magnitude of Xerxes’ army compared to all armies, past 
and present, even those of the Trojan War (7.20). His army moves through territo- 
ry already visited in the Histories, such as Cappadocia, Phrygia, and Lydia. It was 
from Sardis that Xerxes sent out another incitement to Greek city-states (except 
Athens and Sparta) to submit to his authority (7.32).18 Once again, the former Ly- 
dian capital, Sardis, plays a pivotal role in the Greco-Persian drama. 


Xerxes attempts to tame nature, but he encounters its powerful resistance 


several times. Regarding the construction of the canal on the peninsula of Mount 
Athos (intended to avoid the disaster that had struck Mardonius’ fleet), Herodo- 
tus offers this aside: “Thinking it over I cannot but conclude that it was mere os- 
tentation that made Xerxes have the canal dug – he wanted to show his power 
and to leave something to be remembered by” (7.24).19 The Hellespont bridge, 
however, will be the showcase of this ‘showdown’ between mortals and gods. 


These warnings, which Herodotus will illustrate, should cause Xerxes to re- 


consider his plans, but he will have none of it. On the human plane, Artabanus’ 
second warning frustrates his nephew, who then sends his uncle back to Susa

To begin, the march from Asia to Europe was not going to be unchallenged. 


The first bridge over the Hellespont, built by Phoenicians and Egyptians at Aby- 
dos, is destroyed by a great storm. Xerxes’ reaction reveals his insolence towards 
the divine realm by punishing the sea with “three hundred lashes and have a pair 
of shackles thrown into it” and with belittling language, “barbarous and pre- 
sumptuous words” (7.35.1–2).22 His impiety is also reflected in the human sphere 
as he gives command to behead the bridge builders.23 


A new bridge project is commissioned and completed (7.36–37). In the 


spring, Xerxes’ army begins its advance on Abydos. But a second natural warning 
occurs in the form of a solar eclipse (7.37).24 The Magi again offer a favourable 
interpretation to calm the “deeply troubled” Xerxes. They claim that it is a sign 
from the gods that the Greek cities will be eclipsed. The psychological effect is 
immediate: “Having heard this, Xerxes continues the march in high spirits.”25 His 
pompous march is accompanied by the “sacred horses” and the “holy chariot of 
Zeus” and a company of 10 000 spearmen (7.40), which was followed by a squad- 
ron of 10 000 cavalry, and then the massive remainder of the army (all of which 
Xerxes will have counted after the crossing). 


The irony, again, is clear: this massive display of human force is now met by 


still another natural miracle. The entry of Xerxes’ army into the territory of Troy 
met with a storm that killed a great number of his men at the foot of Mt Ida (7.42). 
Herodotus does not dwell on this as a further sign of divine opposition. He does, 
however, follow this up with an anecdote that lends to that interpretation. Xerxes, 
like Darius, wants to visit places of historical or natural significance (cf. 4.85). He

It appears from Xerxes’ subsequent actions in Troy that he is attempting to take on

Herodotus conveys the weight of tension between the hybris of the pseudo god- 
man, Xerxes, and the presence of the gods through the dialogue between Xerxes 
and Artabanus. The sacred territory of Athena was making its displeasure known 
about the Persians’ invasive presence. They were not welcome there. The march 
continues to Abydos where Xerxes sits on a white throne prepared for his use

and physical imbuing this vantage point: Xerxes sees his naval and land forces 
across the Hellespont and enters a state of conflicting emotions, joy and sadness 
(7.45). This provides the occasion for Artabanus and Xerxes to explore the for- 
mer’s theological views on human existence and his persistent reservations about 
the invasion (7.46–52). 


Several points are noteworthy. Xerxes’ comment on the brevity of human 


life arouses Artabanus’ theological comment: “So heavy is the burden of it [life] 
that death is a refuge which we all desire, and it is common proof amongst us that 
the god [ὁ θεός] who gave us a taste of this world’s sweetness has been jealous in 
his giving” (7.46.4).27 This may not be a mirror of Herodotus’ own theology, but 
similar statements on the lips of other characters suggest Herodotus’ consent.28 It 
raises again the question of the ultimate sovereignty of the divine sphere over 
humanity. Next, the question of the vision of the phantom returns and what it 
means now for Artabanus, since he is coming back to his original cautious posi- 
tion. Artabanus hopes that the dream will come true, but he is plagued by 
thoughts of doom since that night. Then, here, he issues again a prophetic-like 
statement for Xerxes: the two greatest enemies are not human, but natural, the 
land and the sea (7.49). The lack of harbours and the threat of storms are support- 
ed by an aphorism “men are at the mercy of circumstance, and not their master,” 
and the calamities created on land through unceasing expansion by still another 
aphorism: “Concerning success, humans are never satisfied” (7.49.4). Herodotus 
raises again the truth that war is not fought in the human sphere alone, for if it

him from conquering Europe before reaching its farthest borders” (7.54.2). His 
concern is above all the Eurasian conquest. Yet Herodotus follows with an aside 
suggesting a trace of genuine piety in Xerxes: “Concerning the preceding, I cannot 
judge with certainty whether he threw them into to the sea as offerings to the 
sun, or whether he gave them as gifts to the sea after repenting for whipping the 
Hellespont” (7.54.3). 


Additionally, Herodotus provides another illustration concerning the cross- 


ing from a theological perspective. Sometime after Xerxes was on the European 
side, a Hellespontine man exclaims (it is not mentioned to whom) with prophetic 
authority: “O Zeus, why do you appear in the likeness of a Persian, change your 
name to Xerxes, and want to lay waste to Greece, leading all men against them? 
For it was within your power to accomplish these things without them” (7.56.2). 
The misperception of human and divine is clear.29 Xerxes, apparently, does not 
refuse honour meant for the gods. 


9.1.3 The Persians’ March from the Hellespont to Therma (Hist. 7.57–131) 


At the beginning of this section and in continuity with the previous one, Herodo- 
tus underlines the above paradox. As he begins to describe the army moving 
ahead after crossing the Hellespont, Herodotus relates two portents (τέρας) that 
were conveniently ignored by Xerxes. The first portent occurred as the march re- 
sumed from the bridge: a mare gave birth to a hare. Herodotus handles this for 
his audience with confident, prophetic skill (i.e., being an easy one to interpret, 
εὐσύμβλητος is mentioned twice): “The meaning of this was easy to divine: Xerx- 
es was going to lead an army against Greece, with great pride and magnificence, 
but that he would return to the same place running for his own life” (7.57.1). 
Then, Herodotus supports this with an analepsis concerning another portent that 
had occurred in Sardis: “a mule gave birth to a mule having double genitals, both 
male and female” (7.57.2). He doesn’t offer an interpretation of this second freak 
of nature but offers the conclusion that Xerxes ignored both portents and contin-

ued the march.30 Two conflicting views constantly surround this central event be-

This seeks to affect the audience’s reception of this long section, which in-

tus then describes those in the cavalry (7.84–88) and the navy (7.88–99). This long 
section serves as a reminder to readers of this war machine involving many peo- 
ples. Real people are involved in the subjugation of other real people. For exam- 
ple, Herodotus introduces here Artemisia, Queen of Halicarnassus (Herodotus’ 
hometown), whom he describes as a ‘great marvel’ (μάλιστα θῶμα, 7.99). She will 
be instrumental in the Battle of Salamis. 


The subsequent dialogue between Xerxes and Demaratus the Spartan 


(7.101–104) sets apart the values animating the Persians and the Greeks. Demara- 
tus does not hesitate to oppose the king because his people fear another ruler, 
their ‘law’ (nomos).31 Xerxes is again represented as foolish with his refusal to 
consider Demaratus’ knowledge as an insider and his boisterous laughing 
(7.104).32 As the army moves forward through various regions, Herodotus com- 
ments on their inhabitants as well as religious annotations adding depth to the 
story without varying the storyline.33 


Herodotus concludes this section by describing a natural marvel, but one 


that is not intrusive on the story. Although this appears to be circumstantial infor- 
mation, Herodotus, as seen in other instances, alerts readers to a place being the 
territory of the gods. Xerxes arrives in Therma, but he wants to see the mouth of 
the river Peneus.34 By ship, Xerxes views this immense gorge, which Herodotus 
describes through the Thessalian belief that it was the work of Poseidon. Herodo-

9.1.4 Greek Leaders and City-States Respond to Athens’ Plea for Help 


(Hist. 7.132–77) 


Herodotus provides a list of Greek cities submissive to Persia as well as an expla- 
nation why Athens and Sparta did not receive a delegation from Xerxes. It was 
due to their previous treatment of Persian delegates (7.132). The Greeks who did 
not submit to Xerxes take a pledge against the submissive city-states by making 
them pay, after the war, a tenth of their property to the god at Delphi (τῷ ἐν Δελ- 
φοῖσι θεῷ, 7.132.2). From 7.133 to 7.137, Herodotus explains that the mistreat- 
ment of Darius’ envoys resulted in divine retribution, possibly for Athens, but 
certainly for Sparta, because they were “unable to obtain favourable omens 
through their sacrifices” (7.134.2, καλλιερῆσαι θυομένοισι οὐκ ἐδύνατο). This act 
of divine justice is said to transpire through Agamemnon’s herald Talthybius 
(who had a temple in Sparta) and was finally assuaged during the Peloponnesian 
War in 430 BCE (chronologically, this is the latest event mentioned in the Histo- 
ries).36 Herodotus appraises this with prophetic authority: “it is clear to me that 
this was a divine act of wrath” (7.137.2, δῆλον ὦν μοι ὅτι θεῖον ἐγένετο τὸ πρῆγμα 
ἐκ τῆς μήνιος).37 Then he says that he needs to get back to his story (7.137.3).

Some Greek city-states chose to submit to the king for obvious reasons. Other 


city-states were in a state of panic, and Athens could have followed suit. Thus, the 
above prolepsis, a reflection on the divine’s ability to carry out retribution many 
years after the end of the Greco-Persian Wars, functions as an interlude to the 
following passage in which Herodotus voices his opinion, as narrator after the 
war, about the role of Athens during the war. He recognises that most people 
might object to it, but here is his prophetic-like expression: “[…] they [the Atheni- 
ans] were the ones who were roused – and after the gods – repelled the king. Not 
even the terrifying oracles that had come from Delphi made them fearful or con- 
vinced them to abandon Greece. Instead, standing firm, they held on to meet the 
invader of their land” (7.139.5–6).38 Herodotus is anticipating the unsettled narra- 
tive question: who, then, is saviour? Herodotus is careful in his remark by recog- 
nising human and divine involvement about which his audience is now famil- 
iar.39 The fact that, at the time of Herodotus’ writing, Athens was now the 
enslaver rather than the liberator, must have caused many to contemplate this 
twist of history.40 Herodotus invites his audience to consider whether Athenian 
dominance was the result of human or divine action. Or was it purely a conse- 
quence of human impiety at the level of the city-state? While he does not spell 
this out here or anywhere else, the rest of the narrative illustrates how the impe- 
rial impulse, fostered by any state, is ultimately brought low by the divine realm. 


Herodotus now comes back to his chronological account and explains the ex- 


changes between Athens and the oracle at Delphi (7.140–4). Herodotus again acts 
as an arbiter and interpreter of the oracles in light of relevant circumstantial in- 
formation. The first oracle of the Pythia to the Athenians should have caused Ath- 
ens to abandon their opposition (7.140).41 Upon Athenian insistence by envoys 
praying to Apollo at Delphi, the Pythia utters “a second prophecy” to the Atheni- 
ans, which causes significant discussion as to its meaning (7.141–144). Viewed as 
less harsh, it is still not perceived as favourable (7.142). There is now an impor- 
tant intervention by Themistocles – introduced at 7.43 – who asserts that the 
chresmologoi were mistaken and he gives the right interpretation: it was the ene- 
my, not the Athenians, who was “the target of the god’s words.”42 The Athenians 
are persuaded by Themistocles’ explanation and exhortation. Herodotus sum- 
marises their resolve: “After discussing the oracle, it seemed best to meet the bar-

Much of the remaining section concerns potential allies joining, which in- 


forms and raises narrative tension. Herodotus often notes exchanges between ci- 
ty-states and oracular centres, which play a part in his critique with a touch of 
irony. Namely, the forces that could have joined did not. This raises the stakes 
and as such helps to appreciate better Athens’ role. As a historian from a post-war 
perspective, Herodotus had the awkward task of describing Athens as the cham- 
pion, who was one of the great powers of the Mediterranean at the time of redac- 
tion, as well as the city-states who had submitted to the Persians. This, he recog- 
nises, did not please some of his audience. 


For instance, interestingly, an oracle from Delphi advises Argos to stay out of 


the war (7.148–149).43 Sicily’s response is disappointing, since Gelon, their tyrant, 
employs a highly pragmatic strategy.44 Having refused to join the coalition, he 
sends ambassadors to Delphi bearing many gifts and waits to see if the Persians 
will win (7.157). Depending on the outcome, he intends to support the victors but 
retrieve the money if the Greeks win (7.153–167). Herodotus also criticises Cor- 
cyra for refusing to help (7.168). Delphi also advises Crete not to join the coalition 
(7.169).45 As described by Herodotus, Thessaly is clearly not interested in helping 
the Greek allies and in fact did its best to assist the Persians (7.172–4). 


Finally, Herodotus helps his audience to imagine the topography and the 


strategic nature of sacred landscapes. The two locations chosen by the Greeks to 
prevent Persian incursion were Thermopylae on land and Artemisium by the sea. 
Both are narrow channels that would force the Persians into a bottleneck. As a 
part of their military strategy, this is more than circumstantial information. 
Throughout Book 7 and the remaining books, Herodotus highlights the Greeks’ 
belief in divine protection near or in sacred places like these. He mentions two 
such sacred precincts here: the temple of Artemis at Artemisium (located on the 
northwest coast of Euboea) and an altar dedicated to Heracles in the passage of 
Thermopylae. The Greek allies then occupied these areas straightaway (7.176– 
177).

9.1.5 Military Conflict on Land and Sea around Thermopylae (Hist. 7.178–239) 


Regarding the Eurasian agōn, narrative tension is mounting. This is expressed 
through the phrases “[…] the Delphians consulted the god dreading for them- 
selves and for Greece” and “[Greece] was exceedingly dreadful of the barbarian” 
(7.178.1, 2). At this point, Herodotus brings in the intervention of the Delphians 
and their famous Panhellenic oracle who tells them what to pray. Would Delphi 
support the Greek coalition? The oracle’s answer was that they should pray to the 
winds, which “would become great allies of Greece” (7.178.1).46 A charge follows 
to make it known to all Greek city-states “who wanted to be free” (7.178.2). This 
key passage reiterates and anticipates human and divine agency, with movement 
from human to divine and back in subsequent scenes. Oracle and nature work 
together to the advantage of the Greeks. The winds, or the gods who control them, 
would certainly play a favourable role.47 But how could this force make a differ- 
ence against Xerxes’ forces numbered, by Herodotus, at 5 283 220 men, including 
all those in positions of service (7.186)?48 Herodotus’ audience does not have to 
wait long to hear of the winds’ intervention. The Persian king faces another sig- 
nificant blow at the hands of nature. The Persians are now in Greek territory and 
are taken by surprise by a storm at dawn when the weather was “clear and 
calm.” Bodies and wrecks from the storm at Pelion caused panic (7.188.2). 
Herodotus estimates that four-hundred ships were lost and an incalculable num- 
ber of lives (7.190.1). 


Our narrator brings in another interpretative element about the winds 


(7.189).49 The Athenians attributed this disaster to the intervention of Boreas, the 
god of the North Wind, and his wife Orithyia. Boreas, according to them, had also 
caused the storm against Mardonius’ fleet in Athos (7.189).50 The storm lasted 
three days during which the Persian Magi offered sacrifices to Thetis and the sea- 
nymphs and cast spells on the wind. The storm, according to Herodotus, may 
have ended because of their prayers or perhaps by natural means (7.192). The 
Athenians recognised Poseidon as saviour on this occasion and offered him pray- 
ers and libations of wine (7.192). Historical causation includes an element of di- 
vine mystery. However, given that Herodotus has already brought Poseidon into 
the narrative at various points, he is expecting his audience to consider divine

Greek confidence is keenly felt in the response by the Opuntian Locrians and Pho-

Thus, there was no cause for alarm – for, after all, it was not a god who threatened 
Greece, but a man, and there neither was nor ever would be a man who was not 
born with a good chance of misfortune – and the greater the man, the greater mis- 
fortune. The present enemy was no exception; he too was human, and was sure to 
be disappointed of his great expectations. (7.203.2, de Sélincourt) 


Xerxes may have had a massive army, but in the Greeks’ eyes, he was not a god 
himself. The battle of Thermopylae provides a showcase for Herodotus’ narrative 
strategy, which is to explore the first major clash, comparing Xerxes with Leoni- 
das, the great leader on the Greek side. He also is not a god, but Leonidas’ family 
claimed descendance from Heracles. If Xerxes’ lineage was from Perseus and 
Leonidas from Heracles, a confrontation is staged and may have raised expecta- 
tions in ancient readers (7.204). The comparison between Xerxes and Leonidas, 
however, is not only on the military level; rather, it asks the audience to consider

what values rouse the opposing forces and their leaders. Along with Herodotus’ 
own running commentary, Demaratus the Spartan also provides several contex-

As the two sides approach, the Greeks again debate the question whether it 


would be better to face the Persian forces or to retreat. Leonidas and others vote 
to stay and fight (7.207). Xerxes wants to know why (7.208). Spartan behaviour is 
interpreted again by Demaratus: they have come to fight and to die. Xerxes again 
is not persuaded (7.209). It was better for the Spartans to go to the underworld in 
defeat with honour than in victory with shame. Thus, the emotional side is partic- 
ularly significant in this text. Xerxes is enraged at the Greeks’ obstinance and re- 
fusal to withdraw their troops (7.210). In the face of initial significant losses, Xerx- 
es expresses rage and terror for his army (7.212). He realises that he has many in 
his troops but few men (7.210). This dilemma baffles Xerxes: the Persians want 
the Greeks to realise that they have no chance and to retreat, but they do not 
(7.212). The king’s hope comes ironically through Ephialtes, a Greek traitor, who 
gives a strategic suggestion about the track that leads over the hills to Thermopy- 
lae.52 Xerxes is delighted by this information (7.215). The clear irony here is that 
the Persians need a Greek traitor to win the battle of Thermopylae. It was not due 
to their own ingenuity or pure force. This move to follow Ephialtes’ advice was 
the winning card. 


Divine activity is reported here to highlight the fate of the Greek soldiers, 


despite their valorous behaviour. This time, a seer, Megistias, prophesies doom as 
a result of the examination of the sacrifices.53 He is an example of a seer who nei- 
ther lies nor proclaims only the positive part of a prophecy. Leonidas and others – 
despite this news from Megistias and other reports of Persian movements – held 
their ground. Herodotus interprets Leonidas’ action theologically. He exalts the 
figure of Leonidas, who was inspired by a Delphic oracle (which Herodotus pro- 
vides textually) that had announced at the outset of the war two possibilities: the 
destruction of their city or the death of a Spartan king (7.220). Leonidas appropri- 
ated this prophecy, therefore he “left great glory behind him, and Sparta did not 
lose her prosperity” (7.220). On the day of Leonidas’ death, Xerxes pours “a liba- 
tion to the rising sun” (7.223). The Greek side fights with great valour knowing 
that they have no chance to survive that day. A conflict then arises over Leonidas’ 
body, which is finally recovered by the Greeks (7.225).
