Following Persia’s victory at Thermopylae, Herodotus provides – through di- 


alogues and asides – an evaluation of this first major battle and an anticipation of 
future ones. Xerxes praises Demaratus for accurately predicting the outcome of 
the battle (7.234). Despite Demaratus’ accuracy, Xerxes, influenced by Achae- 
menes (7.237), refuses to adopt his strategy for conquering Sparta. Demaratus 
had offered this counsel: “But if you take my advice, the Isthmus and Peloponne- 
sian towns will fall into your hands without a blow” (7.235). Xerxes then commits 
an outrage against Leonidas’ body, despite the Persian custom of respecting the 
corpse of the enemy. His uncontrolled animosity towards Leonidas drives him to 
have his head cut off and impaled on a stake (7.238).54 


The final chapter (7.239) may be an addition, described by the narrator as an 


omission in the preceding anecdotes.55 Chronologically, this is plupast material, 
which describes how the Spartans came upon knowledge of the Persians’ plans to 
invade Greece. Even here, a religious element is underlined. First, Demaratus, for 
unclear motives, had sent word to Sparta about Xerxes’ plans. Then, Gorgo, wife 
of Leonidas, guessed that the blank wooden tablets, sent by Demaratus, actually 
contained a message under the wax. Demaratus’ words were then confirmed by 
the Delphic prophecy (7.220). 


The end of Book 7 thus denotes the involvement of both the divine and the 


human in the Greco-Persian Wars, particularly, the role of Sparta as Athens’ 
greatest ally. This is a bittersweet twist of irony at the time of redaction, which 
Herodotus underscores brilliantly, emphasising the perils of the imperial impulse 
in antiquity through two major military conflicts. 


9.2 The Battles of Artemisium and Salamis (Hist. 8.1–144) 


Book 8 covers events during the years 480–479 BCE. Two major battles take place 
in 480 at Artemisium and Salamis. As stated, Herodotus presents the Greeks meet- 
ing the Persians by land at Thermopylae and later by sea at Artemisium. Pride of 
place is, in terms of narrative space and historical importance, the Battle of Sala- 
mis. Salamis, in fact, can be understood as the beginning of the end of the Greco- 
Persian conflict. Consequently, Book 8 can be outlined in four parts: Artemisium 
and the Greek retreat (8.1–39); the prelude to Salamis via the fall of Athens (8.40– 
83); the Battle of Salamis (8.84–96); and Xerxes’ retreat and Mardonius’ actions 
(8.97–144).56 Herodotus provides much theological commentary on divine activity 
surrounding these key events. The emphasis on divine influence continues to be 
displayed in parallel with human actions and words, on the Greek and Persian

tus’ critique. Presented as bad examples, these men are compared, albeit differ- 
ently, to the positive portrayals of Artemisia and Themistocles. 


9.2.1 Artemisium and Greek Retreat (Hist. 8.1–39) 


Book 8 flows naturally out of Book 7 as our author’s attention focuses on the 
naval conflicts near Artemisium. These battles took place at the same time as 
Thermopylae and both concerned strategic passes to the heart of Attica, by land 
and by sea (cf. 8.15). Information about the Greek city-states’ contributions to the 
fleet as well as Themistocles’ clever activity are reported (respectively in 8.1–3 
and 4–5). Xerxes sends two hundred ships to ensnare the Greek fleet (8.7). The 
Greeks, however, are victorious at this first encounter (8.8–11). Herodotus moves 
quickly to his explanation about divine intervention in the war. He follows this 
early victory narrative with a mention of a great summer storm (which were 
rare) with much thunder from the direction of Pelion, a mountain with some 
mythological history. Implicitly, this reinforces the interpretation that the storms 
came from a divine source, by now an established motif. Panic ensued among the 
Persian troops at Aphetae as they witnessed this natural (and divine) force and a 
great number of bodies drifting in the water. 


Herodotus’ commentary on divine activity becomes immediately explicit re- 


garding the divine as the source of the wreck of Persian ships off the island of 
Euboea (8.13). It is one of Herodotus’ strongest opinions on divine intervention: 
“All this was being done by the god so that the Persian side would be made equal 
to the Greek side and not much greater than it” (8.13).57 The purpose of this inter- 
vention is not explicitly stated as punishment for previous acts of sacrilege, but 
rather as a way for the god to ensure a fair fight.58 That being reported, Herodotus 
notes that the Greeks decided to retreat after receiving the news of their defeat at 
Thermopylae (8.21). Between the accounts of the storm and the retreat, Herodo- 
tus presents the oracle of Bacis in textual form, explains that it announced the 
misfortunes of the Euboeans, who had ignored its warning of impending troubles 
from those who speak a barbarian tongue (8.20).59 This ethnic differentiation con- 
tinues to be emphasised in various places, especially regarding true Greek identi- 
ty (e.g., “you have come from us,” ἀπ᾽ ἡμέων γεγόνατε, 8.22.2; Persian surprise at 


57 
Harrison (2002) 93.

Greeks competing for non-lucrative prizes 8.26.3; and the exhortation about same 
customs, language, etc.). Meanwhile, Xerxes and Themistocles use various strata- 
gems to outwit their adversary. Yet Xerxes fails to dupe his sailors (8.22–26), and 
internal struggles among the Greeks also come to the fore in Book 8, beginning 
here with a feud between Thessaly and Phocis (8.27–33).60 The Thessalians, in 
fact, led the Persians through Phocis where the Persians burnt the towns and tem- 
ples that they overran (8.32). This included Abae, where there were an oracle and 
temple of Apollo that was still visible in Herodotus’ time (8.33). Further examples 
of Persian impiety are reported, including sacrilegious behaviour towards wom- 
en. 


The next example of sacrilege and divine activity occurs in Delphi, the Pan- 


hellenic centre of Apollo’s oracle. Owing to the importance of this site, this is a 
major passage for the development of Herodotus’ prophetic voice. Xerxes sent 
troops around Mount Parnassus to plunder the great temple of Delphi, which con- 
tained an enormous treasure, because he was aware of Croesus’ lavish gifts. Un- 
derstandably, the arrival of the Persians produced terror among the Delphians, so 
they consulted their oracle whose response was that the god (Apollo) could take 
care of his own things (8.36.1). Herodotus reports several elements of divine activ- 
ity, which clearly underline his believing posture. This comes close to portraying 
the divine in Homeric fashion, since divine presence is clearly assumed. First, an 
eyewitness, Aceratus the prophet (προφήτης), reported that the sacred weapons 
were lying in front of the temple which no one was permitted to touch. It was a 
sign that the god had moved them himself (8.37.1). Herodotus then writes that 
“even greater portents (τέρεα) happened […] but of the signs from heaven 
(φασμάτων) the next was one was the most worthy of wonder” (8.37.2). As the 
Persians were approaching the shrine of Athena Pronaia, thunderbolts fell from 
the sky and two crags from Mount Parnassus fell on the Persians and killed a 
great number (8.37.3). In addition, simultaneously, “emerged from the sanctuary 
of Athena a loud shout and a battle cry” (8.37.3). 


The punishment of the Persians’ profanation was thus being accomplished, 


which included the ensuing slaughter that the Delphians themselves wrought on 
the fleeing Persians (8.38). Herodotus then authenticates these remarkable occur- 
rences with two pieces of information. First, a testimony from the Persians who 
had escaped reported other miraculous manifestations (θεῖα). They saw a vision 
of two giant hoplites chasing them and slaying people of their army. Further- 
more, the Delphians later interpreted this apparition as their local heroes, Phyla- 
cus and Autonous. Their sacred plots are close to the sanctuary of Pronaia (8.38– 
39).61 Second, Herodotus adds that the rocks were still present in his time and 


60 
In 8.27, Herodotus gives an example of a diviner (an Elean named Tellias) who leads the Pho-

were embedded within the sacred precinct of Athena. Consequently, Herodotus 
does not strictly limit himself to historical commentary, namely, that the battle 
occurred and was won by ‘such and such side’. Rather, he wishes to emphasise 
that the divine was interested in routing the invaders from their territory, not just 
that of the Delphians.62 This war was being fought on two fronts, the human and 
the divine, and theological discourse deserved this space in historical commen- 
tary. To author and audience, including the divine in the equation did not make it 
any less historical. 


9.2.2 Prelude to Salamis via the Fall of Athens (Hist. 8.40–83)63 


Narratively, the defeat of the Persians at Delphi is quickly contrasted by events 
occurring in and around Athens. On sea, the Greek fleet sails to Salamis, while on 
land the Athenians begin to desert their city in obedience to the oracle announc- 
ing that all of Attica would be taken (8.41.1; cf. 7.142). But the oracle was not the 
only reason for evacuating Athens; another divine sign had reached the Atheni- 
ans through the temple priestess (ἱερείη), namely, that Athena in the form of a 
great snake that guarded the Acropolis and lived in the temple had not eaten the 
customary monthly offering in the form of a honey-cake. The interpretation of 
this sign was that the goddess herself had abandoned the Acropolis. Therefore, 
their only hope now was to abandon Athens as well (8.41.3). Herodotus does not 
provide any further commentary on this peculiar report. It is the reverse of the 
situation at Delphi. Based on deduction, the occurrence is deemed divine, the log- 
ic being that the presence of the god(s) leads to Persian defeat, while their ab- 
sence leads to Greek defeat. However, in the light of the Delphi episode, it is un- 
clear why a goddess would abandon her temple. 


Following this, there is much build-up regarding the number of ships gather- 


ing in Salamis and their contributors. In addition, narrative tension is building as 
the Persians move towards Attica burning both Thespia and Plataea (8.50). Four 
months had passed since the Persians had begun their crossing of the Hellespont 
(8.51.1). There was, however, some difference in the interpretation of the oracle 
with the image of the “wooden wall” (already signalled in 7.142). Some Atheni- 
ans, temple servants and poor people, interpreted the “wooden wall” as a barrier 
of protection around the Acropolis (7.142). So, they created a wall made of doors 
and logs. This simple strategy was somewhat successful since Xerxes found it dif-

became clear to the Persians, for it was necessary, according to the prophecy, for 
all of Attica on the mainland to be under Persian control” (8.53.1).64 


In fact, this is what happened, as the Persians were able to take the Acropo-

sary subsequently robbed and burnt to the ground (8.53.2). Xerxes became ‘mas- 
ter of all of Athens’ for which he proudly sent news home to Artabanus, his 
pessimistic uncle (8.54). Herodotus then speculates about the order given by 
Xerxes to the exiled Athenians to offer sacrifices on the Acropolis. Either Xerxes 
had received a dream, or he felt remorse for having burned down the sanctuary 
(8.54). In any case, these acts of cruelty on sacred grounds, from Herodotus’ per- 
spective, were still another sacrilege committed against the gods who would hold 
Xerxes accountable in time.65 


Just when things were looking terribly bleak for the Athenians and their al- 


lies, a ray of hope shone through a sign promising a rebirth for Athens.66 This 
time, the gods are perceived as speaking through the natural realm. The day after 
the Persians burned the sanctuary, the stump of an olive tree, which had also 
been burnt down, sprouted a shoot about a cubit long. This itself was extraordi- 
nary, but it was also a special tree in that it was on the Acropolis because Athena 
had planted it herself, when she and Poseidon had contended for the land (8.55). 
This was referred to the king by the Athenians who had gone up to offer sacri- 
fices, but Herodotus refrains from giving more commentary on this. The interpre- 
tation was clear enough that nothing more needed to be said.67 


In the human sphere, the Athenians feared that having lost Athens, they 


would also lose their allies’ support as well and would have to give up hope for 
routing the Persians and retaking Athens. Through heated discussions (8.56–63), 
Themistocles becomes the hero by exhorting his fellow Greeks to block the Per- 
sians in Salamis: “It is now within your reach to save Greece, if you listen to me 
and stay here to engage in battle on sea, and not listen to those who would have 
you move the ships to the Isthmus.” (8.60α). Herodotus passes on a wisdom saying 
from Themistocles’ speech following his confident appropriation of the oracle’s 
announcement of victory: “When men make good plans, they are usually likely to 
succeed. But if their plans are improbable, then not even god (ὁ θεός) is willing to

Here Herodotus reinforces the idea that divine support was communicating

again announces the gods’ presence in a timely way: there was an earthquake on 
land and on sea which seems to announce the start of the battle of Salamis

muster: the heroes Ajax and Telamon are summoned as well as Aeacus and his 
sons from Aegina (8.64.2; the images of the latter arrive by ship in 8.83).73 No 
favourable interpretation is given at this point, but, in the following lines, 
Herodotus supplies information that the divine was indeed coming to the defence 
of the Greeks. Indeed, an apparition of sight and sound was manifest while the 
Persians were ravaging Attica. A great dust cloud as one might expect from a 
great army and the sound of the procession was divine in that there was no other 
possible source (i.e., Attica being deserted). This interpretation is provided by a 
certain Dicaeus, an Athenian exile who was in the service of Xerxes. Dicaeus was 
familiar with the sacred landscape and rituals. In his description, he mentions the 
Mother and the Maid who are Demeter and Persephone respectively. Demeter is 
later said to have intervened in favour of the Greeks in the battles of Plataea and 
Mycale. Eleusis was nearby, so the cry must have been part of the Iacchus song 
from the Dionysiac Mysteries. Demaratus, on the other hand, required an expla- 
nation of these signs. So Dicaeus answers in a prophetic manner:

parition and to be reassured that the gods would attend to Xerxes’ army. Subse- 
quently, they watched the dust cloud fly to Salamis where the Greeks were en- 
camped. They both knew then, according to Dicaeus’ testimony,74 that Xerxes’ 
fleet was going to be destroyed (8.65.6).75 In light of this series of divine testi- 
monies, Herodotus’ readers (especially those knowledgeable of Eleusis) are well- 
prepared to interpret the miraculous victory in Salamis.76 Moreover, adding a 
touch of irony, Herodotus then returns to the Persians, providing significant cir- 
cumstantial information and including Artemisia’s advice to Xerxes not to risk 
battle at sea (8.68α). Again, a wise counsellor is ignored! Xerxes is destined to fail, 
and, again ironically, he would view the defeat of his fleet with his own eyes (un- 
like at Euboea) from Mt Aegaleos (8.69, 90).77

and at sea during the night. At this point, Herodotus introduces another oracle 
with one of the clearest expressions of his belief in oracular communications

Now I cannot deny that there is truth in prophecies, and I have no wish to discredit 
them when they are expressed in unambiguous language. Consider the following: 


When they shall span the sea with ships from Cynosura 
To the holy shore of Artemis of the golden sword, 
Wild with hope at the ruin of shining Athens, 
Then shall bright Justice quench Excess, the child of Pride, 
Dreadful and furious, thinking to swallow up all things. 
Bronze shall mingle with bronze, and Ares with blood 
Incarnadine the sea; and all-seeing Zeus 
And gracious Victory shall bring to Greece the day of freedom. 


With that utterance of Bacis in mind, absolutely clear as it is, I do not venture to say 
anything against prophecies, nor will I listen to criticism from others. (8.77, trans. 
de Sélincourt) 


Herodotus offers no further interpretation or moral instruction on this matter.78 


Given the divine assistance available to the Greek side, it is clear enough for his 
readers that Xerxes’ defeat is sealed. Indeed, just before the battle began, as the 
Greeks were boarding their ships, a boat arrived from Aegina carrying the images 
of the Sons of Aeacus (8.83.2). Divine presence is underscored again; proof that 
the sailors could count on their gods and heroes. 


9.2.3 The Battle of Salamis (Hist. 8.84–96) 


The crushing defeat of Xerxes’ Persian fleet takes place in the strait between the 
island of Salamis and the mainland of Greece in 480 BCE. Despite the significance 
of this victory for the Greeks, Herodotus does not provide much detail about the 
movements of either side.79 The beginning of the battle is handed down in various 
versions, which merit our attention. The first version is Athenian, which reports

5th cent. BCE onwards (e.g., Hist. 8.20.77 and 9.43, referring to the invasion of Xerxes, and

that Athenian ships reacted first to the Persian attack, some backwatering, others 
engaging battle. The Aeginetans, however, claim that the ship carrying the Sons of 
Aeacus met the Persians first. This is supported by another report of divine inter- 
vention. An apparition of a phantom in the shape of a woman (φάσμα σφι γυναι- 
κός) appeared and raised her voice loud enough for the entire Greek fleet to hear 
her reproaches for retreating (8.84.2). The battle is described as a conflict involv- 
ing divine and human forces.80 There are, however, no indications of gods taking 
sides or of conflict among themselves. Again, Herodotus’ portrayal of divine in- 
tervention is almost always in favour of the Greeks. 


Another report from an Athenian source supports the positive development 


of the battle for the Greeks (8.86).81 The Athenians are convinced about it, but not 
the Corinthians. It concerns the so-called retreat of the Corinthian fleet right at 
the beginning of conflict.82 This sign of cowardice by the commander Adeimantus 
and the Corinthians at Salamis is countered by a scene which has the appearance 
of being divinely orchestrated. A mysterious ship met them at the level of the tem- 
ple of Athena Sciras (8.94). The crew aboard cried out a reproach: “Ademantus, 
while you are playing the traitor by running away with your squadron, the pray- 
ers of Greece are being answered, and she is victorious over her enemies”, which 
they backed up with an offer of self-sacrifice if their story were not true (8.94). 
The result of this divine intervention is that the Corinthians returned to battle, 
but only after military action had ceased. 


As noted, commentators have pointed out the portrayal of the Corinthians as 


an example of the political bias at the time of writing the Histories. There is clear 
recognition of discrepancies in the reports. Nevertheless, the fact that Herodotus 
indicates that the boat was at the level of the temple of Athena Sciras as well as 
the mention of the prayers of the Greeks being answered suggest patterns of per- 
ception of divine presence. That Herodotus does not accept the story uncritically 
is signalled by the detail: “This was spread through a rumour by the Athenians, 
but the Corinthians do not agree, believing themselves to be among the first in the

Chapter 96 concludes the description of the battle scene with details of the 


Persian wreckage being towed by the Greeks to Salamis, while other vessels were 
floating away towards Colias on the Attic coast. Herodotus conveys this victorious 
scene with two prophetic reports. The first hearkens back to the confirmation of 
oracles by Bacis and Musaeus. The second comes from Lysistratus, an Athenian 
chresmologos who had announced, “The women of Colias shall cook with oars” 
(8.96.2). Herodotus adds retrospectively: “This was to happen after the king had 
gone away” (8.96). This is again a confirmation of Herodotus’ belief and use of 
oracles to construct his narrative. In sum, the victory of Salamis was the turning 
point of the Greco-Persian Wars, and Herodotus places the gods’ interventions 
and oracular communication at the centre of his narrative. Moreover, he is quick 
to include various expressions of gratitude by the Greeks to their gods for this 
unexpected rout of the greatest military force on earth.83 


9.2.4 Xerxes’ Retreat and Mardonius’ Actions (Hist. 8.97–144) 


Herodotus continues by describing Xerxes’ decision to depart for the Hellespont 
in order to save his bridge between Europe and Asia. Xerxes pretends to prepare 
for retaliation, but Mardonius was not fooled. Xerxes was fully intent on leaving 
the theatre and had even sent a courier to Susa to bring news of the defeat (8.88– 
89). Artabanus was right, of course, and his quasi-prophetic utterance (cf. 7.10ε 
and 7.49.1) seems to have been fulfilled both on land and sea. Mardonius, howev- 
er, stayed and became again the central commander of the Persian forces for the 
remaining part of the war (or at least, very close to it, since his death was near 
the end). His impressive rhetoric convinces Xerxes not to give up. Mardonius was 
still confident of Persia’s ability to reduce all of Greece to servitude.84 Consequent- 
ly, Mardonius, as the representative of Xerxes and another key personality, will 
also become, narratively, a target of divine retribution and of Herodotus’ cri- 
tique. 


83 
For a helpful evaluation of this victory and its religious aspect, see Mikalson (2003) 80–85. 


84 
Mardonius’ confidence and boastful spirit come through clearly in various statements: “for 
the Greeks cannot possibly escape ultimate subjection”; “My lord, do not give the Greeks the 
chance to laugh at us”, “Persia is not involved in their disgrace. No; it is not we who are re- 
sponsible for what has occurred”; and “I will make it my duty, with 300,000 picked troops to 
deliver Greece to you in chains” (Herodotus 2003, 8.100.3–5). 


9 Xerxes under Divine Rule 
283 


The storyline thus continues with Themistocles and Mardonius as the main 


protagonists. Themistocles allows the Persians to depart without hindrance, and 
he informs Xerxes about this, so that one day he might receive help from the king 
in case of estrangement with Athenian leadership (8.110). This depiction of 
Themistocles is mixed with piety and deception. During a debate about whether 
to pursue the Persians to the Hellespont, one of the strongest affirmations of grat- 
itude to the gods appears. It is arguably an encapsulation of Herodotus’ own 
prophetic voice explaining the Greco-Persian Wars from a theological perspec- 
tive: 


τάδε γὰρ οὐκ ἡμεῖς κατεργασάμεθα, ἀλλὰ θεοί τε καὶ ἥρωες, οἳ ἐφθόνησαν ἄνδρα 
ἕνα τῆς τε Ἀσίης καὶ τῆς Εὐρώπης βασιλεῦσαι ἐόντα ἀνόσιόν τε καὶ ἀτάσθαλον· ὃς 
τά τε ἱρὰ καὶ τὰ ἴδια ἐν ὁμοίῳ ἐποιέετο, ἐμπιπράς τε καὶ καταβάλλων τῶν θεῶν τὰ 
ἀγάλματα· ὃς καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν ἀπεμαστίγωσε πέδας τε κατῆκε. ἀλλ᾽ εὖ γὰρ ἔχει ἐς 
τὸ παρεὸν ἡμῖν, νῦν μὲν ἐν τῇ Ἑλλάδι καταμείναντας ἡμέων τε αὐτῶν ἐπιμεληθῆναι 
καὶ τῶν οἰκετέων, καὶ τις οἰκίην τε ἀναπλασάσθω καὶ σπόρου ἀνακῶς ἐχέτω, παντε- 
λέως ἀπελάσας τὸν βάρβαρον· ἅμα δὲ τῷ ἔαρι καταπλέωμεν ἐπὶ Ἑλλησπόντου καὶ 
Ἰωνίης. 


For it is not we who have won this victory, but the gods and the heroes, who 
deemed Asia and Europe too great a realm for one man to rule, and that a wicked 
man and an impious one who dealt alike with temples and bones, burning and 
overthrowing the images of the gods, – yes, and one who scourged the sea and 
threw fetters into it. But as it is well with us for the moment, let us abide now in 
Hellas and take thought for ourselves and our households. Let us build our houses 
again and be diligent in sowing, when we have driven the foreigner completely 
away. Then when the next spring comes, let us set sail for the Hellespont and Ionia. 
(8.109.3–4, trans. Godley) 


Herodotus provides two points of commentary on this, but nothing about the ac- 
curacy of Themistocles’ theological interpretation. The motives for Themistocles’ 
discourse are criticised (i.e., to secure favour with the Persians) but not his grati- 
tude to the gods for their part in the victory. The Athenians follow him again, be- 
cause he was clever and successful. It is nonetheless a significant statement that 
places the gods and the heroes in the centre of the conflict and victory, explaining 
also that Xerxes, “an impious and reckless man” (ἀνόσιόν τε καὶ ἀτάσθαλον, 
8.109.3) had sparked divine retribution. Indeed, although Greece did not follow 
through in their pursuit of the Persian fleet, it appears that the divine sphere did 
not want to let the Persians get away so easily. A natural miracle is reported: an 
optical illusion of white cliffs resembling ships causing the Persians to fear 
(8.107.2).85 While Herodotus does not describe this scene in detail regarding the

divine, it may have been clear enough to some of his readers. As the Persians 
were passing by Cape Zoster (ζωστήρ, ‘belt’ or ‘girdle’), they mistook the cape’s 
rocks for enemy ships and fled until they realised their mistake.86 This area was 
associated with various deities and was considered sacred. This optical illusion 
may have been perceived as being caused by divine intervention; for example, 
the idea of a soldier’s belt representing divine belligerence. 


On land, Mardonius retreats to Thessaly for the winter, and, per Xerxes’ ap- 


proval, he organises his army for subsequent military operations in Greece 
(8.113). Herodotus, here, informs his readers that Delphi had intervened again in 
the political sphere, since the Spartans had received an oracle from there de- 
manding reparations from Xerxes for the death of Leonidas in Thermopylae. 
Xerxes laughs at this and shifts the responsibility to Mardonius (who was at his 
side): “Mardonius will pay them back all the satisfaction they deserve” (8.114).87 


Mardonius will pay dearly by his own life (9.64.1), but Herodotus does not reveal 
this here, thus creating suspense and anticipation. This is in fact the second 
prophecy about Mardonius’ fate (cf. 7.10η). The Spartan messenger took this re- 
sponse back and nothing more of it is reported. 


In the meantime, Xerxes left for the Hellespont, and Mardonius stayed in 


Thessaly. Of note is that Xerxes could not recover his sacred chariot of Zeus from 
Siris in Paeonia where he had left it (8.115). This may be a symbol of his defeat. 
Again, the absence of the divine (here Zeus’ chariot) leads to a sense of abandon- 
ment, defeat, or destruction. But Herodotus comments no further on this. Xerxes 
and his army return – with much difficulty and death – to the Hellespont where 
they find the bridge in bad shape (“shattered by the storms”). They cross over to 
Abydos, then return to Sardis (8.117). Herodotus offers no further account on 
Xerxes’ retreat (8.118ff.), which he does not find plausible (8.119.1). 


Alongside the abundant reports of divine activity, Herodotus pays much at- 


tention to pious gestures towards divinities for their assistance (requested and 
realised). In 8.121–122, Herodotus turns his attention back to the Greeks and their 
return to Salamis. These sections are significant in that they open a window 
through which readers can better appreciate gestures of recognition towards the 
divine following the unexpected victory against the Persians.88 There is a sense of 
priority here in the mention of ‘the first act on reaching Salamis’ and the choice 
of the ‘first fruits’ (ἀκροθίνια) to offer to their divinities (8.121). Tributes and of- 
ferings are given to the gods and the heroes. Among these gifts were three 
Phoenician triremes: one for Poseidon at the Isthmus, another for Poseidon at

Sunium, and the third to Ajax at Salamis.89 Other ‘first fruits’ were sent to Delphi, 
the material of which was made into a sculpture of a man’s image, eighteen feet 
high, with the beak of a ship in his hand.90 What is clear from these gifts is their 
link to the victory on sea and their perception that the divine had a significant 
part to play in their rout of the Persians. The following lines (8.122) provide an 
example of an exchange between the Greeks and the god of Delphi (Apollo) about 
whether the latter was satisfied with their offerings. The answer was affirmative 
except in the case of the Aeginetans who had not offered a gift to him as part of 
their prize of valour won at Salamis. The god of Delphi, in this sense, confirms 
this honour to the Aeginetans (and not to the Athenians) and desires to be recog- 
nised as well for his part in their victory.91 


After a brief return to the storyline on Themistocles, who is the object of 


both honour and rejection from various sources (8.123–125), Herodotus brings 
back into the narration a counterfigure, Artabazus, a key personage (next to Mar- 
donius) in the Persian military. The reason for this focus on Artabazus appears to 
be Herodotus’ interest in showing the aftermath of Xerxes’ retreat and how his 
generals performed after him. Having escorted Xerxes safely to Asia, Artabazus 
returns to the front during wintertime and finds that Potidaea, and other popula- 
tions of the Pallene peninsula, are in revolt against Xerxes whom they knew had 
been defeated in Salamis. In fulfilment of his duty, Artabazus proceeds to subju- 
gate Potidaea, a major port city (8.126–128). This project proves to be more com- 
plicated than expected, as he faces both human and divine opposition. Even after 
a three-month siege and with the help of a compromised general of Scione, Tim- 
oxenus, the Potidaeans had not been broken. An unusual low tide that lasted for 
some time enticed Persian soldiers to break through to the peninsula via this 
pathway. However, they were taken by surprise by an exceptionally high flood 
which swept away those who could not swim and caused others to be killed by 
Potidaeans who were in their boats waiting for them (8.129.1–2). Herodotus then 
provides a theological interpretation of this extraordinary natural event. The 
Potidaeans reflected on the people who had been killed by it and concluded that 
these were the same Persians who had desecrated Poseidon’s shrine and statue 
outside the town. Herodotus states: “I also think they are right to assert that this 
was the cause” (8.129.3). 


A few items are noteworthy here. First, Herodotus acknowledges again what 


seems clearly to be an instance of divine intervention. But this must be deduced. 
Herodotus leaves it to his audience to consider that Poseidon himself had inter-

tion. 


Book 8 does not contain other reports of divine activity during this time 


frame. Nevertheless, Herodotus concludes it by underlining certain theological 
knowledge that has a bearing on the interpretation of the rest of the book which 
highlights peace negotiations between Mardonius and Athens, and Sparta’s fear 
of it. In the springtime, the Greeks were provoked by Mardonius’ presence in 
Thessaly. Herodotus introduces now the Spartan leader of the fleet whose name 
was Leotychides. He belonged to the younger house of the Spartan royals, and his 
origins could be traced back to Heracles, for whom our author provides a brief 
genealogical list (8.131). 


In 8.133, Herodotus offers to his audience a long section on Mardonius’ idea 


(like Croesus’) to consult numerous oracles via a Carian named Mys. The question 
of the consultation must have been important since several centres of oracular 
activity are mentioned. Herodotus admits his ignorance about the details report- 
ed by Mys to Mardonius, particularly those of Mys’ visit to the precinct of Apollo 
Ptoius near Acraephia, which was quite remarkable to Herodotus. Our author, 
not knowing the content of this last message, deduces that it must have concerned 
the sending of Alexander I of Macedonia to Athens with the hope of winning Ath- 
ens as an ally (see 8.136).93 This, Herodotus surmises, appears to be the gist of the 
oracles, and “it was in obedience to them that he [Mardonius] sent Alexander on 
his mission” (8.136.3).

Herodotus then closes Book 8 by providing a detailed account of Alexander’s 


visit, containing several references to religious practices, the divine, political 
power, and liberty (8.139–144). Herodotus also recounts Xerxes’ offer of alliance 
to Athens and Alexander’s personal plea for it to be accepted. In the meantime, 
the Spartans caught wind of the nature of Alexander’s visit and were deeply con- 
cerned by the threat of an alliance between Xerxes and Athens. The latter could 
evolve from being liberators to enforcers of slavery to Greece. Moreover, the 
Spartans had recalled the oracles that announced that they, with the rest of the 
Dorians, would one day be expelled from the Peloponnese by the Medes and the 
Athenians (ὑπὸ Μήδων τε καὶ Ἀθηναίων, 8.141.1)! The origin of these oracles is 
not mentioned. It was good timing for the Spartans as they were able to respond 
to the Athenians in Alexander’s presence, evoking the imminent danger and their 
support of Athens. Their rhetoric resounds with phrases like “if you are wise” and 
“in foreigners (βαρβάροισι) there is neither truth nor trust” (8.142). This is all 
highly ironic when read in the light of the conflicts between Athens and Sparta at 
the beginning of the Peloponnesian War when Herodotus was still composing his 
work. In fact, some of the most noble words – to ancient Greek sensibilities – in 
the Histories about Greek identity and cooperation are voiced here by the Atheni- 
ans. 


The Athenians’ admirable responses via Alexander (to Mardonius and Xerx- 


es) and to the Spartans evoke faith in the divine for their survival. They, like 
Alexander, acknowledge the superiority in numbers of the Persian forces. Yet 
their love of freedom is so great that they will never surrender to Xerxes. Their 
trust is in “the help of the gods and the heroes for whom he had no reverence 
(οὐδεμίαν ὄπιν) and whose temples and statues he burnt” (8.143.2).94 Their re- 
sponse to the Spartans evokes the greatest reason, which also encapsulates the 
motifs of freedom and religious devotion, for not accepting Xerxes’ offer: 


πολλά τε γὰρ καὶ μεγάλα ἐστι τὰ διακωλύοντα ταῦτα μὴ ποιέειν μηδ᾽ ἢν ἐθέλωμεν, 
πρῶτα μὲν καὶ μέγιστα τῶν θεῶν τὰ ἀγάλματα καὶ τὰ οἰκήματα ἐμπεπρησμένα τε 
καὶ συγκεχωσμένα, τοῖσι ἡμέας ἀναγκαίως ἔχει τιμωρέειν ἐς τὰ μέγιστα μᾶλλον ἤ 
περ ὁμολογέειν τῷ ταῦτα ἐργασαμένῳ, αὖτις δὲ τὸ Ἑλληνικὸν ἐὸν ὅμαιμόν τε καὶ 
ὁμόγλωσσον καὶ θεῶν ἱδρύματά τε κοινὰ καὶ θυσίαι ἤθεά τε ὁμότροπα, τῶν προ-

first and greatest is the burning of the temples and images of our gods – now ashes 
and rubble. It is our bounden duty to avenge this desecration with all our might –

Again, the sacrilegious acts against the gods are highlighted as well as common

religious and ethno-patriotic values. The Athenians’ final words to the Spartans 
are to prepare for the Persian onslaught that is inevitable after the Athenians’ re- 
fusal to become their allies. The audience is being prepared for further animosity, 
which is revealed in the opening lines of Book 9. 


9.3 Xerxes and Mardonius as Co-antagonist and Xerxes’ Downfall 


(Hist. 9.1–122) 


In this final book of the Histories, Herodotus highlights Greek victories at Plataea 
and Mycale, as well as on the Hellespont, which culminates in the retreat of the 
Persians to Asia Minor. Greek success at Plataea is ranked as “the finest victory of 
all known to us” (9.64.1). With other scenes and disclosures, these three events 
provide closure to the main questions driving the intrigue: how and why the 
Greeks defeated the Persians, and who was chiefly responsible for the conflicts 
and victories. Consequently, these final episodes provide a sense of closure to sev- 
eral thematic threads in the Histories: geopolitical, moral, and theological.96 


As regards Persian leadership and the question of overall closure of the His- 


tories, it is helpful to recall Herodotus’ prophetic interpretation of the earthquake 
in Delos (6.98). It was a heaven-sent portent (τέρας), which announced coming 
evils on the world (6.98.1). These evils, he writes, came through Darius, Xerxes, 
and Artaxerxes. Rightly, Herodotus does remind his audience that part of the 
troubles was ascribable to the conflicts among the Greeks themselves (6.98.2). His 
focus, however, in this final part continues to be on the Persian aggressors and 
how the Greeks – despite their internal rivalries for leadership – were able to set 
the Persians to flight. 


As Xerxes – who retreats to Sardis (9.1, 81) then reappears in Susa (9.108) – 


leaves the stage as the main antagonist, the spotlight follows other Persian lead- 


95 
See also Mikalson (2003) 88–89. 


96 
Several studies elucidate elements of narrative closure in Book 9, e.g., Boedeker (1988) 30–

(1997) 62–82.

ers who exemplify foolish behaviour, particularly Mardonius and Artaÿctes.97 Be- 
cause Xerxes’ death is not recounted in Book 9, the change of leadership to Artax- 
erxes does not appear in the narrative.98 The audience, listening to this part of the 
narrative over the span of ca. 430–410 BCE, could most likely envisage some of 
the troubles (outside the narrative limits) subsequently committed by Xerxes and 
Artaxerxes. 


Thus, rather than focusing on Xerxes or his son, Herodotus focuses primarily 


on the Persian general Mardonius (9.1–63). He continues to be depicted as em- 
bodying, more than all others, the ‘imperial impulse’ that Artabanus had warned 
about (7.10η). Mardonius is extremely ambitious and longs to capture Athens, so 
that he can report back to the king, who is now in Sardis. For this reason, Mardo- 
nius takes Xerxes’ place in the narrative, and Herodotus carefully sets up Mardo- 
nius’ downfall for his audience. To this end, Herodotus displays his unique 
prophetic voice through oracles that are both announced and fulfilled, oracles 
that are interpreted incorrectly then corrected by Herodotus himself, and exam- 
ples of divine landscapes and presences in relation to battle scenes. Curiously, 
Xerxes reappears in Susa, where his poor judgement is again thoroughly featured 
(9.108–113). Finally, the first great Persian king Cyrus returns to the narrative, 
anachronistically, to offer advice to his successors. His appearance nicely book- 
ends the imperialistic line of aggressors in the Eurasian agōn. 


9.3.1 On the Way to Plataea (Hist. 9.1–24) 


The depiction of Persia’s series of defeats and rout from Greece enfolds through a 
focus on Mardonius, especially on his inner drive to capture Athens, despite the 
Thebans’ counsel to act otherwise (9.1.1). Herodotus is carefully preparing his au- 
dience for Mardonius’ humiliating ruin. Ironically and comically, Mardonius 
finds Athens empty; thus, he captured a “deserted town” (9.3). The Athenians had 
left for Salamis because of its protection and strategic benefits, hoping for urgent 
support from their slow-acting allies from the Peloponnese (9.6). Thus, Athens 
was once again under Persian rule ten months after Xerxes had captured it 
(September 480 / June 479). But Mardonius did not stop there, for he displays his 
impious nature by burning Athens, about which Herodotus carefully specifies, 
“walls, houses, temples, and all” (9.13). The burning of temples and anything sa- 
cred awakens expectation for some act of divine retribution, which Herodotus 
will not fail to point out in later passages. When Mardonius heard that the Atheni-

ans received help from the Spartans and other allies, he withdrew from Attica 
because it was not optimal for his cavalry’s manoeuvres (9.13). 


In the meantime, Athens had rejected Mardonius’ proposals to surrender 


peacefully (9.4–5, 7). Despite the temptation to submit to him, they send messen- 
gers to solicit once again Sparta’s help. In the message, the Athenians underline 
the grounds for their refusal as being out of “reverence for Zeus of all the Greeks” 
(ἡμεῖς δὲ Δία τε Ἑλλήνιον αἰδεσθέντες, 9.7.α.2). Once again, Greek identity and 
unity are substantiated via the city’s piety. Athenian faith, however, was not 
enough to trust in Zeus’ deliverance. She felt isolated and desperately needed 
help from their Peloponnesian allies, especially Sparta. Herodotus points out that 
part of the perceived slowness of Sparta transpired because of their building a 
wall on the isthmus and their own piety (9.7, 11). In fact, the Spartans wished first 
to respect the Hyacinthia, a festival honouring Hyacinthus and Apollo of Amyclae. 
Finally, Sparta agrees to join the Greek coalition – thanks to the intervention of a 
respected Tegean named Chileus – for fear of Athenian acceptance of Mardonius’ 
offer (9.9). 


The narration continues to move back and forth between Persian and Greek 


strategies and movements. Upon hearing the news of Peloponnese forces joining 
Athens, Mardonius decides to retreat and prepare for battle in Theban territory 
(9.15.1). Herodotus builds up tension regarding the confrontation via an anecdote 
about a banquet conversation in Thebes. The foreboding ruin of the Persian 
forces (and of Mardonius) comes through an unnamed Persian to Thersander of 
Orchomenus, whom Herodotus had met.99 The Persian, weeping greatly, predicts 
that few of the Persians at the banquet and at the camp would survive. He sup- 
ports this with a theological utterance, which echoes previous expressions about 
divine sovereignty and human fate: “that which must happen, coming from a 
god, it is impossible for a man to avert, for even when people say trustworthy 
things, they do not want to believe” (9.16.4). The perception of a divinely or- 
dained defeat was perceived to be in the air. Again, some (“many of us”) were 
more willing to accept its truth than others (i.e., “our commander”). As such, sev- 
eral Herodotean themes are illustrated such as the divine having the last word, 
human frailty, and the refusal of truth.100 Retrospectively, in Herodotus’ view, the 
Persians’ defeat confirmed the prophetic utterance of their fellow countryman. 


The sense of divine assistance on the side of the Greeks is reinforced as the 


Peloponnesian forces received favourable omens in their sacrifices as they 
moved from the Isthmus to Eleusis then to the foothills of Mt Cithaeron (9.19–20). 
Notwithstanding losses, the first military clash in those parts displays a Greek vic- 
tory. The Persian defeat is highlighted by the death of the Masistius, a highly es-

Cf. Asheri et al. (2003) 196.

teemed officer just below Mardonius. Furthermore, his body was not recovered 
and was exposed to all in order to illustrate Greek military prowess (9.20–25). 
The theological background in the anecdote primes Herodotus’ audience to see a 
change in fortune for the sacrilegious Persians. The audience is now prepared to 
experience the “the most splendid victory” at Plataea. 


9.3.2 The Battle of Plataea (Hist. 9.25–89) 


In Herodotus’ account of the discussions between the Athenians and the Tegeans 
about who should lead one of the wings in battle formation, the divine realm and 
responses to it are mentioned. Speakers take turns in evoking their city’s piety, 
that is, former deeds of honour and instances of the divine plupast (cf. 9.26– 
27).101 The sum of these was aimed at obtaining pride of place in leadership for 
such a battle as this. The Spartans, who had overall leadership, found the Atheni- 
an response the most convincing and gave them the more honourable position. 


The Greeks had now taken position in Plataean territory, and Herodotus is 


quick to point out that they were in proximity to the Gargaphian Spring and the 
precinct of the hero Androcrates, the legendary hero thought to have founded 
Plataea (9.25.3).102 This is again one of the many mentions of the sacred landscape, 
which serve as geographical markers and as signals of divine presence in favour 
of the Greeks through the rest of Book 9. 


Having provided statistics on the Greek forces and described the positions 


taken by both sides, Herodotus goes on to provide a thorough and lengthy ac- 
count illustrating the religious rivalry between the two sides in their attempts to 
solicit divine aid and direction through the offering of sacrifices and their subse- 
quent interpretations. The Greeks and the Persians were served by highly sought 
diviners who had their own unique experiences of the divine realm. Tisamenus 
of Elis served the Greeks and was supported by an enigmatic oracle from Delphi. 
Mardonius, too, sought help from a Greek seer, Hegesistratus, who was also from 
Elis (9.33–38). The latter, Herodotus says, was motivated by his hatred of the 
Spartans and by his love of money (9.38.1). The diviners proffered positive omens 
if they fought in self-defence (9.36–37). Interestingly, the Greeks serving on the

Persian side also had their own diviner, Hippomachus of Leucas. As the Greek 
troops increased, Persian divination revealed unfavourable omens regarding the 
crossing of the Asopus. Other military manoeuvres, however, were permitted 
(9.39–40).103 


Due to his impatience, Mardonius decides not to heed the omens (9.41–42), 


rejecting also the counsel of Artabazos to retreat to Thebes (9.41.2). The Persian 
general then gives orders to prepare the troops for battle. Mardonius will pay 
dearly for this act of defiance towards the divine realm. The narrative sequence 
forecasts that Mardonius will be defeated, because the positive omens for the 
Greeks and their obedience are followed by ill-omens for Mardonius. All this 
prompts the audience to expect Greek victory. 


Mardonius is interested in the divine, but he imposes his own will, which is 


to engage in battle. Herodotus further illustrates Mardonius’ folly when he asks if 
any of his commanders or Greek officers know of any prophecies announcing the 
Persian destruction of Greece. There is silence, either for lack of knowledge of the 
prophecies or for fear to speak about them. He states that he knows of one which 
predicts the sack of the temple in Delphi by the Persians and then their subse- 
quent defeat by a man. His solution is that they will not destroy the temple and 
therefore have nothing to fear and will engage in battle the following day (9.42.3– 
4). 


With authority, Herodotus informs his readers of the correct interpretation 


of the oracle in question, as well as other relevant oracles. The prophecy cited by 
Mardonius was actually intended for the Illyrians and the army of the Encheles. 
Furthermore, Herodotus is familiar with some verses by Bacis (a Boeotian oracle 
collector), which apply to the Battle of Plataea: 


τὴν δ᾽ ἐπὶ Θερμώδοντι καὶ Ἀσωπῷ λεχεποίῃ 
Ἑλλήνων σύνοδον καὶ βαρβαρόφωνον ἰυγήν, 
τῇ πολλοὶ πεσέονται ὑπὲρ λάχεσίν τε μόρον τε 
τοξοφόρων Μήδων, ὅταν αἴσιμον ἦμαρ ἐπέλθῃ 


By Thermodon and Asopus, where the grass grows soft, 
Shall be gathering of Greeks and the sound of strange tongues; 
And there beyond lot and portion many Medes shall fall, 
Armed with the bow, when the day of doom comes. (9.43.2, trans. de Sélincourt) 


Herodotus confidently restates that the Persian defeat was predicted: “I know 
that these verses, and others of Musaeus, referred to the Persians” (9.43.2). 


Herodotus resumes the narration of Mardonius’ questioning of the oracles 


by stating that “night fell and sentinels were posted” (νύξ τε ἐγίνετο καὶ ἐς φυλα- 
κὰς ἐτάσσοντο 9.44). Given the ominous presence of failure in the air, known to 
the gods and expected by some of Mardonius’ subordinates, this reference to

Asheri et al. (2003) 234.

nightfall may also carry a symbolic meaning. Suspense is thus created as Herodo- 
tus slows down the narration and shifts the focus from Mardonius to his soldiers, 
who experience nightfall and impending defeat more intensely than their leader. 
The announcement made by the Persian at the Theban banquet is in the air and 
some may also be aware of the oracles cited by Herodotus. During the night, 
Alexander, king and commander of the Macedonians, secretly informs the Greeks 
of Mardonius’ intention to ignore the omens and attack at dawn (9.45.2). All are 
now aware of the Persian general’s obstinacy towards the divine realm. His will 
is too hardened to receive any help from the gods: he has disregarded the omens 
and misconstrued an oracle.104 


The depiction of Mardonius’ arrogance is also conspicuous in his exchanges 


with the Greeks, particularly with the Spartans, whom he ridicules for having 
shifted positions to avoid direct confrontation with his troops. He thus challenges 
them to direct combat to determine the victor of the battle for both armies (9.48). 
But the Spartan strategy had been decided in accord with the Athenians. Spartan 
cowardice was not the cause; rather, the Athenians had already had experience 
in battle against the Persians, whereas the Spartans hitherto had none (9.46–47). 
The Greeks gave no answer to the challenge, so Mardonius gave orders for battle, 
unleashing his cavalry but without hand-to-hand combat (9.49). 


The Greeks decided then to shift their position about which Herodotus care- 


fully points out the significance of the spiritual landscape: they stopped in front 
of Hera’s temple (9.52). The narrative continues by indicating the arguments and 
positions of the Greek forces, particularly among the Spartan regiments (9.53– 
57). Herodotus again is keen to point out the choice of halt: the sanctuary of 
Eleusinian Demeter.105 In that vicinity, the Persian calvary attacks the Spartans, 
who find themselves immediately in serious trouble, which confirmed the un- 
favourable omens resulting from divination (9.60–61). 


Consequently, Pausanias does two things: he sends a request for urgent help 


from the Athenians, and he offers a prayer to Hera in the direction of her temple, 
requesting her help for victory (9.61). Herodotus heightens narrative tension 
through the depiction of Pausanias’ desperation and piety.106 In one of the clear- 
est examples of divine-human interaction in the Histories, Herodotus underlines 
this scene: just when defeat seems immanent, the prayer to Hera appears to be 
answered: “While he was still invoking these things […]” and “[…] immediately 
after Pasaunias’ prayer […]”, a decisive turning point occurs: the Tegeans rose up 
first (προεξαναστάντες) against the Persians, and the Spartan sacrifices were now

receiving a favourable interpretation (9.62.1). When this happened, the Spartans

The perceptions of divine assistance by the actors in the narrative is empha- 


sised by Herodotus’ own retrospective perception of divine presence, which is far 
from passive. He again mentions the proximity of Demeter’s temple during a “vi- 
olent fight” (9.62.2). After which, Herodotus mentions the death of Mardonius and 
many Persian soldiers and subsequently the flight of the remaining troops. For 
Herodotus, this was the fulfilment of the Delphic oracle that demanded justice for 
the murder of the Spartan general Leonidas (9.64.1; cf. 8.114). Xerxes, it may be 
recalled, laughed at this request, blaming Mardonius and saying – unknowingly 
in a prophetic way – that Mardonius would pay for this dishonourable act. 
Herodotus returns to the question of Demeter’s temple and the marvel (θῶμα) 
that none of the Persian soldiers entered or died on its premises. Herodotus inter- 
prets this theologically: “My own view is – if one may have views at all about 
divine matters – that the Goddess herself would not let them in, because they had 
burnt her sanctuary at Eleusis” (9.65, trans. de Sélincourt).107 Both temples, of 
Hera and Demeter, appear again in relation to the Greeks’ reaction to the reversal 
in the battle: they move from one to the other so as to join the battle enthusiasti- 
cally and haphazardly (9.69). 


Several theological items stand out in this passage. Divine retribution is reit- 


erated, owing to Mardonius’ sacrilege and to the burning of Demeter’s temple in 
Eleusis. Sacrilegious acts – particularly the burning of temples and other holy 
sites (those unnamed and named, e.g., Athena’s in Miletus [1.19] and Poseidon’s 
in Potidaea [8.129.3]) – have developed into a strong motif inviting the audience 
to reflect on due respect for τὰ ἱερά. Perhaps more striking is the clear description 
of how it occurred: a positive response to Pausanias’ prayer for help and to the 
Greeks’ sacrifices, as well as Demeter’s action to defend her own sacred precincts 
(cf. the rocks falling to prevent the Persian troops entering the temple of Athena 
Pronaea, 8.39.2). Again, the mentions of divine landscape serve here not only to 
report geographical positions but also to substantiate divine presence and action 
in relation to those holy sites.108 


Herodotus’ prophetic voice is thus elucidated through his theological inter- 


pretation of the battle but also through his audience’s knowledge of subsequent 
battles won later by the Spartans. Herodotus views Plataea as a turning-point and 
“the most splendid victory of all those that we know” (νίκην […] καλλίστην ἁπα- 
σέων τῶν ἡμεῖς ἴδμεν, 9.64). It stands above the victories of Marathon and Sala- 
mis, and it was won by Pausanias, Leonidas’ descendant, which is further proof

Mardonius’ corpse and thus to increase Pausanias’ glory (9.78–79). By refusing 
this flattery, Pausanias shows his respect for the gods and the dead. Mardonius, 
however, as Herodotus relates, appears not to have received an honourable 
burial. His body disappeared the day after the battle, so Herodotus is uncertain 
about a proper burial (9.84).

Poseidon. Proper reverence is given to the gods who helped them in their victo-

These anecdotes and parenthetical remarks serve to underline for the audience 
the necessity of acknowledging divine assistance and respecting customs, which 
are also shown to be held with religious rigour in the Histories. Plataea was in 
Herodotus’ hands a showcase for all of these values. 


9.3.3 The Battle of Mycale (Hist. 9.90–107) 


If Plataea is the showcase battle, that of Mycale is its sidelight. Together, they un- 
derline divine involvement in these victories, which lead to the decline of the Per- 
sian imperial impulse. Herodotus’ prophetic voice remains strong here, as he 
highlights the Greeks’ piety and confidence. The shift from Plataea to Mycale is 
clearly noted at 9.90: “So that is how Artabazus returned home to Asia. It hap- 
pened that on the same day as the Persian defeat at Plataea, they also suffered 
another defeat at Μycale in Ionia” (9.90.1, trans. Waterfield). The rout back to 
Asia and beyond has continued: Xerxes in Susa and Artabazus is in Asia. All this 
leads to a full circle with respect to the Eurasian agōn and the initial tensions be- 
tween the Ionian Greeks and the Lydians under Croesus (1.5.26–27). Herodotus is 
eager to bring this part of Hellas back into the narrative. He is also keen to show 
how knowledge of the victory at Plataea spurred the Greeks on to victory.113 


What better way to approach these questions than to underscore the reli- 


gious tone in this beginning paragraph in which messengers from Samos urged 
Leotychides the Spartan to save them from slavery and expel the Persians. Both 
common stock and common worship are evoked: “By the gods they have in com- 
mon, he urged them to deliver the Greeks from slavery and to drive back the bar- 
barian” (9.90.2).114 


Leotychides is portrayed as a religious man who seeks an omen or an act of 


a god (9.91.1). He finds the omen directly in the name of the main messenger, He- 
gesistratus (‘leader of the army’), which was enough proof for accepting the re- 
volting Samians against Persia. Being a “good omen,” Hegesistratus was sent with 
the Greek fleet. That this was more than chance, Herodotus recounts that a confir- 
mation came through the sacrifice the next day (and again at 9.96.1). 


In light of this, Herodotus’ audience encounters still another diviner, Dei- 


phonus, who supposedly (cf. 9.95) was the son of Euenius of Apollonia in the Ioni- 
an gulf. To this celebrated diviner, Euenius, another divine plupast is dedicated to 
show his divinely bestowed power of divination (9.93–94). This plupast material, 
the story of Euenius, contributes to the sense of reliability of this family of divin- 


113 
This reading is justified by Herodotus’ comment at 9.103.2 and 104.1 where Ionians are in- 
volved in liberating Ionia: “In this way Ionia revolted for the second time from the Persians” 
(Herodotus 1920, 104.1). 


114 
Similar themes appear in the stirring speech by the Athenian messengers to rouse the Spar- 
tans (8.144.2). 


9 Xerxes under Divine Rule 
297 


ers and of diviners’ help in general in the success of the Greeks. The entire logos 
is filled with oracles and prophecy; all serving to show how Euenius received the 
power of divination, and supposedly also his son Deiphonus (9.95). With these 
favourable auspices, the Greeks leave Delos for Samos and strategically prepare 
for battle, dropping anchor near another sacred landscape, Hera’s temple (9.96). 
Experience had shown that it was good for them to have a divine presence near- 
by. This point will be emphasised in the account of the battle. 


As soon as the Greeks decide to march against the Persian troops, the sol- 


diers perceive a confirmation of divine assistance. This is supported in various 
ways. Mysteriously a herald’s staff (e.g., like one of Hermes), is lying on the beach 
and at that time the report of the Greeks’ victory over Mardonius in Boeotia at 
Plataea was diffused through the troops in Mycale (9.100.1). Seeing these signs as 
more than coincidental, Herodotus adds his own perception to this: “It is indeed 
clear, from many proofs, that divine forces are at play in circumstances […]” 
(9.100.2).115 This metaleptic aside strengthens his present argument as well as his 
insistence throughout the nine volumes on divine involvement in the overall, 
grand victory over the massive Persian forces.116 In addition, Herodotus observes 
that the battles of Plataea and Mycale both occurred near the precincts of Deme- 
ter of Eleusis (9.101) and on the same day (verified by him not long after the bat- 
tles, 9.101.2). As in other battles, the perception of divine support emboldened the 
Greeks to fight with all their strength. The victory at Mycale receives little narra- 
tive time, but its significance must be understood in the light of Plataea and des- 
tiny concerning Ionia’s part in defying the giants, first the Lydians then the Per- 
sians. Herodotus concludes this section with reference to the Milesians: “[…] and, 
finally, they themselves became their worst enemies and killed them. In this way, 
for the second time, Ionia revolted from the Persians” (9.104). 


9.3.4 Coda: The Final Victory over the Persians (9.108–122) 


In Immerwahr’s influential work, Form and Thought in Herodotus, the events that 
follow the Battle of Mycale are proposed as the aftermath of this important Greek 
victory. While this is reasonable, the variety of material in this brief section – in 
narratological terms – is too great to be connected to the aforementioned bat- 
tle.117 Herodotus concludes his lengthy work (in its present form) with various 
anecdotes about Persian leaders and their intrigues. It appears that he is inviting 
his audience to shift their gaze from the global level of Persia’s troubles with 
Greece to the personal level of her rulers and their own failures. Herodotus and 


115 
Lachenaud (1978) 212–214. 


116 
Morgan (2022) 55–56. 


117 
Immerwahr (1966) 144–147.

298 


his audience know that Xerxes and Artaxerxes (whom he mentioned as some of 
the causes of the greatest evils for Greece) lived well beyond the narrative limits 
of Book 9. But like all narrators, Herodotus had to stop somewhere, hopefully of- 
fering some degree of closure to the narrative’s main questions for the audience’s 
satisfaction.118 So, what does Herodotus have in store for his audience here, and 
how does his prophetic voice help him to articulate his choices?119 I summarise 
this briefly below. 


First, our author chooses three main subjects to close his long work: Xerxes’ 


personal dilemmas (9.108–113), the siege of Sestos with the sacrilege and judge- 
ment of Artaÿctes (9.116–120), and Cyrus’ word of counsel to his people (9.122). 
Various points are connected in these three accounts to form a circle between the 
beginning and the end of the Histories: the struggle for Europe and Asia, divine 
vengeance against impious leaders, and, finally, Cyrus as the first Persian king to 
attempt conquering both Asia and Europe. Ironically, Cyrus has the final word in 
this history. Secondly, what brings all three of these points together, from the per- 
spective of Herodotus’ prophetic voice, is the sacrilegious acts committed by Ar- 
taÿctes. There can be no doubt that this scene caps off the theme of the futile at- 
tempt to usurp divine rule and appropriate their property. 


Closure to the story of Xerxes, which wraps up Books 7–9 as a unit, begins 


with the violent rivalry between two Persian leaders Artayntes and Masistes 
(9.107). At this point, Xerxes returns to the narrative, not through his folly as an 
oppressive king, but as a stalking paramour. While Xerxes was in Sardis, he sets 
his sights on Masistes’ wife, while Masistes was on the front (9.108).120 This opens 
a rather long logos that explores Persian impetuousness: since the imperial im- 
pulse was squelched militarily, it reaches down to an equally base level with lust 
for Masistes’ wife, then with Masistes’ daughter who was the wife of Xerxes’ son 
Darius. A string of reckless actions led to misinterpretations and heinous crimes 
(9.109–113). Herodotus signals to his audience that this narrative thread on hu- 
man perversion is concluded: “So that is the story of Xerxes’ passion and Ma- 
sistes’ death” (9.113.2). 


With Xerxes now offstage, narratively speaking, the audience encounters an- 


other Persian leader, Artaÿctes, who embodies the impious character exhibited 
by other actors. The stage is the siege on the Chersonese in the town of Sestus. 
Artaÿctes is Xerxes’ governor there. He receives the narrator’s evaluation as 
“both terrible and reckless” (δεινὸς δὲ καὶ ἀτάσθαλος, 9.116.1). The adjective 
ἀτάσθαλος links Artaÿctes with Xerxes, who is described in the same way by 
Themistocles for the latter’s great acts of sacrilege (8.109.3). Herodotus builds on 


118 
Herodotus’ line “nothing else of consequence happened in that year” seems to contribute to 
the winding down of the narrative.

Several studies show convincingly that this ending brings closure to various thematic threads

this description by revealing specific acts of impiety. By tricking Xerxes, Artaÿctes 
robbed the riches of the sanctuary of Protesilaus, the first Greek to fall in the Tro- 
jan War (Homer, Il. 2.701), who was honoured as divine in Elaeus. This is implicit 
plupast material loaded with implications, for the audience knows well what is 
awaiting this evil man Artaÿctes. Second, he had the habit of sleeping with wom- 
en in the inner part of the said sanctuary (9.116.3). Third, he caused great suffer- 
ing to the people of Sestus and abandoned them at their greatest point of misery. 
Fourth, after his capture by the Greeks, he interprets the portent of jumping fish 
in the fire as being a message of vengeance from Protesilaus (granted by the 
gods) for Artaÿctes’ irreverence (9.120.2). Although the interpretation of the por- 
tent may have been correct, Herodotus does not say so. However, he does de- 
scribe it as a ‘wonder’ with a message, and thus also a ‘portent’ (twice τέρας, 
9.120.1, 2). Artaÿctes uses this event to express his guilt and repentance by offer- 
ing a hundred talents to the god and two hundred to the Athenians. His cunning 
nature towards both the gods and humans results in him being nailed to a plank 
at the end of Xerxes’ Hellespont bridge (or on the hill overlooking Madytus, 9.11). 
This marks also the end of another impious man, executed as it were by both the 
gods and his rivals (9.120.4). This leads to the final anecdote about Cyrus. 


The connection between this Artaÿctes and Cyrus is that one of Artaÿctes’ 


ancestors was Artembares who came to Cyrus with a proposal, apparently ap- 
proved by other leading Persians (9.122.1). In a few words, it all concerns what to 
do with God-given power. He addresses this with the preamble: “Since Zeus has 
given sovereignty to the Persians and to you in particular, Cyrus, now that you 
have done away with Astyages [King of the Medes]” (9.122.2, trans. Waterfield). 
The logic that follows is why stop there? There are many other lands to be taken. 
He continues, “This is a perfectly reasonable thing for people with power to do. 
Will we ever have a better opportunity than now, when we rule over so many 
peoples and the whole of Asia?” (9.122.2, trans. Waterfield). This is, in essence, 
the heart of the imperial impulse, the fervent zeal for Eurasian conquest, which is 
both attempted and thwarted throughout the Histories. Cyrus warns them, offer- 
ing in narrative terms the punchline: if they choose to follow this course of action, 
they should prepare themselves for slavery, because it will come upon them hav- 
ing become soft men living in soft places. The links between the natural environ- 
ment, ethnic identity, and geopolitical intrigue are again underlined.121 The moral 
of the story from Herodotus’ prophetic perspective is that Persia’s attempts to 
dominate Asia and Europe, from Cyrus to Xerxes, were not worth it.122 Ironically, 
it is the Athenians who take the spoils and the cables of Xerxes’ bridge as votive 
offerings to their sanctuaries (9.120.4) 


121 
For a balanced discussion of the narrative and political value of this passage, see Xian (2020) 
16–26. 


122 
Taken from Holland’s subtitle, this is “Cyrus’s prognostication in retrospect.” Herodotus 
(2013) xvi–xvii.

9.4 Conclusion 


Books 7–9 describe the campaigns of Xerxes and Mardonius and the five battles, 
which highlight the folly of the imperial impulse as a sacrilegious act against both 
the divine and human spheres. Attempting to usurp the rule of the gods leads to 
divine retribution and disastrous social consequences. The sacred landscape is 
extremely rich, signifying the presence and action of the gods in relation to these 
five battles. Herodotus reports on the many oracles and sacrifices used by both 
sides, often augmenting them with his own authorial interpretations of the ora- 
cles and signs (as well as correcting poor interpretations). 


Our author invites his audience to evaluate acts of piety and impiety, some 


of which are more overt than others. The ethical force of this theological narra- 
tion shows that the Greco-Persian Wars were perceived by the author and the 
protagonists as being engaged on two levels: the divine and the human. Herodo- 
tus uses a variety of literary techniques via his prophetic voice to make this clear 
to his audience, who were witnessing similar acts of folly in their own times 
against the backdrop of the Peloponnesian War. 


The next two chapters move to the first century CE, a time when another 


great power, the Roman Empire, also sought dominion over distant lands. The 
Gospel of Luke and its sequel, the Acts of the Apostles, depict around sixty years of 
history, from Jerusalem to Rome in a similarly prophetic-like fashion. Which 
forces in the divine and human spheres are perceived to be at work in this differ- 
ent yet comparable agōn?

Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 


10 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts (Volume 1: Luke 1:1–24:53) 


10.1 Introduction 


Having ‘listened’ to Herodotus’ prophetic voice, we now turn to that of Luke as 
evidenced in his two-volume work, the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles. 
The justification for bringing these two volumes together under one title ‘Luke- 
Acts’ was provided in Chapter 4. This chapter focuses on the first volume, part of 
which – the ‘divine plupast’ of Luke-Acts – has been discussed in Chapter 5. 


Many differences have been noted between Herodotus’ Histories and Luke’s 


Luke-Acts. However, these authors and their works also have much in common, 
both historically and historiographically. First, spread out in between them is a 
succession of rulers, from the Persians to the Romans, who disputed territory for 
five hundred years, centred on Europe and Asia, and much of the Mediterranean 
Basin.1 Chapter 2 offered a survey of numerous historians who chronicled this 
lengthy period, either as members of the ruling powers or as their subjects. Sec- 
ond, these historians share many literary and methodological elements, one of 
which is the enduring perception that the divine realm – however it may have 
been perceived – was somehow involved in human history, even guiding it. In 
this respect, all the historians gathered around ‘Herodotus’ table’ express various 
theistic perspectives. 


Both Herodotus and Luke wrote with this basic belief underlying their di- 


verse theistic worldviews. Despite the different areas of focus, there is a unifying 
element: the Histories and Luke-Acts both display a geopolitical agōn in the 
Mediterranean Basin, which is not perceived as being limited to human agency.2 


Divine agency is presented as influencing these struggles for freedom against op- 
pression. In the Histories, the main rulers – Croesus, Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius, 
and Xerxes – form a unified yet varied expression of the imperial impulse: hu- 
man rule aimed at subjugating other peoples. Although Luke’s narrative does not 
include accounts of military conflict, it does feature military presence and politi- 
cal intrigue. These elements are presented through a religious lens within the 
flow of history, making them relevant to an audience living under the rule of five 


1 
The Persians (or Parthians), under the Arsacid Empire (247 BCE to 224 CE) were vying for 
political control of territories under Roman rule. They even occupied at one point all of the 
Levant with the exception of Tyre. 


2 
For the significance of agōn in the epic tradition, see Barker (2009). For conflict in narratolo- 
gy, see Abbott (2008) 55–56 and Herman (2008) 83. For a broader view of conflict in the 
Mediterranean, see Horden and Purcell (2000). 


emperors, from Octavian to Nero. Thus, both imperial and regional rule are pre- 
sented in Luke-Acts as encounters with divine rule. 


Rather than viewing these two histories either as political or religious narra- 


tives, they are actually both, with one or the other being more prominent. It is 
precisely here that their prophetic voices exert their influence, as they depict 
agōnes within their own global contexts of conflict and struggle. These narratives 
are real political discourses – as systems of civic influence – expressed through 
the rhetoric of historiography.3 Rather than a desacralisation or depoliticisation 
of ancient narratives, both the sacred and the political should receive attention.4 


Given that several chapters have addressed various issues about Herodotus’ 


work, it is beneficial to resume the discussion of Luke-Acts with a sharper focus 
on the geopolitical conflict that is being constructed in light of the previous dis- 
cussions on Luke’s project (Chapter 4) and the divine plupast in Luke 1:5–4:13 
(Chapter 5). After this introduction, the discussion focuses on how Luke and his 
characters perceive divine rule and agency in Jesus’ movement from Galilee to 
Judea, culminating in Jerusalem. 


10.2 Synopsis of the Periods of Narrated Time and Redaction 


with regard to the Roman Empire 


The events recounted in Luke-Acts and the period during which they were writ- 
ten invite a geopolitical reading.5 The question is therefore not whether Luke’s 
work employs a geopolitical lens, but what kind it is and what apologetic purpose 
it serves. As Eric Barreto acutely observes, “But Luke’s critique of the empire is 
only evident if one knows how to read between the lines. Shrouded in a text 
seemingly accommodating Rome’s claims are the seeds of its downfall, theologi- 
cally speaking.”6 The characters in the narrative lived under Roman rule and ex- 
perienced it first-hand, as did Luke and his audience. This common experience 
binds them together narratively. Just as Luke offers scenes of apologetic signifi-

cance relating to his characters, especially Peter, Stephen, and Paul, he also pro- 
vides his readers with responses to their own social challenges. 


The events described in Luke’s Gospel span a period of about thirty-five 


years (ca. 5 or 4 BCE–30 CE), namely, from the announcements of the birth of 
John the Baptist and the birth of Jesus up until the latter’s death, resurrection, 
and ascension.7 Despite analepses and prolepses, the story follows the chronologi- 
cal stages of Jesus’ life in the land of Israel, concentrating on the three years of his 
public life in Galilee and Judea. The last episode of Luke’s Gospel, traditionally 
called the ascension, closes the first volume (Luke 24:50–53) and it opens the sec- 
ond, since it is repeated in different form at the beginning of Acts (Acts 1:9–11). 
Thus, the episodes narrated in the two volumes are literarily linked and chrono- 
logically sequenced, reinforcing the idea that the two volumes were written by 
the same author and meant to be read together. For ancient historiography, con- 
tinued histories in multiple volumes by the same authors are well attested.8 


Crucial for understanding Luke-Acts is the political backdrop of the Roman 


Empire, which claimed divine sanction for its existence and expansion.9 It is one 
of the key elements that affected the social situation of the narrative’s protagon- 
ists as well as that of the author and his audience.10 Jesus was born during the 
reign of Augustus Caesar (27 BCE–14 CE; Luke 2:1) and died under the rule of 
Tiberius (14–37 CE; Luke 3:1; 20:22, 24; 23:2) by crucifixion under the adminis- 
tration of Pontius Pilate, Prefect of Judea (26–36 CE). Luke follows the practice of 
using the calendars of the ruling powers, mentioning the names of the emperors 
and the events and years associated with them. The narrative leaves no doubt as 
to who is in control during this period. The remainder of Luke-Acts assumes this, 
proceeding from the events in Jerusalem and ending with the apostle Paul’s so- 
journ in Rome in 60–62 CE. In all, the macronarrative covers approximately the 
period from 5 BCE to 62 CE. 


Concerning Luke and his audience (ca. the final quarter of the first century 


CE), some may have lived as early as Tiberius’ reign, but presumably mostly from 
Caligula (37–41 CE) to Trajan (98–117 CE). As recognised in Chapter 4, the dating 
of the redaction of Luke and Acts is approximate. No consensus exists on this 
question. However, most scholars do place the final redaction of both volumes 
after the destruction of Jerusalem and her temple in 70 CE (cf. Ch. 4.1.2). This 
tragic moment in Jewish history was preceded by years of Jewish strife against 
Roman rule in the provinces of Judea and Egypt. Consequently, Luke-Acts was 
written during a time when communities of Christ-followers lived under political 
and military tension, and they gradually became understood as distinct from Jew-

is generally understood that Luke wrote to people somewhere in the Mediter-

lowers were also a part of his readership. In the two volumes, Luke demonstrates 
his dual interest in divine salvation reaching the Jews and other ‘peoples’ (cf. 
Luke 2:31–32; 24:47), which illustrates his aim to reach a global audience through 
the medium of Greek.13 The geographical scope of the narrative, spanning from 
Jerusalem to Rome, also encapsulates the multicultural nature of the movement 
portrayed by Luke, as evidenced especially by Paul’s character. Paul was a Jew 
from Greek-speaking Tarsus, a Roman citizen from birth, and a religious teacher 
trained among the Pharisees.14 As observed in Chapter 2, Luke can be compared 
to other ‘crossover historians’ (e.g., Berossus, Manetho, Josephus) who lived un- 
der foreign rule and imparted to their contemporaries lesser known (and per- 
haps marginalised) narratives about their own peoples. 


As Luke’s narrative progresses from its Jewish cultural and cultic centre to 


the Empire’s capital, several encounters are highlighted with personages of the 
Roman administration, insiders and outsiders, who react in various ways to Jesus’ 
life, teaching, and movement. Luke’s perception of the meaning of Jesus’ life is 
shaped by his understanding that Jesus was not only heir to the Jewish royal 
throne but also saviour of all peoples. The dilemma is clear: this message clashes 
with Roman imperial ideology, which itself had a strong, communicated, religious 
component throughout the Empire.15 Luke-Acts can thus be viewed as a type of 
subversive literature vis-à-vis Rome, because its ideology does not submit to hu- 
man rule as ultimate rule.16 Rather than projecting a posture of outright accom- 
modation or resistance, Luke consistently illustrates a hybrid approach, which

Key differences in the theistic representations of the divine in the works of 


Herodotus and Luke were noted in Chapter 6. Another key distinction, which will 
be discussed in the review of the divine plupast section below, concerns how 
Luke’s narrative framework is shaped by the revelation of a divinely planned te- 
los, events moving towards a goal.20 This contrasts with Herodotus’ exposition of 
a chain of divine reactions to (usually wrong) human decisions and actions (e.g., 
via Candaules, Gyges, Croesus, and the Persian kings). This, in turn, is a key differ- 
ence between Herodotus’ representation of the divine and that of Homer. 
Herodotus does not present the thoughts of the gods or scenes of divine dialogue. 
Instead, we read about interpretations of divine activity after the events have oc- 
curred.21 The review below will clarify this distinction of theistic representation 
within a geopolitical framework.

Empire, mainly through the early narrative construction of various aspects of Je- 
sus’ perceived identity: υἱὸς ὑψίστου (θεοῦ), κύριος, σωτήρ, and χριστός. But is 
this construction meant to introduce a specific narrative agōn between Jesus and

Augustus Caesar, his successors, and other representatives of the Empire? It is
