gest form of human rule against which the story of ‘the kingdom of God’ moves 
from Jerusalem to Rome. In this first section, Luke demonstrates theological and 
political legitimacy of the divine rule of Israel’s God in various ways. 


To sum up the discussion on the geopolitical and religious elements converg- 


ing in the plupast section, Luke portrays Jesus’ identity and mandate as a key part 
in the rule of God in competition with other forms of rule, human and spiritual. 
Three competing rules are thus evoked: Roman rule, Jewish rule, and the usurp- 
ing rule of the devil. The rest of the story will unfold with examples of conflict 
with each of them. With this theological backdrop, Luke’s audience understands 
that Jesus is going to face challenges concerning his identity as Jewish heir of the 
throne and as saviour of all peoples. The agōn, as in the Histories, will be dis- 
played involving human and divine characters. The promises about Jesus’ man- 
date counter the claims of contemporary rulers’ divine nature or mandate.22 This 
is underlined by the reactions of Jewish and non-Jewish groups who view Jesus as 
a provincial agitator competing with their authority (Luke 19:37–40; 22:66–71; 
23:5; Acts 4:7) or with the emperor’s rule (Luke 23:2; Acts 17:7). 


Two competing understandings of Jesus’ identity are expressed through pos- 


itive and negative labels, either as a legitimate ruler or as a deviant usurper.23 


Luke seeks to persuade his audience to opt for the first by supporting the human/ 
divine claims of Jesus. This differs from Herodotus’ depiction of the human/di- 
vine claims of the Persian kings, who, ironically, commit sacrilege. By not sup- 
porting the Persian kings in this way, the portrayal of the agōn between human 
and divine characters in Herodotus morally sides with those humans who do not 
claim divine descent. 


Finally, the preferred expression in Jesus’ teaching, ἡ βασιλεία (τοῦ θεοῦ), is 


viewed with suspicion by Jews and non-Jews.24 Was this rule of God synonymous 
with Luke’s description of Jesus as announced heir of David’s throne and Son of 
God? If so, how could that function in the Roman imperial setting? How is ἡ βασι- 
λεία to be understood? As a physical kingdom or realm? Or a general rule in 
which God’s will is accomplished? Is it in competition with spiritual powers and 
with human rulers? Luke explores these nuances, especially because Israel had 
already had a physical kingdom and hoped for restoration through God’s faithful- 
ness, but not like the Babylonians who had never recovered their kingdom.

Hence, it is through this interpretative lens that Luke’s readers could fathom the

For the treatment of the sections that follow, it is helpful to have an idea of 


Luke’s ulterior construction of divine rule as outlined below (all references are to 
Luke’s Gospel): 


– Divine rule is most often expressed through various expressions involving βασι- 


λεία, especially the idiom ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ, which can be interpreted as the 
kingdom/reign/rule of God (e.g., 4:43; 6:20), that is, the rule of the God of Israel 
and of Jesus’ ‘father’ (1:31, 35; 3:22; 11:2; 22:29). 


– This βασιλεία also belongs to Jesus, as it is expressed through possessive pro- 


nouns: ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ μου (22:30); εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν σου (23:42); and ἐν τῇ 
βασιλείᾳ αὐτοῦ (1:33).25 


– Jesus shares this rule with others (e.g., “the poor,” 6:20) and his disciples: “and 


I bequeath to you, just as my Father has bequeathed to me, a kingdom” (12:32; 
22:29). 


– This rule is depicted as already being manifest, e.g., through healings (10:9), 


exorcisms (11:20), and divine presence among Jesus’ disciples (17:20–21). 


– But it is not completely accomplished on earth, e.g., (disciples’ future participa- 


tion in feast and judgement in 22:30; hence the prayer: ἐλθέτω ἡ βασιλεία σου 
(11:2; and, implicitly, not yet for “the poor” in 6:20). 


– Divine rule is depicted as being accomplished through various agents, both di- 


vine and human, but also opposed by divine and human antagonists (see sec- 
tion 6.2.2 on Luke’s divine constellation). 


Here the prophetic voice of Luke is clearly at work on two levels: narratively and 
existentially in relation to his audience. Using plupast material (Luke 1:5–4:13), 
he prepares his readers for the rest of the narrative by exploring events leading 
to Jesus’ initial public activities beginning in Galilee. Luke connects the story of 
Jesus to the broader metanarrative of Israel’s history, and he anchors it in world 
history. Judea was a part of Roman history, whether people liked it or not. Sec- 
ond, Luke’s audience, who are also living under Roman rule, are invited to ex- 
plore their own existence in light of this broader narrative. They are encouraged 
to see themselves as a part of it, since the divine βασιλεία and σωτήριον are pre- 
sented as continuing up to and beyond Paul’s imprisonment in Rome, the final 
scene of Luke-Acts (Acts 28:28–31). This, then, is one of the primary distinctions 
from Herodotus’ description of divine rule: Luke displays the God of Israel as tak- 
ing the initiative to shape local and world history. We will now turn to the next

10.4 The Development of the Agōn between Divine and Human Rule 


in Galilee (Luke 4:14–9:50) 


Narrative significance of the Galilee section. Commentators represent the plan of 
Luke’s Gospel in various manners based on the content and their analytical meth- 
ods. Most commentaries, however, view Jesus’ activity in Galilee as a distinct sec- 
tion in Luke’s narrative framework.26 Its contribution, especially on the level of 
action, is crucial, and it will receive more attention than the subsequent sections. 


Luke provides several cues that facilitate this summative analysis, based on 


narrative shifts in location. For example, there is a shift from Jesus’ return to Gal- 
ilee in 4:14 to his arrival at the border of Samaria in 9:51. This latter location con- 
tains an explicit statement of Jesus’ intention to travel south to Jerusalem. The 
discussion below, as well as those on subsequent sections, will not offer passage 
by passage commentary. Instead, it continues to explore the author’s and actors’ 
perceptions of human and divine rule in the second major section of the Gospel of 
Luke, which is set in Galilee, the northern part of Palestine, east of the River Jor- 
dan.27 


As narrator, Luke follows his sources by representing Galilee as the initial 


theatre of reception and rejection of Jesus as the divinely mandated υἱός, χρίστος, 
σωτήρ, as well as κύριος. Luke’s narrative advances towards this end.28 The guid- 
ing question here concerns how Luke leads his audience to explore the geopoliti- 
cal and religious agōn based on various perceptions of Jesus’ mandate in support 
of or opposition to other forms of rule. Luke informs his audience about the con- 
flict surrounding Jesus that was announced to Mary by Simeon: “This child is 
established for the falling and the rising of many in Israel and an opposed sign, so 
that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed – and a sword will pierce your

Similar to the method used in the commentary on Herodotus’ perception of 


divine action and speech, various texts will be highlighted here to demonstrate 
how Jesus and his disciples are understood to be assisted by divine action or 
speech towards the said objectives in the divine plupast section. One important 
difference in approach reflects the nature of Luke’s work, namely, because Jesus 
is represented by Luke as a divine agent, my task here will not be to comment on 
every action or speech event by Jesus. Rather, thanks to the plupast section, much 
of the intrigue is constructed upon the actorial awareness (or lack of awareness) 
of Jesus’ identity and the divine realm working through him. Luke’s audience, 
however, has a privileged position concerning this question because they have 
received a proleptic portrait of Jesus (i.e., his identity and mandate).30 For this 
reason, it will be noted how these perceptions are represented among various 
groups: the population in Galilee, the religious and political authorities, and spiri- 
tual beings. Before considering these elements, it is helpful from the outset to con- 
sider some historical background to Galilee in relation to the Roman Empire and 
Jewish political authorities. 


Historical background to Galilee. Galilee, though mountainous, was not isolated, 
given that major thoroughfares between Egypt and Syria-Mesopotamia passed 
through her valleys.31 Flavius Josephus is the main historiographical source for 
the Early Roman Period (63 BCE–125 CE). He describes – in much greater detail 
than Luke – the geographical, political, and cultural makeup of Upper and Lower 
Galilee (see e.g., B.J. 3.35–43). Jewish hostility towards Roman (and Herodian) 
domination flared up in 39–38 BCE at Sepphoris and again there at Herod the 
Great’s death in 4 BCE. Subsequently, Josephus himself was a general in the First 
Jewish Revolt in Galilee against Rome in 66 CE.32 As was true for other parts of the 
traditionally inhabited Jewish regions, Galilee was far from being an idyllic, ho- 
mogenous haven of Jewish cohabitation with Roman constituents. 


After Herod’s death, Caesar Augustus gave Galilee and Perea to Herod’s son, 


Herod Antipas. Jesus’ hometown, Nazareth, was located close to Sepphoris, a 
main political and commercial centre of Galilee (but not mentioned in the NT).

Josephus describes Sepphoris as “the ornament of all Galilee” (Ant. 18.27). Herod 
Antipas used Sepphoris as his capital until he transferred it to Tiberias33 (named 
in honour of Emperor Tiberius) on the Sea of Galilee, between 18 and 20 CE. Her- 
od Antipas ruled this region 4 BCE–39 CE as tetrarch (τετραάρχης, Luke 3:19; 9:7; 
Acts 13:1). During this same period, as Luke reports, Jesus matured and began to 
fulfil his God-given mandate.34 


In the Galilee section, Luke provides only a few hints at Roman presence. 


Herod Antipas is, of course, one of them, due to his family’s ties with the Empire. 
Luke’s treatment of Herod Antipas is consistently portrayed negatively, due to the 
latter’s culpability for the murder of John the Baptist, his immoral acts (3:19), and 
his superficial treatment of Jesus, which ultimately led to his execution (9:7–9; 
13:31; 23:7–15). Interestingly, Luke points out that Joanna, one of Jesus’ female 
disciples, was “the wife of Herod’s steward (ἐπίτροπος) Chuza” (8:3). She and oth- 
er women contributed to the financial support of Jesus and his disciples.35 This 
implies a close, though not direct, link between imperial regional governance and 
Jesus’ movement.36 


Another specific mention of Roman presence comes through an unnamed 


centurion (ἑκατοντάρχης) in Capernaum. He is described as benevolent to the 
Jewish people and whose faith – for the healing of his beloved slave – is praised 
by Jesus himself (7:1–10). No tension is perceived here in Luke’s text, which cor- 
responds, generally, to his positive caricature of centurions. Luke shows that Ro- 
man domination is a simple fact and occasionally illustrates how Rome exercises 
its authority locally (7:8). Next, Luke highlights Jewish collaboration with the Em- 
pire through tax collectors (τελῶναι) through Levi and later with Zacchaeus (Luke 
19:1–10). Since this activity was despised by the Jewish people, Jesus is reportedly 
criticised for having contact with such people of low moral standing (e.g., 5:30; 
7:34). 


Regarding Jewish religious authorities, it is helpful to remember that neither 


Judea nor Galilee were homogenous. Josephus writes of four ‘philosophies’ 
among the Jews that wrestled for power and, at times, collaborated with one an- 
other. These are the Sadducees, the Pharisees, the Essenes, and the Zealots 
(Ant. 18.11–24). Josephus does speak of Jesus and his followers but not as a sep-

another philosophy. This group plays an important part in the Gospel narratives 
because they were the authorities overseeing the transmission of scripture and its 
teaching. Thus, they were ‘teachers of the law’ (νομοδιδάσκαλοι, Luke 5:17; Acts 
5:34) and considered specialists of the interpretation of sacred texts. This func-

that the Pharisees are portrayed as the chief antagonists of Jesus’ mandate. In this 
regard, it is interesting to note that Luke-Acts portrays Jesus, in comparison to the 
other Gospels, as a legitimate competitor among the scribal-literate class. Jesus’ 
training in the temple among the teachers (Luke 2:41–51) is further illustrated by 
the scene in the Nazareth synagogue, which is the only place in the NT where 
Jesus is shown to be reading.38 It also highlights Luke’s portrayal of Jesus as a syn- 
agogue teacher, by omitting certain details, here and elsewhere, that would con- 
nect him to the manual-labour class.39 Also, as a part of the development of the 
agōn with human powers, Jesus is depicted as victorious in all his debates with 
the religious and civil authorities (e.g., Luke 5:17–26; 20:1–8; 20:34–40). 


In his first volume, Luke offers little in the way of temporal and geographi- 


cal description. Temporally, we have an approximate idea of the period when 
events happen, but, generally, Luke often uses descriptions such as “on one sab- 
bath,” “during those days,” “one day,” and “soon afterwards.”40 And, what is gen- 
erally true for his first volume, but much less so for the second in which he shows 
greater interest in geography, Luke appears to take little interest in Galilee’s to- 
pography and demography. Narratively, he is concerned with staying with the 
construction of the agōn, mentioning, as necessary, only a few specific regions, 
cities, or villages, and their various cultural compositions.41 Sepphoris and Tibe- 
rias are not even mentioned. But this may reflect Jesus’ avoidance of these politi- 
cally charged centres, or they may simply have no relevance to Luke’s account. 


In their place, Capernaum is presented as Jesus’ main sphere of action, most 


likely because of its importance to the Jewish population, its security (distance 
from the aforementioned cities), the initial positive reception of his activity (4:23,

This raises the question whether Luke provides any clues as to why Jesus 


chose to leave Galilee. Two intertwining answers can be suggested: sociological 
and theological, which will be further developed below. Narratively, there is a 
growing awareness that local authorities were planning to deal with his presence 
and movement (6:11). A later passage echoes these sentiments by Jesus’ accusers 
in Jerusalem: “But they were insistent, saying, ‘He incites the people, teaching 
throughout all Judea, from Galilee until here’” (23:5). 


Parallel to this growing conflict, several references point to Jesus’ self- 


awareness that it was time to move southward to the final destination, Jerusalem. 
Rejection at the hands of the authorities is explicitly mentioned (5:34–35; 9:22, 
31, 44, 51). This is the teleological drive in the first volume, similar to Rome for 
Paul’s final journey in the second volume. It is pertinent too that this aspect is 
bolstered by Jesus’ own voice and by the narrator’s voice. As for the narrative 
agōn, the section in Galilee may be understood as presenting the point of no re- 
turn for Jesus’ movement.42 This is clearly highlighted in Nazareth, the first focus 
passage, upon which the entire section develops and shapes the rest of Luke-Acts. 


Jesus’ mandate announced and rejected in Nazareth (Luke 4:14–30). The Galilean 
section begins with an ironic twist because, while the first few lines act as a 
bridge between the temptation narrative and the events in Nazareth – readers 
know who Jesus is. These lines show that he was received with enthusiasm in Gal- 
ilee to some degree (4:14–15). It is a way of signalling to readers that something 
had already happened, generally positive (cf. 4:23), before coming to Nazareth. 
This is perhaps Luke’s most important adjustment to the order of the Gospel of 
Mark (Luke’s main source), because the rejection in Nazareth is presented later 
in Mark’s account (Mark 6:1–6a), when Jesus was further along in his mandate. 
By doing this, Luke highlights the episode of Nazareth and sets up the immanent

This very first episode highlights a dramatic part of the macronarrative, 


which is the rejection of Jesus by his own people. It is programmatic for the rest 
of Luke’s narrative because of the discrepancy between Jesus’ identity and how 
he is received or rejected. In the synagogue of Nazareth, the place of local reli- 
gious authority, Jesus is described as claiming divine support for his mission by 
reading an ancient oracle of the prophet Isaiah (61:1–2): “The Spirit of the Lord is 
upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent 
me to proclaim liberation to the captives and regaining of sight to the blind, to let 
the shattered go in liberty, to proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord” (4:18– 
19).43 


He closes the scroll then announces: “Today this scripture has been fulfilled 


in your hearing” (4:21). Jesus claims two things: a divine mandate and God’s pres- 
ence upon him. The mandate, alluded to in the plupast section, is now publicly 
announced by Jesus himself. Initially, this part does not seem to bother the audi- 
ence in the synagogue (4:22), which may have corresponded in part to their ex- 
pectations of their Messiah in light of Roman occupation. The passage echoes 
God’s covenant faithfulness to his people (cf. Zechariah’s prayer, 1:68–75). 


But the initial harmony between Jesus and the internal audience changes 


quickly. Jesus challenges their understanding and perhaps that of Luke’s audi- 
ence. Jesus emphasises his mandate’s focus on the physical and spiritual needs of 
the people rather than on Jewish aspirations for a military insurrection.44 Luke 
reports that Jesus does this – in addition to prophetic support from Isaiah – by 
comparing his mandate to the acts of two prophets of the past, Elijah and Elisha. 
They had performed miracles of compassion on behalf of non-Jewish individuals. 
Here, the direction of events changes dramatically when Jesus quotes the saying, 
“No prophet is accepted in the prophet’s homeland” (4:24). The scene does not 
end the way one would have expected: the people are “all filled with rage” 
(ἐπλήσθησαν πάντες θυμοῦ) and they proceed to expel him from town and at- 
tempt to throw him off the cliff (4:28–30). Narratologically, this episode repre- 
sents another potential end to the story as we know it, similar to the devil’s coun- 
terplot for Jesus to share in the glory and rule of the kingdoms.

In this focus-narrative in the section on Galilee, some clues guide the inter- 


pretation of the rest of the Gospel and Acts. Jesus identifies himself with the 
prophetic tradition of Israel without hesitation, and he shows an openness to 
non-Jewish peoples through the illustrations from the prophetic plupast. Luke 
portrays Jesus as both a faithful son of Israel and a faithful son of God, who en- 
trusted him with a mandate.45 This dual loyalty brought him into conflict with the 
Jewish religious and political authorities. The logic of the story and the narrative 
clues, here and there, show that, if Jesus had been partially rejected in Galilee, 
hopes of a cordial welcome in the south were slim. Luke describes Jesus as being 
aware of this risk. 


We turn briefly to the question of how the God of Israel is depicted as inter- 


vening in the rest of the Galilee section. This can be answered by considering the 
hints that Luke offers about perceptions of activity attributed to God, such as 
works of power (i.e., ‘miracles’), the granting of forgiveness of sins, and theopha- 
nies. We will examine these briefly below. 


Works of power (αἱ δυνάμεις). Generally, the word ‘miracle’ is used to speak of 
divine interventions that go beyond human capabilities.46 I refer here to Luke’s 
own use of δύναμις to designate deeds of divine power (αἱ δυνάμεις, Luke 
10:13).47 This expression covers a broad range of actions that Jesus is shown to 
accomplish for diverse situations and beneficiaries: 


– exorcisms: a man with an ‘unclean spirit’ (4:31–37); demons cast out (4:41); 


people troubled with unclean spirits (6:18–19); people with evil spirits (7:21); 
women who had been healed of evil spirits (8:2); a man of the Gerasenes 
healed of a ‘legion’ of demons (8:26–39); and a boy with an unclean spirit 
(9:37–43). 


– physical healings: fever and unnamed diseases (4:38–41); leprosy (5:12–16); 


paralysis (5:17–26); a withered hand (6:6–11); unspecified illness of a centuri- 
on’s slave (7:1–10); restoration to life of a widow’s son (7:11–17); various 
diseases and blindness (7:21); infirmities of various women (8:2); haemor- 
rhage (8:43–48); restoration to life of Jairus’ daughter (8:49–56); unnamed 
diseases (via Jesus’ disciples, 9:6); and other various healings (9:11). 


– works of power in nature: an abundant catch of fish (5:4–7); the calming of a 


storm (8:22–25); and the multiplication of loaves and fish (9:12–17). 


45

news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also; for I was sent for this purpose” (4:43).

See the interdisciplinary book on miracles and a brief discussion of the vocabulary of miracle

318 


For the macronarrative of Luke-Acts, the significance of these three groups of 
works of power is best understood in the light of the proleptic portrait of Jesus, 
his proclaimed mandate in the synagogue of Nazareth, and his response to John 
the Baptist’s question, “Are you the one who is coming, or should we wait for an- 
other?” (7:19). Luke points to these divinely-operated acts to illustrate for John’s 
disciples that God’s presence (“the Spirit of the Lord is upon me”) was assisting 
Jesus to fulfil his mandate (4:18–19). Luke reports that Jesus had been given au- 
thority (ἐξουσία) over the spiritual realm, the natural realm, and the human 
realm (4:36; 5:24; 9:1). Thus, God is perceived to be operating through Jesus in 
these three areas, which prepares the audience to follow the unfolding story from 
Galilee to Judea and beyond. 


The forgiveness of sins. We have already considered the centrality of the theme of 
forgiveness of sins in Luke-Acts. It was announced in the divine plupast section 
(1.77; 3:3), and it is emphasised several times to show the results of Jesus’ man- 
date (Luke 24:47; Acts 5:31; 10:43; 13:38; 26:18). The various scenes noted above 
illustrate Luke’s emphasis that Jesus also had the authority to declare forgiveness 
of sin. This is perceived as being only God’s work as the scribes and Pharisees 
exclaim, “Who is this one who is speaking blasphemies? Who can forgive sins if 
not God alone?” (5:21). Jesus follows this with a rhetorical question: “Which is 
easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’?” (5:23). In 
response, Jesus heals the paralytic and sends him home. But Luke also highlights 
this authority to forgive sins in the passage in which a sinful woman comes to 
anoint him with alabaster and her tears. Shocked, the Pharisees see Jesus declare 
the woman’s sins to be forgiven (7:36–50). 


Theophanies. The various healings and the authority to forgive people’s sins 
evoke a sense of wonder in the internal audience. God is perceived as accomplish- 
ing works of power in their midst (5:26; 7:16; 9:43). Furthermore, as the devil 
had tested Jesus concerning his identity as Son of God, so the demons are report- 
ed to recognise the divine presence in Jesus, specifically calling him “the son of 
God” (σὺ εἶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, 4:41; cf. 8:28). 


After the resurrection of the widow’s son at Nain, Luke reports: “Fear seized 


them all; and they were glorifying God, saying, ‘A great prophet has risen among 
us!’ and ‘God has visited his people!’” (ἐπεσκέψατο ὁ θεὸς τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ, 7:16, 
cf. 1:68). Even Herod Antipas is intrigued and wonders how these things that he is 
hearing could be done if it were not for some divine manifestation, perhaps 
through a prophet returning to life (9:7–9). The presence of God in Jesus is high- 
lighted in the passage, traditionally called, ‘the Transfiguration’ (9:28–36). There 
Jesus appears enveloped in a cloud and surrounded by Moses and Elijah, two an- 
cient prophets, who prepare Jesus for “his departure, which he was going to ac- 
complish in Jerusalem” (9:31). Jesus’ nature is distinguished from the two proph- 


10 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts I 
319 


ets in that his countenance changed and “his clothes became blazing white” 
(9:29). Also, a voice from the cloud announces, “This is my chosen son; listen to 
him!” (9:35). This echoes the divine utterance at Jesus’ baptism (3:22), as well as 
the point of attack in the devil’s testing of Jesus as son of God (4:3, 9). 


Summary of Galilee section. Despite some success, even reaching a crowd of 5 000 
men in one place, Luke gives no indication of a military uprising in response to 
Jewish aspirations for liberation. Luke counts on his audience’s knowledge and 
expectations with respect to the dissonance emerging from hints of hopes of polit- 
ical deliverance resounding in the early chapters, for example, in the words of 
Mary (toppling of sovereigns from their thrones, 1:52), Zechariah (deliverance 
from enemies, 1:71, 74), Simeon (the consolation of Israel, 2:25), and Anna (the 
redemption of Jerusalem, 2:38). Beginning with Jesus’ public proclamation of his 
divine mandate at Nazareth, Luke underlines Jesus’ focus on the spiritual level, 
that is, reconciliation between God and humanity as well as deliverance from de- 
monic oppression in soul and body. Rather than focusing on a Galilean insurrec- 
tion of Jewish freedom fighters, as had occurred at various points in Israel’s histo- 
ry prior to the redaction of Luke-Acts, Luke presents a harmless movement.48 


Jesus leaves Galilee without any hint of military success or intentions of it. There 
is no fight for Sepphoris or Tiberias, nor instructions about how to overthrow the 
Romans, ambush cargo, or assassinate infidels (as the Sicarii were known to do; 
Jos. A.J. 20.8.10; B.J. 2.13.3). Politically, however, Luke shows that God is making 
his presence felt, challenging the authorities and thus shaping the political lands- 
cape through Jesus’ growing movement headed for Jerusalem. Multiple dimen- 
sions of opposition are depicted in this agōn as a variety of antagonists increas- 
ingly join together to thwart Jesus’ mandate. 


10.5 The Development of the Agōn on the Way to Jerusalem 


(Luke 9:51–19:44) 


Narrative limits and significance. The narrative frame of the longest section in 
Luke’s Gospel is carefully structured. Luke is preparing his audience for a theo- 
logical and geopolitical paradox: while Jesus is recognised as king – at the end of 
the section – by a large crowd at his arrival in Jerusalem, his ‘departure’ and his 
‘being taken up’ are also understood as immanent. If Jesus is heir to the throne of 
David, what does this mean for Israel and the Roman Empire? Luke explores this 
with his audience through his unique prophetic voice, an intertwined theological 
and political narrative. 


48 
Weapons among Jesus’ disciples only appear later in the narrative (22:35–38, 49). 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
320 


At the beginning of the section, Jesus and his disciples leave Galilee, passing 


through the region of Samaria, on his way to Jerusalem in Judea.49 As noted 
above, the turning point between Galilee and movement towards Judea is found 
at 9:51, where Luke reports, “When the days were completed regarding his being 
taken up, he fixed his regard to go to Jerusalem.” The final destination is sig- 
nalled, and the temporal expression alludes to the already mentioned ‘departure’ 
(9:31): Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν τῷ συμπληροῦσθαι τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ἀναλήμψεως αὐτοῦ. His 
‘being taken up’ (ἀναλήμψεως) recalls Jesus’ forewarnings to his disciples that he 
would be handed over to the authorities (9:21, 44) and then be taken up by God 
(cf. Acts 1:11, 22). Luke portrays Jesus’ intention to face this fateful outcome in 
Jerusalem by using the dramatic expression: καὶ αὐτὸς τὸ πρόσωπον ἐστήρισεν 
τοῦ πορεύεσθαι εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ.50 This literally means, Jesus “strengthened his 
face to go to Jerusalem,” denoting his firm resolve.51 


The final limit of the narrative frame is indicated by Jesus’ arrival just out- 


side of Jerusalem at the Mount of Olives with a dramatic approach to the city 
(19:37). While the crowd welcomes Jesus as a king, “Blessed be the one who 
comes, the king, in the name of the Lord,” some Pharisees ask Jesus to silence 
them. But he refuses to do so. This emotional scene culminates in Jesus’ lament 
for Jerusalem (19:41–44), announcing times of destruction and tribulation for its 
inhabitants.52 The final words of this long section are noteworthy: “[…] because 
you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God” (19:44). This under- 
lines the perception that Jesus’ presence was in effect a part of a divine theo- 
phany. Thus, these two outer parts of the section dramatically heighten the devel- 
oping intrigue. Although most of Luke’s readers would have known the outcome 
in Jerusalem, they arguably would have been struck by the tragedy and irony of 
Jesus’ mandate to the Jews and the non-Jews.53 


But unlike the section on Galilee, which includes many works of power and 


less teaching, the long travel section to Jerusalem reverses this by placing greater 
emphasis on Jesus’ teaching and the agōn with the Jewish authorities. For this 
reason, the following discussion on acts of divine rule will be comparatively 
shorter than the previous section, despite the length of ten chapters. It is worth

noting briefly how various literary devices are used in this section at the service 
of Luke’s theology. One of the most distinctive aspects of this section is the use of 
numerous parables, many of which are unique to Luke.54 Moreover, these para- 
bles are often programmatic for Luke’s work, as they deal with themes such as 
discipleship, divine compassion and grace, the hypocrisy of the authorities, as 
well as justice and injustice.55 In this way, the parables sustain the episodes of ac- 
tion and debate to substantiate Luke’s elaboration of the fulfilment of Jesus’ man- 
date within the agōn. In addition, Luke’s parenthetical remarks continue to orient 
his audience in their evaluation of the characters: those who recognise Jesus and 
the coming of God’s reign (even the marginalised, e.g., lepers and Samaritans, 
cf. 17:11–19) and those who, often ironically, such as religious leaders, do not 
recognise it and oppose it (e.g., 15:2; 16:14; 18:9; 19:11; cf. 7:29–30; 9:45).56 


Finally, the manifestation of an alternative kingdom to the Empire, raised 


early in the narrative, is consistently highlighted throughout this long section. 
The number of occurrences of βασιλεία in this section attests to this emphasis.57 


Thus, the journey narrative provides a framework in which Jesus is portrayed as 
the teacher and agent of the kingdom of God, then and in the future.58 More will 
be said about ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ below. In sum, Luke conveys an ethics and the- 
ology on the road, by highlighting various reception and rejection encounters of 
Jesus and his disciples in thoroughfare contexts.59 


Geopolitical introduction to the travel narrative to Jerusalem. As Jesus’ disciples’ 
involvement in his movement grows, so does religious and political opposition to 
him increase. The depiction of the political nature of Jesus’ movement is unmis- 
takable. Regional tension appears immediately when a Samaritan village refuses 
Jesus’ passage because he was headed to the Judean capital (9:51–55).60 Jesus re- 
bukes the violent disposition of his disciples, who inquire whether they should 
pray for divine retribution on this uncooperative village. Also, it is reported for

the third time that Jesus announces his imminent death at the hands of the peo-

pectation of a divine intervention is strong as they drew closer to Jerusalem: “[…] 
and they thought that the kingdom of God was going to appear at the moment” 
(19:11, καὶ δοκεῖν αὐτοὺς ὅτι παραχρῆμα μέλλει ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναφαί-

grasp” (or within/among them, 17:21),62 Luke underlines again the tension be- 
tween perceptions of physical and non-physical expressions of the kingdom of 
God. As was true for the Galilee section, this section also ends without any signs of 
resistance by Jesus’ movement against the Empire. 


Also worthy of note is Luke’s use of geographical markers and indications of 


imperial presence. Like the previous section, Luke’s lack of interest in descriptive 
geography is manifest. What interests him is movement towards the destination 
and what takes place on the way. However, travel notices do occur more fre- 
quently and contribute to the narrative tension in the approach to Jerusalem.63 As 
in the previous section, the precise locations here continue to be unspecified 
through uses of the indefinite pronoun ‘certain’ (τις, e.g., 10:38; 11:1; 18:2, etc.). 


In his earlier geopolitical note (3:1–2), Luke did not specify that, along with 


Judea, Samaria, with its main cities (Samaria, Shechem, and Mt Gerizim), was 
also under direct Roman rule. Augustus had sent Herod Archelaus into exile (Vi- 
enne, France) in 6 CE. Judea had thus more experience under Roman officials. As 
a rival city to Jerusalem, Caesarea Maritima was built by Herod the Great, be- 
tween 22 and 10/9 BCE. It subsequently became the headquarters for Roman 
governors.64 Jesus’ movement was now entering this geopolitical space under the 
authority of Pontius Pilate, Prefect of Judea (rule 26–36 CE). 


The characterisation of imperial presence is mediated through a few charac- 


ters, mainly on regional and local levels. Their description contributes to Luke’s 
construction of the competing geopolitical and religious agendas and actors.65 


Luke makes no mention of emperors here, but he does reveal ongoing Roman

hostility. In Jesus’ third prediction of his death, Luke does not speak of the role of 
the Jewish authorities, nor does he explicitly speak of Rome, but rather the peo- 
ples (ἔθνεσιν, 18:32). It is understood, however, that Rome is intended. Luke also 
mentions the regional rulers: Pontius Pilate’s cruel acts in Galilee (i.e., the Gali- 
leans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices, 13:1)66 and Herod An- 
tipas who wanted to kill Jesus (13:31). This serves to make the audience aware of 
the Empire’s presence.67 


Yet Luke’s focus in this section progresses less on the agōn with the Romans 


than with the Jewish authorities, some of whom are presented as imperial collab- 
orators. Jesus is depicted as superior in thought and character over, mainly, the 
Pharisees and the scribes. Several strong episodes illustrate heated debates and 
the ensuing tension and aggression.68 Consequently, in light of these religio-politi- 
cal victories for Jesus, it is not surprising that Luke highlights the crowd’s enthu- 
siastic welcome of Jesus as their king. In the next section, however, both imperial 
and local authorities will collaborate violently against Jesus’ non-military move- 
ment in Jerusalem. Following this summary of the journey from Galilee to Jer- 
usalem, we now consider Luke’s depiction of perceptions of divine rule, engaging 
with the human and spiritual realms as a part of the overall geopolitical agōn. 


Works of power on the way to Jerusalem. As stated above, the number of “works of 
power” (δυνάμεις) is far fewer than in the Galilee section. Luke prefers to high- 
light Jesus’ teaching about the kingdom. We consider first the works of power, 
then, because of this rhetorical emphasis, how Jesus speaks about himself in rela- 
tion to the kingdom of God. Both are significant for understanding the overall ar- 
gument of a different kingdom that Luke wishes to convey to his audience. 


As in the first section, Luke also offers here perceptions of actions attributed 


to the God of Israel or to his agents. While exorcisms and healings are present, 
there are no events similar to those of Jesus’ transfiguration or the declaration of 
forgiveness of sins. Following an uncertain start involving the Samaritan village’s 
refusal to allow passage to Jesus, Luke again turns his attention to the implication 
of Jesus’ disciples in his mandate. First, three individuals offer clumsy excuses for 
not joining Jesus’ followers, to which one of them Jesus says sternly, “Let the dead 
bury their own dead. But you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God” (9:60) and to 
another “No one who puts a hand to the plough and looks back to things behind is 
apt for the kingdom of God” (9:62). Thus, the kingdom of God is immediately in 
the foreground.

The unity between the God of Israel, Jesus, and his disciples is summed up thus: 
“Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me, and 
whoever rejects me rejects the one who has sent me” (10:16). Again, the expres- 
sion of divine rule is perceived as being in progress. 


Interest in the conflict with the spiritual realm appears in the disciples’ first 


mission. With this shared authority, the disciples return joyfully, claiming victory 
over demons: “Lord, even the demons are obedient to us in your name!” (10:17). 
Jesus’ response sheds light on his perception of the effect of God’s kingdom 
against the competing force in the spiritual world:

The involvement of Jesus’ disciples is understood as a greater threat to the spiri- 
tual world from which the devil had promised Jesus to rule over the peoples (4:5– 
8). 


This part of the agōn receives attention shortly thereafter when Jesus is re-

Again, the reactions are revealing. While “the crowds were amazed” (ἐθαύμασαν

their accusation, concluding, “But if it is by the finger of God that I drive out the 
demons, then the kingdom of God has reached you” (11:20). It is clear then that 
Luke portrays Jesus as the main agent of God’s kingdom and his disciples as co-

agents. This is the last episode in Luke’s Gospel which involves direct confronta- 
tion with the spiritual world. The presence of the devil, however, will reappear in 
connection with Judas Iscariot’s betrayal of Jesus (22:3). 


Luke’s attention now shifts to the human realm where Jesus encounters ad- 


ditional agōnes, primarily arising from the hostility of the Pharisees and scribes 
(11:53–54; 13:10–17) as well as Herod’s intention to kill him (13:31–33). This in- 
cites a lament of condemnation from Jesus, who, like the prophets of the past 
(13:33–35), is destined to be treated dishonourably, even to the point of death. In 
the remainder of the travel narrative, Luke reports four instances of works of 
power in the form of healings: 


– a woman suffering from a physical disability (13:10–17), 
– a man with dropsy (14:1–6), 
– ten lepers (17:11–19), 
– and a blind man on the road to Jericho (18:35–43). 


As in Galilee, the healings here point to the manifestation of divine rule and ac- 
complishment of Jesus’ mandate (4:18–19; 7:18–23). To shed light on the polemi- 
cal context, Luke includes reactions to the healings. These episodes underscore 
Jesus’ superiority in action and in word; that he is the true agent of the kingdom 
of God. 


In the first healing, while the healed woman praises God, the leader of the 


synagogue is said to be indignant at this healing on the sabbath (13:13–14). Jesus 
also uses labels, calling the leader and others in the crowd ‘hypocrites’ (13:15). 
They were “put to shame” by his rebuttal (13:17), and “the whole crowd was re- 
joicing at all the glorious deeds being done by him” (ἐπὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς ἐνδόξοις τοῖς 
γινομένοις ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ). 


In the second healing, Jesus is under surveillance by the experts of the law 


and the Pharisees because it was also the sabbath. Tension is noted: “they were 
observing him” (καὶ αὐτοὶ ἦ σαν παρατηρούμενοι αὐτόν, 14:1). This time Jesus is 
said to ask a question before healing the man with dropsy: “Is it lawful to heal on 
the sabbath, or not?” They are silent before and after the healing, not being able 
to respond to Jesus’ second question about rescuing humans or animals on the 
sabbath. Yet, unlike other contexts, no hostility or plans for harm are noted. 


In the third healing, Luke reports that Jesus cures ten lepers, nine of whom 


are Jewish and one of whom a Samaritan. After their healing, while they are on 
their way to show themselves to the priests required by Jewish law, only the Sa- 
maritan returns to thank Jesus. Jesus observes that the other nine did not come 
who should have done so and thus commends the positive example by a “foreign- 
er” (ἀλλογενής). Within the macronarrative, the episode contains a polemical 
note, recalling Jesus’ comparison of his mandate to that of Elijah and Elisha in the 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
326 


synagogue of Nazareth, who performed acts of compassion towards non-Jews 
(4:24–27). 


The fourth healing also shows resistance to Jesus’ compassion to the margin- 


alised, because the leaders of the moving crowd rebuked the blind man for call- 
ing out: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (18:38). Jesus heals the man 
despite their opposition. The reactions are then positive: the healed man glorifies 
God and follows Jesus, and the crowd also praised God (18:43). 


Summary. Jesus’ teaching about the kingdom of God and his actions are depicted 
as its true manifestation. Throughout the long travel narrative, Luke confirms 
both Jesus’ proleptic portrait and his self-proclaimed mandate. The healings and 
the exorcisms are underscored as evidence of Jesus’ claims: “The kingdom of God 
has come to you” (10:9; 11:20) and that “something greater than [king] Solomon 
is here” (Luke 11:31). His part in divine rule is thus substantiated over human 
and spiritual rule. 


Nonetheless, narrative tension remains through the growing awareness of 


the ongoing reality of the kingdom of God (17:20–21) and the expectation that an 
immanent appearance – “because he was near Jerusalem” – was going to take 
place (καὶ δοκεῖν αὐτοὺς ὅτι παραχρῆμα μέλλει ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναφαί- 
νεσθαι, 19:11). Jesus finally arrives in the vicinity of Jerusalem and is proclaimed 
king by some of the people. But he has no means of removing the Roman and 
Jewish authorities, and Luke does not suggest that Jesus wishes to remove them. 
Hence, the notions of kingship and reign become more nuanced as the narrative 
progresses. We now turn to the last section of Luke’s first volume, in which Jesus 
first receives an enthusiastic welcome in Jerusalem, followed by fierce hostility. 


10.6 The Escalation of the Agōn between Divine and Human Rule 


in Jerusalem (Luke 19:45–24:53) 


Introduction to the narrative of Jesus in Jerusalem. Luke’s prophetic voice is partic- 
ularly forceful in this final section as he shows how Jesus’ mandate and the multi- 
ple strands of the agōn not only intensify but also converge. The geopolitical land- 
scape quickly becomes hostile here, which Luke represents by not affording any 
separation of the political, religious, and divine realms. Jesus is portrayed as one 
who does not negotiate terms with the three realms of opposition (Rome, Jewish 
leaders, and Satan). Luke employs a hybrid approach, which acknowledges impe- 
rial control but shows how that realm neither thwarts the purposes of the king- 
dom of God nor subjugates it multi-ethnic identity. Jesus is recognised as innocent 
by the imperial rulers and executed anyway, but the story does not end here. Ro- 
man and Jewish leadership are indeed the human face of the agōn, but an under- 


10 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts I 
327 


lying darker force is perceived by Luke behind the scenes. Luke explores how Je- 
sus faces these three powers by highlighting scenes and interposing the narrative 
with temporal movements through analepses and prolepses, many of which are 
external to the narrative. In this way, windows to the past and the future are 
opened for understanding the narrative present. 


This final section of the first volume also prepares the audience for the re- 


sumption of the narrative in the second volume in which various themes and 
questions continue to be explored, from Jerusalem to Rome. All this description is 
for readers post 70 CE, when Jerusalem and her temple were razed by the Roman 
forces.72 The cumulative victory of Vespasian and Titus over Judea was well 
known, publicly celebrated by coin and arch.73 Thus, Luke’s prophetic voice con- 
tinues to work on two levels, making sense of ‘the things accomplished among us’ 
(Luke 1:1; the core narrative) and helping readers to understand their own con- 
text, in which they also were confronted by imperial powers. They had their own 
agōn to contend with.74 The emotive aspect of this section is decisive, especially as 
the story becomes increasingly global, entering geopolitical contexts in which 
Luke’s audience lived and worshipped. This is not only Jesus’ story but had be- 
come their story as well. 


In this regard, the discussion below focuses on the following points: Jesus’ 


works of power (accomplished and announced), the convergence of the three 
strands of the agōn, and the multiple epithets for Jesus in relation to his basileia 
towards narrative closure. These elements are placed under the central questions 
driving the overall intrigue, which here reaches its peak of narrative tension. Je- 
sus arrives in Jerusalem perceived as king (19:38), yet crucified (23:33), then wor- 
shipped as a divine being (24:52). Where then is his basileia since he has failed to 
take political possession of Jerusalem? Has divine rule failed in Luke’s eyes? How 
then – to use Theodora Jim’s expression – is Jesus portrayed as a ‘saviour god’?75 


Works of power (accomplished and announced) in Jerusalem. There are few works 
of power in this final section (19:45–24:53). Some of Luke’s audience who were 
unfamiliar with the events surrounding Jesus’ execution may have been sur- 
prised by this ending. The narrative shows that people expected such powerful 
deeds to work in Jesus’ interest or in their own, either ensuring his survival or 
setting them free from their enemies. These expectations, however, are frustrated 
for both internal and external audiences. The works of power are listed below,

with some receiving further discussion in the following sections. Luke continues 
to portray these events as manifestations of divine rule and as an accomplish- 
ment of Jesus’ mandate. These range from punctual acts of lesser importance to 
greater ones indicating Jesus’ states of being, moving from death, to resurrection, 
then to ascension. 


In this section, a noteworthy element is Jesus’ ability to predict future events 


of which several are external prolepses. This ranges from Jesus’ prediction of a 
man carrying a jar of water who met and led his disciples to the room for the 
Passover meal (22:10–13), to Peter’s threefold denial before the rooster crowed 
(22:34, 54–62), and to the accomplishment of his announcements about his death 
and resurrection (20:16–19; 24:25–27, 44–49). That these events are shown to be 
divinely accomplished affirms the faith of internal characters and Luke’s original 
readership. For the latter, various statements attributed to Jesus would be signifi- 
cant to their generation of disciples, for example, the prediction of persecutions 
(21:12–19), the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple (21:5–6, 20–24), and Je- 
sus’ return as “the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory” 
with the promised redemption (21:27; Acts 1:9–11). 


Luke also relates works of power in the human and natural realms. In the 


human realm, Jesus heals the clipped ear of the high priest’s servant who was 
struck by someone defending Jesus (22:50–51). In the natural realm, at the time 
of Jesus’ execution, two signs occur that illustrate that his death was not per- 
ceived as a common incident: darkness appears at daytime, and the curtain of the 
temple was torn in two (23:44–45). But the primary works of power are – within 
the narrative limits – Jesus’ resurrection and ascension. The first is not displayed 
in progress but rather its effects as an accomplished action. The empty tomb and 
Jesus’ appearance are attested by two divine figures (24:4–7) and human wit- 
nesses (24:13–32, 33–49, 50–51). Conversely, at various points, Jesus is taunted to 
demonstrate his ability to perform works of power either for show (23:8) or for 
“saving himself” (23:35–39). But he does not avail himself of the divine resources 
at his disposal. 


Converging narrative strands as a part of the agōn towards Jesus’ arrest. The con- 
flict in relation to the Jewish authorities reaches its culmination in Jerusalem, as 
had been announced at various points through Jesus’ voice (Luke 9:22; 9:43; 
13:33; 17:25). Rather than seeking to come to terms of agreement with the Jewish 
rulers, Jesus is shown to take authority concerning Jewish customs and beliefs, 
thus deepening the conflict with them. Unsurprisingly, the first scene opens in the 
temple complex (ἱερόν) from which Jesus drives out commercial activity (19:45).76 


Jesus justifies this action by appropriating various scriptures: “It is written: ‘My 
house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers’” (19:45; 


76 
Cf. note 25 for Luke’s distinction between ἱερόν (temple complex) and ναός (sanctuary). 


10 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts I 
329 


cf. Isa 56:7; Jer 7:11). He is taking authority in the most sacred location against a 
powerful group of leaders. Jesus also does this by teaching daily in the temple. 
This recalls Jesus’ instruction under the teachers in the temple and his claim to be 
in his “Father’s house” (2:46–49). No discussion is provided here, but Luke re- 
ports that three groups, the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders, were hence- 
forth seeking some way to eliminate Jesus. But there was an obstacle to this: the 
people are portrayed as welcoming Jesus’ teaching. Consequently, the leaders’ 
fear of the people is explicitly noted several times (19:48; 20:6, 19, 26; 22:1, 6; 
Acts 5:26). 


Luke then depicts Jesus’ authority before the Jewish leaders by highlighting 


his superior understanding of God’s actions during their era, as revealed through 
his interpretation of the Jewish scriptures. The leaders demand a justification for 
his presumed authority, and Jesus asks them to state whether they recognise John 
the Baptist as a prophet, as he and the people do. Out of fear, they refuse to state 
their position (20:1–8). As shown above, John and Jesus are depicted as insepara- 
ble in the divine plan. Narratively, both the temple and the prophet are now on 
Jesus’ side. For this reason, Jesus goes on to tell a parable – of only two parables 
in this section – traditionally known as the ‘Wicked tenants’, which depicts the 
leaders’ rebellion against God and the subsequent divine retribution (20:9–19). 
The leaders understand the force of this parable against them, but they dare not 
seize Jesus owing to the people’s support. 


In response to these authoritative actions, Luke portrays the agōn playing 


out through public debate in which the Jewish leaders attempt to ‘trap’ Jesus. 
First, they send ‘spies’ (ἐγκαθέτους) who seek to put him in disfavour with the 
imperial authorities, “Is it lawful for us to give tribute (φόρος) to the emperor, or 
not?” (20:22). It is formulated as a no-win situation vis-à-vis Roman and Jewish 
sensitivities.77 Although their objective is not stated here, it becomes apparent lat- 
er in the form of an accusation before Pontius Pilate: “We found this man cor- 
rupting our people, forbidding us to give tribute to the emperor, and saying that 
he himself is the Christ [anointed one], a king” (23:2). Jesus avoids this trap by 
way of his renowned answer, that is, to give to the emperor what is his and to God 
what belongs to him (20:25).78 Next, the Sadducees seek to show Jesus’ inferiority 
as a religious authority by asking him to solve a puzzle regarding the bodily res- 
urrection. Again, Jesus wins this debate, and Luke reports that his opponents “no 
longer dared to ask him another question” (20:40). So, Jesus asks them a question 
pertaining to his identity and authority in relation to king David: “How can they 
say that the Christ (τὸν χριστόν) is David’s son?” (20:41). Jesus challenges, in his

view, their misinterpretation of Psalm 110:1. He is again claiming David’s throne 
and displaying his interpretative superiority as teacher. He then denounces the 
scribes and announces their condemnation because of their self-righteousness 
and exploitation of widows (20:45–47). 


A narrative hinge now opens again about the temple, the heart of Jewish cult 


and culture. In contrast to the Jewish leaders’ behaviour, Jesus points out the ex- 
emplary attitude of a “poor widow” who places “two small copper coins” in the 
temple treasury (21:1–4). While others comment on the beauty of the Jerusalem 
temple, Jesus prophetically announces its coming destruction. Here, Luke subtly 
connects the Roman strand to the agōn. For readers of Luke’s Gospel, living post 
70 CE, the allusion to imperial authority is unmistakable for “the days will come 
when not one stone will be left upon another that will not be cast down” (21:6). 
Jesus goes on to remind them that other events will happen in response to the 
question: “Teacher, when then will this be and what is the sign when these things 
are going to happen?” (21:7). Global strife, natural calamities, and “dreadful por- 
tents and great signs from heaven” (φόβητρά τε καὶ ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ σημεῖα μεγάλα) 
will occur. Also, various opponents of Jesus’ movement are mentioned: “But be- 
fore all these things, they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, deliver- 
ing you to the synagogues and prisons, and be led before kings and governors 
because of my name” (21:12). Jesus’ prophetic voice now becomes Luke’s, as he 
points out the convergence of imperial and Jewish forces to his readers of post 70 
CE. 


This is further illustrated by Jesus’ announcement of the destruction of Jer- 


usalem and an exhortation to his disciples to remain faithful (21:20–38). That this 
will come by the hand of outsiders is clear: “when you see Jerusalem surrounded 
by troops” (21:20) and “Jerusalem will be trampled on by the peoples (ὑπὸ 
ἐθνῶν), until the times of the peoples are fulfilled” (21:24). The Romans and their 
allies are understood to be the perpetrators of this Jewish national tragedy. 


Jesus again uses prophetic language by pointing to the signs (σημεῖα) in the 


heavens and on earth. He also draws a contrast between “the powers of the heav- 
ens,” which will be shaken at his return. For this, he appropriates Jewish scrip- 
ture, “the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory,” which is an 
allusion to Daniel 7:13–14. This event introduces a turning point in the story, 
which is their coming deliverance (or ‘redemption’, ἐγγίζει ἡ ἀπολύτρωσις ὑμῶν, 
21:28).79 


This subsection concludes with Jesus’ exhortations to his disciples. The sec- 


ond and final parable of this section, ‘the Lesson of the Fig Tree’ (21:29–33), em- 
phasises two key points: the importance of recognising the signs of the approach- 


79 
This resonates with other mentions of redemption or deliverance (λύτρωσις) in the first chap- 
ters of Luke’s Gospel, in Zechariah’s prayer (1:68), and in the prophetess Anna’s testimony 
(2:38).

331 


ing ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ (21:31) and Jesus’ claim to his teaching’s truthfulness and 
durability: “Heaven and earth will disappear, but my words will not disappear” 
(21:33). This is followed by a final exhortation to be alert and faithful, despite 
coming global calamities (ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς καθημένους ἐπὶ πρόσωπον πάσης τῆς 
γῆς, 21:35). Before moving to the third trajectory in the agōn, Luke concludes 
with a summary that underlines Jesus’ authority in relation to the temple and the 
people: “During the day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out 
and spent the night on the mount called the Olivet. And all the people left early to 
come and listen to him in the temple” (21:37–38). 


At this point, Luke brings in the third strand of the agōn, which reintroduces 


the direct intervention of the spiritual being encountered in the temptation scene 
(4:1–13). There, Luke spoke of the διάβολος about whom a return on the scene 
would occur (ἀπέστη ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἄχρι καιροῦ, 4:13). Now Luke presents him as 
σατανᾶς (without the article) who is said to ‘enter’ Judas, one of Jesus’ disciples. 
This now moves the narrative in another direction, since Judas offers his privi- 
leged insider position to the chief priests and officers (τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσιν καὶ στρα- 
τηγοῖς). This treachery must happen at an opportune moment (εὐκαιρίαν) and in 
the absence of a crowd (ἄτερ ὄχλου, 22:6). 


Luke briefly leaves this part of the agōn to focus on Jesus’ final moments 


with his disciples at Passover before being handed over to the authorities (22:7– 
30). Noteworthy are the mentions of the βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ (22:16, 18) and the 
announcement of his (i.e., Son of man’s) impending death (22:22). Talk of the 
kingdom raises a debate among his disciples about who might be the greatest 
among them. In Jesus’ view, they think in terms of “the kings of the peoples,” – 
another remark about abusive imperial authority – which runs counter to his 
teaching about servant leadership. This is followed by a promise to his disciples, 
an external prolepsis in Luke’s narrative (22:28–30), which announces future 
participation as judges of the twelve tribes of Israel in his kingdom (ἐν τῇ βασι- 
λείᾳ μου, 22:30). That is, the kingdom conferred to him by his father is now “my 
kingdom.” In this passage, Luke uses Jesus’ words and contrasts them with those 
of his disciples to demonstrate that Jesus’ understanding of the βασιλεία is both 
present and future. Wherever God reigns, there is his kingdom (cf. Luke 17:20– 
21). In this sense, the rule of God may be opposed, but it cannot ultimately be 
impeded by human or spiritual forces (cf. θεομάχοι in Acts 5:39). 


Luke now returns to the third strand of the agōn, an evil presence, as the 


narrative moves towards Jesus’ betrayal and execution. Jesus speaks directly to 
Simon (i.e., Peter) revealing something that had been said in the divine realm: 
“Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you (ὑμᾶς) like wheat, but I have 
prayed for you (σοῦ) that your own faith (ἡ πίστις σου) may not fail […]” (22:31– 
32a). Jesus does not reveal how he knows this. Narrative tension continues to 
grow as the agōn is explicitly brought to the fore by talk of betrayal (22:34), 
swords (22:36–38), and a ‘time of trial’ (πειρασμόν, 22:46). Then the climactic mo- 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
332 


ment arrives when Judas accompanies a crowd led by “the chief priests, the offi- 
cers of the temple police, and the elders,” equipped with “swords and clubs” 
(22:52).80 The convergence of the two strands, political and spiritual opposition, is 
highlighted by Jesus’ words: “When I was with you daily in the temple, you did 
not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness!” (ἀλλ’ 
αὕτη ἐστὶν ὑμῶν ἡ ὥρα καὶ ἡ ἐξουσία τοῦ σκότους, 22:53). Luke had introduced 
the presence of ‘darkness’ (σκότος) in Zechariah’s prayer (1:79, “[…] to give light 
to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death […]”). He evokes it again 
here, as well as during the hours of Jesus’ execution (23:44, “It was now about 
noon, and darkness came over the whole land until three in the afternoon […]”). 


Through this motif, Luke introduces and underlines the interaction between 


the human and divine realms, as portrayed in Jesus’ arrest and trials before the 
Jewish and imperial authorities. First, however, Luke shows how this manifests 
itself among Jesus’ followers when Peter denies Jesus three times (22:54–62). 
Having joined the three strands in the narrative, highlighted by betrayals (Judas 
and Peter), Luke continues to develop the narrative tension surrounding the 
question of Jesus’ identity and the grounds for his execution under the represen- 
tative of Rome, Pontius Pilate. Here, we consider here how epithets continue to be 
used to describe Jesus in relation to his mandate and the promised basileia, both 
of which are understood as threats to the three realms of opposition. 


Return to Jesus’ epithets in relation to his mandate and divine rule. Luke addresses 
the question of how Jesus can be both king (i.e., Christ, Luke 23:2) and Lord, yet 
still be crucified on a Roman cross. From 22:63 until 23:49, the audience explores 
how the agōn develops as various groups question Jesus, directly and indirectly, 
about his identity. Luke is certainly building on the motifs of innocent victims 
and unlawful trials, which were well-known in the Mediterranean.81 In front of 
the Jewish authorities (τὸ πρεσβυτέριον τοῦ λαοῦ, ἀρχιερεῖς τε καὶ γραμματεῖς), 
Jesus is asked to confirm whether he understands himself as ὁ χριστός and ὁ υἱὸς 
τοῦ θεοῦ (22:67, 70). Jesus responds with the messianic title “the Son of man” (cf. 
Dan 7:13–14), “From now on the Son of man will be seated at the right hand of 
the power of God” (22:69; cf. Acts 7:55–56). This is a clear claim to divine rule 
about which the authorities’ reaction confirms the weight of this statement: 
“What need of testimony do we still have? For we ourselves have heard from his 
own mouth!” (22:71). No negotiation ensues for a peaceful resolution.

This leads to a succession of trials under imperial powers: Pontius Pilate and 


Herod Antipas (23:1–25). Here again Luke shows Jesus making no attempt to seek 
terms of peace. The charges brought against him are three: perverting the Jewish 
people, advocating tribute evasion, and claiming to be the Messiah, a king. Pilate 
explores this last accusation, but he finds Jesus innocent. But the Jewish authori- 
ties retort, “He incites the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee to 
here” (23:5). 


The mention of Galilee prompts Pilate to send Jesus to Herod, the tetrarch of 


Galilee, who was present in Jerusalem for the Passover (23:6–7). Herod is pleased 
to meet Jesus in person and had hoped for some kind of sign (σημεῖον) from him. 
Jesus, however, is silent before Herod and the chief priests and scribes, who bring 
their accusations against him. After verbal abuse by Herod and his soldiers, the 
tetrarch sends Jesus – mockingly dressed in an “elegant robe” – back to Pilate, 
with whom a friendship begins that day despite their own previous agōn (23:11– 
12). 


Pilate decides to release Jesus, because he and Herod did not find the accusa- 


tions convincing. A good flogging would suffice (23:16). But the religious authori- 
ties propose a compromise: release the criminal Barabbas and crucify Jesus. De- 
spite Pilate’s reluctance to condemn Jesus, “their voices prevailed” (κατίσχυον αἱ 
φωναὶ αὐτῶν) and Jesus was led away to be executed (23:23–25). Once more, 
there is no evidence of any attempt at negotiation between Jesus and the rulers. 
Jesus is assumed to be submitting to their unjust forms of religious and imperial 
oppression. 


The narrative ensues with accounts of exchanges between Jesus, anguished 


women, two criminals, and soldiers (23:26–49). Here as well, various epithets are 
explored in the form of mocking accusations by the leaders (ὁ χριστὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ 
ἐκλεκτός, 23:35), by the soldiers (ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων, 23:37), and by one of 
the criminals crucified with Jesus (ὁ χριστός, 23:39). Even the inscription (ἐπι- 
γραφή) is reported to announce publicly Jesus’ identity: ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων 
οὗ τος (23:38).82 


But Luke also reports support for Jesus in which various narrative threads 


come together. In this way, two opposing strands, Jewish and imperial, are coun- 
tered, and narratively weakened by eyewitness reports. One of the criminals de- 
fends Jesus’ innocence and asks to be remembered in Jesus’ kingdom (23:42). The 
second, a centurion, who had witnessed the crucifixion and the omen, praises 
God and declares, “Certainly this man was innocent” (23:47). Then, after Jesus’ 
death, these reports of belief are strengthened by Luke’s characterisation of 
Joseph of Arimathea. He is a Jewish council member (βουλευτής) who is a “good 
and righteous man” (ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς καὶ δίκαιος, 23:50). Luke had begun his narra-

tive by describing Elizabeth and Zechariah as δίκαιοι (1:79), and Simeon as 
δίκαιος καὶ εὐλαβής (2:25), now Joseph, clearly expressing his disagreement with 
the council’s plan and action (οὗ τος οὐκ ἦ ν συγκατατεθειμένος τῇ βουλῇ καὶ τῇ 
πράξει αὐτῶν, 23:51) wishes to ensure proper ceremonial burial for Jesus. Luke 
adds that the women disciples from Galilee followed Joseph to the “rock-hewn 
tomb” and went home to prepare “spices and ointments” for Jesus’ burial. Then, 
they rested on the sabbath as per Jewish customs (23:53–55). 


How does Luke resolve these conflicting voices concerning the identity of Je- 


sus, since, factually, he has failed to liberate Jerusalem and himself? Jerusalem is 
still under Roman rule and Jesus has been publicly executed as a criminal with 
two criminals. How is he then considered a ‘saviour God’ in Luke’s depiction? 
What are the perceptions and epithets used to support Luke’s prophetic voice? To 
conclude the section on epithets used to describe Jesus’ identity, we consider 
Chapter 24, which displays three post-resurrection events: the women at the 
tomb (24:1–12), Jesus’ exchange with two disciples (24:13–35), and his appear- 
ance to his disciples in Jerusalem (24:36–53). Interestingly, these accounts share 
common elements: conflicting perceptions about his identity and reminders of Je- 
sus’ necessary suffering. From 24:1 onward, the agōn has decreased on the narra- 
tive level but traces of it remain in the perceptions of Jesus’ disciples. Also, no 
other conflictual groups are physically present but remain in their thoughts 
(“how our chief priests and rulers handed him over for death sentence and they 
crucified him,” 24:20) and, because of them, Jesus was unable to “redeem Israel” 
(24:21). Luke carefully works through these scenes, seeking to show his readers 
that divine rule has not failed. 


In the first account, the women disciples come to the tomb to complete the 


burial preparations, but they are perplexed to find it empty. “Two men” in daz- 
zling clothes appear to them, reminding the women that “the Son of man must be 
handed over to [the hands of] sinners, and be crucified, and on the third day rise 
again” (24:7). The “Son of man” (Jesus’ preferred self-designation) is “to be hand- 
ed over to the hands of sinners” (παραδοθῆναι εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων ἁμαρτωλῶν). 
This underlines the assessment of the human authorities who are responsible for 
Jesus’ death. Another conflicting perception is depicted: the women’s report 
seems to the male disciples to be “an idle tale (λῆρος)” and they do not believe it 
until Peter has verified the state of the tomb for himself (24:11–12, 34). In con- 
trast, Luke skilfully portrays the women’s perception, as they recognise that these 
were indeed angels, a detail that is reported later in Jerusalem (24:23). 


The second account takes place between Jerusalem and Emmaus (24:13–32). 


The conflicting perceptions are almost comical in that the two disciples (one of 
whom is specifically named, ‘Cleopas’) encounter the risen Jesus but they do not 
recognise him, and they express to him their despair. They perceive him as a 
“stranger residing in Jerusalem” (παροικεῖς Ἰερουσαλήμ), apparently ignorant of 


10 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts I 
335 


the events (τὰ γενόμενα […] τὰ περὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Ναζαρηνοῦ, 24:18–19).83 They de- 
scribe Jesus (to Jesus) as “a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all 
the people” in whom they had hoped that “he was the one to redeem Israel” (ὁ 
μέλλων λυτροῦσθαι τὸν Ἰσραήλ, 24:21). This echoes the enthusiastic hope of the 
crowd who expected that “the kingdom of God was to appear immediately” 
(19:11). They go on to tell Jesus what had happened at the tomb that morning 
(24:21–24). Jesus’ response takes the form of a rebuke (24:25–27), reminding 
them of what he had told them on the basis of the Jewish scriptures. The empha- 
sis on the fulfilment of a divine plan through the construction ‘it is/was necessary’ 
recalls previous uses of δεῖ concerning Jesus’ mandate as a part of a larger divine 
plan (2:49; 4:43; 9:22; 13:33; 17:25; 19:5; 21:9; 22:7, 37; 24:7, 44). In Jesus’ voice, 
he refers to himself as the Christ, asking the two disciples: oὐχὶ ταῦτα ἔδει παθεῖν 
τὸν χριστὸν καὶ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ; (24:26). This is further supported 
by his teaching based on the Jewish scriptures: “Moses and all the prophets” 
(24:27). Luke alerts his readers to two things. Jesus still assumes his divinely giv- 
en role and epithet, and he enters “his glory.” This is the beginning of the narra- 
tive of Jesus who reigns in his glorified state, evoking the transfiguration scene 
(9:28–36). No further epithets are given in this passage, but the two disciples fi- 
nally recognise Jesus, then he disappears from their view (lit. “became unseen/ 
invisible’, καὶ αὐτὸς ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, 24:31). 


The third account displays a similar pattern about conflicting perceptions of 


Jesus, in Jerusalem and Bethany. The dramatic appearance above caused the two 
disciples to return quickly to Jerusalem to rejoin Jesus’ disciples, now without Ju- 
das, “the eleven and those with them” (24:33). The disciples in Jerusalem an- 
nounce their belief in the risen Christ, describing Jesus as κύριος: “The Lord has 
risen indeed, and he has appeared to Simon!” (24:34). Yet, during this enthusias- 
tic discussion about the risen Jesus, he himself appears to them who were “star- 
tled and terrified” (24:37), thinking they perceived a spirit (ἐδόκουν πνεῦμα θεω- 
ρεῖν, 24:37). After proofs that he was indeed the same person and alive (24:38– 
43), Jesus proceeds in much the same way as with the Emmaus disciples, explain- 
ing how the divine plan had to be fulfilled according to the scriptures (24:44– 
47).84 This is followed again by explicit mentions of the sources: “the law of Mos- 
es, the prophets, and the psalms” (24:44). In Jesus’ voice, he thus lays claim to the 
scriptural heritage of Israel, his title (“the Christ”), and his relationship to Israel’s 
God, namely, “my Father” (24:44–49). 


The third account also helps us to grasp how Luke intends to conclude his 


first volume, by depicting Jesus’ form of rule. Despite the obvious fact that Jesus

has not removed power from the Roman or Jewish authorities, nor physically re- 
deemed Israel (λυτροῦσθαι τὸν Ἰσραήλ, 24:21), Jesus is still presented as a ruler. 
First, Luke reports Jesus giving to his disciples a mandate, based on what had 
happened in Jerusalem. Although Jesus has returned to life, no plans for military 
or political takeover are proposed. Jesus does, however, announce a continued 
mandate focused on reconciliation with God: “[…] and that repentance for the 
forgiveness of sins be proclaimed in his name to all peoples” (24:47). In Luke’s 
narrative, this is the equivalent of salvation or deliverance (e.g., Luke 1:77; 2:30; 
19:9; Acts 4:12; 28:28). That this is a continuation of Jesus’ mandate is underlined 
by the phrase “in my name” (ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ, 24:47). Only in this sense is he 
perceived as ‘saviour god’. 


Second, Luke ensures that divine action is announced proleptically to under- 


line the continuity of Jesus’ mandate and that of his disciples. It comes through 
the announcement of a “power from above/on high” (ἐξ ὕψους δύναμιν) that will 
“clothe them” in Jerusalem (24:49). Thus, in Luke’s portrayal, divine rule has not 
displaced human rule – whether Roman or Jewish – but it has not failed to main- 
tain and exhibit its own power, with a global focus, through a coming power, 
namely, the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:5). 


Finally, Luke confirms that the epithets given to Jesus (χριστός, κύριος, ὁ 


υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ) are justified. He does this in two ways. As in the baptism and the 
transfiguration scenes, a final work of power, a divine passive, elevates Jesus to 
heaven: “he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven” (διέστη ἀπ’ 
αὐτῶν καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, 24:51). This is the “departure” of Jesus that 
Luke had mentioned earlier (9:31, 51; cf. Acts 1:11, 22). This work of power is also 
confirmed on the human level. Jesus’ disciples are said to worship Jesus, then 
they “returned to Jerusalem with great joy; and they were continually blessing 
God in the temple” (24:52). Despite the apparent failure to “redeem Israel” (Luke 
24:21), some elements remain the same for the disciples. This explains why Luke 
reiterates the disciples’ joy, which would otherwise be difficult to fathom (24:41, 
52). Israel’s God is still their God, who indeed reigns, and his temple is also still 
theirs as a place of worship and teaching (cf. Acts 2:46; 3:1; 4:1; 5:21). What is 
new is that Jesus is perceived as having entered a new state, confirmed as divine 
saviour worthy of their worship, who brings reconciliation between God and the 
peoples (24:47). 


10.7 Conclusion 


Like all Greek historians before him, Luke recounts perceptions of divine acts and 
speech that intervene in human affairs and shape world history. Through his 
prophetic voice, Luke interprets events in Roman Judea, to help his audience to 
make sense of the present and offer them direction for the future. Writing to- 


10 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts I 
337 


wards the end of the first century CE under the Roman Empire, Luke, like other 
‘crossover historians’, presents an alternative view of human and divine rule to 
that of the Empire. In his first volume, Luke describes the life of Jesus of Nazareth 
and his message about ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ, another way of experiencing power 
and freedom rooted mainly in Jewish scripture and worship. 


Unlike Herodotus whose military campaigns receive much attention in the 


Histories, Luke describes a geopolitical agōn nonetheless, moving between two 
capitals – Jerusalem and Rome – between ca. 4 BCE to 62 CE. The narrative in- 
trigue develops around the proleptic portrait of Jesus who is announced as ὁ υἱὸς 
τοῦ θεοῦ, κύριος, σωτήρ, and χριστός, Jesus’ own understanding of his mandate, 
and responses to these by various individuals and groups. Jesus’ own name, Yah- 
weh saves, is given proleptically in relation to what he will accomplish, so that his 
life is not only portrayed as a divine visitation (19:44) but as a divine offering 
regarding salvation (Luke 1:77; 2:30; 3:6; 7:36–50; 24:47). Jesus is, in this sense, 
understood as a divine being who saves, namely, a ‘saviour god’.85 


While all these honorific titles – including heir of the Jewish royal line – are 


reported to have raised hope with some and apprehension with others, Jesus con- 
firms his own divine mandate in relation to meeting physical and spiritual needs 
of people, especially among the commonfolk who comprised most of the popula- 
tion (cf. Luke 4:16–21; 7:18–23). Rather than developing into a military insurrec- 
tion starting in Galilee, there is a growing awareness that Jesus’ understanding of 
a divine plan must bring him to Jerusalem, not as a military σωτήρ but as a sacri- 
ficial one. For Jesus’ disciples, it is a story of reframing their expectations, as in 
the haunting question by John the Baptist: “Are you the one who is coming, or 
should we wait for another?” (7:19). The perception of Jesus’ opposition, howev- 
er, is different. Therefore, the agōn develops mainly vis-à-vis spiritual, Jewish, 
and Roman rule. 


The narrative ends in a paradoxical way, since Jesus does not die in battle 


but by Roman public execution, which is seen as part of the divine plan. He is 
raised and exalted by God, and he is worshipped by his disciples. However, in this 
volume, Luke has not demonstrated the impact of Jesus’ accomplished mandate 
beyond the circle of his disciples. How are these events perceived as a divine re- 
sponse to the three realms of opposition? Luke’s second volume explores this, be- 
ginning with a highly geopolitical question: “Lord, is this the time when you will 
restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6). For Luke’s post-70 CE audience, the 
temple of Jerusalem no longer stands, but Rome does. What then does stand for 
them? How does Jesus’ βασιλεία manifest itself in relation to the Jewish people 
and to the Roman Empire? Once again, two realms and two reigns are juxtaposed 
in the period of 30 to 62 CE, beginning in Roman Judea and moving north then 
west towards Rome.
