11 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts: From Jerusalem to Asia Minor 


(Volume 2: Acts 1:1–15:35) 


11.1 Introduction to the Ensuing Agōn from Jerusalem to Rome 


The imperial impulse and divine rule in Volume 2. At the end of Luke’s first volume 
and at the beginning of the second, Emperor Tiberius (14–37 CE) and his Gover- 
nor of Judea, Pontius Pilate (26–36 CE), are still in power. Roman rule provides 
the political backdrop to the events of the second volume (ca. 30–62 CE), which 
also concerns Luke and his audience in the latter part of the first century. During 
this turbulent period, power shifted from the Julio-Claudian dynasty (31 BCE–68 
CE) to the Year of the Four Emperors (68–69 CE), and then on to the Flavian (69– 
96 CE) and Nerva–Antonine dynasties (96–192 CE). From Nero to Trajan, nine 
emperors and claimants to the Empire can be counted. 


Despite the Empire’s power and Jewish national expectations for deliver- 


ance articulated in the first volume (cf. Luke 1:51–53, 71, 74; 2:25, 38; 19:11; 
24:21), Luke’s audience – now ethnically mixed – with Theophilus (again, the 
specific narratee in Acts 1:1), may have been puzzled by the Empire’s longevity.1 


How could the kingdom of God – so manifestly demonstrated in Jesus, a ‘saviour 
god’ – not make a greater impact on their world? Or, at least, loosen the Empire’s 
grip so keenly felt throughout the provinces? What deliverance or salvation is 
available to them or still awaits them? It seems that Theophilus, Luke’s probable 
sponsor, and the wider audience desired an explanation of these kinds of ques- 
tions. This chapter and the following one examine how Luke’s prophetic voice 
continues to operate on two levels; it seeks to make sense of the unfolding story 
of Jesus’ movement against the backdrop of the wider historical context of Luke’s 
audience. 


These two chapters on the Acts of the Apostles require a brief justification. 


The circumstances of this story are simply not the same as those of the first one. 
Luke’s narrative world reflects the new situation for the cosmos that he and his 
characters perceive regarding Jesus’ ascension and its meaning for them. To illus- 
trate this, Luke provides a significant amount of material regarding perceptions 
of divine activity (cf. Appendix III). Luke’s literary genius, always in service to his 
theology, comes to the fore in his second volume, as he appears less dependent on 
sources than in his gospel, where he relied on a version of the Gospel of Mark 


1 
Henceforth, references to the Acts of the Apostles will not be preceded by ‘Acts’ except in am- 
biguous cases. 


(cf. 4.3.2 on literary genre). Consequently, what follows is a summary of how the 
agōn evolves in relation to Luke’s worldview and Jesus’ ascension as reflected in 
the literary distinctiveness of Acts.2 Based on this and other narrative cues, an 
outline is provided in the second part of the chapter. 


How the agonistic drive evolves. Still fresh from the previous volume, the theologi- 
cal and geopolitical agōn is hinted at right from the start of the second volume. 
The focus on the “kingdom of God” and the desire for “the restoration of the king- 
dom to Israel” (1:3, 6) resume the competing narratives. But how could they exist, 
or even coexist, as long as the Roman Empire rules? One notes, however, a cer- 
tain optimism, even a triumphant tone, in the opening lines of the prologue of 
Acts. Luke’s story was not going to end with a group of disciples at the temple in 
Jerusalem (Luke 24:52), since Jesus was still present and instructing his disciples 
about the next steps of their mandate (1:1–8). Their part in the story would not 
only continue in their teacher’s ways but also go beyond Israel’s traditional bor- 
ders as his witnesses (μάρτυρες, Acts 1:2–8). In Luke’s narrative, the world would 
never be the same, neither in Jerusalem nor in many places through which “the 
message (of/from God/Lord)” was going to pass (4:4, 31; 8:25 passim). Neverthe- 
less, as in the first volume, although God is said to have initiated and implement- 
ed his plan of reconciliation (4:28), human and spiritual opposition continues in a 
variety of spheres, e.g., religious, commercial, and political. The competing narra- 
tives are at the heart of the agonistic synkrisis that undergirds Luke-Acts from a 
narratological perspective.3 As in the first volume, the second does not depict an 
unhindered journey; opposition and obstacles abound. 


A significant change, however, is that the intrigue is now amplified, because 


the focus has shifted from one person and a few regions to multiple actors on a 
global scale. This change reflects Luke’s dual focus on the scope of Jesus’ mandate 
for the Jewish people and all other peoples. Accordingly, Luke depicts the forma- 
tion of a multicultural people of a kingdom over which Jesus is Lord (2:36; 10:36). 
In fact, as soon as readers assume that the agōn is now restricted to conflicts in- 
volving Jesus’ disciples – because of the book’s traditional title the Acts of the 
Apostles – Luke shows at various points that Jesus is neither removed to heaven 
nor inactive.4 On the contrary, he is depicted as the binding active force in the 
story, in connection with his disciples through bidirectional communication and

persecution about which Jesus exclaims to Saul the Pharisee, “Saul, Saul, why do

In Luke’s representation, Jesus and his disciples function together as joint 


protagonists of the agōn, at times collectively and other times separately. But it 
continues to be a united expression of the movement initiated through Jesus’ 
teaching and acts; hence, the focus may be viewed as the continued acts of Jesus 
through his apostles in volume 2 (1:1).6 In this sense, narratively, Jesus remains 
the hero, the central protagonist of the agōn.7 He was shown to go on the offensive 
from Galilee to Jerusalem in the first volume (10:36–39), but without weapons 
and military insurrections as others had tried against Jewish and Roman authori- 
ties in various provinces.8 Now Jesus continues to direct his disciples and work 
through them. 


For a narrative seeking to provide ἀσφάλεια to his audience (Luke 1:4), vari- 


ous types of proofs (τεκμήρια, Acts 1:3) are provided such as signs (σημεῖα), won- 
ders (τέρατα), and works of power (δυνάμεις). For this, Luke points to the contin- 
ued demonstration of divine activity in recent history. But he also reaches into 
the divine plupast by referring to ancient prophecies. Interestingly, although 
Luke claims later to be a witness to some of the events in the second volume, he 
never claims direct divine assistance for his work.9 He does not resort to ‘Thus 
says the Lord’ in his own voice to settle an issue. He lets others do most of the 
theological interpretation in several speeches. This rhetorical device serves to 
sustain his story, like those of his predecessors. Given this assumed worldview, 
this treatment of Luke’s second volume works primarily on a historiographical 
level, paying attention to the narrator’s techniques in leading his audience to ex- 
perience and welcome his account rather than seeking to prove or disprove its 
factuality.

11.2 Outline and Narrative Focus of Luke-Acts: Volume 2 


Luke organises the second volume so that his audience perceives the advance- 
ment of divine rule, taking the story from Jerusalem to Rome. Various types of 
outline display an organisation of the second volume based on either a central 
theme or an exegetical approach.10 Few outlines are proposed for Luke and Acts 
as a single work comprising two parts.11 Most outlines of Acts logically follow the 
geographical expansion referred to in Jesus’ response to his disciples’ question: 
“But you will receive power from the Holy Spirit coming upon you; and you will 
be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the 
earth” (1:8). Luke follows the general contours of this statement by showing how 
the movement spreads from the cultic centre (Jerusalem) – already known from 
the first volume – to near and far regions, ending in the imperial centre (Rome). 
Luke’s treatment generally follows this movement, but it is not entirely linear ow- 
ing to his characters’ departing from and returning to Jerusalem. Once again, 
Luke’s dual interest comes to the fore: Jerusalem is central to the narrative and 
so is the Aegean region.12 The link between the two geographical focal points is 
Antioch of Syria, where Jews and non-Jews form a community of Christ-followers. 
The corporate life of this community sparks a major debate among church lead- 
ers (Acts 14:21–15:35). 


The framework is clearly based on Acts 1:8 as the opening marker and its 


counterpart in Acts 28:28 with Paul’s words in Rome: “Therefore, let it be known 
to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the peoples (ἔθνεσιν) and they 
will listen.” The audience has been prepared for expansion outside traditionally 
Jewish territory by the first volume’s interest in the peoples. And various sign- 
posts in Acts support this overall framework: e.g., the list of peoples at Pentecost 
(2:5–13); persecution causing emigration from Jerusalem to the regions of Judea 
and Samaria (8:1–3); Cornelius the centurion’s conversion as a highlighted prece- 
dent (10:44–48; 11:18); Paul and Barnabas’ announcement in Antioch in Pisidia 
to “turn to the peoples” (13:46–48; and again in 14:27); the Jerusalem leaders’ let- 
ter of integration of believers from the peoples (15:22–29); a visionary call to

One of the differences in outline titles, but hardly irreconcilable, is the ques- 


tion of focus on human activity or divine activity, namely, who the protagonists 
are and how the narrative is organised around them. Most outlines highlight the 
former, often in relation to ecclesiological and missiological questions.13 Recent 
scholarship in the English-speaking world, however, has given more attention – 
perhaps surprisingly to those outside Acts research – to Luke’s narrative descrip- 
tion of God’s character and acts.14 In another publication, I have demonstrated 
this narratologically, showing that three transformational divine acts form the 
‘pivot’ between the two volumes: Jesus’ resurrection, his ascension, and his send- 
ing of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost.15 These actions bind the two vol- 
umes, and, without them, the entire two-volume narrative would neither hold to- 
gether nor make sense.16 Luke’s second volume reinforces this theological 
structure by showing the continuity of works of power (δυνάμεις) from volume 1, 
thus linking and authenticating this period with preceding ones through actorial 
presentations of divine interventions in ancient and recent history (i.e., the di- 
vine plupast, especially in the speeches, e.g., 7:51–53).17 For example, Luke pres-

ents his characters as reaching into the divine plupast, and so, narratively speak- 
ing, he participates in and facilitates those actions on his characters’ part. As a 
representation of historical discourse, we see how the use of the divine plupast 
informs not only the presentation of the narrative but also the events therein. 
This is very similar to Herodotus when, for example, he is talking to the Egyptian 
priests about lineages (2.2.5–2.3) and to priests in Tyre about Heracles’ sanctuary

The subsequent outline builds on this research, focusing again on the geopo- 


litical agōn and divine agency as in the analysis of Herodotus’ narrative. It high- 
lights Luke’s emphasis on how the divine realm intervenes in various ways to 
form a multi-ethnic people of God’s rule. It is not about geographical or colonial 
conquest in terms relatable to those awaiting physical and political deliverance 
from the Romans, because, in the end, no physical geopolitical territory is con- 
quered.18 It does, however, recognise Luke’s claims that the God of Israel contin- 
ues to set in motion the story and moves in known spaces – as in Paul’s words, 
“for this was not done in a corner” (26:26). Thus, Jesus’ disciples enter spaces that 
traditionally ‘belong’ to other peoples and to other gods, i.e., spaces understood to 
be under the protection of other forms of divine rule.19 Luke’s God – with and 
without human assistance – encounters individuals and groups from Jewish and 
non-Jewish lineage and integrates them into a multicultural movement. As in 
Herodotus’ Histories, human and divine activity are highlighted in parallel (e.g., 
Cambyses’ role in his fated death, Hist. 3.64–66). These spaces, as stated above, 
also include the heavens (i.e., the heavenly sanctuary seen by Stephen, 7:55–56), 
which is no small claim. This is understood as the new state of affairs, because, 
for Luke and his audience, it is as real as other spaces in the earthly realm.20

The ensuing commentary traces the intrigue of the geopolitical agōn as follows: 


(1) Divine rule continues and clashes with human and spiritual rule in Jerusalem 


(Acts 1:1–7:60) 


(2) Divine rule extends the agōn throughout Judea, Samaria, and Syria (Acts 8:1– 


12:25) 


(3) Divine rule moves the agōn westward to Cyprus and Asia Minor (Acts 13:1– 


15:35) 


(4) Divine rule crosses into Europe (Acts 15:36–18:22) 
(5) Divine rule clashes with human rule in Asia Minor with a focus on Ephesus 


(Acts 18:23–20:38) 


(6) Divine rule at the centre of the agōn in Judea and Jerusalem (Acts 21:1– 


23:30) 


(7) Divine rule brings the agōn to Imperial-ruled Caesarea (Acts 23:31–26:32) 
(8) Divine rule comes to Rome and the agōn continues (Acts 27:1–28:31) 


In the analysis below, for each of the eight sections listed above, three parts ex- 
plore the place of the divine in the narrative flow. First, a ‘section summary’ de- 
scribes the narrative and historical framework. This is particularly helpful to 
those who are unfamiliar with the Acts of the Apostles. Second, a ‘summary of 
divine interventions’ outlines divine activity in relation to the first element, offer- 
ing an idea of the types of τεκμήρια (1:3) used in Luke’s theological construction. 
The third element includes ‘focus passages’ concerning Luke’s prophetic voice 
and the agōn. In those sections, a few examples of divine activity are the object of 
sharper focus owing to their programmatic value for Luke-Acts. 


Appendix III may be helpful to readers as it displays the full list of the types 


of divine interventions in their order of appearance.21 Some of the occurrences 
are used in summary-type texts rather than in descriptions of specific divine acts. 
Also, sometimes Luke provides a cluster of divine activity that logically belong 
together in the narrative. These are sometimes listed as separate entries because 
of their distinctive nature (e.g., epiphany, judgement, etc.). Appendix III does not 
include the divine acts or oracles referred to in the speeches as instances of the 
‘divine plupast’. As in the discussions below, the focus of this appendix is rather 
on how Luke himself conveys perceptions of divine acts and speech having oc- 
curred within the limits of the narrative proper. 


The discussion now turns to Luke’s prophetic voice, his depiction of percep- 


tions of divine activity shaping human history between ca. 30–62 CE throughout 
the Mediterranean Basin.

For lists of miracles in Acts, see e.g., Hemer (1989) 435–436; Witherington (1998) 220. McGin-

11.3 Section 1: Divine Rule Continues and Clashes with Human 


and Spiritual Rule in Jerusalem (Acts 1:1–7:60) 


Section summary. This section begins by highlighting both Jesus’ continued pres- 
ence with his disciples (1:1–8) and his ascension (1:9–11). However, it concludes 
with the martyrdom of Stephen (6:8–7:60). This illustrates the intensity of the 
agōn in this section. The events take place in Jerusalem, suggesting that the sec- 
ond book will continue to focus on Jewish themes. The historical period is approx- 
imately 30–32 CE.22 


The tension of competing narratives surfaces quickly in the opening chapter. 


The seemingly logical question posed by Jesus’ disciples is geopolitically charged 
and deeply connected to one’s perception of the divine: “Lord, is this the time 
when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6).23 If Jesus is the Son of 
God and heir to the throne of David, challenging Rome’s imperial occupation and 
the Jewish authorities in Jerusalem would seem to be the next logical step. Jesus’ 
answer, however, leaves the matter open; stating that only “the Father” knows 
(1:7) and instructing his disciples to bring the news about him in “Jerusalem, in 
all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8). This activity, of course, 
raises the issue of expansion in Rome’s provinces, as promoting divine rule 
through a new “saviour god” elsewhere perceived as a direct affront to the Em- 
pire and Jewish communities. 


Luke continues to incorporate ‘works of power’24 within a divinely initiated 


narrative, namely, the metanarrative of Israel and the macronarrative of Jesus in 
volume one (cf. Chapter 5). Luke centres this first part of his narrative on the city 
of Jerusalem with much happening in and around the sacred spaces of the temple 
precincts. Luke continues to depict the intimate relationship between Jesus and 
the temple. Luke claims through his characters that this temple is just as much 
their place of worship as for other Jewish groups, because the God of that temple 
is the same one accomplishing acts and speech through Jesus’ disciples. Unsur- 
prisingly, the temple is the highlight of Stephen’s speech and, ironically, he is put 
to death for it. It continues to be a place of agōn as other sacred spaces are in the 
remainder of Acts. 


Jewish opposition almost always occurs in reaction to divine activity in rela- 


tion to Jesus as the source of works of power or as the object of his disciples’ mes-

sage. The agōn is not due to belief in the Jewish God or miracles themselves, but 
rather to the fact that both are mediated through Jesus. Consequently, Luke de- 
scribes the first judicial arrests and defence speeches, which mirror Jesus’ trials, 
mainly with Peter as spokesperson. This opposition is portrayed as becoming 
more acute, and it culminates climactically in Stephen’s death. 


Two further observations are significant. The judicial interventions involve 


again the highest Jewish authorities but without the aid of imperial personnel or 
structures. Also, there are only a few mentions of spiritual opposition (Satan, 5:3; 
unclean spirits, 5:16). Thus, the agōnes with the Empire and with spiritual antago- 
nists are kept in the background. The end of the first volume and the beginning of 
the second are thus plainly grounded in the Jewish cultural and geopolitical con- 
text. The agōn here develops mainly among those identified as Jewish in ethnicity 
or religion. 


Summary of divine interventions. Through the great quantity and variety of proofs 
of divine activity (τεκμήρια), Luke elicits his audience to evaluate the perceptions 
of and reactions to these interventions (seventeen listed in Appendix III). Luke is 
making a case for a new phase in the plan of God, which is centred on Jesus of 
Nazareth as ‘saviour god’, now proclaimed “Lord and Messiah” (2:36). For Luke, 
continuity is capital; the story of what Israel’s God had done in the past (observed 
in several ‘plupast’ sections) is now corroborated by what he was doing in the 
time period of the narrative. Thus, various types of τεκμήρια support Luke’s em- 
phasis on the ongoing activity of the divine realm: epiphany, guidance, prophetic 
speech, salvation, physical and spiritual healings, works of power, judgement, 
and visions. 


In this section, spiritual opposition is perceived as present, but not highlight- 


ed, through the healing of those disturbed by uncleans spirits (5:16). Luke’s focus 
is on divine activity in the interests of the population in Jerusalem. These acts are 
performed by various divine protagonists. Jesus’ presence is highlighted through 
his epiphany, salvation bequeathed in him, and works of power accomplished 
through him by his followers. The Holy Spirit, who was mentioned several times 
in the first volume, is reported as very active in this section through an epiphany, 
various acts of prophetic speech (discussed below), and an act of judgement. Also, 
as in the first volume, the activity of angels (divine messengers) continues 
through an epiphany and divine guidance (5:17–21). 


While the expression θεός occurs fifty-nine times in this section, it is mostly 


used by Luke and his characters to signify acts of the God of Israel in previous 
epochs and during Jesus’ life on earth. It is only used a few times in the list of 
seventeen divine acts, namely, regarding judgement (5:4), the growth of the word 
of God leading people to salvation (e.g., ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξανεν, 6:7). In some 
occurrences, when no specific divine actor is mentioned, it can be inferred that 
the protagonist of an act is ‘God’ or ‘the divine’, for example, in guiding the choice 


11 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts II 
347 


of Matthias by lot to replace Judas (1:21–26) and the salvation of people “added” 
(προσετέθησαν) to the followers of Jesus. The latter is an example of the divine 
passive, which begins a motif of divine salvation in which a divine actor is the 
logical subject (e.g., προσετίθει, 2:47; προσετίθεντο, 5:14; προσετέθη, 11:24). Al- 
so, the works of power done “by way of the hands of the apostles” are in effect 
wrought by God (e.g., 2:43; 5:12). In sum, all the above activity can be understood 
to be done ‘by God’ and as manifestations of ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ (1:3) and τὰ 
μεγαλεῖα τοῦ θεοῦ (2:11). 


Luke’s noteworthy depiction of divine activity underlines his perception 


that the world is now under divine rule through the agency of Jesus, who is pre- 
sented as the saviour of all peoples, not just one people in a specific region. Conse- 
quently, Luke includes one of the sternest warnings in Greek literature to not re- 
ject divine activity with haste. This is attributed to Gamaliel, a Pharisee of the 
Jewish council: “[…] but if it is of God, you will not be able to bring them down; 
you may even be found fighting against God (θεομάχοι εὑρεθῆτε)” (5:39).25 Since 
this warning is followed by some and rejected by others, the agōn continues in 
Jerusalem. 


Focus Passages of Luke’s Prophetic Voice and the Agōn. 


Pentecost and Peter’s Speech (2:1–42) 


The agōn is not nearly as hostile in this scene compared to later ones, but Luke 
does make it felt through a group of scoffers and in Peter’s response to them. 
Luke’s description of the manifestation of the Holy Spirit (2:1–13) displays vari- 
ous elements: multiple perceptions of divine activity, the convergence of narra- 
tive strands from the first volume, and a forceful claim of global rule of Israel’s 
God. It also introduces the first lengthy speech in the book, which provides a theo- 
logical interpretation of this dramatic event by way of Peter’s response to scoffers 
(2:14–36). 


It is not necessary to rehearse the whole scene; only the key elements are 


pointed out. It is clearly an epiphany-type scene (ὤφθησαν αὐτοῖς, 2:3) in which a 
divine protagonist appears “from heaven” accompanied by signs of the wind and 
tongues as of fire (2:1–4). The latter sign symbolically denotes the divine empow- 
erment of Jesus’ disciples to prophesy in various languages of the first century CE. 
Luke’s dual focus on the Jews and non-Jews is clear. A centripetal force draws 
people to Jerusalem, the focal point, expressing hope for the restoration of the 
kingdom to Israel. But it is also centrifugal, alluding to future movement towards 
the peoples, in light of Luke’s list of ethnic groups and regions and the proleptic 
promises of the Holy Spirit’s manifestation (Luke 3:15–17; 24:47 and Acts 1:8):

προσήλυτοι, Κρῆτες καὶ Ἄραβες, ἀκούομεν λαλούντων αὐτῶν ταῖς ἡμετέραις 
γλώσσαις τὰ μεγαλεῖα τοῦ θεοῦ. 


And how is it that we hear, each of us, in our own native language? Parthians, 
Medes, Elamites, and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and 
Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and 
visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs – in our own lan- 
guages we hear them speaking about God’s deeds of power. (Acts 2:8–11) 


The God of Israel speaks through this group of Galileans to people coming from 
all four directions, gathered in Jerusalem for the Jewish festival. The content of 
the disciples’ utterances is not stated specifically, but it concerns “God’s wonder- 
ful deeds” (τὰ μεγαλεῖα τοῦ θεοῦ, 2:11). This scene is foundational for the rest of 
the book because of its theistic claim to be pertinent to other peoples outside the 
people of Israel. It precedes the movements of Israel’s God to other regions. The 
scene ends with amazement and perplexity (2:12), but also with incredulity and 
scoffing (2:13): “But others were mocking, saying, ‘They are filled with new 
wine’.” Although humorous on the surface, this accusation is sacrilegious because 
it attributes a profane act to the realm of the holy. These mockers are the first 
theomachoi in the second volume. 


Luke shows Peter explaining the significance of the occurrence (2:14–36). 


He claims that the event fulfils an ancient oracle by the Jewish prophet Joel (quot- 
ed in 2:17–21; from Joel 3:1–5 LXX), and it is credited to Jesus: “Exalted therefore 
to the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the 
Holy Spirit, he [Jesus] has poured out (ἐξέχεεν) this that you are both seeing and 
hearing” (2:33).26 This affirmation reaches back to the first volume to John the 
Baptist’s prophecy about the Messiah: “He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit 
and fire” (Luke 3:20). Peter concludes by stating Jesus’ epithets (“both Lord and 
Messiah,” Acts 2:37; proleptically announced in Luke 2:11). Finally, this speech 
ends with a reference to salvation (via an exhortation, σώθητε, 2:4027) when 
around three thousand were baptised and added (προσετέθησαν, i.e., to the num- 
ber of those who believed, 2:41). 


Both the event and Peter’s speech touch upon the agōn in relation to Jesus’ 


life, the one who was “crucified and killed through the hand of lawless ones” 
(2:23); hence, the exhortation, “be saved from this perverse generation” (2:40). 
The first refers most likely to Roman involvement in Jesus’ execution and the sec- 


26 
The resurrection is supported in this speech through the citation of two texts: Ps 15:8–11 
(LXX; Acts 2:25–28) and Ps 109:1 (LXX; Acts 2:34–35). 


27 
The translations NRSV and ESV weaken the force of this aorist passive form: “save your- 
selves.” The logical subject of the verb is divine not human.

ond more generally to the context in which Jesus was depicted as being deceitful- 
ly judged by Jewish and non-Jewish antagonists. 


Finally, the coda (2:43–47) highlights “fear” (φόβος, reverence or awe) in re- 


lation to the wonders and signs accomplished through the apostles. A community 
ethic is expressed through members helping each other with practical needs, 
gathering for worship and teaching in the temple as well as in their homes. The 
final sentence underlines divine reconciliation: “And the Lord added to them dai- 
ly those who were being saved” (ὁ δὲ κύριος προσετίθει τοὺς σῳ ζομένους καθ’ 
ἡμέραν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό, 2:47). 


Healing of a disabled man, Peter’s arrest, and speech evincing the agōn (3:1–4:31). 
This section begins with a deed of power in the form of a physical healing, and it 
ends with a prayer of thanksgiving for the release of Peter and John’s arrest by 
the Jewish authorities. At first sight, it is difficult to understand how much trouble 
the healing of a disabled alms beggar could cause if it had not been attributed to 
the main protagonist, Jesus (3:6, 16; 4:10). For this reason, as observed in the Pen- 
tecost scene, the description of the healing is brief (3:1–10). But Peter’s explana- 
tion of the healing (3:11–26) triggers a sharp reaction from the Jewish authorities, 
which marks the first arrest and appearance before the Jewish council in the sec- 
ond volume (4:1–22). 


The context is again the temple precincts, and it is the time of prayer (the 


ninth hour = three o’clock in the afternoon). Luke shows that this sacred space is 
still available to them. The rupture with the temple’s activities has not yet oc- 
curred and theological continuity is underlined naming the God of the patriarchs 
(3:13). The actual healing takes place outside the temple grounds near the Beauti- 
ful Gate. Peter invites the man, disabled from birth, to stand up “in/by the name 
of Jesus Christ of Nazareth” (ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Ναζωραίου, 3:6, 16; 
4:10). After the healing, they enter the temple area; the healed man is recognised 
as the alms beggar from the Beautiful Gate and “all the people ran to them” in 
Solomon’s Portico (3:11). Peter refuses to take credit for the healing and recounts 
the story about Jesus’ rejection by his people (even killed by them, 3:14–15) and 
the resurrection (3:15, 17, 26). Luke shows Peter reaching into the divine plupast 
(3:17–26) by pointing out the fulfilment of several prophecies which reinforced 
Israel’s identity and destiny through whom “the families of the earth shall be 
blessed” (3:25). 


The agōn is triggered: the priests, the captain of the temple, and the Sad- 


ducees are provoked (διαπονούμενοι, 4:2) and they arrest the disciples, because 
they were teaching in the sacred space, the temple, and announcing the resurrec- 
tion of Jesus (4:2). Peter and John are held in custody for an appearance the next 
day before “[…] their rulers, elders, and scribes […] Annas the high priest, Cai- 
aphas, John, and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family” (4:5–6), 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
350 


whom Luke’s audience know from the previous volume. Luke adds that the num- 
ber of men in Jesus’ movement was growing, now around five thousand (4:4). 


The agōn is centred on the question by the Jewish authorities: “By what pow- 


er or by what name did you do this?” (4:7). The response is unequivocal: “[…] 
that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God 
raised from the dead this man is standing before you in good health” (4:10). Peter 
also points to Jesus as saviour: “There is salvation (σωτηρία) in no one else, for 
there is no other name under heaven given among humans by which we must be 
saved” (ἐν ᾧ δεῖ σωθῆναι ἡμᾶς, 4:12). The problem is Christocentric, because they 
could not refute this “notable sign” (γνωστὸν σημεῖον, 4:16).28 Therefore, the au- 
thorities warn Peter and John “not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus” 
(τὸ καθόλου μὴ φθέγγεσθαι μηδὲ διδάσκειν ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, 4:18). Luke 
shows that the Jewish authorities, as they had acted with Jesus, have once again 
become theomachoi. 


This is reinforced by the coda, which displays a collective prayer for contin- 


ued boldness in testimony, in which the agōn against Jesus is retold and paral- 
leled (synkrisis) with his disciples’ ill-treatment (4:23–31). The narrative struc- 
ture is paralleled in subsequent ‘healing-hostile reaction’ scenes.29 The prayer 
displays an awareness of robust faith in theistic sovereignty as well as in a divine 
plan being accomplished through the ages: “Sovereign God, you who made the 
heaven and the earth, the sea, and all things in them” (4:24). A corroborating 
prophecy is cited (Ps 2:1–2), and the agonistic nature of the story of Jesus is re- 
hearsed, which underlines the participation of Herod and Pontius Pilate with the 
peoples and Israel, “against your holy servant Jesus” (4:27). Luke wishes to incul- 
cate in his audience the belief in a cosmic saviour, not merely a local one from 
Judea. The prayer asks for boldness in witness and for accompanying works of 
power “through the name of your holy servant Jesus” (4:30). Divine approval 
manifests itself immediately with the place being shook and the fullness of the 
Holy Spirit working in each of them (4:31). 


Healings and intense persecution (5:17–42). Luke offers a brief look into the com- 
munity life of Jesus’ followers (4:32–5:11) in which harmony and generosity are 
shattered by the lies and meanness of Ananias and Sapphira (inspired by Satan, 
5:3), resulting in immediate divine judgement. Following this brief reference to 
spiritual opposition, Luke resumes the agōn in Jewish contexts by presenting still 
another example of synkrisis, this time between the suffering of Jesus in Jer-

usalem and that of his disciples at the hands of the Jewish authorities. The context 
is again Solomon’s Portico, and it concerns healings, both physical and spiritual 
(5:15–16). A night arrest of an unknown number of “apostles” follows, and a 
court appearance is supposed to take place in the morning, except that “an angel 
of the Lord” had already set them free and sent them back to the temple to preach 
(5:19–21). A second arrest is made and the charge against them centres on their 
disobedience in teaching “in this name” (5:28). Peter and the apostles (unnamed) 
retell the story of Jesus whom they call “leader and saviour” (ἀρχηγὸν καὶ 
σωτῆρα) by whom “he [God] might give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of 
sins” (5:31). 


Here the council’s violent reaction intensifies and mirrors reactions from 


the first volume in relation to Jesus (19:47; 22:2; 23:18–21): “When they heard 
this, they were cut to the heart and wanted to kill them” (5:33). Luke now pres- 
ents Gamaliel’s intervention to plead for a cautious approach, allowing God him- 
self to deal with this group (5:34–39): “[…] but if it is of God, you will not be able 
to bring them down; you may even be found fighting against God (θεομάχοι)” 
(5:39).30 Luke depicts Gamaliel as a reliable witness (5:34), similar to Herodotus’ 
‘wise adviser’, thus strengthening this episode’s rhetorical force.31 Also, Luke’s 
multicultural audience may have picked up resonances in Greek and Jewish sour- 
ces about ‘fighting against’ the divine realm.32 Although the council was con- 
vinced by Gamaliel, they had the apostles flogged and threatened them not to 
speak in the name of Jesus (5:39–40). Luke’s readers know that Gamaliel’s speech 
has been confirmed, as they interpret the grave error of beating the disciples in 
light of Peter’s miraculous release from prison.33 In addition, while Jesus’ disci- 
ples continue their divinely-given mandate at the temple and in their homes 
(5:41–42), the agōn is not resolved and only gets worse – through the climax of 
the first section – with the martyrdom of Stephen, a Jewish follower of Jesus.

Stephen’s speech and agōn (6:1–7:60). Narratively, this dramatic episode func- 
tions as the climax of the story in Jerusalem. It begins with a brief description of 
an internal complaint of division of food among Jesus’ followers (6:1): the Greek- 
speaking widows were receiving less than the Hebrew speakers (ἐγένετο γογγυ- 
σμὸς τῶν Ἑλληνιστῶν πρὸς τοὺς Ἑβραίους, 6:1). Luke uses this episode to intro- 
duce some key characters among the Greek-speaking Jewish community, espe- 
cially Stephen, “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (6:5). The end of this long 
section features his tragic death by lapidation at the hands of the Jewish authori- 
ties among whom a certain Saul (later ‘Paul’) exercised an authoritative function 
(7:58–60). This section is mainly composed of Stephen’s defence speech, which is 
the longest speech in Acts (7:1–53). It features a summary of the Jewish metanar- 
rative upon which Luke’s two volumes are constructed. Luke’s prophetic voice is 
illustrated well here as the speech must have been didactically invaluable for 
those of his audience unfamiliar with Jewish history and theology. The discussion 
below focuses on the accusations of sacrilege and divine activity. 


Luke highlights the agōn with the Jewish authorities who present false accu- 


sations against Stephen by Greek-speaking Jews of “the synagogue of the Freed- 
men,” in which there were representatives of Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, and 
Asia (6:9). In a perverse manner, their accusations against Stephen concern blas- 
phemous speech: he allegedly spoke against Moses and God (6:11), “the holy place 
and the law” (κατὰ τοῦ τόπου τοῦ ἁγίου [τούτου] καὶ τοῦ νόμου, 6:13) with the 
objective of changing Jewish customs (τὰ ἔθη, 6:14). But Luke foreshadows Ste- 
phen’s innocence by depicting his countenance like the face of an angel (6:15). 


From 7:2 onwards, Stephen responds to the high priest by addressing the 


council, similar to the beginning of speeches to the Athenian assembly in the clas- 
sical period: “O men, brothers and fathers” (Ἄνδρες ἀδελφοὶ καὶ πατέρες), re- 
counting Israel’s story from Abraham, Moses, David, and Solomon who built the 
first great temple in Jerusalem. This rhetorical use of the divine plupast parallels 
the guilt of Stephen’s contemporaries with those Israelites who had rejected Mos- 
es (7:35, 39), practised idolatry (7:40–43; corroborated by Amos 5:25–27 LXX), 
and persecuted prophets (7:52). Stephen offers no diplomatic resolution but rath- 
er – like prophets of old – challenges the authorities’ hypocrisy: “Stiff-necked and 
uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your ances- 
tors did so do you” (7:51). And he adds this judgement: “They killed those who 
foretold the coming of the righteous one and now have become his traitors and 
murderers” (7:52). 


Stephen’s blunt rejoinder encounters immediate wrath: “When they heard 


these things, they were cut to the heart and were grinding their teeth at him” 
(7:54). Here Luke presents Stephen’s vision, which may have been the word that 
pushed the Jewish authorities to execute Stephen on the spot. Luke reports that 
Stephen sees “the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (7:55), 
then it is repeated through Stephen’s voice: “Behold, I see the heavens opened 


11 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts II 
353 


and the Son of man standing at the right hand of God!” (7:56). This vision echoes 
Luke’s depiction of Jesus in volume 1 who is described in divine and filial terms.34 


Luke’s audience was probably prepared to hear this vision, but certainly not Ste- 
phen’s audience who proceeded to drag him out of the city and stone him (7:58). 
Stephen’s innocence is paralleled with Jesus’ innocence before various authori- 
ties, and it is sealed, rhetorically speaking, by Stephen’s prayer to Jesus for him- 
self and for forgiveness of his executioners (7:59–60). In relation to the question 
‘Where is the kingdom of God?’, these divine actions point to two realities from 
Stephen’s perspective. Jesus already reigns with God and those who oppose Ste- 
phen and his faith oppose God (7:51) and are in effect theomachoi. 


11.4 Section 2: Divine Rule Extends the Agōn throughout Judea, 


Samaria, and Syria (Acts 8:1–12:25) 


Section summary. Following the dramatic portrayal of Stephen’s death, Luke dis- 
plays geographic trajectories, leading his audience away from Jerusalem to ex- 
plore divine interventions and ensuing conflicts in the regions of Judea, Galilee, 
Samaria, Phenicia, Cyprus, and Syria (cf. 8:1; 11:19). Jesus and his movement are 
shown to penetrate diverse places and entities within the territory of the Roman 
Empire. Again, the chronology of the events is difficult to establish; it is approxi- 
mately the period from 31/32 to 44 CE.35 What matters to Luke and his audience is 
this outward movement. In addition, the causal connection between the episodes 
is not always clear. However, a key word in this section is ‘scatter’ (διασπείρω, NT 
occurrences only in Acts: 8:1, 4; 11:19), and the ‘scattering’ is perceived as the 
result of human agency in connection with the martyrdom of Stephen: “That day 
a great persecution arose against the church in Jerusalem […] and all were dis- 
persed throughout the lands of Judea and Samaria except the apostles” (8:1) and 
“Saul was damaging the church” (8:3). But Luke quickly introduces the notion of 
how this violence and ensuing flight to other regions influenced the disciples’ 
mandate: “Now then those who were dispersed (διασπαρέντες) spread out, pro- 
claiming the word” (8:4). This summarises well the unity of the section with its 
emphasis on witness, and it underscores the divinely prompted scattering, which 
becomes a centrifugal force from here to the end of the volume. This section also 
relates how the imperial presence reappears in the narrative with characters 
who are favourable (Cornelius) and hostile (Herod Agrippa I) to Jesus’ disciples. 


34 
E.g., announcement of Jesus’ birth (1:32, 35); God’s voice at Jesus’ baptism (3:22); Jesus at the 
temple, his father’s house (2:49); the transfiguration (9:35); ‘the Son of man’ epithet (5:24; 
6:5, 22 and passim); the two epiphanies in Luke 24:13–49; and the two accounts of the ascen- 
sion (Luke 24:50–53; Acts 1:6–11). 


35 
With the opening year marking the persecution of the Hellenists then Paul’s conversion, and 
the final year marking the death of Herod Agrippa I (cf. Acts 12:1–23). See Dunn (2009) 510– 
512 and Bruce and Taylor (1986) 276–278.

354 


To highlight this, Luke focuses on central characters in relation to the re- 


gions mentioned above. Luke makes Saul (‘Paul’ from 13:9 on) the outer frame of 
this section through the portrayal of his spiritual transformation, from witness to 
Stephen’s death in Jerusalem to witness of Jesus in Antioch (cf. 8:1; 12:24). With- 
in this framework, Luke features Philip in Acts 8 in relation to events in Samaria 
and on the desert road of Jerusalem–Gaza. The integration of non-ethnic Jews and 
their corresponding regions are here underlined through the conversion of Sa- 
maritans and of an influential Ethiopian eunuch. 


In Acts 9, Luke turns his spotlight on Saul’s dramatic encounter of Jesus in a 


vision. Saul is on his way to arrest disciples in Damascus, but his plan is thwarted 
by Jesus and Saul is incorporated into Jesus’ movement. Then from 9:32 on, Peter 
is again the protagonist accomplishing works of power on the coast of the Levant 
(Lydda, Joppa, etc.). This focus on Peter continues (10:1–11:18) with another high- 
lighted ‘conversion narrative’ that unexpectedly contributes to the imperial agōn. 
It concerns Cornelius, a Roman centurion, and his family and friends. 


Their integration into the movement then needs justification before the 


movement’s leaders in Jerusalem. In 11:19–30, Antioch of Syria is the focal point 
where Barnabas and Saul collaborate to instruct the “great number” of disciples 
(11:21–25). Luke informs his audience – perhaps proudly, owing to his traditional 
contact with Antioch – that it is here that “the disciples were first called ‘Chris- 
tians’” (11:26; elsewhere only two other times in the NT: Acts 26:28 and 1 Pet 
4:16).36 


In the final part, Luke resumes the agōn with imperial authorities; this time 


with Herod Agrippa I whom Luke designates as βασιλεύς (12:1). This Herod or- 
ders the decapitation of Jesus’ disciple John, brother of James (12:2). The depic- 
tion of this martyrdom receives little attention, while more focus is given to Pe- 
ter’s arrest by Herod (12:3–19). Like other prison scenes in Acts, Peter is 
delivered by divine intervention. Herod’s fate is brought to a deadly end by di- 
vine retribution (12:18–23). The section ends with one of Luke’s progress sum- 
maries (12:24–25), which – via a hendiadys – describes the growth and multipli- 
cation of the word of God (Ὁ δὲ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξανεν καὶ ἐπληθύνετο, 12:24). 


Summary of divine interventions. This section presents a significant number and 
variety of divine activity (see Appendix III), which is perceived as moving the sto- 
ry forward through the regions named above. The God that Luke describes has 
power outside the centre of cultic activity in Jerusalem. Jesus as ‘saviour god’ is 
highlighted through direct works of power, epiphanies, and visions, etc. Again, 
the healings and prophetic speech accomplished by his disciples are understood 
to be through divine power rather than through their own ability or ingenuity. 


36 
For Luke’s alleged connection to Antioch of Syria, cf. Chapter 4.1.2 Luke and his world.

Other divine actors who are specifically named are the Holy Spirit and an 


angel of the Lord, as well as the personifications of the divine such as ‘the word of 
the Lord’ and ‘the hand of God’. By contrast, one of the first reports of illegitimate 
supernatural power comes through the person of Simon in Samaria, known as 
“the power of God that is called Great” (8:10, ἡ δύναμις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ καλουμένη 
μεγάλη). Luke carefully shows the subordination of this ‘power’ in the presence 
of protagonists of the kingdom of God. 


Focus Passages of Luke’s Prophetic Voice and the Agōn 


The section summary above has given an idea of Luke’s prophetic voice at work. 
Here, the discussion turns to a selection of passages that illustrate peaks of narra- 
tive highlights and tension. The section begins with an intensification of the agōn 
in the Jewish context. Luke describes it as a “great persecution” (διωγμὸς μέγας) 
against the “church” or “assembly” (ἐπὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, i.e., an ellipsis of “assem- 
bly of followers/disciples of Jesus,” 8:1). One of the scattered disciples, Philip, en- 
counters little conflict in comparison. As noted above, only Simon, “the power of 
God that is called Great” (8:10), causes some concern and is resolved through a 
successful intervention by Philip’s leaders, Peter and John (8:18–24). The three 
passages below depict how divine rule incorporates a Jewish persecutor and a Ro- 
man official and then deals a death blow to a powerful member of the Herodian 
family. 


Saul’s encounter with the ascended Jesus in Damascus (9:1–9). This passage depicts 
one of the most celebrated scenes in the Acts of the Apostles.37 As a key part of the 
repertoire of Luke’s prophetic voice, it is featured three times in this volume: 
once in Luke’s voice and twice in Saul’s voice (i.e., Paul’s speeches, 22:6–11; 
26:12–18). Luke has already introduced Saul as an antagonistic character in rela- 
tion to the stoning of Stephen. He further characterises Saul’s fierce devotion to 
eradicate Jesus’ disciples: “While Saul was still breathing forth threat and murder 
against the disciples of the Lord, he went to the high priest and asked him for 
letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who were of the 
Way, he might bring men and women bound to Jerusalem” (9:1–2). Being a de- 
vout Pharisee, Saul believed in divine rule, but, as per Luke’s portrayal, his faith 
lacked Jesus of Nazareth. Saul is represented – in narrative terms related to the 
agōn – as the foremost individual antagonist, the θεομάχος in the Jewish world. 
Thus, this scene has two main potential trajectories: either judgement for his vio- 
lence or humble recognition of Jesus as ‘saviour god’ and incorporation with 


37 
For this scene’s reception history, cf. e.g., Cuvillier (2022). 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
356 


“those of the Way” (road, path, τινας τῆς ὁδοῦ ὄντας, 9:2).38 Symbolically, this ‘on 
the road’ encounter functions as a crossroads both for Paul, and, narratively, also 
for Luke’s audience. 


Saul’s authority is presented as originating from the leadership in Jer- 


usalem, which has clout in the Jewish synagogues in Damascus (cf. 9:14). Saul’s 
potential – for either side – is great. As the narrative progresses, Luke positively 
displays Saul’s Jewish training and learning, his Roman citizenship from birth, 
and his excellent understanding of the Greek language and culture. Narratively, 
the stakes are indeed high, because, if Luke can show Saul’s subordination to di- 
vine rule in Jesus, he has shown to his audience how these three cultural realities 
(in one person) present no intrinsic obstacle or ultimate power over those adher- 
ing to the reign of God. Not only this, but Luke also shapes the narrative to show 
that one may take part in one or all of these three realities and still be a follower 
of Jesus.39 


The importance of this scene is underscored by this epiphany of Jesus as the 


showcase epiphany in Acts. Luke presents the ascended Jesus taking the initiative 
to influence the direction of history. This is evinced through sight and sound: “a 
light from heaven flashed around him [Saul]” and a voice heard by Saul and by 
his companions (9:3–4, 7). The exchange is briefly presented here and then am- 
plified in the two parallel passages of Saul’s conversion. The voice challenges Saul 
with a haunting question: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (9:4). The 
vital union between Jesus and his followers is expressed no more strongly than 
this in the two volumes. Saul’s answer recognises that he is facing a greater au- 
thority: “Who are you, Lord?”, and the irony of the response of self-identification: 
“I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But stand up and enter the city, and you 
will be told what you must do” (9:5–6). Saul has been floored (“he fell to the 
ground”) and blinded (“for three days he was without sight”), and he chooses to 
obey Jesus’ order with the help of his travel companions (9:8–9). Divine rule has 
put an end to Saul’s aggression and will put him to service for the kingdom of 
God. 


Through various short indications, Luke authenticates Saul’s integration 


into Jesus’ movement in Damascus: a vision of “the Lord” to Ananias who wel- 
comes and heals Saul (9:10–25); Saul’s preaching about Jesus in the synagogues 
(9:19–22); and his becoming a persecuted disciple that needs to escape (9:23– 
25).40 Luke also cites Jesus, who has ascended, in the vision to Ananias. This fore- 


38

shadows what to expect regarding Saul throughout the rest of the narrative: “Go

Returning to Jerusalem, Saul receives a hesitant but successful welcome to 


Jesus’ movement in Jerusalem (9:26–28), but he must escape from a murderous 
plot by some Greek-speaking Jews (Ἑλληνιστάς). He then flees from Jerusalem to 
Caesarea and Tarsus, his home city (9:29–30). In this short passage, Saul has now 
become – with Peter – a chief protagonist in Luke’s narrative for his audience. 
Peter and Paul become the chief ‘focalisers’ of Luke’s narrative in that it is 
through their ‘eyes’ that some of the key events are viewed by the audience, and 
they progressively embody – for the audience – the central values of the move- 
ment’s faith and practice. Saul will return on the scene in Antioch, one of the ma- 
jor centres of Jesus’ disciples in Luke’s narrative (11:19–30). 


Cornelius’ encounter with divine rule in Caesarea (10:1–48). After this focus on 
Saul, Luke returns to his other main protagonist, Peter, whose acts of healing in 
Lydda and Joppa are briefly presented (9:32–43). Now Luke offers to his audience 
another highlighted conversion scene of an official of the Empire’s military. We 
have seen that Luke has an interest in showing how people of authority, both 
Jewish and non-Jewish, encounter the divine, which is particularly true for Ro- 
man centurions.41 In Luke-Acts, this is the highlighted episode of Roman officials 
who encounter and welcome divine interventions.42 The narrative has all the po- 
tential for an imperial arrest of an agitator. But with a touch of irony, Cornelius is 
far from being a θεομάχος; rather, he is the epitome of a non-Jewish θεόφιλος 
(Luke 1:3).43 The importance of this story to Luke and his audience is confirmed 
by the lengthy narrative of the events surrounding Peter and Cornelius’ meeting, 
which comprises all forty-eight verses of Acts, chapter 10. In addition, Luke helps 
his audience to interpret the events through Peter’s report to the church leaders 
in Jerusalem (11:1–18). This passage offers a glimpse of the institutional accep- 
tance of non-Jews in Jesus’ movement, which is further confirmed in Acts 15. 
More than that, it underscores the divine rule that hinders the unrestrained im- 
perial impulse by integrating insiders of the same human power.

Cornelius is described by his position, a centurion of the Italian cohort, an 


auxiliary unit of the Roman army (10:1), and by his social and religious engage- 
ment: “a pious man who feared God with all his household, giving many alms to 
the people and praying continually to God” (10:2). Luke blends various actions 
leading to the culmination of the event: the Holy Spirit ‘falling’ on Cornelius and 
those with him and their subsequent baptism (10:44–48). This is perceived as a 
work of divine orchestration. Cornelius’ piety to the Jewish God is recognised 
(10:2, 4, 22), and he receives instructions by an angel of God in a vision (ὅραμα) to 
send for Peter who was staying in Joppa.44 The reason is not stated, but Cornelius 
obeys and sends “two of his slaves and a pious soldier” (10:7). The next day Peter 
falls into a trance (ἔκστασις, 10:10; ὅραμα, 10:17). He sees heaven opening and 
hears a voice. The purpose of this divine communication (repeated three times) 
was to remove Peter’s reluctance – due to alimentary and cultural restrictions 
(10:13–15; 11:2–3) – to have table fellowship with people outside the Jewish com- 
munity.45 This is another instance of focalisation through Peter who is also uncer- 
tain about the reason for being sent to Caesarea (10:29). An additional act of di- 
vine speech – via “the Spirit” (τὸ πνεῦμα) – tells Peter to go with the men to 
Cornelius “without hesitation” (μηδὲν διακρινόμενος, 10:19–20). 


Luke carefully points out the conclusion that “the peoples” are now theologi- 


cally and institutionally received through “the gift of the Holy Spirit” (who “fell 
upon all who heard”) and then through baptism (Acts 10:44–47). This is ex- 
pressed through Peter’s conclusion in Caesarea (10:47) and then through the con- 
clusion of church leaders in Jerusalem: “If then God gave them the same gift as to 
us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I [Peter] that I could hin- 
der God? When they heard this, they quieted down and they glorified God, say- 
ing, ‘Then God has given even to the peoples (τοῖς ἔθνεσιν) the repentance that 
leads to life’” (11:17–18). Luke does not show whether Cornelius (and those with 
him) continued to play a role in the spread of Jesus’ movement, but the conver- 
sion story serves as further τεκμήρια for Luke’s multicultural audience to live 
their faith in Jesus, despite still living under the Roman Empire, which included 
some unexpected people – from the narrator’s point of view – like Cornelius and 
his family. The narrative strand about Caesarea and Jesus’ movement will re- 
sume when Luke turns his attention to Paul’s two-year arrest during the adminis- 
trations of the imperial governors, Felix and Festus (23:31–26:32).

Herod Agrippa encounters divine rule in Caesarea (12:1–25). Luke provides an- 
other description of the movement’s progress with a brief focus on Antioch 
(11:19–30) in which Barnabas is the protagonist who responds to the needs of the 
growing community of followers there and consequently fetches Saul from Tar- 
sus for his assistance in teaching. This success story does not last long, narratively 
speaking. Attention is now given to another antagonist of the Herodian family, 
Herod Agrippa I (Herod the Great’s grandson).46 Luke shows his audience how 
political authorities, as high as this Herod, remain subject to divine rule. Similar 
to the judgement narrative about the dishonesty of Ananias and Sapphira within 
Jesus’ movement (5:1–11), this episode also demonstrates divine retribution – a 
massive theme in Greek literature – for his sins of θεομαχία and sacrilegious 
ὕβρις.47 


Agrippa’s full Roman name is Marcus Julius Agrippa I (10 BCE–44 CE). He 


was brought up in the imperial court in Rome. Thanks to Gaius Caligula, Agrippa 
became the successor of Herod Philip. He had control over Galilee, Perea, as well 
as Judea and Samaria during the last three years of his reign. This was approxi- 
mately the equivalent of his grandfather’s territory. Luke refers to Agrippa I as 
Ἡρῳ ́δης ὁ βασιλεύς with language similar to the description of Saul’s persecution 
of those of the Way: “About that time Herod the king set his hands to harm some 
who belonged to the church. He condemned James, the brother of John, to death 
by sword. Seeing that it was pleasing to the Jews, he persisted in arresting Peter 
as well. (This was during the days of Unleavened Bread)” (12:1–3). 


These early martyrs receive, comparatively, little attention, but their deaths 


lead to Agrippa’s fatal judgement. All of this leads to another prison episode. Pe- 
ter is guarded by “four squads of soldiers” until his release at the Passover (12:4). 
His time in prison is interrupted by an “angel of the Lord,” who enables Peter to 
escape to the house of Mary, John Mark’s mother in Jerusalem (12:6–12), and 
then to Caesarea (12:19).48 


Peter’s escape was inexplicable to Agrippa, so he ordered the soldiers to be 


executed (12:18–19). Agrippa appears to be incapable of recognising this as a sign 
of God’s sovereignty over his realm, refusing a divine warning to him to cease his 
persecution of Jesus’ followers. Gradually, Luke moves on to the divine execution 
of Agrippa (12:20–23). The setting is also one of an agōn. For reasons unstated,

pa II appears later in the narrative at Paul’s trial in Caesarea. 


11.5 Section 3: Divine Rule Moves the Agōn westward to Cyprus 


and Asia Minor (Acts 13:1–15:35) 


Section summary. A comparison between the beginning and the end of this sec- 
tion will help us to grasp the significance of its geographical movement, geopoliti- 
cal diversity, and theological import. Luke begins the section with Saul (“Paul” 
from 13:9 on) and Barnabas leaving Antioch in Syria for Cyprus (13:1–4), and he 
concludes it with Paul and Timothy in Lystra in the region of Lycaonia in the Ro- 
man Province of Galatia (16:1–5). Luke’s objective here is to give an idea of some 
of the key moments that took place among Jews and non-Jews, in synagogues and 
public spaces in Cyprus and Asia Minor. The movement of Jesus – now viewed 
mainly through the lens of Saul of Tarsus – continues to develop globally in reach 
and composition. Narratively, tension is building up for the climactic episode in 
Jerusalem where church leaders debate the criteria for non-Jewish integration. 


The narrative displays a pattern of the apostles’ urban visits: they begin in 


the regions’ synagogues among the native Jewish community as well as the 
προσήλυτοι (13:43). This brings conflict within and without Jesus’ movement, 
and the key moments of reception and rejection of the message about Jesus are 
shown to highlight these tensions. Of note is Luke’s use of ἀπόστολοι to describe

Once again, the scene in Cyprus portrays Roman officials in a positive light. 


Here, the focus is on Sergius Paulus, the proconsul (ἀνθύπατος) in Paphos.51 This

more is said about his subsequent integration in the movement, but he is most 
likely responsible for making contact with his family in Antioch in Pisidia for the 
apostles’ ensuing journey.52 Ironically, Luke places this perceptive Roman official 
against a foil in a certain Bar-Jesus (or Elymas), a Jewish magician and false 
prophet who unsuccessfully opposes “the Way.” Like other θεομάχοι before him, 
Elymas is silenced and is not able to impede Sergius Paulus from coming to faith 
in the ‘saviour god’ from Jewish roots (13:6–11).53 Once more, Luke offers yet an- 
other illustration to his audience of how Jesus’ movement integrates Jews and 
non-Jews from diverse social backgrounds. The response to Paul’s teachings re- 
garding Jesus, as opposed to ethnicity, results in the salvation of Sergius Paulus, 
an imperial administrator.

Of note is how Luke elucidates, again, the divine-human agōn, namely, those 


portrayed as religious or devout (Jew or non-Jew) to a competing theological enti- 
ty are often shown to be antagonistic to God’s plan or activity. Here the geopoliti- 
cal and religious spheres are drawn together, since the apostles are driven out of 
Antioch in Pisidia by “pious women of high standing and the leading men of the 
city” (τὰς σεβομένας γυναῖκας τὰς εὐσχήμονας καὶ τοὺς πρώτους τῆς πόλεως, 
13:50). 


From there, Luke’s audience follows the missionary team towards Iconium 


(14:1–7) where “a great number of both Jews and Greeks became believers” 
(14:1). After remaining there “a long time” (14:3), division and conflict follow, 
even an attempt to stone the apostles (14:5). They flee to Lystra and Derbe and 
the surrounding region of Lycaonia. The movement’s success among Jews and 
Greeks – mentioned in the same breath in 14:1 – is contrasted with ensuing vio- 
lent conflicts with some, not all, Jews living in the diaspora. The narrative force of 
this portrayal is that various agōnes are prompted here – human against divine 
resulting in human against human – and demonstrated through subsequent par- 
ticular events. 


Below, the focused scene will be that of Lystra (14:8–20), with the discussion 


centring primarily on its theological significance. The agōn is so dramatic that it 
results in an attempted public execution. Saul who had supported Stephen’s ston- 
ing is now Paul, lapidated and left for dead. From the moment he gets up (14:20) 
until the next major scene in Jerusalem (15:4–30), Luke speeds up narrative time 
by summing up events in Derbe, a return to Lystra, Iconium, Antioch in Pisidia, 
then Perga in Pamphylia, and, finally, by boat from Attalia to Antioch (14:20–28). 


Luke is preparing his audience to experience the tension regarding an in- 


tense debate about those of “the peoples” who wish to become Jesus’ followers. 
The conflict develops on two lines: Paul and Barnabas’ report that God “had 
opened a door of faith to the peoples” (14:27) and the position held by some of the 
“school of the Pharisees” (ἀπὸ τῆς αἱρέσεως τῶν Φαρισαίων, 15:5) according to 
which “If you have not been circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you 
cannot be saved” (15:1; restated in 15:5).56 This debate echoes the heated discus-

sion concerning Cornelius’ conversion and baptism, which was also questioned

Luke describes the tension with one of his well-known litotes: “a no small 


dissension and debate” (στάσεως καὶ ζητήσεως οὐκ ὀλίγης, 15:2). Once again, di- 
vine agency is underlined by Luke in Paul and Barnabas’ defence: “they reported 
all that God had done through them” (15:4); via Peter’s voice: “And God, the 
knower of hearts, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, as he did 
to us” (15:8); and, again, Paul and Barnabas reported “all the signs and wonders 
that God had done through them among the peoples” (15:12), which is conclusive- 
ly supported by James’ voice: “Simeon has related how God first considered care- 
fully to take from among the peoples a people for his name” (15:14). This state- 
ment is supported by a conflation of Jewish prophetic texts.57 James’ statement is 
crucial for understanding Luke-Acts as a whole, and specifically the direction of 
the rest of the book. In Luke’s theological construction, the God of Israel is form- 
ing a people, comprised of all peoples, not only with the covenant people, Israel. 
With James’ authority, the decision is made to send a letter to all those “from the 
peoples” who have received the teaching about Jesus. Integration is confirmed 
and some ethical boundaries and dietary practices are established to facilitate fel- 
lowship with followers of Jewish ethnicity. 


Summary of divine interventions. Although Luke displays only seven occurrences 
of specific acts of divine action (compared to seventeen and twenty in the previ- 
ous sections; cf. Appendix III), divine activity sets the tone for the section in the 
opening lines: “While they [the prophets and teachers in Antioch] were worship- 
ing the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul 
for the task to which I have called them’” (13:2). The divine realm, here via the 
Holy Spirit, is again said to set people in motion (cf. Luke 2:27; 4:1, 14; Acts 
11:12). Divine initiative is highlighted as the whole section displays the apostles’ 
God moving with them into Cyprus and Asia Minor, territories with other gods 
but also with some Jewish communities. 


Divine presence, directly or indirectly conducted through Jesus’ followers, 


does not meet with indifference. This aspect of cultural and cultic encounters be- 
comes more pronounced from this point onwards. Luke’s narrative focuses on 
the reactions of the internal audiences who hear the message from the apostles. 
Despite the considerable distance from Jerusalem, the agōn with the Jewish au- 
thorities continues unabated. For example, Jewish elements in Antioch incited 
(παρώτρυναν58) people and raised up (ἐπήγειραν) persecution (13:50) and in Ico-

and confirmation for Luke’s ethnically diverse audience.60 


Focus Passage of Luke’s Prophetic Voice and the Agōn 


Barnabas and Paul before the gods and their worshippers in Lystra (14:8–20). This 
passage is explored here because it is the first highlighted encounter and clash 
between Jesus’ movement and pagan religions in public spaces. The irony and 
tragedy of this brief story is that it begins with the healing of a man disabled from 
birth, and it ends with Paul being stoned, but not quite to death. The point is that, 
although divine action was manifest, it did not lead to the result of conversion as 
in other instances recounted by Luke. As in other scenes, an example of the apos- 
tles’ teaching and preaching is present, which helps to illustrate the differences in 
worldviews at the scene. 


This passage evokes previous scenes involving agents with divine power en- 


countering disabled persons (e.g., Luke 5:17–26; 18:35–43; Acts 3:1–10; 9:32–35). 
The notion of continuity through synkrisis is emphasised again here. Most of 
Luke’s audience could presumably imagine the cultural context in which Paul

pagan interpretation and agitation of the crowds by Jews from Antioch and Iconi- 
um (14:19). Commentators often point to a historic precedent, an example of θεο- 
ξενία, which is said to have occurred in Phrygia. Ovid (Metam. 8.611–724) tells of 
the legend of Jupiter and Mercury (Roman names for Zeus and Hermes) who 
came disguised as humans and were welcomed by an elderly couple, Philemon 
and Baucis. Epigraphic studies have also supported this legendary material.61 This 
information may explain the enthusiastic reception by the priests as colourfully 
depicted by Luke.62 Confusion is manifest in this cultural clash. On the theological 
level, the crowd in Lystra recognises the intervention of the divine realm, but it is 
interpreted as coming from the wrong source as Paul will forcefully challenge. 
Linguistic differences also contribute to the confusion, as the crowd speaks in the 
Lycaonian language (Λυκαονιστί, 14:11). The apostles understand the crowd’s 
misinterpretation when the priest “brought oxen and garlands to the gates [that] 
he and the crowds wanted to sacrifice” (14:13). 


Luke now moves to Paul and Barnabas’ passionate refusal to receive hon- 


ours, which can only be understood by their worldview about which we receive a 
glimpse through Luke’s summary (14:15–17). It is an emotionally charged plea: 
“they tore their clothes and leapt forth into the crowd, shouting […]” (διαρρήξαν- 
τες τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτῶν ἐξεπήδησαν εἰς τὸν ὄχλον κράζοντες, 14:14). The argument 
follows as such: Paul and Barnabas are mortals. They offer a message from a di- 
vine source, the living God. A critique of their traditional religion is evident: this 
God created everything, and he should not be worshipped vainly in their manner 
(ἀπὸ τούτων τῶν ματαίων ἐπιστρέφειν ἐπὶ θεὸν ζῶντα, 14:15). In the past, this 
God showed generosity and patience towards all the peoples (14:16). Indeed, “he 
has not left himself without a witness in doing good” (14:17), that is, through reg- 
ular provision of natural resources (rain) and rhythms (seasons), resulting in the 
satisfaction of both stomach and heart (ἐμπιπλῶν τροφῆς καὶ εὐφροσύνης τὰς 
καρδίας ὑμῶν, 14:17).

There is some degree of understanding of Paul’s message, but Luke signals 


reluctance among the crowd: “[…] with difficulty they restrained the crowds 
from offering sacrifice to them” (14:18). One can imagine that the scene may have 
continued somewhat peacefully, but some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came 
and “won over the crowds” (14:19). Astonishingly, the result is a public execution 
through lapidation. Unlike other passages, Luke does not report any governmen- 
tal protection or any indication on Paul’s part to assert his status as Roman citi- 
zen. Here, they have no protection: Jews and non-Jews come together to rid Lys- 
tra of this foreign deity and his representatives. The brutal episode concludes 
succinctly. Paul was still alive and was able to get up and go into the city with the 
help of some unnamed disciples (μαθητῶν, 14:20). Barnabas and Paul then leave 
for Derbe. The passage 14:21–28 relates a brief stay in Derbe and various actions 
and movements from Derbe to Antioch in Syria from which the section began. 


11.6 Conclusion for Sections 1–3 (Acts 1:1–15:35) 


As the second volume opens with a recapitulation of the ending of the first vol- 
ume, Luke’s prophetic voice appears confident as he expresses – for his late first- 
century CE audience – his and his characters’ perception of divine activity. The 
narrative frame of the three sections treated above (Acts 1:1–15:35) is Jerusalem, 
the religious and political centre of the Jewish people. By the end of this unit, 
Luke has led his audience to grasp how divine rule via Jesus manifests itself not 
only in Jerusalem but also in other regions (e.g., Syria, Cyprus, Asia Minor). He 
shows how this divine rule integrates individuals from various peoples into Jesus’ 
movement, before moving onto the next significant progression towards Europe 
and then to Rome. 


Luke faces the hermeneutical dilemma concerning the juncture of historiog- 


raphy and divine agency by presenting Jesus’ resurrection, ascension, and rule as 
supported by τεκμήρια (‘proofs’, Acts 1:3). Various types of divine interventions 
are highlighted (e.g., works of power, epiphanies, prophetic speech). Appendix III 
lists forty-four occurrences of divine activity accomplished by multiple actors in 
the first three sections. In addition, Luke shows his characters explaining the 
meaning of these interventions in the first speeches of volume 2 (i.e., via Peter, 
Stephen, Barnabas and Paul, and James). In this way, Luke’s audience, along with 
the internal audience, learns how the movement’s deity drives the narrative for- 
ward by also looking back to many plupast exempla (e.g., prophecies and divine 
interventions). 


Thus, building on the first volume’s intrigue, the driving questions continue 


to be: Where is the kingdom of God? And for whom is it? What difference does 
this divine saviour named ‘Lord Jesus’ make? For Luke’s audience at the end of 
the first century CE, who also lived under Roman rule, these questions must have 


11 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts II 
367 


elicited in the audience the desire for some degree of closure. The difference now 
– compared to the events recounted in the first volume – are perceptions of a 
new state of affairs in heaven and on earth: Jesus has become what had been 
announced about him and his mandate in the first volume. This “kingdom of 
God” is not merely that of a Judean deity but rather the rule of the creator of all 
peoples (Acts 4:24; 7:48–50). Through this, Luke prepares his audience to inter- 
pret and experience the remainder of volume 2. 


Luke’s representation of the story is that the kingdom is indeed restored to 


Israel (i.e., to those of Israel who receive it through belief in Jesus), but it is now 
shared with those from other peoples. It is a divine kingdom, a reign or rule of the 
heavenly realm, even greater than one that is restricted to one people and region. 
Although Luke shows no physical geopolitical territory conquered by Jesus’ fol- 
lowers, people from various groups and regions are “added” to the kingdom of 
God (2:47; 5:14). The perception of divine rule is not reduced to geographical or 
colonial conquest in terms relatable to those awaiting physical and political deliv- 
erance from the Romans. 


In light of the above, this narrative unit has grounded the overall agōn in a 


network of geopolitical and theological agōnes with their competing narratives. 
In the next chapter, the discussion continues to explore how this divine rule ex- 
tends beyond the historical divide, from Asia to Europe, then, finally, to the centre 
of the Empire.

12 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts: From Antioch to Europe 


and Rome (Volume 2: Acts 15:36–28:31) 


12.1 Introduction 


At this turning point in the narrative, Europe is now in Luke’s sights as he leads 
his audience to explore how Paul and his missionary team went beyond Asia to 
preach in the most important cities of Macedonia and Achaia. The significance of 
this crossing is partly understood from historiographical sources. Herodotus 
showed how Persia tried to add Europe to the spoils of Asia, but this was impeded 
by human and divine agency. The Eurasian theme was further developed by oth- 
er historians. For example, Quintus Curtius Rufus, Arrian, and Plutarch tell how 
Alexander III of Macedonia was able to subjugate both. Polybius, Livy, and Diony- 
sius of Halicarnassus recount how this feat was not repeated until Rome made 
both continents her possession. Luke shows how Paul and his team are able to 
make inroads into both Asia and Europe, establishing communities of followers 
of Jesus and remarkably coming out alive. 


12.2 Section 4: Divine Rule Crosses into Europe (Acts 15:36–18:22) 


Section summary. From Luke’s perspective, this religious advance was again the 
fruit of divine prompting, and it had geopolitical consequences. Given the narra- 
tive flow, Luke’s audience would reasonably expect to hear not only about suc- 
cess, but also about resistance and opposition. Luke maintains his approach of 
focusing on multiple sources of conflict, viewed through the lens of key divine 
interventions. Concerning imperial rule, he highlights conflicts with the Empire’s 
representatives in Philippi, Corinth, and Athens. As for Jewish conflict, intense 
flare-ups in Thessalonica, Beroea, and Corinth are presented as failing to prevent 
preaching about Jesus. Additionally, spiritual opposition is illustrated by the exor- 
cism of a spirit of divination in Philippi, which results in political turmoil. To- 
gether, these three themes contribute to the audience’s growing sense that, while 
the rule of God may be obstructed by human and spiritual forces, it is ultimately 
unstoppable. 


As with the previous section, this one also begins and ends with Paul’s 


church in Antioch of Syria (cf. 13:1–3).1 The events recounted took place around 
49–51 CE.2 Specific references to regions and cities help readers to visualise the 
vast expanse of Paul’s travels. As suggested, these regions may be those with 
which Luke’s audience most identified. After describing the departure from Anti- 
och, Luke offers a brief report about visits to Derbe, Lystra, and other unnamed 
locations (16:1–5), then movement through Phrygia and Galatia, and even divine- 
ly impeded preaching in Asia and Bithynia. Luke’s intention is to bring his audi- 
ence quickly from Asia to Europe, and this will be again signalled as the work of 
divine agency (i.e., through a vision). This opens the door to explore scenes of 
great geopolitical and religious value in Philippi, Thessalonica, Beroea, Athens, 
Corinth, and, finally, a brief stay in Ephesus before returning to Antioch via Cae- 
sarea and Jerusalem. Below, the focus passages of Luke’s prophetic voice will con- 
sider the scenes in Troas, Thessalonica, Athens, and Corinth. For this reason, I 
briefly describe here the narrative relevance of some information that is not cov- 
ered in detail below. 


In this section, Luke features the Jewish agōn in the diaspora. Paul’s contact 


with the Jewish communities is given some attention in the narratives on Thessa- 
lonica, Beroea, Corinth, and very briefly in Ephesus (which will receive signifi- 
cant attention in the next section). In Philippi, Paul and his team look for “a place 
of prayer,” assuming it to be near the river (16:13, 16).3 As usual, Luke shows Paul 
beginning his preaching in a Jewish context. Some type of Jewish prayer gather- 
ing seems to have been present. There, Paul found Lydia of Thyatira, a worshiper 
of God (σεβομένη τὸν θεόν), who welcomed Paul’s teaching and was baptised 
along with her household (16:14–15). This passage is unusual in that Luke does 
not mention other Jewish individuals or groups in connection to this place of 
prayer, nor a division among the community, nor ensuing hostility against Paul. 
The remainder of the Philippi narrative transpires within pagan contexts. 


Following this ‘reception episode’, the Jewish agōn comes strongly to the fore 


in Thessalonica. Paul and Silas have some success preaching in the synagogue, so 
much that some Jews believed and “a great number of the pious Greeks and not a 
few of the leading women” (17:4). Yet others from the Jewish community are said 
to be jealous (17:5), and – like other of Luke’s representations of Jewish hostility

In that city, the Jewish community receives Luke’s praise for being “more

er places, Paul and his team leave there without delay. Corinth also becomes a 
setting for Jewish hostility when the synagogue rejects Paul (18:6). Paul is said to 
respond with words like those he used in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia

to the peoples” (18:6). Due to this sharp conflict, some Jews even bring Paul to the 
tribunal with this accusation: “This man is persuading people to worship God 
contrary to the law” (18:13). Yet, Gallio, the proconsul, refuses to intervene con- 
cerning Jewish legal matters and dismisses them from the tribunal (18:15–16). 


Finally, it is worth noting that when Paul arrives in Ephesus, he goes to the 


synagogue and discusses with the Jews (18:19). Paul’s declaration at 18:6 seems 
to function as a local application, namely, his mission would now focus on the 
non-Jewish population of Corinth. It is also worth noting Luke’s focus on and use 
of characters. This section signals the end of close collaboration between Barn-

Mark to Cyprus, and Paul chooses Silas to go westward to strengthen the churches

movements of Paul. Barnabas’ disappearance from the scene is probably due to 
space rather than to a remaining polemic against him, since Luke’s description of 
Barnabas elsewhere is highly favourable (e.g., 4:36; 9:26–27; 11:22–26).6 Luke
