both success and hardship among the local populations and Jewish communities. 
According to Luke’s narrative claim, their God has now made advances in major 
parts of the Roman Empire, from Jerusalem to Athens. As in the previous sections, 
this claim is supported by various types of divine interventions, which are dis- 
cussed below. 


Summary of divine interventions. Although the number of explicitly narrated di- 
vine interventions is only five in this section (see Appendix III), three of them are 
particularly central for the direction of the story as they set in motion a chain of 
events. Paul’s deity continues to be depicted as a ‘saviour god’. No specific men- 
tions of divinely inspired prophetic speech or healings are presented. In fact, the 
Holy Spirit is only mentioned once, and it is in relation to divine guidance (16:6). 
In the narrative flow, it is manifest that Luke’s audience is meant to assume di- 
vine agency in certain reported events. For example, Luke highlights a ‘salvation 
episode’ with the jailer in Philippi, but he does not specifically state that God ‘add- 
ed’ the man and his household to those who were saved (cf. 2:37–42; 5:14; 13:48). 
This unnamed man’s ‘salvation’ is understood considering the circumstances 
(Paul and Silas’ arrest) and effects of an earthquake (cell doors opened and 
chains unfastened, 16:25–28). This will be fleshed out more below as a ‘focus pas- 
sage’. 


Particularly noteworthy is Luke’s mention of Jesus’ presence in expressions 


like “the Spirit of Jesus” and “the Lord” in a nocturnal vision. These instances re- 
mind the audience – as mentioned in the introduction of this chapter – that Jesus 
is not absent in the narrative after his ascension to the heavenly realm. These two 
instances will be discussed below as well. Finally, various verbal exchanges in- 
clude concise statements regarding the teaching about Jesus (i.e., events related 
in volume 1), for example, in Thessalonica (17:1–3) and especially in Paul’s 
speech before the Areopagus in Athens (17:22–31). Thus, Luke’s narrative contin-

Focus Passages of Luke’s Prophetic Voice and the Agōn 


Troas: A nocturnal vision launches the departure from Asia to Europe (16:6–10). 
This short passage underlines not only divine direction in Jesus’ movement but 
also divine initiation. It is crucial and pivotal to the macronarrative, because the 
God of Paul and his team prevent them from entering new regions to preach the 
message about Jesus. Instead, he guides them to leave Asia for Europe, marking 
another turning point in the story. Europe will now encounter God through Jesus’ 
followers. From the beginning of the first volume, Luke claims the spiritual union 
between the divine and human. Some intriguing elements show how crucial this 
issue was for Luke and his audience. First, divine prevention of movement is 
communicated through the “Holy Spirit” (16:6) and then “the Spirit of Jesus” 
(16:7).8 These two actions prevent them from preaching in Phrygia and Bithynia, 
instead directing them to Troas (16:8). 


Second, the long and strategic history of the ancient city of Troy must have 


certainly resonated with some of Luke’s audience. Some illustrations are the vic- 
tory of Achilles against Hector (Il., book 23), Xerxes’ preparation to conquer Eu- 
rope (Hdt., Hist. 7.43–44), and Alexander the Great, a Macedonian who – imitat- 
ing Achilles – crosses over from Greece to Troy which he visits (Arr., Anab. 1.11– 
12; Plut., Alex. 15). It is equally intriguing to consider Paul’s vision in Troas con- 
sidering the dreams of Agamemnon and Xerxes in relation to the reflections of 
preparation for war.9 


Third, Luke relates the source of divine direction: Paul sees a man of Mace- 


donia in a vision pleading (παρακαλῶν, 16:9) him to come (διαβὰς εἰς Μακε- 
δονίαν βοήθησον ἡμῖν). Luke does not pass on any information about who this 
Macedonian might represent, neither in the passage nor later in the story. But the 
person represents a group (ἡμῖν). The sense of urgency in the man’s pleading is 
accentuated by the preparations to leave immediately (εὐθέως) for Troas. This 
raises questions and expectations in the audience. Why do they need Paul’s help? 
What agōn awaits him there? Luke’s audience explores these questions through 
the unfolding narrative. It is clear, however, that Paul and his group interpret this 
as being God’s direction to preach there. The narrator writes here in the first- 
person plural, involving himself in the actions leading to the expanded mandate 
to Europe: “[…] immediately we sought to leave for Macedonia concluding that

God had called us to preach the good news to them” (16:10). Consequently, the 
audience hears from an alleged eyewitness about the crossing from Asia to Eu- 
rope – from Troas, via Samothrace to Neapolis. 


Philippi: an exorcism of a Pythian-type spirit, trouble in the polis, and deliverance 
from prison (Acts 16:16–40). The narrative in Macedonia moves quickly from 
Neapolis to Philippi, “a principal city of the district of Macedonia, a colony” 
(16:12).10 The account begins with Lydia’s conversion and baptism with her 
household (16:13–15). The following parts of the sojourn in Philippi are tightly 
connected, linking an exorcism and strife with local businessmen and the imperi- 
al administration. For Paul and Silas, an unwarranted night in jail leads to the 
salvation of the jailer’s family and then apologies by Philippi’s magistrates. 


All this begins when Paul and his companions were on their way to “the 


place of prayer” mentioned above where they had met Lydia. According to the 
narrator’s voice, this was a habitual route for prayer times, and there “we met a 
slave girl who had a spirit of divination” (πνεῦμα πύθωνα, 16:16). This expression 
is clarified by Luke: “[she] procured much profit for her masters by fortune-tell- 
ing (μαντευομένη)” (16:16). Oddly, this girl begins to reveal something about the 
deity of Paul and his companions: “These men are slaves of the Most High God, 
who proclaim to you a way of salvation” (16:17). Paul, however, is not pleased 
with this exclamation and casts out the spirit. Reasons for this exorcism are main- 
ly three: (1) similar to Jesus (Luke 4:35), Paul does not allow spirits to speak about 
God; (2) the ambiguity of the expression “Most High God” (τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου) 
in this pluralistic context; and (3) potential confusion about the expression “a 
way of salvation” (ὁδὸν σωτηρίας). Based on Luke’s two volumes, Paul’s world- 
view is constructed on Israel’s God who offers reconciliation (salvation) to him 
(not to other deities). It is thus “the way of salvation,” namely, how one can be 
saved.11 This is corroborated by the superiority of Paul’s deity over the spirit and 
by Luke’s emphasis that Paul’s God does not coexist with other gods in a pan- 
theon. 


The action of casting out the spirit leads to direct conflict with the unnamed 


slave girl’s owners, who risk losing significant income via her fortune-telling. 
Their strategy involves bringing Paul and his team before the political authorities 
(ἄρχοντας) and magistrates (στρατηγοῖς). Their accusation is summarised: “[…] 
These men are upsetting our city, being Jews, they are declaring customs (ἔθη) 
that are not lawful for us as Romans to adopt or practice” (16:20–21). The coexis- 
tence between Roman and Jewish culture is set forth as incompatible, thus an- 
other clash ensues. Indeed, charges of political troublemaking, agitating, or per-

Unjustly wielded imperial power is countered in Luke’s report by two very 


different actions: the joyful attitude of Paul and Silas (16:25) and a dramatic di- 
vine intervention in the form of an earthquake that opens cell doors and unfas- 
tens prisoners’ chains (16:26). The irony of this passage is irresistible, since the 
deliverance of the missionaries will lead to the salvation of the jailer, who intend- 
ed to kill himself because of his prisoners’ assumed escape (16:27). The jailer’s 
question provides an opportunity for his prisoners to tell him about their deity, a 
‘saviour god’, whom they were praying to and singing about (16:25): “Sirs, what 
must I do to be saved?” (κύριοι, τί με δεῖ ποιεῖν ἵνα σωθῶ;, 16:30). As in the ac- 
counts about Cornelius and Lydia, both the jailer and his household believe and 
are baptised (16:31–33). The nature of this salvation is not explicit and must be 
understood from preceding passages. 


The culmination of this success story occurs when the magistrates discover 


that they have unjustly punished Roman citizens without condemnation (ἀκατα- 
κρίτους, 16:37). Paul demands that they be publicly escorted out of town, which 
happens, accompanied by an apology (16:37–39). The strength of this narrative 
lies in its convergence of the religious and the political. Paul’s deity is not sub- 
servient to human rule or its procedures. 


Athens: no miracles by “the unknown God” who made the world (Acts 17:16–33). 
Some justification of the inclusion of this passage is necessary, because no explicit 
divine interventions are presented. As the subtitle suggests, however, it is a con- 
cise apology of the God of Jesus’ movement, and it has rightly attracted scholars’ 
attention about resonances between Socrates and Paul’s defence in Athens.14 The 
passage comprises three parts: Paul’s conversation with philosophers in Athens 
(17:16–21); his speech before the Areopagus (17:22–31); and a coda about the 
mixed reactions to his speech (17:32–33).

philosophical (Epicurean and Stoic) and political representatives (the Areopagus) 
of Athens. This “new teaching” (17:19) attracts some attention, and Luke delivers 
one of his poignant asides: “All the Athenians and the foreigners living there had 
the occasion for nothing else but telling or hearing something new” (17:21). This 
remark serves to underline the superiority of Paul’s teaching in the implicit com- 
parison of the two worldviews in light of the alleged superficial nature of Atheni- 
an erudition.15 And, although they are highly knowledgeable and “fearful of the 
gods (god-fearing)” (δεισιδαιμονεστέρους, 17:22),16 they are, ironically, ignorant 
as to the true nature of the divine realm.17 


This is also one of the strongest claims by Luke, namely, that Jesus and his 


followers attracted the attention of the highest authorities in various parts of the 
Mediterranean. The mention of the Areopagus in this passage lends solemnity to 
the representation because of the renowned location and council associated to it. 
Here, it seems, Paul is not being tried; perhaps a preliminary hearing is in view to 
give him the opportunity to explain his beliefs in “foreign divinities” (ξένων δαι- 
μονίων, 17:18), namely, both Jesus and the ‘resurrection’ (ἀνάστασιν, 17:32).18 


Some of the spectators are simply curious to know more (17:20). Also, the ending 
of the passage does not indicate any formal actions taken in this matter (17:32– 
33). 


The contents of this excerpt of Paul’s speech are comparable to others before 


a (fully or partly) polytheistic audience in Acts.19 Paul moves from a general de- 
scription of his worldview, namely, the existence of one benevolent creator of all 
humanity who now – owing to this new revelation in Jesus – exhorts the peoples 
to abandon their gods and manner of living and to turn to him in repentance, 
resulting in forgiveness of sins (cf. 26:18–20). Paul supports his observation of

Curiously, the speech does not contain an explicit mention of “the man” (i.e.,

οἰκουμένην ἐν δικαιοσύνῇ, 17:31). God has provided assurance (πίστιν παρα-

resurrection of the dead” (ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν, 17:32) appears to explain the inter- 
ruption of Paul’s speech: “When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some 
were mocking, but others said, ‘We will hear you again about this’” (17:32).23 


Hence, this may also explain the absence of a key element, the promise of recon- 
ciliation or salvation (cf. e.g., 10:43; 26:18). But a second meeting is not presented 
by Luke. It can be assumed that Luke has achieved his purpose here, as the gospel 
is proclaimed to the highest levels of the Athenian society. Therefore, a second 
meeting would serve no narrative purpose other than repetition. 


Despite the absence of divine interventions, this passage’s religious-philo- 


sophical and political value is invaluable. Paul’s defence is formulated based on a 
general divine plupast expression from the Hebrew prophetic tradition: “The God 
who made the world and everything in it, he who is Lord of heaven and earth 
[…]” (17:24). Luke’s protagonist is able to defend his belief before the highest au- 
thority of Greece’s cultural centre. Paul does not claim private revelation, but he 
does claim to announce what they do not know. No violence or tumults are men- 
tioned as in other episodes, only differences of reception: those who scoffed 
(ἐχλεύαζον); those who wished to hear him again; and those who believed, among 
whom “Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris” (17:33). Follow- 
ing this brief note of reception, no other events in Athens are reported and Luke’s 
audience is quickly led to Corinth by way of a simple temporal μετὰ ταῦτα transi- 
tion: Μετὰ ταῦτα χωρισθεὶς ἐκ τῶν Ἀθηνῶν ἦ λθεν εἰς Κόρινθον (18:1).

In light of Luke’s focus on Jewish antagonism (18:6, 12–13), the second con- 


firmation is an epiphany of Jesus to Paul: “One night the Lord said to Paul in a 
vision, ‘Do not be afraid, but speak and do not keep silent; for I myself am with 
you, and no one will set about to harm you, for many in this city are my people’” 
(διότι λαός ἐστίν μοι πολὺς ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῇ, 18:9–10). Luke highlights once 
more the presence of the ascended Christ, who encourages Paul to continue his 
preaching and assures him of his presence and protection.24 


Finally, highly significant is Jesus’ claim that many people in Corinth are his 


people. Like the expression where Jesus says to Paul on the way to Damascus 
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”, the spiritual union between Jesus and 
his followers is emphasised. Equally, Luke’s audience saw (with Stephen) the as- 
cended and glorified Jesus in heaven (7:55–56). The polis of Corinth is not within 
traditional Jewish borders, but Paul’s deity is again presented as unconstrained 
by space or political borders.25 Likewise, if Jesus is said to have a people, it is not a 
people within a restricted geographical setting. Luke’s representation here is best 
understood in the sense of an earlier expression, “the rule of God is among you” 
(ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν, Luke 17:21). 


The notion of a deity having a people in Luke’s thought is expressed through 


a variety of voices (e.g., Luke 1:68, 77; 7:16; Acts 7:17, 34; 13:17; 15:14). Among 
the other passages underlining the reception of Jesus among the peoples, this one 
in Corinth illustrates well James’ conclusion in Jerusalem: “Simeon has reported 
how God had first carefully chosen to select a people from the peoples for his 
name” (15:14). Through this, Luke reconfirms his audience’s multicultural com- 
position by showing them that this is theologically intentional. They are, by exten- 
sion, also Jesus’ people. 


Luke could have brought the story to a close here when he concludes, “He 


[Paul] stayed there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among 
them” (18:11). Yet the length of the stay in Corinth functions to introduce yet an- 
other anecdote of Jewish and non-Jewish interaction. More irony emerges: that 
which one group wishes to accomplish turns against them (cf. e.g., Saul in Damas- 
cus, 9:1–9; the seven sons of Sceva in Ephesus, 19:13–17). Here, a group of Jews 
brings a complaint against Paul before the tribunal (βῆμα, 18:12), and Gallio the

shows no concern about it. 


12.3 Section 5: Divine Rule Clashes with Human Rule in Asia Minor 


with a Focus on Ephesus (Acts 18:23–20:38) 


Section summary. As a part of Luke’s depiction of Paul’s visits to multiple cities, 
Luke focuses, in this section, on one – Ephesus. Luke had already mentioned 
Paul’s brief contact with the Jewish community there (18:19–21). Now he high- 
lights key events in Ephesus and around western Asia. Significant movement is 
evident throughout this section. Luke’s focus, however, does not lie in providing a 
comprehensive travel log. Instead, he illustrates how Paul, divinely led and em- 
powered, enters and challenges the cultural spaces centred on Ephesus.27 In 
Luke’s account, Ephesus functions as another cultic and cultural centre, being the 
site of Artemis’ worship (19:35). It is therefore both a comparison to and a compe- 
tition with other Mediterranean cities, particularly two subsequent destinations 
for Paul: Jerusalem and Rome (19:21). But first Paul wishes to revisit Macedonia 
and Achaia before returning to Jerusalem (19:21). The chronology of this sojourn 
in Ephesus is approximately 52–55 CE.28 As stated in 20:31, the period in question 
is noted as “three years” through Paul’s voice (20:31).29 


26 
Gallio, brother of Seneca the philosopher, began as proconsul in Corinth ca. 50 or 51 for a 
two-year term. An inscription (SIG 2:801D) found in Delphi mentions Gallio as proconsul dur- 
ing the twenty-sixth acclamation as emperor in 52 CE. See Holladay (2016) 353–354. 


27 
For a historical description of the religious landscape in Anatolia, see Mitchell (1995).

Pichler and Rajič (2017) and Harrison and Welborn (2018).

The section begins after a brief mention of Paul’s stay in Antioch in Syria 


and his visits to “all the disciples” in Galatia and Phrygia (18:23). Luke quickly 
brings his audience to Ephesus in 18:24. Most of the events take place there, ex- 
cept a brief excursion to Macedonia and Greece that is interrupted by a plot 
against Paul (20:1–6) and his short stay in Troas upon returning to Asia (20:7–12). 
The section ends with Paul’s preparations, both practical and pastoral, for his re- 
turn to Jerusalem (20:13–38).30 The narrator intervenes at various points in the 
first-person plural (20:6–7, 13–15), enhancing the narration’s authenticity and 
credibility to his audience. 


All three agōnes are touched upon in this section. The spiritual and political 


conflicts receive the most attention while the agōn with the Jewish community is 
less perceptible. The first two act as narrative foils to foreground the identity of 
Jesus for the audience. The third consists of a plot by a group of Jews (20:3), 
which causes Paul to change his itinerary. Luke, however, does not expand on the 
nature of the plot. Instead of sailing back to Syria, Paul decides to go back through 
Macedonia, then Troas, onward to Miletus en route to Caesarea (20:1–6, 13–16). 
Narrative tension is built up through the agōn with the spiritual realm, and it 
reaches its apex in the scene of a public riot in Ephesus, which again demands 
political intervention and results in Paul’s favour (19:23–41). This scene will be 
discussed further in the focus passages below. 


Before moving to the question of divine interventions and the focus pas- 


sages, a few points merit some attention. The riot in Ephesus is prefaced by two 
scenes of integration of individuals into Jesus’ movement. What they have in 
common is the need for further enlightenment to enter more fully God’s plan of 
reconciliation. They know the baptism of John the Baptist (18:25; 19:3–4), but 
they are ignorant of the full story about Jesus. These may be understood as exam- 
ples of mise en abyme in Luke’s work, which mirror the audience’s need for great- 
er certainty, and, thus, the need for evidence about Jesus and his movement 
(Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1–3). 


In the first example, Apollos of Alexandria becomes a member of Paul’s mis- 


sionary network (18:24–28). Luke describes this Jewish man as “an eloquent 
man” and “capable in the scriptures” (18:24). Although he had been instructed in 
the “Way of the Lord,” he needed further teaching through Priscilla and Aquila 
(companions of Paul from Corinth, 18:2), who “explained the Way of God to him 


also refers to the Jewish calendar: “the days of Unleavened Bread” (20:5) and “the day of Pen- 
tecost” (20:16).

ἀκριβέστερον (18:25–26) with ἀκριβῶς (Luke 1:3). 


Immediately following this, Luke introduces a group of around twelve disci- 


ples (cf. μαθητάς, 19:1) who had received John’s baptism (i.e., “the baptism of re- 
pentance,” 19:4). Given their faith, Paul provides them with further instruction 
and baptises them. Then the Holy Spirit manifests himself upon them (ἦ λθεν τὸ 
πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐπ’ αὐτούς, 19:6), and they speak in tongues and prophesy (19:6). 
This scene has significant precedents in the disciples speaking in tongues on the 
day of Pentecost (2:1–4) and in the case of Cornelius and his household (10:44– 
46). Scenes such as these display Luke’s prophetic voice in shaping his audience’s 
understanding of individual and corporate religious experiences within Jesus’ 
movement. 


Finally, this section offers another glimpse of Paul’s speeches. This time the 


context is a Christian gathering in which no opposition is depicted (20:18–35). 
Once more, key themes come to the fore and serve to recapitulate Paul’s mission- 
ary calling and experiences: his character (20:19), conflicts (20:19, 23), and faith- 
fulness to “the Lord Jesus” (20:24). In addition, as in other speeches in Acts, the 
divine plupast presents to the internal and external audiences key teaching ele- 
ments, effectively summarised in “the whole purpose of God” (πᾶσαν τὴν βουλὴν 
τοῦ θεοῦ, 20:27): “Be attentive to yourselves and all the flock, for which the Holy 
Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he acquired 
for himself through his own blood” (20:28). This metaphor, referring to Jesus’ sac- 
rifice, illustrates Jesus as ‘saviour god’ (τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἣν περιεποιήσατο 
διὰ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ ἰδίου). An exhortation follows, which is buttressed by a pro- 
leptic statement announcing future conflict in the Ephesian community of disci- 
ples: the presence of coming “violent wolves” who distort the truth and lead disci- 
ples away (20:29–30). This emotionally charged speech – with tears (20:19, 31) 
and weeping (20:37) – contributes to the climactic movement towards Jerusalem 
in the next section. 


Summary of divine interventions. The seven occurrences of divine agency in the 
fifth section (see Appendix III) underline the continuity and unity of activity 
working through both divine and human agents. The Holy Spirit is specifically 
mentioned concerning the integration of the group of twelve men into Jesus’ 
movement (19:1–7). Their speaking in tongues and prophetic speech function as 
signs bearing witness to their affiliation to Paul’s group (19:6; cf. 2:3, 11; 10:46). 
The Holy Spirit is also evoked regarding continued guidance of Paul (19:21; 
20:23), who is even described as being “bound in the Spirit” (20:22). “God” (ὁ

For a narrative-critical discussion on the uses of ὁδός in the characterisation of Apollos, see

θεός) is also said to perform – via a classic Lukan litotes – “not ordinary deeds of 
power” (Δυνάμεις τε οὐ τὰς τυχούσας, 19:11). These deeds occur through Paul 
(19:12), even at a distance through his “handkerchiefs or aprons”, ousting both 
diseases (νόσους) and evil spirits (τὰ πνεύματα τὰ πονηρά). Continuity with Jesus’ 
deeds of power and those of his first disciples is thus clearly evoked for the audi- 
ence (cf. Luke 6:18; 7:21; 9:21). In addition to the Holy Spirit and God as divine 
agents, Jesus is also clearly perceived as present (19:15, 17). We now turn to this 
description of a peculiar event. 


Focus Passage of Luke’s Prophetic Voice and the Agōn 


An evil spirit overpowers Jewish exorcists (19:14–20). The mention of evil spirits 
above recalls passages in the first volume with reference to the spiritual agōn 
with Jesus. This parallel is greatly impressed on the audience who hear about an 
evil spirit (τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ πονηρόν, 19:15) who not only resists being cast out by 
Jewish exorcists but also speaks to them. He claims to know Jesus and Paul, but 
not them (τὸν [μὲν] Ἰησοῦν γινώσκω καὶ τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι, ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνες 
ἐστέ; 19:15). The exorcists’ authority had no effect on the spirit, so they were 
overpowered, wounded, and had to flee naked (19:13–16). Luke has shown to his 
audience other examples of malevolent spirits with utterances: ὁ διάβολος (Luke 
4:1–13); πνεῦμα δαιμονίου ἀκαθάρτου (Luke 4:33–35); πνεύματα ἀκάθαρτα (Acts 
8:7); τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἀκαθάρτῳ […] λεγιών […] δαιμόνια πολλά (8:29–31); and 
πνεῦμα πύθωνα (Acts 16:16–18). As in those descriptions, Luke uses this as a 
τεκμήριον that Jesus’ authority is known and respected in the realm of the spirits. 


While the scene above may have amused Luke’s readers, he does not in- 


clude it solely for entertainment. Through the result of the agōn between Jewish 
exorcists and the evil spirit, Luke alludes to the opposite experience of Jesus and 
Paul in order to illustrate that there are no forces that can resist Jesus or his 
movement. Luke draws out consequences of this event, which is said to have an 
immediate impact on “all” residents of Ephesus (19:17): (1) Jews and Greeks 
heard about this and “fear fell upon them all” (19:17); (2) Jesus’ name is magni- 
fied (ἐμεγαλύνετο τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ, 19:17); (3) many of the new believ- 
ers in Jesus renounce their practices of magic (τῶν τὰ περίεργα πραξάντων, 
19:19) and burned their books of magic publicly; and, finally, through a summary 
verse (4) “the word of the Lord grew and prevailed” (ἴσχυεν, 19:20; cf. 19:16, an 
evil spirit’s overpowering of exorcists). Thus, various divine actors are shown to 
be active in Paul’s ministry, paralleling acts of Jesus, Peter, Philip, and Stephen. 
This prepares the audience for another cultic and cultural conflict because of the 
perceived threat that Paul’s teaching brought to Ephesus. 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
382 


The effects of a foreign deity causing “no little disturbance” (19:23–41). Ephesus, as 
said above, serves another focalising function in Luke’s use of cities as cultural 
and cultic spaces and the movement of Paul’s deity through them. Paul and his 
companions are said to be active in teaching about “the kingdom of God” and “the 
Way” “for three months” in the synagogue, and then in Tyrannus’ lecture hall 
“for two years, so that all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the 
word of the Lord” (19:10). The deeds of power discussed above are understood to 
have occurred during this time of preaching and teaching (19:11–20). 


Luke now describes an agōn taking place on multiple levels. As Luke writes, 


“About that time no little disturbance arose concerning the Way” (19:23). A cer- 
tain Demetrius, a silversmith, functions as the spokesperson for those of his guild 
feeling threatened by Paul’s missionary activity. He underlines two risks: their 
trade may lose its reputation, because the temple (ἱερόν) of Artemis would be 
considered nothing (οὐθὲν λογισθῆναι) and her majesty removed (καθαιρεῖσθαι 
τῆς μεγαλειότητος αὐτῆς, 19:27). His claim is thus religious and theological, be- 
cause Asia and the world worship her (ἣν ὅλη ἡ Ἀσία καὶ ἡ οἰκουμένη σέβεται). 


Although Luke does not describe Demetrius as recognising any specific 


deeds performed by Paul’s deity, he also does not report any divine acts in this 
scene. But the cause of the disturbance (τάραχος) is indeed seen as both religious 
and theological. In Demetrius’ voice, Paul has “turned aside a good number of 
people saying that those things made by hands are not gods” (μετέστησεν ἱκανὸν 
ὄχλον λέγων ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοὶ οἱ διὰ χειρῶν γινόμενοι, 19:26). That there is oppo- 
sition to the spiritual challenge represented by Jesus’ movement – as Demetrius’ 
objections portray it – points to the perception of divine activity through Paul. 


As in other cities in which Jesus’ movement is seen as a threat (e.g., Philippi, 


Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth), Demetrius and his co-tradesmen bring their com- 
plaint to the streets of Ephesus, causing it to become an agōn for the entire polis 
and hoping to have the support of the imperial administration. The parallel with 
the owners of the slave girl in Philippi is very close. What Paul is teaching and 
doing is propagated by Demetrius as colliding against local customs (cf. ἔθη at 
16:21) and is therefore unlawful. In Ephesus, however, the authorities’ reaction is 
different. Luke records that the city clerk (γραμματεύς) addresses the citizens di- 
rectly (ἄνδρες Ἐφέσιοι) and displays wisdom. He recognises the theological and 
historical justification of the worship of Artemis in Ephesus: “the city of the Ephe- 
sians is the temple guard of the great Artemis and of the statue fallen from heav- 
en” (19:35). These things, he says, are undeniable (ἀναντιρρήτων). The clerk’s 
τεκμήριον is the object that fell from heaven (διοπετοῦς). What, however, would 
be unlawful is if Demetrius and the tumult failed to bring their complaints to the 
courts (ἀγοραῖοι) and the proconsuls (ἀνθύπατοι). In this way, the γραμματεύς 
prevents a public trial (and potential lynching) of Paul and his colleagues because 
of the rioting (στάσεως) and commotion (συστροφῆς). Similar to Proconsul Gal- 
lio’s intervention in Corinth, Ephesian authorities also act in Paul’s favour. The 


12 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts III 
383 


clerk is the main benefactor, but Luke also mentions that “some of the Asiarchs 
who were friends of his [Paul’s]” had sent him a message discouraging him from 
defending himself before the angry mob (19:31). The Asiarchs were the high 
priests of the koinon (the general council) of Asia, from high nobility, and were 
responsible for imperial cult on the provincial level.32 Once again, Luke charac- 
terises Jesus and his movement as attracting great attention in a major city and 
involving some of the highest instances of the imperial and cultural spheres.33 


Although the clerk’s intervention was successful in breaking up the assem- 


bly, Luke reports that Paul decided to leave the region for Macedonia (20:1), 
which is the beginning of a tortuous journey back to Jerusalem (20:16). Apparent- 
ly, he did not have time to say goodbye to the church leaders in Ephesus, since he 
organises a meeting with them in Miletus (20:17). There, Paul’s speech recaps 
many of the main points of his stay in Ephesus: its duration of three years, faith- 
fulness as teacher in content and lifestyle, and leadership development. This mov- 
ing scene elicits the audience to reflect on the deep affection between Paul and 
the Ephesian church leaders. Paul would soon be detained as a prisoner of the 
Empire, and they would no longer see him (20:38). 


12.4 Section 6: Divine Rule at the Centre of the Agōn in Judea 


and Jerusalem (Acts 21:1–23:30) 


Section summary. Luke’s audience encounters Paul’s final and turbulent visit to 
Jerusalem. Parallel to the other trial and appearance episodes (i.e., with Jesus, Pe- 
ter, and Stephen), Paul will be accused falsely, and he will attempt to demonstrate 
his devotion to the God of Israel and his innocence in preaching about Jesus. This 
will not be received as such, and thus this section is of a tragic nature. As a vi- 
brant example of Luke’s use of synkrisis, echoing the tragic representation of Je- 
sus’ final days in Jerusalem, this section is rightly considered “the passion of 
Paul.”34 Luke resumes the narration with his departure from Miletus, the first 
part by sea and the second by land ending in Jerusalem. It ends with Paul’s deten- 
tion under Claudius Lysias, tribune in Jerusalem. The approximate time period is 
57 CE.35 


One reason for Paul’s return to Jerusalem is to deliver the churches’ collec- 


tion for the poor in Judea. This is based on Paul’s reference to alms (ἐλεημοσύνας) 
for his people (ἔθνος) in Acts 24:17 and mentions of a collection in Paul’s letters 


32 
On the Asiarchs, see Campanile (1994). 


33 
Some of the precedents are Paul’s contact with the Proconsul Sergius Paulus in Cyprus (13:7– 
12); members of the Areopagus in Athens (17:19–34); Gallio the Proconsul of Achaia in Cor- 
inth (18:12–17). 


34 
Dunn (2009) 957–958. 


35 
See Bruce and Taylor (1986) 288–289; Riesner (2011) 15, 23–24. 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
384 


(e.g., 1 Cor 16:3–4; Rom 15:26–28).36 But Luke chooses to omit this and focuses on 
other questions of more pressing interest: Paul’s own passion.37 Indeed, from this 
point on, Paul’s days as a citizen moving freely in the Empire come to an end. But 
the reason for his detention is due to the Jewish agōn, the strongest of the agōnes 
in this section. Imperial presence is indeed strong, but it is portrayed as generally 
benevolent to Paul, once his Roman citizenship has been recognised (22:25–29). 
Additionally, there is no explicit mention of the agōn with adversaries in the spiri- 
tual realm. 


In 21:1–16, the audience follows their course by ship with Paul and others, 


from Miletus to Jerusalem by mentioning several locations: Cos, Rhodes, Patara, 
Cyprus, and Tyre (21:1–3), then onward to Ptolemais and Caesarea (21:7–8), and, 
finally, from there by land to Jerusalem. Multiple uses of the first-person plural 
again signal ‘we passages’, which continue until Paul goes to the temple in Jer- 
usalem (21:26).38 Luke is again claiming his personal experience of Paul’s activi- 
ties and authority as narrator. 


The entire section focuses on Paul as a witness carrying the message of Jesus 


and his experiences with him. His conversations and speeches are with different 
people and vary in length. The long journey – from Miletus to Jerusalem – func- 
tions as an emotional preface for the ensuing mob scene. Narrative tension builds 
through divine warnings (21:4, 11) and human entreaties (21:12) that underscore 
the perilous situation awaiting Paul. But he is portrayed with the same resolution 
found in the description of Jesus who decides to go to Jerusalem despite animosity 
and danger (9:51). Paul bravely responds to his friends’ pleas: “What are you do- 
ing, weeping and breaking my heart? As for me, I am ready not only to be bound 
but even to die in Jerusalem for the cause of the Lord Jesus’ name” (21:13).39 


Paul’s conversations and speeches underline the significance of his presence in 
Judea, which will not go unnoticed. He visits two key figures in Caesarea: Philip 
(21:8–14) and Mnason (21:15). He also meets James and “all the elders” in Jer- 
usalem (21:17–26), after which he is recognised by Asian Jews in the temple area 
(21:27). 


The Jewish agōn concerns again the thorny question of adhesion to Jesus’ 


movement and faithfulness to Jewish identity (cf. 15:1–35). Leaders of the Judean 
Christian community are aware that people have allegedly heard that Paul was 
instructing diaspora Jews not to keep their ancestral distinctions (i.e., Moses, cir- 
cumcision, and customs (ἔθεσιν), 21:21). Their proposal is that Paul should prove

For a detailed discussion of Paul’s collection mentioned in his letters, see Dunn (2009) 932– 
947.

For a summary of proposals concerning Luke’s omission of the collection in this passage, see

The fact that the first-person narration stops at the temple entry may be evidence that the

For a summary of the parallels between the trials of Jesus and Paul, see Pervo (2009) 533–534,

12 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts III 
385 


that he has not renounced his attachment to his Jewish identity by performing a 
rite of purity at the temple, accompanied by four witnesses (21:23–24). This act of 
proof can be understood as a failure in that it leads Paul into conflict with the 
Jewish authorities because of two allegations, namely, that Paul’s teaching was 
against “our people, our law, and this place (ἱερόν)” (21:28) and that he had 
brought a non-Jew, Trophimus, an Ephesian Greek, into the temple (21:29).40 Luke 
prefaces this provocation in public spaces with “[…] the Jews from Asia […] stir- 
red up the whole crowd” (συνέχεον πάντα τὸν ὄχλον, with συγχέω in 21:27, 31).41 


Paul is again depicted as attracting the attention of authorities from the 


highest spheres, both Jewish and Roman. His two appearances before Jewish 
groups serve to defend his Jewish identity, belief in Jesus, and missionary role. 
First, with the tribune’s approval, Paul responds with a harried speech to a vio- 
lent mob at the temple, summarising a second time his encounter with Jesus on 
the way to Damascus and his subsequent missionary calling (21:40–22:21; cf. 9:1– 
22; 26:9–18). The juxtaposition of Jesus as a deity (i.e., as “Lord,” 22:6–11, 17–21) 
in relation to the “God of our ancestors” (22:14) is considered blasphemous and 
worthy of death by the violent mob (22:22–24). Their conduct is thus implicitly 
paralleled by the repetition of Paul’s previous activity as persecutor of Jesus’ fol- 
lowers in Damascus (22:8). The roles have now reversed, both metaphorically 
and spiritually; embodied by his followers, Jesus is persecuted by those who per- 
secute Paul. 


The next day, the tribune summons Paul to appear before the Jewish council 


in the presence of the high priest Ananias (22:30–23:10). Luke presents this as an 
interrupted speech, triggered by Paul’s declaration of belief in the resurrection of 
the dead (23:6), which parallels – but theologically differs from – the Athenians’ 
reaction to Paul’s belief in ἀνάστασις (17:18, 32).42 Both appearances are said to 
end in a violent uproar (22:22–24; 23:10) and in Paul’s rescue by Roman soldiers. 
Again, Paul’s belief in his deity causes agitation in a major urban centre of the 
Mediterranean. This narrative pattern of the human-divine agōn is illustrated by 
the violent opposition to the message of Jesus. This time it marks a turning point 
in that, narratively, it represents Paul’s last chance to bear witness to his faith in 
Jesus in Jerusalem. Some believe while others do not, which confirms the motif of 
mixed reception among the Jewish people. Luke, for example, reports through 
James’ voice that “thousands” (μυριάδες) among the Jews had believed in Jesus 
and are “all zealous for the law” (21:20). 


40

the holy place, and the law (6:11–14). For the Greek inscription prohibiting non-Jews to enter 
the temple (dated 23 BCE–70 CE), see Cotton et al. (2010) 42–43.

and ἐπιγείρω (13:50; 14:2).

Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
386 


The section ends with Paul’s definitive transition into the hands of the Em- 


pire, from here until his arrival in Rome in 62 CE. He is in captivity, but as a Ro- 
man citizen. The Jewish leaders can now no longer act independently to extirpate 
his alleged threat to their customs. The parallels with the trials against Jesus and 
Stephen end here, since Paul is rescued in both cases by Roman authorities. Ironi- 
cally, Jerusalem’s sacred spaces do not offer refuge, as do the barracks of the Ro- 
man military (21:37; 22:24; 23:10). This is evinced through interaction with the 
military hierarchy involving soldiers, centurions, and one tribune. Finally, the 
highest level of regional authority (ἡγεμών) is solicited when another murderous 
plot against Paul is unveiled by Paul’s nephew to the tribune, Claudius Lysias, 
who sends a letter of transfer to Felix the governor at his residence in Caesarea 
(23:16–30). As a Roman citizen, Paul leaves Jerusalem innocent and will also be 
declared innocent in Caesarea (26:32). He is now under the protection of the Ro- 
man Empire, from Caesarea to Rome. 


Summary of divine interventions. This section depicts another of Paul’s conflictual 
visits to Jerusalem (cf. 9:26–31; 15:1–12), but it is not portrayed as being divinely 
orchestrated as in other episodes where a divine intervention initiates movement 
from one place to another. Rather, Luke spotlights Paul’s devotion to Jesus and to 
his own people. This is clearly understood by the people and fiercely opposed, 
because the two are not compatible in their eyes. That the agōn remains on the 
human plane and no conflict with the spiritual realm is mentioned could lead to 
the understanding that it is merely a human conflict. However, the entire section 
is centred on the reception or rejection of Jesus and his messengers; thus, the di- 
vine is at the centre, which is clearly illustrated by Jesus’ epiphany. The guidance 
that Luke attributes to the Holy Spirit and the exhortation by Jesus to Paul 
demonstrate that the agōnes do not merely involve the spiritual dimension as a 
proxy for the human conflict. Rather, the divine actors are perceived as being ac- 
tively involved in this episode. 


Regarding Paul’s decision to return to Jerusalem, the Holy Spirit is said to 


have been active by warning Paul twice not to go to Jerusalem, first via indirect 
speech (21:4) and then direct speech through a prophet (21:11). But Paul is not 
explicitly prohibited from going there, as was the case when he intended to 
preach in Asia and Bithynia (16:6–7). Despite the warnings, Paul chooses to go, 
without fear of suffering or losing his life. After the two violent reactions of the 
Jewish audiences, Luke recounts that “the Lord” appeared to Paul at night in or- 
der to encourage him and command him to bear witness in Rome (23:11). This 
brief interaction does not suggest that Paul’s return to Jerusalem was in vain. In 
fact, it seems to confirm it. This “Lord” is again to be understood as Jesus whose 
previous appearance to Paul in the temple had led him to leave Jerusalem due to 
the threat of rejection, and to preach to the peoples (cf. 22:17–21). This epiphany 
will be examined in more detail below. 


12 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts III 
387 


Additionally, another plot to kill Paul is averted, because Paul’s nephew had 


overheard the conspiracy (συστροφήν, 23:12). Thus, this entire section portrays 
Paul facing danger that possibly could have been avoided, having been divinely 
forewarned, and then is rescued through divine agency. The direction of his next 
move is clearly signposted by Luke through Jesus’ appearance to Paul (23:11). 


Focus Passage of Luke’s Prophetic Voice and the Agōn 


Another epiphany of “the Lord” to direct Paul in his mission (23:11). Although brief, 
Jesus’ appearance and utterance to Paul are of great import for the narrative: 
“That night the Lord stood by him saying, ‘Take courage, for as you have testified 
about things concerning me in Jerusalem, so you must also bear witness in 
Rome’” (Τῇ δὲ ἐπιούσῃ νυκτὶ ἐπιστὰς αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος εἶ πεν· θάρσει· ὡς γὰρ διε- 
μαρτύρω τὰ περὶ ἐμοῦ εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ, οὕτως σε δεῖ καὶ εἰς Ῥώμην μαρτυρῆσαι). 
Indeed, the appearance of Jesus himself, rather than his messengers, attests to the 
significance of this brief occurrence. 


Luke inserts this night epiphany of Jesus to Paul after the two tumultuous 


encounters with the Jewish population on two consecutive days (22:30). In both 
uproars, Paul is brought with great haste into the Roman barracks. The next day, 
some Jews, already the next morning, hatched their plot by oath to murder Paul. 
Jesus’ appearance and this conspiracy will lead to the same result: Paul must 
leave Jerusalem for another destination. The first one, Caesarea, will be tempo- 
rary, and the next one, Rome, will be the final destination in the narrative. Rome 
was in Paul’s sights (19:21), but it was not clear how or when he was going to 
arrive there. Jesus’ utterance serves to confirm the direction, and the next section 
will explain the rest. 


Literarily and theologically, Jesus’ appearance here builds on previous ones 


that the audience has already encountered, namely, all of them in relation to Paul 
in the scenes in Damascus (9:1–19), Corinth (18:9–10), and twice in Jerusalem, 
one retrospectively (22:17–21), and another in this passage. Luke uses these as a 
part of the τεκμήρια of Jesus’ continued existence and activity in the human 
sphere after his death, resurrection, and ascension (Luke 23:44–46; 24:1–11; Acts 
1:1–11). This is the last epiphany of Jesus in Acts. A final night epiphany involving 
an angel of God appears during Paul’s maritime journey to Rome (27:23–24). 


For the audience’s experience, these τεκμήρια have various functions. They 


serve to strengthen the audience’s devotion to Jesus in their own contexts and to 
orient them in their interpretation of divine direction of the apostle Paul in his 
journeys in Jewish and non-Jewish contexts. The audience perceives divine rule 
in Jesus – from one region to the next – who prevents harm to his disciples in 
Damascus (9:4–6), encourages Paul in his testimony in Corinth where Jesus has 
“many people” (18:10), and again reassures Paul to continue his ministry else- 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
388 


where outside of Jerusalem (22:17; 23:11). In these four instances, direct speech 
by Jesus (“the Lord”) to Paul is indicated. Luke’s representation of Paul’s deity is 
not limited by time, sacred spaces, or geopolitical forces. 


A final observation stems from the preceding one, the theme of witness and 


the use of δεῖ. Here, as often elsewhere in Luke and Acts, they contribute to the 
notions of a divine plan or divine guidance.43 In the four cases mentioned above, 
Paul’s role as witness is underlined (9:15–16; 18:10; 22:18; 23:11). These will be 
further underscored by a third narration of Paul’s encounter of the risen Jesus, 
when he appears before Festus and Herod Agrippa (25:23–26:32). There, Paul 
refers again to Jesus’ direct speech to him, which elaborates on Paul’s calling to 
be a witness of Jesus among the Jews and the peoples (26:14–18). This is ground- 
ed in the opening lines of the second volume where Jesus speaks to his disciples 
about being witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth 
(1:8). Paul has been thoroughly established as a worthy apostle in Luke’s narra- 
tive. The story moves forward to Caesarea and as promised, on to Rome. Paul had 
explicitly expressed his own awareness of divine guidance through the familiar 
Lukan idiom using δεῖ: “[…] μετὰ τὸ γενέσθαι με ἐκεῖ δεῖ με καὶ Ῥώμην ἰδεῖν” 
(19:21). 


12.5 Section 7: Divine Rule Brings the Agōn to 


Imperial-ruled Caesarea (Acts 23:31–26:32) 


Section summary. The events of this section are placed entirely in Caesarea Mar- 
itima under the administrations of the Roman Governors, Antonius Felix and Por- 
cius Festus, during the rule of Nero (54–68 CE). The period recounted here is 
around 57–59 CE.44 This section is the link between Paul’s final visit to Jerusalem 
(ca. 57 CE), his journey to Rome (59 CE), and subsequent imprisonment there (60– 
62 CE). Paul’s two-year imprisonment in Caesarea is – compared to the tumultu- 
ous sea journey to Rome – the calm before the storm. 


Given the events told by Luke beforehand and the knowledge of events that 


took place in Judea after this time, a sense of suspense develops among Luke’s 
readers who were unfamiliar with Paul’s story, or curiosity among those who

also important to recognise various nuances of δεῖ in the New Testament, see e.g., Smit (2019)

389 


were ignorant of the means by which Paul was sent to Rome. The stakes are in- 
deed high for Paul as competing narratives converge and clash again. The Jewish 
authorities want to eliminate him once and for all, so an arrangement with the 
Romans would work well for them. Moreover, although Paul is a Roman citizen, 
he is at the mercy of the imperial authorities, given the examples of misconduct 
towards him that Luke mentions (e.g., a bribe, 24:26). The Romans represent, 
then, trajectories of death and salvation. Indeed, a sense of curiosity is manifest: 
How did Paul manage to depart from Caesarea unharmed, despite the presence of 
both Jewish and Roman authorities and subsequently be accompanied to Rome as 
an innocent citizen? What part did Paul’s deity have in making this happen? Nar- 
ratively, Luke’s intention for this section seems clear. Paul will be shown to be 
sent to Rome as an innocent prisoner, a Roman citizen, and a Jewish follower of 
Jesus. It had been announced – in Jesus’ epiphany in the previous section – that 
Paul would be Jesus’ witness in Rome. Now, Luke shows the human agency by 
which this will be accomplished. 


Luke showcases two of Paul’s three hearings in which he is judged by the 


highest regional authorities: Felix, Festus, and Herod Agrippa II. All three declare 
Paul’s innocence with respect to Roman law. Paul also continues to claim his in- 
nocence before Jewish law, which he succinctly states before their judicial pow- 
ers (25:8). All this serves to orient the audience’s reception of the next section: 
Paul’s journey and imprisonment in Rome (27:1–28:31). Although there is no 
mention of divine activity having occurred during this period, the presence of the 
agōnes is clearly illustrated. 


The location and the assemblies of mixed ethnicities are highly significant, 


especially for those in Luke’s audience who were aware of the harrowing events 
that took place not long after Paul’s stay in Caesarea. This provincial capital had 
become the theatre of increasing Jewish hostility towards the Empire’s pres- 
ence.45 This culminated, as Josephus reports, in the massacre of some 20 000 Jews 
in 66 CE and the deportation of any remaining to the galleys, so that Caesarea was 
“completely emptied of Jews” (B.J. 2.18.1 [Thackeray]). This sparked a massive re- 
taliation against Rome in various regions, which, ultimately led to the destruction 
of Jerusalem under Titus in 70 CE. Read in this light, the Caesarean logos about 
Paul’s case helps to explain Luke’s attention to the judicial treatment of Paul by 
the Romans before his aggressive Jewish accusers. The context is already volatile. 
Like Pontius Pilate in the trials of Jesus (23:11–12, 23–24), Felix and Festus are 


45 
Felix and Festus, especially the former, were both acquainted with hostilities with various 
Jewish groups (cf. Josephus, B.J. 2.252–271). Jewish hostility in Caesarea against Paul is indi- 
cated via Festus’ clarification: “[…] the whole Jewish community petitioned me, both in Jer- 
usalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer” (24:24).

390 


both noted as wishing to grant favours to the Jews in their dealing with Paul’s 
case (24:27; 25:9).46 


For further narrative tension, Luke highlights the return of the Herodian 


family to the scene in Caesarea. This resumes the Herodian storyline from 12:20– 
23 where Herod Agrippa I was reported as having been divinely executed in Cae- 
sarea because of his hybris for accepting divine honours (cf. the parallel in Jose- 
phus, Ant. 19.8.2). Representatives of Rome and the Jewish people are now shown 
again to be politically and intimately intertwined in Caesarea, even for a seeming- 
ly insignificant figure such as Paul. Caesarea was Herod the Great’s aggrandising 
project in honour of Augustus Caesar. This was conceived (and perceived) as 
Rome’s provincial rival to Jerusalem. Her commercial and political prowess was 
adorned with sacred spaces such as temples to Roma, Augustus, and Tiberius. But 
this was also a contested space, considered by some of the Jewish population to be 
theirs in that a Jew (i.e., Herod the Great) had built the city in all its grandeur (cf. 
Josephus, B.J. 2.266). 


The aura of the Herodian family continues in the narrative. In addition to 


the retrospective historical significance of the mixed nationalities of those who 
judged Paul’s case, Luke presents the recurrence of the Herodian dynasty as an 
example of the intermingling of regional Roman power with Jewish identity. In 
this regard, there is some irony in the treatment of Paul despite his defence that 
portrays him as a model Pharisee. 


Felix has Paul kept in Herod’s praetorium (23:35), and three of four children 


of Herod Agrippa I are mentioned: Herod Agrippa II, Bernice, and Drusilla.47 Her- 
od Agrippa II is portrayed as a noble and authoritative figure alongside Festus. 
Agrippa is referred to as βασιλεύς eleven times (via direct address by Festus and 
Paul, and in Luke’s own voice). What is more, Luke signals the presence of Felix’s 
wife, Drusilla, who “was Jewish” (οὔσῃ Ἰουδαίᾳ , 24:24) and may have been one of 
the sources for Felix’s accurate knowledge of the things concerning the Way 
(ἀκριβέστερον εἰδὼς τὰ περὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ, 24:22).48 The presence of Bernice, the 
younger sister of Agrippa and Drusilla, also adds to the solemnity of Paul’s hear- 
ing and to the overall agōn between Herod’s family, Jesus, and his followers.49 


Agrippa and Bernice – Luke notes – enter the place of audience (ἀκροατήριον) 
“with great pomp” (μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας, 25:23). Not only this, other signifi-

cant, but unnamed, dignitaries are present: “the military tribunes and the promi- 
nent men of the city” (25:23). 


These were, in short, the people present in various verbal exchanges with 


Paul. Luke reports that Felix – accompanied on occasion by Drusilla – converses 
privately with Paul (24:24–26). But no private conversation with Festus is men- 
tioned. Paul’s defence speeches recap many of the events and themes already en- 
countered in Luke’s second volume. Their theological import is discussed below 
in the ‘Summary of divine interventions’. 


The first hearing takes place before Felix, five days after Paul’s arrival from 


Jerusalem. The high priest, Ananias, is accompanied by other Jewish leaders and 
their attorney, Tertullus (24:1–23). Paul is accused of being “a pestilent man, who 
incites sedition among all the Jews around the world, and a leader of the sect of 
the Nazarenes,” and as one who had tried to profane the temple (24:5–6). Paul 
responds by stating facts that were verifiable and by establishing his devotion to 
his people and their God (24:10–21). Felix adjourns the assembly, stating that he 
would decide after Lysias the Tribune had given his report about Paul in person 
(24:22). 


The second hearing takes place in the presence of Festus and the Jews from 


Jerusalem (25:6–12). This is the shortest of the three hearings and the issue at 
hand is that Paul refuses to appear again before the Jewish authorities in Jer- 
usalem. He appeals to the authority of the emperor. Festus closes the hearing – in 
consultation with his council – granting Paul’s wish to be tried in Rome (25:12). 


This leads to the third hearing, which is occasioned by the fact that Festus 


had no worthwhile report to send to the emperor, and that Agrippa and Bernice 
had come to Caesarea to welcome him at the beginning of his administration 
(25:13, 20). Festus hopes to receive some insight from Agrippa in view of sending 
a report about Paul. This hearing receives the most narrative space (25:23– 
26:32). Paul builds on his defence by elucidating again his full devotion to the 
people of Israel and their God, which was formerly evidenced by his aggression 
against Jesus’ followers (26:9–12) but is now demonstrated by his obedience to 
the epiphany of Jesus (26:13–23). His testimony is supported by some pillars of 
Jewish beliefs: God, the prophets, Moses, and, for some Jewish groups, also the 
Messiah (26:22–23).50 The hearing ends with a lively exchange between Paul, Fes- 
tus, and Agrippa (26:24–29) and concludes with the unanimous statement of 
Paul’s innocence; ironically – they say – Paul could have been released if he had 
not appealed to the emperor (26:30–32). 


Declarations of Paul’s innocence stipple this section, so that Luke’s audience 


fully grasp Paul’s legal status before the authorities in Rome and in Jerusalem. 
Paul’s trials display him as a reliable representative of the Way due to his unwa- 
vering dedication to the same defence, which persuades Roman rulers of Paul’s 


50 
Pomykala (2010) 938. 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
392 


innocence. This enables Luke’s audience to understand that the accusations 
against Paul were not only unfounded but dangerous because of the links that 
were later drawn with the troubles that arose in the following years. Namely, the 
Jewish revolt against Rome in 66 CE and the destruction of Jerusalem and her 
temple in 70 CE. Luke’s audience could be encouraged to know that their move- 
ment was not the cause of this major social upheaval in Palestine. Paul is shown 
to be innocent before Roman law according to the letter by the tribune Claudius 
Lysias (23:29), Felix (implicit, 24:22–23, 26–27), Festus (25:25), and Herod Agrip- 
pa II (26:31–32). Paul claims his innocence before Jewish law, consistently refer- 
ring to his belief in the resurrection of the dead, which the Pharisees in Jerusalem 
had conceded as a valid argument and not as a charge against him (23:10). De- 
spite this, Paul (and the Way) is not set free, because he had appealed to the em- 
peror. 


Interestingly, while noteworthy characters feature in the aforementioned 


scenes, there are two instances of silence: Paul’s companions and any activity 
connected to the divine, such as Paul’s deity. Not many personal names or inter- 
actions are noted among the non-elite. Although Felix allows Paul’s friends to at- 
tend to his needs (24:23), there is no specific mention of them or any suggestion 
of the narrator’s presence. It can be reasonably assumed that Paul was assisted 
during these two years in light of previous mentions of Jesus’ followers in the re- 
gion of Caesarea (e.g., Philip, Cornelius, Mnason) and the resumption of the ‘we 
passages’ in 27:1 when Paul’s escorted journey to Rome begins. 


Summary of divine interventions. Throughout this section, Luke does not mention 
a single instance of perceived divine activity during Paul’s imprisonment in Cae- 
sarea. When mentioned, the divine is told in relation to prior events concerning 
Jesus and Paul’s experiences. Where, then, is Luke’s prophetic voice, showing the 
power and presence of the divine moving human history forward? The hiatus of 
divine activity is obviously a clear narrative break with all of the previous sec- 
tions and with the following (and final) section of Acts in which divine activity is 
reported. One might expect to hear of an epiphany of Jesus or angelic beings in 
the prison precincts (cf. 5:19; 12:7) or earthquakes opening cell doors (cf. 16:26). 
This warrants some reflection about how the divine is represented or even as- 
sumed to be at work in this section. 


First, this section is best understood in theological continuity with Paul’s vi- 


sion of Jesus, who tells Paul that he would bear witness in Rome (23:11). All this 
attention on Paul’s innocence – as a Roman citizen and a devout worshipper of 
Israel’s God – serves to consolidate Luke’s characterisation of Paul and his narra- 
tive function as the key protagonist in bringing the message of Jesus to the peo- 
ples. Paul is portrayed as both prisoner, missionary, and Roman citizen. He repre- 
sents three spheres of society: the Roman Empire, the Jewish people, and Jesus’ 
followers. This is a heavy burden to carry as he is portrayed as an enemy to some 


12 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts III 
393 


and a nuisance to others. In this light, this section serves to confirm the fulfilment 
of the prophecy uttered by Jesus about Paul’s sort. He will be sent to Rome and 
for a purpose. Indeed, Paul’s missionary calling is succinctly highlighted when he 
speaks of his faith in the Messiah to Felix and Drusilla (περὶ τῆς εἰς Χριστὸν 
Ἰησοῦν πίστεως (24:24)), and when he unswervingly states his beliefs (i.e., those 
of “the Way”) as being in line with Moses and the prophets (26:4, 22). Once again, 
divine rule is perceived as overpowering human attempts to bring an end to 
Paul’s mission. 


Second, Luke’s prophetic voice continues to explore – for the benefit of his 


audience – the agōnes on the human plane and the divine-human agōn through 
Paul and the movement that he represents, which are at odds with the Jewish au- 
thorities. The latter’s authority is frustratingly limited by imperial rule – as in 
Jerusalem, so in Caesarea. Luke’s depiction of Paul’s experiences of the divine 
realm provides insights about their implications for Paul’s life, for his fellow dis- 
ciples, and, more broadly, for the world. Paul’s defence speeches thus allow 
Luke’s audience to revisit key divine actions in Paul’s life that elaborate on the 
evidence in support of Jesus’ movement presented in previous sections. 


Third, reactions to Paul’s claims of divine activity invite the audience to re- 


flect on how perceptions of the divine were received by three regional leaders of 
the Empire. Felix responds with fear upon hearing about divine judgement 
(24:24–25). Festus dismisses Paul as mad due to his great learning (26:24). Agrip- 
pa rejects Paul’s invitation to recognise the prophets before the assembly (26:28): 
“Are you persuading me to become a Christian in such a short amount of time?”51 


All of this highlights the didactic nature of Luke’s prophetic voice. The retellings 
of Paul’s conversion inculcate in Luke’s original audience some beliefs of Jesus’ 
movement and encourage them to persevere as his followers in their own con- 
texts towards the end of the first century CE. As stated, no focus passages require 
further attention here. 


12.6 Section 8: Divine Rule Comes to Rome and the Agōn Continues 


(Acts 27:1–28:31) 


Section summary. This final section of Luke-Acts provides closure to a number of 
motifs and themes.52 Luke employs a range of literary topoi that were likely to 
resonate with his audience, e.g., examples of human error, even hybris, a great 
storm at sea, and a shipwreck.53 In addition, the narrative leads the audience

This is one of the three occurrences of Χριστιανός in the New Testament of which twice in

For a concise presentation of parallels between Luke and Acts and parallels between Acts 1– 
12 and 13–28, see Talbert (1974) 15–29.

For some ancient topoi and Acts, see Rapske (1994).

through a complex network of ‘sociomateriality’, namely, frequent mentions of 
place names, social interactions, and nautical matters and objects.54 In all of this, 
Paul’s role as a wise adviser and prophetic mediator are highlighted through four 
interventions.55 Similar to his previous speeches, these discourses orient the audi- 
ence’s reception of this final section by showing that Paul is wise due to his per- 
sonal background and his connection with his God. Again, the literary serves the 
theological. 


The temporal and geographical hiatus in Caesarea provides ample time for 


Luke’s audience to reflect on Paul’s dilemma as a Roman citizen and a Jewish 
follower of Jesus. The narrative now turns towards its climactic ending. Suspense 
builds around a central question. If Paul has not been judged and executed in Jer- 
usalem or Caesarea, the next threat will be destruction at sea, which represents 
an agōn with the natural world and, consequently, the divine world according to 
some ancient worldviews. Luke’s objective here is to demonstrate that just as 
Paul has been judged innocent by human rulers, he will be found innocent by 
God.56 


These two final chapters can be divided into four parts, with the geographic 


indications being consistently provided. The narrative flow of Paul’s journey 
leads the audience from Caesarea to Crete (27:1–12), from there to Malta (27:13– 
44), then to Rome (28:1–16), and, finally, to receive a glimpse of Paul’s two-year 
stay in Rome (28:16–31). Each segment adds to the narrative tension by compli- 
cating the journey with physical dangers, natural deterrents to travel, and vari- 
ous agōnes such as the human disputes onboard the ship about how to get to 
Rome in the face of extreme weather. This finally eases through Paul’s safe ar- 
rival in Rome and summary of his preaching activity there.57 


During the first part of the journey, from Caesarea to Crete (i.e., Fair Havens, 


27:1–12), the narrator’s presence reappears in the scene (e.g., 27:1–8), as does 
the device of naming individuals specifically, such as Julius the centurion (27:1), 
who oversees the transfer of Paul and the prisoners on board the ship, as well as 
Aristarchus, a Macedonian follower of Jesus from Thessalonica (27:2). The first 
part of the journey from Caesarea to Myra (Lycia) is successful but not without 
difficulty. From there, Julius organises the transfer of the passengers – number- 
ing 276 persons including soldiers and prisoners (27:37) – onto an Alexandrian 
wheat cargo ship.

The account of the second leg continues to build narrative tension through 


several mentions of maritime peril58 and through Paul’s first exhortation (παρ- 
ῄνει, 27:9), which fails to convince the pilot, the owner, and the centurion – in- 
deed, the majority (οἱ πλείονες, 27:12). At the risk of losing both cargo and their 
lives (27:10),59 the choice is made to leave Fair Havens for Phoenix in order to 
have a better harbour for wintering. 


The next section (27:13–44) explains how a “northeaster” (εὐρακύλων, 


27:14) blew the ship off course.60 Some control of the ship was managed around 
the leeside of the island Cauda, but danger lurked in the waters because of the 
Syrtis, two major shoals in the Mediterranean. Despite lowering the anchor, the 
ship was being driven by a violent storm. The gravity of the situation is clear, 
echoing Paul’s warning. The cargo and the ship’s tackle are thrown over (27:18– 
19) and “finally all hope of our being saved was taken away” (λοιπὸν περιῃρεῖτο 
ἐλπὶς πᾶσα τοῦ σῳ ́ζεσθαι ἡμᾶς, 27:20). Paul’s second intervention is shown to be 
timely as he reminds them of his warning and encourages them with news that 
his God has promised safety to all the passengers through an appearance of an 
angel (27:22–26). This is discussed further below. 


During the fourteenth night (27:27–38), the sailors who are marked by fear 


and impelled to pray (27:29) secretly decide to abandon the ship. This warrants 
Paul’s third intervention: “If these men do not stay in the ship, you cannot be 
saved” (27:31). This time the centurion and the soldiers heed Paul’s warning and 
prevent the sailors from leaving. Shortly thereafter, Paul now has centre stage. 
Through his fourth intervention, he encourages the passengers to eat some food 
to gain strength in view of their promised deliverance. The theological import of 
this passage is unmistakable. In particular, verse 35 offers a clear parallel with 
Jesus at table with his disciples (Luke 22:19; 24:30–31) when Paul gives thanks to 
God before all for the bread and eats some of it. This encourages others to do the 
same.61 Once they have satisfied their hunger, the wheat is thrown overboard to 
lighten the ship. 


The audience now views the shipwreck (27:29–44) and the subsequent so- 


journ in Malta (28:1–9). The shipwreck, as a literary topos, was both entertaining 
and instructive in antiquity.62 Here the narrator is silent about his own experi- 
ence of this disaster. But he offers much detail as a spectator, preferring to focus

on two failed missions: the sailors’ wish to save the ship and the soldiers’ plan to 
kill the prisoners including Paul. When the former plan is doomed, the latter is 
again obstructed by Julius who wanted to save Paul (27:43; cf. 27:30–32). Imperi- 
al authorities are shown to serve the overall divine plan once again. Luke con- 
firms this twice by stating that all the passengers had reached the shoreline safely 
(27:44; 28:1). 


The scene continues with first-person narration, recounting an unexpected 


experience with the islanders whom Luke calls βάρβαροι (28:2). These, he says, 
showed “us” “not ordinary kindness” (28:2). These βάρβαροι were observant 
about divine workings when they witness Paul surviving contact with a viper. 
Their prior conclusion that he must have been a murderer (28:4) turns into con- 
sidering Paul to be a god (28:6). This pagan interpretation echoes Paul and Barn- 
abas’ experience with pagan religion in Lystra, when they were named Zeus and 
Hermes because of a healing in public (14:12–13). 


This three-month unplanned wintering in Malta (cf. 28:11) features still an- 


other of Paul’s meetings with dignitaries. Publius, “the leading man of the island” 
(τῷ πρώτῳ τῆς νήσου ὀνόματι Ποπλίῳ , 28:7) shows hospitality to the stranded 
group (“us”).63 Paul’s ministry on the island is limited to curing Publius’ father as 
well as those with diseases on the island (28:8–9).64 Curiously, alongside the heal- 
ings, no preaching or conversions are mentioned. A generous sending-off is given 
with “many honours” (πολλαῖς τιμαῖς) and all the necessities for the next leg of 
their journey to Rome (28:10). 


In Lukan laconic fashion, Luke tells this last part of the story, which took 


place approximately in the lapse of two years (60–62 CE), in the space of twenty 
verses (28:11–31). The journey continues first by sea (via Syracuse, Rhegium, and 
Puteoli) with an Alexandrian ship with the “Twin Brothers” (the Dioscuri) on the 
prow, which may be Luke’s subtle, and perhaps ironic, gesture to the protective 
saviour gods on sea.65 Continuing then by land, they passed through the Forum of 
Appius and Three Taverns. Luke provides a glimpse of the Christian community 
there. Some brothers (ἀδελφούς, ἀδελφοί, 28:14–15) provide a week’s stay in 
Puteoli and others accompany Paul in the last part of the journey until Rome. For 
them, “Paul thanked God and took courage” (28:15). 


Luke’s depiction of Paul’s stay in Rome suggests good treatment. He is “al- 


lowed to live by himself, with the soldier who was guarding him” (28:16). Twice 
he enjoys the freedom to receive a delegation from the Jewish community (28:17– 
22, 23–28), and he is said to have lived in that place for two whole years (διετίαν

ὅλην, 28:30), receiving visits and preaching and teaching “with all boldness and 
without hindrance” (μετὰ πάσης παρρησίας ἀκωλύτως, 28:31). 


The two gatherings with the Jewish leaders are succinctly described. In the 


first, Paul discloses his innocence against “the people or the customs of our ances- 
tors” (28:17), his reason for appealing to the emperor, and “the hope of Israel” 
(28:20). Paul’s interlocuters reveal that they had indeed heard about the sect (αἱρ- 
έσεως, 28:22) but had not received letters or reports about Paul (28:21). They 
wanted to know more.66 The second gathering echoes previous encounters with 
Jewish audiences in that Paul exposes his reasons for his faith in the kingdom of 
God in relation to Jesus based on Jewish scriptures. The reaction is depicted as 
mixed: some were convinced while others were unbelieving (ἠπίστουν, 28:24). 
This provokes two reactions: disagreement among themselves followed by a 
weighty rebuke by Paul, who calls as his witness the Holy Spirit who had inspired 
the prophet Isaiah from whom a quotation is evoked (Isa 6:9–10). If the quotation 
is not direct enough – emphasising metaphorical lack of spiritual perception 
(hearing, sight, and heart) – Paul reiterates that the salvation of God has been 
sent to the peoples “and they will listen” (28:28, αὐτοὶ καὶ ἀκούσονται). 


The description of their meeting ends here, as does Luke’s second volume, 


with a final synopsis that connects Paul’s part in the greater theme of the king- 
dom of God arriving in Rome (28:30–31). Modern readers find it strange that 
Luke makes no mention of Paul’s martyrdom, which is attested in later works.67 


Some of Luke’s audience, however, certainly knew of Paul’s death and may have 
been satisfied with this so-called abrupt ending with which Luke has brought clo- 
sure to the main questions, namely, how the message about Jesus passed through 
many regions and arrived at the imperial centre through Paul and other follow- 
ers of Jesus.68 Jesus’ movement, “the Way,” has encountered various agōnes and 
survived through Paul and his companions and, presumably, also through Luke’s 
audience. Here, one fathoms something of the vital significance for them to have 
an account about the teaching of Jesus arriving in Rome. 


Summary of divine interventions. This section interrupts the silence of divine in- 
terventions in the preceding section about Paul’s stay in Caesarea. Five occur- 
rences of divine activity appear here and contribute to closure on various themes 
in Luke-Acts (see Appendix III). The presence of Paul’s deity in other regions, by 
sea and by land, contributes to the confidence that Luke instils in his audience 
about the god of the Way and about Paul as one of his chief representatives 
throughout the Empire.
