The presence of Paul’s deity is signalled through an epiphany of an angel of 


God. This angel encourages Paul that he will indeed “stand before the emperor” 
and that God will ensure the safety of all his fellow travellers (27:23–26). It is evi- 
dent that this situation has consequences for the entire group of passengers, who 
are promised – through Paul – that they too will also find safe passage (27:24, 31, 
34). This promise is portrayed as being fulfilled by God via the verb διασῴζω used 
twice: καὶ οὕτως ἐγένετο πάντας διασωθῆναι ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν (27:44) and again at the 
beginning of the following paragraph, καὶ διασωθέντες τότε ἐπέγνωμεν ὅτι 
Μελίτη ἡ νῆσος καλεῖται (28:1). 


Paul’s innocence echoes highlighted scenes of the innocence of Jesus, Peter, 


and Stephen – and, implicitly, the entire movement, the Way, through the fulfil- 
ment of physical safety during the maritime journey. This is confirmed by an il- 
lustration of divine protection that prevents ill effects or even fatality from the 
viper’s venom, which starkly contrasts with the expectations of the Maltese 
(28:3–6). The divine is not explicitly evoked, but it can be assumed that Luke ex- 
pects his audience to interpret this as another example of God’s protection of 
Paul. 


In Malta, continued demonstration of God’s power outside the traditional ar- 


eas of Israel’s God are expressed through deeds of power. Publius’ father, sick 
with a fever and dysentery, is healed (28:8). Paul also cures those with diseases 
on the island (28:9). These physical healings parallel those accomplished through 
Jesus (4:40), Peter (3:6, 12), and Philip (8:5–7). They function as further τεκμήρια 
to buttress the narrative’s overall didactic function. 


Finally, although there are no specific conversion stories in this section, 


there is a hint that some of the Jewish leaders in Rome may have received Paul’s 
message and later joined the assembly of Jesus’ followers (28:23–24). This 
demonstrates Luke’s intention to show his readers Jewish reception of Jesus in 
various regions. The themes of reception and rejection run throughout the two 
volumes, and the final meeting between Paul and the Jewish leaders confirms 
these themes. To ensure that his other emphasis is not overlooked (i.e., salvation 
among the peoples), Luke provides his audience of mixed ethnic groups and reli- 
gious backgrounds with a resounding conclusion. This is the focus below. 


Focus Passage of Luke’s Prophetic Voice and the Agōn 


The salvation of God has been sent to the peoples (28:23–28). Divine salvation 
(σωτηρία and σωτήριον (1:77; 2:30; 3:6)) and redemption (λύτρωσις, Luke 1:68; 
2:38) have been some of the main objects of Luke’s narrative from the opening 
chapters. Throughout Luke and Acts, Israel’s God is depicted as taking the initia- 
tive to implement his plan (βουλή, e.g., Luke 7:30; Acts 2:23; 4:28) to reconcile 
Israel to himself. As the narrative progresses, this plan is shown to not be restrict- 


12 Divine Rule in Luke-Acts III 
399 


ed to one people but extended to all peoples. This is perhaps most clearly brought 
together in Simeon’s prophecy: “a light for revelation to the peoples and for glory 
to your people Israel” (φῶς εἰς ἀποκάλυψιν ἐθνῶν καὶ δόξαν λαοῦ σου Ἰσραήλ, 
Luke 2:32). 


For this reason, Luke pays close attention to the reception of Jesus and his 


disciples’ message about Jesus among the peoples throughout the Empire. In this 
final episode, Luke cites Paul, using solemn language, “Let it be known to you 
then that this salvation of God has been sent to the peoples and they will listen” 
(γνωστὸν οὖ ν ἔστω ὑμῖν ὅτι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπεστάλη τοῦτο τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ, 
28:28). The passive voice of ἀπεστάλη indicates to Luke’s audience that God is the 
logical subject of sending the salvation. The God of Israel is now preached as the 
God of all peoples, for his σωτήριον is for them as well, and it is mediated through 
Jesus (Acts 28:23, 31). 


Luke does not divulge knowledge of divine activity during Paul’s stay of two 


years in Rome. There is no triumphant welcome nor mass conversions among the 
Jewish and non-Jewish population. But looking back at the geographical develop- 
ment of Luke’s second volume, e.g., the integration of Saul the persecutor into the 
Way and his arrival with the message about Jesus to Rome, underscores that the 
story is essentially about Paul’s deity initiating and accomplishing his plan to 
bring the message about Jesus to the heart of the Roman Empire. It is less about 
Paul’s trial and more about the ‘saviour god’ arriving and challenging competing 
narratives of the divine. 


12.7 Conclusion for Sections 4–8 (Acts 15:36–28:31) 


The beginning of Luke’s second volume opens with a question: “Lord, is this the 
time when you restore the kingdom to Israel?” (1:6). It may also reflect one of the 
driving questions for Luke’s audience towards the end of the first century: Where 
is the kingdom of God? Jesus’ answer does not deny it but defers it, and he directs 
his disciples’ attention to their implication in his shared mandate: to be his wit- 
nesses throughout the world, crossing cultural and geopolitical borders. Luke’s 
narrative addresses the disciples’ question by showing that no military takeover 
has taken place in Jerusalem or Judea or elsewhere. But Sections 1–3 show that a 
divine kingdom or rule does exist, which is confirmed through the apparitions 
and interventions of the ascended Jesus and the Holy Spirit. The result is that in- 
dividuals and groups from among the ‘peoples’ are integrated into ‘the people’ 
following Jesus, and the leaders of the church in Jerusalem confirm this as being 
the accomplishment of God’s plan (15:12–21). 


Sections 4–8 build on this as Luke’s characters perceive divine initiative, fo- 


calised especially through Paul of Tarsus. The narrative continues by shifting dra- 
matically to a new development: the disciples’ mandate moves from Asia to Eu- 


Part IV Hearing Luke’s Prophetic Voice 
400 


rope instigated by a vision in Troas of a Macedonian man asking Paul: “Come 
over to Macedonia and help us” (16:9). Paul and his team never meet this myste- 
rious man, but the underlying agōn awaits them as various forces opposing di- 
vine rule present in Jesus’ witnesses. Their decision to cross from Troas to Neapo- 
lis initiated a string of visits, moving from Macedonia to Achaia then again to Asia 
and Judea, and, finally to Italy. Luke’s audience explores scenes in major cities 
that demonstrate that this divine plan, though opposed, is ultimately unstoppable, 
being superior to spiritual forces in those regions as well as human forces, includ- 
ing representatives of the Roman Empire. The apex of this is the τεκμήριον of 
Paul’s arrival in Rome as an innocent citizen of Rome, which is announced by 
Jesus in Jerusalem (23:11), enacted by Roman leaders in Caesarea, and confirmed 
by an angel on the ship (27:24). 


Luke’s prophetic voice serves not merely for the sake of a good story but for 


the sake of his audience, some of whom, like Theophilus, were needing to know 
the security or certainty (ἀσφάλεια, Luke 1:4) of their collective faith. His prophet- 
ic voice thus manifests itself not only through captivating scenes of Jesus’ contin- 
ued presence, e.g., via healings and epiphanies (i.e., in Corinth and Jerusalem), 
but also through the extensive use of the divine plupast in Paul’s speeches, which 
gives a sense of continuity in the plan of the God of Israel and thus depth to the 
teaching of those belonging to “the Way.” For Luke’s audience, Paul embodies the 
composition of this multicultural group of Jesus’ followers, being a Jewish Phar- 
isee, Roman citizen, and a native of Greek-speaking Tarsus. In this way, Luke sub- 
stantiates his understanding of divine rule: it is the inseparability of “the king- 
dom of God” and “the things concerning Jesus” (28:23, 31).

13 Conclusion: Prophetic-like Voices: 


From Herodotus to Luke? 


13.1 Herodotus’ Table of Historians and the Building Blocks 


of their Craft 


It is intriguing to imagine Herodotus conversing with his successors around the 
table. The Greek language and their love of history would unify the cultural and 
geographical diversity of the participants around the table, hailing from regions 
such as Asia and Attica, Italy and northern Africa, the Levant and Mesopotamia. 
This imaginary framework has helped explore this project’s main questions: How 
did Herodotus and his successors deal with the mythopoetic tradition concerning 
the divine realm (i.e., the ‘hermeneutical dilemma’) bequeathed mainly by the 
Homeric tradition? And is it possible to include ‘Luke’, the author of Luke-Acts in 
this succession of Greek historiographers? Answers to these questions, based on a 
theological and narratological approach, have been addressed with mainly two 
readerships in mind: classicists and biblical scholars. 


In the following outline, I summarise how this study builds on previous re- 


search and breaks new ground in six ways by proposing the following: (1) theistic 
continuity as a strand of Greek historiography; (2) a theological and narrative 
methodology for studying this aspect, termed the ‘prophetic voice’; (3) the devel- 
opment of the Herodotus–Luke historiographical axis; (4) the demonstration of 
theological and narratological readings of Herodotus and Luke, and consequently 
(5) further historiographical justification for including Luke-Acts in classical re- 
search, as well as (6) the justification for further research in the Classics and in 
biblical studies on the theological and rhetorical strands of Greek historiography. 


For this summary of research, it is helpful to return to the imaginary table of 


historians convened by Herodotus. On the cusp of the end of the first century CE – 
i.e., the culmination of the time frame of this research – Greek historiography 
was still being shaped by voices from various regions and cultures. Some of 
Herodotus’ successors would be sympathetic to his views and methods, while oth- 
ers would be clearly antagonistic. However, they may have agreed on at least 
some of the fundamental principles that shaped their approach to history writ- 
ing.1 


1 
E.g., John Marincola has given us – in his introductory chapter – an idea of some of these 
essential components of historiography as well as some thorny questions about methodology 
and composition in his treatment of individual authors, see Marincola (2017) xxix–lxxi. Lu- 


One of these may have been to acknowledge that their craft operated on two 


levels, the redactional and the rhetorical. These two levels worked together to de- 
scribe the past with an eye to the present of their audiences. The narrative aspect 
influenced their selection and description of events and characters (micronarra- 
tives), as well as how – through the arrangement of those smaller units – they 
constructed their overall narrative argument (macronarrative) to investigate 
their main questions. On the rhetorical level, all this redactional activity served 
explicit and implicit existential purposes for their audiences. Like other produc- 
ers of oral and written works, historians played a didactic role for their readers 
and listeners, taking their circumstances, concerns, and interests into account. 
Imparting historical knowledge was vital, as was drawing lessons for contempo- 
rary life, both collectively and individually. 


Herodotus and his fellow historians may also have found common ground in 


the literary and oral traditions that influenced their compositions. Two main tra- 
ditions, the mythopoetic and the rhetorical, would have come to the fore. The 
mythopoetic tradition bequeathed a large lexical stock, some historical knowl- 
edge and poetic elegance, focusing on conflicts (agōnes). It also played a signifi- 
cant role in moral education. The questions that often drive their narrative in- 
trigues are: Who had the right and ability to occupy land and rule there? How 
should they rule and within which boundaries? Who was to blame for the con- 
flicts? Who were the winners and who were the losers? And why? Accordingly, 
some common themes were explored: governance and justice; conquest and op- 
pression through the imperial impulse; freedom, resistance, and liberation (sal- 
vation). This epic heritage also provided Greek historians with the contours of a 
worldview that acknowledged the existence and activity of a divine realm – 
mainly polytheistic, but with some nuances. Not all of Herodotus’ successors 
agreed with his interpretation of this worldview, either because they saw his mis- 
interpretation of the gods as flawed, or because they disagreed with the composi- 
tion of the divine realm itself. However, they all agreed that something greater 
than the human realm ultimately shaped the development and direction of histo- 
ry. Divine rule was perceived as keeping various forms of human rule in check in 
an unbroken sequence of raising and levelling. 


Given the prominence of orality in antiquity, the rhetorical tradition ma- 


tured alongside the mythopoetic tradition before other textual traditions. But it 
continued to evolve alongside historiography and other literary traditions, such 
as tragedy, comedy, and philosophy. Herodotus and his heirs encountered 
rhetoricians and learned from them a good range of techniques – to name a few – 
incipits, accounts of actions and speech; auctorial asides and actorial points of 
view; positive and negative exempla; proofs (tekmēria) for corroboration; as well 


cian of Samosata’s How to Write History helps us to imagine what debates he may have had 
with his generation of historians and rhetoricians. 


Prophetic-like Voices: From Herodotus to Luke? 
404 


as plupast sections for historical depth. The richness and variety of these tradi- 
tions served the existential aims of the historians to educate and entertain their 
audiences, as well as impart valuable lessons. These were intended to persuade 
or dissuade readers in their interpretation of history and in the light of the situa- 
tions that they faced in their own contexts. 


In sum, Herodotus and his successors would have much material to work 


with and much to agree on, but also much to debate. One such debate concerned 
how closely to emulate Homer and Herodotus when writing about the divine 
realm to audiences who still expected this element in historical discourse. 
Herodotus addressed this hermeneutical dilemma posed by Homer, thus giving 
rise to the prophetic-like voice of Greek historiography. To flesh this out, the fol- 
lowing section below summarises six contributions of this study, indicated below 
in italics. 


13.2 The Rhetorical Force of the Historians’ Prophetic-like Voices: 


Perceptions of the Divine to Address their Audiences’ 


Questions and Interests 


Theistic continuity as a strand of Greek historiography. This study has argued that 
one of the ongoing debates among historians was not whether but how they 
should integrate their perceptions of the divine realm and those of their charac- 
ters. Homer and Hesiod’s way of telling stories about the gods and heroes, name- 
ly, through direct participation in action, had almost completely been set aside by 
Herodotus, and his heirs generally followed suit. The historiographical tradition 
was not going to be a mere imitator of the mythopoetic tradition in the represen- 
tation of divine action. Nor was it to be reduced to a worldview as a closed sys- 
tem, focusing only on how their world was being shaped by events and people. 
Their worldviews (for there were several) acknowledged that the divine had a 
role to play in human history. Smaller acts and speeches were seen to be a part of 
a larger narrative, and the divine was perceived as intervening in the smaller sto- 
ries to shape the larger one. 


This research has highlighted some of the ways in which historiography 


built on and distanced itself from the mythopoetic tradition. One of the reasons 
that the divine realm was not set aside was because God, the gods, heroes, and 
other forms of divine presence and activity were still perceived to be real to their 
audiences. This was arguably also the general perception of the historians who 
were addressing their audiences’ questions and concerns. Nevertheless, this cul- 
tural dimension has not always been given due consideration within the frame- 
work of historiographical studies. 


13 Conclusion 
405 


Alongside the didactic voices of tragedians, orators, and philosophers in soci- 


ety, historians offered alternative methods and voices for addressing historical 
and contemporary issues. By evoking the divine in various ways as a part of their 
narratives, they employed interpretative and communicative strategies that have 
prophetic-like qualities. By seeing and making known the past through the lens of 
the divine – through their beliefs, even faith – the historians’ didactic function in 
society claimed an additional depth of field. Their audiences, it was argued, ex- 
pected to hear how the divine realm – however it was understood – had shaped 
human history, culminating in the world in which they lived and the societal 
challenges they faced. This was theological reflection on two situations, for exam- 
ple, Herodotus’ description of the Greco-Persian Wars in the light of the Atheno- 
Peloponnesian conflicts, or Luke’s view of the disputes between Jesus and the 
Jewish authorities against the backdrop of the Jewish revolts against the Roman 
Empire. 


As a study of the history of historiography, Chapter 2 showed that the histo- 


riographical record, though largely incomplete, evinces theistic continuity from 
Herodotus to Luke. This is one of those longitudinal threads that can be traced 
through different periods, regions, and cultural expressions. Rather than indiffer- 
ence and rupture towards the divine realm, historians integrated – consistently 
but with varying intensity – perceptions of divine agency. Historians, then, had 
their own prophetic voice, which allowed them to address the questions of their 
audiences about both the past and the present. These were connected worlds ac- 
cording to their worldviews. While their understanding of the divine can be de- 
scribed as theistic, it was not theologically uniform. Differences in the representa- 
tions of perceptions of the divine were highlighted between authors such as 
Herodotus, Thucydides, Polybius, Josephus, Plutarch, and Luke. 


The ‘prophetic voice’ as an interpretative narrative model to explore this strand. 
Alongside classical studies, this research also bridges the disciplines of theology 
(especially, biblical exegesis) and narratology. This narratological voice can also 
be beneficial in the analysis of various types of narratives, both fictional and fac- 
tual, in which a theistic narrative or even metanarrative contribute to the narra- 
tion. For works of history, Chapter 3 elaborates the concept of the ‘prophetic 
voice’ and examines its narrative and theological functions. While the list of char- 
acteristics of the prophetic voice is not exhaustive, it outlines the main compo- 
nents that I have identified in ancient Greek historiography. The aim is to explore 
how narrative techniques and rhetorical strategies intertwine, integrating autho- 
rial and actorial perceptions of the divine for their audiences. This is achieved 
through the depiction of events and characters (micronarrative level) as a part of 
the overall structure of the narrative argumentation (macronarrative level). 


In rhetorical terms, then, the prophetic voice can convey perceptions of the 


divine using a variety of narrative techniques. For instance, plupast material can 


Prophetic-like Voices: From Herodotus to Luke? 
406 


incorporate the divine and provide a theological reading of events beyond the 
temporal limits of the core narrative. This can then contribute to the characterisa- 
tion of individuals or groups, providing positive or negative exempla for the audi- 
ence. Examples of piety and impiety are often presented to encourage reflection 
on the value of honouring the divine by respecting things associated with the di- 
vine sphere such as temples, rituals, oracles, even nomoi. In summary, the 
prophetic voice as a narratological voice, helps us explore how historians com- 
posed their narratives (emplotment), using techniques to orient their audiences’ 
cognitive and emotional encounter with the narrative’s questions (plot), persuad- 
ing them to adopt and integrate the historians’ interpretations and values in their 
own living narratives (explotment). 


The Herodotus–Luke historiographical axis. Chapters 4–6 provide preparatory 
material for a focused comparison of Herodotus and Luke, examining their writ- 
ings in detail. These two historians were chosen mainly because of the high fre- 
quency with which they integrate perceptions of the divine into their causal 
structures, their different worldviews, and because they bookend the proposed 
time frame. They offer to their audiences not only narrative finesse but also theo- 
logical reflection, and, thus also, rhetorical force through their prophetic voices. 
Their incipits, both pithy and profound, evoke “great and marvellous deeds” 
(Hist. 1.1) and “deeds accomplished among us” (Luke 1:1) as ‘monuments’ to hu- 
man and divine beings who intervene in their stories. Smaller narrative units are 
connected to a larger story, inviting the audience to consider its consequences 
and, secondly, their own part in human history. The plupast sections in the Histo- 
ries and in Luke-Acts use the audiences’ knowledge of the metanarratives to ori- 
ent them as they enter subsequent stories, exploring events and characters (e.g., 
highlights on Solon and Croesus; Zechariah, Mary, and Simeon) to catch a 
glimpse of the themes developed in the core narratives. Although their subjects 
and understanding of the divine (‘divine constellations’ in Chapter 6) differ con- 
siderably, both are interested in exploring events and themes from theological 
perspectives that have global interest and implications. 


Theological and narratological readings of Herodotus and Luke through their 
prophetic voices. Sections three and four (Chapters 7–12) examine the prophet- 
like voices of Herodotus and Luke throughout the Histories and Luke-Acts. The 
chapter summaries provide specific insights. Here, I highlight some of the key 
points. In these chapters, diachronic data was used to focus on how this theologi- 
cal strand contributed to the advancement of major and minor issues that may 
have intrigued their audiences. Diachronic data served to give an idea of what 
our narrators assumed their audiences knew. Much of this is, of course, implicit, 
but it can help us read between the lines and assist modern readers who are un- 
familiar with the narratives under study. 


13 Conclusion 
407 


Chapters 7–9 offer close readings of the Histories, following the flow of the 


overarching narrative. This approach complements other monographs on 
Herodotus’ interest in the divine such as those by Lachenaud, Harrison, and 
Mikalson. This exegetical section provides a rich inventory of how Herodotus’ 
prophetic voice weaves multiple theological and geopolitical threads in his treat- 
ment of the reigns of Croesus, Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius, and Xerxes. Herodotus 
follows the Homeric tradition of focusing on agōnes at the individual and global 
levels. The theological underpinning of the macronarrative has been shown to 
provide a causal chain from Croesus to Xerxes that is consistently kept before the 
audience’s eyes through illustrations of divine intervention (e.g., actions, oracles, 
portents), as well as through Herodotus’ description of bidirectional activity be- 
tween worshippers and their gods. 


In this way, the audience is invited to follow not only the movements of the 


Persian forces and Greek resistance, but also the spiritual landscape, which some- 
times signals divine presence and activity in shaping the conflicts’ themes. In 
Herodotus’ narrative world, the geopolitical is perceived as being imbued with 
divine influence. It is decidedly not Homer’s style, yet temples, shrines, oracles 
and interpreters, sacrifices and priests appear regularly. In terms of theological 
principles, Herodotus conveys certain notions, for example, that divine rule does 
not tolerate the hubristic acts by individuals or peoples, such as the uncontrolled 
imperial impulse to cross borders and oppress others. This is particularly high- 
lighted through the Eurasian agōn. The gods also bring retribution for sacrile- 
gious acts against sacred things that belong to them. Herodotus guides his audi- 
ence to perceive that things are not going to end well for the Persian kings 
because the gods seem to have fought against them – not necessarily because 
they were defending their Greek worshippers – but because they could not allow 
the Persians to rule over Asia and Europe. The gods also could not let the Persians 
go unpunished for the sacrilegious acts committed against their temples, groves, 
and natural boundaries such as rivers. 


Humanly speaking, the Persians should have won these wars. Herodotus’ 


audience would have known this and would have known the main elements of 
the story. But Herodotus extends his investigation by exploring various peoples, 
their ethnographies, and their roles in this great conflict. Throughout his work, 
Herodotus also shows how the gods and the heroes were perceived either to 
make the battles fair for both sides or to level the Persian forces on land and sea. 
It is reasonable to assume that the Greeks’ victory was regarded as a significant 
and marvellous achievement, deserving immortalisation through a literary ‘mon- 
ument’ such as the Histories. However, Herodotus is careful to signal to his read- 
ers through various voices that this victory was achieved, along with other hu- 
man and natural forces, with the help of the gods and the heroes. But Herodotus 
is not setting forth some kind of divine plan at work like Luke does. The theologi- 
cal principles given above are shown to be implemented, but not towards some 


Prophetic-like Voices: From Herodotus to Luke? 
408 


foreknown telos. The gods are not in conflict with one another about some future 
goal, nor are they perceived to be divided as in the Homeric tradition, either for 
the Greeks or for the Persians. Human history moves forward, and the divine 
realm intervenes to maintain order, to keep humans in their place, and execute 
retribution when necessary. If there is a telos, it may be thought of as the gods 
maintaining their rule, that is, divine rule over all forms of human rule. 


What lessons did Herodotus impart to his audience who were facing the 


tragedy of the Atheno-Peloponnesian conflict? As is often the case, Herodotus 
touches on several levels of society. At the level of the city-state, he warned the 
Athenians against their hubristic behaviour and their imperialistic tendencies, 
which saw them oppress not only non-Greeks but also other Greek city-states. The 
warning was that they were likely to suffer the same fate as other great military 
powers. On an individual level, this grand narrative and anecdotal exempla are 
supported by a theological framework that encourages Herodotus’ audience to 
reflect on other lessons. For instance, Herodotus urges them to avoid the risks of 
amassing wealth, individual and familial hybris, and disrespect for the divine. In- 
stead, he encourages them to practise humility and piety in the face of human 
frailty and uncertainty in their experience of an internecine conflict. 


In Chapters 10–12, the same narratological methodology is applied to Luke-Acts, a 
story that may seem alien to Herodotus’ world because of its time frame, geopolit- 
ical situation, and worldview. Despite these differences, I have argued, with oth- 
ers, that Luke’s narrative displays significant knowledge of Greek and Jewish his- 
toriography, which are his primary frames of reference, historical, literary, and 
theological. 


Although Luke does not imitate Herodotus and other historians who focus 


on military strife between peoples and city-states, the threat of military conflict 
looms in the background. Luke thus follows the ancient tradition of developing 
narratives based on one main agōn and several minor ones. Luke’s writings, like 
the other canonical gospels, follow this tradition. In addition, like other ‘crossover 
historians’ who wrote histories to recount the stories of their minority peoples 
under foreign rule (e.g., Berossus, Manetho, and Josephus), so Luke describes the 
history of his ‘people’ within a larger metanarrative characterised by conflict. 
This is the continuation of Jewish history under yet another foreign rule. Thus, 
aspirations for salvation from the Roman Empire emerge early in Luke’s first vol- 
ume, and their rhetorical weight is better appreciated in relation to themes of 
‘salvation’ and ‘saviour gods’ in antiquity.2 


The most significant theological difference is not only the composition of the 


divine realm (cf. Chapter 6), but also the way Luke communicates to his readers 
how the God of Israel takes the initiative to provide a means of salvation that 


2 
Jim (2022). 


13 Conclusion 
409 


would gradually be understood to apply to all peoples everywhere. A clear narra- 
tive telos emerges as a promise of liberation that is being gradually focalised 
through Luke’s characters. It becomes clear that the main agent of salvation will 
be Jesus of Nazareth, who is described by Luke and his characters with a variety 
of human and divine epithets. He is said to inherit both human rule over Israel 
(through the lineage of King David) and to merit divine rule (through the Holy 
Spirit). But this royal and heroic figure, unlike the Persian kings, has no intention 
of raising an army to conquer Jerusalem. Luke is careful to display the expecta- 
tions and tensions of a possible coup d’état. Even the διάβολος tries to offer Jesus 
a share in ruling over the peoples. 


However, when viewed in the context of the overall narrative, the theme of 


divine rule that Luke develops from the outset is that God is creating a people 
from all peoples who recognise and live by his rule. Accordingly, it is understood 
that God has a βασιλεία on earth (cf. Luke 17:20–21). This is understood as a spiri- 
tual rule among those who receive “the word [about Jesus]” (Luke 1:2; Acts 1:1). 
Thus, in classical terms, the development of this claimed spiritual rule through 
Jesus does not go unnoticed and continues unabated. An agōn is unleashed, and 
Luke employs various narrative techniques to advance the story. This account of 
perceived salvation becomes particularly interesting when viewed alongside the 
conceptions of salvation and saviours known in the Mediterranean Basin. Luke’s 
audience explores this salvation story – which ‘must’ happen (cf. the use of δεῖ) – 
primarily through the lens of Jewish divine liberation but also in light of and in 
contrast to Greco-Roman traditions of divine deliverance. 


Opposition takes place in both the spiritual realm and in the human realm. 


This is another theological difference with Herodotus, who does not depict con- 
flict in the divine realm. Throughout Luke-Acts, Jesus and his disciples encounter 
antagonistic agents from the world of the spirits. In this sense, the story reflects 
the contours of a Jewish worldview. But it is not a story of ethereal battles be- 
tween angels and demons behind the scenes. Acts of resistance always centre on 
Jesus and his followers, taking place in the public spaces of the Roman Empire. 
The story begins in the province of Judea, passes through several other provinces 
by land and sea, and ends in the Roman capital. Like Herodotus’ narrative of a 
victory achieved with divine assistance, Luke’s account tells the story of an un- 
likely individual and his group of followers who assert that Jesus has begun his 
reign in heaven, rendering him superior to human rulers of the day and capable 
of intervening in the human realm to assist and guide his followers. This is the 
message of ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ that Luke leaves with his audience in the final act 
of Paul’s preaching in Rome (Acts 28:23, 31). 


On the rhetorical level, much of Luke’s audience, like Herodotus’ audience, 


also lived under foreign, and sometimes oppressive, rule. In this context, it is im- 
portant to consider the expectation of the restoration of the kingdom to Israel (cf. 
Acts 1:6). Luke guides his readers to explore the manifestation of the kingdom of 


Prophetic-like Voices: From Herodotus to Luke? 
410 


God in times of foreign rule, such as that experienced under the Roman Empire. 
Although Jesus does not directly respond to the question about the desire for the 
restoration of the kingdom to Israel, he directs his disciples’ attention to the work 
of the divine realm in their world. It seems likely that Luke wishes to flesh out 
Jesus’ approach by answering the disciples’ question, which may also have been 
a question on the minds of Luke’s audience. The message for them is that the di- 
vine reign is real and has been established through the fulfilment of the divine 
plan of reconciliation, between God and humanity. Like Herodotus, Luke works 
with the principle that divine rule will ultimately level all forms of human op- 
pression. As this study has demonstrated, theological and narratological readings 
of Herodotus and Luke-Acts lead to a rich and holistic interpretation that shows 
how both historians are part of a tradition that uses a ‘prophetic voice’ to illus- 
trate the perceived role of the divine in human events. 


Further historiographical justification for the inclusion of Luke-Acts and other bibli- 
cal narratives in Classical research. As outlined above, this research provides fur- 
ther evidence to support the assertion that Luke is rightly considered one of 
Herodotus’ heirs, and that the field of classical studies should also encompass 
Luke-Acts. Excluding Luke on theological grounds is anachronistic from a histori- 
ographical perspective. Just as other historians anchored their stories in the his- 
torical and theological metanarratives of their peoples, Luke tells a story an- 
chored in the Jewish theological metanarrative. However, he also places the story 
within the context of the overarching metanarrative of the imperial impulse, as 
exemplified by the Roman Empire in his time. As an insider of a religious move- 
ment, Luke effectively communicates the story of his ‘people’ to other individuals 
and groups within the Empire, employing a variety of narrative techniques to ed- 
ucate and engage his audience. 


In this sense, this study builds on John Moles’ research and, particularly, one 


of his seminal contributions: “[…] present-day Classicists should be able to ‘speak 
to them [the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles]’, and they in turn should ‘re- 
spond’ to such Classical addresses, to the benefit not only of New Testament scho- 
larship but also of Classicists, who at a stroke acquire five major new texts […].”3 


The methodology applied here on the works of two key historians from different 
periods and with different approaches, demonstrates the efficacy of this kind of 
research as an effective exegetical tool for investigating other historians, includ- 
ing those outside the Greek historiographical tradition. The final section below 
outlines some proposals for achieving this.

Moles (2011) 117.

13.3 Further Research Building on the Herodotus–Luke Axis 


and Herodotus’ Table of Historians 


The focus on Herodotus and Luke has contributed to broader questions involving 
two main disciplines, the Classics and Biblical studies. This study contributes to 
research in both fields but also aims to stimulate further cross-disciplinary proj- 
ects. This can be described as ‘Reading ancient historians theologically’ and 
‘Reading the Jewish and Christian historians historiographically’. These kinds of 
studies require a polyvalent approach, historical and theological, with a generous 
use of narratology because it is necessary to listen carefully to the prophetic-like 
voices of each historian in their own right. Below I summarise some of the re- 
search questions that can follow on from the contributions of this study. 


The justification for more research on the theological and rhetorical strands of 
Greek historiography. Theological readings of themes and instances of divine ac- 
tivity in the works of Greek historiography are lacking both in consistency be- 
tween authors and in methodology across time periods. Specifically, scholarly 
publications devoted to religious considerations (broadly defined) in the works of 
classical Greek historians enormously overshadow those which are devoted to 
their successors in quantity. Methodologically, scholars of Hellenistic and Roman- 
Greek historians have tended not to approach the subject of divine activity or reli- 
gious beliefs and practices in such a sustained mode as scholars of Classical Greek 
historiography. There are numerous reasons for this, as will become clear below. 


Recent scholarship on ancient Greek religion has shown that historiography 


and other literary genres are useful for its study.4 In scholarly literature, howev- 
er, theological readings of the above-listed historians vary considerably in quanti- 
ty, focus, and assessment. For example, for Herodotus and Thucydides, scholars 
have produced a number of works that vary in focus and draw contrasting con- 
clusions – either amplifying the importance of the religious dimension or min- 
imising it. Yet even those scholars who have defended or taken seriously the reli- 
gious dimensions of these histories have not conducted their theological readings 
– however diverse – of a single historian in the context of a sustained theological 
reading of other comparable histories as proposed in the methodology of this 
study. Instead, they focus on one historian and draw on observations about other 
histories for comparison, which is not sufficient for a robust elucidation of an au- 
thor’s rhetorical use of perceptions of the divine. 


From the historians of the Hellenistic period onwards, there are noticeably 


fewer attempts to examine religious activity in the work of an individual histori- 
an. One reason for this is surely the self-consciousness of their own emerging dis- 
cipline with which historians such as Polybius wrote, particularly in the shadow 


4 
E.g., Harrison (2007); Parker (2011). 


Prophetic-like Voices: From Herodotus to Luke? 
412 


of Herodotus and Thucydides. Incorporating divine intervention into one’s narra- 
tive was to align oneself with Herodotus’ historical approach (and all its negative 
connotations or, at least, that is the impression that we derive from Plutarch). 
Nevertheless, major extant histories of certain historians have received at least 
some attention: Polybius is the subject of various articles on his treatment of reli- 
gion, with a focus on τύχη,5 Diodorus Siculus two articles on prophecy,6 Dionysius 
of Halicarnassus an article on Roman religion,7 and Plutarch a monograph and an 
article.8 


The fragmentary historians are even less well represented in the scholarly 


literature, and there is not one dedicated theological reading of any of them. 
There is one article on Theopompus of Chios and one monograph, neither of 
which focus on religion or divine activity.9 Similarly, for Timaeus of Tauromeni- 
um, there is one monograph which treats religious considerations only in passing 
observations.10 


Further research is crucial to the development of scholarly understanding of 


the deeply religious perspectives through which ancient Greek historians and 
their subjects saw the world. Apart from the studies on Herodotus from Harrison 
onward and some recent studies on Thucydides, there is almost a complete ab- 
sence of intentionally theological readings of Greek historiography. This project 
comes at an important turning point in scholarship, in which emerging scholars 
of ancient Greek historiography have established that religious considerations 
and theological readings are no longer tacitly frowned upon.11 And, the same logic 
applies to the study of historical narratives of other peoples in antiquity. 


More attention to the theological and rhetorical strands of Greek historiography for 
the study of other Jewish and Christian narratives. Further research could also re- 
spond to the research gap in classical historiography that drives a wedge between 
classical and biblical historiography from a theological perspective, assuming 
that Greek historians were not sufficiently interested in the divine and therefore 
are not part of theological research. This research has provided further evidence 
to show that all of Greek historiography can be read in a continuum with Jewish 
and Christian historiography. Therefore, even from a theological perspective, the 
latter fall also under the umbrella of classical research. 


Early Jewish and Christian historians adapted Greek rhetorical devices that 


they had learned from their training (certainly Luke) or from their cultural sett- 
ings. A gap in research that has been identified is to show how Christian histori-

ans used perceptions of the divine in similar ways to historians living under 
regimes who also wrote in Greek to make known and legitimate their peoples’ 
history, culture, and religion. Luke (and other Christian historians) adapted 
Greek rhetoric and a theistic stance to legitimise the worship of Jesus in a vast 
multi-ethnic and religious milieu. In the context of foreign rule, historians em- 
ployed various historiographical strategies to validate their own identity, as seen 
in the works of Berossus, Manetho, and Josephus, and the glorification of the for- 
eign rulers, as exemplified by Polybius and Dionysius of Halicarnassus in relation 
to Rome. Further research could therefore aim to show how early Jewish and 
Christian historiography adapted historiographical rhetoric and a theistic per- 
spective that resonated with Greek-speaking readers from different cultures. 


In today’s complex world, the interests and expectations of modern nations 


are sometimes addressed through historical discourse, reflecting the hermeneuti- 
cal dilemma that originated with and was faced by Herodotus and his successors. 
These are indeed ancient themes. “Who will ultimately have the final word?” the 
Greek historians might ask.

Appendices 


Appendix I: The Meaning of ‘Miracles’ 


in Herodotus’ Miraculous Story 


Despite significant differences between the Greek mythopoetic tradition and 
Herodotus’ portrayal of the divine realm, divine beings are by no means absent 
from the story. This is particularly evident in the programmatic passages of the 
Histories, some of which have been discussed in previous chapters. By ‘program- 
matic’, I mean a line of exploration that develops according to the logic of conflict 
instigated or carried out by divine powers. This hearkens back to the opening 
lines of the Proem in which the causes of the conflict are of central interest (i.e., 
one of the ‘programmes’). Although Herodotus does not spell this out, ‘causes’ 
may be understood as encompassing all types, including divine actions, because, 
according to his worldview, they are a legitimate part of human thought and ex- 
perience.1 


But not all that can be considered miraculous has the same importance in 


Herodotus’ enquiry. For example, Harrison speaks of ‘marvels’ as being in some 
way of a lower order.2 Herodotus occasionally mentions such cases in passing, 
simply because they are noteworthy.3 He writes, for instance, of the priestess of 
Athena who lived in Pedasa and allegedly grew a beard three times as an omen of 
unpleasant things to come. While it appears to be a non sequitur, not having an 
immediate bearing on the story, it does, however, add to the presence of the di- 
vine.4 Anecdotes such as this one would have contributed to the audience’s pro- 
gressive and cumulative experience of the divine in the Histories. By contrast, the 
ensuing discussion will focus on those events that occur at “crucial historical 
junctures.”5 In narratological terms, these events can be considered ‘kernel 
events’ rather than ‘satellite events’, since the story often hinges on them.6 


This narrative development of the divine presence is constructed through 


expressions of belief and unbelief through the voices of Herodotus and his char- 
acters, of which a thread can be traced from beginning to end. It explores a plot 
built on curiosity rather than on suspense about the outcome of the story, since

audiences of the Histories already knew the ending.7 Presumably, audiences were

may have desired to hear the details that flesh out the story and to show how they 
were connected to form a whole. It is comparable to Polybius’ project, which ex- 
plains the unimaginable, rapid spread of Roman power. Some of the main ques- 
tions that engaged Herodotus’ audience, both intellectually and emotionally, may 
have been: How did the Greeks win against this superpower? And how does this 
relate to our current story of oppression (i.e., the Peloponnesian War)? Herodo- 
tus presents a series of events, moving backwards and forwards in time, until 
some degree of closure to these main questions is provided. 


A miraculous story supported by a great number of miracles. One thing is cer- 


tain for Herodotus: military deliverance did not occur without divine help. As 
Herodotus shows – and Mikalson supplements – sanctuaries and gifts scattered 
throughout the Greek territory monumentalised the perception of those divine in- 
terventions that were both temporally punctual and geographically distinct. 
Herodotus provided Greek culture with something it lacked: a literary monument 
that connected these deeds in narrative form,8 showing how the gods achieved 
military deliverance for the Greeks in the face of barbarian oppression. This was 
no less a thing of the gods; the entire story can be received as a macronarrative of 
miraculous scale. The repelling of this omnipotent adversary as a whole is mirac- 
ulous and extraordinary, and in some ways inexplicable in human terms. The sto- 
ry is sustained by regular reports of divine intervention in action and speech. 


This raises the question: What does ‘miraculous’ mean from Herodotus’ per- 


spective? Referring to the Cnidian ditch story (1.174) as exemplary with its hints 
to divine intervention, Harrison offers this definition: “an event deduced to be 
divine on the grounds that it would otherwise be impossible (or at least extreme- 
ly improbable).”9 For Herodotus, a miraculous deed or event is often not mono- 
chrome; rather it may encompass multiple shades of divine traces. This is possi- 
ble because the modern dichotomy of separating the natural and the divine, in a 
hermetically sealed fashion, is absent in Herodotus.10 Nonetheless, it is helpful to 
employ some type of classification of miracles such as answered prayer, fulfilled 
oracles, divine epiphanies,11 and natural miracles.12

Given that miracles in the Histories are recounted by Herodotus, who was 


not an eyewitness, all of these events are received second-hand, and, logically, are 
not verifiable. They are always explained retrospectively based on various factors 
which enable Herodotus to deduce the involvement of divine activity in the 
events.13 Consequently, ‘deduced’ is the key word in the above definition.14 Yet 
this deduction can only be done with the help of Herodotus’ worldview: he be- 
lieves in the possibility of divine intervention. 


Harrison reminds us that the notion of the miraculous is not the same every- 


where in the Histories.15 What does constitute a miracle, an act of the divine? 
Does this also include ‘normal’ natural processes like rain and thunder, which are 
considered miraculous respectively by the Egyptians and Scythians? From which 
perspective then? A good approach is to follow Herodotus’ hints about how he or 
his characters perceive divine activity. This is not always easy to tease out, but 
Herodotus has provided many examples and sufficient narrative clues to allow us 
to have some confidence in understanding better his interpretative methods and 
inclusion of the divine. 


A good example to illustrate this discussion is Herodotus’ commentary on 


the Athenians’ pride in their leadership role in the Greeks’ overall success over 
the Persians. It is a helpful description of the complementary relationship be- 
tween divine and human rule; the recognition of divine assistance alongside hu- 
man bravery in defeating the superior side: 


νῦν δὲ Ἀθηναίους ἄν τις λέγων σωτῆρας γενέσθαι τῆς Ἑλλάδος οὐκ ἂν ἁμαρτάνοι 
τὸ ἀληθές. οὗτοι γὰρ ἐπὶ ὁκότερα τῶν πρηγμάτων ἐτράποντο, ταῦτα ῥέψειν ἔμελλε· 
ἑλόμενοι δὲ τὴν Ἑλλάδα περιεῖναι ἐλευθέρην, τοῦτο τὸ Ἑλληνικὸν πᾶν τὸ λοιπόν, 
ὅσον μὴ ἐμήδισε, αὐτοὶ οὗτοι ἦσαν οἱ ἐπεγείραντες καὶ βασιλέα μετά γε θεοὺς ἀνω- 
σάμενοι. 


As things are, however, anyone who claims that the Athenians proved themselves 
to be the saviours of Greece would be perfectly correct, because the scales were 
bound to tilt in favour of whichever side Athens joined. Once they had decided that 
their preference was for Greece to remain free, it was they who aroused the whole 
of the rest of Greece (except those places which were already collaborating with 
the Persians) and, with the help of the gods, repelled the king’s advance. (7.139.5, 
trans. Waterfield) 


Divine rule is signalled by the brief yet poignant acknowledgement of divine as- 
sistance “with the help of the gods.” But this perception of the gods’ participation

Appendix II: Authorial Profile of Luke the Evangelist 


Some may consider this discussion superfluous, since scholarship generally con- 
siders the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles to be works of the same 
author, whether it was Luke, another fellow missionary (of the ‘we passages’), or 
a Christian from a later generation. The main concern here is the author’s claims 
as a reliable historian and eyewitness. As a concession (recognising that absolute 
certainty is probably not possible for this question), I summarise below the main 
points for a profile of the author, based on information that can be drawn from 
his writings.1 I then presents arguments in support of the traditional position of 
Lukan authorship. 


– Authorship claims. The same author, whose name is omitted in the incipits, 


wrote the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles.2 He collected and organ- 
ised various sources to bring literary, historical, and theological unity to the 
events recounted, beginning in Jerusalem and ending in Rome. This highlights 
his interest in showing how the λόγος about Jesus (Luke 1:2) moved from its 
Jewish origins through various Roman provinces, finally reaching the capital of 
the oikoumenē.3 In this journey, the author claims to be an eyewitness at some 
of the recounted events, through textual indicators such as ἐν ἡμῖν (Luke 1:1), 
the ‘we passages’, and explicit commentary.4 


– Compositional period. On this point, the discussion is complicated by the fact 


that the Gospel of Luke draws heavily on the Gospel of Mark, which is dated 
differently by scholars (before and after 70 CE). This then is the terminus post 
quem year for the Gospel of Luke. Commentators argue that Luke refers to the 
destruction of the temple and Jerusalem in 70 CE in some of Jesus’ words (Luke 
19:41–44; 21:5, 20–24; 23:28–31). Therefore, it would be Luke’s retrospective 
interpretation of Jesus’ announcements after the year 70.5 Knut Backhaus’s 
proposal seems plausible: the dating of Mark’s gospel is shortly before or after

For other profiles or portraits of Luke, see e.g., Bovon (1987) 15–25; Keener (2012) 402–416.

For this question, see Gathercole (2018). 


3

habited world as well as with imperial nuances. E.g., two emperors are mentioned in the con- 
text of οἰκουμένη (Augustus, Luke 2:1; Claudius, Acts 11:28).

70 and that Luke’s gospel is written ten years later circa 80 CE.6 The Acts of the 
Apostles was probably written sometime later (or perhaps concurrently), al- 
lowing time for gathering material and composition.7 Strong arguments sup- 
port the idea that the author of Acts had read Josephus’ Jewish Antiquities 
which is dated circa 93 CE.8 As for the terminus ante quem, the most recent date 
of the writing of the two documents can be fixed approximately via other sour- 
ces. These are the first attested quotations from or mentions of the Gospel of 
Luke in the writings of Justin Martyr and Marcion around 125 CE.9 Further evi- 
dence shows knowledge of the Gospel of Luke in the second century by the au- 
thors of 2 Clement, Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of the Ebionites, the Gospel of 
James (or the Protoevangelium of James) as well as by Tatian and some Valen- 
tinians.10 Thus, most exegetes from various points of view fix the composition 
of Luke and Acts between 70 and 130 CE.11 These questions are still under dis- 
cussion, and there is no consensus even among those who maintain a tradition- 
al position. Given the plausibility of Luke, Paul’s companion, as an author (if 
only as the first editor12), we propose a period of writing of Luke and Acts, in 
various stages, between 80 and 105 CE during the various reigns of the Roman 
Empire between Titus and Trajan.13 


– Knowledge of language and context. From the recounted events and the narra- 


tion, he demonstrates a variety of literary style and knowledge of various re- 
gions, which reveal that he was “at home in the Hellenistic culture.”14 He was 
an educated Greek-speaker whose Greek intimates some rhetorical training.15 


Qualified by Jerome as the “most skilled” (eruditissimus) in Greek among the 
evangelists and whose language “smacked of secular eloquence” (saecularem 
redolet eloquentiam),16 Luke seems to identify himself as a Greek, not just a 
Greek-speaker, when he uses barbaros to describe the inhabitants of Malta

non-Jewish background for Luke. 


– Posture towards authorities. Regarding his relationship to authorities, along 


with several anecdotes, his occasional asides are critical of some of the Jewish 
elite (Luke 6:7; 7:30; 16:14; Acts 12:1) and non-Jewish elite (17:21; 24:26–27). 
His portrayal of Roman authorities is nuanced, showing both negative and pos- 
itive sides. The Roman Empire (and other human rulers) is clearly subordinate 
to God’s purpose and message (ἡ βουλὴ τοῦ θεοῦ and ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ), whose 
forward movement cannot be prevented (Acts 2:23; 5:38–39; 12:21–24; 13:6– 
12, 48–49; 16:35–39, etc.) 


– Knowledge of Jewish scriptures. The multiple citations of the Jewish scriptures 


throughout both volumes show that Luke knew these writings well. This sheds 
some light on his religious identity. It could point to a diaspora Jew like Philo of 
Alexandria who had excellent knowledge of the Jewish scriptures or to an indi- 
vidual, who, prior to reception of the gospel, had contact with the Jewish com- 
munity and may have even proselytised (προσήλυτος, Acts 2:11; 6:5; 13:43), or 
not fully integrated into the Jewish community as ‘one who feared God’ (cf. 
Acts 10:2, 22, 35; 13:16, 26). Alternatively, he may have been an individual of 
pagan background, who, after adhering to Jesus’ movement, received instruc- 
tion in those Scriptures (which Luke himself is doing for his audience). 


– Luke the physician. Those who support Lukan authorship evoke additional 


points about the author. If Luke had been a physician (ἰατρός Col 4:14), his lev- 
el of education is assumed to have been high, and he would have been among 
the privileged in society.20 Based on the ‘we passages’ (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 
27:1–28:16), Luke was with Paul and his missionary team as they travelled

Appendix III: Divine Activity in the Acts of the Apostles 


This appendix lists specific mentions of divine agency, which underline Luke’s 
narrative intention to highlight divine initiative and action. A few preliminary 
comments are necessary. 


– Given that the story of the second volume, like that of the first volume, is per- 


ceived by the narrator as an overall act of God, the list does not claim to be an 
exhaustive list of divine activity. For example, the occurrences below focus 
mainly on how Luke shows – through his own voice and actorial perceptions – 
how the divine sphere is moving the story forward. This means that I omit 
many mentions of divine activity which are used to describe divine activity 
outside the narrative limits (e.g., uses of the divine plupast, which is particular- 
ly important in speeches). 


– Some actions occur as clusters and are not always listed separately. 
– Some divine activity is expressed through metaphor and personification. This 


was a way of talking about God doing something, even if it is merely divine 
presence. A clear example of this is the repetition of expressions attributing di- 
vine action to λόγος, e.g., “the word of God grew” (ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξανεν, 
6:7); and “the word of the God grew and multiplied” (Ὁ δὲ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξα- 
νεν καὶ ἐπληθύνετο, 12:24); but some doubt with “the word of the Lord spread 
through the whole region” (διεφέρετο δὲ ὁ λόγος τοῦ κυρίου δι’ ὅλης τῆς χώρας, 
13:49, see comments below); and in a summary verse, “Thus the word of the 
Lord grew and prevailed” (Οὕτως κατὰ κράτος τοῦ κυρίου ὁ λόγος ηὔξανεν καὶ 
ἴσχυεν, 19:20). 


– The distinction between some categories may not be immediately understood, 


but they are all used to indicate actions of divine agency even humans may be 
involved: 
– ‘Epiphany’, some physical manifestation of the divine (via sight, sound, etc.); 


‘presence’ may simply indicate that God’s presence was with an individual 
or a group, e.g., to strengthen or encourage them. 


– ‘Communication’: divine agent speaks; ‘Prophetic speech’: humans empow- 


ered by a divine agent to speak. 


– ‘Salvation’ is most often used to indicate that people have been reconciled to 


God; but it can also indicate physical rescue. 


– When there is a degree of uncertainty regarding divine agency, the occurrence 


is preceded by a question mark.

b. Salvation: the speaking of tongues and baptism are signs of this (10:47– 


48). 


(16) Presence: “the hand of the Lord was with them” in Antioch (11:21). 


a. Salvation: “a great number became believers and turned to the Lord” 


(11:21, 24). 


(17) Prophetic speech: Agabus in Antioch predicts a famine; Luke confirms that 


it occurred “during the reign of Claudius” (11:27–28). 


(18) Epiphany: an “angel of the Lord” appears to Peter in a prison in Jerusalem, 


then he frees him (12:6–11, 17). 


(19) Judgement/retribution: an “angel of the Lord” kills Herod Agrippa I for blas- 


phemy (12:20–23). 


(20) Salvation: via a personification of “the word” and metaphor of growth and 


expansion; “the word of God” reached more people and thus was “multi- 
plied”:7 Ὁ δὲ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ηὔξανεν καὶ ἐπληθύνετο (12:24; cf. 6:7 where 
the subject of ἐπληθύνετο is specific: ὁ ἀριθμὸς τῶν μαθητῶν). 


7 
LSJ, s.v. πληθύνω as the causal of πληθύω; hence, to cause to increase (or multiply).

Section 3: Divine Rule Moves the Agōn westward to Cyprus 


and Asia Minor (Acts 13:1–15:35) 


(1) Communication/Guidance: Understood as one action in two steps, the Holy 


Spirit speaks to the leaders in Antioch (εἶ πεν τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, 13:2) to set 
apart Barnabas and Saul for their ministry, then it is said that they were also 
sent by the Holy Spirit (ἐκπεμφθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος, 13:4). 


(2) Presence and judgement: Also, two actions connected (i.e., “filled” as in em- 


powered in view of another action): Saul (also known as Paul) in Paphos is 
filled with the Holy Spirit (13:9) when announcing that “the hand of the 
Lord” (13:11) was against Bar-Jesus (or Elymas), blinding him (with mist and 
darkness, ἀχλὺς καὶ σκότος) “for a while” (ἄχρι καιροῦ). 


(3) Salvation: those of the peoples (τὰ ἔθνη, i.e., non-Jews) who heard Paul and 


Barnabas’ preaching in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia received the word 
about Jesus, “and as many as had been destined for eternal life became be- 
lievers” (13:48). 
– ? “Thus the word of the Lord spread (διεφέρετο, pass. litt: “was carried/ 


spread”) throughout the region” (13:49); i.e., as a personification in middle 
voice; more likely, an act of human agency, namely, the message about the 
Lord was brought by people to others in the region. 


(4) Presence: “And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit” in 


Iconium (οἵ τε μαθηταὶ ἐπληροῦντο χαρᾶς καὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου, 13:52). 


(5) Works of power: Paul and Barnabas’ preaching in Iconium is supported by 


“the Lord,” “who testified to the word of his grace by granting signs and won- 
ders (διδόντι σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα) to be done through them” (14:3). 


(6) Physical healing: a man disabled from birth in Lystra is enabled to walk 


(14:10). 


(7) Guidance: the apostles and the elders in Jerusalem claim to have received di- 


vine guidance and confirmation (“For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit 
and to us,” 15:28) in their writing to the followers of Jesus from non-Jewish 
background. 


Section 4: Divine Rule Crosses into Europe (Acts 15:36–18:22) 


(1) Divine guidance: the Holy Spirit forbade Paul and his team from preaching in 


Asia and the Spirit of Jesus does the same regarding Bithynia (16:6–7). The 
means of these two actions are not specified. 


(2) Vision: Paul sees a man of Macedonia calling him to come and help; this is 


interpreted as being God’s direction to preach there. The narrator writes 
here in the first-person plural (16:9–10). 


Appendix III 
429 


(3) Work of power: Paul casts out a spirit of divination (πνεῦμα πύθωνα [or πύθο- 


νος]) from a slave girl through the power of Jesus Christ (16:18). 


(4) Deliverance/salvation/work of power: a violent earthquake, understood as di- 


vine intervention, shakes the prison’s foundations, opens the cell doors, and 
unfastens the prisoners’ chains (16:25–28). 


(5) Vision: “The Lord” appears to Paul in a nocturnal vision and speaks to him, 


encouraging him to continue to preach in Corinth and reassuring him of his 
presence and that many people are his (18:9–10). 


Section 5: Divine Rule Clashes with Human Rule in Asia Minor: 


Focus on Ephesus (Acts 18:23–20:38) 


(1) Epiphany: “the Holy Spirit came upon them” (19:6; cf. 10:44, 46). 


a. Prophetic speech: The spoke in tongues and prophesied.” 


(2) Works of power: “God did extraordinary miracles through Paul” (19:11). 


a. Physical healings (19:12). 
b. Exorcisms (19:12). 


(3) Epiphany: an evil spirit manifests itself, speaks to the seven sons of Sceva 


who are false exorcists (because of using Jesus’ name) and are subsequently 
beaten by the spirit (19:13–16). 


(4) Divine presence: through personification of λόγος, God’s presence and activi- 


ty is described as “the word of the Lord,” which “grew and prevailed” (Οὕτως 
κατὰ κράτος τοῦ κυρίου ὁ λόγος ηὔξανεν καὶ ἴσχυεν, 19:20). 


(5) Divine guidance (?): “Paul resolved in the Spirit to go through Macedonia and 


Achaia” (19:21). The expression (middle voice of τίθημι) can be understood as 
Paul allowed himself to be guided by the Spirit or that Paul planned it 
through reflection.8 


(6) Work of power: Eutychus, a young man, dies after falling out of a window 


but receives life through Paul (divine agency assumed but the agent is not 
specified; mode of resurrection not indicated; 20:9–12). 


(7) Divine guidance: the Holy Spirit testifies to Paul that “imprisonment and per- 


secutions” await him (20:23). 


8 
The text reads: ἔθετο ὁ Παῦλος ἐν τῷ πνεύματι διελθὼν τὴν Μακεδονίαν καὶ Ἀχαϊ ́αν Holladay 
(2016) 375. For divine guidance: Bruce (1988) 413. For personal reflection and decision-mak- 
ing (cf. similar expression in Luke 21:14 and Acts 5:4 with τίθημι and καρδία); LN 30.76; Culy 
and Parsons (2003) 370.

Section 6: Divine Rule at the Centre of the Agōn in Judea 


and Jerusalem (Acts 21:1–23:30) 


(1) Divine guidance: the disciples in Tyre are led by the Spirit to tell Paul not to 


go to Jerusalem (οἵτινες τῷ Παύλῳ ἔλεγον διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος μὴ ἐπιβαίνειν 
εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα, 21:4). 


(2) Divine speech and guidance: Agabus, a prophet from Jerusalem, comes to 


Caesarea to tell him what the Holy Spirit says through direct speech signalled 
by the locution τάδε λέγει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον (21:11). 


(3) Epiphany: Reports of divine action appear in Paul’s defence in Hebrew (i.e., 


Aramaic; τῇ Ἑβραϊ ́δι διαλέκτῳ , 22:2) before the mob in Jerusalem. The first 
two are repetitions, but the third offers new information about Paul’s move- 
ment away from Jerusalem (recounted in 9:26–30). 
a. Retelling of Jesus’ appearance to him on the road to Damascus (22:6–11). 
b. Retelling of healing through Ananias in Damascus (22:12–16). 
c. 
First report of a trance in which – in the temple of Jerusalem – Paul saw 
Jesus who tells him to leave Jerusalem because of immanent rejection and 
that he might be sent by Jesus to the peoples (22: 17–21). 


(4) Epiphany and divine speech: “The Lord” appears to Paul at night, while he is 


held prisoner in the barracks in Jerusalem, encourages him, and tells him 
that he must bear witness in Rome, just as he had done in Jerusalem (23:11). 


(5) Divine protection: Although divine agency is not evoked here, Luke’s audi- 


ence most likely understood this as providence to rescue Paul from imminent 
danger. Paul’s nephew hears about the Jews’ plot to kill Paul, and he reports 
it to Paul. This information is passed on to the centurion then to the tribune, 
which results in a militarily-escorted journey from Jerusalem to Caesarea 
(23:16–30). 


Section 7: Divine Rule Brings the Agōn to Imperial-ruled Caesarea 


(Acts 23:31–26:32) 


This section does not report any new divine activity. However, before Festus and 
King Agrippa, Paul recounts again his encounter with Jesus on the road to Damas- 
cus (Acts 26:12–18). He also claims to have received divine assistance up to the 
day of his speech: ἐπικουρίας οὖν τυχὼν τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄχρι τῆς ἡμέρας ταύ- 
της, 26:22). 


Appendix III 
431 


Section 8: Divine Rule Comes to Rome; the Agōn Continues 


(Acts 27:1–28:31) 


(1) Divine epiphany and communication: Paul encourages the men on the ship 


by stating that an angel of God had stood next to him and said that Paul 
would indeed “stand before the emperor” and that God would bring to safety 
all his fellow travellers (27:23–26). 


(2) Divine salvation: The promise and reassurance of physical safety (27:24, 31, 


34) during the perilous journey from Crete to Malta is shown, implicitly, to 
have been fulfilled by God via the verb διασῴζω used twice: καὶ οὕτως 
ἐγένετο πάντας διασωθῆναι ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν (27:44) and again at the beginning of 
the following paragraph (Καὶ διασωθέντες τότε ἐπέγνωμεν ὅτι Μελίτη ἡ 
νῆσος καλεῖται, 28:1). 


(3) Divine protection: Paul is bitten by a viper, but nothing happens to him in 


contrast to what the Maltese expected (28:3–6). It can be assumed that the 
narrator expects his audience to understand this as another example of God’s 
protection of Paul. 


(4) Works of power: Likewise, here, the narrator assumes that his audience un- 


derstands that God brings healing through Paul who cures Publius’ father, 
sick with a fever and dysentery (28:8). Paul also cures those with diseases on 
the island (28:9). These physical healings parallel those accomplished 
through Jesus (4:40), Peter (3:6, 12), and Philip (8:5–7). 


(5) Divine salvation: Luke cites Paul who states that the salvation of God has 


been sent to the peoples (γνωστὸν οὖ ν ἔστω ὑμῖν ὅτι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἀπεστάλη 
τοῦτο τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ, 28:28). The passive voice of ἀπεστάλη invites the 
audience to understand that God is the logical subject of sending the salva- 
tion.

Schwabe Verlag’s signet was 
Johannes Petri’s printer’s mark. 
His printing workshop was 
established in Basel in 1488 and 
was the origin of today’s Schwabe 
Verlag. The signet refers back to 
the beginnings of the printing press, 
and originated in the entourage of 
Hans Holbein. It illustrates a verse of 
Jeremiah 23:29: ‘Is not my word 
like fire, says the Lord, and like a 
hammer that breaks a rock in pieces?’ 


SCHWEIZERISCHE BEITRÄGE ZUR ALTERTUMSWISSENSCHAFT | 65 


Perceptions of the Divine in Greek Historiography 


Writing history in the shadow of the Homeric tradition and drama, Greek 


historians contended with each other about issues such as the choice of 


subject, genre, and style. A persistent question concerned the legitimate 


use of perceptions and experiences of the divine sphere in historical dis- 


course. A hermeneutical dilemma arose from this and was approached in 


different ways from the inception of Greek historiography with Herodotus, 


Thucydides, and Xenophon, continuing well into the first century CE with 


authors such as Flavius Josephus, Plutarch, and Luke. This book surveys 


this enduring feature of history-writing, proposes an interpretative narra- 


tological model for reading historians theologically, and then applies it to 


the works of Herodotus and Luke, who, despite their differences, exempli- 


fy how historiography exhibited tradition and innovation through theo- 


logical reflection for their audiences’ edification and entertainment. 


James M. Morgan is a lecturer and researcher in the Department of Bibli- 


cal Studies at the University of Fribourg, Switzerland. His research inter- 


ests lie in ancient historiography, biblical exegesis and narratology. He has 


taught and conducted research in Italy, Niger, and Switzerland.
